At baseline, parental carers of children with COVID-19 reported worse health and well-being than parents of healthy children on EQ-HWB-S, EQ-5D-5L, and EQ VAS.
Among carers of children with COVID-19, the EQ-HWB-S identified substantially fewer respondents in full health than the EQ-5D-5L, consistent with a lower ceiling.

Both instruments supported known-groups validity, but EQ-HWB-S showed stronger discrimination than EQ-5D-5L across child infection status, caregiving time, and work impact; EQ-HWB-S was especially sensitive to emotional and social caregiver burden.

Adjusted gamma-log models associated child infection, severe or prolonged illness, and greater work impact with lower parental summary scores; longer daily caregiving time was associated with EQ-HWB-S but not significantly with EQ-5D-5L.
Summary-score test-retest reliability was good and similar for EQ-HWB-S and EQ-5D-5L, while dimension agreement ranged from fair or moderate to good.
Both instruments were responsive when children recovered or improved, with EQ-5D-5L summary scores slightly more responsive than EQ-HWB-S and EQ VAS showing the largest effects.

Child COVID-19 affected parental physical functioning more than emotional functioning; EQ-HWB-S better captured caregiving-related exhaustion, loneliness, cognition, and work or time burden, while EQ-5D-5L better captured physical recovery and changes in anxiety/depression.
Of 313 recruited respondents, 300 successfully completed the interview and entered the primary analysis; 40.0% reported full health and median EQ VAS was 80.
Among 3,000 cTTO observations, 20.0% were worse than dead and 78.7% were better than dead; values showed clustering at -1, 0, and 1.
cTTO- and DCE-predicted values for all 243 EQ-5D-3L states had similar patterns, and the coefficient sets had relative and approximately linear agreement, which supported joint hybrid modeling.
The heteroskedastic hybrid model without a constant was selected as the preferred model because it had the best AIC, BIC, MAE, and RMSE among the hybrid models; it predicted -0.503 for state 33333.

Adding the 13 non-traders in sensitivity analysis increased the GLS prediction for state 33333 by 0.06 utility units, which the authors did not consider meaningful.
The authors produced an interim Russian EQ-5D-5L crosswalk value set from the new EQ-5D-3L values with the Van Hout crosswalk algorithm.
The targeted search selected 27 papers to inform the report; historical evidence also came from EuroQol grey literature and published books.

Digital EQ VAS versions can differ from the paper form in response interaction, hash marks, and numerical labels. The review found that the measurement effect and equivalence of these digital formats were uncertain.
The self-reported EQ VAS originated as a warm-up task that familiarized respondents with the visual analogue scale before they valued hypothetical health states.

The original EQ VAS format reflected its valuation purpose: a vertical 20 cm line, 0-100 numerical scale, millimetre hash marks, extreme best-imaginable-health and worst-imaginable-health labels, and line-drawing responses. These features were not selected to measure self-reported overall health.

In 1994, the EuroQol Group endorsed the EQ-5D profile and own-health VAS pages as an independent questionnaire, and the own-health page became known as the EQ VAS. In 2009, the response changed from drawing a line to writing a number, and the instructions were revised.
The review found little literature that directly addressed a conceptual framework for the EQ VAS as a measure of self-rated general health.

The relevant evidence was largely indirect: six studies addressed conceptual frameworks or measurement theories for general VAS scales rather than the EQ VAS, two qualitative studies gave direct insight into what EQ VAS respondents consider, and seven empirical EQ VAS studies examined associations with demographic, economic, behavioral, health, or environmental factors.

Qualitative source studies showed variable interpretations of the EQ VAS endpoints. Best imaginable health included physical health, mental well-being, social relationships, treatment and medical conditions, and health knowledge or behavior; worst imaginable health included death, disease, and disability. Some respondents found best imaginable health difficult, unattainable, or hard to use as a reference.

The synthesized psychometric evidence indicated satisfactory to strong construct validity in general and clinical populations, but validity was less consistent in Asian populations, and test-retest performance and responsiveness were less satisfactory.

The endpoint labels and hash marks can affect responses. The bipolar best-to-worst format, difficulty imagining the endpoints, possible endpoint aversion, and reports that the marks were too granular raised questions about whether the current format is optimal.

Automated item selection placed all nine EQ-HWB-S items on one scale below an item-scalability lower bound of 0.448; at 0.448, it separated six psychosocial items from three physical items. Results were materially unchanged when the original mobility and concentration/thinking items replaced the composite items.

The combined EQ-HWB-S formed a strong Mokken scale. The main results text and complete-case subgroup table reported stronger psychosocial and physical subscales, with the psychosocial coefficient higher than the physical coefficient; the source reports conflicting subscale values elsewhere.

The combined dataset had no manifest monotonicity violations. In stratified single-scale analyses, mobility violated monotonicity among participants with long-term conditions, and mobility and daily activities violated monotonicity in the United Kingdom sample; no subscale violations occurred across the examined subgroups.

Invariant item ordering was weak: all items in the single scale had violations, with backward selection removing No Control and Pain. The psychosocial subscale had no pairwise violations, but H-T values indicated that item ordering was generally unavailable or had low accuracy; the physical subscale violations appeared to be driven by Pain.
Exploratory factor analysis supported a two-factor physical and psychosocial structure, but the dominant first factor also supported the practicality of a single overall score.
Internal consistency was excellent for the overall and psychosocial scales and good for the physical subscale. All three level summary scores had moderate negative correlations with EQ VAS.

The overall, psychosocial, and physical level summary scores discriminated between carers and non-carers and between participants with and without long-term conditions. Carers and participants with long-term conditions reported more symptoms and problems; results remained similar by country and after adjustment for age, gender, and race.

Score distributions showed no problematic skew or irregular response patterns. Floor effects were larger for the physical subscale than for the full scale or psychosocial subscale, and no respondent had the worst possible full-scale score.
In the Australian subset, a composite sad/depressed item produced results similar to the sad item alone, with slightly better scalability.
Across the major cohort studies, myocarditis after COVID-19 mRNA vaccination was rare, occurred most often in young males, and was concentrated after the second dose.
The authors summarized overall cumulative post-vaccination myocarditis incidence as 0.6 to 4 cases per 100,000 vaccinated males and 0 to 2 cases per 100,000 vaccinated females.
Most vaccine-associated myocarditis cases had a mild or moderate, self-limiting course with rapid symptom resolution and normalization of cardiac findings.

Joint CAPACITY-COVID and LEOSS data showed that 37 of 16,368 hospitalized patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection had myocarditis; the text reports myocarditis and pericarditis diagnoses in 0.2% and 0.15% of patients, respectively.
The reviewed evidence indicated that myocarditis risk in the context of SARS-CoV-2 infection was substantially higher than the risk after COVID-19 vaccination.
A CDC benefit analysis estimated that one million second mRNA vaccine doses in males aged 12 to 17 would prevent thousands of COVID-19 cases and substantial numbers of severe outcomes over 17 weeks.

The authors formulated 23 criteria for developing, assessing, and selecting candidate EQ-5D bolt-on descriptors.
The development group contained five dimension-structure criteria and six dimension-language-and-framing criteria.
The selection group contained four face-and-content-validity criteria and eight numbered classical psychometric criteria in Table 4.

Development criteria favored short and parsimonious items, consistency with the target EQ-5D version and its negative severity framing, translatability, generic wording where possible, and language informed by qualitative work with relevant populations.

Assessment and selection criteria covered comprehensibility, salience, relevance across populations and severity levels, response distributions and missingness, ceiling effects, test-retest reliability, divergent and convergent construct validity, known-groups validity, and responsiveness.

Itch was the most frequently reported symptom in both groups. All original EQ-5D-5L and bolt-on dimensions were spontaneously reported by at least 20% of each group, and the authors judged that data saturation was attained.

All participants found the EQ-5D-5L with the skin irritation and self-confidence bolt-ons easy to complete. Almost all regarded the seven dimensions as relevant and important, and all said that adding these two bolt-ons reflected the effect of their condition better than EQ-5D-5L alone.
Every participant regarded skin irritation as relevant and important and preferred its addition to EQ-5D-5L. Skin irritation was also the bolt-on most often ranked as most relevant or important.

Every participant regarded self-confidence as relevant and important. All participants with atopic dermatitis spontaneously described an effect on self-confidence, compared with about half of those with chronic urticaria.
More than half of each condition group regarded the sleep bolt-on as relevant and important, and most participants who were asked preferred its addition to EQ-5D-5L.

The social relationships bolt-on had weaker support: it was relevant and important to some participants, but it was most frequently ranked as the least relevant or important bolt-on in both condition groups.

Participants identified possible conceptual overlap between skin irritation and pain or discomfort, between self-confidence and anxiety or depression, and between self-confidence and social relationships. Most participants nevertheless regarded the overlapping dimensions as sufficiently distinct.

Views on the EQ-5D-5L current-day recall period were mixed. Fourteen participants said that their responses would differ for a past-week recall period, and two participants with chronic urticaria said that one day did not represent their fluctuating symptoms.

Participants proposed wording or content changes, including clearer or expanded dimension wording, splitting anxiety and depression, and using broader skin-irritation response wording rather than wording focused only on itch.
Both EQ-5D-Y versions had complete responses at baseline.
The EQ-5D-Y-5L reduced the full-health-state ceiling relative to the EQ-5D-Y-3L, but the difference was not significant; floor reporting was also rare.
Response inconsistency between corresponding 3L and 5L dimension levels varied by dimension and was highest for doing Usual Activities.
The five-level version increased absolute informativity across all dimensions while it retained similar response evenness.
Both EQ-5D-Y versions showed similar low-to-moderate concurrent validity with related PedsQL items and self-rated health; emotional, social, and school associations were generally poor.

Both EQ-5D-Y versions detected improvement during acute orthopaedic recovery, with the greatest change from baseline to 48 hours; dimension-level change was generally greater for the five-level version.

Among participants who reported improved self-rated health, both level sum scores changed significantly, with moderate-to-large effects; neither version detected significant change in participants who reported worse self-rated health.
Mean EQ VAS scores increased during follow-up, with significant improvements from baseline to 24 hours and from baseline to 48 hours.
Of 1,321 respondents, 1,237 met the inclusion criteria and contributed data to modelling.

All tested models were logically consistent. The selected weighted hybrid model combined cTTO and DCE data, used eight parameters without an intercept, accounted for censoring, respondent random effects, and linear heteroskedasticity, and had the best overall predictive performance.
The Norwegian value set predicted values from -0.453 to 1 across all 3,125 EQ-5D-5L states.
Anxiety/depression made the largest contribution to health-state values, followed by pain/discomfort, self-care, mobility, and usual activities.
The Norwegian value set classified 333 states as worse than dead, fewer than the UK crosswalk, Danish, and United States value sets but more than the Swedish value set.
Weighting the sample to the Norwegian population by age, sex, education, and geographic region made very little difference to results.
Norwegian predicted values were generally higher than values from the currently recommended UK crosswalk, and sensitivity across severity was closely parallel to the Danish value set.
Protocol compliance was high; the main quality-control flags concerned short cTTO completion time and inconsistent valuations of state 55555 or other states.

outcome: Suitability of alternative approaches for identifying domains of a cross-sector quality-of-life measure
statement: Drawing on existing measures, quality-of-life theory, and the views of future respondents each had strengths and limitations; the authors judged that a combined approach was more useful than relying mainly on one source.

The project specified that the measure must reflect domains important to service users and informal carers, meet predefined measurement and routine-use requirements, and align with policy-maker needs.

The theoretical position was extra-welfarist and multidimensional, drew on an objective-list account and the capability framework, and focused on actual functioning unless capability itself emerged as important and could be measured fit for purpose.

outcome: Conceptual framework, candidate domains, and criteria used to structure EQ-HWB content
statement: A large literature review of qualitative evidence supplied lived-experience domains across health, social care, disability, and caring; Framework analysis organized and revised these domains using an adapted Wilson and Cleary model.

Candidate domains had to show broad importance, be acceptable for self-report, avoid mainly instrumental content and double counting where possible, and be merged when they covered very similar or nested concepts.

The domain process adapted the initial framework when evidence did not support its distinctions, including separating autonomy and control from self-identity and combining mental-health symptoms with feelings and emotions.

outcome: Stakeholder-informed relevance, acceptability, and fit for purpose of EQ-HWB domains
statement: Iterative decisions to retain, drop, or merge domains used discussion, return to the qualitative literature and service-user terminology, and consultation with patient, public, policy, EuroQol, steering, and advisory groups.
The process produced EQ-HWB as a generic measure intended to capture health-, social care-, and carer-related quality of life for consistent use across sectors.

outcome: Ceiling effects of EQ-5D-5L versus EQ-5D-3L by dimension and health state 11111
statement: Ceiling effects fell substantially with the EQ-5D-5L: the proportion reporting health state 11111 decreased by 25.55% in the Malay version and 15.74% in the English version.

outcome: Response redistribution and inconsistency between 3L and 5L
statement: Inconsistencies in response redistribution were below 6% for all dimensions in both languages, peaking in pain/discomfort for the Malay version and anxiety/depression for the English version.

outcome: Informativity (Shannon entropy and information efficiency)
statement: Absolute informativity was higher for the EQ-5D-5L in all dimensions, and relative information efficiency was higher for the 5L except for mobility and pain/discomfort in the English version.

outcome: Convergent validity with EQ VAS
statement: Convergent validity with EQ VAS was stronger for EQ-5D-5L dimensions than for EQ-5D-3L in both languages, with Malay pain/discomfort the strongest correlation.

outcome: Two-week test-retest reliability of EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: Two-week test-retest agreement for EQ-5D-5L dimensions was moderate to poor: kappa 0.208 (self-care) to 0.382 (anxiety/depression) in Malay and -0.015 (self-care) to 0.553 (mobility) in English.

In every country with both value sets except Spain, the EQ-5D-Y-3L value range is shorter than the EQ-5D-5L value range, that is the value for the worst health state is higher for the child instrument.

In eight of the nine countries with both value sets, the percentage of health states valued below 0 (worse than dead) is lower for the EQ-5D-Y-3L than for the EQ-5D-5L, and the child-adult differences are especially marked in Asian countries.

All EQ-5D-Y-3L value sets published to date rate pain/discomfort as the worst aspect of child HRQoL, and all except one rate self-care as the least important dimension, an order that differs from EQ-5D-5L value sets.

Four factors could produce the higher child values: less severe wording of EQ-5D-Y-3L severity labels; a genuine adult view that children are less badly affected; the other-person rather than own-health perspective of the valuation task; and special considerations about child survival invoked by anchoring at dead = 0.

Existing evidence does not rule out that the other-person perspective and considerations about child survival exert an upward bias on values, so the first two explanations alone cannot account for the observed differences.

Because the utility function for life-years is not observed, it is perfectly confounded with the utility function for HRQoL in time trade-off values; a marginal utility of life-years that diminishes with age produces a higher marginal rate of substitution and therefore higher TTO values for child health, even if the marginal utility of HRQoL is constant with respect to age.

The problem is not specific to the time trade-off: a study testing a range of methods for anchoring child HRQoL values at dead = 0 found child values exceeded adult values in every case, so incommensurability is a property of the value scale rather than of one elicitation method.

Alternative valuation approaches already in use produce age-invariant values: the UK and Dutch CHU9D value sets ask adults to value child-instrument states from their own adult perspective, and the Health Utilities Preschool instrument is preference-weighted by mapping to HUI3 values.
The FACIT-COST total score had no floor or ceiling effect; no participant reported the best or worst possible total score.
PCA identified two components, and CFA supported a well-fitting two-factor structure that separated adverse reactions to financial burden from perceived ability to manage finances.
Both FACIT-COST factors had adequate internal consistency, although the positive-item factor had lower reliability than the negative-item factor.

FACIT-COST scores discriminated as hypothesized by age, education, residence, income, employment, metastasis, symptom burden, several financial coping strategies, and FT12 response; they did not discriminate by number of children, disease duration, or savings or pension withdrawal.
Among participants with unchanged FT12 status, all items had strong agreement and the total score had excellent test-retest reliability.
FACIT-COST was responsive to improvement in financial-toxicity status and showed smaller change for worsening status.
FT12 correlated strongly with the FACIT-COST total score and was used as the anchor for classifying improved, worsened, and unchanged status.

Implementation was facilitated by the Innovation Learning Collaborative infrastructure, contextualized local coaching, operational and management support, electronic capture and visualization infrastructure, APERSU expertise, and teams that already had outcome-measure and quality-improvement practices.
Across community rehabilitation programs, 56% of patients had a clinically significant improvement in self-reported health status after rehabilitation.

The data-collection mode changed clinical access to results. Paper forms made it easier to review responses with patients, while iPad collection made responses less accessible to clinicians and created a barrier to clinical use.

Routine EQ-5D-5L use supported patient conversations and goal setting at the clinical level, aggregate service evaluation and quality improvement at the program level, and planned performance comparison and data linkage at the health-system level.

Provider views were mixed. Some clinicians valued direct patient input and the ability to examine program effectiveness, while others judged the generic EQ-5D-5L insufficiently specific for their patients or practice. The mobility wording was not relevant for some wheelchair users, and teams saw value in adding condition-specific PROMs.
The pilot began with 18 early-adopter teams. Lessons from 2017–2018 informed spread and scale to 152 additional adult community rehabilitation sites across Alberta.
Among 1,992 patients with complete intake and end-of-episode data, the mean EQ VAS score increased from 64 at intake to 73 at the end of care.

PROPr utilities were substantially lower on average and had a narrower range than EQ-5D-5L utilities, and the best PROPr state based on PROMIS-29 (0.905) does not equal full health, whereas both EQ-5D-5L value sets reach 1.
All value sets were sensitive to pain, depression and anxiety at a strong level, insensitive to high blood pressure, and PROPr was more sensitive to tiredness than either EQ-5D-5L value set.
PROMIS-29 domain mean T-scores were between 47 and 53 (SD 8.6-10.2), close to the US reference mean of 50, and internal consistency of all domains was positively rated (Cronbach alpha 0.86-0.95).

EQ-5D-5L showed a ceiling effect that PROMIS-29 did not: 17.5% of respondents reported the best EQ-5D-5L health state versus 1.8% reporting the best PROMIS-29 profile, and only 192 (6.1%) of possible EQ-5D-5L states were observed.
The distributions of the value-weighted data differed: EQ-5D-5L utilities were negatively skewed with a tail of negative values, while PROPr values were more evenly spread across the positive range.
Bland-Altman plots showed generally good agreement between the EQ-5D-5L value sets and PROPr across the utility range, with disagreement limited to respondents reporting higher impairment.

Convergent validity was supported for hypothesised dimension pairs, which correlated strongly, while PROMIS fatigue and sleep correlated less strongly with EQ-5D-5L dimensions, indicating these concepts are only indirectly captured by EQ-5D-5L.

PROMIS-29 domains correlated with the EQ-5D-5L value sets more strongly than EQ-5D-5L dimensions correlated with PROPr, with self-care showing the weakest link to PROPr; the two utility scores themselves correlated strongly.
Correlation patterns were consistent across condition subgroups, but were almost uniformly lower in respondents with a mental health condition than in those with a physical health condition.

All three value sets discriminated between most known groups, but PROPr detected differences in self-reported health, health satisfaction and higher levels of multimorbidity more strongly, while EQ-5D-5L discriminated slightly better between no condition and one to two conditions; the number of general practitioner visits was the weakest known group for all value sets.

outcome: Uptake of EQ-5D-Y measured by registered studies over time, by design, country and disease area
statement: Registered use of EQ-5D-Y with the EuroQol Group increased steadily from its first publication to 2018.

outcome: Uptake of EQ-5D-Y measured by registered studies over time, by design, country and disease area
statement: EQ-5D-Y was registered across a range of study designs and countries.

outcome: Feasibility, convergent validity, test-retest reliability and sensitivity of EQ-5D-Y
statement: EQ-5D-Y is feasible and reliable in children and adolescents, but its sensitivity is limited, probably because of high ceiling effects.

In pilot work respondents reported more problems on EQ-5D-Y than on EQ-5D-3L for mobility, pain or discomfort and feeling worried, sad or unhappy, EQ-5D-Y had fewer missing values, and participants found it easier to understand.

outcome: Differences between values for child health states and adult health states
statement: Published valuation work using EQ-5D-Y health states shows that values differ by perspective: adults gave lower VAS values for children's health states than for their own or other adults', whereas a composite TTO and DCE study reported higher mean TTO values for the child perspective than for the adult perspective.
No value set exists for EQ-5D-Y, and use of the adult EQ-5D-3L value set as a proxy value set is not recommended, so use of EQ-5D-Y in cost-utility analysis is limited.

The self-complete EQ-5D-Y is available in around 40 languages, proxy versions in several languages, and electronic data capture versions exist; a cognitive bolt-on is being tested in Germany and a version with additional levels is under development.

Only three generic preference-based instruments developed for younger age groups currently provide value sets (16D/17D, HUI2/HUI3, CHU9D); 16D/17D and HUI use traditional techniques with adult respondents, while CHU9D valuation also used DCE and best-worst scaling with adolescents.

The qualitative evidence review identified 32 subdomains grouped into seven high-level domains: feelings and emotions, cognition, self-identity, autonomy, relationships, physical sensations, and activity.

The coping item caused inconsistent interpretation and sometimes acted as an overall judgment that produced lexicographic preferences; the team replaced it with the highly correlated control item and simplified some response wording.

The team generated 687 candidate items, then used iterative researcher and stakeholder selection to take 97 items covering 28 subdomains into face validation; no retained item remained in its original form.
Face validation eliminated 36 items, modified 14, and added three, which produced a 64-item pool covering 26 previously identified subdomains plus self-confidence; dignity or respect was dropped.

Participants often wanted simpler layouts and more contextual information or definitions, had no consistent preference for item framing or response options, and often forgot or ignored instructions such as the recall period.

Factor analysis broadly confirmed the conceptual model in the United Kingdom, Australia, United States, Argentina, and Germany, with some country-specific modifications; fit was poorer in China, where several feelings subdomains had to be combined.

Candidate items had similar missing-data rates, no unjustified floor or ceiling patterns, and most distinguished physical and mental health groups and severity where tested; known-group evidence for carers was mixed.

Item response theory results showed ordered response levels for most items, although some items functioned differently across groups; 32 items performed well, 25 had mixed evidence, and seven performed poorly.

Stakeholder evidence and international-team review produced the 25-item EQ-HWB and a nine-item EQ-HWB-S covering mobility, day-to-day activities, exhaustion, loneliness, concentration or clear thinking, anxiety, sadness or depression, control, and pain.
The pilot suggested that TTO and DCE were suitable for valuing draft EQ-HWB-S states, but respondents needed more deliberation than for EQ-5D-5L states.

outcome: Root mean squared error of predicted versus observed health state values, overall and by inclusion and commonness
statement: The large orthogonal design with 54 health states produced the lowest overall root mean squared error across all 243 health states, and the small orthogonal design with 18 states outperformed all published designs.

outcome: Root mean squared error of predicted versus observed health state values, overall and by inclusion and commonness
statement: Restricting the design to common health states did not improve prediction of common states and worsened prediction of rare states.

outcome: Number of health states with absolute prediction error above 0.05 and above 0.10
statement: Orthogonal designs produced far fewer health states with large absolute prediction errors than published or random designs.

outcome: Stability (variance) of prediction error across 100 design variants
statement: Random selection designs performed well on average but showed greater variation in prediction error across the 100 generated variants than the orthogonal designs, whose errors were consistently below 0.04 for the large design.

In the reference data, 143 of 243 EQ-5D-3L health states (55%) were observed and were classified as common; 43% of those common states occurred at least five times, and 11111 was the most frequent state.
Descriptive values in the saturated dataset after rescaling on 11111 and 33333 showed a compressed valuation range.
At three months postburn, itching was common but cognition problems were less common.

Adding bolt-on items increased the number of observed health profiles and reduced the proportion classified as perfect health, with the largest ceiling reduction for configurations that included itching.
The itching configuration had the highest absolute and relative informativity; cognition produced a smaller informativity gain, while the combined configuration had lower relative evenness.
Convergent validity with EQ VAS improved slightly with cognition but became weaker with itching.

Extreme itching often occurred without problems on the standard EQ-5D-3L dimensions, while standard extreme problems rarely occurred without itching; no clear dominance pattern occurred for cognition.
Cognition materially increased the variance in EQ VAS explained by the EQ-5D-3L regression model, while itching contributed very little additional explanatory power.
The analyzed group reported generally high mean EQ-5D-3L utility and EQ VAS scores.
Responders differed from non-responders: they were older and had longer hospital stays.

outcome: Ceiling effect and descriptive efficiency
statement: At baseline, the standard EQ-5D-5L had a 46.7% ceiling, while adding R1, R2, or both reduced the ceiling to zero.
Among 120 follow-up participants, clinical criteria classified 43.3% as better, 33.3% as stable, and 23.3% as worse; SGRQ criteria classified 35.8%, 36.7%, and 27.5%, respectively.

outcome: Construct and known-groups validity
statement: All four versions correlated at least moderately with SGRQ; R2 and R1R2 showed stronger correlations than standard EQ-5D-5L, and all bolt-on versions had higher mean C-statistics across eight known clinical groups.

outcome: Appropriateness, acceptability, comprehensiveness, and comprehensibility of R1 and R2
statement: All interviewed patients and clinicians considered both respiratory bolt-ons appropriate, compatible with intended use, readily understood, and easy to answer; data saturation was reached across 20 interviews.

outcome: Appropriateness, acceptability, comprehensiveness, and comprehensibility of R1 and R2
statement: Participants identified conceptual overlap: R1 activity limitation could overlap with mobility, self-care, and usual activities, while R2 breathing symptoms could overlap with pain/discomfort; they still valued the respiratory specificity and clarifying examples.

The culturally adapted Simplified Chinese R1 and R2 versions were finalized after forward-backward translation, bilingual review, and pretesting in 10 Mandarin-speaking patients; no further semantic refinement was needed.

outcome: Construct and known-groups validity
statement: The ability of item scores to explain EQ VAS increased across the standard, R1, R2, and R1R2 versions, with the highest adjusted R-squared for R1R2.

outcome: Test-retest reliability
statement: Reliability showed good agreement across all four versions without statistically significant differences; item-level kappa values were statistically significant and generally moderate to good.

outcome: Responsiveness to health-status improvement
statement: R2 and R1R2 had higher standardized effect sizes and C-statistics than standard EQ-5D-5L under both clinical and SGRQ change definitions; R1 did not show this consistent improvement, and R1R2 had the highest C-statistics.
Psychometric gains from the respiratory bolt-ons were small overall; R2 performed better than R1, and combining both bolt-ons appeared to improve performance further.

Adding a palliative-care context increased the proportion of EQ-5D-5L health states valued worse than dead in all three countries. The largest increase occurred for a 3-month life expectancy with limited support.

Life expectancy and support level affected valuation, with effects most consistent for the death attribute. Limited support interacted significantly with death in all three countries, and life expectancy generally had the larger effect.

Effects of palliative context on individual EQ-5D-5L dimension decrements were mixed and did not show a consistent pattern across study arms or countries. The worst-case vignette did not consistently cause larger dimension decrements than milder vignettes.
Mobility was the most important EQ-5D-5L attribute in every country and context. Relative-attribute-importance differences between context and no-context tasks were generally small.

Australia had the largest proportion of health states valued worse than dead, and Ireland had the smallest. Context-related increases were more pronounced in Australia and the United Kingdom than in Ireland.

outcome: EQ-5D EQ-Index health state utility values for hematologic malignancy health states
statement: Fifty-nine studies described in 63 articles met the inclusion criteria; data from 21 635 respondents provided 796 health state utility value estimates (590 utilities and 206 utility changes) with EQ-Index scores ranging from -0.025 to 0.980.

outcome: Reporting quality of included studies (measures of variability, response rate, handling of missing data, Jadad score, value set reporting)
statement: Health state utility values came from RCTs in 28 studies (48%), cross-sectional studies in 24 studies (41%) and longitudinal studies in 7 studies (12%); 28 studies (45%) were multi-country and 14 (31%) were single-center, and the median number of respondents per publication was 243 (IQR 98-540, range 31-1960).
A formal meta-analysis was attempted but could not be performed because of high heterogeneity in the patient subgroup definitions used by the authors of the individual studies.

outcome: EQ-5D EQ-Index health state utility values for hematologic malignancy health states
statement: In the single histiocytosis study, patient utilities ranged from 0.283 (Sweden) to 0.854 (Germany) and caregiver-reported utilities from 0.217 (Sweden) to 0.880 (Italy).

The majority of included articles (41 of 63, 65%) were published after 2010, with the earliest identified EQ-5D hematology study published in 1995; most single-country evidence came from the Netherlands (9 publications), the United Kingdom (5), the United States (4) and Japan (3).

outcome: EQ-5D EQ-Index health state utility values for hematologic malignancy health states
statement: Multiple myeloma was the most represented area, with 24 studies (26 publications), 11 112 patients and 249 utilities (165 HSUVs and 84 HSUV changes), ranging from -0.025 to 0.923.

outcome: EQ-5D EQ-Index health state utility values for hematologic malignancy health states
statement: More than 50 utilities were identified for chronic myeloid leukemia (164), acute myeloid leukemia (82), chronic lymphocytic leukemia (72), non-Hodgkin lymphoma (65) and mantle cell lymphoma (54).

outcome: EQ-5D EQ-Index health state utility values for hematologic malignancy health states
statement: Hodgkin lymphoma was poorly represented, with only 4 cross-sectional studies, 166 patients and 13 HSUVs ranging from 0.73 to 0.92, and no utility increments or decrements.

outcome: Coverage of hematologic malignancy indications by available EQ-5D-based utilities
statement: No EQ-5D-based health utilities were found for polycythemia vera, primary myelofibrosis, essential thrombocythemia, mastocytosis, myeloid sarcoma, chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, eosinophilic leukemia or neutrophilic leukemia.

outcome: Reporting quality of included studies (measures of variability, response rate, handling of missing data, Jadad score, value set reporting)
statement: The EQ-5D-3L was used in 55 of 59 studies (93%), the EQ-5D-5L in 4 studies, and no included study used the youth version EQ-5D-Y; in all studies except one the questionnaire was self-completed by patients.

outcome: Reporting quality of included studies (measures of variability, response rate, handling of missing data, Jadad score, value set reporting)
statement: Twelve different value sets were used to derive the EQ-Index; the UK time trade-off value set was the most common (26 EQ-5D-3L studies), most value sets were TTO-based, and only the Belgian and European value sets were VAS-based.

outcome: Reporting quality of included studies (measures of variability, response rate, handling of missing data, Jadad score, value set reporting)
statement: The value set used was not reported in 14 studies (18 publications), and in 2 further studies the value set was named but not fully specified.

outcome: Reporting quality of included studies (measures of variability, response rate, handling of missing data, Jadad score, value set reporting)
statement: Reporting quality of the included evidence was limited: 21 of 59 studies (35.6%) reported no measure of variability, response rate was absent in 46 studies (78.0%), handling of missing data was absent in 50 studies (84.7%), and the mean Jadad score of included RCTs was 2.5 (SD 1.1).

outcome: Profile-level EQ-5D ceiling effect: proportion reporting full health state 11111
statement: The pooled profile-level ceiling effect was higher for EQ-5D-3L than for EQ-5D-5L.

outcome: Risk of bias and reviewer agreement
statement: Most included articles had low risk of bias, but non-response reporting and sample-specific psychometric reporting were common weaknesses.

outcome: Risk of bias and reviewer agreement
statement: Agreement among the three study-selection reviewers was high.

outcome: Between-study heterogeneity and small-study or publication bias
statement: The analyses found no evidence of publication bias for the overall profile-level ceiling effects; additional analysis suggested that suspected bias in three EQ-5D-5L dimensions was unlikely to be a concern.

outcome: Profile-level EQ-5D ceiling effect: proportion reporting full health state 11111
statement: Moving from EQ-5D-3L to EQ-5D-5L reduced the pooled profile-level ceiling effect.

outcome: Dimension-level proportion reporting no problems
statement: At dimension level, self-care had the highest no-problems proportion and pain/discomfort had the lowest for both versions.

outcome: Profile-level EQ-5D ceiling effect: proportion reporting full health state 11111
statement: East/Southeast Asian studies had higher profile-level ceiling effects than European studies, with a larger difference for EQ-5D-3L.

outcome: Profile-level EQ-5D ceiling effect: proportion reporting full health state 11111
statement: After adjustment for mean age and the proportion of male participants, the regional profile-level difference remained large for EQ-5D-3L but not for EQ-5D-5L.

outcome: Profile-level EQ-5D ceiling effect: proportion reporting full health state 11111
statement: Profile-level ceiling effects did not differ significantly by sampling method, administration mode, survey venue, or survey language.

outcome: Dimension-level proportion reporting no problems
statement: For EQ-5D-5L dimensions, interviewer-administered studies had higher no-problems proportions than self-administered studies across all five dimensions.

outcome: Dimension-level proportion reporting no problems
statement: Adjusted regional differences remained significant for EQ-5D-3L mobility, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression, and for EQ-5D-5L mobility, self-care, and usual activities.

outcome: Between-study heterogeneity and small-study or publication bias
statement: Profile-level ceiling-effect estimates showed very high between-study heterogeneity.
EQ-5D was rarely the primary endpoint and was usually a secondary or exploratory endpoint in the included randomized clinical trials.
Health utilities were the most frequently analyzed EQ-5D data, followed by EQ VAS; both were analyzed almost entirely as numerical variables, while dimension responses were much less often analyzed.

For utility analyses, the linear fixed-effect model was the most common model for a single postbaseline assessment, and the linear mixed-effect model was the most common model for multiple postbaseline assessments.
Only a small minority of trials that analyzed numerical EQ-5D data reported examining model assumptions, and fewer than one quarter adjusted for baseline EQ-5D score.
Missing EQ-5D data were explicitly examined in less than one third of trials; about half of these trials used imputation, most often multiple imputation or last observation carried forward.
No single analysis method dominated across studies, and the review found substantial variation in model selection and reporting practice.

outcome: Frequency and type of EQ-5D-5L response issues by Tourangeau stage (comprehension, recall, judgement, response mapping) and by dimension
statement: Response issues occurred at every Tourangeau response stage, in every EQ-5D-5L dimension and in both cognition sub-groups, with the usual activities dimension producing the most issues.
Higher education level was associated with no cognitive impairment; no other socio-demographic differences by cognition sub-group were significant.

outcome: Frequency and type of EQ-5D-5L response issues by Tourangeau stage (comprehension, recall, judgement, response mapping) and by dimension
statement: The usual activities dimension showed a high co-occurrence of comprehension and judgement issues, because the listed examples (work, study, housework, family or leisure activities) did not match residential aged care life and drew respondents to their lives before entering care rather than to today.

outcome: Frequency and type of EQ-5D-5L response issues by Tourangeau stage (comprehension, recall, judgement, response mapping) and by dimension
statement: Total issue frequency was not associated with cognition sub-group for most dimensions and all response stages; the exception was mobility, where the no cognitive impairment sub-group recorded a greater proportion of issues, driven by the comprehension stage.

outcome: Frequency and type of EQ-5D-5L response issues by Tourangeau stage (comprehension, recall, judgement, response mapping) and by dimension
statement: No significant differences in response issue frequency were found by age, education or gender.

outcome: Qualitative interpretation problems with EQ-5D-5L dimension descriptors, examples and the today recall period
statement: Participants were unsure whether to factor mobility aids, personal care assistance and pain medication into their answers, and some reported no or slight problems with personal care despite receiving daily assistance.

outcome: Qualitative interpretation problems with EQ-5D-5L dimension descriptors, examples and the today recall period
statement: Participants used strategies to handle fluctuating health and the combined anxiety/depression dimension, including averaging over a longer period, choosing the middle response option, and crossing out part of the item.

outcome: Qualitative interpretation problems with EQ-5D-5L dimension descriptors, examples and the today recall period
statement: On the EQ VAS participants were more aware of the today timeframe, but the most common issue was rating health against others of the same age or age-based expectations rather than against the best health they could imagine.

outcome: Inter-coder reliability of response-issue coding
statement: Inter-coder reliability from independent coding before group discussion was modest, and consensus on all response-issue codes was reached after discussion.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility score scored with the Australian pilot value set
statement: Utility and EQ VAS scores were slightly higher in the cognitive impairment sub-group than in the no cognitive impairment sub-group, but no differences between cognition sub-groups were statistically significant.

outcome: Root mean squared error of predicted VAS values for all 3125 health states
statement: The EQ-VT 86-state design predicted VAS values for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L states well, and a 25-state orthogonal design performed similarly with a marginally smaller error.

outcome: Root mean squared error of predicted VAS values for all 3125 health states
statement: At small design sizes the orthogonal design outperformed the D-efficient and random designs; the random 25-state design performed very poorly and the D-efficient 25-state design was the worst of the plotted designs.

outcome: Root mean squared error of predicted VAS values for all 3125 health states
statement: The small orthogonal design mispredicted mild health states, because orthogonal sets contain at most one mild state; adding or weighting the five mildest states improved prediction for mild states but worsened prediction for moderate and severe states.

outcome: Count of large mispredictions (absolute error above 5 and above 10)
statement: Values generated from the 25-state orthogonal design contained fewer large mispredictions (absolute error above 5 and above 10) than values generated from the EQ-VT design, and large mispredictions were least frequent in orthogonal designs regardless of size.

outcome: Observed mean EQ-VAS values of EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: In the saturated dataset a gap existed at the top of the scale between full health and the next best state, and inclusion of state 11111 drove outlying performance of orthogonal design variants.
In the Vietnamese general-population sample, the mean EQ VAS was 81.10 and the mean EQ-5D-5L index was 0.94.
Full health was reported by 54.4% of participants; reported problems increased with age, while self-care and usual activities had fewer problems than the other dimensions.
EQ VAS and EQ-5D-5L index scores were generally higher in younger people, men, people with at least high-school education, employed people, and single people.
Participants with diagnosed hypertension had lower mean EQ VAS and EQ-5D-5L index scores than both non-hypertensive participants and participants with undiagnosed hypertension.

In adjusted models, diagnosed hypertension and each additional comorbidity were associated with lower EQ VAS and lower EQ-5D-5L index scores. Older age and female sex were also associated with a lower EQ-5D-5L index.
The proportions reporting full health were similar in the non-hypertensive and undiagnosed-hypertension groups, but lower in the diagnosed-hypertension group.

outcome: Problems in recruitment, interviewing and technical tools, and solutions applied
statement: Interviewers most often reported problems in recruiting respondents, especially finding respondents with required quota characteristics such as non-Jawa/Sunda ethnicity and age over 50, and obtaining local authority permission.

outcome: Problems in recruitment, interviewing and technical tools, and solutions applied
statement: Problems perceived in respondents were dominated by cognitive difficulties with EQ-5D-5L levels and TTO/DCE tasks, followed by religious beliefs conflicting with the instant death and worse-than-dead options, and distraction by other people present.

outcome: Problems in recruitment, interviewing and technical tools, and solutions applied
statement: Solutions applied were selective search and use of personal networks with detailed explanation of study goals for recruitment, and stimulating the respondent's thought process plus developing the interviewer's own skills during interviews; technical problems with laptops, EQ-VT software and internet connections were solved independently or with help from fellow interviewers and the EuroQol Office.

outcome: Protocol compliance indicators: zero TTO values, wheelchair explanation moves, inconsistencies flagged, wheelchair explanation time flagged, TTO interview time flagged, wheelchair lead time flagged, percentage of flagged interviews
statement: The percentage of flagged interviews fell sharply after retraining and continued quality control feedback.

outcome: Protocol compliance indicators: zero TTO values, wheelchair explanation moves, inconsistencies flagged, wheelchair explanation time flagged, TTO interview time flagged, wheelchair lead time flagged, percentage of flagged interviews
statement: All seven protocol-compliance indicators improved significantly after retraining, including fewer zero TTO values, more wheelchair explanation moves, and fewer flagged inconsistencies and durations.

outcome: Protocol compliance indicators: zero TTO values, wheelchair explanation moves, inconsistencies flagged, wheelchair explanation time flagged, TTO interview time flagged, wheelchair lead time flagged, percentage of flagged interviews
statement: The first quality control report showed 53% flagged interviews, above the 40% threshold, so the team discarded the first 98 interviews and paused sampling until interviewers were retrained.
At the individual level, PROM feedback to patients or health-care providers improved at least one patient-related outcome in 10 of 23 studies.
The abstract reports that PROM monitoring linked to symptom thresholds, treatment adaptation, or care pathways improved outcomes in 17 of 25 studies; Table 3 reports a different numerator.
PROM-based screening improved outcomes in 10 of 14 studies, although one study reported deterioration.
All three decision-aid studies reported improved decision quality, and all three studies that collected PROMs without feedback reported improved outcomes.
None of the four PROM benchmarking studies found benefit, and one reported possible worsening.
All three studies that used PROMs for in-depth performance analysis and the one study that used a plan-do-study-act cycle reported improved outcomes.
Individual-level studies that used disease-specific PROMs reported improvement more often than studies that used generic PROMs or a combination.

PROM interventions improved general health perceptions and decision readiness or conflict more often than HRQoL, physical functioning, or mental functioning; no included study found improved survival.
The included evidence was of moderate quality at best, which raised concerns about the validity of the synthesized findings.
Conversation analysis identified 20 positive and 14 negative patterns. The patterns formed five subthemes under two main themes: task execution and communication skills.
Across the scored interviews, the mean normalized score was 0.68 for positive checks and 0.49 for negative checks.

Most interviewers had moderate increases in positive-pattern scores or decreases in negative-pattern scores over time. Interviewers 3 and 7 improved on both score types, while interviewer 1 had worse results on both.

Qualitative scoring showed preliminary consistency with quantitative quality-control indicators: interviewer 3 performed above average on key cTTO duration and move indicators, while interviewer 1 performed below average on several corresponding indicators.
Clarity was the only subtheme for which all assessed items improved from batch 1 to batch 2.

The analysis found instances in which interviewers moved on without confirming understanding, gave incomplete or incorrect explanations, spoke too fast, interrupted respondents, or tried to force a response.
Independent scorers had relatively small discrepancies in their total normalized scores.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L value set coefficients from cTTO and from three DCE anchoring methods
statement: All cTTO and latent DCE coefficients were significantly below zero and showed no logical inconsistency across levels in any of the four analyses.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L value set coefficients from cTTO and from three DCE anchoring methods
statement: Mapping and hybrid value sets closely resembled the cTTO value set, while anchoring to the worst cTTO state overestimated the observed cTTO scores of almost all health states.

outcome: Agreement of predicted values with observed mean cTTO scores (RMSE, number of states with error above 0.05 or 0.1, logical consistency)
statement: The hybrid model gave the lowest root mean square error against observed mean cTTO scores and the fewest states with error above 0.05, marginally better than the cTTO model and clearly better than worst-state anchoring.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L value set coefficients from cTTO and from three DCE anchoring methods
statement: Few EQ-5D-5L health states were valued as worse than dead, in contrast with the EQ-5D-3L, and the 5L value distribution was monomodal with lower density at poor health states.
The replication in a more diverse Chinese sample produced a factor structure that was more comparable with the structure found in other countries.
Model fit improved in the new face-to-face sample. RMSEA met the prespecified criterion, but CFI and TLI remained below 0.95.
The Chinese-adjusted model was replicated in the prior online sample, but all three fit indices failed the prespecified criteria.

outcome: Distributional characteristics of utility values: ceiling and floor, evenness (Shannon's H' and J'), clusters and gaps
statement: The 5L produced smoother and more evenly distributed utility values than the 3L for every country value set; Shannon's H' and J' were consistently higher for 5L, including after binning the utility scale into 0.05-wide categories.

outcome: Distributional characteristics of utility values: ceiling and floor, evenness (Shannon's H' and J'), clusters and gaps
statement: The ceiling was always lower with 5L than with 3L, while floor effects were negligible for both versions.

outcome: Distributional characteristics of utility values: ceiling and floor, evenness (Shannon's H' and J'), clusters and gaps
statement: The 3L systematically overestimated reported health problems relative to 5L across almost all dimensions and condition groups, mainly because about 85% of respondents at 3L level 2 chose 5L level 2 or 3; the exception was mobility, where 'confined to bed' was rarely endorsed on 3L.

outcome: Discriminatory power (relative efficiency F statistic ratio and AUROC ratio, 5L over 3L)
statement: Both versions discriminated significantly between groups, but relative performance depended on the comparison: 3L generally showed higher relative efficiency in the healthy versus disease comparison while 5L performed better in the mild versus moderate/severe comparison; AUROC results supported this pattern and favoured 5L overall more often than the F statistic did, except for Japan.

outcome: Discriminatory power (relative efficiency F statistic ratio and AUROC ratio, 5L over 3L)
statement: Value set model characteristics affected discriminatory power: an intercept reduced it, while the modelled range did not significantly affect the F statistic; removing the N3 term from the UK and Dutch 3L value sets markedly improved 3L performance, mainly through lower dispersion.

outcome: Mean country-specific 3L and 5L utility values by condition group
statement: Absolute mean utilities differed substantially between countries, but 3L-5L differences were mostly a constant upward or downward shift; between-country valuation effects were larger than version effects, and value sets of the Asian countries showed higher discriminatory power than the non-Asian ones.

outcome: Non-completion of the TTO part of the valuation interview
statement: 29 of 534 respondents (5.5%) failed to complete the TTO tasks, while 522 completed the DCE tasks and only one respondent failed to complete both TTO and DCE.

outcome: Non-completion of the TTO part of the valuation interview
statement: Among respondents reporting age over 65 years, an EQ VAS score of 50 or below, or an immigrant background, 12% did not complete the TTO.

outcome: Non-completion of the TTO part of the valuation interview
statement: Non-completers of the TTO differed from completers on age, immigrant background and self-reported health, but not on sex or education.

outcome: Non-completion of the TTO part of the valuation interview
statement: In adjusted mixed-effects logistic models, age over 65 years, EQ VAS at or below 50 and immigrant background each predicted non-completion of the TTO, while higher education did not.

outcome: Slow completion (upper quartile) of the TTO introduction, defined as more than 12.7 min
statement: Age over 65 years, immigrant background and low EQ VAS predicted slow completion (upper quartile) of the TTO introduction.

outcome: Slow completion (upper quartile) of the 10 TTO tasks, defined as more than 16.4 min
statement: Age over 65 years and immigrant background predicted slow completion of the 10 TTO tasks, whereas low EQ VAS did not reach statistical significance.

outcome: Slow completion (upper quartile) of the TTO introduction, defined as more than 12.7 min
statement: For those who completed the TTO, the introduction took a median of 10.2 min and the 10 following tasks a median of 12.3 min; 25% of respondents were slow completers of either part.

outcome: Violations of defined data quality standards, mainly inconsistent valuation of the worst possible health state
statement: Violations of defined data quality standards occurred in 17 cases, primarily inconsistent valuation of the worst possible health state.

outcome: Non-completion of the TTO part of the valuation interview
statement: Findings were robust in repeated analyses that controlled for the interviewer as a fixed effect using dummy variables.

outcome: Reported influence of spiritual or religious beliefs on valuation task responses
statement: Most respondents said their answers to the valuation tasks were influenced by their spiritual or religious beliefs.

outcome: Themes describing how Islamic beliefs shape perception of health states
statement: Thematic analysis of 88 free-text answers produced 146 coded themes grouped into two overarching categories, fatalism and preservation of life, with subthemes of inevitability and invincibility, powerlessness or submission, unacceptance of certain ideas, appreciation, fear, and acceptance and patience.

outcome: Reported influence of spiritual or religious beliefs on valuation task responses
statement: Respondents reported discomfort with core elements of the valuation tasks, in particular being asked to choose between death and living with illness and to trade away life time, because life and death are held to be in God's power; some avoided choosing death deliberately.

outcome: Themes describing how Islamic beliefs shape perception of health states
statement: Fear of disability and diminished mobility was prominent, and respondents ranked mobility as the most important dimension of health, while pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression were ranked least important, in contrast with findings in England.
Mean EQ-5D-3L utility was highest in the full sample, lower among participants with chronic conditions, and lowest among participants with asthma.

Participants with asthma consistently had the lowest mean utility across categories of general health, and their health utility curve was below the curves for participants with chronic conditions and the full sample.

Residents generally supported air pollution control and preservation of public space; the highest mean acceptability was for a clean, fast, reliable regional transportation system connecting San Joaquin Valley communities.

The policy-item analysis produced eleven factors: electric or hybrid vehicle charging, expense, and attributes; local and non-local organizations; policy costs and who pays; air pollution control; public space; symptoms; and personal protective actions.

Political ideology, socioeconomic characteristics, and health state predicted policy favorability. The authors reported that left-wing views favored charging polluters, emissions control, public-space preservation, and interventions to reduce health symptoms, while right-wing views negatively predicted concerns about charging infrastructure and vehicle attributes and support for local-organization interventions.
Lower health utility was associated with more symptoms attributed to poor air quality. Having asthma or a child with asthma also predicted more symptoms and more personal protective actions.

Participants with chronic conditions felt less informed about local air quality than participants without chronic conditions. Television or radio and local health authorities were the most trusted information sources, and visual inspection of mountain-range clarity was the most common way to assess air quality.
Participants identified charging availability, purchase expense, and vehicle attributes as distinct concerns about adopting hybrid or electric vehicles.

outcome: Self-rated health on the EQ VAS
statement: Controls had higher mean EQ VAS scores than the combined former COVID-19 groups at 24 months.

outcome: Association of post-COVID symptoms and condition with health-related quality of life
statement: Former COVID-19 patients with post-COVID condition had substantially lower EQ VAS and utility scores than former patients without post-COVID condition.

outcome: Prevalence of post-COVID condition at 24 months
statement: At 24 months, post-COVID condition remained common and was more prevalent among formerly hospitalised patients than among non-hospitalised patients.

outcome: Association of post-COVID symptoms and condition with health-related quality of life
statement: Long-term EQ VAS and utility scores were similar across the non-hospitalised, ward, and ICU patient groups, contrary to the expectation that greater acute severity would predict worse long-term health-related quality of life.

outcome: Association of post-COVID symptoms and condition with health-related quality of life
statement: After mutual adjustment for symptoms, fatigue, cognitive problems, shortness of breath, and loss of appetite were associated with lower EQ VAS; muscle weakness or pain was also associated with EQ VAS, while a similar pattern was seen for utility except for muscle weakness or pain and swollen ankles or feet.

outcome: Prevalence and severity of 14 post-COVID symptoms
statement: Fatigue was the most common symptom in all patient groups; sleep problems, muscle weakness or pain, breathing problems, and cognitive problems were also prominent, with hospitalised groups generally reporting symptoms more often.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility score using the Netherlands value set
statement: Controls had higher mean EQ-5D-5L utility scores than the combined former COVID-19 groups at 24 months.
The analyzed sample included 301 adults and matched the Jordanian population quotas for region, age, and gender.
The mean self-reported EQ VAS score was 81; 40% reported EQ-5D-3L state 11111, and pain/discomfort was the most frequent reported problem.
Residuals were not normally distributed and heteroskedasticity was present; the analyses corrected heteroskedasticity in the mixed-effects and random-intercept models.

outcome: Regression model fit and assumptions
statement: The multivariable multilevel mixed-effects model had the lowest AIC and BIC and was selected as the best-fitting model.

outcome: cTTO health-state valuation score
statement: After adjustment for health-state severity and other retained factors, unemployed respondents gave significantly lower cTTO values than employed respondents.

outcome: cTTO health-state valuation score
statement: After adjustment, respondents with more than one comorbidity gave significantly lower cTTO values than respondents with no comorbidities.
Age, gender, marital status, education, geographic region, exercise, and COVID-19 vaccination were not statistically significant predictors in the selected multivariable model.

The hybrid model combining c-TTO and DCE data produced logically consistent coefficients, with all parameters statistically significant except pain/discomfort level 3, and this model provided the final Ethiopian value set.
Predicted EQ-5D-5L values in the final hybrid model ranged from -0.718 for state 55555 to 1 for full health, with the highest value below full health being 0.974 for state 11112.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility values and dimension-level utility decrements for Ethiopia
statement: Anxiety/depression had the largest utility decrement at level 5 and self-care the smallest, with pain/discomfort and mobility intermediate.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-5L problems by dimension and EQ VAS score
statement: Self-reported health showed most problems in anxiety/depression and fewest in self-care, with a high mean EQ VAS score.

outcome: Data quality indicators: model logical consistency, censoring at -1, clustering of values, interviewer effects and protocol compliance
statement: 8.04% of c-TTO observations were left-censored at the lowest possible value of -1, a higher proportion than in other published valuation studies, and there was a spike of values at 1 indicating nontrading for mild states.

The c-TTO ordinary least squares responses were all logically consistent, whereas the rescaled conditional logit DCE model produced two inconsistent (negative) coefficients at level 3 of self-care and usual activities.

outcome: Feasibility and acceptability of the EQ-PVT valuation protocol in Ethiopia
statement: In the pilot, acceptability of the c-TTO and DCE tasks was good with no special concerns about thinking or talking about death, but respondents frequently found health states difficult to imagine, which was resolved with locally tailored practice examples.
The achieved sample matched the Ethiopian general population closely for residence, gender, age and religion, and all 10 interviewers were retained after quality control.
Very few states were flagged in the TTO feedback module, so all flagged states were retained in the analysis.
Of 533 eligible registrants, 500 completed an interview and all 500 were analyzed; no respondent met the predefined exclusion rules and no cTTO task value was missing.
Observed cTTO values covered the full scale from -1 to 1, with the largest spikes at -1 and 1.
All six model specifications predicted better when heteroskedasticity was accounted for. The heteroskedastic ADD20-I model had the best cross-validation performance.
The selected ADD20-I value set covered all 3,125 EQ-5D-5L states. It ranged from -0.851 for 55555 to 1.000 for 11111, and 1,263 states had a negative value.

Pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression had the largest level-5 disutilities. Mobility by anxiety/depression and pain/discomfort by anxiety/depression were the two significant interactions; the negative interaction terms indicated that combined problems had less disutility than the sum of separate problems.

No model produced logically inconsistent state-pair predictions. The final directly elicited EQ-5D-5L value set differed substantially from the mapped Singapore EQ-5D-5L values based on the local EQ-5D-3L value set.

outcome: Dimension-level and overall ceiling effects
statement: Overall ceiling effects were lower for Y-5L than Y-3L, but the reduction was small; KIDSCREEN-10 had a much lower overall ceiling effect.

outcome: Convergent validity across EQ-5D-Y, EQ VAS, and KIDSCREEN-10
statement: Y-5L and Y-3L summated dimension scores and EQ VAS correlated moderately with the KIDSCREEN-10 index. Similar dimensions generally had moderate to strong correlations, and Y-5L correlations were generally stronger than Y-3L correlations.

outcome: Missing responses to Y-5L, Y-3L, EQ VAS, and KIDSCREEN-10
statement: All three questionnaires had low missing-response rates. Dimension-level missingness was 0% to 0.4% for Y-5L, 1.5% to 4.2% for Y-3L, and 0% to 1.1% for KIDSCREEN-10.

outcome: Known-groups validity and relative efficiency for overweight and shortsightedness
statement: Y-5L and Y-3L summated scores did not show the expected difference between pupils with and without overweight. EQ VAS and KIDSCREEN-10 differences were in the expected direction but were not significant.

outcome: Consistency and redistribution of responses from Y-3L to Y-5L
statement: Response inconsistency between Y-3L and Y-5L was low across dimensions, and no participant chose Y-5L level 5. The extra Y-5L response levels produced only a modest advantage over Y-3L in this school sample.

outcome: Known-groups validity and relative efficiency for overweight and shortsightedness
statement: Scores generally distinguished pupils with and without shortsightedness. Y-5L summated scores and EQ VAS differed significantly, and EQ VAS had the highest relative efficiency.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L-derived health utility within 3 months after a major cardiovascular or bleeding event
statement: Mean EQ-5D-3L utility within 3 months after an event was lowest for stroke and was higher for heart failure, venous thromboembolism, myocardial infarction, and major bleeding.

outcome: Change from baseline SAGE functional-status score
statement: Changes in SAGE functional-status scores and IPAQ physical-activity scores did not show material differences between treatment arms.
Sensitivity analyses that assigned utility 0 at death or used multiple imputation gave treatment-effect estimates consistent with the primary utility analysis.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L health-state change category from baseline
statement: The distribution of improved, unchanged, worsened, and mixed EQ-5D-3L health states was similar between treatment arms.

outcome: Change from baseline EQ-5D-3L health utility at final visit
statement: Change from baseline EQ-5D-3L health utility did not differ significantly between rivaroxaban plus aspirin and aspirin alone.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L utility deterioration exceeding the 0.089 minimum important difference
statement: Utility deterioration was reported by 14.4% of patients in each arm, with no evidence of a treatment difference.

outcome: Change from baseline EQ VAS at final visit
statement: Change from baseline EQ VAS and the odds of EQ VAS deterioration were similar between treatment arms.
Workshop participants broadly agreed that DCE works well as the principal valuation method in the EQ-5D-Y protocol.

The most appropriate method for anchoring latent-scale DCE values at dead equals 0 remained unresolved; participants preferred using all available cTTO data and somewhat larger cTTO state sets instead of using cTTO only to value state 33333.

Participants considered adolescent preferences relevant to some users, but did not agree whether adolescent and adult preferences require separate value sets, should be combined, or whether adolescents should complete life-death trade-off tasks.
Very few completed or ongoing value-set studies had consulted local HTA bodies or end users about the acceptability of the valuation methods.

Participants agreed that no single normative basis will fit all uses or countries; they supported limited local flexibility while staying close to the core protocol to preserve cross-country comparability.

EQ-5D-Y values and adult EQ-5D values may not be directly comparable because the perspective differs and adults may be less willing to trade life-years for a child, which can compress the child value scale and create discontinuities across age transitions.
Until innovative anchoring methods show superior properties, participants expected the protocol to continue using a combination of DCE and cTTO.

Participants expressed mixed preferences, but jointly favored recall periods longer than today; 1-week and 4-week periods each received the largest vote shares, and the preferred instruction described health on a usual day.
All qualitative participants found the proposed variants relevant, acceptable, and easy to understand and answer; four variants were selected for testing.
All four variants reduced the proportion reporting the 11111 profile compared with standard EQ-5D-5L, with more problems reported especially for usual activities and pain or discomfort.

Variant utility, level-sum, and VAS scores were generally moderately to strongly correlated with standard EQ-5D-5L and condition-specific measures and generally discriminated clinical-status groups; average clinical-discrimination c-statistics tended to be higher for variants, but differences were not statistically significant.
Among patients classified as stable, reliability for variant utility, level-sum, VAS, and dimension scores was the same as or higher than for standard EQ-5D-5L under most comparisons.

All variants showed greater responsiveness than standard EQ-5D-5L in ROC analyses that contrasted patients whose health improved with those whose health was stable or worse, using either SGRQ or clinical change criteria.
All administered questionnaires were completed, indicating high feasibility under interviewer administration.
The conceptual model organized reporting into five non-hierarchical modules: four modules for methods used to obtain child HRQoL values and one module for characteristics of the values.
Five structured team meetings and full-team review reduced and refined an initial 147-item draft into an 83-item modular long checklist.
Author scoring and revision produced a 14-item short checklist that followed a CHEERS-like format in which users record the manuscript location of each item.

Paired independent application to four studies showed that the modular approach could cover two value-set reports, for EQ-5D-Y-3L and CHU9D, and two vignette valuation reports; the authors state that this application suggests feasibility.
Six external expert reviews chiefly suggested wording changes and possible additional questions; the team incorporated comments and workshopped proposed additions before finalizing the checklists.

The long checklist has detailed modules A through D for samples, health states, stated-preference methods, and modelling, plus module E for characteristics of reported values; the short checklist gives decision makers and researchers a concise 14-item assessment tool.
Anxiety/depression was more important relative to self-care for adults than for adolescents.

Adolescents generally completed the DCE successfully and had a dominance-test pass rate close to that of adults, although they reported more difficulty differentiating profiles and imagining the health problems.
Adolescents reported substantially better current EQ-5D-Y-3L health than adults.
The mixed logit results showed statistically significant preference heterogeneity for nearly all EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions and levels and fit the choice data better than the multinomial logit models.
Adolescents were less likely than adults to choose the less severe option when the level-sum-score difference was small.

Adult and adolescent EQ-5D-Y-3L latent preferences differed; the Swait-Louviere test showed that coefficient differences were not explained only by scale, and the pooled model found differences for both pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression levels.
Pain/discomfort was more important relative to self-care for adults than for adolescents.
In both samples, severe pain/discomfort was the most important level, severe anxiety/depression was second, and moderate self-care problems were least important.
Usual activities was more important relative to self-care for adults than for adolescents.

outcome: Test-retest agreement of EQ-HWB-S dimension ranks
statement: Dimension ranking showed low test-retest consistency: fewer than half of participants selected the same top-ranked dimension, and only about one third had significant positive rank correlations.

outcome: Test-retest agreement of dimension swing weights
statement: Individual dimension swing weights had mainly poor-to-moderate agreement, with worse performance in the patient sample than in the general-population sample.

outcome: Test-retest agreement of intermediate-level ratings
statement: Intermediate-level ratings had mainly poor agreement; illogical ratings were common, and reliability was lower in the patient sample.

outcome: Test-retest agreement of worst-state versus dead choice and anchoring factor
statement: The pairwise choice between the EQ-HWB-S worst state and dead was the main task with good test-retest agreement.

outcome: Test-retest agreement of worst-state versus dead choice and anchoring factor
statement: Anchoring-factor values showed poor agreement even though the preceding pairwise choice was consistent.

outcome: Individual-level utility-decrement and health-state rank reliability
statement: Individual utility decrements and the resulting rankings of health states showed poor-to-moderate or low test-retest reliability.

outcome: Aggregate-level utility-decrement and value-set reliability
statement: Aggregate utility decrements were highly similar between test and retest, which produced stable group-level value sets.

outcome: Illogical-response frequency and demographic predictors of test-retest differences
statement: Age effects on cumulative utility-decrement differences were not uniform across samples; male gender was associated with smaller differences, while patient-group status was not independently significant in the reported regressions.
Among 212 informal caregivers, the mean EQ-5D-5L utility score was 0.88 and the mean EQ VAS score was 72.47.
No respondent reported the 55555 floor profile, but 54 respondents reported the 11111 full-health profile, which met the study criterion for a substantial ceiling effect.
Twelve of 15 a priori known-group hypotheses were confirmed: nine of ten strong hypotheses and three of five weak hypotheses.

Lower EQ-5D-5L scores were associated with poorer self-rated health, lower happiness, existing health conditions, more emotional and physical exhaustion, relationship problems, difficulty getting support, inability to do enjoyable activities, more weekly caregiving hours, longer caregiving duration, older age, and unemployment.
Partners, parents, and children of the person with dementia had lower EQ-5D-5L scores than friends and other caregivers.
The EQ-5D-5L distinguished caregivers of people with mild dementia from those caring for people with moderate or severe dementia, but it did not distinguish moderate from severe dementia.
