Income and the presence of household members younger than 16 years did not show statistically significant known-group differences.
Anxiety/depression had the smallest proportion reporting no problems, and it had the highest proportion reporting extreme problems among the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions.

outcome: Model fit of hybrid and adapted hybrid models (Akaike information criterion) and significance of subgroup dummy parameters
statement: Group membership affected cTTO and DCE responses differently, so an adapted hybrid model with separate subgroup parameters for the cTTO and DCE parts fitted the data better than the standard hybrid model.

outcome: Model fit of hybrid and adapted hybrid models (Akaike information criterion) and significance of subgroup dummy parameters
statement: After backward selection in the adapted hybrid model, three subgroup dummies remained significant: reporting a health state other than 11111 and reporting problems with pain/discomfort in the cTTO part, and severity level 8 or worse in the DCE part.

outcome: Model fit of hybrid and adapted hybrid models (Akaike information criterion) and significance of subgroup dummy parameters
statement: Age and sex did not significantly influence the estimated values and were left out of the final estimations.

outcome: Agreement between subgroup-based and published German value sets (mean absolute deviation, Pearson correlation, value distribution densities)
statement: The six subgroup-based value sets deviated only marginally from the published German EQ-5D-5L value set, with mean absolute deviations between 0.004 and 0.013.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index values and dimension-level utility decrements from subgroup-based value sets
statement: Values for the worst health state 55555 in the subgroup value sets ranged from -0.676 to -0.639 against -0.661 in the published German value set, with the largest deviations for the pain/discomfort subgroups.

outcome: Agreement between subgroup-based and published German value sets (mean absolute deviation, Pearson correlation, value distribution densities)
statement: All subgroup-based value sets correlated strongly and significantly with the published German value set, and the density curves and scatterplots of predicted index values showed only minor deviations.

outcome: Relative importance and ranking of EQ-5D-5L dimensions (functional dimensions versus symptoms)
statement: Dimension ranking by level 5 decrement was PD-AD-SC-MO-UA in all value sets except the subgroup reporting health state 11111, where mobility and self-care swapped (PD-AD-MO-SC-UA) with a difference of only 0.006 in the level 5 decrements.

outcome: Relative importance and ranking of EQ-5D-5L dimensions (functional dimensions versus symptoms)
statement: Relative importance of the symptom dimensions exceeded that of the functional dimensions in every value set, with subgroup deviations of up to about 2 percentage points from the published German value set.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index values and dimension-level utility decrements from subgroup-based value sets
statement: Subgroup sizes showed that most participants reported no or only mild impairment: 36.36% reported health state 11111, 6.39% reported problems with self-care, 55.61% reported problems with pain/discomfort, and 29.97% had severity level 8 or worse.
The heteroskedastic conditional logit fit substantially better than the conditional logit, while the resulting 3125 profile values remained almost identical.
After control for heteroskedasticity, paired-comparison and best-worst-scaling profile values were highly correlated and had substantial, but lower, concordance.

Task sequence and task type affected response scale: scale increased through about task 14 and then decreased; paired comparisons had lower scale, while best choices had higher scale than worst choices.
The heteroskedastic SALC model gave the best model fit and separated a consistent value-set taste class from a largely uninformative garbage class.
The garbage taste class included 29% of respondents, expressed little consistent attribute importance, and was associated with younger age and male sex.
The lower-scale, more-random class included 59% of respondents; failure of the paired-comparison dominance task increased the odds of membership in this class.
The SALC pits-scale values showed the highest correlation and agreement with the original Dutch EQ-5D-5L values among the models tested.
Best-worst scaling was reported as difficult by fewer respondents than paired comparison, and 72 respondents failed the paired-comparison dominant task.

outcome: Consistency and logical ordering of level coefficients
statement: All level coefficients in both the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L conditional logit models were logically ordered and statistically significant, with no inconsistencies.

outcome: Relative overall weights of the five EQ-5D attributes
statement: Relative attribute weights differed between versions: mobility carried the highest weight in the EQ-5D-3L whereas anxiety/depression carried the highest weight in the EQ-5D-5L; self-care carried the least weight in both.

outcome: Attribute-level regression coefficients and derived health-state values
statement: Level 3 mobility ('confined to bed') had the largest single effect on EQ-5D-3L values, while the corresponding worst EQ-5D-5L level ('unable to walk') had a smaller effect.

outcome: Attribute-level regression coefficients and derived health-state values
statement: For the EQ-5D-5L, the increment from level 4 to level 5 was smaller than the increment from level 3 to level 4 for every attribute.

outcome: Attribute-level regression coefficients and derived health-state values
statement: The distribution of values across all attainable health states differed between versions: the EQ-5D-5L placed a higher proportion of states in the severe (low-value) region and a lower proportion in the mild/moderate region than the EQ-5D-3L.
The two version arms differed significantly in age distribution, but adding age group to the choice model produced no statistically significant effect on the estimated coefficients.
The proxy EQ-5D-Y-5L had very few missing responses and almost no full-health profiles, which showed good data completeness without a ceiling effect.
Children with intellectual disability had marked problems in self-care and usual activities and had more problems on the EQ-5D-Y-5L dimensions than most comparison populations.
Test-retest reliability was substantial for mobility and self-care, fair for usual activities and worry/sadness/unhappiness, and poor for pain/discomfort and EQ-VAS.

Health and EQ-VAS scores changed substantially for some children during the repeat interval, and eight families reported illness, hospital admission or surgery, constipation, or self-harm that could affect health and well-being.

Convergent validity was strong for mobility, self-care, and pain/discomfort; moderate to strong for worry/sadness/unhappiness and EQ-VAS; and weak to strong across usual-activities comparators, with weaker associations for involvement than participation frequency.
The descriptive dimensions showed extensive disability-related problems, but the median EQ-VAS was 80, comparable with values reported for healthy adults.

Fewer respondents reported any impairment on the composite EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort item than on at least one of the separate pain severity and discomfort severity items, confirming the study hypothesis.

Correlation of EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort with the other items was strongest for pain-related items and weakest for discomfort frequency; the expected pattern of severity items correlating more strongly than frequency items was not confirmed.
Discomfort frequency correlated most strongly with EQ-5D-5L anxiety/depression rather than with EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort.

In univariate ordered logistic regressions with EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort as dependent variable, pain severity gave the best model fit and the largest coefficients; discomfort frequency gave the poorest.
Among respondents reporting no problems on EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort, agreement with level 1 was higher for the severity items than for the frequency items.
Considered as single items, pain frequency had the highest absolute and relative informativity and discomfort severity the lowest.
Adding any pain or discomfort item to the EQ-5D-5L increased absolute informativity (Shannon H') but reduced relative informativity (Shannon J'), confirming the study hypothesis.

Replacing EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort in a modified EQ-4D-5L with pain frequency, discomfort frequency or pain interference improved both Shannon indices, while replacement with severity items improved only Shannon H'; adding both frequency items gave the largest gain.

The 0–3-year range was broadly supported, but experts questioned equal relevance and score comparability across developmental stages, especially for children younger than 3 months, premature children, and children with chronic or neurodevelopmental conditions.
Experts generally considered the wording appropriate, easy to follow, and understandable, and considered the six Version 2.0 dimensions to give adequate HRQoL coverage for infants and toddlers.

Experts across groups recommended age-specific observable examples in place of, or to clarify, age-appropriate behaviour to improve proxy comprehension and consistency across ages, literacy levels, cultures, and socioeconomic settings.
Sleep and emotional functioning received substantial support as potentially relevant missing dimensions that require further testing; bowel habits received little support.
Experts identified possible overlap between communication and social interaction, and sometimes between play and movement, but reached no consensus on combining dimensions.

Proxy responses can reflect caregiver experience, expectations, resources, relationship to the child, and caregiver burden; experts recommended a proxy familiar with the child and collection of proxy characteristics and caregiver HRQoL separately.

Today was generally considered the most suitable recall period, especially for acute conditions or repeated measurement, although a longer period might better represent chronic or fluctuating health; the three response levels were broadly accepted, with some support for testing more levels for sensitivity.

Experts considered EQ-TIPS necessary and potentially useful for health research, clinical assessment, clinical trials, routine outcome measurement, health technology assessment, and clinical or economic decision-making because few preference-weighted measures cover this age group.

outcome: Agreement between child or adolescent self-report and parent or caregiver proxy report
statement: Agreement between self- and proxy-reported EQ-5D-Y-3L dimension levels was fair at admission, and the worried, sad or unhappy dimension had especially poor agreement at discharge despite higher exact agreement percentages after hospitalization.

outcome: Agreement between child or adolescent self-report and parent or caregiver proxy report
statement: Agreement on EQ-5D-Y-3L utility index and EQ VAS scores was moderate overall, with lower agreement in the youngest children and older adolescents and higher agreement for many ages from 7 to 15 years.

outcome: Convergent validity of EQ-5D-Y-3L index and EQ VAS
statement: EQ-5D-Y-3L index and EQ VAS scores had statistically significant moderate positive correlations for both respondent types at admission and discharge.

outcome: Responsiveness from admission to discharge
statement: Reported problems decreased substantially across all five EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions; the largest reductions were looking after myself for self-report and worried, sad or unhappy for proxy report.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L utility index score
statement: Mean EQ-5D-Y-3L utility index scores increased significantly from admission to discharge for both self and proxy reports.

outcome: Responsiveness from admission to discharge
statement: Paretian Classification of Health Change showed that most participants improved from admission to discharge in both self- and proxy-reported measures, while worsening was uncommon.

Self-reported problems increased with age in looking after myself, usual activities, pain or discomfort, and worried, sad or unhappy; insufficient household income was associated with more emotional problems, and residence differed for self-reported mobility.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L dimension problems and EQ VAS health status
statement: Mean EQ VAS scores increased significantly from admission to discharge for both self and proxy reports.

outcome: Utility values for EQ-5D health states from each value set
statement: The three value sets differ in range and in the proportion of health states valued as worse than dead, with the English EQ-5D-5L value set having a much narrower range and far fewer negative values.

outcome: Utility values for EQ-5D health states from each value set
statement: For the 243 matched health states, EQ-5D-3L values are consistently lower than English EQ-5D-5L values, and the difference grows with severity.

outcome: Difference in utility between adjacent and matched health states
statement: The change in utility between adjacent matched states is substantially larger for the EQ-5D-3L and crosswalk than for the English EQ-5D-5L value set across all five dimensions; within the EQ-5D-5L the largest step is from severe to moderate, whereas within the crosswalk the largest step is from extreme to severe.

outcome: Dimension level response distributions on the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L in patients
statement: In patient data, adding the slight and severe levels spread EQ-5D-3L 'some problems' responses across levels 2 to 4 of the EQ-5D-5L and modestly reduced the ceiling effect.

outcome: Utility values for EQ-5D health states from each value set
statement: In the patient sample the English EQ-5D-5L value set produced higher mean utility values than the EQ-5D-3L and crosswalk value sets overall and in every condition, with significant differences in the four largest condition groups.

outcome: Agreement between value sets in patient data
statement: Bland-Altman plots show disagreement between the value sets across the severity scale, with greater variation in more severe health states.

outcome: Utility values for EQ-5D health states from each value set
statement: The value sets rank the severity of health conditions in a broadly similar order, consistent for 7 of 12 conditions, with multiple sclerosis the most variable ranking.

outcome: Utility values for EQ-5D health states from each value set
statement: Dimension importance is similar across value sets, with pain/discomfort most important in all three; only mobility and anxiety/depression change rank order in the EQ-5D-5L value set.

outcome: Agreement between predicted and observed HNHC risk
statement: Most models were well calibrated, but enhanced random forest models tended to underestimate low HNHC risk and emergency-department artificial neural networks tended to overestimate low risk.

outcome: Cost capture
statement: Adding patient-reported data produced larger gains in cost capture than in the c-statistic for the primary logistic regression models.

outcome: Discrimination measured with the c-statistic and ROC curve
statement: For the primary logistic regression models, adding patient-reported data increased the mean c-statistic by 0.02 in both cohorts.

outcome: Clinical usefulness measured as decision-curve net benefit
statement: Enhanced logistic regression models had the highest overall net benefit across risk thresholds of approximately 0.05 to 0.70.

outcome: HNHC status in the year after survey completion: health care costs in the top 5% of British Columbians
statement: HNHC status was common in both analytic cohorts, and the annual top-5% cost thresholds were $7,968 for the inpatient survey year and $8,177 for the emergency department survey year.

outcome: Relative importance of predictors
statement: Clinical history and prior resource use and costs were important predictors, while patient-reported variables accounted for 6 of the top 20 inpatient predictors and 12 of the top 20 emergency-department predictors. Important patient-reported variables included inpatient discharge information, VR-12 physical and emotional health items, EQ-5D-5L mobility or usual activities, and emergency-care experience items.

outcome: Accuracy, balanced accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity
statement: The models generally had high specificity and lower sensitivity. Artificial neural networks increased cost capture and sensitivity but reduced specificity compared with the primary logistic regression model.

outcome: Agreement, bias, and posterior uncertainty
statement: For Irish estimates, combined analysis had narrower Bland-Altman limits of agreement, smaller average bias, and a smaller standard deviation of differences than single analysis.

outcome: Prediction accuracy of combined versus single-country modeling
statement: Using Polish-migrant results as informative priors improved prediction of native-Irish mean utilities compared with modeling Irish data alone.

outcome: Agreement, bias, and posterior uncertainty
statement: For Polish-migrant estimates, combined analysis had narrower Bland-Altman limits of agreement and a smaller standard deviation of differences than single analysis; mean bias was close to zero in both analyses.

outcome: Prediction accuracy of combined versus single-country modeling
statement: Using native-Irish results as informative priors improved prediction of Polish-migrant mean utilities compared with modeling Polish data alone.

outcome: Agreement, bias, and posterior uncertainty
statement: Posterior standard deviations of utility estimates were generally smaller in combined analyses than in single-country analyses.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D index scores by arthritis status and severity indicators
statement: EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D index scores were lower in participants with arthritis than in those without, with a moderate effect size for both.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D index scores by arthritis status and severity indicators
statement: Overall mean scores in the full sample were 0.86 for the EQ-5D-5L index, 81.9 for EQ VAS and 0.79 for SF-6D, with ceiling effects of 23% for EQ-5D-5L and 7% for SF-6D.

outcome: Discriminative (known-groups) validity of EQ-5D-5L and SF-12/SF-6D dimensions, domains and index scores
statement: Conceptually related EQ-5D-5L dimensions and SF-12 domains correlated moderately to strongly, and the two index scores correlated strongly.

outcome: Discriminative (known-groups) validity of EQ-5D-5L and SF-12/SF-6D dimensions, domains and index scores
statement: Pain/discomfort and mobility were the EQ-5D-5L dimensions that separated arthritis groups best, while bodily pain had the largest effect size among SF-12 domains; self-care and anxiety/depression separated groups poorly.

outcome: Discriminative (known-groups) validity of EQ-5D-5L and SF-12/SF-6D dimensions, domains and index scores
statement: Both instruments failed to separate participants with moderate from those with severe 6-month chronic pain, and the SF-6D showed a reversed pattern.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D index scores by arthritis status and severity indicators
statement: Among participants with arthritis, EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D index scores declined with more comorbidities and with poorer self-rated health, as hypothesised.

outcome: Estimated disease cases, prevalence, severity, and mortality
statement: The model estimated 2015 national case counts for low back pain, osteoarthritis, and rheumatoid arthritis; osteoarthritis had the most cases.
The burden model was programmed in Microsoft Excel for transparency and external usability, with the ability to apply it to other rheumatic disease scenarios.

outcome: Disability-adjusted life years and DALY rates per 100,000 population
statement: Low back pain produced the greatest estimated burden among the three diseases.

outcome: Disability-adjusted life years and DALY rates per 100,000 population
statement: Osteoarthritis produced the second greatest estimated burden among the three diseases.

outcome: Disability-adjusted life years and DALY rates per 100,000 population
statement: Rheumatoid arthritis produced the lowest estimated burden among the three diseases but its rate was substantially higher than the GBD 2019 estimate for Colombia.

outcome: Years lived with disability
statement: Years lived with disability accounted for almost all estimated DALYs for each rheumatic disease.

outcome: Estimated disease cases, prevalence, severity, and mortality
statement: Recorded 2015 mortality was low: rheumatoid arthritis had no attributable deaths, low back pain had nine, and osteoarthritis had 86.

outcome: Estimated disease cases, prevalence, severity, and mortality
statement: Severity mapping placed 44% of low back pain cases, 63% of osteoarthritis cases, and 55% of rheumatoid arthritis cases in the mild category; the remaining cases were distributed across moderate, severe, and, for low back pain, most-severe categories.

outcome: Expert validation of model inputs, structure, methods, and results
statement: The expert panel unanimously judged the total case estimates reliable, approved the DALY methodology and results, agreed with low back pain and osteoarthritis severity distributions, and requested redistribution of rheumatoid arthritis severity.

outcome: Disability-adjusted life years and DALY rates per 100,000 population
statement: The estimated disease burden was greater among females than males, especially for osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.

outcome: Caregiver self-reported EQ VAS score
statement: Caregiver health as measured by the EQ-5D-3L did not differ across the three child health groups, and reported problems were concentrated in pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression; no caregiver reported self-care problems.

outcome: Child's proxy-reported TANDI VAS score
statement: Children in the general population group were rated significantly higher on the TANDI VAS than acutely-ill and chronically-ill children, who did not differ from each other, and had the fewest reported problems in every TANDI dimension.

outcome: Caregiver self-reported EQ VAS score
statement: The child's TANDI VAS correlated positively and significantly with the caregiver's EQ VAS in all three groups, most strongly in the acutely-ill group, whereas the caregiver's EQ-5D-3L index score correlated with the child's VAS only in the acutely-ill group.

outcome: Caregiver self-reported EQ VAS score
statement: In the forward stepwise regression on the caregiver's EQ VAS, anxiety/depression problems explained the most variance and the child's TANDI VAS was the next largest contributor, ahead of the caregiver's own pain/discomfort, diagnosis and mobility problems.

outcome: Child's proxy-reported TANDI VAS score
statement: In the forward stepwise regression on the child's TANDI VAS, problems with play explained the most variance and the caregiver's own EQ VAS was the second largest contributor; problems with eating, movement and pain significantly reduced the child's VAS.

outcome: Caregiver self-reported EQ VAS score
statement: There was no association between the presence of a health condition in the caregiver and the health classification of the child, and reported mental health conditions were not more common among caregivers of chronically-ill children.

outcome: Caregiver self-reported EQ VAS score
statement: A ten point change in the VAS score of one member of the dyad corresponded to a change of about three to four points in the VAS of the other.
CHU9D had a substantially lower ceiling effect than either EQ-5D-Y instrument at baseline.
Almost all prespecified convergent-validity hypotheses were met for each instrument, although several dimension-level correlations were lower than expected.
All prespecified known-groups validity hypotheses were met; EQ-5D-Y-5L had the greatest relative efficiency for three of five known-group definitions, while EQ-5D-Y-3L was more efficient for two.

Change scores followed the expected direction, but differences between improved and worsened-or-unchanged groups were not statistically significant; CHU9D had the largest standardized effect size in improved patients.
In the exploratory analysis that excluded patients at full health at baseline, standardized effect sizes increased for all instruments and were largest for EQ-5D-Y-5L.
EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L had no statistically significant difference in ceiling effects on any individual dimension.

outcome: Proportion reporting any problem on each EQ-5D-3L dimension
statement: Reported problems increased with age and were generally more frequent in females in all countries except Slovenia; pain/discomfort was the most prevalent problem and self-care the least prevalent in every country.

outcome: Mean self-rated EQ VAS score
statement: Age-standardized mean EQ VAS varied substantially across countries, with Hungary and Korea lowest and Denmark and the United Kingdom highest.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L index value norms by value set
statement: EQ-5D index norms declined with age under all value sets, and the level depended on the value set used: European VAS norms were generally at or above country-specific VAS norms (except Germany), while country-specific TTO norms were higher than country-specific VAS norms.

outcome: Mean self-rated EQ VAS score
statement: Country GDP per capita and health expenditure per capita correlated with mean EQ VAS, unemployment correlated only in age groups over 45, and physicians per 1000 people and life expectancy showed no significant association.

outcome: Mean self-rated EQ VAS score
statement: Regression analyses showed GDP and health expenditure per capita explained a substantial share of between-country variation in mean EQ VAS, with China and Thailand as outliers of low GDP and relatively high EQ VAS.

outcome: Proportion reporting any problem on each EQ-5D-3L dimension
statement: Country rankings on the EQ VAS did not consistently match rankings on reported dimension problems; China reported the fewest problems but only average EQ VAS, while Hungary and Korea had the lowest EQ VAS despite fewer reported problems than Slovenia and Thailand.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L index value scored with the UK value set
statement: SUD patients reported substantially lower EQ-5D-3L index values and EQ VAS scores than the general population sample, overall and in every sex and age subgroup.

outcome: Reported problems by EQ-5D-3L dimension and level, and distribution of self-assigned health states
statement: Almost all patients reported at least one problem, and reports of extreme problems were about ten times more common than in the general population sample.

outcome: Reported problems by EQ-5D-3L dimension and level, and distribution of self-assigned health states
statement: Patients reported more problems on every EQ-5D-3L dimension than general population respondents, with the largest differences for usual activities, pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression; no patient reported the worst mobility level.

outcome: Reported problems by EQ-5D-3L dimension and level, and distribution of self-assigned health states
statement: Patients self-assigned a wider spread of EQ-5D-3L health states than general population respondents.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L index value scored with the UK value set
statement: In multivariable regression, cocaine dependence and phobic anxiety predicted higher (better) EQ-5D-3L index values, and cocaine dependence also predicted higher EQ VAS scores; the association with female sex was not significant after adjustment.

outcome: Convergence of EQ-5D-3L index values and anxiety/depression responses with HSCL-25 total scores
statement: EQ-5D-3L index values and anxiety/depression responses correlated strongly with HSCL-25 total scores.
Heteroscedasticity was detected in most regressions, but Box-Cox transformation of the dependent variables changed neither direction nor statistical significance, so OLS results were reported.

outcome: Intertemporal agreement of recalled pre-injury EQ-5D-3L summary score and EQ-VAS
statement: Mean recalled pre-injury EQ-5D-3L summary scores did not differ between 1 week and 12 months post-injury, with moderate intertemporal agreement.

outcome: Intertemporal agreement of recalled pre-injury EQ-5D-3L summary score and EQ-VAS
statement: Mean recalled pre-injury EQ-VAS was significantly higher at 12 months than at 1 week, with moderate agreement.

outcome: Stability of recalled pre-injury EQ-5D-3L profiles and dimensions
statement: About 38% of respondents reported a different recalled pre-injury EQ-5D-3L profile at 12 months than at 1 week, with changes symmetrical in both directions; pain/discomfort was the least stable dimension.

outcome: Stability of recalled pre-injury EQ-5D-3L profiles and dimensions
statement: Comorbid disease, PTSD symptoms and increasing age were independent predictors of change in the recalled pre-injury EQ-5D profile; no factor predicted EQ-VAS change.

outcome: Intertemporal agreement of recalled pre-injury EQ-5D-3L summary score and EQ-VAS
statement: Neither severe injury (ISS >= 16) nor PTSD produced a significant group-level gap between recalled pre-injury scores at the two occasions, contrary to the cognitive dissonance and memory-disturbance hypotheses.

outcome: Intertemporal agreement of recalled pre-injury EQ-5D-3L summary score and EQ-VAS
statement: Agreement was lowest in patients without pre-existing comorbidity and highest in older patients.

outcome: Observed TTO values for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Mean TTO values did not differ significantly between lead-time and lag-time variants for nine of the ten EQ-5D-5L states; only state 33133 differed significantly.

outcome: Task process measures: completion time, number of steps to indifference, resets, logical inconsistency, non-trading and zero responses
statement: Marked peaks of values at zero occurred in all valued states, with a higher share of zero values for the last state valued than the first, indicating ordering effects.

outcome: Task process measures: completion time, number of steps to indifference, resets, logical inconsistency, non-trading and zero responses
statement: Non-trading responses and process measures (time per state, number of moves, resets) were similar between the two TTO variants.

outcome: Task process measures: completion time, number of steps to indifference, resets, logical inconsistency, non-trading and zero responses
statement: Logical inconsistency between orderable pairs of states was high and did not differ between blocks or TTO variants.

outcome: Observed TTO values for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: A subgroup analysis excluding states valued in only two steps produced no major differences between variants; the difference for 33133 disappeared and a new difference emerged for state 11145.

outcome: Respondent-reported clarity and difficulty of the valuation tasks (cognitive debriefing)
statement: Respondents reported that instructions were clear and easy to understand, though about half found deciding an answer difficult, and over half considered the possibility of a future treatment when valuing states.
Higher EQ-5D index, EQ VAS, GHQ-12 and WEMWBS scores were associated with an increased probability of reporting no social care need.

The EQ-5D self-care and pain/discomfort dimensions were statistically significantly associated with need for social care in both binary logit and ordered probit models; mobility was significant only in the binary model and usual activities only in the ordered model, and extreme anxiety/depression predicted greater social care need.

None of the GHQ-12 dimensions were significantly associated with the Barthel index, while only two WEMWBS dimensions, 'been feeling useful' and 'had energy to spare', were significantly associated with it.

Older age, having a degree and limiting long-standing illness were predictors of social care need across all six EQ-5D models, and being underweight or overweight predicted social care need in some models.

In exploratory models of well-being, ability to perform usual activities and being less anxious or depressed on the EQ-5D were associated with better WEMWBS and GHQ-12 scores; WEMWBS scores were higher in 2012 than 2011, possibly because of the change in administration from interviewer visit to nurse visit.

A small group of respondents with the greatest reported social care need (Barthel index below 5) reported unexpectedly high health status and well-being and were better educated; most of them reported that their needs had not been met.

Missing data were substantial and unevenly distributed: missing responses were 3.8% for the EQ-5D index, 9.7% for EQ-VAS, 24% for WEMWBS and 50.5% for GHQ-12, and were more frequent among older respondents, those with lower education, and those not married or cohabiting.
The recommendation stream included 22 records, divided equally between health economics and PROM development or evaluation.

outcome: Synthesized best-practice recommendations for collaborative engagement
statement: The thematic synthesis produced 15 recommendations that covered planning and design, conduct, evaluation, and reporting of collaborative engagement.

outcome: Reported collaborative-engagement practices in health state valuation studies
statement: The current-practice stream included 15 valuation studies; most were vignette studies and most were conducted in the United Kingdom or Australia.

outcome: Reported collaborative-engagement practices in health state valuation studies
statement: Most reported collaborative engagement involved patients, people with lived experience, and/or experts helping to inform or review health states and related valuation content.

outcome: Alignment of valuation-study practice with synthesized recommendations
statement: No valuation study provided evidence for 9 of the 15 recommendations, and the remaining six recommendations had only limited evidence across studies.

outcome: Alignment of valuation-study practice with synthesized recommendations
statement: Evidence that suitable representatives were involved was sufficient in three studies and uncertain in nine; evidence of engagement at key stages was uncertain in three studies.

outcome: Alignment of valuation-study practice with synthesized recommendations
statement: One study sufficiently showed that collaboration added value and ten had uncertain evidence; two studies sufficiently reported feedback to collaborators or communities.

outcome: Alignment of valuation-study practice with synthesized recommendations
statement: Two studies had uncertain evidence of sustained meaningful engagement and full transparent reporting, despite providing more engagement detail than other valuation studies.
Greater predicted disutility for compromised health was associated with a higher probability of using each of the five preventive services after adjustment for the reported covariates.
Health preferences were not significantly associated with general practitioner use.
The error-term correlation between each preventive-service equation and its paired GP-use equation was positive and statistically significant in all five bivariate probit models.
Reported service-use prevalence varied from 32% for urine tests to 80% for GP use.
After rescaling state 55555 values as disutility from 0 for full health to 2 for worse than dead, the mean estimated health-preference value was 1.8.

Focus-group participants preferred the second-person wording and standardized guidance of the official interviewer-administered version. However, all considered strict use infeasible in a long population survey, and they thought that reading every response option at once could burden older respondents.

Skipping questions, focusing on observable problems, and leading no-problem questions could omit mild problems and increase ceiling effects. Interviewer cross-checking could instead increase reported problems. The study did not quantify either pathway.
No analysed interview fully followed expected interviewer administration. Six recordings had no EQ-5D conversation because the respondent appeared to self-complete the form.

Six non-standard approaches occurred in the 46 EQ-5D-3L recordings: skipping questions, altering wording, combining dimensions, altering response options, selecting responses from interviewer interpretation, and asking no descriptive-system questions. Multiple approaches often occurred in one interview.

Three linked themes explained non-standard administration: comprehension and response problems among older, rural, or low-literacy respondents; a long survey with EQ-5D near the end and resulting burden and time pressure; and limited interviewer knowledge of EQ-5D and self-reported-health principles, including an observer-assessment and quality-control mindset.

Interviewers expected that moving EQ-5D to the start would initially increase care and respondent attention, but they might later develop time-saving adaptations. They also suggested visual aids, smiley faces for response levels, and standardized examples.
The selected 2020 recording sample had a lower EQ-5D-3L ceiling and EQ VAS mean than the full 2020 survey, but both showed high ceiling levels. The 2021 full survey also had a high EQ-5D-5L ceiling.
For EQ VAS, interviewers commonly changed or led the wording and assigned scores from their interpretation of respondents' answers, sometimes by proposing a range or a specific value.

The distributions of reported problems across the five EQ-5D dimensions, EQ VAS scores, and utilities showed little variation between the baseline and the three weekly follow-up waves; EQ VAS and utility differences between waves were not statistically significant.

Compared with the 2011-2012 reference sample, the pooled 2020 study sample reported substantially more anxiety/depression and more pain/discomfort; the largest anxiety/depression increase was for slight problems.
The pooled 2020 study sample had a lower mean utility than the reference sample but a higher mean EQ VAS score; both differences were statistically significant.

Weighted proportional-odds models indicated that 2020 respondents had higher odds of problems in usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression after adjustment for age; age-interaction models showed that the 2020-versus-2012 increase in problems was greatest in the youngest age group across all dimensions.
Regional epidemic-severity groups did not differ significantly in pooled EQ-5D dimension scores, EQ VAS scores, or utilities.

The Spanish adult population was estimated to accrue fewer QALYs than expected from the 2011-2012 reference utilities, with a loss of 60,520 QALYs over 21 days and an extrapolated loss of 285,310 QALYs over the 99-day lockdown.
The estimated lifetime QALY loss associated with 15,956 reported COVID-19-related deaths through 28 April 2020 was 146,584 QALYs.

outcome: Implementation and reporting of HRQoL, health utility, mortality, and QALYs in critical care research
statement: Critical care trials have not routinely measured or reported HRQoL, and no HRQoL instrument has been rigorously validated as the gold standard for critically ill patients.

outcome: Suitability of HRQoL and utility instruments for critical care
statement: The authors identify EQ-5D-5L as the most promising critical care instrument because it is brief, includes EQ VAS, covers low and negative utility states, and has many language versions and country-specific scoring systems.

outcome: Implementation and reporting of HRQoL, health utility, mortality, and QALYs in critical care research
statement: An aggregate QALY result can conceal whether the main contribution comes from survival time or health utility; the same total QALYs can represent clinically different trajectories.
Patient incapacity makes proxy measurement important in critical care, but patient and proxy ratings can differ.

outcome: In-hospital death, Glasgow Coma Scale category, and length of hospital stay
statement: Almost half of admissions were due to injury, mostly motor vehicle crashes, and 17% of admitted patients died in hospital.

outcome: In-hospital death, Glasgow Coma Scale category, and length of hospital stay
statement: Length of hospital stay was significantly shorter for injury patients than for illness patients.

outcome: Pre-discharge health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L dimensions and EQ VAS)
statement: Before discharge, one third or fewer patients reported no problems on EQ-5D-5L mobility, self-care, usual activities, and pain/discomfort, while 70% reported no problems with anxiety/depression and 76% no problems with intellectual functioning.

outcome: Pre-discharge health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L dimensions and EQ VAS)
statement: A considerable proportion of patients reported extreme problems pre-discharge, most often with usual activities, and no patient reported severe or extreme pain/discomfort.

outcome: Pre-discharge health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L dimensions and EQ VAS)
statement: Illness patients reported extreme problems with mobility and self-care more often than injury patients, while moderate pain/discomfort was less common in illness patients.

outcome: Pre-discharge health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L dimensions and EQ VAS)
statement: The mean EQ VAS score pre-discharge was high despite the reported dimension problems.

outcome: In-hospital death, Glasgow Coma Scale category, and length of hospital stay
statement: Glasgow Coma Scale on admission was mild for 63%, moderate for 31%, and severe for 3% of admitted patients; pre-discharge all interviewed patients were mild (69%) or moderate (29%).
In the mental-health arm, the poor-health vignette had no statistically significant effect on any ASCOT coefficient compared with the full-health vignette.

In the physical-health arm, health context significantly modified control over daily life level 4, personal safety level 2, and accommodation cleanliness and comfort level 4; the control and safety decrements became smaller, while the accommodation decrement became larger under poor physical health.

Control over daily life was the most important ASCOT attribute in both mental-health contexts and under full health in the physical-health arm, but personal safety was most important under poor physical health. Control, safety, and cleanliness together accounted for more than half of relative attribute importance in every arm-context case.

Prior experience with physical or mental health problems did not significantly affect most ASCOT coefficients. The exception was personal safety level 4 under poor-health contexts: physical-health experience increased its weight, while mental-health experience decreased its weight.
Social interaction, accommodation cleanliness and comfort, and dignity were consistently the three least important ASCOT attributes.
Participants generally rated the visual appeal favorably. They asked for larger fonts and images and stronger contrast between elements.
For Part 1, patients preferred the grouped icon-array presentation. For Part 2, they preferred the visual appeal of Version 1 and the additional information in Version 2.
The tests found no statistically significant differences between versions for any reported variable or category in either part.

Most participants gave both post-surgery versions a comprehension rating of 4 or 5. Version 2 gave a fuller before-and-after view, but some participants thought that the extra information was distracting.
Participants showed an overall preference for Version 2 of the one-year post-surgery visualization.

About three fifths of participants rated each post-surgery version as useful or very useful. Patients valued information about possible benefits, unchanged outcomes, and worse outcomes, but some had already made a treatment decision.

Almost all participants said that the shared instructions were clear. About half gave each version a comprehension rating of 4 or 5. Most said that the displays helped them compare themselves with similar people.
Some participants interpreted the pre-surgery comparison as evidence of condition severity or priority for surgery, although this was not its intended purpose.
Participants showed a slight overall preference for Version 1 of the pre-surgery visualization.

Half of participants rated each pre-surgery version as useful or very useful. Some participants did not know how to use the comparison, did not value comparison with other people, or had already made a treatment decision.

outcome: Out-of-sample EQ-5D-5L health-state prediction error, measured as RMSE against full-sample censored mean values
statement: Increasing sample size improved prediction accuracy, but the marginal improvement decreased rapidly; gains above approximately 300 to 500 respondents were small.

outcome: Out-of-sample EQ-5D-5L health-state prediction error, measured as RMSE against full-sample censored mean values
statement: In the pooled linear regression, doubling sample size and each alternative modeling choice reduced RMSE.

outcome: Out-of-sample EQ-5D-5L health-state prediction error, measured as RMSE against full-sample censored mean values
statement: For TTO-only analyses, the 8-parameter CALE model had lower out-of-sample RMSE than the 20-parameter ADD20 model at every tested sample size in all three national data sets.

outcome: Sample size at which a candidate model matched the maximum-sample 20-parameter TTO-only model
statement: Alternative model specifications permitted smaller samples to reach the reference accuracy of the maximum-sample 20-parameter TTO-only model.

outcome: Out-of-sample EQ-5D-5L health-state prediction error, measured as RMSE against full-sample censored mean values
statement: At the maximum Norwegian sample, the 8-parameter random-intercept TTO model and 8-parameter random-intercept hybrid model achieved prediction accuracy similar to the Netherlands and United States analyses.

outcome: Out-of-sample EQ-5D-5L health-state prediction error, measured as RMSE against full-sample censored mean values
statement: Across all tested models and sample sizes, mean RMSE ranged from 0.178 to 0.077 in the Netherlands data, 0.209 to 0.084 in the United States data, and 0.174 to 0.099 in the Norway data.

outcome: Missing data and ceiling effects of the bolt-ons
statement: Most respondents reported no or slight breathing or cognition problems at about 30 months; severe or extreme responses were rare.

outcome: Construct validity of the EQ-5D-5L breathing bolt-on
statement: The breathing bolt-on had moderate correlation with mMRC and stronger correlations with Dyspnoea-12 than the standard EQ-5D-5L dimensions, while correlations with earlier pulmonary measures were low to moderate.

outcome: Construct validity of the EQ-5D-5L cognition bolt-on
statement: The cognition bolt-on correlated strongly with DSQ-SF neurocognitive items and the CFQ-11 mental-fatigue score, but correlations with objective CANTAB tests measured about 20 months earlier were low.

outcome: EQ VAS score and variance explained by EQ-5D-5L dimensions and bolt-ons
statement: The five standard EQ-5D-5L dimensions explained about half of EQ VAS variation. Adding breathing produced a small increase in adjusted explained variance, while adding cognition produced almost no increase.

outcome: Missing data and ceiling effects of the bolt-ons
statement: Adding either bolt-on reduced the proportion at the descriptive-system ceiling, and adding both produced the largest reduction.
At about 30 months, mean EQ-5D index and EQ VAS scores indicated residual health problems in the analyzed cohort.
A total of 238 people from 45 countries and 65 HTA agencies completed the survey. Most respondents were public-sector employees, and most had QALY-related responsibilities.

outcome: Reported use and perceived fitness for purpose of utility instruments and preference-elicitation methods in HTA
statement: EQ-5D was the most frequently used utility instrument and was used very often. SF-6D and EQ-5D-Y ranked next and were used occasionally overall.

outcome: Reported use and perceived fitness for purpose of utility instruments and preference-elicitation methods in HTA
statement: Most respondents said that instrument choice matters. EQ-5D, including EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L in open comments, was most often judged fit for purpose because of low burden, psychometric evidence, available value sets, guideline support, familiarity, and comparability. A reported weakness was limited sensitivity in some conditions.

outcome: Reported use and perceived fitness for purpose of utility instruments and preference-elicitation methods in HTA
statement: TTO, VAS, and SG were the three most frequently used elicitation methods and were used often overall. Most respondents said that method choice matters. TTO was most often named fit for purpose because it is choice based, theoretically grounded, validated, and yields cardinal utility, although respondents identified cognitive burden as a limitation.

outcome: Use and preferred source of health-state preference data
statement: Preferences from the general public in another country were used more often than local public preferences overall. Respondents strongly agreed that preference source matters. Qualitative responses more often favored general-public values and local-country values, although many respondents favored patient values because they reflect patient voice and disease experience.

outcome: Frequency and types of HRQoL and utility data-quality problems
statement: Frequently encountered data-quality problems were poorly representative patient samples, small samples, mismatch between available health states and cost-effectiveness model needs, and use of utility values generated with different methods or instruments in one model. Outdated data were encountered less often.

outcome: Global and regional HRQoL research priorities
statement: The highest global research priorities were more recent utility data and tariffs, instruments for children and adolescents, and instruments that capture both health-care and social-care effects.

outcome: Global and regional HRQoL research priorities
statement: Priorities differed by region: social-care measurement ranked first in Asia and Western Europe; recent tariffs ranked first in Central and Eastern Europe and the Middle East and Africa; caregiver effects ranked first in the Commonwealth; and inequality in care ranked first in Latin America.

outcome: Regional and national EQ-5D-5L scoring algorithm coefficients and predicted health state utilities
statement: Models including region-by-fixed-effect interactions fitted the valuation data substantially better than the model ignoring region, indicating that regional variation in health state preferences is present.

outcome: Regional and national EQ-5D-5L scoring algorithm coefficients and predicted health state utilities
statement: Some coefficients (mobility, anxiety/depression, MO45, SC45, AD45) did not vary by region, while self-care, usual activities and pain/discomfort coefficients did, with Quebec attaching the largest and Alberta the smallest disutility to losses in self-care.

outcome: Predictive accuracy (mean squared error, mean absolute error) and limits of agreement between algorithms
statement: Regional shrinkage algorithms predicted regional preferences with smaller mean squared and mean absolute errors than the Canada-wide algorithm in all provinces except Alberta.

outcome: Population mean utility and incremental mean utility under national versus regional algorithms
statement: Applying regional instead of the Canada-wide algorithm to the EQ-5D-5L health states reported by the study population changed estimated population mean utility appreciably.

outcome: Population mean utility and incremental mean utility under national versus regional algorithms
statement: In simulated populations, the national algorithm almost always overestimated population mean utility relative to the British Columbia algorithm and underestimated it relative to the Ontario algorithm for mean utilities above 0.5.

outcome: Population mean utility and incremental mean utility under national versus regional algorithms
statement: Differences between national and regional algorithms in estimated incremental mean utility were smaller, with limits of agreement of about plus or minus 0.05.

outcome: Child-reported health concepts classified under physical, mental, and social health
statement: The analysis generated 126 codes; 39 codes not describing health-status outcomes were excluded, and 87 retained codes were consolidated into 50 distinct concepts.

outcome: Comprehensiveness of EQ-5D-Y-3L coverage of child-reported health concepts
statement: The 50 concepts comprised 16 physical-health, 30 mental-health, and four social-health concepts. All five EQ-5D-Y dimensions were represented, but children frequently described social health, which the instrument does not explicitly include.

outcome: Relevance and comprehensibility of the EQ-5D-Y-3L descriptive system
statement: Participants found no odd or difficult wording and generally understood the instrument, but some had difficulty applying the stated reference period or interpreting broad dimension wording and examples.

outcome: Relevance and comprehensibility of the EQ-5D-Y-3L descriptive system
statement: Many children had difficulty distinguishing looking after myself from doing usual activities and cited overlapping examples such as eating, household chores, studying, and sleeping.

outcome: Relevance and comprehensibility of the EQ-5D-Y-3L descriptive system
statement: All selected response options matched participants' verbal accounts, but two participants thought that the three-level response scale lacked an intermediate option and suggested five levels.

outcome: Relevance and comprehensibility of the EQ-5D-Y-3L descriptive system
statement: Participants suggested additional coverage of social relationships, disease, diet, sleep, economic conditions, and more mental-health concepts; they also requested more specific examples and clearer questions.

outcome: Comprehensibility and score-selection issues for the EQ VAS
statement: No participant reported a clarity problem with the EQ VAS, but three were uncertain about the criteria for assigning a health score, and participants found the dense numeric labels visually confusing.

Children across the sampled age range, including the youngest eight-year-old participant, could communicate health concerns when given appropriate prompts; participants with diseases were generally less forthcoming than healthy participants.
Respondents in the 10-year-old arm were more likely than respondents in the self arm to report difficulty distinguishing and choosing between health states and to rate the tasks as difficult.
The estimated exponential discount rate was above zero in both perspectives, which supported nonlinear time preferences.
All EQ-5D-Y-5L QALY-scale decrements were significant at the 95% confidence level and were ordered across severity levels in both arms.
Parent and nonparent results were similar in the 10-year-old arm. In the self arm, nonparents had a longer utility scale and classified more states as worse than dead than parents.

Pain and discomfort had the largest decrement in both arms. Adults gave larger decrements to pain and discomfort and to being worried, sad, or unhappy when they imagined a 10-year-old; mobility was relatively more important from the self perspective.
Exclusion of the 243 respondents who failed the traffic-light quality check produced results consistent with the main self-arm analysis.
The 10-year-old perspective produced a longer utility scale and more health states valued as worse than dead than the self perspective.

For the 243 comparable profiles, the 10-year-old EQ-5D-Y-5L results agreed better with the Australian EQ-5D-Y-3L value set in distances between states, while the self results agreed better in scale but varied more in distance.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L index value
statement: In the final Tobit model, refugee status was associated with a small reduction in EQ-5D-3L index value after adjustment for retained sociodemographic and health indicators.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L index value
statement: In the age- and sex-matched sample, Ukrainian refugees had a significantly lower mean EQ-5D-3L index value than general-population controls (p = 0.005).

outcome: EQ-5D-3L index value
statement: The refugee-control coefficient became non-significant after economic variables and then health indicators were added, but it became significant after non-significant variables were removed for the final model; OLS sensitivity analyses gave similar results.

outcome: Reported problems in the five EQ-5D-3L dimensions
statement: Refugees reported significantly more pain or discomfort and anxiety or depression than controls.

outcome: Reported problems in the five EQ-5D-3L dimensions
statement: Refugees reported significantly fewer problems with mobility, self-care, and usual activities than controls.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L index value
statement: In the final model, female sex, older age, household financial difficulty, worse self-rated health, perceived stress, depressiveness, and overtiredness were associated with lower EQ-5D-3L index values.
All children in Spain and New Zealand found the three pre-tested exercises easy to understand and complete; completing all three exercises and instructions took less than 20 minutes.
Card ranking was the clear preferred exercise among children who stated a preference.
Card ranking was easier to revise than line-drawing exercises and let interviewers observe difficult ordering decisions as children rearranged cards.

The linguistic review judged card ranking and its instructions generally translatable but identified culturally or linguistically problematic colours, colloquial wording, and instructions that required revision.
Children who completed the South African and Indonesian pilots understood the card-ranking task, and the introductory warm-up was useful.
Card ranking identified severity-qualifier order inversions that interviewers stated would not have been detected without the exercise.
Qualifier inversions occurred in four of 19 pilot participants, and disruption from the intended ranking was greatest in the youngest age group.
The Version Management Committee incorporated card ranking into the translation protocol for beta EQ-5D-Y-5L versions.
EQ-HWB-S had a substantially smaller instrument-level ceiling effect than EQ-5D-5L, and no floor effect was detected.
Conceptually overlapping EQ-HWB and EQ-5D-5L items generally had moderate to strong correlations; the EQ-HWB-S index also correlated strongly with the EQ-5D-5L index.
EQ-HWB-S and EQ-5D-5L had similar discriminatory power for symptomatic chronic conditions.
EQ-HWB-S discriminated social care users from nonusers slightly better than EQ-5D-5L.
EQ-HWB-S and EQ-5D-5L index differences by caregiver status were trivial, while the EQ-HWB psychosocial level summary score showed a small difference.
Both index measures showed very large discrimination between respondents with and without depression; sensitivity of EQ-HWB subscales varied by condition.
The EQ-5D-3L anxiety/depression dimension showed limited responsiveness: most patients with anchor-defined change in depressive or anxiety symptoms reported no change on the dimension.
Discriminative ability of change on the EQ-5D-3L anxiety/depression dimension against anchor-defined change was poor.

The EQ-5D-5L anxiety/depression dimension was slightly more responsive than the 3L version but still below acceptable thresholds; about a third of patients with anchor-defined improvement had no change on the dimension.

C-indices for the EQ-5D-5L anxiety/depression dimension ranged from 0.64 to 0.75, with best performance for detecting deterioration in overall mental health measured by the SF-12 mental component summary.
Effect sizes of change on the anxiety/depression dimension were small in both cohorts and smaller than those of the anchor measures.
Change on the anxiety/depression dimension correlated weakly with anchor change in the 3L cohort and moderately in the 5L cohort.

outcome: Predictive performance, logical consistency, fit, and agreement of candidate valuation models
statement: The hybrid heteroskedastic Tobit model with cTTO censoring at -1, combining cTTO and DCE data, gave the most consistent results and the lowest mean absolute error for commonly observed health states; it was selected to generate the value set.

outcome: Predicted utility values for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Predicted values across all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states ranged from -0.9227 for 55555 to 1.000 for full health 11111.

outcome: Predicted utility values for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: The value set classified 874 of 3125 health states as worse than dead.

outcome: Predicted utility values for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Pain/discomfort had the greatest effect on preference values, while anxiety/depression had the smallest effect in the final model.

outcome: Predictive performance, logical consistency, fit, and agreement of candidate valuation models
statement: Predictions from the final hybrid model agreed closely with predictions from the cTTO-only and rescaled DCE models.

outcome: Respondents' self-reported EQ-5D-5L health and EQ VAS
statement: In the analyzed sample, mean self-reported EQ-5D-5L utility was 0.849 and mean EQ VAS was 75.18.
Of 3548 completed interviews, 788 pilot interviews and 351 substantive interviews were excluded, leaving 2409 interviews for final analysis.
The framework classifies PROMs by measurement focus, by generic or condition-specific scope, and by profile or preference-based type.

The proposed approach has eight steps: establish a selection committee; define measurement focus, scope, and type; identify candidate PROMs; review practical considerations; review measurement properties; review patient acceptance; recommend one or more PROMs; and pilot the selected PROMs.

PROM selection must balance workflow integration, measure length, administration mode and frequency, recall period, technology and resources, value-set availability, data security and ownership, interoperability, licensing costs, measurement properties, and patient acceptance.

The authors recommend selecting measures that can support individual patient care and aggregate organizational and system uses, while allowing a common generic PROM to be combined with targeted measures when needed.
The proposed process is iterative, and the weight of each selection criterion depends on the clinical context, setting, patient population, and available resources.
Before large-scale use, the selected PROMs should be piloted in the target setting with feedback from patients, data collectors, and management.

The all-state hybrid model had lower MSE across the 10 C-TTO states, but this result was driven by states 22223 and 22232; after their removal, pits-state anchoring predicted the remaining states better.
The hybrid model that used all 10 C-TTO states produced a narrower utility range than pits-state anchoring and predicted state 33333 at -0.364, compared with -0.539 under pits-state anchoring.

The four classes showed substantial unobservable preference heterogeneity: the largest class emphasized pain/discomfort, worry or unhappiness, and usual activities; the second emphasized pain/discomfort and mobility; the third strongly emphasized mobility; and the fourth had no homogeneous preference pattern.
For EQ-5D-Y-3L state 33333, the observed population-weighted C-TTO mean was -0.389 and the censoring-adjusted mean was -0.539.

In the selected value set, all utility decrements between consecutive levels were logically consistent and statistically significant; pain/discomfort had the greatest relative importance, followed by worry/sadness/unhappiness, mobility, usual activities, and self-care.
The four-class latent-class model had the lowest BIC and was selected; all tested latent-class models had better MAE, MSE, and BIC than the multinomial and mixed logit models.
After adjustment for age and education, administration mode had no significant effect on EQ VAS or EQ-5D utility scores, and its effect was negligible in both ANCOVA models.
The mandatory digital form had no missing EQ-5D responses, while the paper version had 6.0% missing data.
Adjusted analyses identified older age, food insecurity, financial insecurity, and elevated common mental disorder symptoms as significant correlates of lower HRQoL.

Response distributions did not differ significantly between digital and paper modes in any EQ-5D-5L dimension; effect sizes were negligible or very small. Pain or discomfort and anxiety or depression were the most commonly reported problems.
The analysis included 611 participants. Their mean age was 37.5 years; 70.7% were female, 68.7% reported financial inadequacy, and 51.2% reported food insecurity.

EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS scores were comparable between digital and paper administration. The mean differences and Cohen d values were within the prespecified 0.3-standard-deviation equivalence framework.
The observed differences between groups expected to differ in HRQoL supported known-groups validity of the EQ-5D-5L Shona.

outcome: Role and normative interpretation of the social tariff within the health policy decision-making framework
statement: In the decision framework set out, the social tariff determines incremental QALYs and therefore has a central influence on whether a health program is judged cost-effective, so the aggregation function itself affects societal decisions.

outcome: Role and normative interpretation of the social tariff within the health policy decision-making framework
statement: Research into the conceptual and normative basis of social tariffs has been scarce, and it is not yet established what types of aggregation function are admissible or what social value sets are supposed to represent.

outcome: Role and normative interpretation of the social tariff within the health policy decision-making framework
statement: Because the change in an individual's health is valued by the aggregate societal preference rather than by that individual's own preference, maximizing societal QALYs is not the same as maximizing health-related utilities, so the current tariff framework is incompatible with utility maximization and fits an extra-welfarist reading better.

outcome: Correspondence between mean, mode and median aggregation of health state values and the majority view
statement: The arithmetic mean weights preference intensity and is sensitive to extreme values, so it conflicts with one person, one vote: for EQ-5D-3L state 11131 the mean is 0.24 while 58% of respondents would prefer a higher value.

outcome: Correspondence between mean, mode and median aggregation of health state values and the majority view
statement: The mode of a distribution of cardinal preference values is largely an artefact of measurement accuracy and rounding: for state 11131 the most frequent value is 1 (n = 72) while 90% (n = 663) prefer a lower value, and in the MVH (1995) data every health state has a mode of 1, 0 or -1.

outcome: Correspondence between mean, mode and median aggregation of health state values and the majority view
statement: The median for state 11131 (0.43) is supported in the sense that neither a higher value (49.5%) nor a lower value (48.3%) has majority support, but the Median Voter Theorem only holds in one dimension, so medians combined across multiple health states need not represent the majority view globally.

outcome: Correspondence between mean, mode and median aggregation of health state values and the majority view
statement: A three-person example shows the median health state paradox: two of three individuals prefer state h1 to h2, yet the median values (0.65 vs 0.83) and geometric medians (0.68 vs 0.72) both indicate a group preference for h2.

outcome: Role and normative interpretation of the social tariff within the health policy decision-making framework
statement: Reformulating the decision rule as majority voting over programs, in which each individual evaluates incremental QALYs with their own preference function and the program is adopted when more than half vote for it, gives every individual equal weight and makes support for a decision transparent.

outcome: Requirements for democratic representativeness of health state valuation samples
statement: Democratic representativeness requires random selection of valuation participants and confinement of the tariff to members of the society for which decisions are made; the exclusion of 399 (12%) of MVH (1994) participants for missing values, the ignoring of missing values, and the automatic removal of seemingly irrational preferences all conflict with this, as does NICE's use of a UK-wide rather than an English tariff.

outcome: Requirements for democratic representativeness of health state valuation samples
statement: Using participants' stated preferences to inform policy without informed consent violates their autonomy and is undemocratic, yet informing participants about the purpose of the valuation may invoke strategic responding.

outcome: Mean square error of predicted health state utilities
statement: Shrinkage estimators produced smaller mean square error than naive country-specific estimators on average, with the largest reductions at small simulated sample sizes.

outcome: Mean absolute error of predicted health state utilities
statement: Mean absolute error was also reduced on average by shrinkage estimation, most clearly at small sample sizes.

outcome: Mean bias (mean error) of estimators
statement: The reduction in error achieved by shrinkage did not substantially increase bias; mean bias remained small for both estimators.

outcome: Mean square error of predicted health state utilities
statement: For a given sample size, the probability that predicted MAE or MSE fell below specified thresholds was generally higher with shrinkage estimators than with naive estimators.

outcome: Mean square error of predicted health state utilities
statement: For a few countries (for example Poland, Portugal and Taiwan) shrinkage produced slightly larger errors than the naive estimator, and the average magnitude of improvement was small because between-country variation in EQ-5D-3L value sets was large relative to within-country sampling variation.

outcome: Psychological distress measured with BDS-22
statement: The sample had a mean BDS-22 score of 15.3, which the authors described as minimal psychological distress.

outcome: Psychological distress measured with BDS-22
statement: In the adjusted BDS-22 model, food insecurity, older age, female gender, employment status, and crisis-related job loss were significant predictors of greater psychological distress.

outcome: Food insecurity prevalence and severity
statement: Food insecurity severity correlated with greater psychological distress and lower EQ VAS, and greater psychological distress correlated with lower EQ VAS.

outcome: Psychological distress measured with BDS-22
statement: Participants more often reported that the socioeconomic crisis affected mental health than physical health.

outcome: HRQoL measured with EQ-5D-5L dimensions and EQ VAS
statement: EQ-5D-5L results showed few self-care problems, while pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression were prominent problem dimensions.

outcome: HRQoL measured with EQ-5D-5L dimensions and EQ VAS
statement: The mean EQ VAS score was 74.18, which the authors interpreted as a moderate level of HRQoL.

outcome: HRQoL measured with EQ-5D-5L dimensions and EQ VAS
statement: In the adjusted EQ VAS model, food insecurity, older age, crisis-related job loss, and lower household income were significant predictors of lower HRQoL.

outcome: Food insecurity prevalence and severity
statement: Most participants were food secure, while 14.3% were classified with moderate or severe food insecurity.

outcome: Internal consistency of FIES and BDS-22
statement: FIES and BDS-22 had high internal consistency in the study sample.

outcome: HRQoL measured with EQ-5D-5L dimensions and EQ VAS
statement: Because Lebanon had no EQ-5D-5L value set, the HRQoL regression focused on EQ VAS and did not use an EQ-5D index score.
The final analytical sample had a mean age of 38.23 years; 57.7% were female and 96.7% were Lebanese.

outcome: FIES Rasch item fit and unidimensional performance
statement: FIES Rasch analysis showed satisfactory overall fit; all items had acceptable infit and no item had substantial misfit that warranted exclusion.

outcome: Sensitivity to change of index scores, assessed by area under the ROC curve for discriminating 'improved' from 'not improved' groups
statement: No instrument demonstrated superior sensitivity to change: six of the 10 highest AUC estimates were for the HUI3, three for the EQ-5D-5L and one for the EQ-5D-3L, while 'moderate' AUC classifications (0.70-0.90) were identified in 12 of 22 analyses for each EQ-5D instrument compared with eight for the HUI3, with no 'high' classifications.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L, EQ-5D-5L and HUI3 index scores and change scores at baseline, 12 weeks and 24 weeks
statement: Mean HUI3 index scores were statistically significantly lower than EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L scores at every time point, and the HUI3 had the widest interquartile range and the lowest individual values.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L, EQ-5D-5L and HUI3 index scores and change scores at baseline, 12 weeks and 24 weeks
statement: The magnitude of change scores was similar across instruments under the strict data quality criteria, with no statistically significant differences between EQ-5D-3L, EQ-5D-5L and HUI3 change scores.

outcome: Prevalence and pattern of data quality violations across near-identical EQ-5D and EQ VAS items
statement: Of 272 trial participants, 160 (58.8%) provided complete preference-based instrument data at baseline and at least one follow-up point, and 90 of these 160 (30% at baseline; at least 24% at each time point) had at least one data quality violation; ethnicity was the only baseline characteristic that differed significantly between participants with and without a violation.

outcome: Difference in mean index change scores between 'improved' and 'not improved' groups defined by eight external anchors
statement: Differences in mean change scores between 'improved' and 'not improved' groups were positive and statistically significant in 53 of 57 analyses across seven anchors, whereas the Brief Substance Craving Scale anchor gave non-significant differences in eight of nine analyses and accounted for seven of the 10 lowest AUC estimates, including directional inconsistencies for the EQ-5D instruments from baseline to 24 weeks.

outcome: Dimension-level response distributions and proportions reporting full health or negative index values
statement: Baseline proportions reporting the highest level of impairment differed markedly between instruments for pain (17.9% EQ-5D-3L, 3.6% EQ-5D-5L, 1.8% HUI3) and mental health (18.8% EQ-5D-3L, 9.8% EQ-5D-5L, 3.6% HUI3).

outcome: Sensitivity to change of index scores, assessed by area under the ROC curve for discriminating 'improved' from 'not improved' groups
statement: Sensitivity analyses using soft or no data quality criteria did not change the key conclusions, although the mean HUI3 change score from baseline to 24 weeks was then significantly higher than the EQ-5D change scores, and the number of 'moderate' AUC classifications fell for the EQ-5D instruments and rose for the HUI3.
None of the C-TTO-only models (Tobit, heteroscedastic Tobit, panel Tobit) produced logically consistent coefficients, whereas the rescaled DCE Logit model was consistent.

Predictions from the DCE Logit model agreed strongly with predictions from the C-TTO Tobit and heteroscedastic Tobit models, supporting a single hybrid estimation; the censored hybrid heteroscedastic model gave disordered parameters while the regular censored hybrid model was consistent, so the regular censored hybrid model was selected.
In the selected hybrid model, mobility carried the largest disutility, closely followed by pain/discomfort, then usual activities, anxiety/depression and self-care.
The Vietnamese value set ranges from 1 for full health (11111) to -0.5115 for the worst state (55555), with 8.3% of the 3125 predicted values negative.
The feedback module reduced the number of respondents with inconsistent C-TTO responses.
The self-reported health of the sample showed a large ceiling effect and most problems in pain/discomfort.
Usual activities was ranked third in Vietnam, higher than in many other countries, while anxiety/depression ranked only fourth, in contrast to Western value sets.
The value for the worst EQ-5D-5L state in Vietnam is lower than in neighbouring Asian value sets.

Pilot interviews showed that directly asking respondents about being dead was culturally sensitive and that elderly respondents lost concentration after long C-TTO sessions, so the study adopted a third-person C-TTO framing and a coloured card visual aid for the DCE tasks.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L health utility index and dimension-level HRQoL
statement: Across the pooled cohort, EQ-5D-3L utility declined with each year of disease duration, and it declined significantly in all four SCA subtypes; the decline was smallest in SCA6.

outcome: PHQ-9 depressive symptom severity
statement: PHQ-9 depressive symptom severity increased with disease duration in the pooled cohort, but subtype-specific increases were significant only in SCA2 and SCA3; SCA6 showed a small, nonsignificant improvement.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L health utility index and dimension-level HRQoL
statement: In multivariable models, greater ataxia severity and greater depressive symptom severity were each independently associated with lower EQ-5D-3L utility.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L health utility index and dimension-level HRQoL
statement: Mobility problems were already common at disease onset, but self-care showed the fastest worsening with disease duration; usual activities and mobility also worsened more than pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression.

outcome: PHQ-9 depressive symptom severity
statement: Problems with anxiety/depression, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and self-care predicted higher PHQ-9 scores, whereas mobility problems did not.
Women had higher average PHQ-9 scores over time, and later disease onset was associated with lower average PHQ-9 scores in SCA3.

outcome: EQ VAS self-rated health
statement: At baseline, mean EQ-5D-3L utility was 0.64, mean EQ VAS was 62.38, and 77% of participants had a PHQ-9 score below 9.
Greater speech disturbance was associated with a higher probability of clinically relevant depression in an exploratory mixed-effects analysis.

outcome: Ceiling effects and distributional properties of the three-level EQ-5D-Y items
statement: The EQ-5D-Y showed severe ceiling effects, most pronounced for self-care, so the self-care item was excluded and the remaining items were dichotomised for analysis.

outcome: Self-reported problems on EQ-5D-Y dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression)
