statement: More health complaints were associated with a higher likelihood of problems on every analysed EQ-5D-Y dimension and with a worse EQ VAS score.

outcome: Self-reported problems on EQ-5D-Y dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression)
statement: More parent-reported mental health problems were associated with more problems in pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression and with a worse EQ VAS score.

outcome: Self-reported problems on EQ-5D-Y dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression)
statement: Good disease control was associated with fewer mobility problems and a better EQ VAS health state.

outcome: Self-reported problems on EQ-5D-Y dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression)
statement: Participants with diabetes were less likely than those with juvenile arthritis to report problems in mobility, usual activities and pain/discomfort, and longer disease duration was associated with fewer mobility and usual-activities problems.

outcome: Self-reported problems on EQ-5D-Y dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression)
statement: Age and gender effects were found: problems in mobility and pain/discomfort decreased over time for boys but increased for girls, older girls were more likely than older boys to report pain, and older age was associated with a lower EQ VAS score.

outcome: Self-reported problems on EQ-5D-Y dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression)
statement: Lower socio-economic status was associated with a higher probability of pain/discomfort, while migration background, study centre and comorbidity showed no significant effects.

outcome: Self-reported problems on EQ-5D-Y dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression)
statement: Substantial between-individual variance was found in the null models, with about half of the EQ VAS variance explained by differences between individuals; the EQ VAS showed no systematic change over six months.

outcome: Personal utility function weights for EQ-5D dimensions and levels, anchored at dead = 0
statement: Pain/discomfort and mobility were the most important EQ-5D dimensions in both the ranking and rating tasks, while usual activities was ranked lowest.

outcome: Internal consistency of rankings and ratings, and performance of the tailored task algorithm
statement: Rankings from the dimension ranking task correlated highly with the rankings implied by the dimension rating task.

outcome: Personal utility function weights for EQ-5D dimensions and levels, anchored at dead = 0
statement: Weights given to intermediate (level 3 to level 2) improvements were heterogeneous within and between respondents; most respondents used a mix of ratings above, below and equal to 50.

outcome: Personal utility function weights for EQ-5D dimensions and levels, anchored at dead = 0
statement: Almost a quarter of respondents indicated that no EQ-5D health state, including 33333, is worse than dead.

outcome: Internal consistency of rankings and ratings, and performance of the tailored task algorithm
statement: The tailored paired comparison tasks behaved as designed: respondents favoured the higher-utility state in the task designed to be easy, and split evenly in the task designed to be difficult.

outcome: Personal utility function weights for EQ-5D dimensions and levels, anchored at dead = 0
statement: Most respondents preferred a one-level improvement when no problems existed on other dimensions, indicating the presence of interaction effects.

outcome: Personal utility function weights for EQ-5D dimensions and levels, anchored at dead = 0
statement: The social utility function aggregated from individual PUFs had a minimum value of -0.667 and showed smaller variation across dimension decrements than existing UK value sets, with pain/discomfort most important.

outcome: Feasibility and acceptability of the PUF interview approach
statement: Respondents and interviewers generally found the approach acceptable, although views on which tasks were most difficult were split and the interviews averaged 46 minutes.

outcome: Internal consistency of rankings and ratings, and performance of the tailored task algorithm
statement: Protocol deviations occurred: one interviewer never triggered the tailoring macro in all 17 of their interviews, so those tasks used default settings, and nine respondents failed to rate any dimension at 100.

Global implementation of clinical genomic sequencing remains limited by nonstandard practices, insufficient indication-specific economic assessment, limited meaningful patient engagement, implementation costs and resource demands, and disparities between populations and health systems.

outcome: System-readiness barriers and proposed solutions for clinical genomic sequencing
statement: System readiness requires trusted and transparent testing, equity-informed evaluation, coordinated sequencing and informatics capacity, workforce and operational changes, and financial incentives that support appropriate uptake.

outcome: Evidence, assessment, and approval barriers and proposed solutions for clinical genomic sequencing
statement: Implementation and approval decisions need a stronger multi-stakeholder evidence base that combines economic modeling, prospective trials, real-world data, and iterative assessment across the technology life cycle.

The current evidence base emphasizes diagnostic yield and gives insufficient attention to QALYs, psychosocial outcomes, and broader patient and family benefits; the paper states that preference-based HRQoL instruments such as EQ-5L might not fully capture these benefits.
Confirmatory factor analyses gave moderately well-fitting one-factor solutions with high factor loadings for all five EQ-5D-5L items.
The best fitting internal MIMIC model defined mobility, anxiety/depression and pain/discomfort as causal indicators and self-care and usual activities as reflective indicators.

In linear regression, all EQ-5D-5L items except self-care were important predictors of other health-related quality of life measures, with the best explanatory power for the SF-36/SF-12 physical component score and the poorest for the EQ VAS.

Standardized coefficients of the external MIMIC generally reflected the regression results; results did not differ across gender, education and disease subgroups, but model fit was poor in healthy populations.

outcome: Self-rated health measured by EQ VAS score
statement: Unadjusted mean EQ VAS scores and the distribution of high VAS scores were similar in 2002 and 2017.

outcome: Reported problems on EQ-5D-3L dimensions (any/no problems)
statement: After adjusting for reported problems on each EQ-5D dimension, mean VAS scores in 2017 were significantly higher than in 2002; adjustment for sociodemographic characteristics and presence of disease had negligible effects.

outcome: Agreement between EQ-HWB-S and EQ-5D-5L utility scores
statement: Utility-score concordance was classified as excellent, with greatest visual agreement near the upper part of the scales, although outliers showed lack of agreement.

outcome: Convergent construct validity between EQ-HWB-S and EQ-5D-5L dimensions and utility scores
statement: Participants who reported full health on EQ-5D-5L could report problems in EQ-HWB-S domains, supporting added coverage of exhaustion, loneliness, cognition, and control.

outcome: Ceiling, floor, and score-distribution performance
statement: EQ-HWB-S had a lower whole-instrument ceiling than EQ-5D-5L, but the EQ-HWB-S mobility item had a potentially problematic ceiling; all item-level floor proportions were below 5%.

outcome: Convergent construct validity between EQ-HWB-S and EQ-5D-5L dimensions and utility scores
statement: All conceptually overlapping dimensions had strong correlations, and EQ-HWB-S and EQ-5D-5L utility scores were strongly correlated; nonoverlapping EQ-HWB-S wellbeing dimensions generally had weaker associations with EQ-5D-5L dimensions.

outcome: Known-groups validity of EQ-HWB-S and EQ-5D-5L utility scores
statement: Known-group effects were small for carer status and age, but large for employment compared with unemployment or long-term sickness; effect sizes were similar across instruments.

outcome: Known-groups validity of EQ-HWB-S and EQ-5D-5L utility scores
statement: EQ-HWB-S successfully discriminated all prespecified health and wellbeing known groups, with large effects for EQ VAS healthy status, long-term condition, life satisfaction, and health satisfaction; EQ-5D-5L gave similar conclusions.

outcome: EQ-HWB-S and EQ-5D-5L utility values
statement: Mean utility values were similar in the combined sample, with a mean EQ-HWB-S score of 0.83 and mean EQ-5D-5L index score of 0.81.

outcome: Country baseline measures of EQ-5D-5L health inequality
statement: The five countries had different patterns of EQ-5D-5L health inequality; men generally had higher health status than women, and EQ-5D measures generally declined with age.

outcome: Kakwani index of inequality in health problems
statement: The Kakwani inequality indices were 0.1051 in Barbados, 0.0805 in Belize, 0.1047 in Colombia, 0.0795 in Jamaica, and 0.096 in Trinidad and Tobago.

outcome: EQ VAS score
statement: Age and female gender were negatively associated with EQ VAS scores, and age was positively associated with disutility in all five countries; no other PROGRESS-Plus variable had a significant coefficient across all five countries.
Higher education was generally associated with better EQ-5D health status, and the highest income group had the highest health level where income had a significant association.
Problem reporting showed an unambiguous inverse relationship with income in Barbados, Colombia, and Trinidad and Tobago, but not in Belize or Jamaica.

outcome: Kakwani index of inequality in health problems
statement: Pain/discomfort contributed the largest share of the quality-of-life decomposition in Barbados, Colombia, Jamaica, and Trinidad and Tobago, while self-care contributed the largest share in Belize.

outcome: Frequency and severity of problems on each EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: Age had higher odds of reported problems on all EQ-5D-5L dimensions except for restricted patterns in Jamaica and anxiety/depression in Barbados; gender, education, income, and region effects differed by country and dimension.

outcome: Kakwani index of inequality in health problems
statement: The baseline results placed Jamaica, Belize, and Trinidad and Tobago in the first quartile and Colombia and Barbados in the second quartile when compared with published Kakwani indices for 17 other countries, but the comparison mixed EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L data and included only 22 countries.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index value and disutility
statement: Only Trinidad and Tobago had an available national EQ-5D value set; the analysis used Trinidad and Tobago crosswalk values for four countries and the Uruguayan EQ-5D-5L value set for Colombia.
In the 85-entry comparison subset, GPT-4o identified 12 candidate bolt-on dimensions; nine were also identified by qualitative analysis and five were also identified by topic modeling.
The most frequent GPT-4o dimensions in the 85-entry subset were dietary restrictions, social participation, energy or fatigue, gastrointestinal symptoms, and emotional well-being.
Agreement between GPT-4o and qualitative coding was generally moderate to almost perfect, but the LLM underdetected social support and overdetected dietary restrictions.
Sensitivity analyses with four other LLMs gave similar agreement results; newer models showed a small improvement, and GPT-5-Mini had the highest agreement overall.
The full 1977-entry analysis largely reproduced the subset dimensions, except that self-efficacy was absent and social stigma was newly identified.
Most LLM-identified dimensions had face validity through consistency with existing bolt-ons or generic and disease-specific PROM content; nutritional status was the stated exception.
The four generated item wordings received generally favorable expert appraisal scores, but translatability and grounding in other qualitative work scored lower.

The LLM sometimes proposed concepts that researchers did not consider operationalizable as self-reportable bolt-ons, including bone health and immune function, and it missed some qualitatively identified dimensions such as physical appearance.

outcome: Test-retest reliability of the paper EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS scores (ICC and mean difference)
statement: Paper test-retest administrations of the EQ-5D-5L gave mean differences near zero and ICC values above 0.90 for both the index and the EQ VAS.

outcome: Test-retest agreement on the five EQ-5D-5L dimension responses (kappa and quadratically weighted kappa)
statement: Test-retest agreement on the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions was substantial to almost perfect, except the weighted kappa for self-care, which was moderate because one participant moved from level 1 to level 5 between administrations.

outcome: Test-retest reliability of the paper EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS scores (ICC and mean difference)
statement: Half of the paper test-retest standard deviations (0.080 for the index and 8.0 for the EQ VAS) set the equivalence intervals of -0.040 to 0.040 for the index and -4.0 to 4.0 for the EQ VAS, and the paper ICC lower confidence bounds set the ICC equivalence thresholds of 0.911 for the index and 0.940 for the EQ VAS.

outcome: Equivalence of EQ-5D index scores across data collection modes (mean difference confidence interval within -0.040 to 0.040 and ICC lower 95% confidence bound >= 0.911)
statement: In the paper-handheld-web crossover, all index and EQ VAS mean-difference confidence intervals fell inside the equivalence intervals and all ICC point estimates exceeded 0.950, with ICC lower bounds above the equivalence thresholds.

outcome: Equivalence of EQ-5D index scores across data collection modes (mean difference confidence interval within -0.040 to 0.040 and ICC lower 95% confidence bound >= 0.911)
statement: In the paper-handheld-tablet crossover, all index and EQ VAS mean differences fell inside the equivalence intervals and all ICC point estimates were at least 0.980, with ICC lower bounds above the equivalence thresholds.

outcome: Equivalence of EQ-5D index scores across data collection modes (mean difference confidence interval within -0.040 to 0.040 and ICC lower 95% confidence bound >= 0.911)
statement: In the paper-web-interactive voice response crossover, all index and EQ VAS mean differences fell inside the equivalence intervals and all ICC point estimates were at least 0.982, with ICC lower bounds above the equivalence thresholds.

outcome: Equivalence of EQ-5D index scores across data collection modes (mean difference confidence interval within -0.040 to 0.040 and ICC lower 95% confidence bound >= 0.911)
statement: In the handheld-tablet-web crossover among electronic modes only, index mean differences were 0.000 for all pairs, EQ VAS mean differences stayed inside the equivalence interval, and all ICC point estimates were at least 0.960.

outcome: Mode-by-order interaction in the split-plot ANOVA models
statement: No significant mode-by-order interaction was present in any ANOVA model.
Missing data were rare: one participant in the paper-handheld-tablet sample and one in the handheld-tablet-web sample had missing tablet responses, and no imputation was performed.

Participants described caregiver-burden antecedents in the caregiving situation, financial resources, and sociocultural environment, including health severity and disability, available support, cultural expectations, relationship quality, and competing caregiver roles.

Caregiver burden included physical, emotional, financial, and social attributes; financial burden covered direct and indirect costs and financial distress, and social burden included changed relationships and family conflict.

Reported consequences were financial hardship that could change or delay treatment and care-seeking decisions, and reduced caregiver health-related quality of life through physical, emotional, and social strain.
Participants described caregiver burden and the care recipient's self-perceived burden as interdependent and as changing with progression of the health condition.
All participants considered self-perceived burden highly relevant and important to understanding their experience, family impact, well-being, and health-care decision-making.
The preferred final wording was “I feel like a burden (physical, emotional, social, and financial) to my family/friends,” with a severity response scale from “Not at all” to “Very much.”

Most participants distinguished burden from bother and stress: bother suggested annoyance or inconvenience, stress was mainly emotional, and burden covered broader financial, social, physical, emotional, time, energy, and sacrifice effects.
Participants thought that burden broadly covered the construct, but their feedback supported adding examples in parentheses to prompt consideration of the main burden attributes.

outcome: Elicited TTO and discrete choice values for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Mean lead-time TTO values in the core multinational pilot ranged from 0.73 to -0.23 and showed substantial clustering at 0 and 1, and to a lesser extent at -1, 0.5, 0.6 and 0.8.

outcome: Feasibility of the composite TTO in a face-to-face interview setting
statement: The composite TTO administered face-to-face markedly improved data quality: clustering at 0 disappeared for the mild state 12112 and almost disappeared for the moderate state 33133, clustering at 1 was strongly reduced for the severe state 53555, and a new cluster at -1 appeared for that severe state as expected.

Discrete choice models performed adequately in all four core countries: all 20 dummy parameters were statistically significant except level 2 of Usual Activities in The Netherlands, only three modest logical inconsistencies in coefficient ordering were seen, and predicted values for the 3125 states correlated highly between countries.

outcome: Response clustering (heaping) at focal values and shortcutting of the TTO iteration sequence
statement: In Argentina, lead-time and lag-time TTO produced only slight differences in mean values and very similar response distributions, giving no evidence of superiority of either variant; in China a 5-5 lead-time ratio changed mean values but not clustering; in Singapore stronger visual separation of the lead-time and disease-time bars increased clustering.

outcome: Response clustering (heaping) at focal values and shortcutting of the TTO iteration sequence
statement: Clustering was markedly lower with face-to-face interviews at home (England) than with group interviews (Canada, The Netherlands, United States).

outcome: Response clustering (heaping) at focal values and shortcutting of the TTO iteration sequence
statement: Online TTO data collection without an interviewer worsened response clustering and shortcutting; lag-time TTO gave slightly lower values than lead-time TTO, longer time frames gave slightly higher values, and an adapted iteration procedure did not resolve clustering but shifted it to different values.

The programme produced the standardized EQ-5D-5L valuation protocol: a face-to-face computer-assisted personal interview in the EQ-VT comprising EQ-5D-5L self-report and EQ VAS, background questions, composite TTO valuation of 10 states with debriefing, and 7 forced-choice discrete choice pairs with debriefing.

outcome: Response clustering (heaping) at focal values and shortcutting of the TTO iteration sequence
statement: Many respondents reached their final TTO answer after only one or two steps in the iteration sequence, indicating shortcutting of the task, and most possible iteration paths were rarely used.
At baseline, depressive and anxiety symptoms were common among adults receiving in-centre hemodialysis, and many patients screened positive for both.
Documented follow-up was much less common than positive symptom screens, and PROM-triggered management was usually limited to patient handouts rather than formal screening, referral, or prescribing.

Routine ESAS-r: Renal or EQ-5D-5L use could identify mental-health concerns that might otherwise be missed and could make it easier for nurses to discuss them, although some patients and nurses thought the PROMs added little to usual conversations.
Participants agreed that mental-health resources in dialysis care were inadequate, with barriers in access to providers, nurse knowledge and training, and privacy.

Patients and nurses differed on whether mental-health management belonged within dialysis care; some supported its inclusion, but more evidence indicated that it was viewed as limited or outside the dialysis role.

outcome: Test-retest reliability of C-TTO values (mean differences, ICC, better/worse-than-dead crossover)
statement: For C-TTO, most health states showed no significant change in mean value between test and retest.

outcome: Test-retest reliability of C-TTO values (mean differences, ICC, better/worse-than-dead crossover)
statement: Multilevel regression showed a small but statistically significant upward shift of C-TTO values at retest.

outcome: Test-retest reliability of C-TTO values (mean differences, ICC, better/worse-than-dead crossover)
statement: Agreement per health state measured by ICC was mixed, and most responses did not cross the dead anchor between tests.

outcome: Test-retest consistency of DCE choices and stability of dimension weights
statement: For DCE, most individual choices were repeated at retest.

outcome: Relative importance of EQ-5D-5L dimensions and relative utility decrements across levels at test and retest
statement: The relative importance of the EQ-5D-5L dimensions shifted between test and retest in the DCE model but not in the C-TTO or hybrid models.

outcome: Test-retest reliability of C-TTO values (mean differences, ICC, better/worse-than-dead crossover)
statement: Highly inconsistent C-TTO responses were uncommon and clustered among a few interviewers; change in respondents' own health was not associated with change in C-TTO values.
Respondents used fewer iteration steps in the second C-TTO interview, consistent with a process learning effect.
The corresponding EQ-5D-3L health state values ranged from -0.594 to 1, so the profile standard errors were small relative to the value range.

Uncertainty is generated and inherited across valuation studies, profile-data studies, mapping, disease-state studies, meta-analysis, and cost-effectiveness models, so multiple sources combine in final QALY estimates.

The authors recommend that valuation studies report profile-level health state value standard errors or the variance–covariance matrix needed to derive them, and that researchers and decision makers account for uncertainty more fully.

Current value-set reporting and guidance often provide point estimates and coefficient uncertainty but not profile-level health state value uncertainty, which prevents full sensitivity analysis in cost-effectiveness models.
For every possible EQ-5D-3L profile, the worked example produced health state value standard errors from the regression variance–covariance matrix that ranged from 0.008171 to 0.012203.
The authors classified uncertainty about health state values into variability, heterogeneity, statistical uncertainty, and methodological variation.

Within valuation studies, uncertainty arises from study-design choices, preference elicitation, and modelling, including population and sample selection, state selection, valuation method, administration and interviewer effects, response quality, summary measure, model specification, and parameter uncertainty.

The Shams model with spatially correlated state-level misspecification was selected because it achieved adequate out-of-sample interval coverage and slightly narrower intervals than the independent misspecification model.
The original model substantially undercovered out-of-sample state means, while both misspecification models increased credible-interval coverage.
The selected Shams model was used to create 100 Canadian multiply imputed EQ-5D-5L value sets, each covering all 3,125 health states.
For the Canadian general-public data, multiply imputed scoring changed the mean utility little but increased its standard error by 2.60-fold compared with the original value set.
For women with invasive breast cancer, multiply imputed scoring changed the mean utility little but increased its standard error by 2.56-fold compared with the original value set.
Only 2 of 756,250 dominance pairs had logically inconsistent posterior means, and both inconsistencies occurred in the third decimal place.
Both generic preference-based measures had high completion rates.
Neither EQ-5D-5L nor AQoL-8D met the prespecified 15% threshold for a ceiling or floor effect.
EQ-5D-5L showed good two-week test-retest reliability in carers who reported no change in HRQoL; dimension agreement was moderate to substantial.
Both generic measures showed convergent validity with carer-specific measures, with consistently stronger correlations for AQoL-8D than for EQ-5D-5L.
Both measures discriminated all prespecified groups based on caring intensity and situation, with utility lower in the groups expected to have greater caring burden.
The nine-factor exploratory factor analysis showed limited overlap between EQ-5D-5L and carer-specific content, while AQoL-8D overlapped with more carer-specific items.
EQ-5D-5L utilities were higher on average than AQoL-8D utilities in the same survey sample.

outcome: Utility decrements for EQ-5D-Y dimension severity levels on a QALY scale by age frame and country
statement: In the Netherlands, health state values agreed closely across the 10-, 15- and 40-year age frames, except for the dimensions pain or discomfort and feeling worried, sad or unhappy, where respondents traded off more time to avoid problems in children than in adults.

outcome: Value of the worst EQ-5D-Y health state (33333) by age frame and country
statement: The value of the worst EQ-5D-Y state (33333) in the Netherlands was lowest in the 10-year arm and identical for the 15- and 40-year arms.

outcome: Value of the worst EQ-5D-Y health state (33333) by age frame and country
statement: In China, the value of the worst EQ-5D-Y state (33333) for the 70-year age frame was far lower than for the other age frames, which were close together.

outcome: Utility decrements for EQ-5D-Y dimension severity levels on a QALY scale by age frame and country
statement: The coefficient for life years was positive in both countries, showing that additional life years generate utility; in the Netherlands the interaction terms had the expected negative sign except mobility level 2, while in China level 2 terms for self-care, usual activities and pain or discomfort had unexpected positive signs.

outcome: Estimated discount rate for future health by age frame and country
statement: Estimated discount rates indicated strong discounting of future health in both countries and were higher than rates normally applied in economic evaluation.

outcome: Distribution of Likert responses over the QALY composition scenarios by age frame
statement: The distribution of Likert responses in the QALY composition task showed no clear pattern of differences across age arms in either country; response distributions varied most when life years or quality of life were at the extremes.

outcome: Distribution of Likert responses over the QALY composition scenarios by age frame
statement: In the Netherlands the no-preference response category was used most often in the 10-year child arm, whereas the Chinese data showed more no-preference responses overall and similar or less clustering in the child arm.

outcome: Self-reported difficulty of the A versus B and B versus C choice tasks
statement: Dutch respondents found the choice tasks more difficult in the child arm than in the adult arm, while perceived difficulty was similar across the four arms in China.

outcome: Reported difference between choices made for the hypothetical person and choices the respondent would make for themselves
statement: The proportion of respondents stating that their choices would have been the same if the health problems concerned themselves differed by arm in the Netherlands and was low in all Chinese arms.

All participant groups were open to generic P-PROM use and saw potential for better communication, shared decision making, detection of concerns, longitudinal monitoring, patient engagement, and more holistic care; some service providers were unsure how to act on broad generic results or viewed condition-specific and clinical information as more actionable.
Participants strongly stated that P-PROM data must be discussed and acted on in the individual clinical encounter rather than collected as a token exercise.

Implementation enablers included introduction by a trusted clinical team, clear explanation of purpose, completion before appointments, short and easy completion, integration with existing electronic systems, clinician education and action resources, and provision of results to families.

Participants were largely supportive of EQ-5D-Y-5L because it was brief, clear, and provided a broad health snapshot, but some raised concerns about its health-today recall period, negative framing, ambiguity between response levels, possible effects on child self-esteem, and missing context or domains.

Most participants preferred clinicians and families to see responses for each EQ-5D-Y-5L item and changes over time rather than one combined score. Views on benchmarking were mixed because it could help interpret concern but could also harm self-esteem.

Suggested additions or adaptations included optional contextual comments and coverage of treatment burden, social relationships, eating, sleep, toileting, or schooling; participants also noted that added items could increase burden and that EQ VAS can capture uncategorised concerns.

Mapping the themes to the Theoretical Framework of Acceptability identified both enablers and barriers across affective attitude, burden, ethicality, intervention coherence, opportunity costs, perceived effectiveness, and self-efficacy.

outcome: Individual-level logical inconsistency category (none, slight, severe) based on inconsistency rate, distance and delta-TTO
statement: Fourty-four percent of respondents gave at least one logically inconsistent valuation; 499 respondents were classified as slightly inconsistent and 74 as severely inconsistent.

outcome: Individual-level logical inconsistency category (none, slight, severe) based on inconsistency rate, distance and delta-TTO
statement: In the multilevel model, slight inconsistency was associated with interview process indicators: more time spent on the TTO tasks increased the risk, while more time on the wheelchair example and a later interview sequence reduced it.

outcome: Individual-level logical inconsistency category (none, slight, severe) based on inconsistency rate, distance and delta-TTO
statement: Severe inconsistency was associated with male gender and with earlier interview sequence.

outcome: Individual-level logical inconsistency category (none, slight, severe) based on inconsistency rate, distance and delta-TTO
statement: Two interviewers stood out in the single-level model; interviewer 7 had a strongly raised risk of both slight and severe inconsistency relative to a median-performing interviewer.

outcome: Individual-level logical inconsistency category (none, slight, severe) based on inconsistency rate, distance and delta-TTO
statement: The likelihood ratio test confirmed that both the interviewer and respondent levels were needed in the model, and age and education were not associated with inconsistency in this study, unlike earlier EQ-5D-3L valuation studies.

outcome: Individual-level logical inconsistency category (none, slight, severe) based on inconsistency rate, distance and delta-TTO
statement: Respondents classified as severely inconsistent showed a much higher inconsistency rate, larger inconsistency distance and larger delta-TTO than slightly inconsistent respondents.

At baseline, more than two-thirds of children reported no problems in each EQ-5D-Y dimension, and about half reported no problems in all five dimensions. Pain or discomfort was the most frequently affected dimension.
Self-complete EQ-5D-Y summary scores showed satisfactory test-retest reliability, while proxy-report reliability was lower.

Well- or partially-controlled asthma patients had fewer reported problems, higher EQ-5D-Y-3L index and EQ VAS scores, and lower level sum scores than uncontrolled patients. All summary-score comparisons except self-reported EQ VAS were statistically significant and effect sizes were generally moderate.

For children whose overall health improved by OHA, all EQ-5D-Y summary scores improved significantly. Changes defined by improved GINA asthma control were smaller and significant only for selected self- and proxy-reported scores.

Child-parent agreement was strong for the EQ-5D-Y-3L index and EQ VAS, moderate for the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L level sum scores, and generally lower for pain or discomfort and worried, sad, or unhappy than for mobility or looking after myself.

The self-complete EQ-5D-Y-5L had slightly better level-sum-score test-retest reliability, but the EQ-5D-Y-3L showed slightly better discrimination and responsiveness. The five-level version could not be assessed with a preference-weighted index because no Chinese value set was available.
The proxy versions generally supported known-groups validity and responsiveness, but their test-retest intraclass correlations were sometimes below the recommended 0.70 threshold.

outcome: Selection of logically dominated health state options in fixed pairs
statement: Fewer respondents in the context arm chose the dominated option in the fixed pair contrasting 'severe' and 'extreme' problems (33344 vs 33355).

outcome: Selection of logically dominated health state options in fixed pairs
statement: For the fixed pair contrasting 'slight' and 'moderate' problems (22211 vs 33311), dominated-option selection did not differ between arms.

outcome: Conditional logit coefficients and level decrements by arm
statement: Conditional logit coefficients were ordered as expected in both arms except mobility levels 2 and 3 in the control arm, where the difference was not statistically significant; all context arm coefficients were statistically significant whereas PD2 was not significant in the control arm.

outcome: Conditional logit coefficients and level decrements by arm
statement: Decrements between adjacent levels were generally larger in the context arm, especially between levels 4 and 5, most markedly for anxiety/depression.

outcome: Conditional logit coefficients and level decrements by arm
statement: The heteroscedastic conditional logit comparison rejected preference homogeneity between arms, indicating scale differed significantly between the two models.

outcome: Respondent feedback on task difficulty and comparison strategy
statement: Fewer context arm respondents reported difficulty telling the difference between health state descriptions; other feedback items and reported comparison strategies did not differ by arm.

outcome: Respondent feedback on task difficulty and comparison strategy
statement: When asked directly which label sounded worse, most respondents said 'extreme', with no difference between arms.

outcome: Conditional logit coefficients and level decrements by arm
statement: In subgroup analyses by device, laptop users in the control arm produced three pairs of illogically ordered coefficients while desktop users produced none; the context display reduced disordered coefficients for laptop users but increased non-significant coefficients for desktop users.

outcome: Feasibility of the context display in a web-based DCE
statement: The context display was feasible on desktop and laptop screens but problematic on smartphones and tablets, so access was restricted to computer users.
The final cohort contained 403 completed interviews, with near-balanced randomized arms.
Interviewer effects were significant overall and for moderate and severe states, but there was no overall interviewer-by-mode interaction.
Across all 10 health states, mean cTTO values were equivalent between online and face-to-face modes and differed by only 0.004.
At the individual-state level, equivalence at the 5% level was shown for two mild states; no state had a significant between-mode difference in mean, median, or standard deviation.
Interview mode did not significantly affect cTTO values after adjustment for health state, sociodemographic characteristics, and interviewer effects.

People randomized to face-to-face interviews were much more likely to decline before booking and had a lower overall attendance proportion than people randomized online; mode did not predict attendance after acceptance.
Participants more often preferred online than face-to-face interviews, while about half had no preference; convenience was the main reason for preferring online.
Overall cTTO data quality was good, with no significant between-mode differences in clustering, problematic response patterns, number of trades, or interviewer-rated understanding and engagement.
Self-reported understanding and engagement were high and did not differ significantly between modes.

The completed arms had no significant demographic differences. The overall sample was representative for age and approximately for household income, but included more women and university-educated people than the Australian population.
A larger proportion of post-MBS participants than non-MBS participants reported no problems in all five EQ-5D-5L dimensions.

All post-MBS participants reported improved physical functioning, including less breathlessness, relief of pain, better sleep and energy, better mobility and agility, and improved ability to perform usual activities.

Most post-MBS participants reported improved social participation, family or friendship roles, self-esteem, self-confidence, and happiness, although reduced food intake could diminish participation in food-centred gatherings.

Post-MBS participants reported easier clothing choice and improved appearance, but some reported excess skin or hair loss. Smaller portions, vomiting when overeating, reduced appetite or food enjoyment, and worry about wasting food were balanced by healthier eating habits.
Obesity was associated with breathlessness, pain, sleep problems, tiredness, and low energy that limited mobility, housework, work, driving safety, usual activities, and physical intimacy.

Participants described appearance and clothing problems, difficulty with romantic relationships or intimacy, discrimination, humiliation, social exclusion or avoidance, low self-esteem, fear, sadness, and depression; fear of burdening others was a notable social concern.
Appearance dissatisfaction and weight-related low self-esteem were reported mainly by women; only one man briefly reported poor appearance, and no men reported obesity-related depression.
During the lockdown, patients selected for both THA and TKA were younger, had a lower BMI, and more often had surgery in private clinics than patients in the 2018–2019 control periods.
Preoperative EQ-5D-3L index and Oxford Hip Score were slightly worse during the lockdown, while the analogous preoperative outcomes in TKA patients did not differ.
At 3 and 12 months after THA, adjusted EQ-5D-3L index and Oxford Hip Score were slightly better during the lockdown than during the control periods.
After TKA, EQ-5D-3L index and Oxford Knee Score did not differ at 6 months and were slightly better at 12 months during the lockdown.
All observed PROM differences and their confidence-interval bounds remained below the prespecified minimal clinically important differences.

PROM responders were generally slightly younger, more often male, more often treated for osteoarthritis, and had better ASA and Charnley classifications than nonresponders; similar patterns occurred during the lockdown.

At 12 months after THA, living in a region with at least 50 COVID-19 infections per 100,000 inhabitants reduced the small lockdown-associated improvement in EQ-5D-3L index and Oxford Hip Score, but the effect was minimal.

outcome: Median response time by task sequence
statement: Median response times fell sharply over the first tasks and then flattened, for both TTO and paired comparison tasks, indicating learning within about the first three tasks.

outcome: Relative risk of a changed response by task sequence
statement: The relative risk of a changed response decreased over the initial tasks, consistent with learning or heuristic formation.

outcome: Relative risk of a modal response by task sequence
statement: The relative risk of a modal response was essentially flat across the sequence, showing no loss of response precision with later tasks.

outcome: Frequency of rounded TTO responses (5-year, 1-year, half-year units) by sequence
statement: TTO responses showed rounding that changed with sequence: 5-year unit responses increased in the Dutch data while half-year unit responses fell well below the expected 50% in both EQ-5D-5L studies.

Sensitivity analyses by task difficulty showed longer response times for more difficult comparisons, but sequence effects on response times, changed responses, modal responses and rounding did not differ by difficulty.

outcome: Distribution of self-reported EQ-5D levels by dimension and country, including pain/discomfort and the full health ceiling
statement: On the EQ-5D-3L, more respondents in Japan than in the UK reported no problems with pain/discomfort.

outcome: Distribution of self-reported EQ-5D levels by dimension and country, including pain/discomfort and the full health ceiling
statement: Sample characteristics differed between countries: the English EQ-5D-5L sample was older and reported more experience of serious illness than the Japanese and Spanish samples, while ages were similar in the Japanese and UK EQ-5D-3L samples.

outcome: Distribution of self-reported EQ-5D levels by dimension and country, including pain/discomfort and the full health ceiling
statement: On the EQ-5D-5L, reporting of no problems with pain/discomfort was highest in Spain, followed by Japan and then England; adjusting for age and gender raised the English proportion to about 64%.

outcome: Distribution of self-reported EQ-5D levels by dimension and country, including pain/discomfort and the full health ceiling
statement: The proportion of respondents reporting full health was highest in Japan for both EQ-5D versions, and the reduction in the ceiling effect moving from 3L to 5L was similar in Japan and the UK/England.

outcome: Number of distinct EQ-5D profiles used by respondents in each country
statement: Japanese respondents described their health with far fewer distinct EQ-5D profiles than respondents in England or Spain.

outcome: Self-reported EQ VAS score explained by the five EQ-5D dimensions
statement: In OLS models of self-reported EQ VAS, pain/discomfort was the most important dimension only for the Japanese EQ-5D-3L data; usual activities dominated for the UK 3L and Japanese 5L data, and anxiety/depression dominated for the English and Spanish 5L data.

outcome: Observed mean TTO values for hypothetical EQ-5D health states by country
statement: EQ-5D-3L TTO values in Japan were lower than UK values for the five mildest states but higher for the more severe states, and no Japanese mean value was below zero whereas six UK states were valued worse than dead.

outcome: Observed mean TTO values for hypothetical EQ-5D health states by country
statement: For the EQ-5D-5L, Japanese mean TTO values exceeded English values for most health states without a clear severity pattern, and only state 55555 was valued below zero in either country.

outcome: Observed mean TTO values for hypothetical EQ-5D health states by country
statement: For pairs of health states differing only in pain/discomfort, Japanese respondents traded less time than UK or English respondents, and the between-country gap was much smaller with the EQ-5D-5L than with the EQ-5D-3L.

outcome: Observed mean TTO values for hypothetical EQ-5D health states by country
statement: Linking self-reported and valuation data showed that a respondent's own pain/discomfort level generally did not explain the TTO values they gave, except in the English EQ-5D-5L data.

outcome: Agreement between EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L index scores
statement: Agreement between EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L index scores was high and was higher for caregiver ratings than for care-manager ratings.

outcome: Floor and ceiling effects
statement: EQ-5D-5L reduced ceiling effects in every dimension and for the overall index in both proxy-rater contexts.

outcome: Convergent validity
statement: EQ-5D-5L generally had better convergent validity with the comparison measures, and caregiver ratings generally showed larger correlations than care-manager ratings.

outcome: Response redistribution and inconsistency
statement: Response inconsistency between EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L was low in both proxy-rater contexts.

outcome: Absolute and relative informativity
statement: EQ-5D-5L increased absolute and relative informativity for both proxy-rater contexts.

outcome: Known-groups validity and discriminative ability
statement: Both EQ-5D versions discriminated between several known groups, but superiority was context-dependent: caregiver 5L ratings better distinguished depression and pain, while care-manager 3L ratings better distinguished several health and impairment stages.

outcome: Acceptability based on missing values
statement: Missing values were rare and similar across EQ-5D versions and proxy-rater contexts.

outcome: Acceptability based on missing values
statement: Across acceptability, ceiling effects, informativity, discriminative ability, and convergent validity, the evidence indicated a small overall psychometric advantage for EQ-5D-5L, especially when informal caregivers rated health.

outcome: Proxy-rated EQ-5D index score
statement: Mean EQ-5D-5L proxy index scores were higher than EQ-5D-3L scores in both proxy-rater contexts; the care-manager difference was larger.
The review included 152 papers from 145 distinct studies in only 22 of 75 LMICs, with nearly half of the papers from India and Egypt.
Most papers stated that they used a linguistically validated instrument, but validation status was unclear in more than one quarter of papers.
The included evidence was predominantly cross-sectional, with few cohort or quasi-experimental studies.
Eight generic HRQoL instrument families were identified; PedsQL 4.0 Generic Core Scales dominated, while EQ-5D instruments had only appeared in eligible papers after 2020.
Most source papers used generic HRQoL instruments for general HRQoL assessment, with smaller groups evaluating interventions or conducting cross-cultural adaptation or psychometric studies.
General-population evidence, population norms, and evidence for children aged 4 years or younger were scarce.
Self-report and proxy-report were both common, but reporting practices varied and were sometimes unclear.
Source instruments were most often self-completed and administered on paper; electronic and telephone modes were uncommon.
Among papers that compared child or adolescent self-report with proxy-report, results ranged from agreement to proxy ratings that were worse or better than self-ratings.
Psychometric evidence was incomplete: none of the psychometric studies assessed all nine COSMIN measurement properties, and no study assessed responsiveness or measurement error.

outcome: Reported problems by EQ-5D-Y-3L dimension and EQ VAS score
statement: Children aged 5-7 years reported significantly more problems in Looking After Myself than children aged 8-10 years, while the older children reported more Pain or Discomfort; the other three dimensions did not differ across age-groups.

outcome: Comprehensibility of the EQ-5D-Y-3L IA reported at cognitive debriefing
statement: Cognitive debriefing showed most reported problems with Looking After Myself in the younger group were due to needing help with advanced dressing tasks unrelated to a medical condition, significantly more often than in the older group.

outcome: Comprehensibility of the EQ-5D-Y-3L IA reported at cognitive debriefing
statement: Significantly more 5-7-year-olds than 8-10-year-olds reported difficulty understanding the instrument, most often that Usual Activities required a lot of thinking, or unfamiliar words such as "about" and "discomfort".

outcome: Completion time, ceiling effect and number of unique health states
statement: The younger children took significantly longer to complete the EQ-5D-Y-3L IA, but both age-groups completed it within two and a half minutes.

outcome: Completion time, ceiling effect and number of unique health states
statement: The ceiling effect (health state 11111) did not differ between age-groups, but the younger group reported significantly fewer unique health states.

outcome: Known-group validity of EQ-5D-Y-3L IA dimension responses and EQ VAS across health condition groups
statement: Known-group validity was supported at dimension level: all dimensions except Worried, Sad or Unhappy differed significantly by health condition in the 8-10-year group, whereas only Looking After Myself and Usual Activities differed in the 5-7-year group, with orthopaedic children reporting most problems on physical dimensions.

outcome: Known-group validity of EQ-5D-Y-3L IA dimension responses and EQ VAS across health condition groups
statement: EQ VAS scores differed significantly across condition groups in the 5-7-year group only, and the lowest median EQ VAS in that age-group was in the general population sample.

outcome: Convergent validity of EQ-5D-Y-3L IA dimensions with WeeFIM, FPS-R and MFQ scores
statement: Convergent validity of Looking After Myself with WeeFIM self-care items was moderate to high in both age-groups, and significantly stronger in the 8-10-year-olds for dressing upper body, dressing lower body and self-care total.

outcome: Convergent validity of EQ-5D-Y-3L IA dimensions with WeeFIM, FPS-R and MFQ scores
statement: EQ-5D-Y-3L Mobility correlated moderately to highly with WeeFIM mobility items and Pain or Discomfort correlated moderately with the FPS-R, with no significant difference between age-groups; WeeFIM social interaction was not associated with Usual Activities in either group.

outcome: Convergent validity of EQ-5D-Y-3L IA dimensions with WeeFIM, FPS-R and MFQ scores
statement: Worried, Sad or Unhappy showed only low correlations with MFQ items, and correlations with unhappy, enjoyment and crying were significant in the older group only.

outcome: Test-retest reliability of EQ-5D-Y-3L IA dimensions and EQ VAS at 48 hours
statement: Test-retest agreement over 48 hours was fair to moderate for the dimensions in both age-groups, and EQ VAS reliability by intraclass correlation was above 0.70 in both age-groups although Fleiss kappa and Kendall's W agreement were weak.

outcome: Linguistic and conceptual equivalence of the Chichewa versions
statement: Six items required cultural adaptation to establish linguistic and conceptual equivalence between the Chichewa and US English child and teen self-report versions.

outcome: Known-groups validity by health status
statement: Healthy participants had better scores than sick participants as expected; known-groups effect sizes were generally small for the child version and ranged from small to large for the teen version.

outcome: Item convergent and discriminant validity within scales
statement: All multitrait-multimethod within-scale ratios met the prespecified threshold, although the highest ratios were close to the threshold.

outcome: Linguistic and conceptual equivalence of the Chichewa versions
statement: Cognitive interviews identified that the initial Chichewa wording for bathing could connote menstruation for adolescent girls; adding a word for body resolved the meaning.

outcome: Feasibility of self-completion and comprehension
statement: Some participants circled every response option until the interviewer clearly explained the instructions, which indicated problems with unassisted self-completion.

outcome: Item missingness, endorsement distribution, and redundancy
statement: Item missingness was more problematic for the child version than the teen version.

outcome: Item missingness, endorsement distribution, and redundancy
statement: Most items in both versions failed the adjacent aggregate endorsement criterion, but no items failed maximum endorsement frequency or item redundancy criteria.

outcome: Internal consistency reliability
statement: Internal consistency reliability met the prespecified threshold for all subscales, summary scores, and total scores.

outcome: Convergent validity
statement: Between-subscale correlations generally supported convergent validity in both age versions.

outcome: Discriminant validity by gender, age, and school grade
statement: Gender and age results generally supported discriminant validity, although the child social-functioning score differed by gender.

outcome: Discriminant validity by gender, age, and school grade
statement: School-grade results supported discriminant validity for the child version, but the teen version differed significantly across grades for the total score, both summary scores, and all subscales except emotional functioning.

outcome: Preferred EQ-5D-Y descriptive-system version for measuring child health
statement: Most participants preferred EQ-5D-Y-5L because its additional response options could improve discrimination and detection of change; participants who preferred EQ-5D-Y-3L were concerned that children may have difficulty distinguishing five response levels.

outcome: Recommended respondent source and perspective for child health valuation
statement: Most participants recommended that children and adolescents supply preferences for child health valuation because their perspectives may differ from adults; participants generally considered adolescents aged 12 years or older cognitively able to respond.

outcome: Recommended respondent source and perspective for child health valuation
statement: The 12 participants who supported child and adolescent respondents also supported framing valuation tasks from the child's own perspective.

outcome: Ethical acceptability of asking children about valuation tasks involving death
statement: Views on ethical concerns were split: eight participants reported no ethical concern, while seven urged caution about discussing death with children, including possible fear, incomplete understanding, and the need for parental permission.

outcome: Preferred preference-elicitation method
statement: Most participants preferred DCE to TTO because they viewed DCE as more direct, easier, and closer to reality.

outcome: Preferred DCE anchoring variant
statement: Among the 11 participants who preferred DCE, six preferred DCE with duration because it appeared more detailed, realistic, and potentially safer than immediate death; two preferred DCE with death because duration could add cognitive burden, and three had no strong preference.

outcome: Preferred preference-elicitation method
statement: Preference for DCE differed by prior utility-measurement experience: all six participants without such experience preferred DCE, compared with five of nine participants with experience.

outcome: TTO values and pairwise choices across perspectives and EQ-5D-Y-3L profiles
statement: TTO values and pairwise choices changed across valuation perspectives, which indicates that the imagined person affected stated preferences for the same EQ-5D-Y-3L profiles.

There was no strong support for prioritising child health over working-age adult health; many preferred equal treatment, although many supported a fair-innings priority for younger people over elderly people.

Twenty-seven themes were grouped into eight categories and three topics: interpreting health states, differences by perspective and task, and views about resource allocation and being informed; no new themes first appeared in the final two groups.

Participants were generally least willing to trade life years under the other-child perspective, especially for the physical-health-aligned state; this reluctance was weaker when pain or mental suffering was perceived as severe.

Participants usually preferred the physical-health-aligned state over the mental-health-aligned state in the pairwise task, except for the own-adult comparison of severe profiles; they also generally traded more years to avoid severe states.

Participants found it difficult to imagine a 10-year-old child, and they imagined different children, including their own child, another family child, an ill child known to them, or a hypothetical child.

The same health profile was often perceived to affect a child and an adult differently because participants considered resilience, support, responsibilities, whether illness was present from birth, and capacity to adapt.

outcome: Interpretation, imaginability, and perceived plausibility of EQ-5D-Y-3L states
statement: Participants sometimes found EQ-5D-Y-3L descriptions vague or implausible, added concrete conditions or personal experiences, and assumed treatment, change, or adaptation during the 10-year period.

Problems linked to being worried, sad, or unhappy and to pain or discomfort were often, but not always, viewed as more serious than mobility or self-care problems, especially when a child was imagined.

Participants were split in their preference for TTO or the pairwise DCE: DCE was easier and avoided trading life, while TTO gave more granular information; perspective appeared to change TTO responses more than pairwise choices.

outcome: Acceptability and difficulty of perspectives and elicitation techniques
statement: Participants found the own-adult perspective most acceptable and were less comfortable making life-shortening decisions for other people, which they described as playing God.

outcome: Overall face and content validity of the draft Italian EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S
statement: All participants described the questionnaires as easy or quite easy to complete. They generally considered the items relevant and comprehensive, and no participant identified an important missing health or quality-of-life domain; one participant considered EQ-HWB too long.

outcome: Comprehension and interpretation of items
statement: Participants generally interpreted the measures readily, but interpretation difficulty occurred 15 times. Items on day-to-day activities, control over day-to-day life, hopelessness, and acceptance caused difficulty for more than one participant. Ambiguity often concerned physical versus emotional meaning, and the Italian wording for control and hopelessness needed clarification or examples.

outcome: Acceptability, response-option suitability, and recall-period suitability
statement: Four patients identified acceptability concerns. Hopelessness was associated with stigma or emotional burden, feeling good about oneself was considered inappropriate during illness by one participant, and unable was considered heavy or potentially judgmental in Italian.

outcome: Acceptability, response-option suitability, and recall-period suitability
statement: Response options were generally suitable, but five participants had difficulty distinguishing only occasionally from sometimes. The seven-day recall period was generally suitable, although one participant found emotion recall harder than activity recall.

outcome: Perceived importance of EQ-HWB items and fit of the EQ-HWB-S item set
statement: The most important content concerned day-to-day activities, support from other people, control over life, basic care, autonomy, mobility, and ability to do desired activities. Patients and carers prioritized support, assistance, control, and mobility more often than the general public, while the general public more often prioritized loneliness and acceptance.

outcome: Perceived importance of EQ-HWB items and fit of the EQ-HWB-S item set
statement: The ranking broadly supported the EQ-HWB-S item selection, and EQ-HWB-S items were less often identified as problematic. However, support from others was ranked in the top five by four of nine patients and three of six carers but was not in EQ-HWB-S, while exhaustion was in EQ-HWB-S but was not selected in the ranking exercise.

outcome: Participant concepts of health and quality of life
statement: Participants described health and quality of life through physical and mental wellbeing, disease consequences, activities and participation, social relationships, emotional functioning, living conditions and autonomy, and access to services. Many found a sharp distinction between health and quality of life difficult.

outcome: Comprehension and interpretation of items
statement: Participants proposed clearer examples, different wording, and more distinct response labels for some Italian items. The authors noted that unresolved interpretation and response-option issues could bias scores and comparisons.

The review of existing child and adolescent HRQoL instruments and of dictionaries produced 65 candidate German labels for dimensions 1-4 (mobility, looking after myself, doing usual activities, pain or discomfort) and 56 for dimension 5 (feeling worried, sad or unhappy); after two researchers independently removed labels that were not child-friendly or fitted the item wording badly, 50 labels for dimensions 1-4 and 29 for dimension 5 entered the focus groups.

outcome: Comprehensibility and preference of candidate German response labels reported by children and adolescents
statement: When talking freely about health, the children and adolescents mostly used labels describing strong or large health problems (for example "starke", "sehr viele", "dolle") and rarely labels for mild problems; this was more pronounced in the younger group. Of the labels identified in the review, only three were not understood and ten were named as disliked, while 26 understandable everyday labels were particularly preferred.

outcome: Severity position of each candidate label on the impairment continuum (median, mode and standard deviation of the VAS or smiley rating)
statement: Finally 14 labels for dimensions 1-3, 16 labels for dimension 4 and 12 labels for dimension 5 were tested in 64 sorting and response scaling interviews; the included labels covered the whole continuum of impairment, and median and mode lay very close together for labels describing small impairments, indicating little differentiation at the mild end.

outcome: Self-reported health of the interview participants on the EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions and the EQ VAS
statement: Among the 64 interview participants the most frequently reported problems on the EQ-5D-Y-3L were in the pain or discomfort dimension, followed by feeling worried, sad or unhappy; no participant reported the third (severe) level in any dimension, and the mean EQ VAS score was high.

outcome: Severity position of each candidate label on the impairment continuum (median, mode and standard deviation of the VAS or smiley rating)
statement: The selected German EQ-5D-Y-5L labels are "keine", "leichte", "einige", "große" and "kann nicht" for dimensions 1-3, "keine", "leichte", "einige", "große" and "extreme" for pain or discomfort, and "gar nicht", "ein bisschen", "etwas", "sehr" and "extrem" for feeling worried, sad or unhappy; "extreme" was dropped for dimensions 1-3 because participants said they would not use "extreme Probleme" themselves, and "leicht" was replaced by "ein bisschen" in dimension 5 for the same reason.

outcome: Preference for the EQ-5D-Y-5L over the EQ-5D-Y-4L version
statement: Both versions were understandable and unproblematic to self-complete for both age groups, took at most 3-4 minutes, and raised no comprehension questions; 88% of the 33 participants judged the EQ-5D-Y-5L the better version because they could report their state more precisely, and several participants said it was harder to choose a fitting answer in the 4L version.

The new EQ-5D-Y-5L describes 3,125 health states, compared with 243 states in the original EQ-5D-Y-3L, without losing the brevity and user-friendliness of the questionnaire. The share of participants with a chronic illness in the study (about 30%) was only slightly above the German average of 26% reported in the DAK child and adolescent report.

outcome: Quality-adjusted life expectancy (undiscounted and discounted at 3% and 5%), estimated by the Sullivan method
statement: In the multivariable linear regression, undiscounted QALE fell significantly with increasing geographic remoteness relative to major cities.

outcome: Life expectancy from remoteness-specific life tables
statement: In the multivariable model for life expectancy, only participants in remote or very remote areas had significantly lower life expectancy than those in major cities, and the QALE gap was larger than the life expectancy gap.

outcome: Quality-adjusted life expectancy (undiscounted and discounted at 3% and 5%), estimated by the Sullivan method
statement: In univariable analysis QALE was lower for inner regional residents but not significantly lower for outer regional or remote/very remote residents.

outcome: Variance partition coefficient of the intersectional MAIHDA models (discriminatory accuracy of intersectional strata)
statement: The MAIHDA null models attributed most variance in QALE and life expectancy to differences between intersectional strata, but the variance partition coefficients fell to near zero in the main effects models, indicating additive rather than multiplicative intersectional effects.

outcome: Quality-adjusted life expectancy (undiscounted and discounted at 3% and 5%), estimated by the Sullivan method
statement: Predicted mean QALE differed markedly across age and sex strata but varied little across SEIFA strata.

outcome: Quality-adjusted life expectancy (undiscounted and discounted at 3% and 5%), estimated by the Sullivan method
statement: Female sex, higher household income, tertiary education, and absence of chronic health issues were associated with higher QALE and life expectancy, although education was not significant after adjustment.

outcome: Quality-adjusted life expectancy (undiscounted and discounted at 3% and 5%), estimated by the Sullivan method
statement: Applying an A$50 000 per QALY threshold, closing the QALE gap for the remote/very remote population (493 386 persons in 2019) would require about 1.6 million QALYs, valued at about A$165 000 per person.

outcome: Variance partition coefficient of the intersectional MAIHDA models (discriminatory accuracy of intersectional strata)
statement: The secondary MAIHDA using five social dimensions could estimate QALE for only 178 of 216 strata and had reduced precision.
The surveyed cohort was broadly representative of the Australian adult population except for a high proportion reporting ongoing medical conditions.

EQ-HWB-9 responses were well distributed. Caregivers reported significantly worse health and wellbeing than non-caregivers on all nine items; the between-group effect was largest for mobility and smallest for cognition.
Known-groups analyses supported the prespecified hypotheses for caregiver status, mental distress, chronic health condition, disability, and sleep problems.

Caregivers had worse EQ-HWB-9 sum and index scores than non-caregivers. Low income differentiated groups only after application of the UK pilot preference weights, which showed that weighting affected the result.

Convergent-validity hypotheses were supported. The EQ-HWB-9 sum score and index score correlated strongly with the K6 total score, while mobility, activities, and pain showed weak correlations with K6 items as expected.

Convergent-validity results were consistent across Australia and New Zealand. In New Zealand, caregiver-group differences were not significant, and country-specific analyses indicated that some known-group results differed by country.

Gender differences in known-group effect sizes were minimal. Differences associated with mental distress increased with age, and disability-related quality-of-life differences were larger from age 40 onward.

outcome: Inferred attribute non-attendance and full attendance class probabilities by design
statement: Attribute level overlap increased the estimated probability of attending to all five EQ-5D-5L attributes for every construction method.

outcome: Inferred attribute non-attendance and full attendance class probabilities by design
statement: Among designs with overlap, modified Fedorov designs constructed in Ngene and SAS achieved the highest full attendance rates, while the Bayesian D-efficient design in R achieved the lowest.

outcome: Inferred attribute non-attendance and full attendance class probabilities by design
statement: Overlap also increased the estimated probability of ignoring all attributes in the generator-developed, Ngene and SAS designs, but not in the R design.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility decrements and relative attribute importance before and after excluding non-attenders
statement: Many interaction terms between full attendance and EQ-5D-5L attribute levels were statistically significant, and utility decrements were generally larger for full attenders, especially at levels 4 and 5.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility decrements and relative attribute importance before and after excluding non-attenders
statement: Relative attribute importance changed after excluding non-attenders, with mobility consistently more important before exclusion and anxiety/depression more important among full attenders, but no clear overall pattern across designs.

outcome: External validity indicators of attendance classes (straightlining, completion time, self-reported task difficulty)
statement: External validity checks supported the ECLC attendance classification: non-attenders straightlined most, completed tasks fastest, reported the most difficulty and least often said they considered the whole description.
Non-attenders were more likely to be male, younger and single, while education, household income and region did not differ across attendance classes.
The matched analyses found no within-dimensional effect of serious self-reported pain/discomfort or anxiety/depression on preferences for the same EQ-5D-5L dimension.

Respondents with serious self-reported anxiety/depression assigned significantly larger utility decrements to every pain/discomfort problem level than matched respondents without serious anxiety/depression.

Evidence for cross-dimensional effects of serious pain/discomfort was limited: the matched analysis identified a positive effect for slight self-care problems, while the authors emphasized that the overall evidence was limited.

Respondents with a serious pain/discomfort or anxiety/depression problem assigned higher utility to EQ-5D-5L state 55555 than matched respondents without the respective serious problem, which implies a narrower disutility range.
Akaike and Bayesian information criteria generally showed that adding serious-health-problem interactions did not improve model fit over the baseline conditional logit model.

The serious anxiety/depression effect on preferences for pain/discomfort persisted in the unmatched valid sample and was not contradicted by the simulation, relative-attribute-importance, or non-constant proportional time trade-off analyses.

outcome: Proportion of respondents preferring the better-labelled statement in each pair (preference inversion)
statement: No significant preference inversions were found for EQ-5D-3L or EQ-5D-Y item labels; proportions preferring the better statement ranged from 0.98 to 1.00.

outcome: Proportion of respondents preferring the better-labelled statement in each pair (preference inversion)
statement: EQ-5D-5L pairs between Levels 4 and 5 showed significant preference inversion, while other 5L pairs did not.

outcome: Proportion of respondents preferring the better-labelled statement in each pair (preference inversion)
statement: For anxiety/depression, respondents were indifferent between severely and extremely anxious or depressed; indifference could not be rejected.

Cross-version comparisons showed the EQ-5D-3L measured worse mobility than the EQ-5D-5L, and the EQ-5D-5L measured worse anxiety/depression and pain/discomfort than the EQ-5D-Y; inversions appeared in three of six pairs.
The original 10-item, two-factor adult Vaccine Hesitancy Scale structure had acceptable overall fit; seven items indicated lack of vaccine confidence and three items indicated perceived vaccine risk.
Internal consistency was excellent for lack of vaccine confidence and acceptable for perceived vaccine risk.
Lack of vaccine confidence was negatively associated with influenza and COVID-19 vaccine acceptance, while perceived vaccine risk was negatively associated with Tdap and influenza vaccine acceptance.
Higher adult Vaccine Hesitancy Scale scores were associated with lower adjusted odds of receipt of each recommended prenatal vaccine.
Vaccine uptake declined across increasing adult Vaccine Hesitancy Scale quintiles, with a weaker and later decline for Tdap than for influenza or COVID-19 vaccination.
The mean adult Vaccine Hesitancy Scale score was 20.2 and the median was 20.

Higher educational attainment was associated with higher EQ VAS scores in all ten selected EQ-5D-5L profiles. High education was significant at p < 0.10 in seven profiles and at p < 0.01 in four profiles.
Subjective income status showed a stronger and more consistent positive EQ VAS gradient than education. Significant income gradients occurred in nine of the ten profiles.

Within EQ-5D-5L profile 11121, EQ VAS was higher for medium and high education than for low education, and higher for respondents who were coping or comfortable than for respondents who reported income difficulty.

Country-stratified results supported a stable income gradient. For profile 11111, comfortable versus difficult income was positive and significant at p < 0.05 in all eight countries. For profile 11121, it was positive in all eight countries and significant at p < 0.10 in seven countries, including six at p < 0.05. Education effects varied more across countries.

Median EQ VAS declined with increasing profile severity, from 89 for full health profile 11111 to 69 for profile 21231. Within-profile distributions were concentrated near the median and showed mild left skew.

Across the tested dimensions, most participants correctly ordered the five severity levels with the water-glass scale, but adjacent levels overlapped: slight versus moderate problems and severe versus unable to function were difficult to distinguish, while extreme problems were more distinct.
Review of interviewer debriefing notes found meaning saturation after approximately 23 to 24 interviews; data collection ended after 26 participants.

The water-glass anchors required an explicit explanation. Without it, some participants interpreted a full glass as wellbeing or good luck and an empty glass as a lack of wellbeing, which reversed the intended problem-severity direction.

Cognitive testing led to several wording changes: a colloquial term replaced the original discomfort wording, physical was added before pain, a phrase meaning neither too much nor too little clarified moderate problems, a colloquial phrase replaced unable to function, and a frustration prompt was added to depression.

Interpretations varied by age and gender. Younger participants understood mobility mainly as exercise, working-age participants as movement needed for livelihood tasks, and older participants as physical and cognitive movement; women usually described usual activities as household duties, while men emphasized work outside the home.

Younger participants linked anxiety and depression to unexpected outcomes, unfulfilled expectations, and dissatisfaction with work or life. Older participants linked anxiety to pain, lack of care, inability to work, or unfulfilled desires, and linked depression to pain, grief, severe sadness, and lack of motivation.

Self-care extended beyond hygiene to physical, emotional, social, and sometimes financial wellbeing. Pain was understood readily and could include physical, emotional, or spiritual experiences, whereas the original Nepali term for discomfort was difficult to understand.
Most participants understood the EQ VAS. For participants who were confused, explaining it as a tree or ladder in which greater height meant better health substantially improved understanding.

Some participants gave very high EQ VAS ratings despite moderate or severe problems in several EQ-5D-5L dimensions. Their explanations indicated that overall health was anchored to ability or obligation to work despite age or impairment.

The today recall period was identified as problematic because morning and evening interviews provide different exposure windows and because it can miss symptoms that occur later in the day, such as sleep disruption related to anxiety.
Proxies generally judged that the EQ-HWB covered domains that were relevant to daily life in residential aged care, and they did not identify a major missing domain.
Proxies identified ambiguous terms, double-barrelled items, examples that did not fit residential aged care, perceived repetition, and item meanings that depended on the care provided.
Suggested changes concerned response options, additional or more positive content, the 7-day recall period, layout, instructions, and examples of day-to-day activities that fit residential aged care.

Although most proxies used the proxy-person perspective, some shifted to their own view or were uncertain about the required perspective, especially when a resident had severe cognitive impairment or dementia.

Proxies sometimes disagreed with the resident’s presumed self-assessment. Observable physical domains were usually easier to judge than psychosocial domains, sleep, coping, pain, and other internal experiences.

Proxy-report quality depended on knowledge of the resident, frequency and timing of contact, proxy type, and access to evidence such as resident statements, body language, events, or medication records.
When unsure, some proxies selected middle response categories. Interviewer reminders helped some respondents maintain the proxy-person perspective.

For groups whose health deteriorated by ECOG, Overall Health Assessment, or chemotherapy initiation, all EQ-5D-Y scores worsened, although some changes were not statistically significant; five-level level-sum-score changes were generally more responsive than three-level index or EQ VAS changes.
At baseline, the five-level version generally produced fewer no-problem responses than the three-level version, although the two instruments had similar full-health ceiling proportions.
