Among small groups whose health improved, most scores changed in the expected direction, but most changes were not statistically significant and most standardized effect sizes were below 0.2.

Both self-complete and proxy versions of EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L showed construct validity and responsiveness to deterioration; proxy and five-level versions were slightly more sensitive in this patient group.

Known-groups results followed the prespecified direction: patients in poorer health by ECOG or Overall Health Assessment reported more dimensional problems, lower EQ-5D-Y-3L index and EQ VAS scores, and higher EQ-5D-Y-5L level sum scores.
Known-groups effect sizes were generally larger for proxy than self-complete reports and for EQ-5D-Y-5L level sum scores than EQ-5D-Y-3L index scores.

outcome: Framework and classification of design components for clinical dashboards incorporating PROMs
statement: The authors identified 25 dashboard design components: 16 from the prior literature search and 9 additional components from inductive interview coding. They organized these components into generic dashboard, PROM-related, adjacent information, and adoption-requirement groups.

outcome: Stakeholder preferences for dashboard content, PROM display, users, setting, and patient access
statement: Software producers and users did not consider different dashboard designs essential for chronic conditions versus acute conditions with a one-time intervention. They preferred consistent components across care episodes, with adaptation mainly for disease-specific PROMs.

outcome: Stakeholder preferences for dashboard content, PROM display, users, setting, and patient access
statement: Stakeholders mainly viewed dashboards as tools for patient-physician communication and better clinical decisions in outpatient care. Most preferred disease-specific PROMs alone or a combination of generic and disease-specific PROMs; none preferred a generic PROM alone.

outcome: Stakeholder preferences for dashboard content, PROM display, users, setting, and patient access
statement: Longitudinal past-assessment PRO scores and peer-group comparison were among the most valued design components. Stakeholders also wanted some customizability, usually from a standard set, while views on alerts and score aggregation varied.

outcome: Perceived dashboard benefits, workflow requirements, and adoption barriers
statement: The main perceived benefits were clearer visualization, better workflow efficiency, and improved comparability. The leading implementation barrier was interoperability between systems; users also reported burdensome data collection.

outcome: Stakeholder preferences for dashboard content, PROM display, users, setting, and patient access
statement: Most interviewees supported patient access to dashboard information because it could improve understanding of health status. Users stressed that explanations and suitable aggregation are needed to prevent misinterpretation and avoid overwhelming patients.

outcome: Reported problems on the five EQ-5D-Y dimensions
statement: Special school children reported significantly more problems than open school children in Mobility and Looking after myself, but not in Doing usual activities, Pain or discomfort or Feeling worried, sad or unhappy.

outcome: Self-reported EQ VAS score
statement: Mean self-reported EQ VAS did not differ between special school and open school children.

outcome: Self-reported EQ VAS score
statement: In multiple regression, grade and problems in Doing usual activities, Pain or discomfort and Feeling worried, sad or unhappy predicted a lower child VAS, while gender and special school attendance did not; the model explained 13% of variance.

outcome: Child-proxy agreement and correlation
statement: Agreement between children and female care-givers on the EQ-5D-Y dimensions was only slight to fair in open schools but fair to moderate in the special school.

outcome: Child-proxy agreement and correlation
statement: Correlation of VAS scores between children and female care-givers was low in open schools and not significant in the special school, whereas the two care-givers of the same child agreed well.

outcome: Self-reported EQ VAS score
statement: Female care-givers of open school children rated their child's health significantly higher than the child did, while special school care-givers rated it lower than the child, non-significantly.

outcome: Reported problems on the five EQ-5D-Y dimensions
statement: The EQ-5D-Y was completed with few missing responses, supporting its feasibility in this age group; Pain or discomfort and Worried, sad or unhappy were the most commonly reported problems in open schools.

outcome: Child-parent agreement in preference-weighted EQ-5D-Y-3L values
statement: Agreement between child self-report and parent proxy preference-weighted EQ-5D-Y-3L values was low and similar for both proxy perspectives.

outcome: Child-parent agreement at the EQ-5D-Y-3L dimension level
statement: The largest perspective-related difference in dimension-level child-parent agreement was for feeling worried, sad, or unhappy; proxy-child agreement was stronger than proxy-proxy agreement.

outcome: Child-parent agreement in preference-weighted EQ-5D-Y-3L values
statement: Median preference-weighted health values did not differ significantly between child self-report and either parent-proxy perspective.

outcome: Child-parent agreement and differences in EQ VAS scores
statement: EQ VAS medians were 90 for all three report types, but child self-report and proxy-child scores differed significantly.

outcome: Agreement between proxy perspectives in preference-weighted EQ-5D-Y-3L values
statement: The two proxy perspectives had moderate agreement for preference-weighted values and no significant difference in those values, but their EQ VAS scores differed significantly.

outcome: Agreement between proxy perspectives at the EQ-5D-Y-3L dimension level
statement: Intra-proxy dimension agreement was very good for three dimensions but lower for pain or discomfort and feeling worried, sad, or unhappy.

outcome: Child-parent agreement in preference-weighted EQ-5D-Y-3L values
statement: Children aged 11 to 12 years had poor agreement with parent proxies for preference-weighted values from both proxy perspectives.
Use of the German EQ-5D-Y-3L value set in sensitivity analysis produced similar inter-rater and intra-proxy agreement estimates to the primary Australian EQ-5D-3L value set.
The review included 21 studies published from 2001 to 2024; nine studies evaluated more than one generic preference-based measure.

outcome: Known-group validity
statement: Known-group validity evidence was available for all reviewed measures except HINT-8, and more than 60% of analyses for EQ-5D-3L, EQ-5D-5L, EQ-HWB-9, HUI3, and SF-6Dv1 showed discrimination.

outcome: Convergent validity
statement: Convergent validity was generally supported against other generic preference-based measures, carer-specific preference-based measures, and carer health and well-being measures, but correlations with carer burden, relationship measures, and patient health were mostly weak.

outcome: Responsiveness to change
statement: Responsiveness evidence was limited and mixed: EQ-HWB-9 and EQ-5D-5L were responsive to some changes but not others, and SF-6Dv1 did not respond to changes in care-recipient health status or hours of care in the study that tested it.

outcome: Test-retest reliability
statement: The available test-retest evidence supported reliability of EQ-5D-3L, EQ-5D-5L, and EQ-HWB-9; reported index-level intraclass correlation coefficients ranged from 0.657 to 0.987.

outcome: Ceiling effects
statement: All five EQ-5D-3L studies that assessed ceiling effects found them, with 21% to 33% of carers reporting full health; one of two EQ-5D-5L studies found a ceiling effect, while no ceiling effect was observed for EQ-HWB-9 or SF-6Dv1.

outcome: Structural validity
statement: The sole structural-validity study found that four EQ-5D-3L dimensions loaded on one factor, anxiety/depression did not load on the other factors, and no EQ-5D-3L items overlapped with ASCOT-Carer or Carer Experience Scale items.

outcome: Risk of bias of included psychometric analyses
statement: Across 50 psychometric-property assessments, the COSMIN risk-of-bias review rated 36 as very good, 12 as adequate, and 2 as doubtful; none were inadequate.
No eligible psychometric evidence was identified for the 15D, Assessment of Quality of Life instruments, or the PROMIS preference score.
Including indicators for problems in the other EQ-5D-3L dimensions produced the largest improvement in prediction accuracy.
Adding age and gender reduced AIC but did not improve prediction accuracy, whereas the common latent factor further reduced AIC and slightly improved predictive accuracy.

For in-sample prediction, the ordinal logistic model without demographic variables or the latent factor had the lowest mean absolute error and root mean squared error. For disease-group holdout prediction, the model with the latent factor but without age and gender performed best.
The ordinal logistic mapping without age and gender was more accurate than the copula comparator overall and generally across age and gender strata.
The ordinal logistic models did not produce the logical inconsistencies observed for some predictions from the copula approach.
The recommended model is an ordinal logistic regression that includes other-dimension problem indicators and a common latent factor but excludes age and gender.

outcome: Extent and pattern of PROM implementation across Alberta PCNs
statement: Twenty-nine of the 41 Alberta PCNs were registered and licensed to use EQ-5D, commonly together with a condition-specific measure.

outcome: Extent and pattern of PROM implementation across Alberta PCNs
statement: PROM selection, administration, implementation training, analysis, and reporting varied substantially across PCNs and were often unique to each network.

outcome: Extent and pattern of PROM implementation across Alberta PCNs
statement: For program evaluation, most PCNs used paper-based PROMs before and after programs, although many were moving toward online capture.

outcome: Use of PROM information in program evaluation and decision-making
statement: PROMs added the patient perspective to clinical and other program indicators, supported description of program populations, and enabled examination of trends across programs and time points.

outcome: Use of PROM information in program evaluation and decision-making
statement: PROM results contributed to decisions about program development, program components, administrative features, resource allocation, and service delivery.

outcome: PROM data capture, workflow, reporting, and analytical capacity
statement: Incompatible or absent electronic data systems created problems with workflow, data fidelity, storage, export, display, sharing, and analysis.

outcome: PROM data capture, workflow, reporting, and analytical capacity
statement: PCN size and capacity affected the ability to analyze and report PROM data, and many networks did not use data at micro, meso, and macro levels.

outcome: Extent and pattern of PROM implementation across Alberta PCNs
statement: Four early-adopter PCNs showed different combinations of generic and condition-specific PROMs, administration schedules, and reporting arrangements for locally tailored programs.

outcome: Composite TTO values for ten EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Mean composite TTO values ranged from -0.104 for the most severe state 53555 to 0.946 for the mild state 21111, with larger standard deviations and skewed distributions for more severe states.

outcome: Feasibility of the composite TTO: clarity of instructions, ease of understanding, difficulty of finding the point of equivalence
statement: Debriefing indicated the composite TTO was feasible: instructions were clear to 98% and the task was easy to understand for 95%, both higher than in the earlier multinational and Internet lead-time TTO studies, although 60% found it difficult to decide the exact point of equivalence.

outcome: Task engagement indicators: number of iteration steps and task duration per health state
statement: Respondents used more iteration steps and more time per health state than in earlier lead-time TTO studies, indicating that short-cutting of the task was avoided.

outcome: Face validity of composite TTO values across mild, moderate and severe health states
statement: Face validity was supported: mean values exceeded 0.90 for the three mild states and were below 0.42 for the four severe states, with moderate states in between.

outcome: Composite TTO values for ten EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Compared with the multinational and Internet studies, the composite TTO removed the clustering of values at 0 for mild and moderate states and reduced clustering at 1 for the severe state 53555, while producing a new cluster at -1 for that severe state.
The number of QALY-based cost-utility analyses targeting Asian populations increased over 1999-2019, with most published in 2017-2019 and a marked rise after 2013.

outcome: General characteristics of the included cost-utility analyses (country, intervention type, perspective, time horizon, model type, sensitivity analysis, discount rate)
statement: Included analyses most often targeted mainland China, Japan or Thailand, evaluated a therapy, took a provider or payer perspective, used a time horizon of more than 10 years, and were Markov model based with probabilistic sensitivity analysis.
Only a small minority of the included cost-utility analyses reported using a review to identify health-state utility values.

outcome: Percentage of health-state utilities for which the estimation method, HRQoL data source, preference data source or sample size was not reported
statement: Key characteristics were not reported for the majority of the 4,052 health-state utilities.

outcome: Distribution of health-state utility estimation methods (EQ-5D, SF-6D, HUI, QWB, TTO, SG, VAS, mapping, expert opinion, unjustifiable methods)
statement: Among health-state utilities with a reported estimation method, the EQ-5D was the most frequent method, and its use increased markedly after 2010.

outcome: Country or region of the HRQoL data and of the preference data used to estimate each health-state utility, and match with the country targeted by the analysis
statement: Among health-state utilities with a reported HRQoL data source, most used Asian HRQoL data and most used data from the country targeted by the analysis.

outcome: Country or region of the HRQoL data and of the preference data used to estimate each health-state utility, and match with the country targeted by the analysis
statement: Among health-state utilities with a reported preference source, most were derived from an Asian value set and most used preference data from the target country.

outcome: Sample size used to estimate each health-state utility
statement: Among health-state utilities with a reported estimation sample size, nearly half were estimated with 100 or more individuals, a proportion that increased after 2010.

outcome: Percentage of health-state utilities for which the estimation method, HRQoL data source, preference data source or sample size was not reported
statement: Nonreporting decreased after 2010 overall and for the three countries with most publications, except that Thailand had higher nonreporting of the estimation method after 2010.
The mean EQ-HWB VAS score was significantly lower than the mean EQ VAS score, and the EQ-HWB VAS had a slightly lower ceiling.
EQ-HWB VAS and EQ VAS scores had very strong correlation and good absolute agreement.
The EQ-HWB VAS had moderate-to-strong correlations with EQ-5D-5L, EQ-HWB-9, ReQoL, and PROPr scores; its strongest reported instrument-level correlations were with EQ-HWB-9 scores.

Both VAS measures significantly distinguished all prespecified known groups in the expected direction. The EQ-HWB VAS had slightly larger effect sizes for caregiving, income, exercise, sleep, fatigue, and anxiety or depression, whereas EQ VAS often performed slightly better across physical chronic-disease groups.

EQ-HWB-9 items explained more variance in EQ-HWB VAS than EQ-5D-5L dimensions did, whereas their explanatory power for EQ VAS was nearly equal. PROMIS-29+2 domains explained similar variance to EQ-HWB-9 items for EQ-HWB VAS.

Shapley decomposition identified exhausted and pain as important EQ-HWB-9 contributors to both VAS scores; sadness or depression and loneliness contributed more to EQ-HWB VAS, while control contributed more to EQ VAS. Sleep and fatigue were major contributors in PROMIS models.
The difference between EQ VAS and EQ-HWB VAS scores became smaller with older age and with average or above-average income.
More than half of respondents reported a lower EQ-HWB VAS score than EQ VAS score, while fewer than one fifth gave identical scores.
In THA patients, the most deprived quintile had poorer preoperative health than the least deprived quintile after adjustment for patient characteristics.
In THA patients, the deprivation difference at 12-month follow-up was about half the preoperative difference but remained present.
In THA patients, the most deprived quintile had a higher unadjusted and adjusted mean change score than the least deprived quintile.
TKA patients showed the same pattern as THA patients, with a larger deprivation gap on the Oxford Knee Score at 12 months and no significant deprivation effect on the OKS mean change.

After stratification by preoperative score quintile, the most deprived patients had a lower mean change than the least deprived patients across all preoperative strata, showing that the higher crude mean change among deprived patients was confounded by their lower preoperative health; the difference narrowed as preoperative scores increased and was larger in TKA than THA patients.
Erreygers-corrected concentration indices showed that better cross-sectional health was concentrated among affluent patients, while mean change was slightly concentrated among deprived patients.
Decomposition showed that the measured patient and surgical variables explained only a minority of the observed inequality, with the remainder attributed to socio-economic status.
The regression coefficients for the most deprived group generally exceeded the coefficients for Charnley score C, that is multiple affected joints or severely impaired quality of life.

Deprivation was associated with higher BMI, higher ASA score, surgery in non-private hospitals, and, in THA, more cemented fixation and more posterolateral rather than anterior approach; the most deprived patients also had slightly lower PROM response rates.
EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L had comparable feasibility, with more than 97.7% complete descriptive-system responses.

For both versions, problems were most frequent in mobility, pain or discomfort, and usual activities; EQ-5D-5L produced more unique health profiles and a slightly less clustered index distribution, while ceiling proportions were low and similar.
EQ-5D-5L had higher absolute and relative Shannon informativity in every dimension, with the largest relative improvement in mobility.
Convergent-validity correlations were generally stronger for EQ-5D-5L; strong correlations with comparison measures occurred only for EQ-5D-5L.
Only EQ-5D-5L discriminated significantly between transtibial amputation and higher amputation levels; neither version showed a significant index difference by underlying diagnosis.
At six months, mean EQ-5D index values were similar between the instrument-period groups, and the median EQ VAS in the EQ-5D-5L group was 70.
At six months, approximately 60% described their overall situation as an amputee as good or very good, while residual limb pain and phantom limb pain remained common.
Worse health-related quality of life was observed among women, older patients, and patients with transfemoral amputation or knee disarticulation.
Mean Danish EQ-5D-5L utility was high; utility did not differ significantly across age groups or between sexes.
Mean EQ VAS was high and showed the same socio-demographic association pattern as EQ-5D-5L utility.

Utility and EQ VAS differed significantly by educational attainment, occupational status, household income, and living situation: better health was associated with higher education, employment, higher income, and not living alone.
Pain/discomfort was the most frequently reported problem overall, while anxiety/depression was especially frequent among young women.
The EQ-5D-5L ceiling effect was lower than the previously reported Danish EQ-5D-3L ceiling effect.

Self-perceived general health correlated significantly with all five EQ-5D-5L dimensions; the association was strong for usual activities, moderate for mobility and pain/discomfort, and weak for self-care and anxiety/depression.
EQ-5D-5L utility and EQ VAS were strongly and significantly correlated, but age was not significantly correlated with either score.
Known-group results supported expected associations for education, occupational status, income, and living situation, but relationships with age and sex were less clear.
The probability that dietitian supplementary prescribing was cost-effective at £30,000 per QALY was about 37%, which showed high decision uncertainty.
Dietitian supplementary prescribing cost less than non-prescribing after referral savings. Estimated savings were £4,386 per prescriber in year one and £64,269 over five years.
Adjusted mean QALY was slightly lower for patients managed by dietitian prescribers than for those managed by non-prescribers, but the difference was not statistically significant.

Patient satisfaction differences were small. The tables reported a lower patient experience score for therapeutic radiographer prescribers, although the text stated that experience differences were not significant.
Prescribers referred fewer patients to other prescribers than non-prescribers: 2% versus 30% for dietitians and 7% versus 23% for therapeutic radiographers.
Results were sensitive to referral cost, whether prescription management was required, referral probability, and use of prescribing rights.
The probability that therapeutic radiographer independent prescribing was cost-effective at £30,000 per QALY was about 44%, which showed high decision uncertainty.
Therapeutic radiographer independent prescribing cost more in year one but was estimated to save £16,570 per prescriber over five years.
Adjusted mean QALY was slightly lower for patients managed by therapeutic radiographer prescribers than for those managed by non-prescribers, but the difference was not statistically significant.

outcome: Patient completion rate, follow-up response rate, and completion time
statement: Electronic EQ-5D-5L/VAS completion was nearly complete at all three assessments, and follow-up response rates were about 90%.

outcome: Patient completion rate, follow-up response rate, and completion time
statement: Mean patient completion time decreased after baseline, with a significant difference across the three assessments.

outcome: Patient perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness
statement: Patient perceived ease of use improved with repeated use, while perceived usefulness remained high and stable.

outcome: Doctor time to interpret and address the EQ-5D-5L/VAS report
statement: Doctors usually needed less than two minutes at follow-up to interpret and address a report; their perceived ease of use improved over time.

outcome: Doctor perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness
statement: Most doctors rated at least one usefulness item positively, and their mean perceived-usefulness score increased over time.
Older age and lower education predicted lower patient baseline perceived ease of use.

outcome: Patient and staff barriers and facilitators for routine electronic HRQoL measurement
statement: Patients and research assistants reported technology, vision, literacy, and question-comprehension barriers, but understanding improved after repeated use.

outcome: Patient and staff barriers and facilitators for routine electronic HRQoL measurement
statement: Doctors found the reports clear and useful for a holistic view, monitoring, discussion, counselling, and treatment selection, but limited consultation time and competing medical problems constrained use.

outcome: Qualitative acceptability of the electronic assessment and clinical report
statement: Some patients questioned the value of repeated assessment when doctors did not review the report or treatment did not change.

After adjustment for measured sociodemographic and health covariates, the 2011 survey year remained significantly associated with higher problem reporting in every EQ-5D-3L dimension and with a lower EQ VAS score.

Older age, lower educational attainment, economic inactivity, lower household income, acute illness, long-standing illness, and greater deprivation were generally associated with worse EQ-5D-3L responses; government office region and marital status were not significant for most dimensions.
Mean EQ VAS was lowest in 2011 among the four waves that collected it and was significantly lower than in the other reported years.
The temporal pattern in EQ-5D-3L index scores largely replicated the pattern observed in the descriptive profile.
The study calculated weighted 2014 EQ-5D-3L population norms by age and sex and reported them in the supplementary material.
Standardized dimension problem rates generally fell between 1996 and 2003, were relatively stable to 2006, rose to a peak in 2011, and then fell by 2014 to levels close to those in 2003.
Pain/discomfort was the most common problem, followed by anxiety/depression and mobility; self-care problems were uncommon.
The pooled primary analysis identified 100,825 records with complete responses to all five EQ-5D-3L dimensions.
Analyses repeated with HSE sampling weights from 2003 onward produced results similar to the unweighted analyses.

Most included publications identified representation gaps and supported gender-inclusive or gender-neutral language; eight articles described exclusion from health care or research when binary gendered language was used.

Five articles reported better reliability or validity with gender-neutral or gender-inclusive wording, and two reported improved response rates; inclusive wording could also improve the accuracy of self-reported data.

Three articles reported good acceptance of gender-inclusive language, while one study found irritation among some cisgender men after a non-binary response option was added but found no overall reduction in data quality.

The review found few concrete examples of gender-inclusive wording in health questionnaires and found no study that directly examined preferred gender-inclusive linguistic options for health instruments.
No included article directly reported facilitators or barriers to developing or using gender-inclusive health measures, apart from difficulty agreeing on optimal inclusive terminology.

Only one included paper addressed PROM development and reported a lack of evidence about the effects of diversity in gender identity, gender expression, or sexual orientation on rheumatoid arthritis PROMs.
The median EQ-5D-5L index value was 0.669 and the median EQ VAS score was 60.0.

Malay ethnicity and higher pain self-efficacy were associated with higher EQ-5D-5L index values, while back-to-lower-limb pain, more pain medication use, and greater pain magnification were associated with lower values.
Only 4.1% reported the EQ-5D-5L full-health state 11111; moderate-to-severe problems were most frequent for pain or discomfort, followed by usual activities, mobility, and anxiety or depression.
Of 360 patients approached, 255 participated and 246 completed the survey and entered the final analysis; the response rate was 70.8%.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L utility distributions, scale length, and negative values
statement: The value of the worst EQ-5D-Y-3L state, 33333, ranged from -0.691 in Slovenia to 0.289 in Japan, a difference of 0.980.

outcome: Within-country differences between EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-5L value-set properties
statement: Youth and adult value distributions were broadly similar in Belgium, Germany, Hungary, Spain, and Slovenia, but differed in the Netherlands, China, Indonesia, Australia, and Japan. Dimension-importance rankings also differed for several countries.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L utility distributions, scale length, and negative values
statement: The share of EQ-5D-Y-3L states with negative values ranged from 0% in Japan and Australia to 20.6% in Slovenia; China, Indonesia, and Brazil each had about 0.4% negative states.

outcome: Relative importance of EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions and level decrements
statement: Pain/discomfort at level 3 had the largest weight in all 11 EQ-5D-Y-3L value sets. Looking after myself at level 3 had the smallest weight in 8 of 11 value sets.

outcome: Relative importance of EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions and level decrements
statement: State 22222 was located between 23.7% and 49.6% of the EQ-5D-Y-3L scale length. Most value sets had larger decrements from level 2 to level 3 than from level 1 to level 2.

outcome: Fit of regional aggregate preference patterns to national value sets
statement: The European aggregate preference pattern ranged from -0.448 to 1, while the Asian pattern ranged from 0.038 to 1. The Asian pattern had consistently small mean absolute errors; the European pattern fit the Netherlands and Slovenia less well than the other four European sets.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L utility distributions, scale length, and negative values
statement: European value sets generally had flatter distributions over wider intervals and more negative states than Asian value sets. Australia and Brazil had scale lengths similar to the Asian sets but differed in other characteristics.

outcome: Variation in source valuation designs, models, and anchoring strategies
statement: All 11 source studies used the same DCE design. Six used expanded cTTO health-state designs. Seven used mixed logit models, two used latent class models, one used a garbage-class mixed logit model, and one used a joint hybrid model.

outcome: Variation in source valuation designs, models, and anchoring strategies
statement: Of the 10 studies that modeled DCE data separately, seven anchored through mapping to cTTO data and three rescaled by the censoring-adjusted cTTO mean for state 33333.

outcome: Within-country differences between EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-5L value-set properties
statement: EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-5L value sets differed substantially in some countries. In Indonesia, the worst value was -0.0861 for EQ-5D-Y-3L and -0.865 for EQ-5D-5L, with 0.41% and 35.46% negative states, respectively.
All participants understood six modified items as intended: activities, exhausted, lonely, difficulty concentrating or thinking clearly, anxious, and sad or depressed.

Most participants placed the five modified frequency response options in the intended order, although a minority treated adjacent levels as equivalent or reversed them, and one participant did not understand the task.
The modified EQ-HWB-9 was generally well understood, relevant, and acceptable, and participants preferred the revised version in all tested instances except use of the abbreviated item stem.

Comprehension problems remained for mobility, control, and pain: six participants had difficulty with mobility, four partly interpreted pain severity as frequency, and one did not connect control with day-to-day independence.

Every item was judged not relevant by at least one participant; loneliness and control had the most reports of non-relevance, and some apparent non-relevance of mobility resulted from misunderstanding the item.

Among participants who discussed comprehensiveness, four reported no missing content and seven identified missing information, including spiritual health, access to health care, access to support, and contextualization of problems.
The original full-sentence layout was slightly preferred to the abbreviated item stem, but participants with a clear order preference more often preferred activities before mobility.

Most participants perceived a difference between mobility wording that used inside or outside and wording that used inside and outside; among those with a clear preference, most preferred or because it allowed health problems to differ by setting.
Participants generally preferred difficulty to trouble in the thinking item because they considered it more appropriate and less ambiguous.
Participants strongly preferred lacked control to no control because the modified phrase was less absolute, covered partial loss of control, and was less distressing.

Participants generally preferred a little of the time to only occasionally and moderate difficulty to some difficulty, mainly because the modified labels better fit their respective response scales and were easier to interpret.

The EQ-5D-5L full-health ceiling was higher in China than in the Netherlands. Vision, tiredness, and sleep produced the largest individual ceiling reductions in both countries, breathing produced the smallest, and cumulative reduction largely plateaued after four bolt-ons.

About 84% of prespecified convergent and divergent validity hypotheses were confirmed. Sleep showed moderate-to-strong correlations with PROMIS sleep items in both countries, while tiredness associations were stronger in the Netherlands.

Bolt-on performance varied by population subgroup and country. The cognition item was not conceptually equivalent across countries because the Chinese survey assessed memory only, while the Dutch survey assessed a broader cognition construct.

Core EQ-5D-5L dimensions explained more variance in EQ VAS in the Netherlands than in China. Adding bolt-ons increased explained variance incrementally, with tiredness and self-confidence providing the largest contributions.

Several bolt-ons improved known-groups discrimination, but retained bolt-ons differed by country and comparison. Hearing best improved age-group discrimination in China, while self-confidence had the largest age-group effect in the Netherlands. Breathing was informative for respiratory and cardiovascular disease, sleep for migraine and sleep disorders, tiredness for irritable bowel syndrome, and self-confidence for mental health conditions.

Pooled principal component analysis identified seven factors and placed all eight bolt-ons on factors separate from the core EQ-5D-5L dimensions; country-specific analyses also supported seven-factor structures with no major cross-country differences.

outcome: Achievement of country sample targets and quota-based representativeness procedures
statement: The United Kingdom pilot and all 15 round 1 and round 2 country surveys were completed; every main-round country reported more than 4,500 completed responses.

outcome: Implementation of standardized multicountry population health survey and data infrastructure
statement: The implemented survey combined a standardized four-section core questionnaire with country adaptation, quota sampling, pre-testing, a soft launch review, and continuing data-quality checks.

outcome: Implementation of standardized multicountry population health survey and data infrastructure
statement: Instrument content varied by country because of language availability and survey burden, but EQ-5D-5L was included in every listed pilot and main-round country.

Most experts and non-experts stated that the five core EQ-5D-5L dimensions did not comprehensively reflect HRQoL in the Chinese population; appetite, sleep, and tiredness or lack of strength were the most frequent missing areas.
Sleep, tiredness or lack of strength, appetite, and social adaptation were generally judged relevant to HRQoL by both experts and non-experts.

Climate adaptation and emotional control received substantially stronger relevance support from non-experts than from experts; experts viewed them as influenced by geography, behavior, personality, and life events rather than health alone.
Social support performed poorly: most non-experts did not consider it closely related to HRQoL, and even supportive experts often did not think that it reflected differences in health status.

Expert and non-expert comments led to iterative changes in titles, explanatory examples, and five-level wording; after expert-led revisions, almost all non-experts understood the seven candidate items and judged them aligned with EQ-5D-5L.
No additional bolt-on dimension was proposed by more than two respondents after the candidate set was presented.

Respondents identified possible overlap of emotional control and sleep with anxiety or depression, overlap of social adaptation with social support, and a strong association between sleep and tiredness or lack of strength.

The final qualitative-phase set retained sleep problems, tiredness or lack of strength, appetite, climate adaptation, emotional control, and adaptation to society for quantitative testing, and excluded social support.
In open discussion, non-experts most often described health through mobility, physical fitness, spiritual appearance, sleep, mood, susceptibility to illness, and tiredness or lack of strength.

outcome: Modelled utility values and dimension level decrements for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: The preferred age- and sex-adjusted hybrid main effects model gave a French EQ-5D-5L value set with all coefficients logically consistent and values from -0.525 (state 55555) to 1 (state 11111).

outcome: Interview and interviewer quality control flags, exclusions, task durations and model logical consistency
statement: The sample deviated from the French general population, with more women than expected, an excess of respondents aged 25-34 and 55-74 years and a deficit of women aged 75 years and over, plus overrepresentation of Paris and its Petite Couronne.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-5L profile and EQ VAS of respondents
statement: Respondents reported 181 of the 3125 possible health states for their own health; five states (11111, 11112, 11113, 11114, 11121) covered half the reported states, and mean EQ VAS was 79.0.

outcome: Modelled utility values and dimension level decrements for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: The French value of the worst state 55555 (-0.525) differed from other European value sets: Germany -0.661, United Kingdom -0.285, Spain -0.416, Ireland -0.974.

outcome: Interview and interviewer quality control flags, exclusions, task durations and model logical consistency
statement: Seven models were tested; the cTTO Tobit model and the DCE conditional logit model each had one illogically ordered coefficient (MO3 and UA3 respectively), which the hybrid models corrected.

outcome: Modelled utility values and dimension level decrements for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Age was weakly significant in the hybrid model with age and sex (p = 0.023, coefficient 0.00250) and not significant when entered alone (p = 0.066), but weighting was retained for representativeness; adjusted versus unadjusted values differed little (55555: -0.5255 versus -0.5217) and 2402 of 3125 states had higher values in the unadjusted model.

outcome: Modelled utility values and dimension level decrements for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: The ranking of dimensions by cumulative decrement in the adjusted 5L model was pain/discomfort, mobility, self-care, anxiety/depression, usual activities, whereas the French 3L value set ranked mobility and self-care first, followed by pain/discomfort.

outcome: Modelled utility values and dimension level decrements for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: The 5L value distribution shifted towards higher values than the 3L value set, and fewer health states had negative values (401/3125, 12.8% for 5L versus 78/243, 32% for 3L); the crosswalk distribution resembled the 3L value set.

outcome: Modelled utility values and dimension level decrements for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Maximum dimension decrements were smaller in the 5L value set than in the 3L value set (mobility 0.3250 versus 0.5602; pain/discomfort 0.4439 versus 0.4517).

outcome: Interview and interviewer quality control flags, exclusions, task durations and model logical consistency
statement: Of 1143 interviews, 95 were excluded for poor quality, leaving 1048; interviewers completed on average 71.4 interviews (SD 30.9) lasting on average 39.2 minutes (SD 9.4).

outcome: Composite TTO values and DCE choices for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: In the cTTO data, 20.2% of values were negative, 2.3% were at -1, 13.7% of responses showed unwillingness to trade full health, and heaping occurred at 0.5 (9.29%) and -0.5 (5.2%) without interviewer dependence.

outcome: Composite TTO values and DCE choices for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: cTTO and DCE estimates agreed closely (theta rescaling coefficient 5.226) and the DCE model converged better with the adjusted hybrid model than the cTTO model, supporting proportionality and the hybrid approach.

outcome: Proportion of missing responses on the self-reported and proxy-reported EQ-5D-3L-Y
statement: Both versions were highly feasible: the proxy-reported EQ-5D-3L-Y had no missing dimension data, one patient failed to complete the self-report questionnaire and one self-reported item was missing, and less than 3% of VAS responses were missing.

outcome: Patient-proxy agreement on EQ-5D-3L-Y dimension responses (Gwet agreement coefficient and percent agreement)
statement: Agreement between self-reported and proxy-reported EQ-5D-3L-Y dimension responses was very good for mobility, looking after myself, doing usual activities and having pain or discomfort, and good for feeling worried, sad or unhappy.

outcome: Patient-proxy agreement on the EQ VAS score (intraclass correlation coefficient)
statement: Agreement on the EQ VAS score between patients and proxies was poor overall and in every known subgroup.

outcome: Ceiling effects: proportion of "no problems" responses by version and their absolute and relative reduction
statement: Mobility was the only dimension with a significantly reduced proportion of "no problems" responses from the self-report to the proxy-report version.

outcome: Self-reported and proxy-reported EQ VAS scores and their absolute difference
statement: Mean EQ VAS scores did not differ significantly between the self-report and the proxy version, but the mean absolute patient-proxy difference was about nine points.

outcome: Patient-proxy agreement on EQ-5D-3L-Y dimension responses (Gwet agreement coefficient and percent agreement)
statement: In the regression models, proxies with tertiary or university education agreed significantly more often with patients on mobility, whereas thoracic and lumbar curve type and bracing treatment were associated with significantly lower agreement on doing usual activities and on having pain or discomfort respectively.

outcome: Patient-proxy agreement on EQ-5D-3L-Y dimension responses (Gwet agreement coefficient and percent agreement)
statement: In subgroup analyses agreement was similar to the overall sample except that proxy education level was associated with mobility agreement and treatment modality with agreement on having pain or discomfort; no factor was significantly associated with agreement in EQ VAS scores.

outcome: Acceptability of each TTO method from three debriefing questions
statement: cTTO had statistically better results than LTTO and CGTTO on all three debriefing questions. LTTO and CGTTO did not differ significantly at the reported .05 threshold.

outcome: Administration burden from wheelchair-example time, task time, and iteration count
statement: cTTO had the lowest wheelchair-example time, time per valuation task, and iteration count. CGTTO took the longest for the wheelchair example and formal tasks, while LTTO used the most iterative moves.

outcome: Effects of respondent parental status and age on TTO values

The review included 106 studies. EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L had the largest evidence bases, followed by ICECAP-O and ASCOT.

EQ-5D-3L showed acceptable missing-data, internal-consistency, and test-retest results, but it had ceiling effects and limited interrater reliability; validity and responsiveness findings were mixed. EQ-5D-5L showed better known-group validity and interrater reliability, but evidence remained incomplete.

ICECAP-O had low missing-data and ceiling effects and acceptable internal consistency, but validity and responsiveness were mixed and reliability was insufficient. ASCOT had similar reliability concerns and some ceiling effects. Evidence for QOL-ACC and WOOP was promising but too limited to establish responsiveness or reliability.

Content and face validity studies found recurring problems with relevance, missing domains, ambiguous or double-barreled wording, use of aids or assistance, and interpretation of response levels. Generic measures had more reported content problems than older adult-specific measures.
Age-specific evidence was sparse. Ceiling effects were more common in studies with mean ages of 65 to 74 years, while missing values were more frequent in studies with mean ages of 85 years or older.
No instrument had high-quality evidence across all psychometric properties. Most evidence was moderate or low quality because of risk of bias, inconsistency, and insufficient evidence.
Most studies examined adults aged 75 to 84 years, used self-report, and were conducted in community settings. Evidence for the oldest-old, residential aged care, and subgroup comparisons was limited.
No eligible psychometric study was identified for the PROMIS-Preference Score (PROPr).

All 14 invited stakeholders consented and participated in the roundtable; 13 returned the pre-meeting survey.
Most survey respondents had used HRQoL measures, about half used utility measures or estimated QALYs, and most reported high familiarity with HTA.

Views on paying more per QALY gained for children were mixed. Supporters cited children's future contribution, avoidance of undervaluation, and access to innovation; opponents cited double counting of life-years, limited evidence of long-term benefit, and risks of prioritizing one age group.

Most stakeholders supported direct inclusion of adolescents, alone or with adults, because adolescents were thought able to complete valuation tasks and relate better to a 10-year-old perspective. Stakeholders with greater HTA and valuation familiarity more often favored adult respondents to represent voters and taxpayers.

Stakeholders advised collecting adult respondents' parental and child-care experience and considered population weighting of adolescent respondents, but generally opposed multiple US value sets because end-users could be confused or select the set that produced the most favorable QALY gains.

The investigators incorporated the stakeholder input into the subsequent US valuation methodology by including adolescent participants for DCE preference elicitation and adding adult background questions about children and children's illness experience.

The review included 18 studies after screening 4273 deduplicated database records and assessing 98 reports in full text; four included reports were found through citation chasing.
Valuation studies were the largest design group, followed by mapping studies, randomized controlled trials, and outcome-measure development studies.
Preference-elicitation methods varied. The narrative reports DCE with duration as the most common method, followed by standard gamble, while TTO, BWS, standard DCE, and VAS were each used once.
Adults were the most common valuation respondents. Only two studies used children or young people in preference-elicitation tasks, and both also used adult preferences.

Own perspective was the most common valuation perspective. Some adult respondents valued a hypothetical child or young person, and one study changed perspective according to whether the respondent was an adult or a young person.
For methods that produced preferences on a latent scale, DCE with duration was the most common anchoring approach and was used only with adults in this review.
The included valuation studies varied considerably in their choice of condition-specific HRQoL instrument, preference-elicitation method, anchoring method, respondent, and perspective.
The review identified only decompositional approaches for obtaining utility values from condition-specific descriptive systems.

The authors define a broader measurement system as a combined descriptive system drawn from existing instruments plus one value set based on trade-offs across the included quality-of-life dimensions.

The proposed approach can increase sensitivity to wider quality-of-life effects, use existing evidence about the source instruments, support comparison with their separate value sets, and be applied to datasets that contain both instruments.

The main theoretical and practical challenges are incomplete construct coverage, overlap and double counting, redundant items, inconsistent item wording and response scales, many dimensions, and increased cognitive burden during valuation.

The general process has five stages: establish the conceptual basis and select instruments; assess measurement properties and relationships; generate and test the descriptive system; value it to develop a combined value set; and assess applications and decision implications.
For the EQ-5D-5L and ASCOT-SCT4 example, the paper proposes a combined 13-dimension system and recommends psychometric assessment, cognitive testing, pilot valuation, and a main valuation study.
The paper identifies online discrete choice experiments, especially DCE with duration for anchoring on the full-health-to-dead scale, as a flexible valuation approach for the combined system.

The framework predicts that, when an intervention improves both health and broader quality of life, a combined value set can produce larger incremental QALYs and lower ICERs than a health-only value set, although effects will vary across interventions.
All 1047 participants completed both valuation components, yielding 6082 cTTO values and 10458 DCE choices; two DCE responses were not recorded.

outcome: Observed cTTO values for EQ-5D-Y-3L health states
statement: The worst EQ-5D-Y-3L state, 33333, had a mean observed cTTO value of 0.20; most respondents valued it as better than dead.

outcome: Latent DCE coefficients and anchored EQ-5D-Y-3L index values
statement: DCE decrements were largest for pain or discomfort and feeling worried, sad, or unhappy; level 3 pain or discomfort was least preferred, followed by level 3 worried, sad, or unhappy.

outcome: Latent DCE coefficients and anchored EQ-5D-Y-3L index values
statement: The preferred mixed logit and DCE-to-cTTO mapping produced a logically consistent Japanese value set with predicted values from 0.288 for 33333 to 0.957 for the second-best state 12111.

outcome: Protocol compliance, interviewer effects, model fit, and logical consistency
statement: Predicted values closely matched observed cTTO means for the 26 valued states.

outcome: Protocol compliance, interviewer effects, model fit, and logical consistency
statement: Protocol compliance and task engagement were high, few interviews were flagged, no data were excluded through quality control, and no important interviewer effects were detected.

outcome: Bayesian D-error of the DCE design
statement: Designs optimized for a nonlinear multiplicative utility function with a discount function achieved the lowest Bayesian D-errors, and the choice of discount function used for optimization made almost no difference.

outcome: Bayesian D-error of the DCE design
statement: Conventional designs were less efficient for time-preference-corrected QALY tariff estimation, with average relative design efficiencies of 0.91 for the linear multiplicative design, 0.80 for the heterogeneous linear additive design with severity stratification, and 0.69 for the homogeneous linear additive designs without severity stratification.

outcome: Asymptotic standard error and required sample size for the discount rate parameter
statement: Standard homogeneous linear additive designs gave 2.5 to 3.5 times larger asymptotic standard errors and up to 11 times larger required sample sizes for the discount rate parameter than the TPC-optimized designs.

outcome: Asymptotic standard error and required sample size for the discount rate parameter
statement: The exponential discount rate parameter was best identified: its asymptotic standard error was about half that of the hyperbolic and a quarter of the power discount rate parameter.

outcome: Bayesian D-error of the DCE design
statement: Nearly all design improvement occurred early in the optimization and the number of Bayesian draws did not change the ranking of successive designs.

outcome: Feasibility measured as proportion of missing values
statement: Feasibility was good for both instruments, with fewer missing values for the 5L than the 3L.

outcome: Redistribution and inconsistency of responses between 3L and 5L
statement: Inconsistent responses between 3L and 5L averaged 2.9% by dimension, highest for Pain/Discomfort and lowest for Mobility.

outcome: Redistribution and inconsistency of responses between 3L and 5L
statement: Redistribution from 3L to 5L was valid for all 35 consistent 3L-5L level combinations, since mean dimension-specific rating scale scores decreased monotonically from the healthiest to the most disabled response pair.

outcome: Discriminatory power (Shannon and Shannon Evenness indices)
statement: The 5L observed many more unique health states than the 3L.

outcome: Ceiling (proportion reporting 11111)
statement: The ceiling was reduced with the 5L overall, with variation across subgroups and countries.

outcome: Discriminatory power (Shannon and Shannon Evenness indices)
statement: Absolute discriminatory power improved considerably with the 5L and relative discriminatory power (evenness) improved slightly.

outcome: Convergent validity with WHO-5 and dimension-specific rating scales
statement: Convergent validity with the WHO-5 was demonstrated for both versions and was slightly better for 5L, with correlations highest for Anxiety/Depression and the largest 3L-to-5L gain for Mobility.

outcome: Known-groups validity by age, education and smoking status
statement: Known-groups validity was confirmed for both versions: reported problems increased with age and decreased with higher education, and smokers and ex-smokers reported more problems; correlations were generally similar for 3L and 5L.

outcome: Known-groups validity by age, education and smoking status
statement: Accounting for clustering by country left age associations significant but rendered education and smoking associations nonsignificant for all 3L and 5L dimensions.

outcome: Framework of health concepts nominated by Singaporean participants
statement: Participants nominated 70 health concepts, organised into 17 themes and 53 subthemes across five domains: physical health, mental well-being, social relationships, medical conditions and treatment, and health promotion knowledge and behaviours; participants of all three ethnicities nominated concepts in all five domains.

outcome: Relevance of the five EQ-5D descriptive system dimensions to Asians in Singapore
statement: All five EQ-5D descriptive system dimensions were present among the health concepts nominated spontaneously before participants saw the questionnaire: mobility (basic functions), self-care and usual activities (activities), pain/discomfort (undesirable bodily sensations), and anxiety/depression (worry/anxiety and happy/sad).

outcome: Framework of health concepts nominated by Singaporean participants
statement: The most undesirable health problems fell into physical health (mobility, vision, self-care, work, pain, inability to enjoy food), mental well-being (for example anxiety after a serious diagnosis) and social well-being (confinement at home, isolation from social networks).

outcome: Comprehensiveness (adequacy) of the EQ-5D descriptive system and dimensions suggested for addition
statement: Participants generally judged the EQ-5D descriptive system adequate and easy to understand, and of suitable length, but some proposed additional dimensions: appetite, ability to eat and dietary restrictions, sleep, vision, cognitive function/dementia, family relationships, available support, burden to others, medical diagnosis and treatment, and financial burden.

outcome: Comprehensibility of EQ-5D wording and severity labels and participant suggestions for improvement
statement: Reported comprehension and format problems included difficulty with the words anxiety, depression, mobility and discomfort, difficulty distinguishing slight from moderate problems, sensitivity of the anxiety/depression item, perceived overlap of usual activities and self-care with mobility, and suggestions to separate anxiety from depression, add concrete examples, and rate pain on a numeric or face scale.

outcome: Choice blindness (failure to detect the switched card)
statement: Choice blindness was substantially more common in adolescents than adults, both unadjusted and after adjustment for gender and personality traits.

outcome: Logical inconsistency: choosing a dominated health state
statement: Rates of logical inconsistency (choosing the dominated state) did not differ significantly between adolescents and adults.

outcome: Health-state choices across the six pairwise scenarios, including preferring dead to the worst state
statement: The proportion preferring dead over the worst health state '333' did not differ significantly between adolescents and adults.

outcome: Choice blindness (failure to detect the switched card)
statement: Mean conscientiousness score was significantly lower among respondents who were choice blind than among those who were not.

outcome: Health-state choices across the six pairwise scenarios, including preferring dead to the worst state
statement: Higher conscientiousness was associated with lower adjusted odds of several health-state choices, including choosing dead over '333', extreme depression over extreme pain, and extreme pain over extreme dysmobility.

outcome: Health-state choices across the six pairwise scenarios, including preferring dead to the worst state
statement: Higher openness to experience was associated with increased adjusted odds of preferring a health state with extreme pain over extreme dysmobility.

outcome: Health-state choices across the six pairwise scenarios, including preferring dead to the worst state
statement: Adolescents tended more than adults to prefer extreme depression (113) over extreme pain (131), at the exploratory alpha of 0.1.
Pre-existing cardiac disease was common and patients with it were older, more often male, and had more cardiovascular risk factors and other comorbidities than patients without cardiac disease.

Crude in-hospital mortality was higher with pre-existing cardiac disease, but the association between any cardiac disease and mortality was not significant after multivariable adjustment and correction for multiple testing.

Heart failure, especially severe heart failure, had the strongest adjusted association with in-hospital mortality; the other cardiac disease subtypes, including ischaemic heart disease, were not significant after adjustment.
Serious cardiac complications were uncommon during hospitalization, while pulmonary embolism was the most frequent thrombo-embolic complication.
COVID-19 symptoms at hospital presentation varied mainly by age and did not materially differ according to pre-existing cardiac disease.

outcome: Self- and proxy-rated EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS
statement: People living with dementia reported higher mean EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS values than caregiver proxies.

outcome: Agreement and individual-level discrepancy between self- and proxy-rated EQ-5D-5L profiles
statement: Approximately 95% of dyads differed on at least one EQ-5D-5L dimension; only nine dyads had identical profiles.

outcome: Agreement and individual-level discrepancy between self- and proxy-rated EQ-5D-5L profiles
statement: Paretian classification most often placed profiles in the self-better group, followed by mixed, proxy-better, and same ratings.

outcome: Agreement and individual-level discrepancy between self- and proxy-rated EQ-5D-5L profiles
statement: The body text and table show that 62.6% of dyads differed in at least three of five EQ-5D-5L dimensions.

outcome: Agreement and individual-level discrepancy between self- and proxy-rated EQ-5D-5L profiles
statement: Agreement was fair across EQ-5D-5L dimensions and was lowest for usual activities; pain/discomfort had the highest reported weighted kappa.

outcome: Proxy response distribution and central tendency bias
statement: Caregiver proxies chose moderate problems about twice as often as people living with dementia; the contrast was largest for usual activities.

outcome: Agreement and individual-level discrepancy between self- and proxy-rated EQ-5D-5L profiles
statement: Proxy ratings tended to report worse health when self-ratings showed no or few problems, but better health when self-ratings showed more problems; adjusted regression analyses confirmed this pattern, especially in more observable dimensions.

outcome: Self- and proxy-rated EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS
statement: Self-rated EQ-5D results were most strongly associated with self-reported depressive symptoms, while proxy-rated EQ-5D results aligned more closely with proxy-reported functional impairment.
The selected indirect model overpredicted the proportion at the highest possible utility, whereas the selected direct Tobit model predicted almost no observations at the ceiling.
The adjusted limited dependent variable mixture model did not converge for any predictor set, and the robust mixture model failed to converge for several predictor sets.
Adding child age, gender, and report type to the predictor sets did not materially improve predictive accuracy, so the final algorithms excluded these variables.

The selected direct mapping was a Tobit model using the 25 PROMIS-25 raw item scores to predict Australian EQ-5D-Y-3L utilities. Candidate OLS, Tobit, generalized linear, and mixture models had similar average errors, but the selected Tobit model better represented the lower utility range.

The selected indirect mapping was a generalized ordered logit model using six PROMIS-25 raw domain scores. It predicted EQ-5D-Y-3L responses and outperformed ordered logit; generalized ordered logit and multinomial logit otherwise had similar errors.

PROMIS-25 and EQ-5D-Y-3L showed moderate-to-high domain correlations and construct overlap. EQ-5D-Y-3L worried/sad/unhappy correlated strongly with all PROMIS-25 anxiety and depressive-symptom items, and pain/discomfort correlated strongly with several PROMIS-25 pain items.

Sensitivity analyses with Netherlands EQ-5D-Y-3L utilities selected the same generalized ordered logit and Tobit specifications. Performance was similar, although the Australian-utility models had slightly lower errors.
Using the Singapore value sets, EQ-5D-5L utilities showed a larger and statistically significant mean improvement after cataract surgery, whereas the EQ-5D-3L change was smaller and not significant.

All three responsiveness statistics were higher for EQ-5D-5L than EQ-5D-3L utilities with the Singapore value sets, and the same pattern held with the UK/England value sets with slightly smaller magnitude.
EQ-5D-5L utilities derived with the crosswalk algorithm were slightly more responsive than utilities derived from the EQ-VT-based EQ-5D-5L value sets.
SF-6D utilities were slightly more responsive than EQ-5D-5L utilities, and HUI3 and the non-preference-based VF-12 were markedly more responsive than all EQ-5D and SF-6D utilities.

More patients reported problems with EQ-5D-5L than EQ-5D-3L in most dimensions, and pre- to post-operative improvement was concentrated in mobility, pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression, with greater change captured by EQ-5D-5L.
Cataract surgery produced a clear clinical benefit in the sample, with mean best spectacle-corrected visual acuity improving from 0.53 to 0.07 LogMAR.

outcome: Standardized factor loadings of the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions on a single latent HRQOL factor (confirmatory factor analysis)
statement: In the single-factor confirmatory factor analysis, Mobility, Self-Care, Usual Activities and Pain/Discomfort loaded well on one latent HRQOL factor, while Anxiety/Depression loaded distinctly lower in nearly all data sets and subgroups.

outcome: Model fit statistics (chi-square, RMSEA, SRMR, CFI, TLI) for reflective, formative and combined measurement models
statement: Modelling the EQ-5D-5L item responses as categorical variables gave better fit than modelling them as continuous variables in the confirmatory factor analysis.

outcome: Model fit statistics (chi-square, RMSEA, SRMR, CFI, TLI) for reflective, formative and combined measurement models
statement: External MIMIC models, with EQ-5D-5L items as composite indicators and SF-36, HUI3, QWB and VAS scores as reflective indicators, had poor absolute fit, and the two-factor model fitted only marginally better than the one-factor model; adding HUI3, VAS and QWB indicators did not substantially improve fit.

outcome: Standardized regression coefficients of EQ-5D-5L dimensions as formative/composite indicators in external MIMIC models
statement: In all external MIMIC models the standardized coefficient of Self-Care was much smaller than those of the other dimensions and was not statistically significant in several specifications.

outcome: Model fit statistics (chi-square, RMSEA, SRMR, CFI, TLI) for reflective, formative and combined measurement models
statement: Internal MIMIC model 3b (formative indicators Mobility, Anxiety/Depression, Pain/Discomfort; reflective indicators Self-Care, Usual Activities) had the best fit across almost all subgroups and data sets, exceptions being the Spanish valuation data set and liver disease.

outcome: Standardized factor loadings of the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions on a single latent HRQOL factor (confirmatory factor analysis)
statement: The Spanish valuation data set behaved as an outlier: Anxiety/Depression had the highest factor loading of all dimensions while Usual Activities and Pain/Discomfort loaded low, and internal MIMIC model 3b did not fit best.

outcome: Model fit statistics (chi-square, RMSEA, SRMR, CFI, TLI) for reflective, formative and combined measurement models
statement: Model fit was better for healthy and general population respondents than for respondents with at least one self-reported illness across all three model types, while the mixed patient/general population data sets (crosswalk and MIC) fitted most poorly.

outcome: Distribution of EQ-5D-5L dimension responses and EQ VAS scores across the nine data sets
statement: The pooled analysis covered 26 521 respondents from nine data sets, representing 25 types of diseases or conditions from 13 countries, with individual data sets ranging from 230 to 8022 respondents.

outcome: Conceptual challenges and proposed recommendations for infant and toddler HRQoL measurement
statement: Six conceptual challenges for infant and toddler HRQoL measurement were identified: what concepts to measure; how to identify which concepts matter; proxy reporting; rapid developmental change; transitioning between instruments; and spillover effects.

outcome: Conceptual challenges and proposed recommendations for infant and toddler HRQoL measurement
statement: Eight recommendations are proposed, including greater consensus on a core HRQoL conceptual model, operationalising subjective aspects through observable behavioural correlates, prioritising primary caregiver perspectives, using the primary caregiver as default proxy with an observer-based response perspective, designing items to detect HRQoL change rather than developmental change, deciding between continuity and age-based sensitivity, and minimising capture of caregiver or family spillover.

Existing HRQoL instruments for very young children are heterogeneous in the concepts they capture and do not reflect a shared core conceptualisation of HRQoL, which limits comparability and adds uncertainty in health technology assessment.

Submissions to NICE and in Australia for children under five have mostly used generic HRQoL measures and value sets designed for adults, which lack content validity for infants and toddlers and can yield biased utility estimates.

In its development EQ-TIPS prioritised age-related content validity over continuity with the EQ-5D-Y, adding dimensions such as eating or drinking and sleep that the EQ-5D-Y does not cover, so implications of transitions between descriptive systems require further research.

EQ-TIPS experimental version 3.0 contains seven observably operationalised dimensions (movement, eating or drinking, sleep, pain, managing emotions, interacting with others, play) with three-level and five-level variants, retains the EQ VAS and a 'Today' recall period, and is completed by a proxy, typically the parent.

outcome: Hospital ward and accident-and-emergency admissions during the first year
statement: During the first year, the functional model had fewer hospital ward admissions and fewer accident-and-emergency admissions per patient than the integrated model.

outcome: Cumulative hospital ward days per patient during the first year
statement: Cumulative hospital ward days per patient were lower under the functional model in both the unadjusted comparison and analyses adjusted for baseline differences.

outcome: Institutionalization and respite-care use during the first year
statement: Institutionalization was less frequent under the functional model, while use of respite care was more frequent.

outcome: Home visits, specialist contacts, tests, and other service use during the first year
statement: The functional model provided more intensive home follow-up and requested more complementary tests, without a difference in the number of prescribed drugs or in-person referrals to hospital specialists.

outcome: Mortality during the first year
statement: First-year mortality did not differ significantly between the care models after adjustment.

outcome: Baseline health-related quality of life
statement: Baseline perceived health status measured with EuroQol did not differ between groups, while patient experience of care measured with IEXPAC differed statistically.
Participants in the functional-model group had higher baseline comorbidity and dependency and more private caregiver support than participants in the integrated-model group.

outcome: Ceiling and floor of items, health-state profiles and utilities
statement: A much larger share of respondents reported the best possible health state on the EQ-5D-5L than on the PROMIS measures, and respondents at the EQ-5D-5L ceiling still reported some impairment on PROMIS items.

outcome: Informativity measured by Shannon's index and Shannon's evenness index
statement: Most matched PROMIS items had lower ceilings and higher relative informativity than the corresponding EQ-5D-5L items, while the EQ-5D-5L had lower floor in most pairs.

outcome: Convergent and divergent validity between EQ-5D-5L and PROMIS items, domains and utilities
statement: Convergent validity was supported: most matched PROMIS items and domains correlated at least moderately with their paired EQ-5D-5L items and domains, whereas PROMIS sleep disturbance and cognitive function, which have no EQ-5D-5L counterpart, correlated weakly.

outcome: Agreement between EQ-5D-5L and PROPr utilities (ICC, Bland-Altman)
statement: Mean EQ-5D-5L utilities were substantially higher than PROPr utilities, EQ-5D-5L utilities exceeded PROPr utilities in 97.1% of respondents, and agreement between the two was only fair.

outcome: Informativity measured by Shannon's index and Shannon's evenness index
statement: PROPr used a much narrower utility range but more evenly, giving higher absolute and relative informativity of the utility distribution than the EQ-5D-5L.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L and PROPr utility scores derived with US value sets
statement: EQ-5D-5L utilities decreased with age while PROPr utilities slightly increased with age.

outcome: Known-group validity and relative efficiency (F-statistic ratio, AUROC ratio) of EQ-5D-5L versus PROPr utilities
statement: EQ-5D-5L utilities discriminated significantly better than PROPr across many known groups defined by age, self-perceived health status and physician-diagnosed conditions.

EQ-HWB items 1 to 20 had no missing responses. Item 22 had 23 missing responses, possibly because respondents overlooked it in the survey layout; items 23 and 24 each had 2 missing responses and item 25 had 1.
Physical items generally showed fewer problems than psychosocial items. Exhaustion and sleep problems had the largest proportions reporting often or most or all of the time.

EQ-HWB level sum scores and EQ-HWB-S index scores differed in the hypothesized direction across caregiver chronic health condition, caregiving time, caregiver general health, dementia severity, and shared caregiving comparisons. Their effect sizes were similar to C-DEMQOL and generally larger than CarerQoL-7D effect sizes.

At item level, 13 of 25 EQ-HWB items discriminated caregivers by caregiving time and 23 of 25 items discriminated them by general self-reported health. Seeing and hearing did not discriminate either grouping.

Adjusted gamma-log generalized linear models retained significant differences in EQ-HWB-S index scores for caregiving time and caregiver general health after control for caregiver age and gender; recruitment source was not significant.
Of 45 hypothesized EQ-HWB and CarerQoL item correlations, 39 reached at least 0.3. All 15 hypothesized correlations between EQ-HWB items and C-DEMQOL domains reached at least 0.3.
Exploratory factor analysis produced a 9-factor solution that explained 99.4% of cumulative variance. Four EQ-HWB items did not load on a factor: seeing, hearing, sleep, and exhaustion.
The study completed five co-design workshops, nine feedback sessions, and two optimisation sessions.

The final P-PROM ROCK Program combined six elements: clinician training, patient and caregiver information, EQ-5D-Y-5L displays, integration into journeys and clinical systems, family resources, and clinician resources.

Participants preferred item and response-level wording in a table because it was easier to interpret than a single summary score; the longitudinal graph showed each item separately and reversed the usual item-score direction so that higher values indicated better health.
Patients or caregivers control which EQ-5D-Y-5L items are flagged for discussion; flagged items appear only in the clinician display as red text with yellow highlighting.

The program links EQ-5D-Y-5L completion to a specific outpatient visit, permits completion up to seven days before the visit through Epic MyChart or on paper, and makes the clinician allocated to the visit responsible for review.
Response support includes clinician training, a four-part decision support tool, family resources for mild or moderate concerns, and clinician resources for urgent concerns.
The authors found that joint involvement of adolescent patients, caregivers, and service providers was feasible and essential to a user-centred design.

The three EuroQol TTO protocols differ mainly in trade-off framework, iteration algorithm, termination rule, mode and method of administration, respondent training and quality control: MVH and Paris use conventional TTO with a 10-year horizon administered on paper with a time board, whereas EQ-VT uses composite TTO with computer-assisted personal interviewing.

The Paris protocol simplifies MVH iteration by terminating at an indifference interval of one year rather than six months, halving the number of possible x values, which the authors expect to improve efficiency without materially changing mean values.

Use of the MVH protocol revealed within-respondent logical inconsistency, large variance between respondents, interviewer effects and a non-continuous value distribution, and MVH-like variants used in other studies hampered comparability of value sets.

EQ-VT design choices were informed by empirical work: composite TTO was selected after comparing conventional, lead-time and lag-time TTO, and face-to-face interviewing was retained because group interviews and internet surveys produced many respondents stating indifference after only one or two iteration steps, indicating poorer comprehension or engagement.

Interviewer effects on protocol compliance and on obtained TTO values were detected in studies using EQ-VT version 1.0, prompting the addition of quality control software for real-time monitoring in version 2.
DCE cannot replace TTO for QALY weights because DCE values are on an arbitrary scale, but TTO and DCE data can be combined in a hybrid maximum likelihood model linking the two scales.

outcome: Prevalence of reported problems by EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: Most respondents reported no problems on all EQ-5D-5L dimensions. Pain or discomfort had the highest prevalence of slight-to-extreme problems, followed by anxiety or depression.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state utility score using the Philippine value set
statement: EQ-5D-5L utility scores were strongly concentrated near full health. No analyzed respondent had a negative utility or a health state scored as worse than dead.

outcome: EQ VAS score from 0 to 100
statement: EQ VAS scores were also concentrated near the top of the scale.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state utility score using the Philippine value set
statement: In the main Tobit model for EQ-5D-5L utility, savings of about one year of earnings were positively associated with HRQoL. Student status, Protestant affiliation, monthly or weekly religious attendance, family caregiving, urban residence, residence in Visayas or Mindanao, and diagnosed disease were significantly negatively associated with HRQoL.

outcome: EQ VAS score from 0 to 100
statement: In the reported EQ VAS model, student status and diagnosed disease were significantly associated with lower scores.

outcome: Self-rated health, analyzed as good or very good versus fair or poor
statement: Older age, partnered status, residence in Mindanao, caring for others, and diagnosed disease were associated with lower odds of good or very good self-rated health. Longer available savings were associated with higher odds of good or very good self-rated health.
Beta-regression, nested-model, and ordinal-logistic sensitivity analyses generally preserved the directions and conclusions of the main analyses, with some changes in significance levels.

The 12 national valuation studies were sufficiently comparable in their methods, procedures, and analyses to support pooling, although sample size, valued health-state count, exclusion criteria, model specifications, and some translations differed.
