Ten national studies used the British MVH protocol as their starting point; the Hungarian and Romanian studies used cTTO within EQ-VT. All studies used face-to-face TTO interviews, a 10-year duration, and a VAS or ranking warm-up task.
The 2,916 simulated country-health-state utilities ranged from -0.865 to 1.000.
OLS was the preferred model because it balanced model fit, prediction error, and convergence; its values formed the reported pan-European EQ-5D-3L value set.
The two-component finite mixture model had the lowest AIC but the largest RMSE of the candidate models, and its population-weighted specification did not converge.
Population-size weighting made only small changes to the OLS coefficients, but the weighted usual-activities level-2 coefficient was not statistically significant.
The residual plot showed no visible heteroskedastic pattern, and the Breusch-Pagan/Cook-Weisberg test supported the OLS homoskedasticity assumption.

outcome: Proportion of respondents choosing scenario B (the shorter time in full health) in each binary-choice question
statement: Health-state preferences were not independent of the duration of the state, but no clear pattern emerged: pooling across states only the 10-week duration differed significantly from the 10-year reference, and coefficients varied by dimension and severity, so the study produced no strong evidence for or against constant proportional time trade-off.

outcome: Failure of the logical dominance consistency test
statement: A small minority of online respondents failed a logical dominance test embedded in the type I questions; failure was associated with being male, having continued education past the minimum school leaving age and poorer self-reported health, but not with the time taken to complete the module.

outcome: Proportion of respondents choosing scenario B (the shorter time in full health) in each binary-choice question
statement: Changing the person perspective from "you" to "somebody else" or "somebody else like you" produced no consistent effect across states; the "somebody else like you" perspective modestly reduced the probability of choosing full health overall, with the clearest state-specific differences for extreme mobility problems and extreme depression.

outcome: Proportion of respondents choosing scenario B (the shorter time in full health) in each binary-choice question
statement: Adding lead time changed responses in 6 of 16 matched scenario pairs, but with no clear pattern across dimension, severity, duration or lead-time-to-duration ratio; the proportions choosing scenario B with and without lead time correlated highly.

outcome: Propensity to exhaust lead time when valuing the worst EQ-5D-5L state
statement: Exhaustion of lead time when valuing state 55555 fell as the lead time to duration ratio rose, but fewer than half of respondents exhausted lead time only once the ratio reached 5:1, a much higher incidence than the 20-25% observed in earlier face-to-face iterative lead-time TTO.

outcome: Implied minimum rate of time preference consistent with the observed choices
statement: Implied minimum rates of time preference were positive in most scenarios, fluctuated by state and duration, reached very high values for short durations, shifted leftwards (lower rates) as duration increased, and did not differ systematically by perspective.

outcome: Proportion of respondents choosing scenario B (the shorter time in full health) in each binary-choice question
statement: Attaching a satisfaction level to the health-state description significantly changed preferences: low health satisfaction increased the probability of choosing the shorter time in full health, while high health satisfaction, high life satisfaction or having learnt to live with the condition reduced it; respondents' own satisfaction with their health or life had no consistent effect.

outcome: Anchored EQ-5D-5L dimension-level coefficients and predicted health-state values from DCE with duration
statement: The PRET-AS DCE with duration produced coefficients that were logically ordered within every dimension except mobility level 2, which had the wrong sign but was not significant, and produced a unimodal distribution of predicted values for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L states without arbitrary transformation of negative values or exogenous anchoring of dead.

outcome: Anchored EQ-5D-5L dimension-level coefficients and predicted health-state values from DCE with duration
statement: The smaller PRET DCE-with-duration data set (two tasks per respondent) produced several disordered and non-significant coefficients, showing that two observations from about 3000 respondents were insufficient for a satisfactory EQ-5D-5L value set.

outcome: Anchored EQ-5D-5L dimension-level coefficients and predicted health-state values from DCE with duration
statement: Compared with the MVH TTO tariff for the 243 comparable EQ-5D states, the DCETTO predictions differed by a mean absolute value of 0.11, agreed on the classification of most states as better or worse than dead, and diverged most for the worst mobility level, whose wording changed between the three-level and five-level instruments.

outcome: Time-trading behaviour, learning and fatigue effects, and the effect of the number of tasks per respondent
statement: Most respondents traded time when duration differed across a scenario pair, and the proportion choosing the scenario with more QALYs increased with the absolute QALY difference, although a few pairs with small QALY differences produced highly uneven response splits.

outcome: Time-trading behaviour, learning and fatigue effects, and the effect of the number of tasks per respondent
statement: Predicted values across the three task modules correlated very highly, but the estimated scale parameters fell across the choice sequence, indicating a fatigue effect, and a likelihood ratio test narrowly rejected preference stability across batches; batches of 10 or 15 tasks per respondent gave more concentrated predictions than 5 tasks from a larger sample.

outcome: Predicted median health-state values for five EQ-5D-3L states from binary-choice lead-time TTO
statement: Binary-choice lead-time TTO responses were explained by the value V presented, by duration and by lead time, and yielded median health-state values, but the values for severe states were highly sensitive to the model and to assumptions about duration and lead time.

outcome: Equivalence of responses to binary-choice valuation questions across administration modes
statement: The proportion of respondents choosing scenario B did not differ significantly between the online and CAPI administrations for any of the twelve experimental questions, and neither mode of administration, time taken, nor their interaction predicted responses.

outcome: Self-reported health status, health satisfaction and life satisfaction of the online and CAPI samples
statement: The online and CAPI samples matched on age and gender but differed on other characteristics: the online sample was more educated and reported significantly worse health, health satisfaction and life satisfaction, while the CAPI sample contained more married or partnered respondents and took longer to complete the survey.

outcome: Acceptability and reported difficulty of the three binary-choice valuation tasks
statement: About half of stage 3 respondents found the two task types equally difficult, but when a difference was reported the binary-choice TTO and lead-time TTO tasks were judged easier than the DCE with duration.

outcome: Perceived importance of EQ-5D-5L dimensions and ability to distinguish adjacent severity levels
statement: Duration, whether in full health or in the health state, was ranked the most important attribute in the decision, and among the EQ-5D-5L dimensions mobility was ranked most important and anxiety/depression least important, matching the order in which they are presented in the descriptive system.

outcome: Perceived importance of EQ-5D-5L dimensions and ability to distinguish adjacent severity levels
statement: A substantial minority of respondents could not always distinguish severe from extreme problems, and many respondents attended only to the subjectively most important attributes rather than to all of them.

outcome: Attribute attendance and the influence of personal and subjective factors on responses
statement: Personal and subjective factors influenced responses: most respondents imagined themselves in the state, most said their answers were influenced by how the state would affect people close to them, and being married or partnered was significantly associated with that influence.

outcome: Respondent-reported strategies, complexity and acceptability of the valuation tasks
statement: Think-aloud interviews showed that respondents used a range of strategies, comparing dimensions, severity levels, duration or combinations of these; some attended to every attribute and others only to selected components.

outcome: Respondent-reported strategies, complexity and acceptability of the valuation tasks
statement: Adding duration to the DCE made duration an important part of the choice for many respondents, supporting the DCE-with-duration approach, but respondents differed in whether they prioritised length or quality of life and were sensitive to the particular duration levels used.

outcome: Comprehensibility and plausibility of EQ-5D-5L health states and severity levels
statement: Respondents incorporated personal factors such as their own and others' illness experience, coping, life stage, family responsibilities and assumptions about treatment, and some judged particular EQ-5D-5L state combinations implausible or found the immediate-death option hard to conceptualise.

outcome: Comprehensibility and plausibility of EQ-5D-5L health states and severity levels
statement: Uncertainty about the relative ordering of severe and extreme problems recurred in the think-aloud interviews, although at the aggregate level the PRET-AS data produced significantly different coefficients for every pair of adjacent levels within each dimension.

All EQ-HWB response options and a broad score range were used. EQ-HWB-S showed a low risk of ceiling or floor effects in both samples, although full health was more common in the general-population sample.
The EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-9 level-sum scores were very highly correlated in both samples, which indicates similar score-level behavior of the long and short forms.
Convergent validity was supported most strongly by EQ-5D-5L and ICECAP-A at score level. Correlations were generally higher in the health-condition sample than in the general-population sample.
Item-level convergence was strongest for related EQ-HWB and EQ-5D-5L items. Correlations with conceptually related SWEMWBS, ICECAP-A, and ASCOT items were often lower than hypothesized.

The EQ-HWB measures discriminated all tested prespecified known groups. They had the largest standardized effect sizes for groups defined by emotional problems and were broadly comparable with EQ-5D-5L for physical-health comparisons.

Within condition groups, poorer EQ-HWB outcomes were associated with more diabetes complications, more affected joints in arthritis, and respiratory symptoms; the arthritis pattern was not strictly monotonic.
All three EQ-HWB scoring approaches had very good score-level test-retest reliability in both samples, with intraclass correlation coefficients above 0.866.

Item-level test-retest agreement was weaker than score-level reliability. Kappa values ranged from fair to moderate or substantial, and some items that were expected to be stable had only fair or moderate reliability.

All four instruments had high profile-level ceiling effects in the total sample. Adapted versions usually had lower dimension-level ceiling effects than originals, except for looking after themselves, but their profile-level ceiling percentages were slightly higher. Ceiling effects fell substantially in children with special healthcare needs and were absent by the prespecified 15% threshold when caregiver-rated health was poor, fair, or good.

The instruments discriminated children with specific chronic conditions from healthy children, except for asthma with the original EQ-5D-Y-5L. The adapted EQ-5D-Y-3L had larger effect sizes for 8 of 10 conditions, and the adapted EQ-5D-Y-5L had larger effect sizes for all 10 conditions. The largest effects occurred for autism, behavioural problems, and developmental delay.
The adapted and original EQ-5D-Y-3L versions converged strongly, as did the adapted and original EQ-5D-Y-5L versions.

Adapted versions generally produced more responses at severe levels than original versions, especially for mobility and usual activities and among children with special healthcare needs; the difference was more marked for EQ-5D-Y-5L.
Most proxy respondents found all four EQ-5D-Y versions easy to complete, with no significant differences in reported difficulty.

Probability-of-superiority analysis showed little or no difference between adapted and original versions. Supplementary utility-score analyses for EQ-5D-Y-3L were broadly comparable with level-sum-score analyses.
Adapted versions had stronger four-week test-retest reliability than original versions for level sum scores and for most dimensions. Utility-score analysis also favored the adapted EQ-5D-Y-3L.

Level sum scores for all versions changed in the hypothesized direction for better, unchanged, and worse health at 4 weeks. The adapted EQ-5D-Y-5L showed a statistically significant small response for improved health. Small worse-health samples prevented formal comparison of adapted and original versions.
All instruments discriminated the main known groups. Adapted versions generally produced wider level-sum-score differences and larger Cohen d effect sizes than original versions.
A latent-scale DCE can establish the relative importance of EQ-TIPS dimensions, but it cannot by itself anchor values at 0 and 1 for QALY estimation.
The standard 10-year cTTO duration is not suitable for EQ-TIPS because it extends far beyond the 0-to-3-year target range and uses descriptions that are not relevant to older children.

A shorter TTO duration can increase non-trading and reluctance to sacrifice life-years, while a composite EQ-TIPS and EQ-5D-Y-3L scenario creates problems of equivalence, comprehension, additive independence, and interpretation.

Parents or caregivers of infants and toddlers may be better able than other adults to conceptualize EQ-TIPS states; however, a parent-based sample departs from the usual general-public approach and evidence about preference differences is limited.
Proxy 2 valuation is conceptually problematic because it asks an adult to represent preferences that an infant or toddler might not be able to form; the authors therefore favor Proxy 1 options.

Respondents may include future developmental, health, social, educational, employment, and socioeconomic consequences in current infant health-state values, which can cause double counting in economic models.
Poor infant health can affect parents, caregivers, and siblings, and these spillover effects are difficult to separate from the value assigned to the child's health state.

Mapping EQ-TIPS responses to EQ-5D-Y-3L or EQ-5D-Y-5L values could avoid direct age-specific elicitation and reduce discontinuities across age groups, but it assumes that values elicited for older children apply to EQ-TIPS states.

outcome: Mean utilities for hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis health states
statement: All EQ-5D utilities showed better quality of life for hemodialysis than peritoneal dialysis; 5L value set utilities were generally higher and showed slightly smaller HD-PD differences than crosswalk-based utilities.

outcome: Incremental QALYs of hemodialysis versus peritoneal dialysis
statement: In the model for non-diabetic ESRD patients, incremental QALYs based on the 5L value set and the crosswalk were similar across the seven countries.

outcome: Incremental QALYs of hemodialysis versus peritoneal dialysis
statement: In the model for diabetic ESRD patients, the 5L value set generally produced more incremental QALYs than the crosswalk, whereas in the model for all ESRD patients it produced fewer.

outcome: Incremental QALYs of hemodialysis versus peritoneal dialysis
statement: The magnitude of the difference between 5L- and crosswalk-based incremental QALYs varied by country, being largest with the Chinese value sets and smallest with the Dutch value sets; the 5L value set gave more incremental QALYs for China and the crosswalk gave more for South Korea in all three models.

outcome: Incremental QALYs of hemodialysis versus peritoneal dialysis
statement: In all models, incremental QALYs were a positive linear function of both the utility of peritoneal dialysis and the difference in utilities between the two dialysis treatments.
In the preferred mixed-effects model, the lead-time TTO frame B substantially increased the odds of a worse-than-dead classification relative to regular TTO frame A.

Frames C and D did not differ clearly from regular TTO frame A, contrary to the hypotheses that removing immediate death or changing wording about death would increase worse-than-dead classifications.
The longevity frame E increased the odds of a worse-than-dead classification relative to regular TTO frame A.
The quality-of-life-improvement frame F greatly decreased the odds of a worse-than-dead classification relative to frame A, but it also produced much poorer response quality.
Respondents were mostly in good self-reported health.
Respondent heterogeneity was substantial. The mixed-distribution model estimated a subgroup with an extremely low propensity to classify states as worse than dead.
Frame F showed markedly more comprehension and consistency problems than the other frames; the respondent-frame garbage-class model estimated much more inattentive responding for frame F.

Acceptance of euthanasia and age younger than 40 years independently increased the propensity to classify a health state as worse than dead; caring responsibilities were not associated with a greater preference for life.

outcome: Thought processes and reasoning expressed while responding to the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system, EQ VAS and the open-ended TTO question
statement: Two themes were developed from four categories: participants personalized the questions and considered which aspects to include in the response, and they used reference points and comparators to enable assessment of their own health; the four categories were contextualizing and interpreting instructions, relating the questions to one's own health, using different recall periods and time perspectives, and using personal, interpersonal or normative comparators.

outcome: Number of life years in full health traded in the open-ended TTO question for own current health
statement: The concepts of full health and best imaginable health were difficult to define, imagine or relate to; two participants gave no TTO answer because full health was not a realistic scenario for a person with a lifelong chronic disease.

outcome: Thought processes and reasoning expressed while responding to the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system, EQ VAS and the open-ended TTO question
statement: Participants used comparators to anchor their assessments, most often their own previous health or earlier experiences, and less often the health of other people; in the EQ VAS most related their health to 100 as best imaginable health, some used only part of the scale, and little attention was given to the worst imaginable health end point.

outcome: Thought processes and reasoning expressed while responding to the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system, EQ VAS and the open-ended TTO question
statement: Participants reflected that adaptation of expectations and activities, self-image, having rather than being a chronic disease, and age influenced their responses, and only problems that prevented them from doing what they wanted were considered in the TTO trade-off.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-5L health profiles and EQ VAS scores
statement: Reported responses across the three assessments did not always follow similar patterns: most participants reported no or slight problems on the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system while EQ VAS scores ranged widely and almost all TTO answers indicated no trade of life years.

outcome: Thought processes and reasoning expressed while responding to the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system, EQ VAS and the open-ended TTO question
statement: Before answering, participants reasoned about the purpose and context of the assessment, who asked the questions, and whether their answers could lead to action, and they wanted to explain their answers and discuss areas for improvement.

outcome: Perceived relevance, comprehensiveness and comprehensibility of the EQ-5D-5L dimensions and instructions
statement: Instructions for the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system and EQ VAS were generally comprehensible, but participants found it challenging to reduce the experience of their own health and everyday life into a single response option or number, especially when problems were severe but rare.

outcome: Perceived relevance, comprehensiveness and comprehensibility of the EQ-5D-5L dimensions and instructions
statement: Interpretation of the anxiety/depression dimension varied, and it was generally read as two separate constructs, while pain/discomfort was not read as two constructs: discomfort was interpreted as a consequence of pain, so problems such as low blood sugar were not reported on that dimension.

outcome: Perceived relevance, comprehensiveness and comprehensibility of the EQ-5D-5L dimensions and instructions
statement: Some participants found one or more EQ-5D-5L dimensions irrelevant or intended for someone older or more severely ill, and named missing aspects including sleep, stress, physical capability, treatment burden and positive abilities, while the anxiety/depression dimension was seen as relevant for worry about future diabetes complications.

outcome: Thought processes and reasoning expressed while responding to the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system, EQ VAS and the open-ended TTO question
statement: The EQ VAS allowed participants to include any aspect they considered important, including diabetes and other health problems, physical activity, diet, sleep, stress, well-being, relationships and job satisfaction, and it was described as representing their feeling about being in a certain state of health.

outcome: Thought processes and reasoning expressed while responding to the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system, EQ VAS and the open-ended TTO question
statement: Recall periods and time perspectives differed from the instructions: responses to the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system and EQ VAS were often based on typical or usual health over recent weeks or months rather than health today, with temporary problems overlooked, whereas the TTO question shifted the focus to the future, plans, goals and expected health deterioration.

outcome: Number of life years in full health traded in the open-ended TTO question for own current health
statement: All participants considered the trade-off between life years and health in the TTO question, although some had to read the instructions several times, some found the scenario too hypothetical or complex, and some were unsure where to put the mark on the 0-10 year line.

outcome: Number of life years in full health traded in the open-ended TTO question for own current health
statement: Most participants did not want to trade any life years, explaining that their lives were good, that they did not want to give up other parts of life, and that they wanted to give as much time as possible to family or people depending on them; impact on others, personal goal achievement and expectations of future health were more clearly integrated in the TTO than in the other two assessments.

The task force judged all five EQ-5D dimensions and the VAS concept applicable to children and adolescents, with only minor changes to the operational definitions, mainly to make clear that items refer to health-related and not age-related limitation.

Wording was changed to uniform response options ('no', 'some', 'a lot of' problems; 'not', 'a bit', 'very' worried, sad or unhappy), which made the third level less extreme than in the EQ-5D, and dimension labels were reworded (for example 'Looking after myself' and 'Feeling worried, sad or unhappy').

outcome: Comprehensibility and interpretation of EQ-5D-Y items and VAS by young respondents
statement: Cognitive interviews with 103 children and adolescents in four countries showed the EQ-5D-Y was well accepted and comprehensible, and almost all respondents answered without assistance; the 'Looking after myself' item was misinterpreted by a small number of younger or chronically ill respondents but was retained.
Testing of several VAS variants in Italy and Germany led to a youth VAS with simplified instructions, marking an X directly on the scale instead of drawing a line from a box, and a finer graduation.

outcome: Frequencies of reported problems by dimension and mean VAS score
statement: Pupils reported more problems on the EQ-5D-Y than on the EQ-5D for mobility, pain or discomfort, and feeling worried, sad or unhappy, with no consistent pattern for looking after myself or usual activities.

outcome: Frequencies of reported problems by dimension and mean VAS score
statement: Mean VAS scores did not differ significantly between the two versions in any country.

outcome: Percentage of missing values on the descriptive system and the VAS
statement: The EQ-5D-Y produced fewer missing values than the EQ-5D, significantly so for all five dimensions in Germany and for the VAS in all three countries.

outcome: Acceptance and ease of completion of the two questionnaire versions
statement: German pupils rated the EQ-5D-Y as easier to understand than the EQ-5D.

outcome: Death thought accessibility score, range 0 to 11
statement: Mean death thought accessibility scores were similar in the TTO, EQ VAS, and television-control conditions and were highest in the mortality-salient condition.

outcome: Death thought accessibility score, range 0 to 11
statement: Death thought accessibility differed across the four conditions, but Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise differences occurred only because the mortality-salient condition exceeded every other condition; the mortality-salience manipulation check passed.

outcome: Death thought accessibility score, range 0 to 11
statement: Contrary to the hypothesis, death thought accessibility in the TTO condition tended to be lower than in the television-control condition.

outcome: Death thought accessibility score, range 0 to 11
statement: Death thought accessibility was not associated with TTO scores, but it had weak negative correlations with EQ VAS scores for wheelchair and self-experienced health.

outcome: TTO score for living 10 years in a wheelchair
statement: Worse attachment anxiety and avoidance were weakly and negatively associated with TTO and EQ VAS scores for self-experienced health, but associations with hypothetical wheelchair scores were absent or judged not meaningful.
Attachment anxiety moderated the association between death thought accessibility and the wheelchair EQ VAS score in Study 2.

outcome: Consistency of TTO response sequence
statement: Most TTO observations had a consistent preference-switch sequence, and response-time and non-trader sensitivity analyses gave comparable results.

outcome: Unconscious cultural worldview defense strength
statement: The unconscious cultural worldview defense measure did not differ significantly between mortality-salient and control conditions and was discarded from further analysis.

outcome: Conscious defense strength measured by emotional lability bias
statement: The conscious emotional-lability defense measure followed the expected direction but did not differ significantly between conditions and was discarded from further analysis.

Pain/discomfort was the most frequently reported EQ-5D-3L problem in most registers and in the general population at baseline and 1-year follow-up; respiratory failure was the main exception, with mobility problems most prevalent.
Mean EQ VAS scores varied widely across diagnoses at both time points.
Mean EQ VAS scores increased over 1 year in most patient groups, with the largest overall gains in hip and spine patients; scores decreased in fracture and respiratory-failure patients.

The improved Paretian category had the largest proportion for many diagnoses, especially in intervention-based ankle, hip, knee, and spine registers. Respiratory-failure and fracture groups most often worsened, while heart-failure patients had similar improved and worsened proportions.

After adjustment for age and sex, most diagnoses had lower mean EQ VAS scores than the general population at baseline. At 1 year, most diagnoses improved but generally remained below the general-population level; fracture patients were the principal exception.

Women had significantly lower age-adjusted mean EQ VAS scores in most registers and in the general population. Exceptions occurred for fracture and respiratory failure at baseline and for BOA, fracture, heart failure, and respiratory failure at follow-up.
Changes in EQ VAS scores generally corresponded to EQ-5D-3L profile change: scores increased in Paretian improved categories and decreased in worsened categories.

Analyses that included all complete baseline records or all complete follow-up records showed patterns comparable with the paired main analysis, supporting use of the reported tables as diagnosis reference data except for fracture baseline values.

outcome: Revised EQ VAS ratings for 11111, 55555, and dead on the 0-100 scale
statement: In the matched samples, the 2020 mean rating for full health state 11111 was lower than in 2018, and the adjusted Tobit survey-period coefficient was also negative.

outcome: Revised EQ VAS ratings for 11111, 55555, and dead on the 0-100 scale
statement: In the matched samples, the 2020 mean rating for extreme-problems state 55555 was higher than in 2018, and the adjusted Tobit survey-period coefficient was positive.

outcome: Revised EQ VAS ratings for 11111, 55555, and dead on the 0-100 scale
statement: In the matched samples, the 2020 mean rating for dead was lower than in 2018, and the adjusted Tobit survey-period coefficient was negative.

outcome: Rescaled value for EQ-5D-5L state 55555 on the full health = 1, dead = 0 scale
statement: On the full health = 1, dead = 0 scale, state 55555 had a higher mean value in 2020; more respondents rated it better than dead, and the adjusted Tobit coefficient was positive.

outcome: Revised EQ VAS ratings for 11111, 55555, and dead on the 0-100 scale
statement: Interaction models indicated that COVID-19-period differences varied by age, sex, ethnicity, education, and own EQ-5D-5L health for some raw ratings; age was the only demographic characteristic with a significant interaction for rescaled 55555 values.
Results were qualitatively unchanged with multiple imputation for illogical responses, genetic rather than nearest-neighbor matching, and alternative censoring points for rescaled 55555 values.

outcome: Illogical VAS responses and censored rescaled values
statement: Illogical VAS responses were more frequent in the 2020 survey than in the 2018 survey.
The value sets showed moderate-to-good concordance, with slightly higher agreement before surgery and negligible or no sex differences.
The 2023 value set produced a small increase in post-operative full-health scores because health states 11111 and 11211 both received utility 1.00.
The 2023 value set produced smaller mean pre-operative to post-operative improvements; effect sizes were smaller after hip and knee replacement and unchanged after shoulder replacement.
The proportion of procedures with a clinically important improvement of at least 0.28 utility units was lower with the 2023 value set in all cohorts.
Mean 6-month post-operative utility scores were 0.11 to 0.14 units higher with the 2023 value set.
Mean pre-operative utility scores were substantially higher with the 2023 value set in all three procedure cohorts.
The 2023 value set had a narrower scoring range and produced fewer and less extreme negative utility scores than the 2013 value set.
The 2023 value set classified fewer pre-operative observations as worse than dead in every cohort.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index value, EQ VAS score and proportion reporting problems per EQ-5D-5L domain
statement: In the 245 analysed burn patients the mean EQ-5D-5L index value was 0.87 and the mean EQ VAS 81.6; pain/discomfort was the most affected domain, with 39.2% reporting at least slight problems.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index value, EQ VAS score and proportion reporting problems per EQ-5D-5L domain
statement: In multivariable regression on the EQ VAS, neither POSAS pain nor POSAS itching was significant, while the EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort domain, age and comorbidity were significant predictors.

outcome: Self-reported scar pain and itching on the POSAS patient scale
statement: The POSAS pain and itching items themselves were moderately correlated with each other (Spearman rho = 0.489, p < 0.001), and patients with comorbidity had significantly worse EQ-5D-5L and POSAS outcomes than those without.

outcome: Self-reported scar pain and itching on the POSAS patient scale
statement: On the POSAS patient scale 25.7% reported pain (score >= 2) and 48.2% reported itching (score >= 2), so more patients reported problems on the single POSAS items than on the composite EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort domain.

outcome: Correspondence of reported problems between the EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort domain and the POSAS pain, itching and worst-count items
statement: Most patients gave corresponding answers on the EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort domain and the POSAS pain item (73%); of the 27% with non-corresponding answers, 75% reported no POSAS pain but slight to severe EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort problems, and the two items were statistically related.

outcome: Correspondence of reported problems between the EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort domain and the POSAS pain, itching and worst-count items
statement: Most patients gave corresponding answers on the EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort domain and the POSAS itching item (70%); of the 30% with non-corresponding answers, 65% reported POSAS itching but no EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort problems, and the two items were statistically related.

outcome: Convergent validity of the EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort domain against the POSAS pain and itching items (Spearman rank correlation)
statement: The EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort domain correlated moderately with both the POSAS pain item and the POSAS itching item, with correlations of similar magnitude, and correlated more strongly with the POSAS worst-count variable.

outcome: Convergent validity of the EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort domain against the POSAS pain and itching items (Spearman rank correlation)
statement: In the subgroup reporting pain but no itching the correlation of the pain/discomfort domain with POSAS pain was strong but not statistically significant (n = 10), while in the subgroup reporting itching but no pain the correlation with POSAS itching was moderate and significant.

outcome: Convergent validity of the EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort domain against the POSAS pain and itching items (Spearman rank correlation)
statement: The other EQ-5D-5L domains correlated less strongly with the POSAS pain and itching items than the pain/discomfort domain, with usual activities showing the highest and self-care or mobility the lowest correlations.

outcome: Convergent validity of the EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort domain against the POSAS pain and itching items (Spearman rank correlation)
statement: In multivariable regression adjusted for demographic and clinical variables, both POSAS pain and POSAS itching were significantly associated with the EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort domain score, with a larger coefficient for pain than for itching.

outcome: Convergent validity of the EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort domain against the POSAS pain and itching items (Spearman rank correlation)
statement: In the comorbidity subgroup only POSAS pain remained significantly associated with the pain/discomfort domain, whereas in patients without comorbidity both POSAS pain and POSAS itching were significantly associated.

outcome: Support for legalisation of euthanasia
statement: Three quarters of the sample favoured access to physician-provided euthanasia for a person with a painful incurable disease who requested it, while over 40% attended religious services at least monthly.

outcome: Support for legalisation of euthanasia
statement: Greater religiosity significantly reduced support for euthanasia; weekly attenders were much less likely to support euthanasia than those attending a few times a year or less, although over 40% of weekly attenders still favoured access.

outcome: Probability of assigning a worse-than-dead value in composite TTO
statement: Support for euthanasia significantly increased the likelihood of assigning a worse-than-dead value to a health state, and older age also increased that likelihood.

The correlation between the error terms of the euthanasia and worse-than-dead equations was large, negative and significant, supporting endogeneity between attitudes to euthanasia and readiness to assign worse-than-dead values.

outcome: Probability of assigning a worse-than-dead value in composite TTO
statement: The probability of assigning a worse-than-dead value increased with the severity of the EQ-5D-5L state valued, with the largest effects for extreme pain/discomfort and severe or extreme anxiety/depression.

Results were robust in sensitivity analyses that grouped equal-to-dead valuations with worse-than-dead valuations; in a reduced-form probit religiosity was less significant and had a smaller effect than attitudes to euthanasia.

EQ-5D-5L had lower ceiling effects than EQ-5D-3L in every dimension and condition group; the largest reductions were in pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression, and the HIV/AIDS group had relative reductions above 30% in every dimension.
Both versions distinguished each of the four condition groups from the healthy group in dimension-response distributions, which supports known-groups validity.

EQ-5D-5L had higher relative efficiency than EQ-5D-3L when the healthy group was compared with the condition groups; the EQ-5D-3L index did not show a statistically important difference between the healthy and HIV/AIDS groups.
EQ-5D-5L produced more unique reported health states in every group than EQ-5D-3L.

EQ-5D-5L index values had a wider, smoother, and less clustered distribution than EQ-5D-3L index values, although EQ-5D-5L values clustered at 0.734 for the HIV/AIDS group because health state 22222 was frequent.

Mean EQ-5D index values were highest in the healthy group and lowest in the generalized anxiety disorder group for both descriptive systems; condition-group mean values were broadly comparable between versions.
EQ-5D-5L detected mild problems that EQ-5D-3L did not detect in some physical-condition groups: the HIV/AIDS median profile was 22222 with EQ-5D-5L but 11111 with EQ-5D-3L.

outcome: Occurrence and prevalence of cardiac arrhythmias and conduction disorders during hospitalisation
statement: Atrial fibrillation and/or atrial flutter was the main electrical disorder during hospitalisation; most affected patients had new-onset AF/AFL, while ventricular arrhythmias were rare.
Among examined baseline characteristics, pre-existing heart failure had the strongest reported association with development of new-onset AF/AFL.

outcome: In-hospital mortality
statement: In univariable analysis, new-onset AF/AFL during hospitalisation was associated with higher in-hospital mortality.

outcome: In-hospital mortality
statement: After modeling age continuously and allowing interactions with sex and new-onset AF/AFL, increased mortality associated with new-onset AF/AFL was restricted to males aged about 60–72 years.

outcome: In-hospital mortality
statement: The mortality association was not observed in female patients and was largely attenuated in older male patients.

The EQ-HWB uses response-level descriptions based on frequency, severity, and difficulty. The authors state that switching between these formats can be cognitively demanding for self-report and for valuation tasks.

The 25-item EQ-HWB creates challenges for preference elicitation and may be unattractive in applied studies. Cited uptake reviews showed that the three shortest generic preference-based measures accounted for approximately 87% of use in published cost-utility analyses.

For the 9-item short form, a four-level system would produce 4^9 health-state combinations instead of 5^9 and could reduce space, response time, complexity, and the difficulty of estimating preference weights.
The circumstances in which EQ-HWB should be used instead of EQ-5D have not been determined, and EQ-HWB is not intended to replace EQ-5D.
It is not yet clear whether findings about EQ-HWB translate across cultures and languages. The Argentina work provides an early framework for face-validity assessment in a non-English setting.
Both infliximab products improved EQ-5D utility from very poor pretreatment levels after at least 12 weeks of treatment.
Mean utility improvement was slightly larger with Remicade than with Remsima, but the between-group difference was not statistically significant.
At follow-up, limitation in usual activities was lower in the Remicade group than in the Remsima group; this was the only EQ-5D dimension with a significant between-group difference.
The two groups had no significant follow-up differences in mobility, self-care, pain or discomfort, or anxiety or depression.
Using 2019 prices, Remicade produced slightly more QALYs at a higher annual direct cost, with an ICER of 40,909 USD per QALY.
Using 2021 prices, Remicade was less costly and produced slightly more QALYs than Remsima, so Remicade was dominant.
Infliximab treatment duration was substantially longer in the Remicade group than in the Remsima group.

outcome: Utility decrements associated with levels of the respiratory bolt-on dimension
statement: Observed mean TTO values for health states with level 4 or 5 on the respiratory dimension were significantly lower than for the same states in the Dutch EQ-5D-5L valuation study without a respiratory dimension, and DCE choice probabilities for these states were also lower.

outcome: Utility decrements associated with levels of the respiratory bolt-on dimension
statement: In hybrid models, the bolt-on 'limitations in physical activities due to shortness of breath' produced significant utility decrements at levels 3 to 5.

outcome: Utility decrements associated with levels of the respiratory bolt-on dimension
statement: The 'breathing problems' bolt-on produced larger utility decrements than the physical activity bolt-on at the same levels.

outcome: Distributional performance: proportion reporting full health (ceiling) on EQ-5D-5L versus EQ-5D-5L+C
statement: Adding the cognitive domain slightly reduced ceiling: 26.3% of respondents reported full health on the EQ-5D-5L at 6 months versus 24.1% on the EQ-5D-5L+C; the reduction was largest in TBI patients (36.3% to 28.9%) and absent in PTSD patients (0.9% on both).
Responders differed significantly from non-responders in age, education level, number of chronic conditions, hospitalisation and presence of PTSD, but not in sex or TBI.

outcome: Self-reported health of trauma patients: EQ-5D-5L+C domain problems, level sum scores and EQ VAS at 6 and 12 months
statement: Cognitive problems at 6 months were reported by 26.2% of responders, a prevalence similar to anxiety/depression (25.6%) and higher than self-care (20.8%).

outcome: Classification efficiency (informativity): Shannon Index H' and Shannon Evenness Index J', crude and adjusted for underestimation bias
statement: Only 308 of 3125 possible EQ-5D profiles and 460 of 15,625 possible EQ-5D+C profiles were observed; crude Shannon Evenness was lower for EQ-5D+C, but after adjustment for underestimation bias the adjusted H' and J' were higher for EQ-5D+C in every subgroup, indicating more captured information.

outcome: Convergent validity: Spearman correlation of level sum score with EQ VAS
statement: Convergent validity with the EQ VAS was slightly higher for EQ-5D+C than for EQ-5D in every group, and was markedly lower in PTSD respondents than in other groups.

outcome: Explanatory power: adjusted R-squared of multivariable regression of EQ VAS on domain levels
statement: Explanatory power of EQ VAS variance increased slightly when cognition was added; in the TBI/PTSD group the best five-domain model replaced anxiety/depression with cognition.

outcome: Discriminatory power: mean level sum score differences between clinical subgroups
statement: Mean level sum scores of EQ-5D and rescaled EQ-5D+C differed significantly in all groups except TBI patients, and level sum scores discriminated between TBI, PTSD and neither, and between numbers of chronic conditions.

outcome: Responsiveness: Paretian classification of health change and probability of superiority between 6 and 12 months
statement: With the cognitive domain, the Paretian classification shifted respondents from unambiguous change into the non-categorisable (mixed change) category, most strongly in PTSD respondents, because cognition often changed in the opposite direction to the other domains.

outcome: Responsiveness: Paretian classification of health change and probability of superiority between 6 and 12 months
statement: In TBI patients the addition of the cognitive domain reduced the 'no problems' category by 6.9 percentage points and increased the 'improve' category by 1.8 percentage points.

outcome: Responsiveness: Paretian classification of health change and probability of superiority between 6 and 12 months
statement: Probability of superiority over 6 to 12 months was highest for usual activities and pain/discomfort (0.58) and lowest for cognition (0.50), but cognition improved more in TBI and PTSD respondents (0.52 each) than in respondents with neither (0.50).

Full-health profiles were uncommon: the paper reported full health for 15 participants on EQ-5D-Y-3L, 17 on EQ-5D-Y-5L, and 5 on CHU9D. Dimension-level no-problem responses nevertheless showed ceiling effects.

Most hypothesized correlations between EQ-5D-Y or CHU9D dimensions and PedsQL subscales were statistically significant. EQ-5D-Y pain/discomfort correlated more strongly with emotional than physical functioning, and usual activities correlated only mildly with PedsQL school functioning.
Cross-instrument concordance was moderate for EQ-5D-Y-3L versus EQ-5D-Y-5L, poor for EQ-5D-Y-3L versus CHU9D, and higher for EQ-5D-Y-5L versus CHU9D.
Scale-level test-retest reliability was good for EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, and CHU9D among the 88 participants who reported unchanged health.

Item-level agreement was mostly moderate for both EQ-5D-Y versions. EQ-5D-Y usual activities had only fair agreement, while CHU9D join-in-activities had poor agreement; CHU9D sleep, annoyed, and pain showed good agreement.

The EQ-5D-Y instruments distinguished more OI-related known groups than CHU9D and PedsQL. Only EQ-5D-Y-5L detected a significant difference by number of symptoms, and no instrument detected significant differences for bluish sclera or short stature groups.
EQ-5D-Y-3L showed slightly stronger convergent correlations in some comparisons, whereas EQ-5D-Y-5L showed a lower ceiling effect and greater known-group discriminatory ability.
The sample had poor HRQoL relative to cited general-population values, with low mean EQ-5D-Y-3L and CHU9D utilities and a low mean rescaled EQ-5D-Y-5L level-sum score.
Nearly half of respondents reported some type of sleep problem on CHU9D, while EQ-5D-Y has no sleep dimension.

outcome: Agreement between cTTO and BTD methods, logical consistency, and test-retest reliability
statement: Overall agreement between the ternary cTTO and binary BTD responses was high, with a pooled polychoric correlation of 0.791; agreement was lowest for health states valued close to dead.

outcome: Classification of health states as better than, equal to, or worse than dead
statement: Health states were classified as worse than dead far more often in the BTD method than in the cTTO, while equal-to-dead responses in the cTTO were rare.

outcome: Agreement between cTTO and BTD methods, logical consistency, and test-retest reliability
statement: Logical inconsistencies were rare and comparable across methods, with about 91% of respondents having no inconsistency in either task.

outcome: Agreement between cTTO and BTD methods, logical consistency, and test-retest reliability
statement: Test-retest reliability was equal for both methods at 88% identical responses, with correlations of 0.865 (BTD, tetrachoric) and 0.897 (cTTO, polychoric).

outcome: Task difficulty ratings and time needed per valuation question
statement: The two tasks were rated similarly easy to understand and to discriminate between health states, but BTD questions took much less time than cTTO questions.

outcome: Agreement between cTTO and BTD methods, logical consistency, and test-retest reliability
statement: Task order did not affect agreement between methods for any health state, and mean cTTO utilities were independent of order except for state 33444.

outcome: Perceived benefits and uses of routine quality-of-life measurement
statement: Participants saw routine quality-of-life measurement as a way to formalize assessment, identify resident needs and practice improvements, support person-centred care planning, monitor provider performance, and inform families, managers, government, and prospective consumers.

outcome: Implementation barriers and feasibility
statement: Participants expected resistance from providers and staff, administrative burden, limited time and resources, competing care priorities, and resident survey fatigue or refusal. Some participants thought a government mandate was needed for sector-wide uptake.

outcome: Preferred routine quality-of-life collection process
statement: Workshop participants generally preferred integration into existing care-plan evaluations. They considered registered nurses well placed to organize or administer collection because nurses have a holistic view, administrative and clinical skills, and authority to act on results.

outcome: Preferred routine quality-of-life collection process
statement: The most common preferred collection frequency across groups was six monthly. Participants also favored a private and relaxed setting, a staff member who had good rapport with the resident, and flexible timing that reflected resident capacity, preferences, and staff workload.

outcome: Validity and data-quality concerns
statement: Participants warned that time pressure could cause box-ticking or staff substitution of professional opinions for resident responses. They also described incentives for staff or providers to manipulate responses that could reflect poorly on care quality.

outcome: Validity and data-quality concerns
statement: Residents could withhold negative experiences because they feared repercussions or did not want to implicate liked staff. Some residents were skeptical about the benefit of surveys and reported being tired of repeated questions and forms.

outcome: Validity and data-quality concerns
statement: Participants considered proxy reporting necessary for some residents but questioned its validity. Family knowledge varied with contact, family members might rate quality of life lower or seek to influence care, and staff might present care too positively.

outcome: Resident, family, and staff acceptability of routine surveys
statement: Participants estimated that only about half of residents might self-complete with adequate support. They recommended brief measures, simple wording, and adaptation to communication, vision, cognition, and fluctuating capacity.

outcome: Number, scope, and identity of pictorial paediatric HRQoL PROMs
statement: The review identified 22 paediatric pictorial PROMs comprising 28 unique versions; 15 versions were generic, 11 were condition-specific, and two were domain-specific.

outcome: Instrument design, format, recall period, length, and administration characteristics
statement: Recall periods varied: eight versions used today or current health, eight used periods from the past week to the past month, three used a general period without a specific duration, and nine did not state a recall period.

outcome: Evidence about the performance of pictorial versus text-only PROMs
statement: The review found some evidence that pictorial PROMs facilitate child self-report and can improve measurement properties compared with text-only PROMs, but it did not perform a comprehensive psychometric appraisal.

outcome: Number, scope, and identity of pictorial paediatric HRQoL PROMs
statement: Only two of the 28 versions were preference-weighted measures with value sets: CHU9D animation/CHILDSPLA and 17D.

outcome: Instrument design, format, recall period, length, and administration characteristics
statement: The reviewed PROMs targeted ages from 3 to 18 years, contained 4 to 45 items, and had reported completion times from 3–5 minutes to 20–30 minutes.

outcome: Instrument design, format, recall period, length, and administration characteristics
statement: Most versions used pictorial Likert response scales, usually with happy–sad faces or cartoons and pictures.

outcome: Development methods and child involvement in pictorial content
statement: The review reported that 13 of 28 versions involved children in development of pictorial elements; literature reviews and focus groups each informed 12 versions, expert consultation informed nine, and interviews informed 17.

outcome: Instrument design, format, recall period, length, and administration characteristics
statement: Self-administration was intended for 71% of versions, interviewer-assisted administration for 29%, and seven versions used electronic data collection.

outcome: Cross-cultural considerations in instrument development
statement: Only three reviewed measures addressed cross-cultural issues during development.

outcome: Number, scope, and identity of pictorial paediatric HRQoL PROMs
statement: Physical health was the most common synthesized domain, followed by emotional health and social functioning; environment was least common.

outcome: Instrument design, format, recall period, length, and administration characteristics
statement: Reviewer agreement for study selection was reported as good.

All three stakeholder groups received EQ-TIPS positively and identified potential uses in primary-care surveillance, clinical practice, applied and interventional research, health-economic decision making, and policy.

Caregivers generally interpreted the dimensions correctly and supplied appropriate examples, but relevance was less certain for infants than for toddlers, particularly for children younger than six months.

Stakeholders largely supported the relevance and overall content validity of the six current dimensions, but they identified wording and comprehensibility changes that need further testing, especially examples to reduce subjective interpretation.
Sleep and emotional functioning or mood were the most frequent candidate dimensions for further multinational investigation.

Stakeholders questioned whether social interaction and communication were distinct enough as currently worded and whether the dimensions captured age-related nuances, particularly in infants younger than six months.

Proxy reporting was the main measurement concern. Caregiver perspective, knowledge of child development, family and environmental context, and wide normal developmental variation could bias judgments, especially judgments based on the term age-appropriate.

Views on the Today recall period and the three severity levels were mixed, and response rates for these later survey questions were low. Some respondents preferred examples, clearer severity anchors, a frequency scale, or a longer recall period.

outcome: Perceived severity score (0-100) of EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-3L response labels and its deviation across language versions
statement: EQ-5D-5L labels describing different levels of health problems received clearly different severity scores, while labels describing the same level received similar scores across dimensions.

outcome: Perceived severity score (0-100) of EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-3L response labels and its deviation across language versions
statement: Cross-language variation was minimal for the EQ-5D-5L labels 'slight(ly)' and 'severe(ly)': no group mean deviated from the grand mean by more than 5 points on the 0-100 scale for 'slight(ly)' in any of the five dimensions after adjustment for age, gender and education.

outcome: Perceived severity score (0-100) of EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-3L response labels and its deviation across language versions
statement: The Chinese label for 'moderate(ly)' was rated as more severe than the average of the four language versions in all five EQ-5D-5L dimensions, while French respondents rated it lower.

outcome: Perceived severity score (0-100) of EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-3L response labels and its deviation across language versions
statement: For the EQ-5D-3L label 'some problems', Spanish respondents gave significantly lower and French respondents significantly higher severity scores than the four-language average in the three functional dimensions.

outcome: Proportion of respondents violating the hypothesised ordinality of EQ-5D-5L labels
statement: Violations of the hypothesised ordinality of the EQ-5D-5L labels occurred in only a small proportion of respondents, mainly for 'slight(ly)' versus 'moderate(ly)' in the Spanish group and for 'severe(ly)' versus 'extreme(ly)' in the English, French and Chinese groups on the symptom dimensions.

outcome: Proportion of respondents violating the hypothesised ordinality of EQ-5D-5L labels
statement: Ordinality violations were more prevalent among respondents with lower educational level.

Translation produced few linguistic problems. Cognitive debriefing identified overly formal Afrikaans terms for proxy, grimacing, and adequate oral intake; caregiver-proposed vernacular alternatives were implemented before psychometric testing. The resulting descriptive system was generally understood and accepted.

All 162 caregivers completed every EQ-TIPS dimension and the EQ VAS. Seventy-five children had the best descriptive profile 111111, and no child had the worst profile 333333. In contrast, 75 caregivers had some missing ASQ responses and 5 could not be scored.
Known-groups testing showed more reported pain among inpatients than outpatients. Other individual dimensions and the overall 111111 ceiling did not differ significantly by care group.
Outpatients had better caregiver-rated general health and fewer reported EQ-TIPS problems than inpatients, shown by higher EQ VAS and lower level sum scores.
Children aged 0 to 12 months had fewer reported movement problems and a higher 111111 ceiling than older children. EQ VAS and level sum scores did not differ significantly among the three age groups.
Concurrent validity was moderate for EQ-TIPS pain against FLACC. Hypothesized associations for other dimensions were weak but significant, except the play and ASQ fine-motor association.

After six regression outliers were excluded, EQ-TIPS dimension levels explained 38% of EQ VAS variance. Severe pain and eating problems and some play problems had significant negative coefficients; the largest negative coefficient was for severe pain.
The EQ-TIPS had no preference-based score. The study therefore summarized the six three-level dimensions with a level sum score from 6, best descriptive profile, to 18, most severe profile.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L item acceptability assessed by non-response
statement: Mobility-item non-response was concentrated in wheelchair users; no mobility responses were missing in the no-MAT and walking-aid groups.

outcome: Response distribution and discriminatory informativity of EQ-5D-3L dimensions
statement: The mobility item had the poorest response distribution and informativity. All walking-aid users selected “some problems,” and the mobility Shannon indices were zero in this group.

outcome: Convergent and divergent validity of EQ-5D-3L dimensions and index
statement: In wheelchair users, mobility showed moderate convergent correlations with ataxia severity and activities of daily living. A mobility correlation could not be calculated for walking-aid users because all responses were identical.

outcome: Convergent and divergent validity of EQ-5D-3L dimensions and index
statement: Among wheelchair users, the EQ-5D-3L index had stronger associations with SARA and ADL than were present in less-supported groups, while INAS associations with EQ-5D outcomes were weak or negligible.

outcome: Responsiveness of EQ-5D-3L dimensions and index over three years
statement: Over three years, the mobility item showed almost no change in walking-aid users but substantially more deterioration in wheelchair users.

outcome: Responsiveness of EQ-5D-3L dimensions and index over three years
statement: SARA and ADL showed moderate-to-large longitudinal effect sizes, while EQ-5D-3L changes were generally absent-to-small; walking-aid users had no significant EQ-5D-3L effect sizes over three years.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L index and EQ VAS health status
statement: Baseline EQ-5D-3L index scores were lower with greater mobility-support use, while EQ VAS scores did not differ significantly across support groups.
The updated value set ranged from 1 for full health to -0.723 for health state 33333.
Pain/discomfort had the largest level-3 decrement, followed by mobility, anxiety/depression, self-care, and usual activities.
Agreement with the existing Dutch EQ-5D-3L value set was limited; the concordance coefficient was 0.890 and the error measures showed material differences.

Compared with the existing value set, the updated set gave slightly lower values for mild states, slightly higher values for moderate states, and substantially lower values for severe states, especially states below zero.
Mild-to-severe anxiety and depression symptoms were common in the full sample.
Suboptimal self-confidence and social-connectedness outcomes were common in the full sample.
Anxiety and depression prevalence differed across countries and was lowest in China and highest in Italy.

In pooled exploratory factor analysis, two interpretable correlated factors were identified: internal states, dominated by GAD-7 and PHQ-9 with some contribution from self-confidence, and social connectedness, defined by social participation, contact with others, and feeling connected.
The country-specific factor pattern was broadly similar, but Greece had the reversed factor order and China had a third factor that separated objective social participation from felt connectedness.

Younger respondents generally reported more anxiety, depression, and problems with self-confidence and social connectedness; female respondents reported more anxiety and depression than male respondents.

Across countries, more chronic conditions, perceived COVID-19 risk, and feeling less protected against COVID-19 were associated with worse internal-state and social-connectedness factor scores; not living alone was associated with better social connectedness.
More than 80% of respondents who met the mild-to-severe anxiety criterion also met the mild-to-severe depression criterion.
In the full sample of 750 respondents, the default garbage-class mixed logit model estimated that about 34% of respondents belonged to the garbage class.

After the model accounted for random response patterns, mean preference estimates for faster, more convenient, and more reliable tests moved farther from zero, relative standard deviations became smaller, and posterior correlations changed from positive to mainly negative.
Changing the class-membership prior from Bernoulli(0.5) to Bernoulli(0.8) reduced the estimated garbage-class share to about 28%, but the main contrast with the standard mixed logit results remained.

A standard mixed logit model fitted after removing respondents with posterior garbage-class probability of at least 0.5 retained 540 respondents and produced estimates similar to the Bernoulli(0.8) garbage-class model.

The garbage_mixl and JAGS implementations produced nearly identical standard and garbage-class mixed logit estimates within Monte Carlo sampling precision, which confirmed the correctness of the implementation.
All commands produced similar standard panel mixed logit estimates, but garbage_mixl completed the reported benchmark much faster than the comparison implementations.
The achieved Metropolis-within-Gibbs and MALA acceptance rates were close to their targets, and Monte Carlo standard errors were generally less than 5% to 10% of posterior standard deviations.
Within-person recall-period profile agreement was much higher for EQ-5D-5L than for EQ-HWB-9, and agreement fell further when best-health profiles were excluded.
For both instruments, last-week recall produced lower scale-level ceilings, more reported problems, and generally greater response informativity than today recall.

Most hypothesized item associations were at least moderate. Last-week EQ-HWB-9 items consistently correlated more strongly with related external content than today items, while EQ-5D-5L showed a mixed or negligible recall-period pattern.
Absolute informativity was higher for last-week recall for all items except EQ-5D-5L usual activities, and recall-related informativity differences were larger for EQ-HWB-9.
Last-week versions distinguished slightly more prespecified known groups with moderate or large effects, and the clearest advantage was for mental health subgroups.
Differences between today and last-week recall were generally small, but recall-period effects were slightly larger for EQ-HWB-9 than for EQ-5D-5L.
Analyses stratified by educational attainment showed no meaningful differences in the psychometric findings.

Principal component analysis found five common domains under both recall periods; factor loadings for both EuroQol instruments changed little, although a separate sleep factor appeared only in the today analysis.

outcome: Uncertainty, fear, worry, and anxiety during childbearing
statement: Uncertainty was prominent in experiences of COVID-19 infection, vaccination decisions, and birth. Participants worried about unknown effects on themselves, fetuses, newborns, and other children, and about changing hospital restrictions and support at birth.

outcome: Uncertainty, fear, worry, and anxiety during childbearing
statement: Participants described fear, worry, anxiety, hypervigilance, isolation, and prolonged rumination. Pandemic conditions made even low-risk pregnancy resemble the uncertainty that is often associated with high-risk pregnancy.

outcome: Coping, resilience, and concealed well-being needs
statement: Participants developed resilience through deliberate calm, acceptance of limited control, gratitude for survival, solidarity with others, humility, courage, and support from community or therapy.

outcome: Coping, resilience, and concealed well-being needs
statement: Resilience was sometimes only an external appearance. Some women concealed depression, fear, stress, or vulnerability while they protected family members and met expectations to be strong, resilient mothers.

Compared with annual family income above CAD 150,000, the lowest income category and undisclosed income were associated with significantly lower EQ-5D-3L utilities in both primary multivariable models.
Lower income was associated with more severe problems in the EQ-5D-3L pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression dimensions; the other three dimension correlations were not statistically significant.
Mean utility differed across cancer sites, and colorectal cancer had a significantly higher adjusted utility than head and neck cancer in both primary models.
The interaction between categorical age and birth sex was not statistically significant.
Five-level bolt-ons performed better than three-level bolt-ons on the item-level ceiling criterion that used a 70% cutoff.
No included publication reported content-validity evidence or qualitative evidence on acceptability.

Divergent validity against unrelated domains was generally good, but convergent-validity performance was mixed. Some bolt-ons had moderate or strong correlations with the EQ-5D usual activities and anxiety/depression dimensions.
The review included 101 publications from 72 unique studies and assessed 15 three-level and 13 five-level cognition bolt-ons.

Adding a cognition bolt-on produced limited and variable ceiling reduction. Absolute informativity increased in all reported cases, but relative informativity decreased slightly. Associations with EQ VAS usually improved only slightly.
The Janssen 2013 five-level global cognition bolt-on and the Haagsma 2005 three-level thinking-ability bolt-on had the most assessments; every other bolt-on had fewer than 10 assessments.
Five-level cognition bolt-ons had a more favorable positive-to-nonpositive assessment ratio than three-level bolt-ons.
Evidence was mixed in the two populations represented by at least 10 studies: head or brain injury and dementia.

Evidence was sparse and generally unfavorable for responsiveness and test-retest reliability. Only two publications assessed patient-proxy agreement, and no publication assessed differential item functioning.

Two publications assessed structural validity. In both, cognition bolt-ons grouped with the EQ-5D anxiety/depression item; in one study, the bolt-on did not load on a separate cognition factor defined by PROMIS cognition items.

Known-groups validity was the most frequently assessed property. Bolt-on items differentiated 56% of known groups for 3L and 29% for 5L, while EQ-5D plus bolt-on differentiated 88% for 3L and 80% for 5L. Positive evidence was most common for injury characteristics, acute or chronic conditions and comorbidities, and sociodemographic groups.

outcome: Presence of at least one logically inconsistent composite TTO valuation
statement: Inadequate health literacy was reported by 7% of respondents and 11% had at least one logical inconsistency in their valuations.

outcome: Presence of at least one logically inconsistent composite TTO valuation
statement: Logical inconsistencies were more common in respondents with inadequate health literacy (23%) than in those with adequate health literacy (10%).

outcome: Presence of at least one logically inconsistent composite TTO valuation
statement: In adjusted logistic regression, inadequate health literacy roughly doubled the odds of an inconsistent valuation.

outcome: Presence of at least one logically inconsistent composite TTO valuation
statement: Two of the three health literacy components were associated with inconsistency, while lacking confidence in completing medical forms was not.
Respondents with inadequate health literacy had lower socio-economic and health status, including lower education, unemployment, rural residence and lower EQ VAS scores.

outcome: Self-reported difficulty of the TTO task
statement: Respondents with inadequate health literacy reported understanding the valuation questions as often as those with adequate health literacy, despite more inconsistencies.
Immunologic and musculoskeletal conditions had the strongest associations with greater pain frequency.

Condition-specific associations differed by response format: depression was associated with pain and discomfort frequency but not severity; cancer and dermatologic conditions were associated with pain frequency only; neurologic conditions were associated with pain severity only.

All EQ-HWB pain and discomfort frequency and severity items and the EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort item had strong, statistically significant correlations. The strongest reported full-sample correlations were between EQ-HWB pain severity and pain frequency and between pain severity and discomfort severity.
Frequency and severity response formats showed large differential item functioning for pain, driven mainly by uniform DIF, but negligible DIF for discomfort.
Frequency response scales had higher absolute and relative informativity than severity scales for pain and discomfort in the full sample and in most examined subgroups.
The graded response model showed that severity items had higher discrimination and wider threshold ranges, while frequency items were more sensitive at lower latent-trait levels.

outcome: Feasibility: time to complete tasks and perceived task difficulty
statement: DCE tasks took less time than BWS tasks overall, although per-question times were similar.

outcome: Feasibility: time to complete tasks and perceived task difficulty
statement: More participants reported severe difficulty choosing among three health states than between two health states, and about 70% reported some difficulty imagining EQ-5D-5L health states.

outcome: Test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient) of DCE and BWS responses
statement: Test-retest reliability was higher for the DCE than for the BWS.

outcome: Agreement between choice-task rankings and VAS rankings, and dominance-task pass rates
statement: Almost all participants passed the dominance validity checks in both tasks.

outcome: Agreement between choice-task rankings and VAS rankings, and dominance-task pass rates
statement: Choice task rankings agreed closely with VAS rankings of the same health states.

outcome: Latent utilities (regression coefficients) for EQ-5D-5L dimension levels
statement: Estimated dimension-level coefficients were similar between methods, but confidence intervals were wider for the DCE estimates than for the BWS estimates; each method showed one level ordering violation.

outcome: Test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient) of DCE and BWS responses
statement: Participants who completed the BWS tasks first were more consistent in the repeated DCE tasks, while BWS consistency did not improve with task order.

The effect of a bolt-on depended on its severity. No, mild, or moderate problems usually increased health-state values, while severe or extreme problems decreased them. The effect was stronger at the lower end of the value scale.
Mean values were slightly lower after self-care was added to EQ-4D, but the overall difference was not statistically significant.
Mean values were lower after vision was added to EQ-5D-5L, and the overall difference was statistically significant.
Scaling factor models had better out-of-sample prediction than conventional models in both arms.
CALE specifications generally predicted better than additive specifications. The gain was clear in arm 1 and small in arm 2.
The estimated scaling coefficients indicated about 10% shrinkage for self-care addition and about 15% shrinkage for vision addition.
All 600 students completed the tasks. The mean completion time was 36.7 minutes, and the mean number of moves to indifference was 6.77.
In the CALE scaling models, self-care had the smallest dimension weight and vision had the largest dimension weight.

outcome: Agreement between care-recipient proxy assessments and caregiver self-assessments
statement: Care-recipient proxy assessments had fair-to-moderate agreement with caregiver self-assessments across EQ-5D-5L dimensions, and moderate agreement for the EQ-5D-5L Index and EQ VAS.

outcome: Directional bias of care-recipient proxy assessments of caregiver HRQL
statement: Care recipients consistently overestimated caregiver HRQL across all EQ-5D-5L dimensions and summary scores; the largest dimension-level differences were for usual activities and anxiety/depression, while summary-score bias was small.

outcome: Agreement between caregiver proxy assessments and care-recipient self-assessments
statement: In the traditional proxy direction, caregivers had moderate-to-excellent agreement with care-recipient self-assessments and substantially higher agreement than care recipients assessing caregivers.

outcome: Directional bias of caregiver proxy assessments of care-recipient HRQL
statement: Caregivers slightly underestimated care-recipient HRQL on summary scores, with smaller bias than in the reversed proxy direction.

outcome: Stability of agreement and bias patterns across caregiving subgroups and weighted-kappa sensitivity analyses
statement: Agreement and directional-bias patterns remained consistent across subgroup analyses of caregiving duration, baseline HRQL, living situation, and care-recipient memory issues; weighted-kappa sensitivity analyses supported the findings.

outcome: Agreement between care-recipient proxy assessments and caregiver self-assessments
statement: The hypothesis that more observable dimensions would have higher agreement was not supported; usual activities had the lowest agreement when care recipients assessed caregivers.

outcome: Sensitivity of the HSDI and Shannon evenness J' to random variation and to rare profiles
statement: The HSDI is strongly reduced by rare profiles (regression slopes near -1 in simulated data and about -0.8 to -0.9 in real data) whereas the Shannon evenness J' declines more slowly with rare profiles; conversely the HSDI is highly sensitive to purely random variation in profile counts, falling from 1 to 0.8 in a total-evenness simulation where J' stayed near 0.99.

outcome: Absolute and relative discriminatory power of the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L descriptive systems
statement: EQ-5D-5L data from Cambridgeshire were much less clustered than EQ-5D-3L data from HSE and PROMs, with higher Shannon indices, HSDI and J' values for the 5L.

outcome: Sensitivity of the HSDI and Shannon evenness J' to random variation and to rare profiles
statement: The Shannon index is underestimated in finite samples by (S-bar - 1)/2N, and because the theoretical maximum number of profiles is 243 for the 3L and 3,125 for the 5L, this bias is larger for the 5L and can make the 5L appear more discriminating even when H' is equal.

outcome: Observed distribution of EQ-5D dimension levels and health state profiles across NHS data sets
statement: EQ-5D-3L data were highly concentrated, with the ten most frequent profiles covering more than 90% of observations in all data sets and 11111 the most frequent profile in the general population survey and after surgery; EQ-5D-5L data were more dispersed, with the ten most frequent profiles covering about 10% (rehabilitation) to 30% of observations.

outcome: Absolute and relative discriminatory power of the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L descriptive systems
statement: In the NHS PROMs data, EQ-5D-3L profile distributions were more concentrated and less discriminating after surgery than before, as patients moved from a wide range of poor states to a narrow set of mild states.

outcome: Sensitivity of the HSDI and Shannon evenness J' to random variation and to rare profiles
