statement: Power law (Pareto) functions fitted the cumulative distributions well, better for the 5L than the 3L and best where the proportion of rare profiles was moderate; the estimated slope was largest for rehabilitation patients, indicating the least concentrated distribution.

outcome: Sensitivity of the HSDI and Shannon evenness J' to random variation and to rare profiles
statement: The specialist nursing sample showed a non-linear relationship between J' and the proportion of rare profiles (R2=0.29), revealing two distinct subgroups: about a quarter of patients concentrated in five profiles and the remainder spread almost uniformly across 727 profiles.

outcome: Proportion of logically inconsistent C-TTO health state pairs
statement: The proportion of inconsistent health state pairs did not differ significantly across arms.

outcome: Proportion of tied C-TTO values across dominance pairs
statement: The proportion of tied C-TTO values was statistically significantly lower in both ranking arms than in the control arm.

outcome: Rate at which state 55555 was not valued as the worst state
statement: The rate at which state 55555 was not valued as the worst state did not differ significantly across arms.

outcome: Interview duration, task times, flagged interviews and estimated extra data collection cost
statement: Adding the ranking task lengthened interviews by about 7 minutes and increased data collection cost by at least 15%.

outcome: Proportion of logically inconsistent C-TTO health state pairs
statement: Within the ranking and sorting arm, inconsistency rates were similar between ranking responses and C-TTO responses, but ties were far less frequent in the ranking task.

outcome: Interview duration, task times, flagged interviews and estimated extra data collection cost
statement: Quality control flagging rates were low and did not differ significantly across arms, and no interviewer reached the 40% retraining threshold.

outcome: Proportion of logically inconsistent C-TTO health state pairs
statement: Value distributions were broadly similar across arms, with one significant mean difference for state 35311 between the control and the ranking and sorting arms.

outcome: Respondent-reported task difficulty and understanding
statement: Respondents in the ranking arms reported the tasks as more complex than respondents in the control arm.

Some participants treated concentrating and thinking clearly as different experiences, and sadness as a transient state distinct from clinical or longer-lasting depression. These compound items could therefore be difficult to answer with one response.

Half of the participants regarded the EQ-HWB-9 as comprehensive. Suggested additions included more specific mental or emotional content, a global health assessment, environmental or resource factors, sleep, self-care, and social support; many suggested domains occur in the long-form EQ-HWB.

The control item was less consistently understood than most items. It resonated more strongly with caregivers and social care users than with participants classified by chronic illness alone, and the parenthetical example could conflict with the less absolute modified wording.

Most modified EQ-HWB-9 items had strong face and content validity. Participants generally interpreted daily activities, exhaustion, loneliness, anxiety, sadness or depression, and pain as intended and supplied relevant examples from chronic illness, caregiving, and social care.

More participants preferred full repeated questions to a shared item stem because repetition was clearer and reduced the need to remember the stem. Preferences for whether mobility or daily activities should appear first did not form a strong consensus.

Mobility caused the clearest comprehension problem. The parenthetical examples led some participants to think that the item applied only to people who used mobility devices; participants also questioned whether driving and other transport counted and noted different indoor and outdoor obstacles.

Most participants correctly ordered each modified response scale, but incorrect ordering affected about one quarter of the sample and was most frequent for the frequency scale. Fully reversed orders were treated as task-instruction misunderstandings and counted as correct.

Participants generally preferred the proposed modified terms: difficulty rather than trouble for cognition, lack of control rather than no control, a little of the time rather than only occasionally, and moderate difficulty rather than some difficulty.

EQ-5D-3L index and EQ VAS showed the expected convergent relationships with ataxia severity, functional impairment, non-ataxia signs, and depressive symptoms; correlations were generally weaker in SCA 6.
Physical EQ-5D-3L dimensions correlated most strongly with SARA and ADL, while pain or discomfort and anxiety or depression correlated more strongly with PHQ-9.
At baseline, the mean EQ-5D-3L index was 0.65, with limited ceiling effects for the EQ-5D-3L index and EQ VAS.

In SCA 1-3, EQ-5D-3L index values were lower in older patients and in groups with more severe ataxia, more non-ataxia signs, more depressive symptoms, and lower EQ VAS; in SCA 6, age and INAS groups did not differ significantly.
Non-item response was low for both the EQ-5D-3L index and EQ VAS.
Among 27 patients classified as stable at 12 months, EQ-5D-3L item agreement and index and EQ VAS intraclass correlations met the study thresholds for acceptable test-retest reliability.
Patients with no SARA score change showed no responsiveness in the EQ-5D-3L index or EQ VAS.
Among patients whose SARA score deteriorated, EQ-5D-3L index and EQ VAS changes were almost none to small across follow-up, while SARA changes increased from small to moderate.

Predicted absenteeism and presenteeism generally increased as EQ-5D-5L health-state severity increased. The fitted relationship showed a diminishing marginal effect of disutility, although very severe states were not studied.

In linear mixed-effects models based on dimension-specific utility losses, mobility, self-care, usual activities, and anxiety/depression were associated with higher absenteeism and presenteeism, while pain/discomfort was not significant. Self-care, mobility, and usual activities had the largest effects.

In the non-linear multiplicative models, all five EQ-5D-5L dimensions had significant effects. Pain/discomfort had only a marginal effect, and mobility, self-care, and usual activities remained the most influential dimensions.
The relative effects of levels 2 and 3, compared with level 4, were larger for absenteeism and presenteeism than their relative effects on disutility in the Polish EQ-5D-5L value set.

In the reported linear models, remote work was associated with higher absenteeism and presenteeism, sedentary work with lower absenteeism, work with other people with higher absenteeism, and creative-thinking work with lower presenteeism.

In the non-linear models, remote work and sedentary work remained significant for absenteeism, while remote work and creative thinking remained significant for presenteeism. Adding job characteristics did not change RMSE.
Models that tested interactions between EQ-5D-5L dimensions and job characteristics found no significant interactions.
Within respondents, valuations of state 33333 were often equal at the cTTO floor in both perspectives; when valuations differed, the proxy 1 valuation was usually lower.
All-in trading at utility -1 and clustering at or below the value for state 33333 were more frequent under proxy 1 than under proxy 2.
Between-respondent variances differed for some states, but the direction of the difference was not consistent across states.
Proxy 2 respondents were more likely to give no negative utilities, and fewer observations were valued worse than dead under proxy 2 than under proxy 1.
The perspectives did not differ significantly on the other assessed response patterns, including few unique utilities, non-trading, rounding, strict dominance violations, and feedback flags.
There was no significant overall main effect of proxy perspective across all valued health states.

Proxy perspective changed valuations mainly for severe pain or discomfort and severe sadness, worry, or unhappiness; these states had lower valuations when adults decided what was best for a child than when adults considered what the child would want.
Within-respondent valuation variance was lower under proxy 2 (substitute) than under proxy 1, which indicates more compressed valuations under proxy 2.

Pain or discomfort and mobility were the two most important dimensions in both main modelling approaches, but worried, sad, or unhappy ranked least in the mixed logit model and third in the A3 hybrid model.
cTTO values were concentrated at 0.5 or higher, with a long negative tail and a small spike at -1.
The cTTO interviews took longer and required an average of 13.21 moves, while DCE interviews were shorter.
A large observed value gap separated the worst state 33333 from the second-worst state 33323.
The hybrid model with an A3 term had the lowest reported MAE, no inconsistent or non-significant coefficients, and predicted a negative value for state 33333; it was selected as the value set.
Among the 28 cTTO states, state 11112 had the highest observed mean value and state 33333 had the lowest; 33333 was the only state with a negative observed mean.
The authors judged the completed sample representative of the Chinese population against the sixth National Population Census quotas.

outcome: Modelled utility decrements (parameter estimates) and predicted utilities of the Hungarian value sets
statement: The Hungarian value sets span nearly the same range, with the EQ-5D-3L reaching a slightly lower minimum utility than the EQ-5D-5L.

outcome: Model prediction accuracy (mean absolute error, correlations, illogical and insignificant parameters) and logical inconsistency rates
statement: Pooled heteroscedastic Tobit models produced logically ordered and statistically significant parameters and were selected as the final value sets, with the 5L intercept constrained to 1 because it did not differ significantly from 1.

outcome: Self-reported EQ VAS scores and self-perceived health of the respondents
statement: The achieved sample matched national age and sex quotas, with higher-educated respondents and residents of Central Hungary somewhat overrepresented.

outcome: Relative importance ranking of the 5 EQ-5D dimensions
statement: Mobility was the most important dimension and usual activities the least important in both value sets; the ranking differed only in that self-care outranked pain/discomfort in the 3L.

outcome: Modelled utility decrements (parameter estimates) and predicted utilities of the Hungarian value sets
statement: The EQ-5D-5L showed lower ceiling effects than the EQ-5D-3L, with a narrower and higher band of utilities for the mildest health states.

outcome: Proportion of health states valued as worse than dead and range of utilities
statement: A higher proportion of health states was valued as worse than dead with the 3L value set than with the 5L value set.

outcome: Single-level and mean transition utilities between adjacent health states
statement: Changing the most severe mobility label from "confined to bed" (3L) to "unable to walk" (5L) produced a large positive impact on utilities and explained most of the difference between the two value sets.

outcome: Single-level and mean transition utilities between adjacent health states
statement: More negative wording in the other dimensions, including "very much anxious/feeling down a lot" (3L) versus "extremely anxious/depressed" (5L), had only a modest negative impact on utilities.

outcome: Single-level and mean transition utilities between adjacent health states
statement: Mean single-level transition utilities were substantially larger and less consistent across the scale for the 3L than for the 5L, and increased significantly as baseline utility fell for both instruments.

outcome: Modelled utility decrements (parameter estimates) and predicted utilities of the Hungarian value sets
statement: Agreement between 3L and matched 5L utilities was good, but most matched states had a higher 3L utility except where the most severe mobility level was involved.

outcome: Model prediction accuracy (mean absolute error, correlations, illogical and insignificant parameters) and logical inconsistency rates
statement: The feedback module strongly reduced logical inconsistencies in the 5L cTTO data, while 3L inconsistencies were rare without any feedback module.
Any cardiovascular complication occurred in 13% of female participants and 17% of male participants.
Pre-existing cardiovascular disease did not significantly modify the sex difference in any cardiovascular complication.
After full adjustment, female participants had lower odds of in-hospital death than male participants.
The study found no sex difference in the risk of heart failure or stroke.
After full adjustment, female participants had lower odds of any cardiovascular complication than male participants.
Complete-case analyses and analyses restricted to sites with universal or random sampling showed patterns similar to the main analysis.
Female participants had lower adjusted odds of arrhythmia, supraventricular tachycardia, cardiac ischaemia, and pulmonary embolism than male participants.

outcome: Construct validity (convergent and known-groups) of each preference-based measure by country and disease group
statement: Seventy-nine papers containing 1504 individual studies were included; EQ-5D was the most frequently assessed measure and construct validity the most frequently assessed property, with no eligible evidence for 15D, AQoL or the Philippines.

outcome: Methodological quality (risk of bias) of included studies
statement: Methodological quality was 'very good' or 'adequate' for almost all construct validity studies and most responsiveness studies, but for only a small minority of test-retest reliability studies.

outcome: Construct validity (convergent and known-groups) of each preference-based measure by country and disease group
statement: Study-level results were positive for most construct validity and test-retest reliability studies and for just over half of responsiveness studies.

outcome: Construct validity (convergent and known-groups) of each preference-based measure by country and disease group
statement: EQ-5D showed 'sufficient' construct validity in 6 of 10 countries/districts and 17 of 20 disease groups, and 'sufficient' responsiveness in 5 of 6 countries/districts and 8 of 11 disease groups, with no population rated 'insufficient' for these properties.

outcome: Test-retest reliability of each preference-based measure by country and disease group
statement: Test-retest reliability of EQ-5D was 'inconsistent' or 'insufficient' in every country/district assessed and in most disease groups.

outcome: Construct validity (convergent and known-groups) of each preference-based measure by country and disease group
statement: EQ VAS construct validity was 'sufficient' in only half of the countries/districts and in 8 of 14 disease groups, but its responsiveness was 'sufficient' in all four countries/districts assessed.

outcome: Construct validity (convergent and known-groups) of each preference-based measure by country and disease group
statement: SF-6D showed 'sufficient' construct validity in only 2 of 5 countries/districts and 6 of 11 disease groups, and 'sufficient' responsiveness in only 1 of 3 countries/districts.

outcome: Construct validity (convergent and known-groups) of each preference-based measure by country and disease group
statement: Evidence for HUI and QWB was scarce; HUI showed 'sufficient' construct validity in all three countries/districts and four disease groups assessed, and QWB construct validity was 'sufficient' in China and Japan for neurological and respiratory disease.
The 36 candidate items had a wide distribution of reported problem rates.
The thematic analysis identified eight recurring types of item problem.
Most reported problems were generic wording or comprehension problems and were not specific to Chinese culture.
Three items showed possible Chinese linguistic or cultural equivalence problems. The daily-life control item was the only one of these with a problem rate above 50%.
Longer and more complex items received more comments, which indicated worse understandability and readability.
The analyzed sample had high psychological distress: 45.2% were classified by K10 as likely to have a moderate or severe disorder.

Both EQ-HWB-9 versions had response distributions and psychometric results that supported use in this population. Problems were more frequent for exhaustion, cognition, and anxiety than for mobility, activities, and pain.

The modified activities item, which appeared before mobility, had a higher mean score and a wider response distribution than the original activities item. The between-version mean difference was statistically significant and had a moderate effect size.

Compared with the original version, the modified activities item had a lower correlation with mobility and higher correlations with exhaustion, cognition, and sadness or depression. These differences supported a broader interpretation of activities when the item appeared first.
The study found no statistically significant item-score differences for the three modifications other than item order, and the other changes had little observable effect on psychometric outcomes.

Known-groups analyses for both versions were in the hypothesized directions. The instruments discriminated between groups defined by psychological distress, wellbeing, stress, life satisfaction, sleep problems, mental health support, unpleasant meditation experiences, and meditation-related functional impairment.
All hypothesized correlations of EQ-HWB-9 with K10, SWEMWBS, and PSS-4 exceeded 0.30 for both versions, with no material difference between versions.

All responsiveness analyses followed the hypothesized directions. Changes in psychological distress, wellbeing, stress, and life satisfaction were associated with corresponding changes in EQ-HWB-9 quality-of-life sum scores.
The original and modified randomized groups had no significant baseline demographic or measured-outcome differences; the baseline groups were comparable.
Almost all patient/caregiver participants and all clinicians found the EQ-5D-Y-5L quick, simple, and easy to complete or interpret; simplicity and engagement supported completion and use.

Short specialist appointments and limited external support, especially community mental health support, constrained the response to wider concerns and could create unmet expectations or harm if problems remained unaddressed.
The patient PROMpt gave patients and caregivers agency to identify EQ-5D-Y-5L items for discussion and helped to prioritize limited appointment time.

Brief practical resources, clinician response guides, administrative support, and integration with the patient portal and electronic medical record supported implementation; participants requested clearer completion flags and discussion reminders.
Clinicians perceived little overall negative effect on clinic time, and normal results could make an appointment quicker, although some discussions of identified concerns took considerable time.
EQ-5D-Y-5L results were not always reviewed or discussed in appointments; patients, caregivers, and clinicians considered acknowledgment and discussion necessary for the program to affect care.
When results were discussed, participants reported more holistic care, improved patient-clinician communication, and greater satisfaction because concerns beyond the clinic specialty could be raised.
Completing the EQ-5D-Y-5L helped some caregivers gain new perspectives on their child's health and feelings.

Views on generic measurement were mixed: some caregivers wanted more condition-specific questions, while a clinician valued the generic instrument because it supplied information that routine condition-specific assessment might miss.
Participants wanted a larger and longer trial with repeated measurement so that child health could be tracked over time and program effects could be better understood.
The cohort had substantial frailty, multimorbidity, and medication burden at baseline.
EQ-5D-5L index scores were progressively lower with greater frailty severity, with the lowest median score in the very severe frailty group.
Participants with severe CKD had lower EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS scores than participants with moderate CKD.
Frailty severity was similar across the moderate and severe CKD groups, and the age and sex patterns expected from prior frailty research were not observed.
Greater frailty severity was associated with more comorbid conditions and a higher medication burden.
Perspective differences were associated with education, region, parental status, and the normative view that a child’s life is more valuable than an adult’s.
Among observations classified as better than dead, child-perspective values were higher overall, with the largest difference for severe or worst states.
Adult-perspective values showed more clustering at the cTTO endpoints of -1 and 1 than child-perspective values.
Perspective sometimes changed whether the same state was classified as better or worse than dead, mainly for severe states.
Paired differences were centered near zero, but variability increased with health-state severity.
The overall mean child-minus-adult cTTO difference was zero and was not statistically significant.
Adjusted random-intercept regression found no systematic effect of perspective on cTTO values.
Child-perspective values were slightly lower for mild states, while mean differences for moderate and severe or worst states were not statistically significant.
Among observations classified as worse than dead, child-perspective values were lower overall and for severe or worst states.
A linear transformation applied to the United States and Netherlands relationships would systematically underestimate TTO utilities at the upper and lower ends of the latent scale.

Under the simplifying linear model, prediction MSE decreases as the number of TTO-valued health states, the spread of their latent utilities, the number of respondents, or the number of tasks per respondent increases.

Simulations with hypothetical TTO distributions supported all three theoretical hypotheses: endpoint-weighted selection gave larger latent-utility variance and smaller RMSE and MAE, and its advantage decreased as more states were assessed or scatter increased.

For Indonesian data, where mean TTO utilities showed random scatter around an approximately linear DCE relationship, endpoint-weighted selection was only marginally better than even selection, and 10 or 20 valued states performed better than 2 or 5.

Valuing more distinct health states generally improved predictive precision; designs with 20 states outperformed designs with 10 states when respondents valued 10 states, even though the selected-state variance was smaller.
Having each simulated respondent value 10 health states rather than one reduced RMSE and MAE in every assessed scenario.

For the United States and Netherlands data, which showed nonlinear TTO-to-DCE utility relationships, even selection generally had lower RMSE than endpoint-weighted selection when more than two states were valued; the exception was the 20-state Netherlands scenario.

The authors recommend that each respondent value multiple TTO states, that at least 20 distinct health states be valued, and that states be spread evenly across severity; for EQ-5D-Y-3L, states should be added toward the middle of the latent scale.
State 11111 was the most frequent health state and was reported by 52.2% of the sample; 216 of 3,125 possible states were observed, and 28 states accounted for 90% of respondents.
Self-reported health was higher for men, declined with age, and was lower in the lowest income and education groups. Age, sex, income, and education were the main drivers of inequality.
Pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression had the highest prevalence of reported problems. More than 70% of the inequality share associated with EQ-5D dimensions was linked to these two dimensions.
The overall mean EQ-5D-5L index value, scored with the Uruguayan value set, was 0.953.
The EQ VAS Kakwani inequality index was 0.1047. Demographic variables explained 3.43% of inequality, and EQ-5D dimensions explained 27.78%.
Compared with earlier Colombian EQ-5D-3L population studies, EQ-5D-5L had substantially lower ceiling levels and more observed health states, which the authors interpreted as increased sensitivity.
The overall mean EQ VAS score was 85.3.

outcome: Model fit (in-sample mean squared error) and predictive power (out-of-sample mean squared error)
statement: All four modeling approaches produced similar in-sample fit, with mean squared error between 0.013 and 0.015.

outcome: Model fit (in-sample mean squared error) and predictive power (out-of-sample mean squared error)
statement: Out-of-sample predictive power was slightly better for the indirect methods than for the direct linear methods.

outcome: Model fit (in-sample mean squared error) and predictive power (out-of-sample mean squared error)
statement: The nonparametric indirect model was selected as the recommended crosswalk because it was simple, transparent, value-set independent, and performed comparably to the more complex models; its mean squared error of 0.014 equals a root mean square error of 0.12.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index values derived from EQ-5D-3L value sets
statement: Crosswalk values tended to underpredict observed 3L values at the upper end of the scale and overpredict them at the lower end.
Ordered logistic regression fits showed that level 5 on the 5L represents more extreme problems than level 3 on the 3L, and level 1 on the 5L is healthier than level 1 on the 3L.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index values derived from EQ-5D-3L value sets
statement: The large gap between full health and the next best health state in the UK 3L value set (0.117) was reduced by all models, most by the linear models and least by the nonparametric and ordered logistic regression models.

outcome: Frequency of logically inconsistent 3L/5L response combinations
statement: Logical inconsistencies between 3L and 5L responses were uncommon, and the item response theory model could not be estimated on the consistent data set because the excluded variation was needed to identify parameters.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index values derived from EQ-5D-3L value sets
statement: Crosswalk index values closely tracked mean observed 3L values for frequently occurring health states under the UK value set.

outcome: OPUF-derived EQ-HWB-S value-set coefficients and state utilities
statement: OPUF produced plausible aggregate EQ-HWB-S value sets with consistent, logically ordered coefficients in all four samples; the aggregate worst-state utilities ranged from 0 to -0.17.

outcome: Technical feasibility and data quality of OPUF for EQ-HWB-S valuation
statement: Despite analyzed sample sizes of 99 to 311, uncertainty around mean OPUF coefficients was comparable to the published EQ-VT pilot study based on 520 respondents.

outcome: Respondents self-reported EQ-HWB-S states and EQ-HWB VAS scores
statement: Self-reported health and wellbeing was broadly similar in three samples, while the rheumatic disease sample consistently reported more severe problems and a lower median EQ-HWB VAS score.

outcome: Preference differences across respondent samples and valuation methods
statement: Physical pain was the most important dimension in all samples, with a tied first rank for mobility in the diabetes sample; mobility and day-to-day activities were also consistently among the three most important dimensions, and the four leading dimensions in both United Kingdom methods were pain, mobility, day-to-day activities, and sadness or depression.

outcome: Preference differences across respondent samples and valuation methods
statement: The United Kingdom OPUF value set differed from the published EQ-VT pilot value set in relative dimension weights, intermediate-level positions, and overall scaling; 17 of 36 coefficient differences were statistically significant, and the EQ-VT worst-state utility was more negative.

outcome: Preference differences across respondent samples and valuation methods
statement: The four OPUF value sets were fairly consistent with one another, and only a few between-sample coefficient differences were statistically significant.

outcome: Technical feasibility and data quality of OPUF for EQ-HWB-S valuation
statement: Median main-survey completion time was 11 to 16 minutes across samples, with the two patient samples taking longer than the general population samples.

outcome: Technical feasibility and data quality of OPUF for EQ-HWB-S valuation
statement: Completion was high for the Prolific United Kingdom sample but lower for the Bilendi German samples, where noneligibility and a stricter response-quality rejection rule also affected completion.

outcome: Respondent comprehension, ease, feedback, and survey duration acceptability
statement: Most respondents rated the survey as understandable, answerable, and an appropriate length, although free-text feedback included recurring descriptions of some questions as difficult, confusing, complex, or complicated.

outcome: Technical feasibility and data quality of OPUF for EQ-HWB-S valuation
statement: Invalid top-anchor responses caused exclusion of 5% to 10% of recruited respondents, and other suspect patterns included zero dimension weights, all weights equal to 100, and illogical level ratings.

outcome: OPUF-derived EQ-HWB-S value-set coefficients and state utilities
statement: Preferences between the worst EQ-HWB-S state and being dead varied across samples; 31% to 54% preferred state 555555555 over being dead, and uncensored anchors included very negative outliers, so analysis censored anchor points at -1.
Paired responses to proxy EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L were highly consistent across all five dimensions.
EQ-5D-Y-5L had small ceiling-effect reductions in four dimensions, but the pain or discomfort ceiling effect increased slightly; the full-health ceiling effect was nearly unchanged.
EQ-5D-Y-5L had higher absolute informativity than EQ-5D-Y-3L in every dimension, although relative informativity decreased for mobility, pain or discomfort, and feeling worried, sad or unhappy.
Both instruments generally showed the expected known-groups patterns by curvature magnitude, curvature type, treatment modality, and bracing status.
Dimension responses had good to very good overall test-retest agreement for both instruments, with looking after myself most reliable and feeling worried, sad or unhappy least reliable.
Proxy-reported EQ VAS scores had poor-to-moderate test-retest reliability and showed a significant mean decline between baseline and retest.
EQ-5D-Y-5L often improved test-retest reliability in hard-to-observe dimensions for clinically defined subgroups, but improvement was not uniform across all patient and caregiver subgroups.

outcome: TTO-derived health utility values for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: The preferred model produced utilities ranging from -0.148 for the worst state (55555) to 0.949 for the best state (11111).

outcome: Distribution of composite versus traditional TTO values and model prediction error
statement: Composite TTO values were distributed toward the positive side of the scale and were consistently higher than traditional TTO values for the same severe health states; about a quarter of composite TTO values were nonpositive.

Models using 20 dummy variables or dimension-specific level 4/5 terms alone showed logical inconsistency between levels 4 and 5; adding the squared additional-number-of-level-4-or-5 term produced logically consistent estimates with the best fit.

outcome: Self-reported health status of the valuation sample
statement: The analysed sample resembled the Canadian general population on age, sex, marital status, employment, country of birth and language spoken at home, but was more educated and had lower income; excluded participants were older, less healthy and of lower socioeconomic status.

outcome: Distribution of composite versus traditional TTO values and model prediction error
statement: The preferred model retained the smallest mean absolute error in sensitivity analyses that censored only negative values or that included all participants.

outcome: Item missingness and survey completion
statement: Among respondents with at least one EQ-5D-5L item response, missingness was low for the five core dimensions and both bolt-ons; EQ VAS missingness was higher, and 234 respondents completed none of the EQ-5D-5L items.

outcome: Response distributions and item- and profile-level ceiling effects
statement: Both bolt-ons had acceptable response distributions. Cognition reduced the profile-level ceiling more than social participation.

outcome: Convergent and divergent construct validity
statement: Construct validity was supported by moderate-to-high correlations with related measures and weak correlations with less-related constructs; cognition related most strongly to post-COVID symptoms, and social participation related strongly to disability.

outcome: Known-groups validity and relative efficiency
statement: The cognition bolt-on significantly improved discrimination in 10 of 13 known-group comparisons, while social participation significantly improved 6 of 13 comparisons.

outcome: Known-groups validity and relative efficiency
statement: Cognition improved discrimination of baseline and most-severe-episode PCS severity, work ability, and several mental-health groupings; social participation performed similarly to the core instrument for PCS severity but better distinguished current post-COVID sick leave.

outcome: Incremental explanatory power beyond the five core EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: In the total-sample multivariable model for PCS severity, cognition produced a meaningful incremental gain beyond the core EQ-5D-5L, while social participation produced little gain.

outcome: Incremental explanatory power beyond the five core EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: Across the six prevalent health-condition subgroups, cognition consistently added explanatory power for PCS severity, while social participation changed model performance negligibly.

outcome: Incremental explanatory power beyond the five core EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: For EQ VAS, cognition made a modest additional contribution across the total sample and health-condition subgroups, while social participation generally made a negligible contribution.

outcome: Response distributions and item- and profile-level ceiling effects
statement: Cognition and pain or discomfort captured a wider spread of reported problems than most other dimensions; severe or extreme problems were most frequent for cognition.

outcome: Criteria for selecting items for preference-based measures
statement: The authors present 22 item-selection criteria. Criteria 1 to 12 concern accurate completion, criteria 13 to 19 have greater importance for preference-based measures, and criteria 20 to 22 address requirements that are specific to valuation.

outcome: Suitability of items for questionnaire completion, QALY measurement, and preference valuation
statement: Items should be readable, brief, unambiguous, free of jargon and colloquial wording, not double-barrelled, acceptable to respondents, relevant across respondents, answerable from personal experience, and neutrally worded.

outcome: Suitability of items for questionnaire completion, QALY measurement, and preference valuation
statement: Items used for QALY measurement should cover the domain range, avoid differential item functioning and comparisons with other people, expectations, or other time periods, refer clearly to the specified period, and use clearly ordered response options.

outcome: Suitability of items for questionnaire completion, QALY measurement, and preference valuation
statement: For preference valuation, each domain should support meaningful trade-offs, each item should avoid attributing a problem to a specific cause, and response options across items should use a consistent direction.
Translatability must be assessed in the translated language and cultural context because accurate literal translation alone does not ensure consistent interpretation.

When one health state was omitted at a time, the Shams Bayesian spatial-correlation model reduced RMSE relative to each country's published model in all seven countries; no published functional form performed best.
When whole 10-state blocks were omitted, CALE had the smallest prediction error in four countries and a Bayesian model had the smallest error in three countries.
When 10 randomly selected health states were omitted, CALE was preferred in three countries and the Shams model in four countries.

Both Bayesian spatial-correlation models produced logical inconsistencies for fewer than 0.2% of dominant health-state pairs; the Shams model generally had fewer inconsistencies than the Kharroubi model.
The relative performance of the alternative models varied by health state, but there was no evidence that the Bayesian advantage changed systematically across the utility scale.
The 8-parameter CALE models outperformed corresponding 20-parameter additive models. The selected hybrid CALE model had monotonic coefficients and strong out-of-sample prediction accuracy.
The small valuation design produced usable cTTO data in the cancer sample. Mean cTTO task time was 16.93 minutes, and observed mean state values ranged from -0.463 for 55555 to 0.916 for 11112.

Cancer-patient values were generally higher than Chinese general-population values, but the direction depended strongly on pain/discomfort: patient values were higher for no, slight, or moderate pain/discomfort and lower for extreme pain/discomfort.

Cancer patients assigned less disutility than the general public to all slight problems, moderate-to-extreme mobility, self-care and usual-activity problems, and moderate anxiety/depression, but more disutility to moderate-to-extreme pain/discomfort and severe-to-extreme anxiety/depression.
The cancer-patient value for the worst state 55555 was lower than the general-population value, while the proportions of all 3,125 states with negative values were similar.
Of the 221 patients who completed cTTO, 193 completed DCE; 28 did not complete DCE because of fatigue.
In the analyzed sample, 23.08% reported full health on EQ-5D-5L and the mean EQ VAS score was 74.15.

outcome: Consistency between paired 3-level and 5-level responses
statement: Paired 3-level and 5-level EQ-5D responses were inconsistent in 3.5% of observations on average and 7.8% after weighting for severity. Vision had the greatest bolt-on inconsistency, whereas breathing had the least.

outcome: Convergent validity
statement: Breathing had strong convergent validity against the MG-ADL breathing item in both response systems. Vision had only moderate convergence with the HUI-3 vision item, which the authors attributed in part to construct differences.

outcome: Response distributions, unique profiles, ceiling, and floor effects
statement: Across the six bolt-ons, the 5-level versions reduced ceiling effects by an average of 35% and floor effects by an average of 55% relative to the 3-level versions. Vision had the largest ceiling reduction, and sleep had the largest floor reduction.

outcome: Divergent validity
statement: Most bolt-ons had weak to moderate correlations with the core EQ-5D dimensions. Social relationships correlated strongly with anxiety/depression and with self-confidence; correlations were about 5% stronger for the 5-level bolt-ons.

outcome: Known-groups validity and relative efficiency
statement: Bolt-ons reduced ceiling effects in respondents with multiple chronic conditions and in those who needed caregiver assistance, but they did not generally improve relative efficiency over the core EQ-5D. Breathing produced the only modest improvement among respondents with multiple chronic conditions.

outcome: Longitudinal responsiveness and health-state change
statement: Paretian health-state classification also showed greater sensitivity for the 5-level system, chiefly through more mixed changes and fewer unchanged profiles. The probability of a better wave-2 state was about 0.50 in both systems, which indicated little overall population HRQoL change.

outcome: Absolute and relative informativity
statement: The 5-level systems captured 3.2 to 3.5 times as many profiles as the 3-level systems. The 5-level bolt-ons also had higher item and instrument informativity, except that breathing reduced relative instrument informativity by 2%.

outcome: Reliability and agreement
statement: Level sum scores for EQ-5D-5L plus 5-level bolt-ons and EQ-5D-3L plus 3-level bolt-ons showed excellent reliability and agreement.

outcome: Longitudinal responsiveness and health-state change
statement: The 5-level bolt-ons detected more longitudinal change than the 3-level versions: they classified fewer respondents as stable and detected substantially more improvement and worsening. Vision, tiredness, and sleep captured the most changes, whereas breathing captured fewer changes.

outcome: Composite TTO values for EQ-5D-5L health states by arm
statement: Mean TTO values were higher in the full health (control) arm for all health states except 21111, but most differences were small and not statistically significant.

outcome: Composite TTO values for EQ-5D-5L health states by arm
statement: Almost all respondents who valued health state 11111 gave it a value of 1.

outcome: Data quality and face validity: logical inconsistencies, value distributions, interviewer effects, completion time
statement: Data quality and face validity were similar in the two arms: mean values fell as the level sum score increased, and inconsistency rates and completion times did not differ significantly between arms.

outcome: Data quality and face validity: logical inconsistencies, value distributions, interviewer effects, completion time
statement: Regression analysis showed significant interviewer and sequence effects, while the study arm coefficient was not significant.

outcome: Respondents' interpretations of full health versus 11111 and aspects of health not covered by EQ-5D
statement: Many respondents did not regard 11111 and full health as identical, and full health was rated and ranked higher than 11111.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-5L profile and EQ VAS score of respondents
statement: Half of respondents self-reported health state 11111, but most of them rated their own health below 100 on the EQ VAS.

outcome: Respondents' interpretations of full health versus 11111 and aspects of health not covered by EQ-5D
statement: A sizeable minority of respondents named aspects of health or quality of life important to them but not covered by the EQ-5D dimensions, including vision, hearing, energy and sociability.

outcome: Respondent-reported ease of understanding and difficulty of the TTO tasks
statement: Most respondents found the tasks easy to understand, but opinion was divided about the difficulty of identifying the point of indifference.

outcome: Composite TTO values for EQ-5D-5L health states by arm
statement: The low mean values for very mild health states seen in the EQ-5D-5L value set for England study were not reproduced in either arm of this study.
Most respondents agreed that the DCE tasks were easy to understand and that they could distinguish between the paired health states.
The youth and adult United States EQ-5D value sets had comparable overall ranges, but the EQ-5D-Y-3L value set had more states above 0.5 and a value for state 33333 that was about 0.10 higher.
For health state 33333, the observed mean cTTO value was 0.020 from 190 retained observations and the censored population-weighted estimate was -0.026.
Pain or discomfort was the most important dimension in the final model, followed by feeling worried, sad, or unhappy.
The mapping model with an intercept produced values above 1.0 and was rejected; ordinary least squares without an intercept was selected, with a rescaling parameter of 0.089.
DCE quality-control criteria excluded 37.5% of adolescent completers and 38.5% of adult completers; 12 of 211 completed cTTO interviews were excluded for insufficient understanding or engagement.
Final EQ-5D-Y-3L utilities ranged from 0.079 for health state 33333 to 0.976 for health state 12111; health state 11111 was fixed at 1.0.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L index value
statement: HRQoL had a nonlinear association with age. Scores were relatively low among the youngest adults, rose through midlife, and then declined, with the largest decline among adults aged 80 years and older.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L index value
statement: Chronic health conditions, long-term illness, and multimorbidity were associated with progressively lower HRQoL after adjustment. Chronic pain, heart failure, and COPD showed some of the largest differences.

outcome: Prevalence of problems in each EQ-5D-3L dimension
statement: Pain or discomfort and anxiety or depression were the most common reported problems, while self-care problems were uncommon. Anxiety or depression followed a bathtub-shaped age pattern, with high prevalence among the youngest adults and another rise among the oldest adults.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L index value
statement: The weighted adult population mean was 0.81 for the EQ-5D-3L index and 76.97 for EQ VAS.

outcome: Distribution of EQ-5D-3L health-state profiles
statement: The sample contained 169 observed EQ-5D-3L health states. The full-health profile 11111 accounted for about 37% of respondents, and 14 respondents reported the worst profile 33333.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L index value
statement: Higher BMI, daily smoking, and longer daily sitting time were associated with lower EQ-5D-3L index and EQ VAS values after sociodemographic adjustment. Hazardous alcohol consumption was associated with higher HRQoL than abstention, but the authors noted possible health-related selection into abstention.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L index value
statement: The 2021 estimates were largely similar to pre-pandemic 2014 cohort estimates. A two-part model gave similar patterns, and the Swedish experience-based value set produced higher index estimates in every age group than the United Kingdom value set.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L index value
statement: Lower income and lower education showed clear gradients toward poorer HRQoL. After age adjustment, respondents born outside the European Union and United Kingdom also had lower HRQoL than respondents born in Sweden.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L index value
statement: Female respondents had lower mean EQ-5D-3L index and EQ VAS values than male respondents. The index difference remained after age adjustment.

outcome: Feasibility of EQ-5D-Y (missing values and ambiguous answers)
statement: The EQ-5D-Y was feasible: nearly 96% of respondents completed all items, with only three missing values and no ambiguous answers.

outcome: Distribution of reported problems by EQ-5D-Y dimension, health profiles and EQ VAS scores
statement: Problems were reported mainly in 'having pain or discomfort', 'doing usual activities' and 'feeling worried, sad or unhappy'; 'doing usual activities' was the only dimension where 'a lot of problems' was reported.

outcome: Distribution of reported problems by EQ-5D-Y dimension, health profiles and EQ VAS scores
statement: Twelve different EQ-5D-Y health profiles occurred, and almost half of the sample reported full health (11111).

outcome: Distribution of reported problems by EQ-5D-Y dimension, health profiles and EQ VAS scores
statement: Mean EQ VAS was 80.7, and younger children reported significantly higher VAS than adolescents.

outcome: Convergent validity of EQ-5D-Y against PAQLQ and self-rated health
statement: Convergent validity was supported: EQ-5D-Y 'doing usual activities' correlated highly with the PAQLQ 'activity limitations' domain and total score, and the EQ VAS correlated highly with the PAQLQ total score and activity limitations.

outcome: Convergent validity of EQ-5D-Y against PAQLQ and self-rated health
statement: The EQ-5D-Y 'feeling worried, sad or unhappy' dimension did not correlate as expected with the PAQLQ 'emotional functions' domain, and 'mobility' and 'looking after myself' showed low or negligible correlations.

outcome: Convergent validity of EQ-5D-Y against PAQLQ and self-rated health
statement: PAQLQ scores were lowest for 'activity limitations', and respondents reporting EQ-5D-Y health profile 11111 reported better PAQLQ scores than the rest of the sample in all domains.
Most respondents rated their overall health as excellent or very good on the self-rated health question.
For better-than-dead values elicited with the comparable conventional TTO method, adjusted mean valuations were 0.05 higher in 2017 than in 2002.
For worse-than-dead values, adjusted 2017 valuations were lower than 2002 valuations under both transformations, but the estimated difference depended strongly on the transformation.
When all values were analyzed, 2017 valuations were lower with the linear transformation of 2002 WTD data, but there was no statistically significant difference with the nonlinear transformation.
After adjustment, respondents in 2017 were slightly less likely than respondents in 2002 to value a health state as worse than dead.

Better-than-dead valuations for the 16 common profiles had high rank correlation and absolute agreement across years; all-value agreement was also high and was highest with the nonlinear transformation.
In better-than-dead interaction models, only Self-Care level 3 differed significantly by year after correction, so no specific EQ-5D dimension appeared to drive the overall mean difference.
The review included 29 studies that covered 27 EQ-5D-5L country value sets from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, and South America.
None of the reviewed papers reported involvement of steering committees, decision makers, patients, or members of the public in selection of the recommended value set.
All included studies used general-population samples. Most sample sizes were close to the EuroQol recommendation of 1,000, but sampling and recruitment methods varied substantially across countries.

Most value-set studies followed the international EQ-5D-5L valuation protocol. They usually used EQ-VT computer-assisted face-to-face interviews, 86 TTO health states, and 196 DCE choice sets; one study used video interviews, one used a postal survey, and two used different study designs.
Of the 27 value sets, 10 used TTO data only and 17 used a hybrid model that combined TTO and DCE data.

TTO modelling varied across the 22 studies that reported separate TTO analyses. Tobit models censored at -1 were common, 15 studies explicitly addressed heteroscedasticity, and no TTO study accounted for preference heterogeneity.

Sixteen studies reported DCE analyses. Thirteen used conditional logit models, 10 anchored DCE estimates to the full-health-to-dead scale, only one accounted for heterogeneity, and three reported robustness assessments.

Eighteen studies, reported in 20 papers, estimated a hybrid TTO-DCE model. Fifteen used the Stata hyreg command, but only 10 assessed, explicitly or implicitly, whether TTO and DCE data could be combined; one study concluded that combination was not appropriate.

Model performance was most often assessed with logical consistency, coefficient significance, goodness of fit, prediction errors, suitability for data characteristics, and parsimony. Five studies had no reported model-performance assessment.
Studies used different model-performance assessments and reasons to select a recommended country value set. Some selected models did not account for important features of the valuation data.

Young and middle-aged patients generally had worse long-term outcomes than older patients. Older age remained associated with better HRQL, EQ VAS, fatigue, post-exertional malaise, depression, and anxiety in multivariable analyses, but not with the number of complaints.
Participants reported many persistent complaints. Fatigue, concentration problems, and physical exhaustion were most common, and nearly two thirds reported all three.

In multivariable analyses, living alone was associated with more complaints; absence of comorbidity with better HRQL and EQ VAS; male sex with higher depression risk; and low education with higher anxiety risk. Acute antibiotic treatment and hospitalisation were not associated with less severe long-term outcomes.
Energy was less than half of the recalled pre-infection level, and fatigue was high across MFI-20 domains. Older patients reported significantly less fatigue than young and middle-aged patients.
HRQL and self-rated health were low. Almost all patients reported pain or discomfort, and nine of ten reported limitations in usual activities.
More than one quarter screened positive for likely depression and about one fifth screened positive for likely anxiety; 55.4% of those with likely depression also had likely anxiety.
Post-exertional malaise was almost universal, with all but four participants reporting at least mild problems on one or more domains.
Each of the four primary models produced a logically consistent value set with all 20 incremental parameters non-negative.

Sensitivity analyses showed that removing the worst and five mild cTTO profiles increased cTTO-DCE correlations; logit and ZBT parameters were highly correlated; and DCE parameters were nearly invariant across power, exponential, and hyperbolic temporal functions.
The planned hybrid pooling was not used because cTTO and DCE parameters were not equivalent and DCE rejected constant proportionality.
The value-set floors and proportions of profiles worse than dead differed substantially across cTTO and DCE models.
Within the 300-person Lite subsample, cTTO and DCE incremental parameters showed only moderate agreement.
The DCE estimates were more precise than the cTTO estimates: all DCE incremental parameters were significant, compared with 12 of 20 cTTO parameters.
The DCE parameters from the 300-person and 700-person samples were similar in relative pattern, but the 700-person model gave higher values and no negative profile values.
Each DCE model rejected the constant proportionality assumption that is implicit in cTTO.
Prior completion of cTTO was associated with more choices of immediate death in matched-pair DCE tasks.
The study had a 49% response rate; some respondents did not complete the matched-pair section, but no respondent was excluded from the analysis.
Quality control flagged 31 cTTO interviews, and the frequency of worse-than-dead responses varied across interviewers.

outcome: Attribute attendance and non-attendance by EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: The six-class ECLC model estimated that 40% of respondents considered all five EQ-5D-5L dimensions and that 60% used some form of attribute non-attendance strategy.

outcome: Attribute attendance and non-attendance by EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: In the ECLC model, estimated non-attendance was highest for self-care and usual activities, followed by mobility, anxiety/depression, and pain/discomfort.

outcome: Attribute attendance and non-attendance by EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: The sensitivity EAA model also estimated substantial non-attendance, with the largest difference from the ECLC estimate occurring for pain/discomfort.

outcome: Attribute attendance and non-attendance by EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: Respondents were less likely to consider physical-functioning dimensions; pain/discomfort was the most attended dimension in the ECLC model.

outcome: Comparative choice-model fit
statement: Both ANA models improved fit over conditional logit: EAA had the lowest AIC, while ECLC had the lowest BIC among the three reported models.

outcome: Difference in DCE-derived EQ-5D-5L health-state utility scores under alternative ANA interpretations
statement: Under a decision-heuristics interpretation of ANA, utility-score differences between the conditional logit and ECLC models were substantial across the 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states.

outcome: Difference in DCE-derived EQ-5D-5L health-state utility scores under alternative ANA interpretations
statement: Under a preference interpretation of ANA, utility-score differences between the conditional logit and probability-weighted ECLC estimates were small for almost all health states.
The pooled survey contained 2,707 of the 3,125 possible EQ-5D-5L states; 418 states were not reported.

Health-state reports were highly concentrated: state 11111 accounted for about one-third of respondents, the three most prevalent states accounted for just over half, and the 33 most prevalent states accounted for just over 80%.
Problems in self-care were the rarest dimension-level reports, while problems in pain or discomfort were the most prevalent.

All 250 possible two-way level combinations occurred in the data, but some were extremely rare; only 122 respondents reported SC4 together with UA1. The combinations previously treated as implausible were not consistently the rarest.

After task exclusion, the treatment designs retained 90, 86, 84, and 90 of the 120 choice tasks for T1 through T4. Correlations between two-way combinations remained below 0.3, and the authors found no other design problems that threatened statistical identification.

Several models produced reversed coefficient ordering between severity levels 2 and 3. Usual activities was monotonic in all models and was the dimension most sensitive to state removal, followed by anxiety or depression.

The random-exclusion comparator estimates were close to the full-data model. The four criterion-based treatment models showed additional deviations, with no consistent direction across dimensions or exclusion criteria.

Predicted values were similar across models for state 11122 but differed more for the other selected states. The two evidence-based rare-state criteria produced different results, and T4 was more similar to the judgment-based T1 than to T3.

outcome: Face validity: understandability, appropriateness, relevance, and response-process issues
statement: Response issues occurred across all four measures. The most common issues involved comprehension and response mapping, including unclear instructions, non-adherence to recall periods, ambiguous or double-barrelled items, missing suitable response options, and positive responding. These issues can affect response validity and bias scores.

ASCOT SCT4 produced ambiguity from questions embedded in response options and from double-barrelled content. Food and drink, dignity, social participation, home cleanliness, and occupation caused interpretation or response-option problems. Residents sometimes could not separate functional ability from services offered by the facility, and positive responding was noted for care-linked items.

For EQ-5D-5L, some residents did not understand that one response per dimension was required, and the layout and EQ VAS instructions caused difficulty. Residents were uncertain about mobility aids, assistance with personal care, medication use, and combined pain/discomfort or anxiety/depression items. The usual-activities examples were often inappropriate for residential aged care.

Relative to its 25-item length, EQ-HWB generated fewer response issues than EQ-5D-5L. Its activity domain was most problematic: residents varied by indoor versus outdoor mobility and aid use, found day-to-day activity examples unsuitable, and needed different answers across self-care activities. Pain versus physical discomfort, assistance, and the 7-day recall period also caused difficulty.

QOL-ACC had fewer response issues than the other measures. The main problems were how residents without mobility aids should answer the mobility item and how residents without pain should answer the pain-management item. Some residents also had difficulty with response-frequency labels or considered family and friends separately.

Residents sometimes judged their health or quality of life relative to worse-off peers and gave more positive responses, particularly for psychological or care-linked domains. The authors related this pattern to positive responding and response shift in older people.

outcome: Reasons given for valuing a health state as same as dead or worse than dead
statement: Most participants believed some health states could be worse than dead, and described such states as the worst EQ-5D state 55555, vegetative state, severe depression, extreme pain, coma, serious illness, paralysis or complete dependence on others.

outcome: Respondent understanding of the tTTO to LT-TTO transition and of same-as-dead versus worse-than-dead valuations
statement: Twelve participants who said in the interview that a state such as 55555 could be worse than dead had not valued any state as worse than dead in the TTO task, and explained the discrepancy by confusion about the task or insufficient thought.

outcome: Reasons given for valuing a health state as same as dead or worse than dead
statement: Participants gave the same kinds of reasons for valuing a state same as dead and worse than dead, without distinguishing between the two: severity of the state or a dimension, dependence and burden on others, quality over quantity of life, ability to contribute to society, impact on others, and loss of control.

outcome: Respondent understanding of the tTTO to LT-TTO transition and of same-as-dead versus worse-than-dead valuations
statement: Most participants found it hard to express the concept of a state being worse than, rather than the same as, dead; only a few could articulate the distinction, and some believed dead is the worst possible state so nothing can be worse.

outcome: Respondent understanding of the tTTO to LT-TTO transition and of same-as-dead versus worse-than-dead valuations
statement: Among the nine participants who traded all years in tTTO but traded none in LT-TTO, six were confused about the transition and four did not realise they had changed their valuation from worse than dead to same as dead.

outcome: Respondent understanding of the tTTO to LT-TTO transition and of same-as-dead versus worse-than-dead valuations
statement: A few participants understood the task and said that the presentation of the LT-TTO, in particular the added 10 years of full health and the longer life span, influenced them not to trade further years.

outcome: Respondent understanding of the tTTO to LT-TTO transition and of same-as-dead versus worse-than-dead valuations
statement: Many participants who traded years in LT-TTO (scenarios c and d) were confused by questions about the transition and could not relate them to the task, suggesting they did not realise they were valuing a state as worse than dead.
Participants who valued at least one state as same as dead or worse than dead did not differ on any measured characteristic from those who valued all states as better than dead.
The recent Chinese CALE model had a wider value range, placed the largest disutility on pain/discomfort instead of mobility, and classified more EQ-5D-5L states as worse than dead.
Compared with the early Chinese study, the recent study produced higher observed values for mild states and lower observed values for severe states.
The recent Chinese study had better cTTO logical consistency than the early study and more respondents who were consistent across all tasks.
After adjustment, recent study time remained associated with higher mild-state values and lower severe-state values in China; no tested study-time interaction was significant.
The recent Singapore CALE model had a wider value range, placed the largest disutility on pain/discomfort instead of anxiety/depression, and classified fewer EQ-5D-5L states as worse than dead.
Compared with the early Singapore study, the recent study produced higher observed values for mild and moderate states.
The Singapore studies had similar mean logical consistency, but the recent study had far fewer respondents consistent across every task; it also had more values at 1 and fewer values at -1.
After adjustment, recent study time was associated with higher mild-state values in Singapore; study time interacted with age 65 years or older for mild and moderate states.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health index value using the Hong Kong value set
statement: The mean EQ-5D-5L index value for the Hong Kong general adult population using the Hong Kong value set was 0.92, left-skewed towards full health.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension responses and EQ VAS score
statement: Mean EQ VAS was 82.7 and about 46% of respondents reported no problems on all five dimensions; the most reported problems were in pain/discomfort.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension responses and EQ VAS score
statement: Younger respondents reported more problems with anxiety or depression, while older respondents reported more problems with pain or discomfort and mobility.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health index value using the Hong Kong value set
statement: In the Tobit model, higher educational attainment and higher life satisfaction were associated with a significantly higher health index, while receiving government allowance, experiencing serious illness and having a longstanding condition were associated with a lower index; sex and age were not significant.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health index value using the Hong Kong value set
statement: Hong Kong mean index values were similar to Australia and Vietnam, higher than Portugal and Poland, and lower than the USA and mainland China norms.

outcome: Consistency of cTTO responses (inconsistencies overall and for health state 55555)
statement: Both arms produced better cTTO data quality than the first wave of EQ-5D-5L valuation studies, with more worse-than-dead valuations, fewer inconsistencies for 55555, fewer spikes and higher values for mild states.

outcome: Consistency of cTTO responses (inconsistencies overall and for health state 55555)
statement: Inconsistent cTTO responses were fewer in the test arm than in the control arm, without reaching statistical significance.

outcome: Consistency of cTTO responses (inconsistencies overall and for health state 55555)
statement: The feedback module halved the level of inconsistencies and reduced the share of respondents with at least one inconsistency, while leaving mean cTTO values unchanged.

outcome: Observed cTTO value distribution, mean values by severity and proportion of worse-than-dead valuations
statement: Mean cTTO values fell with increasing severity in both arms, with a marginally wider value range and higher discrimination for severe states in the test arm.

outcome: Observed cTTO value distribution, mean values by severity and proportion of worse-than-dead valuations
statement: More respondents gave at least one worse-than-dead valuation in the test arm, although the overall share of worse-than-dead health state valuations did not differ significantly between arms.

outcome: Interview and task duration, protocol compliance and homogeneity of the wheelchair example explanation
statement: The ranking task lengthened and complicated the interview without the expected benefit, and was judged burdensome by respondents and interviewers.

outcome: Interview and task duration, protocol compliance and homogeneity of the wheelchair example explanation
statement: Splitting the better-than-dead and worse-than-dead explanations shortened and homogenised the worse-than-dead part of the wheelchair example while keeping protocol compliance.

outcome: Acceptability of the valuation tasks and modifications to respondents and interviewers
statement: Respondents and interviewers found the valuation protocol feasible and acceptable, favoured parking severe states for later worse-than-dead valuation, and welcomed the chance to review answers in the feedback module.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-5L profile and EQ VAS of the sample
statement: The sample was young and highly educated with good self-reported health, and the arms differed significantly in age, gender, some EQ-5D-5L dimensions and EQ VAS.

The hybrid heteroskedastic model without a constant was selected as the final model because it had monotonic and statistically significant coefficients, good fit and prediction accuracy, and the best out-of-sample prediction.
The final value set ranged from full health at 1 to the worst EQ-5D-5L state, 55555, at -0.683.
Pain/discomfort had the largest effect on preference values in the final model, while usual activities had the smallest effect.
Quality control excluded 43 live interviews and retained 1000 interviews for the final analysis.
The cTTO feedback module flagged 8.4% of states, and inconsistency decreased after feedback. Model performance became worse when flagged states were excluded, so the authors retained them.
The study completed the standard valuation work in Arabic with a nationally representative quota sample.

outcome: Linearity between TTO utilities and DCE latent utilities
statement: The United States valuation data rejected a linear scalar-multiple relationship between DCE latent utilities and TTO utilities. The departure was mild and was mainly in the central utility range and very mild health states.

outcome: Heteroscedasticity of TTO responses
statement: TTO residual variation increased with increasing disutility, which gave strong evidence against homoscedasticity.

outcome: Within-subject dependence of TTO responses
statement: TTO responses from the same individual were dependent, based on the within-subject permutation test.

outcome: Value-set prediction error across EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Across the simulations, correctly specified models had maximum state-level mean absolute errors below 0.05, while models that ignored nonlinearity or heteroscedasticity had maximum errors above 0.1.

outcome: Value-set prediction error across EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: When DCE latent utilities were a linear transform of TTO utilities, a correctly specified hybrid model improved prediction over TTO-only analysis. When this relationship was nonlinear, hybrid analysis was less accurate than TTO-only analysis.

outcome: Value-set prediction error across EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Ignoring TTO heteroscedasticity increased prediction errors and distorted the utility scale. The direction of scale distortion depended on the data-generating model.

outcome: Value-set prediction error across EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Ignoring within-subject dependence did not increase mean absolute error when heteroscedasticity was modeled, but the heteroscedastic Tobit still produced a stretched utility scale compared with the marginalized mixed Tobit.

outcome: Value-set prediction error across EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: The TTO-DCE transforming approach performed poorly in the simulated latent-class and mixed-model settings, including settings in which linearity held.

Among 9,197 analyzed patients, 48.3% had documented pre-existing hypertension and 22.0% died in hospital; crude mortality was higher in patients with hypertension than in patients without hypertension.

Pre-existing hypertension was associated with in-hospital mortality in the unadjusted analysis, but the association was no longer significant after adjustment for age, sex, and other hypertension-related covariates.

No antihypertensive medication class was associated with increased mortality in fully adjusted models; pooled prior ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker use showed a small protective association.

Sensitivity analyses that excluded clinically suspected but laboratory-unconfirmed infections, or excluded patients taking antihypertensive drugs without documented hypertension, gave results consistent with the primary adjusted analysis.

outcome: Area under the life-duration utility curve
statement: Adult- and child-perspective AUC values were weakly and positively correlated.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L TTO utility corrected for time preference
statement: Correction for time preference had little effect on mean utilities and did not reduce the adult-child perspective difference in a systematic way.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L TTO utility corrected for time preference
statement: Regression models showed that the positive child-adult utility discrepancy was larger with LT-TTO in the combined model and in the corrected-utility model; the perspective main effect was not significant for cTTO in those interaction models.

outcome: Uncorrected EQ-5D-Y-3L TTO utility
statement: Utilities were generally lower with LT-TTO than with cTTO; the regression condition coefficients indicated about 1.2 additional life-years traded with LT-TTO.

outcome: Uncorrected EQ-5D-Y-3L TTO utility
statement: Utilities were generally slightly higher from the child perspective than from the adult perspective, with an average uncorrected difference of 0.048; state-specific differences appeared more often in the LT-TTO condition.

outcome: TTO response pattern and data quality
statement: LT-TTO produced more negative utilities than cTTO, while strict dominance violations were uncommon across conditions and perspectives.
The analyzed sample contained 219 students, with a mean age of 21.6 years; 141 were female and 78 were male.

outcome: Area under the life-duration utility curve
statement: Time preference was heterogeneous. Median AUC values showed only slight negative time preference and no overall adult-child difference, although many individuals had different time preferences across perspectives.

outcome: Floor and ceiling effects of EQ-5D-5L and EQ VAS
statement: A ceiling effect was present at baseline: 28.0% of patients reported EQ-5D-5L health state 11111, while 5.6% reported EQ VAS 100.

outcome: Responsiveness to self-reported health improvement or worsening over 6 months
statement: Among 41 patients who reported improved health at 6 months, neither EQ-5D-5L index nor EQ VAS change was statistically significant and the effect sizes were small.

outcome: One-month test-retest reliability and agreement
statement: Among 64 patients who reported unchanged health at 1 month, dimension-level agreement was substantial to almost perfect and index-score and EQ VAS test-retest reliability was moderate.

outcome: Convergent validity of EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS against ThyPRO-39 summary scores
statement: At baseline, EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS scores had moderate to strong negative correlations with ThyPRO-39 overall QoL-impact and composite scores, consistent with the prespecified convergent-validity hypothesis.

outcome: Responsiveness to self-reported health improvement or worsening over 6 months
statement: Among 21 patients who reported worsened health at 6 months, EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS scores decreased significantly; responsiveness was moderate for the index by standardized effect size and large for EQ VAS.
The Netherlands and United Kingdom experiments gave similar intervention patterns, although absolute attribute attendance and choice consistency were higher in the United Kingdom sample.
Without level overlap or color coding, respondents attended to only about half of the five EQ-5D-5L attributes. The best combined arms produced almost full attribute attendance.
Color coding alone increased attribute attendance but reduced choice consistency.
Level overlap alone increased attribute attendance and choice consistency.

Combining level overlap with intensity color coding gave the best joint performance: attribute attendance approached all five attributes and relative choice consistency increased by about 30% in both datasets.

Level overlap reduced the relative importance of the most important attribute and increased the relative importance of the least important attribute. Anxiety/depression was most important in both no-overlap samples; self-care was least important in the Netherlands and usual activities was least important in the United Kingdom.

Color schemes changed level importance differently. Shades of purple increased the importance of moderate relative to slight problems without changing the best-to-worst distance, whereas highlighting emphasized worse levels and traffic-light coding significantly increased attention to the extreme levels shown in dark red.

Supplemental sensitivity models and models with warm-up and fatigue terms gave nearly identical attribute-attendance and relative-scale effects. Warm-up effects occurred in arms without level overlap, no warm-up effects occurred in overlap arms, and no fatigue effects were found.

Missing data were low where item skipping was possible, averaging 2.3% in the UK paper survey and 0.6% in the US online survey, with one UK item reaching 19.5% missing because of a printing problem in one questionnaire version.

Differential item functioning was evident for many items, most commonly related to age, with higher occurrences in self-care, happiness and self-worth items and additional DIF in control and anxiety items for respondents reporting a mental health condition.

Overall item performance ratings judged 32 of the 64 items to perform very or fairly well in at least 5 countries, 27 items to have mixed evidence and 7 items to perform poorly in at least one country.

Most items had responses distributed across all levels; high ceiling effects were limited to self-care, mobility, hearing and seeing items, and few respondents used the worst level for activity, safety, severity-scaled pain and discomfort, and the items "I felt calm" and "I got along well with people around me".

Most items discriminated between respondents with physical or mental health conditions and healthy respondents with moderate to large effect sizes, but discrimination across carers was weak, with moderate to low effect sizes for high- versus low-hour carers.

The item "I had support when I needed it" performed poorly for physical and mental health known-group differences in all countries, while the similar item "I felt unsupported by other people" had moderate to high effect sizes; self-care items with frequency response options performed worse than those with difficulty response options.

Exploratory factor analysis found a positively worded wellbeing factor, a negatively worded wellbeing factor and a SWEMWBS factor, indicating the need for a bifactor confirmatory model with separate positive and negative measurement factors alongside the domain factors.

A well-fitting bifactor CFA model with 15 domains was attained on the UK data and also fitted the Australian and US data; German data required dropping energy and merging mobility with self-care, Argentine data required merging self-worth and coping, and the Chinese data fitted least well with several feelings subdomains needing to be merged.

Most of the item variance (at least 69% for all domains in the UK data) was explained by the domain factors rather than by the positive and negative measurement factors, which supported running IRT on separate domains.
