Three items intended for a daily activity domain were not highly correlated and the domain was not identified, so "I could do what I needed" was moved to meaningful/valuable activity, "I was able to do daily activities" to mobility, and "I was able to do the things I wanted to do" to the control subdomain.

IRT showed that response categories worked well for most items, but self-care items with frequency response options had non-functioning categories in every country and five items showed merged categories in at least one country, suggesting fewer response levels may be needed.
The pre-meeting survey showed limited prior use of health utility methods and mixed familiarity with HTA among the 12 stakeholders.

Stakeholders reported that QALYs had not yet been used in Pakistan's healthcare system, although researchers increasingly used EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L for HRQoL evidence; they endorsed generating local adult and child health utilities for economic evaluation and resource allocation.
Views on paying more per QALY for children than adults were divided: the roundtable Results section reports support from 5 stakeholders and caution or disagreement from 7.

Stakeholders agreed that adolescents aged 11 years and older could complete valuation tasks and should participate; 4 of 12 specifically recommended adult taxpayer preferences for the initial value set because of budget, capacity, and policy constraints, while the others emphasized adolescent involvement in parallel or later phases.

Stakeholders generally considered it acceptable to ask respondents to imagine child health states and compare life-year quantity with quality or immediate death, but all expected many respondents to find trading a child's life length for better quality difficult; responses could depend on personal relationships with children.

Stakeholders consistently preferred parents or primary caregivers as proxies when a child could not self-report, because they understood the child's daily function, emotional well-being, and health challenges better than teachers or healthcare professionals.

Key barriers to use of health preference values in Pakistan were low awareness of QALYs, scarce local utility data, limited trained staff and institutional HTA capacity, constrained health budgets, possible cultural resistance, and weak routine use of cost-effectiveness evidence.

Despite the barriers, stakeholders noted growing government interest and called for collaboration among government, academia, and industry to support the generation, acceptance, and use of health preference data.
In the analyzed longitudinal sample, 77.0% were vaccine accepting at wave 1 and 89.0% reported vaccination at wave 2.
Wave 1 intention and wave 2 vaccination status were consistent for 77.3% of respondents.
The direct intention question had high sensitivity but low specificity for later vaccine uptake.
Wave 1 vaccine intention was the strongest individual-level predictor of wave 2 uptake in the selected logistic model.

After Bonferroni correction, university education was associated with less sentiment switching, while right-leaning or undisclosed political ideology was associated with more switching; some country effects also remained significant.
After Bonferroni correction in the directional switching models, having one chronic condition was associated with lower odds of changing from initial hesitancy to later acceptance.

outcome: Missing responses and practical completion feasibility
statement: Neither EQ-5D-Y version had missing answers, and the authors judged feasibility to be excellent and comparable.

outcome: Ceiling effects, response redistribution, and inconsistency
statement: EQ-5D-Y-5L did not significantly reduce the overall or dimension-level ceiling effect compared with EQ-5D-Y-3L at baseline or follow-up.

outcome: Ceiling effects, response redistribution, and inconsistency
statement: Most responses redistributed consistently from EQ-5D-Y-3L to EQ-5D-Y-5L; the extra levels gave more precise reporting of moderate-to-severe problems, although dimension-level inconsistency ranged from 8.7% to 16.1%.

outcome: Convergent validity against generic and disease-specific HRQoL measures
statement: EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L had broadly similar convergent validity with PedsQL Generic Core Scales and the condition-specific instruments; correlations varied from weak to strong by dimension and diagnostic group.

outcome: Test-retest reliability among patients reporting stable health
statement: Among the 44 patients reporting stable health, EQ-5D-Y-5L showed slightly better test-retest stability in every dimension and at least substantial agreement.

outcome: Responsiveness to post-treatment health improvement
statement: Among follow-up respondents, 95.6% reported improvement; in the analyzed improved group, a larger proportion showed aligned positive dimensional change on EQ-5D-Y-5L than on EQ-5D-Y-3L.

outcome: Convergent validity against generic and disease-specific HRQoL measures
statement: The additional response levels produced small improvements in stability, responsiveness, and accuracy, especially for severe states, without evidence of poorer feasibility or validity; they did not establish clear overall superiority of EQ-5D-Y-5L.

outcome: Predictive accuracy of EQ-5D-5L utility values under standard and extended EQ-VT cTTO designs
statement: For predictions evaluated across all 150 observed health states, the standard EQ-VT design had an average RMSE of 0.055 and MAE of 0.041.

outcome: Predictive accuracy of EQ-5D-5L utility values under standard and extended EQ-VT cTTO designs
statement: All three design extensions reduced RMSE and MAE relative to the standard design. The designs that included more directly valued health states had the lowest overall errors, and adding more observations to the more-states design produced no additional gain.

outcome: Predictive accuracy of EQ-5D-5L utility values under standard and extended EQ-VT cTTO designs
statement: When the overall sample was held near the standard-design size, the extended design with more health states still had marginally lower prediction error than the standard design.

outcome: Predictive accuracy of EQ-5D-5L utility values under standard and extended EQ-VT cTTO designs
statement: For the 64 new health states, designs with more states gave the best predictions. For the conventional 86 states, the design with more observations per state gave the best predictions.

outcome: Predictive accuracy of EQ-5D-5L utility values under standard and extended EQ-VT cTTO designs
statement: Prediction patterns were similar across designs in Bland-Altman plots. Prediction was adequately precise for milder states with level sum scores 6 to 9 when more states or more observations were used; none of the extensions lowered the higher MAE seen for level sum score groups 10 and 24.

outcome: Ability to differentiate consecutive EQ-5D-Y-5L ordinal severity levels without preference inversion
statement: No statistically significant positive incremental-dummy coefficients were observed in either adults or adolescents, so the study found no preference inversions across the ten cohort-by-country models.

outcome: Relative preference importance of EQ-5D-Y-5L dimensions
statement: The latent-scale DCE results were not anchored at 0 and 1 and did not measure preferences for the dead state.

outcome: Ability to differentiate consecutive EQ-5D-Y-5L ordinal severity levels without preference inversion
statement: Adults generally differentiated the EQ-5D-Y-5L levels in their intended severity order; more than 80% of incremental dummies were statistically significant and negative in every country, with only a few country-specific cases of indifference.

outcome: Choice consistency and error variance by cohort and country
statement: Adolescents largely differentiated the level labels, but they had more nonsignificant level transitions and more random choices than adults.

outcome: Relative preference importance of EQ-5D-Y-5L dimensions
statement: Among adults, Pain/Discomfort was the most important dimension in Australia, Canada, the Netherlands, and Spain, while Mobility was most important in China; Looking After Myself and Usual Activity were generally the least important.

outcome: Relative preference importance of EQ-5D-Y-5L dimensions
statement: Adolescent dimension preferences varied more across countries: Mobility was most important in Canada, China, and Spain and second most important in Australia and the Netherlands.

outcome: Relative preference importance of EQ-5D-Y-5L dimensions
statement: After adjustment for overall choice consistency, adolescents placed more relative importance on Mobility and less on Pain/Discomfort and Worried, Sad, or Unhappy than adults in every country.

outcome: Self-reported task understanding, state differentiation, decision difficulty, and completion time
statement: Adult and adolescent respondents reported broadly similar task feasibility: most found the tasks easy to understand and could tell the difference between health states, while deciding between states was more difficult.

outcome: Online survey response quality and exclusion
statement: Online recruitment produced substantial suspected fraudulent data in the Australian parent-recruited adolescent subsample, and the investigators removed the whole subsample.

outcome: Choice consistency and error variance by cohort and country
statement: Adult preferences and choice consistency were more similar across countries than adolescent preferences; Chinese adults and Canadian and Chinese adolescents showed relatively lower choice consistency.

outcome: Estimated EQ-5D health-state utilities under standard and proposed anchoring
statement: Across all reported model specifications, maximal-health-gain anchoring reduced dimension-level disutilities, increased health-state utilities, and had little effect on the relative importance of EQ-5D dimensions.

outcome: Estimated EQ-5D health-state utilities under standard and proposed anchoring
statement: For EQ-5D-5L, maximal-health-gain anchoring made the utility of state 55555 substantially less negative in ordinary least squares and Bayesian models.

outcome: Change in the proportion of health states with negative utility
statement: For EQ-5D-5L, maximal-health-gain anchoring reduced the proportion of health states with negative utility from approximately 3% to 4% to less than 1% in most models and 0.1% in the Bayesian model without discounting.
In the EQ-5D-5L data, most respondents valued their worst reported health state as worse than dead, while pits-state data were available for nearly all respondents.

outcome: Estimated EQ-5D health-state utilities under standard and proposed anchoring
statement: For EQ-5D-3L, maximal-health-gain anchoring made the utility of state 33333 less negative across ordinary least squares, weighted least squares, and Bayesian estimation.

outcome: Change in the proportion of health states with negative utility
statement: For EQ-5D-3L, maximal-health-gain anchoring reduced the proportion of health states with negative utility from 13.2% to 3.3% to 5.3%, with little effect on relative dimension importance.
In the EQ-5D-3L data, 79.3% of respondents valued their worst reported state as worse than dead, and 29% did not value 33333 as their worst state.
Accounting for censoring increased the effect of anchoring, while individual power discounting attenuated but did not remove the effect.
The analyzed sample comprised 1,000 adults and broadly mirrored the Philippine general population by age, sex, ethnolinguistic group, and region; unemployment had the largest demographic discrepancy.

Respondents provided 10,000 cTTO observations; 1,164 values were flagged by respondents as having an incorrect severity order and were excluded. All 7,000 DCE observations were retained, although 42 respondents showed unusual response patterns.

All three reported 20-parameter models violated monotonicity. The authors selected the homoscedastic eight-parameter TTO-only model with a respondent random intercept because it was logically consistent and parsimonious, and hybrid cTTO-DCE models did not materially improve performance.
Pain/discomfort and mobility had the largest dimension coefficients in the preferred model, followed by self-care, usual activities, and anxiety/depression.
After linear adjustment, full health (11111) had utility 1.000 and the most severe state (55555) had utility -0.4381; 169 health states had negative values and were classed as worse than dead.

Philippine utility values were generally higher than Thai values: 72% of Philippine health-state values were higher, with a mean difference of 0.041, although Thai utilities tended to exceed Philippine utilities for level-sum scores of 23 or more.
Health fluctuations were nearly universal and occurred on about half of observed days.
The dimensions that most often triggered reported fluctuations were memory, mobility, concentration, sleep, pain/discomfort, and usual activities.
Both self- and proxy-reported EQ-5D-5L health states commonly changed between weekly assessments; repeated utility values had moderate agreement.

Absolute EQ-5D-5L utility change from day 1 to day 14 was larger in the moderate- and high-fluctuation groups than in the low-fluctuation group, although group differences were not statistically significant.
Diary-defined improvement was associated with increased EQ-5D-5L utility and improved level sum scores, whereas deterioration was associated with lower utility; EQ VAS results were inconsistent.

One quarter of caregivers did not follow the EQ-5D-5L recall period of today. Nonadherence tended to increase with fluctuation frequency and was significantly higher for patients whose diary-defined health improved than for those whose health deteriorated.
In the base case from the Brazilian Unified Health System perspective, standard care was more effective than best supportive care and was cost-effective at the Brazilian threshold.
Donanemab produced only a negligible QALY gain over lecanemab at a high incremental cost and ICER.
Annual indirect costs increased sharply with Alzheimer disease severity and included substantial family home-help costs.
Lecanemab produced a small QALY gain over standard care at a very high incremental cost and ICER.
Lecanemab and donanemab had no probability of being cost-effective over standard care within the willingness-to-pay range evaluated.
Standard care remained the lowest-ICER drug strategy across scenarios, but its cost-effectiveness was sensitive to the perspective and source of cost and utility inputs.
Study-based EQ-5D-5L utility decreased with Alzheimer disease severity, but the moderate and severe utilities were higher than the cited literature inputs.

outcome: Raw VAS scores and VAS range (full health minus pits) for each instrument
statement: On the joint VAS the individual-level range between full health and pits was wider for EQ-5D than for SF-6D, indicating the descriptive system contributes to the narrower SF-6D value range.

outcome: Raw VAS scores and VAS range (full health minus pits) for each instrument
statement: The Sheffield protocol produced lower joint VAS scores than the York protocol, and the VAS scores in variant 3 differed significantly from the original York study VAS scores.

outcome: Raw VAS scores and VAS range (full health minus pits) for each instrument
statement: Raw VAS scores for full health did not differ between EQ-5D 11111 and SF-6D 111111 at the aggregate level, and most respondents gave both states the same value.

outcome: TTO and chained SG utility values for EQ-5D and SF-6D states standardised on the -1 to +1 dead-full health scale
statement: Effects of the preceding valuation task were not statistically significant: EQ-5D states tended to have a narrower range when valued first and SF-6D states tended to have lower values when preceded by EQ-5D.

outcome: TTO and chained SG utility values for EQ-5D and SF-6D states standardised on the -1 to +1 dead-full health scale
statement: The Sheffield protocol using chained SG gave higher mean values overall than the York protocol using TTO, but the protocol effect was statistically significant in only one of four comparisons; a marginally significant interaction consistent with a TTO-SG cross-over appeared when SF-6D states were valued first.

outcome: TTO and chained SG utility values for EQ-5D and SF-6D states standardised on the -1 to +1 dead-full health scale
statement: The difference between the EQ-5D and SF-6D pits values was much smaller within this study than across the two original valuation studies.

outcome: TTO and chained SG utility values for EQ-5D and SF-6D states standardised on the -1 to +1 dead-full health scale
statement: Values in the present study were higher than in the original studies, significantly so for EQ-5D with a larger discrepancy for the more severe states.

outcome: Logical inconsistencies in the ranking exercise
statement: Few respondents produced logically inconsistent rankings, and over two-thirds ranked the states in the intended severity order.

Self-reported health of respondents was similar on the two instruments and similar to the original valuation study samples, though no respondent reported full health on SF-6D while 51% reported EQ-5D 11111.

outcome: Redistribution of responses from 3LY levels to 5LY levels, including proportion of inconsistent response pairs
statement: Redistribution from the 3LY to the 5LY was largely consistent: the proportion of inconsistent response pairs was low in every dimension, ranging from 0.0% for "Doing usual activities" to 3.9% for "Pain/discomfort".

outcome: Ceiling effects (proportion of "no problem" responses) per dimension and for full health, with absolute and relative reduction from 3LY to 5LY
statement: Ceiling effects were reduced in four of five dimensions when moving from the 3LY to the 5LY, significantly for "Usual activities" and for "Feeling worried/sad/unhappy"; "Looking after myself" showed identical ceiling in both versions and the difference in reporting full health (11111) was not significant.

outcome: Ceiling effects (proportion of "no problem" responses) per dimension and for full health, with absolute and relative reduction from 3LY to 5LY
statement: Floor effects were absent in all dimensions of both versions, and no patient selected the "extreme problems/cannot" level of any 5LY dimension.

outcome: Test-retest reliability of dimension responses over 2-3 weeks (Gwet agreement coefficient and percentage agreement)
statement: Test-retest agreement over 2-3 weeks was very good for both versions, except the "Feeling worried/sad/unhappy" dimension of the 3LY; in that dimension the 5LY performed markedly better, especially among patients reporting stable health (GRS = 0).

outcome: Discriminative power measured by Shannon index (H prime) and evenness index (J prime)
statement: Discriminative power measured by the Shannon index was slightly higher for the 3LY in all dimensions except "Usual activities", and the evenness index was higher for the 3LY in all dimensions.

outcome: Known-groups differences in proportion of "no problem" responses across clinical subgroups
statement: Known-groups results were similar for the two versions: no dimension differed by modified Lenke classification, only "Pain/discomfort" in the 3LY differed by Cobb angle group, and both versions distinguished treatment modality groups in several dimensions.

outcome: EQ VAS self-rated health score
statement: Sample health was high overall: mean EQ VAS was 84.3 (SD 16.4), and 19 and 20 distinct health states were observed with the 3LY and 5LY respectively.
Patients who completed the retest interview did not differ significantly from those who did not on any demographic or clinical characteristic, giving no evidence of selection bias.
Multinomial propensity-score weighting improved covariate balance for all examined exposures, but balance was notably weakest for the reported effect of COVID-19 on health.

In Tobit models, respondents who said COVID-19 affected their health rated 55555 higher whether the reported health effect was negative or positive; those reporting a positive health effect also rated dead substantially higher.

There were no significant effects of regional COVID-19 cases or deaths, and the analyses found no consistent significant effects for COVID-19 effects on quality of life, shopping frequency, or exercise frequency after propensity-score weighting.
After multinomial propensity-score weighting, higher subjective infection risk was associated with higher raw VAS ratings for dead and state 55555.

Most alternative treatments of extreme rescaled 55555 values gave similar results, but the significant effects of worry and subjective risk on rescaled 55555 were not reproduced in about half of the robustness analyses.
Significant raw VAS differences could be large, but differences in rescaled 55555 values were usually small, with reported magnitudes of about 0.005 to 0.07.
After multinomial propensity-score weighting, greater worry about infection was associated with lower ratings for dead but higher rescaled values for 55555.
Most rescaled values for 55555 were positive but low, while many respondents valued 55555 below zero and thus as worse than dead.
The heteroskedastic conditional logit model fit better than the conditional logit model, gave coherent positive quality-of-life coefficients, and improved precision.
Among converged models, the model with two scale classes and three taste classes had the lowest BIC and was selected as the best-fitting model.
The quality-of-life-oriented taste class placed the largest weights on EQ-5D-5L severity and the smallest weight on lifespan; several severe profiles were valued as worse than dead.
The middle taste class had health-attribute and lifespan effects between the other two classes; EQ-5D-5L profile 55555 was worse than dead, but profiles 44444 and 33333 had positive values.
The quantity-of-life-oriented taste class placed the smallest weights on health attributes and the largest weight on lifespan; even EQ-5D-5L profile 55555 had a positive value.
Prior completion of cTTO tasks strongly predicted membership in the quality-of-life-oriented class; respondents with cTTO exposure treated health problems as more burdensome on the QALY scale.
The model identified two scale classes. Task type produced the main scale-class differences, and none of the tested scale-class membership covariates was statistically significant.

All taste classes had lifespan power parameters below one, consistent with decreasing marginal value of lifespan; the decrease was strongest in the quality-of-life-oriented class and weakest in the quantity-of-life-oriented class.

outcome: Problems in the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions and health-state profiles
statement: The full sample reported worse EQ-5D-5L health than published Chinese population norms, with the largest difference in anxiety/depression.

outcome: Problems in the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions and health-state profiles
statement: After adjustment for sex, age group, education, marital status, and chronic disease, Hubei respondents had more mobility, usual-activity, and anxiety/depression problems and lower utility than respondents outside Hubei.

outcome: Problems in the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions and health-state profiles
statement: Overseas respondents had poor descriptive health, including a high prevalence of anxiety/depression and a mean utility close to that of much older people in Chinese population norms; their adjusted utility remained lower than that of respondents outside Hubei.

outcome: Problems in the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions and health-state profiles
statement: Contrary to usual population patterns, younger respondents tended to report more problems, especially with usual activities and anxiety/depression, and lower utility.

For the Proxy-CB perspective, the CarerQoL-7D index had moderate agreement and the CarerQoL VAS had substantial agreement with caregiver scores; CarerQoL item agreement was highest for financial problems and lowest for fulfillment from care tasks.
Care recipients generally overestimated caregiver burden from the Proxy-CB perspective and underestimated it from the CR-SPB perspective; the largest intra-proxy difference was for overall burden.

The five-item caregiver-burden level summary score had substantial agreement between caregiver and Proxy-CB ratings and moderate agreement between caregiver and CR-SPB ratings, with small systematic mean differences for both comparisons.

Proxy-CB had moderate to substantial agreement with caregiver self-assessment across the caregiver-burden domains; agreement was strongest for financial burden and weakest for emotional and social burden.
CR-SPB agreed less closely with caregiver self-assessment than Proxy-CB did across all reported caregiver-burden domains.

outcome: Construct validity
statement: Construct validity was sufficient with high certainty for the EQ-5D-3L index and dimensions: 86% of 43 index tests and 100% of 210 dimension tests were positive.

outcome: Construct validity
statement: Construct validity was sufficient with high certainty for the EQ-5D-5L index and dimensions: 90% of 186 index tests and 100% of 395 dimension tests were positive.
The review included 16 studies from 31 countries and synthesized 996 individual EQ-5D measurement-property tests; 96% of tests met the review criteria.

outcome: Test-retest reliability
statement: Test-retest reliability results were sufficient where assessed, but evidence was sparse. The EQ-5D-5L index had two positive tests with moderate certainty; the EQ-5D-5L dimensions had five positive tests with high certainty; the EQ-5D-3L index and dimensions had one and five positive tests, respectively; and EQ VAS had one positive test with low certainty.

outcome: Responsiveness
statement: Responsiveness was assessed in 104 tests for the EQ-5D-5L index, EQ-5D-3L index, or EQ VAS, and 101 tests showed the expected direction of change. No included study assessed responsiveness of EQ-5D-5L or EQ-5D-3L dimensions.

Eleven of 16 included studies used EQ-5D-5L, and the source-study sample sizes ranged from 20 to 674 patients with a median of 259. All studies used patient self-completion, and one also used family-member or caregiver proxy reports.

outcome: Construct validity
statement: EQ VAS construct validity was sufficient overall with high certainty: 93% of 44 tests were positive. Known-groups validity was inconsistent in the only study that assessed it, with 40% of five tests positive; the lymphoma subgroup result was also inconsistent at 70%.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L item missingness, descriptive-system completion, and incomplete-response probability
statement: EQ-5D-5L completion decreased with age, from 96.01% in respondents aged 18–24 years to 85.92% in respondents aged 85 years or older; overall completion was 93.11%.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L item missingness, descriptive-system completion, and incomplete-response probability
statement: EQ-5D-3L completion decreased with age, from 94.88% in respondents aged 18–24 years to 83.14% in respondents aged 85 years or older; overall completion was 91.57%.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L item missingness, descriptive-system completion, and incomplete-response probability
statement: Anxiety/depression had the largest item-missingness among the oldest respondents: 7.56% for EQ-5D-5L and 9.14% for EQ-5D-3L at age 85 years or older; missingness in the other dimensions was below 5%.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L item missingness, descriptive-system completion, and incomplete-response probability
statement: After adjustment for gender and long-term condition, the predicted probability of an incomplete response increased more quickly after age 64 and reached 13.9% for EQ-5D-3L and 11.5% for EQ-5D-5L at age 85 years or older.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L item missingness, descriptive-system completion, and incomplete-response probability
statement: Item missingness was associated with age in chi-square tests, but Cramer's V showed negligible or very weak associations; EQ-5D-5L had less missingness than EQ-5D-3L at each age and dimension.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L response distribution by dimension and age
statement: Reported problems generally increased with age. EQ-5D-5L had a lower ceiling and spread responses across more severity levels than EQ-5D-3L.

outcome: Model fit (deviance information criterion) and logical consistency of coefficients
statement: Models with separate parameters for all dimensions and levels (20-parameter) fitted best for DCE-only, TTO-only and combined data, as judged by the deviance information criterion, and restricting the parameter space improved the hybrid model.

outcome: Estimated utility decrements per dimension and level (value set coefficients)
statement: Censoring decisions had important effects on estimates: 749 TTO observations were censored at zero, and dropping censoring assumptions narrowed the range of predicted index values.

outcome: Estimated utility decrements per dimension and level (value set coefficients)
statement: Unrestricted 20-parameter hybrid estimation produced two logical inconsistencies (usual activities and anxiety/depression between levels 4 and 5), which disappeared when the parameter space was restricted, with little change in coefficients.

outcome: Model fit (deviance information criterion) and logical consistency of coefficients
statement: Accounting for respondent heterogeneity improved fit, and the multinomial slope model with three latent groups performed best, identifying groups with disutility slopes near 1, about 2 and about 3.6.

outcome: Estimated utility decrements per dimension and level (value set coefficients)
statement: Pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression received the largest dimension weights, and the assumed slope distribution mainly affected the predicted values of the most severe states.

outcome: TTO values for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Predicted values for mild states exceeded observed mean TTO values, which the authors attribute to asymmetry of the error distribution near the top of the scale.
Of 1032 participants, 1000 provided usable responses according to quality-control criteria and interviewer judgment; 9787 cTTO observations remained after response-level exclusions.
The analyzed sample closely matched the 2010 Mexican Population Census for age, sex, and region and followed the AMAI socioeconomic structure.

The feedback module flagged 2.1% of cTTO responses; no other data were excluded, no respondent gave the same value to all states, and 70.6% had no logical inconsistencies after exclusions compared with 67.3% before exclusions.
Observed mean cTTO values ranged from 0.96 for state 11121 to −0.66 for state 55555; 1925 of 9787 analyzed valuations were below zero.
Residual variance increased with health-state severity, which supported use of a heteroscedastic model.
The preferred Bayesian heteroscedastic censored model addressed respondent clustering, censoring at −1, and heteroscedasticity; all dimension-level coefficients were logically ordered.
The Mexican value set ranged from 0.984 for state 21111 to −0.596 for state 55555, and 9.1% of modelled EQ-5D-5L health states were worse than dead.

Pain/discomfort had the greatest level-5 utility decrement, followed by anxiety/depression, usual activities, mobility, and self-care; the largest level 4-to-5 increases were especially marked for pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression.
The mean interview duration was 44.2 minutes, including background questions, task explanations, cTTO tasks, and DCE tasks.

outcome: Latent health-state values derived from the discrete choice probit model
statement: DC-derived values per country correlated almost perfectly with the pooled DC values of the 400 EQ-5D-5L states.

outcome: VAS values for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: VAS values per country correlated strongly, but less closely than DC values, with the pooled VAS values.

outcome: Agreement and correlation between DC-derived and VAS values within and across countries
statement: Individual intraclass correlation coefficients showed high similarity of DC values (>0.85) and only moderate correspondence of VAS values across the four countries.

outcome: Latent health-state values derived from the discrete choice probit model
statement: Pooled DC and pooled VAS values correlated strongly, but the relationship between the two methods was nonlinear, with larger differences between severe states under DC and larger differences between relatively good states on the VAS.

outcome: Latent health-state values derived from the discrete choice probit model
statement: All pooled discrete choice coefficients were statistically significant and increased logically with level severity, except that slight pain/discomfort (PD2) had a more negative coefficient than moderate pain/discomfort (PD3).

outcome: VAS values for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Mean VAS values clustered in a narrow band of roughly 40 to 70 on the scale, indicating range reduction and end-aversion, whereas states scored low or high on VAS were also predicted low or high by the DC model.

outcome: Task completion time and drop-out per valuation method
statement: The VAS task took less time to complete than the paired comparison task, and drop-out was low in all countries.

outcome: Latent health-state values derived from the discrete choice probit model
statement: Mean values over all 400 health states were highest in the US, followed by Canada and the Netherlands, and lowest in the UK for both DC and VAS.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state values on the dead-full health scale estimated by each model
statement: The DCdead and DCWTD models produced very similar rescaled value sets, with high concordance and small mean square difference, although coefficients in the DCdead model were slightly lower in absolute size.

outcome: Agreement and consistency between value sets from the four models (CCC, MSD, coefficient ordering, log-likelihood)
statement: Agreement between the DC models anchored on dead and the models anchored on or based on lead-time TTO was much weaker.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state values on the dead-full health scale estimated by each model
statement: Lead-time TTO produced the largest utility decrements and the lowest values, driven by a large intercept, while the DC models anchored on dead gave much higher values for the worst state 55555.

outcome: Feasibility and comprehension of the discrete choice and lead-time TTO tasks
statement: About half the respondents rated at least one health state worse than dead, and states were judged worse than dead more often in the indirect lead-time TTO task than in the direct discrete choice question.

outcome: Agreement and consistency between value sets from the four models (CCC, MSD, coefficient ordering, log-likelihood)
statement: No model was fully consistent: all showed some positive or non-monotonic level coefficients, for example a positive coefficient for level 3 pain/discomfort in every model and lower coefficients for level 2 than level 3 self-care in the three DC models.

outcome: Feasibility and comprehension of the discrete choice and lead-time TTO tasks
statement: Respondents found the lead-time TTO task harder than the discrete choice task; many did not realise the health condition changed at the indifference response and needed the interviewer to complete the first exercise with them, while inconsistent mean lead-time TTO values were observed, for example state 55253 valued lower than the more severe state 55255.

TTO values are inconsistent with random and expected utility theory: empirical evidence on constant proportional trade-off is mixed and utility independence is often violated, so the value of a health state depends on the duration spent in it and on the order in which states are presented.

TTO is confounded by time preference, by the framing effect of the chosen time frame, and by respondents' own life expectancies, which may be longer or shorter than the conventional 10 years; no practical correction for these prospect-theory effects is yet available.

The iterative indifference procedure shapes the values obtained: the quarter-year increments of the MVH protocol produced many very negative predicted values (lowest possible value -39), and the EQ-VT computer-assisted procedure accumulates indifference at three specific iteration steps, producing many values of -1.0, 0.0 and 1.0.

In the English EQ-5D-5L value set respondents were more likely to give 0.0, 0.5 or 1.0 than intermediate values, with very few values between -0.5 and 0.0, suggesting crude rather than cardinal responses; values recorded at -1.0 are censored, so averaging individual values should account for censoring.

TTO requires a trained interviewer or specialised software, and trained interviewers do not explain the tasks in the same structured way, so values are interviewer dependent; similar interviewer effects were traced for VAS values in the MVH study.

Qualitative research shows respondents often cannot distinguish the health states to be valued, struggle with the hypothetical nature of the states, and have difficulty conceptualising being dead, including religious or spiritual beliefs about death.

Different procedures are used for states better and worse than dead; valuation studies based on the composite TTO showed almost no discrimination among values for states worse than dead, and lag-time TTO produced lower values than lead-time TTO with the difference increasing over longer time frames.

TTO does not satisfy measurement-theoretic requirements of unidimensionality and invariance, mainly because it measures two distinct elements at once, health status and life years, and it is better described as a matching method than a choice method.

A UK government-commissioned review by NICE and the Department of Health and Social Care raised several concerns about the English EQ-5D-5L values, many of them associated with the TTO; later EQ-VT versions used in other countries produced more balanced results with smaller interviewer effects.

outcome: Comprehensibility of EQ-HWB-9 items, instructions, recall period, and response options
statement: Eight EQ-HWB-9 items were understood as intended by all participants, but the mobility item produced unintended or narrowed interpretations for four participants.

outcome: Perceived differences and preferences for mobility wording and cognition response scales
statement: Most participants perceived meaning differences between the three mobility wordings, and preferences varied; participants who first saw the version without an example consistently preferred a version that included an illustrative mobility-aid example.

outcome: Perceived differences and preferences for mobility wording and cognition response scales
statement: Participants understood both cognition response scales. Seven perceived differences between frequency and difficulty, and preferences were split between the difficulty and frequency scales.

outcome: Relevance of EQ-HWB-9 items
statement: Most items were relevant to most participants, although loneliness, sadness or depression, and control were each judged not relevant by five participants.

outcome: Perceived overlap and redundancy between EQ-HWB-9 items
statement: Participants noted overlap between mobility and activities and between cognition and exhaustion, anxiety, or pain, but they did not regard the items as redundant and valued their separate measurement.

outcome: Comprehensiveness of the EQ-HWB-9
statement: Only two participants considered the measure fully comprehensive; ten identified missing information, mainly medical management, support, mental-health impact, or space for free-text context.

outcome: Comprehensibility of EQ-HWB-9 items, instructions, recall period, and response options
statement: The seven-day recall period and instructions were generally understood, although some participants preferred a shorter recall period or reported unclear response or instruction wording.

outcome: Feasibility of routine QoL data collection
statement: Of 103 consenting residents, the study obtained 90 resident self-reports, 101 staff proxy assessments, and 49 family proxy assessments.

outcome: Barriers and facilitators to routine QoL data collection
statement: Staff proposed dedicated time and staff, quiet morning interviews, repeated approaches when residents were unavailable, accessible rephrasing, and selecting proxies who know the resident well.

outcome: Barriers and facilitators to routine QoL data collection
statement: Staff identified possible interviewer, social-desirability, and proxy bias; time pressure could also lead staff to complete assessments without adequately involving residents.

outcome: QoL measure completion and missing data
statement: Most residents with an evaluation record completed the EQ-5D-5L; resident EQ-5D-5L data had low missingness.

outcome: Resident engagement, understanding, and support needs
statement: Staff rated most residents as very or somewhat engaged in QoL collection, although many questions had to be repeated or explained across all four measures.

outcome: Proxy difficulty and perceived proxy-report accuracy
statement: Staff reported more difficulty with proxy completion than relatives.

outcome: Proxy difficulty and perceived proxy-report accuracy
statement: Staff commonly expected residents to rate their own QoL more positively, while most relatives expected their rating to align with the resident.

outcome: Fit with staff workflow and data collection protocol
statement: Most staff assessments fitted within the work schedule, but a notable minority did not.

outcome: Barriers and facilitators to routine QoL data collection
statement: Staff said that standardized QoL questions improved their knowledge of residents, revealed unmet issues, and could support more person-centred care.

outcome: Barriers and facilitators to routine QoL data collection
statement: The main implementation barriers were time pressure, competing duties and interruptions, resident illness or communication and cognitive difficulties, limited familiarity between proxy and resident, and instrument-specific problems.

outcome: Barriers and facilitators to routine QoL data collection
statement: Staff generally viewed EQ-5D-5L length and directness as acceptable and QOL-ACC wording as positive; they found ASCOT and EQ-HWB more difficult because of length or complex wording, and some ASCOT topics and mental-health questions were sensitive.

outcome: Growth, geographic spread, and practical administration of DCE valuation studies
statement: The review included 65 studies after screening 1172 deduplicated records and assessing 109 full articles.

outcome: Anchoring and statistical modelling practices
statement: Sixty-one studies anchored latent DCE coefficients to a QALY scale, most often with duration attributes or cTTO data.

outcome: Anchoring and statistical modelling practices
statement: More than 60% of included studies reported some degree of coefficient or health-state ordering inconsistency with conditional logit models.

outcome: Use and design characteristics of DCE-based health-state valuation studies
statement: The review identified growing use of DCE health-state valuation across more countries and measures, but it found no gold standard for design, presentation, anchoring, or model selection.

outcome: Growth, geographic spread, and practical administration of DCE valuation studies
statement: Publication volume increased during the review period, and the share of studies from developing countries was higher than in the 1999–2018 literature.

outcome: Growth, geographic spread, and practical administration of DCE valuation studies
statement: Most source studies sampled the general population and used large samples, although study sample sizes varied widely.

outcome: Growth, geographic spread, and practical administration of DCE valuation studies
statement: Online panels were the most common administration mode; most offline studies used software-assisted data collection.

outcome: Use and design characteristics of DCE-based health-state valuation studies
statement: EuroQol measures were the most frequently valued preference-based measures, and studies also covered generic, condition-specific, carer, child, older-person, and broader well-being measures.

outcome: Use and design characteristics of DCE-based health-state valuation studies
statement: DCE task designs varied in attribute count, duration or death anchoring attributes, numbers of choice sets, and tasks per respondent, but paired choices were dominant.

outcome: Use and design characteristics of DCE-based health-state valuation studies
statement: Efficient experimental designs dominated, with Bayesian-efficient and D-efficient approaches more common than factorial or manually selected designs.

outcome: Use and design characteristics of DCE-based health-state valuation studies
statement: Studies used overlap, colour highlighting, blocking, and several forms of randomization to reduce cognitive burden and balance task presentation.

outcome: Anchoring and statistical modelling practices
statement: Main-effects and duration-interaction utility functions were most common; conditional logit was the usual starting regression model, while mixed logit and latent-class models were widely used for heterogeneity.

outcome: Composite of in-hospital mortality or discharge with palliative care
statement: The composite primary outcome occurred in 1,108 patients (23%): 1,066 died in hospital and 42 were discharged with palliative care.

outcome: Composite of in-hospital mortality or discharge with palliative care
statement: Age 70 years or older was strongly associated with the primary outcome in univariable analysis, and mortality risk increased steeply from about age 60.

outcome: Composite of in-hospital mortality or discharge with palliative care
statement: After adjustment with a restricted cubic spline for age, female sex was associated with lower mortality, while diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease remained associated with higher mortality; other comorbidity effects were attenuated.

outcome: Composite of in-hospital mortality or discharge with palliative care
statement: Each individual comorbidity significantly mediated the association between age 70 years or older and the primary outcome, but every individual mediation proportion was below 6%; a comorbidity count greater than two mediated 8% of the association.

outcome: Referral to an intensive care unit during hospitalization
statement: During hospitalization, 1,312 patients (27%) were referred to intensive care; patients aged 70 years or older made up 34% of these referrals.

outcome: Missing questionnaire responses
statement: Both proxy forms had few missing responses and showed similarly good feasibility.

outcome: Ceiling, response redistribution, and classification consistency
statement: At baseline, the EQ-5D-Y-5L proxy classified fewer children as having no problems on all five dimensions than the EQ-5D-Y-3L proxy; the difference was small and was not present at follow-up.

outcome: Ceiling, response redistribution, and classification consistency
statement: Logical response-redistribution pathways dominated when 3L responses were projected onto 5L responses, which supported the 5L proxy as a valid extension. Inconsistent redistribution varied by dimension, and the added detail was most useful for pain or discomfort.

outcome: Convergent validity with generic and disease-specific HRQoL measures
statement: The 3L and 5L proxy forms showed similar convergent validity. Associations with PedsQL Generic were mostly weak to moderate, while associations with matched disease-specific measures were generally higher and ranged from weak to strong.

outcome: Test-retest reliability among children reported as stable
statement: Test-retest reliability was high and comparable for the two proxy forms among 59 stable-health pairs.

outcome: Responsiveness to proxy-reported health improvement
statement: Among proxies who reported improved child health, the 5L proxy showed a larger proportion of improvement-aligned dimension changes than the 3L proxy for all dimensions except self-care.

outcome: Agreement between child self-report and proxy report
statement: At baseline, patient-proxy agreement was generally higher for EQ-5D-Y-5L than for EQ-5D-Y-3L. Agreement was at least moderate except in acutely ill children; after recovery, agreement was generally high and comparable between versions.
In the primary GLS Tobit model, private health-insurance status was not a statistically significant determinant of EQ-5D-5L health-state preferences.

Interaction analyses gave limited evidence of insurance-related differences: most insurance-by-dimension-level interactions were not significant, although the most severe usual-activities level was significant in the interaction model and the most severe mobility and usual-activities levels were significant after covariate adjustment.
When models were estimated separately by insurance status, the 95% confidence intervals for every level of each EQ-5D-5L dimension overlapped between groups.
The simple comparison of valuations for EQ-5D-5L state 55555 found no statistically significant difference between insured and uninsured respondents.
Health-state disutility generally increased as the described EQ-5D-5L health state became poorer, which supported the face validity of the models.

The analyses found preference heterogeneity related to age, marital status, and income, showing that the study could detect some sociodemographic differences even though it found no compelling insurance effect.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state values for the 3125 states
statement: The main effects robust regression model was selected as the Uruguayan EQ-5D-5L value set; predicted values ranged from -0.264 for the pits state to 1 for full health.

outcome: Model logical consistency, goodness of fit and prediction accuracy
statement: The OLS model showed a logical inconsistency between slight and moderate problems in usual activities, while both robust models were logically consistent; adding interaction terms improved AIC/BIC by only about 0.4 % with equal prediction accuracy (MSE = 0.002).

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state values for the 3125 states
statement: Uruguayan values were higher than the Argentinian EQ-5D-5L crosswalk values across the whole misery index spectrum, by about 0.05 for states differing from full health by one dimension at level 2.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-5L profiles, EQ VAS and index-based population norms
statement: Population norms: the mean EQ-5D-5L index value for the Uruguayan general population sample was 0.954, decreasing with age, and slightly higher in males than females though not significantly.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-5L profiles, EQ VAS and index-based population norms
statement: Self-reported health: 44 % of respondents reported no problems on any EQ-5D-5L dimension; older respondents reported more problems in all dimensions and mean EQ VAS decreased with age.

outcome: Model logical consistency, goodness of fit and prediction accuracy
statement: Discrete choice models showed several logical inconsistencies, so the hybrid C-TTO/DCE approach was abandoned and the value set was based on C-TTO data only.

outcome: Model logical consistency, goodness of fit and prediction accuracy
statement: Quality control led to dropping 10 of 21 interviewers and excluding 220 interviews; excluded participants were similar in age, gender and educational level to the retained sample.

Preference values did not differ significantly by educational level in ANOVA of crude preferences or when education dummies were added to the final model; 43.7 % of respondents had low health literacy despite over 80 % having at least some secondary education.

Caregiver descriptions aligned fairly closely with mobility, self-care, and pain or discomfort response levels, less closely with usual activities and worry, sadness, or unhappiness levels, and poorly with EQ VAS ratings.

Caregivers considered the instrument too brief and insufficiently comprehensive to describe children with intellectual disability. Common missing areas were communication, social engagement, broader mental-health indicators, and the human or equipment support that the child required.

Responses depended on whether activities meant independent or supported performance and whether the comparison was with the child’s own usual state or a typically developing peer. Caregivers also preferred attention to functional impact and support needs rather than only problems or deficits.

Proxy reporting was especially uncertain for pain or discomfort and for worry, sadness, or unhappiness because many caregivers could not observe the child’s internal state and believed their own response could differ from the child’s response.

Caregivers considered the five questions clear and largely relevant, although some wanted mobility broadened beyond walking, self-care expanded to include toileting, and usual activities separated or clarified.
Of 34 invited families, 28 completed interviews. The 28 interviews included 30 caregivers and represented 28 children or young people with intellectual disability.
Caregivers questioned the single-day time frame because health or emotions could fluctuate within a day, the day could be atypical, and the child could be away from the caregiver at school.

Caregivers who discussed use did not want the brief instrument alone to determine funding or compare different children because it did not capture need in enough detail and children’s usual activities and expectations differed.

The median caregiver EQ VAS rating was 78 out of 100, but caregivers used different aspects of health and well-being to form ratings, and severe fixed impairment did not necessarily produce a low rating.

outcome: Severe fatigue and cognitive-problem prevalence
statement: Severe fatigue and cognitive problems were common in the analyzed Q-fever sample, and most respondents reported both.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility and EQ VAS by fatigue and cognitive-problem status
statement: Respondents with severe fatigue or cognitive problems had significantly lower mean EQ-5D-5L utility and EQ VAS scores than their comparison groups (all p < 0.001).

outcome: EQ-5D-5L coverage and sensitivity for fatigue and cognition
statement: Fatigue and cognition were associated with all EQ-5D-5L dimensions. Fatigue correlated most strongly with usual activities and pain/discomfort, while cognition correlated strongly only with usual activities; 99% of severe-fatigue respondents and 98% of respondents with cognitive problems reported a problem on at least one EQ-5D-5L dimension.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L coverage and sensitivity for fatigue and cognition
statement: The EQ-5D-5L dimension models explained more variance in fatigue than in cognition.

outcome: Added explanatory power of fatigue and cognition for EQ VAS
statement: Adding fatigue to the EQ-5D-5L model increased adjusted explained variance for EQ VAS by about six percentage points, whereas cognition added about 0.1 percentage point; adding both did not improve on fatigue alone.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L coverage and sensitivity for fatigue and cognition
statement: Only 5% of analyzed respondents reported the EQ-5D-5L 11111 profile, indicating a small ceiling in this symptomatic sample.

outcome: Factor structure and dimensionality
statement: Separate exploratory factor analyses of EQ-HWB and each comparator instrument resulted in four-factor structures.

outcome: Factor structure and dimensionality
statement: For all 44 pooled items, a five-factor solution was more meaningful than the four-factor solution and comprised emotional functioning, self-care and usual activities, leisure and enjoyment, cognition and senses, and pain.

outcome: Factor structure and dimensionality
statement: EQ-HWB items covered all five pooled factors, whereas EQ-5D-5L and ASCOT items covered three factors and QOL-ACC items covered four factors.

outcome: Convergent validity between instrument items
statement: All EQ-5D-5L items correlated strongly with at least one EQ-HWB item; the strongest correlation was between EQ-5D-5L pain or discomfort and EQ-HWB physical pain.

outcome: Convergent validity between instrument items
statement: Most QOL-ACC items correlated strongly with at least one EQ-HWB item, but social relationships did not; ASCOT showed less convergence, with only one strong correlation with EQ-HWB.

outcome: Item loadings, cross-loadings, and uniqueness
statement: Several items did not meet the 0.32 loading threshold, including ASCOT food and drink, accommodation, safety, and dignity; QOL-ACC mobility; and EQ-HWB difficulty hearing and physical discomfort.

outcome: Item loadings, cross-loadings, and uniqueness
statement: Three positively worded EQ-HWB items loaded negatively on the leisure and enjoyment factor, and some items cross-loaded across emotional, functional, and leisure factors.

outcome: Item loadings, cross-loadings, and uniqueness
statement: The polychoric factor correlation matrix was non-positive definite because of high inter-item correlations between EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB, so the primary results used the complete item set with principal-factor EFA.

outcome: Mean directly reported and recalled EQ-5D-3L summary scores
statement: Recalled EQ-5D-3L summary scores were systematically lower than the directly reported scores, with larger deviation at longer recall intervals.

outcome: Mean directly reported and recalled EQ-VAS scores
statement: Recalled EQ-VAS scores were also lower than directly reported EQ-VAS scores, significantly so for the longer recall intervals.

outcome: Correspondence (ICC) between directly reported and recalled EQ-5D-3L summary, dimension and EQ-VAS scores
statement: Correspondence between directly reported and recalled scores was fair overall for both EQ-5D summary and EQ-VAS.

outcome: Correspondence (ICC) between directly reported and recalled EQ-5D-3L summary, dimension and EQ-VAS scores
statement: Among the EQ-5D dimensions, mobility was recalled most consistently while anxiety/depression and pain/discomfort showed the largest distortion.

outcome: Correspondence (ICC) between directly reported and recalled EQ-5D-3L summary, dimension and EQ-VAS scores
statement: Correspondence was lowest in patients with major trauma (ISS >= 16) and in patients with a middle educational level, and highest in patients with high education.

outcome: Correspondence (ICC) between directly reported and recalled EQ-5D-3L summary, dimension and EQ-VAS scores
statement: Correspondence was better when the recovery phase (3 months) was recalled than when the acute phase (1 week) was recalled, despite the longer interval.

outcome: Correspondence (ICC) between directly reported and recalled EQ-5D-3L summary, dimension and EQ-VAS scores
statement: Only a minority of patients recalled exactly the score they had reported directly, and exact agreement was much rarer on the EQ-VAS than on the EQ-5D summary.
Content-validity evidence found broad relevance in some populations but gaps for spinal cord injury and asthma; research professionals also regarded self-care as narrow and usual activities as broad.

The EQ-5D-5L index showed moderate-to-strong convergence with other multi-attribute utility, physical or functional, and pain measures, but weak convergence with life satisfaction and cognition or communication measures.
Two studies of dimension-level change found the EQ-5D-5L more sensitive than the EQ-5D-3L, although both versions had limited responsiveness in anxiety/depression in one study.
Missing responses and floor effects were generally not problematic, but substantial ceiling effects remained, especially in general-population samples and for the self-care dimension.
The review included 99 publications from 32 countries; musculoskeletal or orthopedic conditions and cancer were the most frequently studied patient areas.
Pooled EQ-5D-5L index values were generally lower in disease groups than in healthy populations and lower in disadvantaged socioeconomic or sociodemographic groups.
The EQ-5D-5L generally distinguished disease groups, severity, symptoms, age, and education, but did not consistently distinguish groups defined by some clinical and sociodemographic factors.
EQ-5D-5L index scores had good test-retest reliability, but individual dimensions showed instability; fair agreement occurred in some studies and was most evident for pain/discomfort.

Across 15 studies, EQ-5D-5L index responsiveness was typically moderate among people who improved or were expected to improve; comparisons generally found performance as good as or better than other instruments, but evidence was heterogeneous.
The standard formula can calculate a standard error for any health state described by a modeled HRQoL instrument, including states outside the valuation modeling data.
The replicated model estimates were identical to those reported by Gray et al.; small discrepancies from the published MVH model may reflect different statistical software.
Across all 243 EQ-5D-3L profiles, the calculated standard errors ranged from 0.008171 to 0.012203.
The replicated health-state values ranged from -0.594 to 1, so the standard-error range was small relative to the value range.
The nine patient groups reported 204 distinct EQ-5D-3L health states at baseline and 202 at 1-year follow-up; the general-population sample reported 152 states.

Mean EQ VAS was lower in patient groups than in the general population at baseline and increased by 1 year in almost all patient groups except respiratory failure; increases were largest in most intervention-based registers.

For the nine selected EQ-5D-3L states, mean EQ VAS scores were generally higher for milder states and lower for more severe states at both time points, but values for the same state differed across patient groups and over time.

EQ VAS and the EQ-5D-3L index had mostly moderate correlations at baseline. Correlations increased at 1 year in every patient group and were strong for spine and hip patients; correlations between changes were low to moderate.

OLS and two-level models produced mostly severity-consistent EQ VAS decrements. The main inconsistency was self-care level 3, with some mobility inconsistencies; anxiety/depression had the largest decrement in most patient groups and in the general population.
The variance in EQ VAS explained by EQ-5D-3L dimensions was lower at baseline and increased at 1 year across patient groups; respiratory failure had the lowest explained variance.

Age- and sex-adjusted models were similar to unadjusted models, multilevel models gave narrower confidence intervals than OLS models, and EQ-5D-5L analyses in the BOA and hip groups were broadly comparable to the main EQ-5D-3L analyses.
In the complete-case pooled sample, mean EQ-5D-5L index was 0.794 and mean rescaled EQ-5D-5L health was 0.871.
Better health was associated with fewer chronic conditions, better practice experience, younger age, male gender, not smoking, and residence in areas with less income and education deprivation.

The association between white ethnicity and health was heterogeneous: it was negative through age 64 and positive from age 65, positive in five of eight condition samples, and negative in all regional samples except London and Yorkshire and the Humber.

Practice clinical quality was positively associated with health in the pooled sample but in only 4 of 23 region-, age-, and condition-specific samples; condition-specific quality was positively associated with health only for diabetes, and GP supply was not associated with health.

Income was positively associated with health in the pooled sample and all subgroups. Income-related health inequality was greatest for patients with a mental health problem, was highest in the northwest and northeast regions, and peaked at ages 55–64.

The standard and absolute concentration indices were strongly positively correlated across condition, region, and age samples, while the partial index had much weaker correlations with them across regions.

Multiple-imputation and mixed-effects results were very similar to the complete-case pooled OLS results, and practice-level and CCG-level random effects accounted for very small proportions of residual variance.
Exploratory factor analysis supported two related but distinct CARE-2B factors: CR-SPB and Proxy-CB.
Confirmatory factor analysis showed good fit for the CR-SPB model and less favorable fit for the Proxy-CB model, although all item loadings were high and statistically significant.

Convergent validity patterns differentiated the perspectives: CR-SPB related most strongly to the established SPB Scale and care recipient health and well-being, while Proxy-CB related most strongly to caregiver-reported burden and CarerQoL.

Item response theory results showed that CARE-2B items generally discriminated well and provided high information across a wide latent-trait range; the financial burden item had overlap in response-category curves.

The multivariate exploratory factor analysis found that CR-SPB items loaded on a distinct factor, while Proxy-CB items loaded on the caregiver-burden factor. The CR-SPB financial item also cross-loaded on caregiver burden.
Both CARE-2B subscales had high internal consistency in the analyzed sample.

outcome: Acceptability of the online EQ-5D-Y: completion rate and response distribution
statement: Acceptability was high: all 136 participants answered the EQ-5D-Y at the first visit and 119 (87.5%) at the fourth visit, with complete responses to the five dimensions and the EQ VAS.
Problems were most frequent in "having pain/discomfort" and "feeling worried/sad/unhappy" and rare in "mobility" and "looking after myself".

outcome: EQ-5D-Y dimension distribution, unweighted summary score, EQ VAS and KIDSCREEN scores in children with T1DM
statement: The unweighted EQ-5D-Y summary score had a mean of 8.5 (SD 10.9) with a large ceiling effect (50.7% reporting no problem in any dimension) and no floor effect; the EQ VAS mean was 80.4 (SD 14.7).

outcome: Construct validity: known-groups differences and multitrait, multimethod correlations with KIDSCREEN
statement: Known-groups analysis showed statistically significant differences by self-rated general health and by mental health in three EQ-5D-Y dimensions ("doing usual activities", "having pain/discomfort", "feeling worried/sad/unhappy") and in the summary score, with larger effect sizes for the EQ-5D-Y summary score than for the KIDSCREEN-10 index.
Acute diabetic decompensations were associated only with problems in "looking after myself", and dysfunctional family function only with problems in "having pain/discomfort".

outcome: Construct validity: known-groups differences and multitrait, multimethod correlations with KIDSCREEN
statement: Three of four hypothesised substantial convergent correlations were confirmed; the EQ-5D-Y "mobility" dimension correlated only weakly with KIDSCREEN-27 "physical well-being", while the three hypothesised discriminant correlations were insignificant (0.02-0.06).

outcome: Test-retest reproducibility (intraclass correlation coefficient) in the stable subsample
statement: Test-retest reproducibility between the first and fourth visits in the stable subsample (n=18) was good, with an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.83 for the summary score and 0.74 for the EQ VAS.

outcome: Responsiveness: change and effect size between first and fourth visit in the improved subsample
statement: In the improved subsample (n=58) the EQ-5D-Y detected significant change between the first and fourth visits in three dimensions, in the summary score and in the EQ VAS, with moderate-to-large effect sizes.
The analysis produced 734 codes in four categories: health definition and conception; significant health factors; perceptions of EQ-5D-5L; and perceptions of EQ VAS.

Dementia was the most concerning and most influential health problem for quality of life, principally because of loss of control, incurability, and burden on family members. Cancer, pain, mental illness, bereavement, disability, and other conditions were also described as threats to quality of life.

outcome: Perceived relevance, adequacy, comprehensibility, and comprehensiveness of EQ-5D-5L
statement: Usual activities was most often considered the most important EQ-5D-5L dimension because it was seen to encompass other dimensions. Some participants said that five broad dimensions could not show detailed health and proposed more mental-health content, social relationships, diet, sleep, or more specific physical-function content.

outcome: Perceived relevance, adequacy, comprehensibility, and comprehensiveness of EQ-5D-5L
statement: Eighteen of 20 main participants reported no difficulty understanding and answering EQ-5D-5L. Most found its five physical and mental dimensions simple, familiar, distinct, and broadly adequate, although anxiety/depression or questionnaire intent was difficult for two participants and some found response options extreme or ambiguous.

outcome: Perceived clarity, ease, scoring behavior, and limitations of EQ VAS
statement: Participants said EQ VAS scores may not be comparable across respondents because people use different standards. Some found today’s health ambiguous or disliked reducing health to one score. Many used 5-point or 10-point increments rather than 1-point units, and some viewed 100 as an unreachable ideal.

outcome: Perceived clarity, ease, scoring behavior, and limitations of EQ VAS
statement: Participants usually based their current EQ VAS score on physical discomfort. When explaining a 5-point improvement, they more often described relief of mental difficulties; when explaining a 5-point decline, they described increased physical discomfort.

outcome: Perceived clarity, ease, scoring behavior, and limitations of EQ VAS
statement: Most participants found EQ VAS visually clear, simple, easy to understand, and easy to answer. The thermometer-like display and 0-to-100 range were viewed as useful.

outcome: Korean general-public concepts and important dimensions of health
statement: Participants viewed health as multidimensional. They emphasized physical health most strongly, but also identified mental health, social relationships, vitality, and the ability to pursue desired activities as important. Urban participants gave broader definitions, while all four rural participants focused only on physical health.

Corresponding EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB dimensions showed moderate-to-strong convergent associations, while sight, hearing, feeling unsafe, acceptance, and ability to do wanted activities had weaker associations with EQ-5D-5L dimensions.

EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S had fewer highest-response concentrations and more lowest-severity responses than EQ-5D-5L, which suggests better discrimination across health and well-being in this general-population sample.

Exploratory factor analysis supported four factors: anxiety or depression; mobility, pain, or discomfort; activities of daily living or personal care; and self-identity. The first three were shared across measures, while self-identity was unique to the full EQ-HWB.
Participants with current health problems had lower adjusted utility values on both measures, with a larger relative decrement for EQ-HWB-S than for EQ-5D-5L.
EQ-HWB-S was more sensitive than EQ-5D-5L to depression and chronic pain in the multivariable utility models, while effects for most physical conditions were broadly comparable.
The nine-item EQ-HWB-S items did not cross-load in the four-factor solution, while several broader full-form EQ-HWB items captured content not represented by EQ-5D-5L.

The video and in-person samples were similar for age, gender, and deprivation, but differed significantly in ethnicity and income. Both samples were highly educated, and older adults and the lowest deprivation quintile were underrepresented.

Understanding and overall feedback were positive in both modes. In-person interviews had better results for boredom and hearing the interviewer, while about one in six video respondents reported technical issues.
There was no clear overall preferred mode. Participants most often preferred the mode that they received, and the characteristics of people who preferred video and in-person interviews differed.

Both modes produced good-quality data. Video interviews had marginally poorer results on some criteria, but only two of the many assessed criteria differed significantly: repeated zero values without negative values and interviewer doubt about participant understanding.

TTO distributions and mean values were largely similar by mode. Mean differences exceeded 0.05 for four moderate or severe states, and the clearest difference was for state 55555, which had lower values and lower dispersion in in-person interviews.

Interview mode was not significant in the main random-effects Tobit models after adjustment. Mode-by-state interactions were significant for states 21345 and 55555; gender and some interviewer effects also affected values.
The video group was larger because invitation acceptance was higher for video and in-person data collection stopped when COVID-19 transmission increased.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index score
statement: Weighted mean EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS scores did not differ significantly between the two 2020 survey waves.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index score
statement: The pooled pandemic-period sample had significantly lower mean EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS scores than the pre-pandemic Alberta population norms, although the overall differences were smaller than the stated minimally important differences.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension-level problem prevalence

Pulmonary embolism was diagnosed in 201 of 939 analyzed patients.
In-hospital death occurred in 260 of 939 analyzed patients.
After adjustment for calendar time, age, sex, hospital transfer, and weight, a doubling of protocolised LMWH dose was not associated with clear evidence of a change in pulmonary embolism risk.

After adjustment for calendar time, age, sex, hospital transfer, and weight, a doubling of protocolised LMWH dose suggested a lower in-hospital mortality risk, but the confidence interval included no effect.
Restricted cubic spline analysis suggested a non-linear relation between protocolised LMWH dose and in-hospital mortality.
Protocol validation in two academic hospitals found that the actual starting LMWH dose agreed with the protocolised dose in 45 of 58 patients in one hospital and 58 of 92 patients in the other.

Sensitivity analyses that converted nadroparin doses, removed six patients with 18,000 IE anti-Xa exposure, or added selected covariates did not materially change the pulmonary embolism results; adding sex, dyslipidaemia, and baseline blood pressure moved the mortality hazard ratio toward no effect.
The cTTO distribution was largely smooth and concentrated between 0.5 and 1. Negative values were present, but values at the lower bound of -1 were uncommon.

Participants completed the cTTO valuation interview in a mean of 35.70 minutes and required a mean of 13.21 pairs of alternative lives to reach an indifference point in one task; the interview was longer and required more moves than the published Chinese EQ-5D-5L comparator.

For each of ordinary least squares, heteroscedastic, and random-intercept models, the main-effects-plus-A3 specification had better predictive accuracy than the main-effects-only specification. Only one participant was a nontrader, which the authors treated as further support for the suitability of cTTO for EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation.

Mean values decreased with level sum score. State 11112 had the highest observed mean cTTO value, and state 33333 had the lowest and was the only state with a negative mean; there was a large drop between state 33323 and 33333.
The 2020 census-weighted population norms indicated generally high self-reported health.
EQ-5D-5L showed less ceiling and more observed health-profile diversity than EQ-5D-3L in the same respondents.
Pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression were the most frequently reported problems on both EQ-5D versions.
Doctor-diagnosed disease was the strongest and most consistent independent correlate of lower HRQoL across index and EQ VAS models.

Older age and unemployment were associated with lower EQ-5D-5L health utility, while rural residence, unemployment, and never-married status were associated with lower EQ-5D-3L utility in reported models.
EQ VAS models found lower scores with diagnosed disease, Chinese ethnicity, and never-married status, and higher scores among females.
Norm estimates were robust to use of 2010 rather than 2020 census weights.
The EQ-5D-5L had a low ceiling and no floor: 17 participants reported profile 11111, none reported profile 55555, and 115 distinct profiles were observed.
Correlations across EQ-5D-5L dimensions were mostly weak to moderate; mobility and usual activities had the only strong correlation, so divergent validity was only partly sufficient.
Convergent validity was sufficient: the EQ-5D-5L index correlated strongly with EQ VAS and moderately with self-rated health.
Known-group validity was acceptable. EQ-5D-5L index, level sum score, EQ VAS, and ceiling differed in the expected direction across low, moderate, and high symptom-severity groups.

All five EQ-5D-5L dimensions explained 41.3% of EQ VAS variance, with mobility and usual activities explaining 39.0%; explanatory power was much lower in the high-severity group and did not meet the study criterion.
Median one-year changes in EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS were zero; 30.3% of participants had mixed profile changes.

Responsiveness was insufficient. EQ-5D-5L index change had weak correlations with self-rated health change, Global Rating of Change, and symptom-severity change, and it poorly discriminated change groups.

statement: The Italian EQ-5D-5L value set ranged from full health at 1 to -0.571 for state 55555, and 523 health states were worse than dead.

outcome: Candidate-model consistency, significance, prediction error, and robustness
statement: Sensitivity analyses supported robustness of the selected model to removal of pilot data and removal of health states flagged in the feedback module.

outcome: Experience-scale value of each incremental EQ-5D-Y-3L child HRQoL improvement
statement: Parents valued relief across all five EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions positively; fathers were ambivalent about relief from some to no self-care problems and from a bit to not worried, sad, or unhappy.

outcome: Differences in child HRQoL preferences between mothers and fathers
statement: Mothers placed a higher value than fathers on improving a child's feelings from a bit worried, sad, or unhappy to not worried, sad, or unhappy.

statement: From the parent perspective, the worst EQ-5D-Y-3L profile 33333 had an experience-scale value below no experience, represented by being in a coma.
