statement: The empirical example produced parent-, mother-, and father-perspective estimates with fewer than 100 respondents in each gender subgroup, which the authors present as evidence of feasibility for brief value assessments.
The provincial PROM database included more than 60,000 unique patients and more than 300,000 digitally captured patient reports.

Patients reported that the Symptom Tracking Report supported communication, understanding of symptom trends, recognition of self-management and support needs, and a positive clinic experience.

outcome: Reported problems in EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions and health profiles
statement: Most problems overall were reported in the dimensions 'having pain or discomfort' and 'feeling worried, sad or unhappy'; 94 unique health profiles occurred and 11111 was most frequent, while 33333 was reported by two respondents.

outcome: Reported problems in EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions and health profiles
statement: Girls reported more problems than boys in 'doing usual activities', 'having pain or discomfort' and 'feeling worried, sad or unhappy', and had a lower mean VAS score.

outcome: Reported problems in EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions and health profiles
statement: The youngest age group reported the highest mean VAS score, and adolescents aged 15-16 years were more likely to report mood problems and less likely to report mobility problems than 13-14 year olds.

outcome: Reported problems in EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions and health profiles
statement: Adolescents with one or both parents unemployed reported more problems with usual activities, pain/discomfort and mood, and a lower mean VAS score, than those with both parents working.

outcome: EQ VAS score (0-100)
statement: In the fully adjusted linear regression, always feeling depressed in the past 3 months had the largest negative association with VAS score.

outcome: Reported problems in EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions and health profiles
statement: There was a gradient of increasing reported problems and decreasing VAS score from 'very good' to 'very bad' self-rated health, and feasibility was good with few missing answers.

outcome: Ceiling effect (proportion reporting perfect health)
statement: Ceiling was only marginally lower with the EQ-5D + C than with the EQ-5D, in the full sample and in both subgroups.

outcome: Convergent validity with EQ VAS

outcome: Explanatory power for EQ VAS (adjusted R-squared)
statement: Adding the cognition dimension raised the explained variance of the EQ VAS by about 3 percentage points in TBI patients and about 1.5 percentage points in non-TBI patients.

outcome: Explanatory power for EQ VAS (adjusted R-squared)
statement: All EQ-5D and cognition dimension levels were significantly associated with the EQ VAS in both groups, except that usual activities level 2 in the non-TBI group had an unexpected positive coefficient.

outcome: Explanatory power for EQ VAS (adjusted R-squared)
statement: Any selection of five out of the six dimensions gave similar explained variance, so the cognition dimension performed like the existing dimensions rather than adding unique information.

outcome: Classification efficiency (Shannon and Shannon Evenness indices)
statement: Absolute classification efficiency was higher for the EQ-5D + C than for the EQ-5D in both groups, while relative efficiency (Shannon Evenness) was similar after adjustment for underestimation bias.

The review of 25 COPD-specific HRQoL instruments identified 18 recurring dimensions. Every instrument contained at least one respiratory symptom. Dyspnea appeared most often, in 18 instruments (72%). Social functioning, impact on daily life, mobility, emotional functioning, energy or fatigue, and sleep each appeared in more than 15 instruments.

The exploratory interviews reached thematic saturation after 8 physicians and 18 patients; two additional patients produced no new codes. The analysis yielded 31 subthemes and 11 themes. The most frequent themes were breathing problems, limitations in physical activity, social interaction effects, psychological problems, sleep problems, appetite or digestive problems, and fatigue.

The final Version 4 candidate set contained five EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons: Breathing problems; Limitations in physical activities due to shortness of breath; Social activities; Tiredness or lack of strength; and Sleep problems.

Successive expert and patient review changed item wording and examples. The team replaced dyspnea with shortness of breath for comprehension, separated social activities from going out, replaced fatigue with lack of strength, added examples for sleep problems, and removed the appetite item because it was not considered a typical COPD symptom and combined distinct concepts.

Respondents identified conceptual overlap between Limitations in physical activities due to shortness of breath and the EQ-5D-5L Mobility, Self-care, and Usual activities dimensions. Some respondents nevertheless judged the bolt-on to describe their COPD experience more accurately. Breathing problems received stronger support as the more appropriate respiratory bolt-on.

Patients, physicians, and experts welcomed relevant bolt-ons as a way to represent COPD HRQoL more comprehensively. Respondents considered an eight-dimension form acceptable when the three newly identified generic dimensions were added to the existing five EQ-5D-5L dimensions, although the authors noted that valuation and complexity require further study.
The review included 81 eligible reports from 63 unique studies after 3,139 records were identified.
Use of preference-based measures with Indigenous people increased recently and was concentrated in Australia and New Zealand, with fewer reports from the United States and Canada.
Indirect multi-attribute preference-based measures dominated the evidence; EQ-5D was the most common instrument, but many reports did not identify the EQ-5D version.
Most reports used a preference-based measure to measure health status, while few examined measurement performance, directly elicited preferences, developed a measure, or translated a measure.
Only four publications evaluated psychometric performance in Indigenous populations; the limited evidence included mixed findings for EQ-5D across populations.
Only 31 reports described an ethically engaged research approach, while most reports did not provide sufficient information about engagement or Indigenous-specific ethical approaches.
Only 14 reports clearly stated which value set was used.

outcome: Completion time and reported difficulty
statement: Both instruments were quick and easy for proxy respondents to complete.

outcome: Ceiling and floor effects
statement: CHU9D had no overall ceiling effect in the total sample or the special-health-care-needs sample and no floor effect, but its pain dimension had a high best-level response rate. PedsQL had no ceiling or floor effect.

outcome: Test-retest reliability
statement: CHU9D showed moderate overall test-retest reliability and lower reliability than PedsQL, with fair-to-moderate agreement across individual CHU9D dimensions.

outcome: Convergent and divergent validity
statement: CHU9D showed convergent and divergent validity against PedsQL: total scores correlated strongly, similar items correlated moderately to strongly, and prespecified unrelated items correlated weakly.

outcome: Known-group validity
statement: CHU9D distinguished groups with expected health differences and specific chronic conditions, with medium-to-large or large effect sizes that were similar to or better than PedsQL.

outcome: Responsiveness to health change
statement: CHU9D detected health change with mainly small responsiveness for general or existing-condition change and medium-to-large responsiveness for worsening linked to a new illness; the worsening groups were small.

Use of Australian adolescent versus United Kingdom adult CHU9D weights produced similar conclusions about reliability, known-group validity, and responsiveness, although mean utility values differed substantially.

outcome: Item-level and instrument-level ceiling and floor effects
statement: All 300 patients reported a problem in at least one EQ-HWB item. Seven EQ-HWB items had item-level ceiling effects, but neither EQ-HWB nor EQ-HWB-S had an instrument-level ceiling effect.

outcome: Item-level and instrument-level ceiling and floor effects
statement: At instrument level, the EQ-HWB-S had a lower ceiling than EQ-5D-5L and SWEMWBS but a higher ceiling than FACT-8D.

outcome: Convergent and divergent validity
statement: Convergent validity was supported by moderate-to-strong correlations between conceptually similar items and strong correlations of the EQ-HWB-S index with EQ-5D-5L and FACT-8D index values. EQ-HWB level sum scores correlated strongly with FACT-G and moderately with WEMWBS.

outcome: Known-group validity
statement: EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S significantly distinguished groups defined by EQ VAS, general health, and symptom count with large effect sizes and groups defined by comorbidity count with small effect sizes. Cancer-stage discrimination was small for EQ-HWB-S and trivial for EQ-HWB.

outcome: Test-retest reliability
statement: Across 25 EQ-HWB items, 7 had almost-perfect, 10 strong, 5 moderate, and 3 fair test-retest agreement. Anxiety, exhaustion, and sleep had the lowest agreement.

outcome: Test-retest reliability
statement: EQ-HWB-S index and EQ-HWB level sum score had excellent instrument-level test-retest reliability. EQ-5D-5L had higher ICCs; FACT-8D and FACT-G had slightly lower ICCs; and SWEMWBS and WEMWBS had the lowest ICCs among the compared instruments.

outcome: Responsiveness to change
statement: EQ-HWB-S showed small responsiveness in the improved subgroup and moderate responsiveness in the worsened subgroup. EQ-HWB showed small responsiveness in the improved subgroup and large responsiveness in the worsened subgroup. Unexpected score changes also occurred in the unchanged-health subgroup.

Exhaustion, pain, discomfort, and sleep were particularly relevant EQ-HWB domains in this breast cancer sample, and EQ-HWB-S performed comparably with established generic and cancer-specific measures across the principal psychometric tests.

outcome: Use of the feedback module: responses flagged for removal
statement: About a third of respondents used the feedback module to flag responses, covering around 5% of all responses, and most of those respondents had no logical inconsistency.

statement: Worse-than-dead responses were common and mean health state values did not differ significantly between study arms, while Hong Kong values were lower than Dutch values.

outcome: Five-year healthcare costs and longitudinal cost-trajectory membership
statement: Healthcare expenditure was highly concentrated in 2017: 27% of residents incurred no cost, while the top 10%, 5%, and 1% accounted for 79%, 66%, and 36% of expenditures, respectively; the top-5% threshold was C$7,968.

outcome: Five-year healthcare costs and longitudinal cost-trajectory membership
statement: Among people who were high-need high-cost in 2017, 39% met this definition in one study year and 61% met it in two or more of the five years.

statement: The selected five-group trajectory model identified persistent very-high-cost, persistent high-cost, rising-cost, declining-cost, and cost-spike groups; more than three quarters were in one of the two persistent high-cost groups.

statement: The multinomial model had limited explanatory fit, with McFadden pseudo-R-squared of 0.10 and Nagelkerke R-squared of 0.16, which indicated that important predictors were absent from the administrative data.

outcome: Fit and classification adequacy of trajectory and multinomial models
statement: Sensitivity analyses using adjacent index years, top-1% and top-10% high-cost thresholds, monthly costs, and rolling costs produced similar trajectory groups.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index reference values
statement: The mean EQ-5D-5L index value in the full elderly sample was 0.84.

outcome: EQ VAS reference values
statement: The mean EQ VAS value in the full elderly sample was 73.2.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension-level health profile and reported health states
statement: Of the sample, 21.4% reported no problems in all five EQ-5D-5L dimensions, and health state 11111 was the most frequent state.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension-level health profile and reported health states
statement: Pain or discomfort was the most frequently affected dimension, followed by mobility, usual activities, anxiety or depression, and self-care; extreme problems or inability were rare.
Both index and EQ VAS reference values decreased with age; the mean index declined from 0.92 at ages 65 to 69 to 0.68 at age 80 or older, and mean EQ VAS declined from 82.6 to 61.9.
Men had a significantly higher mean index value than women, but the two-point difference in mean EQ VAS was not statistically significant.
Women reported more problems than men in mobility, usual activities, pain or discomfort, and anxiety or depression; the gender difference in index values was largest in the oldest age group.
The search found 308 unique records; 31 full-text articles were assessed, and 28 peer-reviewed articles were included. Nine conference presentations were also included and reported separately.
Of the 28 included articles, 23 were cross-sectional survey studies, four were longitudinal survey studies, and one was a case study; 16 used the EQ-5D-5L.

The evidence base included three identification or development-only studies, 13 psychometric-only studies, six valuation-only studies, three studies classified as both identification or development and psychometric, and three classified as both identification or development and valuation.
The review identified 26 bolt-on dimensions. Cognition was most frequent, followed by vision, relationships, sleep, hearing, energy, and tiredness.

Bolt-ons came from diverse sources, including existing HRQoL instruments, literature or systematic reviews, expert groups, patient or public input, interviews, and focus groups. Terminology varied, especially for cognition, which included cognition, cognitive functioning, speech or cognition, concentration, and memory or concentration.

Psychometric studies used diverse analyses. Explanatory power was reported by most studies, and ceiling effects were the next most common performance outcome. Only two studies assessed dimension dependency.

On the COSMIN risk-of-bias checklist, 27 of 28 studies had an overall inadequate rating and one had a doubtful rating. The author-developed checklist gave ratings from doubtful to very good and better distinguished study quality.

Valuation studies used varied methods; EQ VAS and time trade-off were the two most frequent valuation measures. The effect of a bolt-on on preferences often depended on the severity of the core EQ-5D state and the severity and type of the bolt-on.

Some reviewed bolt-ons showed added descriptive or valuation value, but most source studies did not conclude that a bolt-on should be implemented and recommended more research. The psoriasis bolt-on alone had beta status; the others were experimental versions at the review date.
If cTTO is insensitive for worse-than-dead states, value sets compress differences between severe states and can underestimate gains from improvements in health-related quality of life.
In the original Polish data, overall and nonnegative utilities decreased with severity, but negative utilities had virtually no association with severity.

Replacing original values with sensitivity-imposed values changed the nonnegative-utility slope only slightly but increased the absolute negative-utility slope and its explained variance, which indicates that positive values were already sensitive while negative values were largely insensitive.
Random reshuffling of negative utilities left the GRL-style negative-utility result almost unchanged, which indicates that the original negative values already lacked sensitivity to severity.
The RDS-style M1 and M2 parameter patterns were strikingly similar before and after negative utilities were reshuffled, even though reshuffling guaranteed insensitivity.

When individual-level sensitivity was imposed by regression-based simulation, significant negative severity-utility associations appeared among negative observations in both the raw-prediction and empirical-distribution-preserving data.
The preferred heteroscedastic censored hybrid model combined cTTO and DCE data and was the only examined approach that produced logically consistent parameter estimates.

The hybrid model removed inconsistencies found in individual cTTO and DCE models, although mobility level 3, self-care level 3, and usual activities level 3 were not significantly different from the preceding levels.
Quality-control indicators showed high protocol compliance and face validity, and none of the 13 interviewers was classified as performing poorly.
The final Danish EQ-5D-5L value set covered all 3125 health states, with predicted utility values from -0.757 for state 55555 to 1 for full health.
Anxiety/depression had the largest level-5 utility decrement, followed by pain/discomfort, mobility, self-care, and usual activities.
The directly observed cTTO data contained 10140 valuations; 22% were worse than dead, and greater health-state severity was associated with lower means and higher variation.

After respondents used the feedback module, 712 cTTO state valuations judged to be incorrectly ranked were removed, leaving 9428 observations for main cTTO modelling. Reintroduction of these observations did not qualitatively change model estimates.
All 1014 analyzed respondents completed seven DCE pairs, which produced 7098 choice observations.

The analyzed sample was similar to the adult Danish population for gender, age, marital status, and geographical region, but it included more people with higher education and under-represented people aged 18 to 24 years.
The EQ-5D-5L value set assigned 21.7% of health states a value worse than dead, similar to the Danish EQ-5D-3L value set and higher than the Danish crosswalk value set.
Only seven respondents were non-traders in the cTTO tasks.

outcome: Alignment between the longest-fixated response level and the selected response level

statement: Residents with cognitive impairment showed trends toward less attention to relevant questionnaire wording areas, including some headings, examples, and first-level descriptors, but subgroup differences were generally not statistically significant.
