outcome: Visual attention to EQ-5D-5L wording and response areas of interest
statement: Participants in all cognition groups engaged with the screen, and participants with cognitive impairment had broadly similar fixation patterns to participants without cognitive impairment.
The analyzed residents contributed an average of 290 whole fixations and 158 saccades per participant.

outcome: Patterns and sequences of eye movement during EQ-5D-5L completion
statement: Visual review found more haphazard fixation sequences, less fixation on questionnaire text, and larger eye movements that did not follow the text more often among residents with mild or moderate cognitive impairment.

outcome: Visual attention to EQ-5D-5L wording and response areas of interest
statement: Attention to instructions and the recall period was uncommon: 23 participants fixated on the instructions area and only 3 fixated on the word TODAY.
Of 45 residents who expressed interest, 41 supplied usable data and were analyzed; cognition groups included 9 residents with no impairment, 20 with mild impairment, and 12 with moderate impairment.
Across the five countries, 19.8% of respondents reported insufficient outpatient healthcare access; prevalence ranged from 11.7% in the United States to 29.2% in Greece.

Insufficient healthcare access was more frequent among younger respondents, respondents with at least one chronic disease, and respondents from Greece and the United Kingdom than among their counterparts.

outcome: Change in EQ-5D-5L index from T1 to T2
statement: Healthcare access was not significantly associated with one-year HRQoL change in almost all age, gender, socioeconomic-status, and chronic-disease strata, and the full factorial models found no significant interaction effects.

outcome: Change in EQ-5D-5L index from T1 to T2
statement: Respondents with insufficient access more often had either improved or deteriorated HRQoL, while respondents with sufficient access more often had unchanged HRQoL.

outcome: Change in EQ-5D-5L index from T1 to T2
statement: In the final main-effects model for EQ-5D-5L index change, sufficient healthcare access and chronic disease status were statistically significant predictors, but the model explained little variance.

outcome: Change in EQ VAS from T1 to T2
statement: For EQ VAS change, no predictor remained significant in the final reduced model; gender had only borderline significance in the reported final model.
Mean EQ-5D-3L utility declined steadily from baseline through three years; the baseline-to-three-year decline was statistically significant.
Among EQ-5D-3L dimensions, self-care had the largest three-year deterioration, while anxiety/depression and usual activities deteriorated moderately.
Worse ataxia severity and more depressive symptoms were strongly associated with lower HRQoL at baseline.
In the panel model, increases in ataxia severity and depressive symptoms and higher baseline BMI predicted a larger decline in EQ-5D-3L utility.
Male patients had a larger HRQoL decline, and earlier disease onset showed a borderline association with larger decline.
Change in non-ataxia signs, SCA6 type, and restless legs syndrome were not statistically significant predictors in the main panel model.
The main panel model explained substantial between-person and overall variation in EQ-5D-3L utility.

Increasing the duration attribute to six levels (6 months to 10 years) and raising the proportion of choice sets where duration varies remained feasible and produced a model with generally logically ordered coefficients in the zero prior value design.

outcome: Precision (standard errors), logical ordering of coefficients, choice set difficulty distribution, scale parameters and duration-based non-trading
statement: The design using non-zero prior values (Type Ib) produced more logical inconsistencies and less precise anchored coefficients than the zero prior value design (Type Ia).

outcome: Precision (standard errors), logical ordering of coefficients, choice set difficulty distribution, scale parameters and duration-based non-trading
statement: The two-stage design (Type II) produced ordered and significant coefficients with precision similar to Type Ia despite half the sample size.

outcome: Precision (standard errors), logical ordering of coefficients, choice set difficulty distribution, scale parameters and duration-based non-trading
statement: Choice set difficulty, proxied by the split of respondents across the two options, differed markedly across designs; the non-zero prior design contained the most difficult choice sets.
A pooled heteroscedastic model rejected the hypothesis of equal parameters across sub-samples; choices were noisiest for the non-zero prior design and least noisy for the two-stage design.
About one in eight respondents never chose the shorter duration option, but excluding these duration-based non-traders did not change the character of the models.

outcome: Unanchored and anchored EQ-5D-5L utility coefficients and predicted health state values
statement: Predicted anchored values for the worst EQ-5D-5L state (55555) were negative in all designs, indicating states worse than dead.
Both the conditional and mixed logit DCE models were logically consistent, and Bland-Altman and scatter plots indicated good agreement between cTTO and DCE results.
The investigators estimated 34 models: 16 cTTO models, two DCE models, and 16 hybrid models. Six shortlisted models were logically consistent.
Pain/discomfort was the most important dimension, followed by anxiety/depression, mobility, usual activities, and self-care; disutility coefficients rose sharply between levels 3 and 4.

The Hausa cTTO coefficients were logically consistent and had the same dimension order as the overall cTTO model, but MO4, MO5, PD2, and PD4 coefficients were significantly lower than in the English version.

Model 26, a hybrid heteroskedastic Tobit model with an intercept that excluded flagged responses, was selected because it was logically consistent and had better predictive accuracy than the comparable all-response hybrid model.
Eight interviews met EuroQol quality-control flag criteria, respondents flagged 392 cTTO responses in the feedback module, and all flagged responses together represented about 4% of cTTO data.
The study completed 1,200 interviews and analyzed 1,197 respondents after three records were missing because of technical problems; the analyzed sample closely matched Nigerian adult demographics.
The preferred value set assigned utility 1 to 11,111, 0.963 to 21,111, -0.733 to 55,555, and -0.653 to 54,555.
About 3.3% of cTTO responses were censored at -1, which reflected respondents who were willing to trade all available years to avoid the most severe health states.

outcome: Self-reported health status (EQ-5D-5L profile, index score, EQ VAS)
statement: Ciliwung respondents reported higher EQ VAS scores than each comparison group, while EQ-5D-5L index scores were essentially equal across groups.

outcome: Quality of life across WHOQOL-BREF physical, psychological, social and environment domains
statement: Ciliwung respondents reported the lowest WHOQOL-BREF physical domain scores, with a moderate effect size against the matched controls and the general population.

outcome: Self-reported health status (EQ-5D-5L profile, index score, EQ VAS)
statement: A larger proportion of Ciliwung respondents reported full health (11111) and fewer reported any anxiety/depression problems than in the comparison groups.

outcome: Personal happiness and life satisfaction
statement: Ciliwung respondents reported less happiness but higher life satisfaction at all three time points than the comparison groups.

outcome: Perceived family financial situation
statement: Ciliwung respondents perceived their family financial situation as better than the matched controls and the general population, despite lower actual incomes.

outcome: Self-reported health status (EQ-5D-5L profile, index score, EQ VAS)
statement: MANOVA showed the Ciliwung group differed significantly from the matched controls in quality of life and life satisfaction, but not in health status or happiness; differences from Jakarta and the general population were significant on all outcome sets except health status versus the general population.

outcome: Relevance, salience, acceptability, comprehensiveness, comprehensibility, and conceptual distinctness of the four bolt-ons
statement: Participants regarded the final four bolt-ons as appropriate, salient, acceptable, comprehensive, comprehensible, and conceptually distinct from the EQ-5D core items; their suggestions led to revisions of labels and phrasing.

outcome: Ceiling and floor effects and health-profile distributions
statement: The four-item module substantially reduced the ceiling effect compared with standard EQ-5D-5L: full-health reports fell from 42.7% with EQ-5D-5L to 5.5% with EQ-5D-5L plus all four bolt-ons.

outcome: Convergent validity against SAQLI, FOSQ, and PSQI
statement: Each bolt-on correlated more strongly with the condition-specific PROMs than EQ-5D-5L did, and the combined module gave the strongest correlations with FOSQ, PSQI, and SAQLI.

outcome: Discriminatory power for polysomnographic known groups
statement: All four single-bolt-on versions and the combined module had greater mean known-group discriminatory power than EQ-5D-5L; the sleep, tiredness, and combined-module differences were statistically significant. The combined module also explained more EQ VAS variation than EQ-5D-5L.

outcome: Responsiveness in treated and condition-specific PROM-defined improved groups
statement: The bolt-on versions were more responsive than EQ-5D-5L in treated participants and in SAQLI-, PSQI-, and FOSQ-defined improved groups; the four-item module generally produced the largest effect sizes and c-statistics.

outcome: Test-retest reliability in untreated and condition-specific PROM-defined no-change groups
statement: Level-sum-score reliability was at least moderate for all versions except EQ-5D-5L and the relationship-bolt-on version in the FOSQ-defined no-change group; item-level weighted kappa values were generally fair to good, with specified weak exceptions.

Among individual bolt-ons, sleep performed best and tiredness was close behind; relationships performed worst. The combined module generally performed best overall, except that its discriminatory power was lower than that of the sleep bolt-on alone.

EQ VAS and utility scores declined with age. Men had higher overall scores than women, and mobility, self-care, usual-activity, and pain or discomfort problems increased with age in both sexes. Anxiety or depression was more prevalent in younger male groups but increased with age among women.

In the generalized linear model with identity link and maximum-likelihood estimation, significant predictors of utility included age, education, marital status, alcohol use, presence of ailments, state or region, household dependants, and mobile-phone time. Older age, more dependants, more mobile-phone time, and ailments were associated with lower utility.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension-level health profile and problem prevalence
statement: Pain or discomfort and anxiety or depression were the most frequently affected EQ-5D-5L dimensions; self-care had the largest proportion reporting no problems.

Unadjusted HRQoL was higher with greater educational attainment, was highest among never-married people and private-sector employees, and was lowest among people with both acute and chronic ailments. Rural and urban respondents did not differ significantly.

outcome: EQ VAS score
statement: Among 2311 analyzed respondents, the mean EQ VAS was 75.18 and the mean Indian EQ-5D-5L value-set utility was 0.849 in the Results section; the Abstract reports the utility as 0.848.
The study produced the first Indian EQ-5D-5L population norms, including profile prevalence, EQ VAS, and utility values by age, sex, and other sociodemographic groups.
The EQ-HWB-S index had strong positive correlations with the EQ-5D-5L, ASCOT-Carer, and CarerQoL-7D indices, which supports convergent validity.
Only EQ-5D-5L showed a ceiling effect above the prespecified 15% threshold, and no evaluated measure showed a floor effect.
For employment interference due to caregiving, CarerQoL-7D had the largest effect size, followed by ASCOT-Carer, EQ-HWB-S, and EQ-5D-5L.
EQ-HWB-S had the largest effect size among the compared measures for distinguishing caregivers with better versus worse general health.
Known-group effects for caregiving intensity were small for all measures; EQ-HWB-S had the largest effect for the Level of Care Index and for weekly hours of care.
Pilot feedback indicated that no further changes to the survey were necessary.
Relationship dissatisfaction produced medium-to-large known-group effects, with ASCOT-Carer showing the largest effect.
The analyzed sample contained 504 informal caregivers with a mean age of 49.2 years; 57.5% were female, 69.9% had Level of Care Index level 4 or 5, and 68.3% lived with the care recipient.
Care recipient self-perceived burden distinguished caregiver scores on all four indices; EQ-HWB-S showed the largest effect, and CarerQoL-7D and EQ-5D-5L also showed medium effects.

The EQ-HWB psychosocial subscale correlated most strongly with the caregiver-focused indices, while physical-sensation and activity subscales had mostly moderate-to-weak correlations with them, which indicates coverage of different aspects of caregiver health and well-being.
Fourteen of 19 carers had previously provided a report about the health and well-being of the person with dementia, most often during joint medical appointments.

Carers used two main retrieval strategies: they extended the recall window to include important events or self-report just outside seven days, and they used earlier behavior, personality, and pre-dementia history to interpret recent behavior.

The seven-day period was easier to use for observable domains or experiences that the person expressed, including mobility, day-to-day activities, concentration, exhaustion, and pain. Carers relied more on past context for less observable feelings.

Carers interpreted response options in different ways. For difficulty items they averaged behavior, focused on the hardest moments, or considered frequency; for frequency items most counted days but some counted occurrences.

Adherence to the recall period did not appear to vary with how often carers saw the person with dementia. Carers with less frequent contact also used telephone interactions or information from other carers.

All carers answered from their own observations and judgments, which is the proxy-proxy perspective. They used observable behavior as an indirect indicator when feelings such as loneliness, acceptance, and control were difficult to assess.
Nearly half of carers also imagined how the person with dementia might answer, which is the proxy-patient perspective, but no carer used only this perspective.
Carers sometimes disagreed with the person's self-assessment, especially for pain and control, and some were concerned that reduced insight could affect proxy-patient responses.
No new concepts or themes emerged after the tenth interview.
PROPr based on PROMIS-29+2 had a much narrower theoretical range than all three EQ-5D-5L value sets, with a maximum below full health.
The share of theoretical health states valued as worse than dead was much smaller for PROPr than for the EQ-5D-5L value sets.
PROPr values were skewed and concentrated in a narrower, lower range, and they had fewer unique theoretical values than the EQ-5D-5L value sets.

Dimension importance differed strongly: pain/discomfort ranked first in the US and England EQ-5D-5L value sets, while pain interference ranked next to last in PROPr based on PROMIS-29+2; physical function ranked first in PROPr.
For hypothesized comparable states, PROPr gave lower utilities for mild and moderate health but higher utilities for severe and worst health than all three EQ-5D-5L value sets.

When other dimensions were held at best or moderate health, EQ-5D-5L had its largest adjacent utility change between moderate and severe problems, while PROPr had its largest change near the most severe corner states.
When all other domains were held at their worst level, improvement in one PROPr domain produced no or almost no utility change, and PROPr utilities exceeded the corresponding EQ-5D-5L utilities.
Sensitivity analyses that defined PROMIS severity by T-scores and calculated PROPr from PROMIS-29 produced qualitatively similar matched-state and adjacent-state conclusions.

The adapted Wilson and Cleary model accommodated all analyzed items. Authors resolved the limited high-disagreement classifications through two joint discussion rounds; one pandemic-related item was uninformative and was excluded.

Parallel analysis, scree plots, and the minimum average partial method suggested extraction of 9 to 15 factors. Oblique 14- and 15-factor solutions were the most interpretable; psychological functioning, physical or daily functioning, and social relationships or functioning were the most differentiable factors.

The final model contained 12 factors: psychological symptoms, social relationships, physical functioning, emotional resilience, pain, cognition, financial needs, discrimination, outlook on life or growth, access to public services, living environment, and control over life. Its fit in the testing sample was acceptable to good.

Bifactor tests supported combining social participation and relationships as one social-relationships factor and combining daily functioning and physical mobility as one physical-functioning factor. Nine items were excluded during CFA model building after theoretical and statistical review.

PHDT and CAP-AWB showed the broadest factor coverage. EQ-5D-5L items loaded on psychological symptoms, pain, and physical functioning, while ICECAP-A items loaded on four separate factors. Emotional resilience, cognition, and discrimination were each represented by only one instrument.

All 12 factor scores had positive, statistically significant correlations with both overall health and happiness. Pain had the strongest correlation with overall health, while psychological symptoms had the strongest correlation with happiness.

Social relationships, living environment, psychological symptoms, outlook on life, and emotional resilience were more strongly related to happiness than to health. Pain and physical functioning were more strongly related to health. Cognition, financial needs, public-service access, and discrimination had similar relationships with the two VAS outcomes.

outcome: Utility values (disutility decrements) for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Utility decrements for movement from the best to the worst level differed by dimension, with anxiety/depression and pain/discomfort weighted most heavily.

outcome: Utility values (disutility decrements) for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Utility values were non-linear with respect to severity in all dimensions, with larger decrements between levels 3 and 4 than between levels 1 and 2 or 2 and 3.
Approximately 36% of the 3125 estimated health state values were negative, similar to the 35% reported for Indonesia using the same protocol version.

outcome: Utility values (disutility decrements) for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Weighted and unweighted TTO and DCE models produced no substantive differences, and boosted or de-selected samples confirmed the main results.

outcome: Logical inconsistency rates in cTTO responses before and after the feedback module
statement: Data quality was high: logical inconsistencies were few and fell further after the feedback module, no interviewer required retraining and no interviewer's data were removed.
Irish respondents attached a much larger decrement to extreme anxiety/depression than other populations.
The achieved sample broadly reflected the Irish population but over-represented older people, women, those with third-level education and those with private health insurance.
CHU9D had the lowest ceiling effect, followed by EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-Y-3L; moving from Y-3L to Y-5L reduced the ceiling by 6.1 percentage points, or 17.5% relative.
All three instruments showed convergent validity, although several correlations with CDLQI and conceptually similar CDLQI items were weaker than hypothesized.

All known-groups hypotheses were met: worse clinician-rated skin status and more frequent scratching were associated with worse scores on all three instruments, and EQ-5D-Y-5L had the strongest discrimination.

Among 39 patients who reported improved health, CHU9D had moderate responsiveness and was relatively more responsive than either EQ-5D-Y instrument in the principal analysis, although the differences were not statistically significant.
After exclusion of patients in full health at baseline, responsiveness estimates increased for both EQ-5D-Y instruments, and EQ-5D-Y-5L had the largest standardized effect size.
The divergence in hospital classifications was explained almost entirely by valuation technique rather than valuation source or experience of the health state.

outcome: Preoperative and six-month postoperative EQ-5D index and EQ VAS scores
statement: Hip-replacement patients had substantial improvement in EQ-5D index and EQ VAS scores six months after surgery.

outcome: Availability of well- or poorly-performing hospitals within each patient's five closest hospitals
statement: Value-set choice changed the mix of well- and poorly-performing hospitals in patients' local five-hospital choice sets.

outcome: Agreement in hospital performance rankings across value sets
statement: Hospital national rankings were stable across the four value sets.
Value sets based on direct valuations of current health produced higher average index scores and a narrower spread of hospital mean scores than value sets based on stylized health-state valuations.

outcome: Hospital good, average, or poor outlier classification across value sets
statement: Changing from the general-population TTO value set to the patient current-health VAS value set changed national outlier status for a non-negligible set of hospitals.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L health-state values and dimension-level decrements
statement: Both newly estimated current-health VAS value sets were internally consistent; patient decrements were generally equal to or smaller than general-population decrements, but patients had a larger global decrement for any health problem.
The 300 completed interviews produced 4500 cTTO responses and 4200 DCE paired-choice responses.
At level 5, mobility had the largest utility decrement, followed by pain/discomfort, self-care, anxiety/depression, and usual activities.
Respondents reported generally good current health: mean EQ VAS was 84.61, but no respondent reported the EQ-5D-5L full-health profile 11111.

Model 9, a constrained hybrid random-effects Tobit model with heteroscedasticity, was selected because it combined all cTTO and DCE data, handled left censoring at -1 and heteroscedasticity, and produced logically ordered, statistically significant parameters.
The main analysis retained flagged responses because their exclusion did not qualitatively change estimates or dimension rankings; parameter differences ranged from -0.001 to 0.009.
The preferred model predicted -0.493 for EQ-5D-5L state 55555 and 0.969 for state 11112, the best state other than full health.
The sample represented Ghanaian distributions for religion, education, and marital status, but included more men than the Ghanaian population.

outcome: Distinct shared viewpoints on quality of life
statement: Eight factors initially met the eigenvalue and exemplar criteria, but factors five through eight did not add distinct viewpoints. The retained four-factor solution explained 44% of total variance.

outcome: Distinct shared viewpoints on quality of life
statement: Factor 1, “Eat, sleep and other basic needs,” prioritized sleep, appetite, physical senses, and freedom from discomfort. It gave lower priority to negative emotions, which exemplars often viewed as common, temporary, infrequent, or resolvable.

outcome: Distinct shared viewpoints on quality of life
statement: Factor 2, “Positive relationships, belongings and well-being,” prioritized social relations, social adaptation, communication, socializing, and dignity. Physical functioning and several negative emotions were less important in this viewpoint.

outcome: Distinct shared viewpoints on quality of life
statement: Factor 3, “My own physical and mental health first,” prioritized freedom from pain and discomfort and freedom from negative emotional states. Social approval, support, adaptation, and social relationships were less important. Four negative exemplars expressed the opposing pattern.

outcome: Distinct shared viewpoints on quality of life
statement: Factor 4, “Physical health is the foundation of well-being,” prioritized freedom from pain and discomfort, self-care, daily activities, mobility, coping, and control of daily life. Mental and social aspects were less important.

outcome: Relative importance assigned to quality-of-life aspects
statement: Physical pain, physical discomfort, and sleep were consistently toward the important end of the rankings across the four viewpoints.

outcome: Differences and similarities in quality-of-life priorities across participant roles
statement: The social-relationship viewpoint was predominantly represented by carers, while the personal physical-and-mental-health viewpoint was predominantly represented by patients. The physical-health-foundation viewpoint included similar numbers from all three participant groups.

outcome: Predicted utility values for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states and dimension weights
statement: The constrained eight-parameter hybrid model (MULT8_HYBRID) was chosen for the Malaysian EQ-5D-5L value set, giving values from -0.442 for state 55555 to 1 for full health, a median of 0.336 and 8.99% of the 3125 states with negative values.

outcome: Out-of-sample predictive accuracy over mean C-TTO values (MSE, MAE, Lin CCC, ICC, Pearson R) and logical consistency of parameters
statement: All four estimated models (ADD20_TTO, MULT8_TTO, ADD20_HYBRID, MULT8_HYBRID) were logically consistent, with higher disutility for more severe levels within every dimension.

outcome: Out-of-sample predictive accuracy over mean C-TTO values (MSE, MAE, Lin CCC, ICC, Pearson R) and logical consistency of parameters
statement: Cross-validation by leaving out one C-TTO block at a time showed the constrained eight-parameter models predicted left-out mean C-TTO values better than the 20-parameter models, and the hybrid version outperformed all others.

outcome: Predicted utility values for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states and dimension weights
statement: Dimension importance ranking differed between data sources: C-TTO-only models ranked pain/discomfort first, while hybrid models ranked mobility first; usual activities was least important in all models.

The analysed sample matched the Malaysian general population on gender, age, ethnicity and residential area, but people employed full time or self-employed were under-represented and those outside the labour force over-represented.
The intercept was statistically significant for the C-TTO-only models and was retained, but was non-significant in the hybrid models and was dropped.

outcome: Out-of-sample predictive accuracy over mean C-TTO values (MSE, MAE, Lin CCC, ICC, Pearson R) and logical consistency of parameters
statement: Hybrid models produced a slightly wider range of utility values and smaller bootstrapped standard errors than their C-TTO-only counterparts.
Using the selected value set, the index value for health state 12345 is 1 - 0.062 - 0.064 - 0.259 - 0.300 = 0.315.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-3L problems and EQ VAS score of the respondents
statement: 225 of 1,000 sampled individuals completed the interview, producing 2,717 VAS and 2,831 TTO values; the sample was broadly representative of the Slovenian population for age, education and activity, but women were overrepresented.

outcome: Model monotonicity/logical consistency and out-of-sample predictive accuracy (Pearson R, Lin CCC, MSE, MAE) in leave-out-by-state cross-validation
statement: The standard additive 10-parameter model ADD10 (with or without intercept) produced non-monotonic, logically inconsistent parameters for both TTO and VAS data, while the constrained MULT6 and MULT6P models without intercept were monotonic for both.

outcome: Model monotonicity/logical consistency and out-of-sample predictive accuracy (Pearson R, Lin CCC, MSE, MAE) in leave-out-by-state cross-validation
statement: MULT6P, the constrained 6-parameter model with a supplementary power term, gave the best out-of-sample predictive accuracy in leave-out-by-state cross-validation for both TTO and VAS data and was selected for both value sets; ridge regression improved accuracy for ADD10 and MULT6 but not for MULT6P.

outcome: TTO values for EQ-5D-3L health states and modelled TTO based value set coefficients
statement: In the selected MULT6P models, mobility carried the largest dimension weight and the power term was well below 1, indicating diminishing sensitivity to accumulating health problems.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-3L problems and EQ VAS score of the respondents
statement: Respondents most often reported problems with pain/discomfort, and mean self-rated EQ VAS was 72.15; mean rated interview difficulty was 2.87 on a 1-5 scale.

outcome: TTO values for EQ-5D-3L health states and modelled TTO based value set coefficients
statement: The Slovenian TTO value set differs considerably from the UK MVH and Polish TTO value sets, mainly because mobility has a substantially greater weight in Slovenia; the UK set gives lower and the Polish set higher values for mild states, whereas the Slovenian VAS value set is close to but somewhat higher than the European VAS value set.

outcome: Model fit and convergence (deviance, deviance information criterion, potential scale reduction factor) and interview quality flags
statement: Between June and October 2016, 15 interviewers completed 1570 interviews; after exclusions, data from 1252 respondents (11,480 composite TTO valuations and 8764 DCE pairs) entered the modelling, and only 2.3% of interviews were flagged by quality control.

outcome: Self-reported health of respondents (EQ-5D-5L profile, EQ VAS, SF-1)
statement: The achieved sample matched the Polish general adult population on age, sex, education, employment status, geographical region and size of locality, and was similar in self-reported health (EQ-5D-5L, EQ VAS mean 79.9 vs 73.7, SF-1).

outcome: Composite TTO utility values for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: In the observed composite TTO data, 13.5% of valuations were worse than dead, time was not traded in 10.7% of experiments, and the average utility of state 55555 was − 0.408 with 33.5% of respondents assigning − 1.

outcome: Model fit and convergence (deviance, deviance information criterion, potential scale reduction factor) and interview quality flags
statement: The TTO feedback module led respondents to remove 1040 (8.3%) valuations and reduced the number of respondents with inconsistencies for state 55555 from 49 (3.9%) to 22 (1.8%).

outcome: Modelled disutilities per dimension and level, and utilities for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L states
statement: In the final hybrid model, pain/discomfort had the largest level-5 disutility, followed by mobility, self-care, anxiety/depression and usual activities.

outcome: Model fit and convergence (deviance, deviance information criterion, potential scale reduction factor) and interview quality flags
statement: Adding random parameters, error scaling with a t-Student distribution, religiosity scaling, DCE data and censoring at − 1 improved model fit and produced a level-consistent final model, while lowering the utility of the pit state relative to intermediate models.

outcome: Modelled disutilities per dimension and level, and utilities for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L states
statement: The new Polish EQ-5D-5L value set ranges from 1 (11111) to − 0.590 (55555), assigns 0.982 to the second-best state, has a mean value of 0.476 (SD 0.286), and classes 137 states (4.4%) as worse than dead.

outcome: Modelled disutilities per dimension and level, and utilities for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L states
statement: The three Polish value sets are highly similar in range and dimension ordering, but the directly measured EQ-5D-5L set gives higher values to mild states and a slightly lower worst value than the EQ-5D-3L and crosswalk value sets.
About 15% of respondents reported difficulty understanding a TTO task, with no statistically significant difference between task groups.
Better self-rated overall health on EQ VAS was associated with a higher TTO value and therefore less willingness to trade life-years.
The three task groups did not differ significantly in reported background characteristics, clinical characteristics, or health outcome measures.
Mean experience-based TTO values differed across the three task groups.
The modified open-ended task did not produce a statistically significant TTO-value difference relative to the iteration-based task.
The original open-ended TTO task produced significantly higher TTO values than the iteration-based task, and adjustment for measured covariates changed this effect only modestly.
The original open-ended task produced significantly higher TTO values than the modified open-ended task.
Respondents traded the most life-years in the iteration-based task and the fewest in the original open-ended task.

outcome: Health state values for the 3,125 EQ-5D-5L states
statement: The final 20-parameter hybrid model with three latent classes produced a value set ranging from -0.285 for state 55555 to 0.950 for states 11211 and 12111, with 5.1% of the 3,125 states valued as worse than dead.

outcome: Health state values for the 3,125 EQ-5D-5L states
statement: Pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression received the greatest weight in both TTO and DCE data; at level 5 the decrements were pain/discomfort 0.335, anxiety/depression 0.289, mobility 0.274, self-care 0.203 and usual activities 0.184.

outcome: Face validity and quality of TTO and DCE data, including clustering, interviewer effects and exclusions
statement: The data showed face validity: mean TTO values fell as level sum scores rose, and the probability of choosing a state in the DCE increased with its severity advantage.

outcome: Face validity and quality of TTO and DCE data, including clustering, interviewer effects and exclusions
statement: Data quality issues included clustering of TTO values at 1, 0.5 and 0, digit preference, interviewer effects, and 4.0% of TTO observations at the -1 boundary; 84 participants (8.4%) were excluded and values of 177 further participants were censored at 0.

outcome: Health state values for the 3,125 EQ-5D-5L states
statement: The distribution of EQ-5D-5L values is approximately normal, unlike the bimodal distribution of the EQ-5D-3L value set, and values for mild states are considerably higher than in the 3L and crosswalk value sets.
The achieved sample over-represented people aged 75 and over, retired people, women and people with health-related limitations relative to the English general population.

outcome: Self-reported understanding and difficulty of DCE tasks
statement: Most adolescent and adult respondents agreed that the DCE questions were easy to understand and that they could distinguish the presented health states.

outcome: Adult and adolescent scale-adjusted contribution to the combined latent-class model
statement: After adjustment to approximate equal adult and adolescent sample sizes, adults supplied 65.0% and adolescents supplied 35.0% of model contribution.

outcome: Latent preference classes, dimension priorities, and preference strength
statement: All 6 classes contained both age groups. Adolescents were more represented in classes that prioritized mobility, while adults were more represented in classes that prioritized pain or discomfort and feeling worried, sad, or unhappy.

outcome: Adult and adolescent scale-adjusted contribution to the combined latent-class model
statement: In the observed unequal samples, adults supplied 78.7% and adolescents supplied 21.3% of total scale-adjusted class-share contribution to the combined model.

outcome: Latent-class model fit and predictive performance
statement: The 6-class latent-class model had similar prediction errors and a lower Bayesian information criterion than the 7-class model, so the authors selected it for further analysis.

outcome: Dominant-pair and speeding quality-control violations
statement: Overall quality-control exclusion proportions were similar, but adolescents were more often excluded for choosing dominated states and adults were more often excluded for speeding.

outcome: Adult and adolescent scale-adjusted contribution to the combined latent-class model
statement: Class 4 combined the largest class share with the strongest preferences and supplied most model weight, while class 5 had largely indifferent preferences and supplied the least weight despite its large class share.
Missing responses were uncommon for all three EuroQol measures and were lowest for EQ VAS.
Responses generally redistributed from EQ-5D-3L to the expected adjacent EQ-5D-5L levels; the mean percentage of inconsistent transitions was 4.4%.
The full-health-state ceiling effect was significantly lower for EQ-5D-5L than for EQ-5D-3L, while dimension-level ceiling effects did not differ significantly.

EQ-5D-5L had higher absolute Shannon informativity, but relative informativity increased for mobility, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression and decreased for self-care and usual activities; no clear overall advantage was established.
Known-groups analyses found lower EQ-5D index values with older age, female sex, and self-reported diabetes for both EQ-5D versions, as hypothesized.

EQ-5D-5L showed convergent validity with EQ-5D-3L, EQ VAS, and the SF-12 general-health item; most correlations were moderate and matching EQ-5D dimensions had the strongest cross-version correlations.
In the random-forest assessment, the training and test error distributions overlapped almost completely, and 85.6% of test errors were below the 95th quantile of the model error distribution.
The mean SWEMWBS score was 24.73, with a standard deviation of 5.71 and a range from 7 to 35; 10.7% reached the maximum score.
The anxiety/depression dimension of EQ-5D-5L correlated more strongly with SWEMWBS items than the four physical dimensions; deleting anxiety/depression increased EQ-5D-5L Cronbach’s alpha.
The mean EQ-5D-5L utility was 0.86 with a standard deviation of 0.17; 31.2% had a utility of 1, and only one participant had a value below zero.
The mean EQ VAS score was 76.52 with a standard deviation of 18.96 and a range from 0 to 100.
Both instruments had good internal consistency; Cronbach’s alpha was 0.811 for EQ-5D-5L and 0.922 for SWEMWBS.
SWEMWBS scores had a moderate positive correlation with EQ-5D-5L utility and a strong positive correlation with EQ VAS.

In adjusted ordered logistic models, each higher SWEMWBS point was associated with lower odds of reporting more severe problems in every EQ-5D-5L dimension; the association was present in separate analyses of both survey modes.
In adjusted linear models, higher SWEMWBS scores were associated with higher EQ-5D-5L utility and EQ VAS scores.

Health condition group had the largest adjusted association with EQ-5D-5L dimension problems; participants with physical conditions, mental conditions, or both generally reported more and more severe problems than healthy participants.
Online participants reported more EQ-5D-5L problems than face-to-face participants after adjustment, although this mode comparison also involved different samples and collection periods.

Overall cTTO completion time did not differ significantly between perspectives. Mild states were sometimes completed faster from the child perspective, while the most severe states took longer from the child perspective.

cTTO utilities clustered differently by perspective: all-in trading at -1 and utility 0.5 were more frequent for adult perspectives, while utilities 0, 0.8, and 1 were more frequent for child perspectives.
Child-perspective respondents more often produced fewer than five unique cTTO values, while the associations between level sum score and utility were similar and negative in both groups.

DCE speeding was more frequent for child perspectives at the 4-second and 5-second thresholds. Flatlining or alternating paths did not occur, and dominance and transitivity violation rates did not differ significantly.

Tallying predicted the direction of all four choice-pair differences with p<0.10, but only about 15% of respondents followed tallying across all nine paired comparisons. Other deterministic strategies gave mixed results.
Heuristic-constrained multinomial logit models generally did not improve fit over the standard model. The only marginal improvement was an adult-perspective model that ignored self-care.

The analyses provided limited and indirect evidence of perspective-related heuristic valuation processes, with no systematic evidence that heuristics occurred more often for child perspectives across all data sources.
The search identified 4444 records, left 1704 unique records after deduplication, assessed 603 full texts, and included 90 studies; full-text reviewer agreement was substantial with kappa 0.79.
The 90 included studies reported 840 MID estimates: 436 for EQ-5D-3L index scores, 177 for EQ-5D-5L index scores, 173 for EQ VAS, and 54 for an EQ-5D index score whose version was unknown.

For EQ-5D-3L, the 436 estimates ranged from 0.003 to 0.952 with median 0.089; method-specific ranges were 0.02 to 0.952 for distribution-based estimates, 0.003 to 0.720 for anchor-based estimates, and 0.038 to 0.082 for instrument-defined estimates.

For EQ-5D-5L, the 177 estimates ranged from 0.005 to 0.410 with median 0.065; method-specific ranges were 0.023 to 0.115 for distribution-based estimates, 0.010 to 0.410 for anchor-based estimates, and 0.037 to 0.101 for instrument-defined estimates.
For EQ VAS, the 173 estimates ranged from 0.04 to 51.0 with median 9.0; distribution-based estimates ranged from 0.96 to 16.6 and anchor-based estimates ranged from 0.42 to 51.0.

MID estimates varied by estimation method, direction of change, clinical condition, intervention, and baseline score; improvement estimates were generally larger than deterioration estimates, and estimates from studies with surgical interventions were larger than estimates from studies without interventions.

Higher baseline index scores were associated with smaller MID estimates for EQ-5D-3L and especially EQ-5D-5L, with reported r-squared values of 0.2 and 0.5, respectively; baseline scores did not appear to affect EQ VAS MID estimates.

Anchor-based approaches produced wider MID ranges than distribution-based and instrument-defined approaches; more than half of all MID values used anchor-based estimation, with variability attributed to diverse anchors, statistical methods, and assessment timeframes.
More than half of included studies focused on chronic conditions, 24.2% involved patients undergoing surgery, 9.9% involved cancer, and 6.6% used general-population samples.
Censoring-adjusted mean cTTO values ranged from -0.3497 for health state 33333 to 0.9700 for health state 21111.
The German EQ-5D-Y-3L value set had logically ordered parameters and predicted health-state utilities from -0.283 for 33333 to 1 for 11111.

Pain/discomfort was the most important dimension, followed by feeling worried/sad/unhappy, usual activities, looking after myself, and mobility. The two symptomatic dimensions each accounted for about 30% of relative attribute importance.

DCE preferences differed little by parental status. In cTTO, adjusted mean utilities were always higher for parents than for non-parents, but only three state-level differences were statistically significant.
Separate parental-status value sets had significantly different scales: the value for 33333 was -0.210 for non-parents and -0.358 for parents.
Respondents removed 296 of 2150 cTTO valuations (13.77%) through the feedback module, leaving 1854 observations for analysis.

All DCE level coefficients were logically ordered. Movement from level 2 to level 3 produced larger utility decrements than movement from level 1 to level 2 for all dimensions except usual activities.
Health problems increased and EQ-5D-5L utility declined from early pregnancy to month 9, when utility was lowest.
EQ-5D-5L utility increased in the first postpartum month and then remained stable; month 9 postpartum had the highest reported median utility.
EQ VAS scores showed little variation and no statistically significant change across pregnancy or postpartum months.

Anxiety or depression and pain or discomfort were the most common EQ-5D-5L problems; changes by pregnancy stage were mainly associated with pain or discomfort, usual activities, mobility, and self-care rather than anxiety or depression.
Worse PHQ-4 and GAD-7 severity showed dose-response associations with lower EQ-5D-5L utility and EQ VAS scores and more reported problems in all EQ-5D-5L dimensions.
EQ-5D-5L ceiling effects were more common postpartum, and no participant reported the EQ-5D-5L 55555 floor health state.
Results were similar across survey waves, and conception quarter and year showed little overall variation; pain or discomfort increased from the second to third quarter of 2020.
In Barbados, the mean EQ-5D-5L index value was 0.943 and the mean EQ VAS score was 81.9.
In Jamaica, the mean EQ-5D-5L index value was 0.948 and the mean EQ VAS score was 87.8.
Full health (state 11111) was reported by about two thirds of respondents: 66.4% in Barbados and 68.9% in Jamaica.
Men had significantly higher EQ VAS and index values than women in both countries, and reported health declined with increasing age.

Pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression were the most frequently reported problem dimensions. Anxiety/depression problems were more prevalent across all age-gender groups in Jamaica than in Barbados, while women in both countries reported more pain and mobility problems than men.

In age- and gender-adjusted Poisson generalized linear models, lower income, unemployment, and lower educational attainment were significant predictors of EQ VAS in Barbados; unemployment was a positive significant predictor in Jamaica. No demographic variable was significant for index disutility.
EQ VAS values of 100 were reported by 14% of respondents in Barbados and 30% in Jamaica, contributing to high mean EQ VAS values.
The study observed 216 EQ-5D-5L health states; 12 states accounted for at least 90% of each country sample and of the Caribbean composite.

Among 6,141 members in the acceptability analysis, 3.14% did not complete EQ-5D-3L and 8.57% did not complete MSIS-8D; the difference was statistically significant (p < 0.001), which favored EQ-5D-3L acceptability.
EQ-5D-3L had a larger ceiling effect than MSIS-8D (11.13% versus 3.86%, p < 0.001); floor effects were below 1% for both measures.

MSIS-8D responses were more evenly distributed across health states than EQ-5D-3L responses: the health-state density index was 0.577 for MSIS-8D and 0.215 for EQ-5D-3L, and the five most frequent states covered 8.19% and 49.32% of their respective samples.
Both measures discriminated between groups defined by multiple sclerosis subtype, disability, walking impairment, fatigue, depression, and anxiety (all p < 0.0001).

Both measures correlated strongly with disability, fatigue, walking impairment, and depression measures and moderately with anxiety. EQ-5D-3L correlated slightly more strongly with disability and walking, while MSIS-8D correlated more strongly with fatigue, depression, and anxiety.

During relapse, mean utility decreased by 0.047 for both instruments. Only MSIS-8D met the prespecified statistical and non-negligible-change criteria (p = 0.0001; SES = -0.228), and its SRM was significantly larger in magnitude than that of EQ-5D-3L. No individual dimension change was significant after correction.

After onset of two or more new symptoms, mean utility decreased by 0.022 for EQ-5D-3L and 0.034 for MSIS-8D. Neither instrument met the prespecified criteria for responsiveness, although the MSIS-8D SRM was significantly larger in magnitude. No individual dimension change was significant after correction.

outcome: Meaning and usefulness of better-than-dead and worse-than-dead classifications
statement: The authors interpret differences in health-state values caused by including dead as anchoring bias. This bias can affect values for all health states, not only states with negative values.

outcome: Theoretical necessity and conceptual validity of anchoring health-state values at dead equals zero
statement: Neither scale measurement theory nor utility theory requires dead to be the zero anchor. In standard-gamble and time trade-off reasoning, the choice of the zero-valued health state is arbitrary.

outcome: Theoretical necessity and conceptual validity of anchoring health-state values at dead equals zero
statement: Dead is not a health state that can be described with health attributes. A value assigned to dead cannot affect QALYs because a dead person generates zero QALYs regardless of the value or time horizon.

outcome: QALY-first interpretation of health-state values, zero, and negative values
statement: QALYs, or the value of a healthy year, can be treated as the foundational measurement unit. Health-state values can then be derived from the QALYs generated over time or from the corresponding shortfall relative to full health.

outcome: Meaning and usefulness of better-than-dead and worse-than-dead classifications
statement: The better-than-dead and worse-than-dead distinction mixes preferences for health with the value of being alive, adds elicitation and modelling complexity, and has no stated practical use for health-care resource allocation.

outcome: QALY-first interpretation of health-state values, zero, and negative values
statement: A health-state value of zero denotes a one-year QALY shortfall equal to one healthy-year value and does not need a named health-state descriptor. Negative values remain meaningful as shortfalls greater than one healthy-year value, without being labelled worse than dead.
The review identified 86 unique methods for measuring discount rates; most were designed for monetary outcomes, while health was the main non-monetary domain.

Most methods imposed restrictive theoretical assumptions: most used one discount function, assumed linear utility, did not model reference dependence, and could not estimate negative discount rates; non-parametric methods were rare.

Operational designs varied widely. Most methods used choice-based elicitation and individual-level estimation, about half used real incentives, and reported task counts and completion times showed substantial heterogeneity and missing data.
Method development was concentrated in Western, higher-income settings and frequently used student samples, which limits external validity and leaves little development for low-income settings.
Citation-network analysis showed limited cross-disciplinary overlap, especially between economics and psychology and between health economics or health policy and other fields.
The proxy for theoretical advancement increased with publication year and was lower for methods published in psychology and other journals than for methods in economics journals.

The authors grouped methods into four useful clusters: neuroimaging methods that favor brief and simple tasks, flexible methods with fewer assumptions but greater burden, efficient adaptive choice methods with stronger restrictions, and experiential methods limited to short real-time delays.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility score
statement: Adults aged 18–24 had substantially lower mean EQ-5D-5L utility during the pandemic than the pre-pandemic sample and both online and face-to-face US norms.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility score
statement: Adults aged 25–34 had lower utility than face-to-face norms only; adults aged 35–64 had higher utility than online norms; and utility for adults aged 65 years or older was similar across samples.

outcome: EQ VAS score
statement: EQ VAS scores were lower than face-to-face norms in all age groups except 45–54 years; only ages 18–24 had a lower score than online norms.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L anxiety/depression problems
statement: The HRQoL difference was mainly driven by more anxiety/depression problems during the pandemic, especially among women, people reporting another gender, and respondents who were underweight or obese.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility score
statement: Higher age and income were associated with higher utility. Lower utility was associated with factors that included living alone, a family COVID-19 diagnosis, fear of health effects, arthritis, diabetes, self-reported depression, and the selected stroke-by-fear and underweight-by-California interactions.

outcome: Regression model fit and robustness to unmeasured confounding
statement: The post-lasso OLS model fitted the data significantly better than the standard OLS model, and the reported E-values indicated that relatively strong unmeasured confounding would be needed to attenuate all lasso-selected effects.

outcome: Population QALY change and lives affected
statement: Population extrapolation produced different QALY totals according to the comparator: a 2.6 million QALY loss versus the pre-pandemic sample, a 3.5 million gain versus online norms, and an 8.4 million loss versus face-to-face norms. The average across comparators was a net gain of 18,385 lives affected, but this average included large losses for ages 18–34.

outcome: Item-level and aggregate association between EQ-5D-5L and GHQ-12
statement: EQ-5D-5L utility and EQ VAS scores had moderate or small-to-moderate negative aggregate correlations with GHQ-12 scores.

outcome: Item-level and aggregate association between EQ-5D-5L and GHQ-12
statement: The first four EQ-5D-5L dimensions had only trivial or small correlations with all GHQ-12 items; anxiety/depression had small-to-moderate correlations with GHQ-12 items.

outcome: Latent construct and cluster structure of EQ-5D-5L, GHQ-12, EQ VAS, and life satisfaction
statement: Multidimensional scaling produced three clusters: the first four EQ-5D-5L dimensions with EQ VAS; positively phrased GHQ-12 items; and EQ-5D anxiety/depression with negatively phrased GHQ-12 items and overall life satisfaction.

outcome: Latent construct and cluster structure of EQ-5D-5L, GHQ-12, EQ VAS, and life satisfaction
statement: Exploratory factor analysis supported an interpretable four-factor solution for positive GHQ-12 items, loss of confidence, worry and stress, and the first four EQ-5D-5L dimensions; EQ-5D anxiety/depression loaded with negative mental-effect items.

outcome: Item-level and aggregate association between EQ-5D-5L and GHQ-12
statement: Worse aggregate GHQ-12 scores predicted lower EQ-5D-5L utility and EQ VAS after adjustment, but individual GHQ-12 items did not consistently predict EQ-5D-5L responses. Anxiety/depression was associated with most GHQ-12 items, unlike the first four EQ-5D-5L dimensions.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility, EQ VAS, and GHQ-12 score patterns
statement: Weighted descriptive results showed that health status generally declined with age, while younger respondents reported worse mental well-being; worse mental well-being categories had lower utility and EQ VAS scores across gender, age, and education groups.
The review included 1,512 oncology CUAs and examined 8,714 reported health-utility inputs; 1,428 CUAs were model based.
The original health-utility source could not be verified for 2,096 inputs because the trail led to a non-utility study or an unidentifiable source, or because no reference was given.
Of the 6,618 health-utility inputs with an identified original source, 1,718 came from an original utility study embedded in the CUA and 4,900 came from external published sources.
For embedded original utility studies, expert opinion was the most frequent derivation method, followed by EQ-5D.
For external published utility sources, standard gamble was the most frequent derivation method, followed by EQ-5D.
Among the 4,900 externally published utility inputs, 4,180 cited the original source directly, 640 required second-level citation tracing, and 80 required third-level or higher tracing.
Multiple measurement methods were used for 728 of the 6,618 utility inputs with verified sources; selection or synthesis of values was often not reported clearly.
Breast and female genital neoplasms were the most common cancer group, and health-care payer was the most common analysis perspective. Nearly half of the CUAs used a lifetime horizon.
The EQ-5D-5L reduces the ceiling effect seen with the EQ-5D-3L, where more than 40% of subjects often self-report full health.
The EQ-5D-5L produces considerably more unique health states and less clustering of observations than the EQ-5D-3L.

The EQ-5D-5L discriminates better between patient subgroups defined by severity and requires smaller sample sizes; the apparent superiority of the 3L in separating patients from general population groups is an artefact.

Replacing the 3L mobility descriptor 'confined to bed' with 'unable to walk about' is an improvement, because level 3 mobility problems are rarely observed with the 3L, so the 3L underestimates benefits of treatments that improve severe mobility problems.
Compared with the UK 3L value set, the England 5L value set distribution is shifted to the right, has a shorter tail, a higher minimum value, fewer negative values, and a more even distribution.

Differences between the UK 3L and England 5L value sets arise from different elicitation of negative values, use of both time trade-off and discrete choice experiment data in the 5L, two decades of protocol and modelling advances, changed mobility descriptors, and possible change in preferences between 1997 and 2017.
The UK 3L value set is unusual relative to other 3L value sets and to a UK replication study, while the England 5L value set broadly agrees with other 5L value sets.

outcome: Dimension-specific reference dependency scaling factors and their effect on the social tariff
statement: All five dimension-specific reference dependency scaling factors were negative and statistically significant: respondents whose own health was equal to or worse than the level under evaluation attached roughly 30% smaller decrements to that level.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state decrements on the latent utility and QALY scales
statement: Health state values on the QALY scale were almost identical with and without the reference dependency correction, with only minor differences for usual activities and pain/discomfort that fell within the 95% credible intervals.
Few respondents reported severe impairment, notably in self-care where 96% reported no problems, and 42% of the combined sample would have to be excluded to obtain a strictly healthy sub-sample.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state decrements on the latent utility and QALY scales
statement: The online and paper-and-pencil samples produced comparable EQ-5D-5L estimates on the QALY scale, with only the most severe mobility and self-care levels differing in magnitude, which justified pooling the two samples.

outcome: Self-reported problems by EQ-5D-5L dimension and level
statement: Most respondents reported no problems in each EQ-5D-5L dimension, with pain/discomfort the most affected dimension.

outcome: EQ VAS score and EQ-5D-5L crude sum score
statement: Mean EQ VAS and mean crude sum score for the whole sample, with both declining with age.

outcome: Self-reported problems by EQ-5D-5L dimension and level
statement: Health state 11111 was the most frequently reported state, followed by 11121 and 11112; the six most common states were ranked in the same order as in England.

outcome: EQ VAS score and EQ-5D-5L crude sum score
statement: In the generalised linear model with Poisson family and power link of 0.6, age, education and income were significant determinants of the crude sum score, while gender and urban/rural status were not.
Marginal effects from ordered logit models per dimension show a dose-response income gradient in the probability of reporting no problems, which varies by dimension.

Private health insurance was associated with better self-reported health in univariate analysis, but after controlling for other socio-economic characteristics the association remained significant only for anxiety/depression.

Concentration indices for the sum score and individual dimensions were negative and highly significant, showing that poor health is disproportionately concentrated among those with lower equivalised income.
Compared with other countries, self-reported health in Ireland was similar to England and Germany and better than Poland and the USA for pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression.

Most EQ-HWB items were relevant and well understood. Psychosocial items, sleep, exhaustion, support, memory or cognition, anxiety, frustration, depression, looking forward, and control were especially pertinent to the caregiver role.

Some participants considered seeing and hearing simple opening items, while others viewed them as a disincentive at the start and suggested later placement. Two participants suggested moving positive items to the end so that respondents finish on a positive note.

Seeing and hearing were less relevant and caused confusion about item purpose and the role of aids; 12 of 17 participants said these items did not support their concept of health and wellbeing, while five supported their inclusion.

Feeling unsafe was relevant to only a few participants but was considered important, including for family violence and violent child meltdowns. Pain and discomfort were generally understood, although some participants found severity levels harder to distinguish for discomfort.
Participants strongly supported the nine items selected for EQ-HWB-S. Most did not want to replace an item, and no participant spontaneously identified a missing concept at the end of the interview.

Of the CarerQoL domains not represented directly in EQ-HWB, finance was most often judged important. Fulfilment and the caregiver-care recipient relationship received mixed support, and some respondents found the relationship wording problematic.
Views on changing the frequency response from “only occasionally” to “a little of the time” were mixed and not strongly held.
Most respondents to the control wording comparison preferred “lacked control” over “no control” because it allowed limited rather than absent choice.

Participants generally wanted to retain the three positively framed items. For acceptance, all nine respondents either disliked negative wording or considered exclusion a different concept; many said positive items balanced the emotional effect of the questionnaire.
Four of seven respondents favored placing activities before mobility in EQ-HWB-S because activities is broader and mobility can then provide a more specific follow-up; two were neutral.
The mean censored value for the worst EQ-5D-Y-3L state 33333 was -0.475; 65% of its valuations were worse than dead.

The Belgian youth utility distribution had a similar shape to Spanish and Slovenian youth value sets but slightly higher values, and it was close in shape and scale to the Belgian adult EQ-5D-5L value set.

A four-class latent-class model had the lowest BIC and was selected; all final value-set coefficients were statistically significant and logically ordered, with greater disutility at level 3 than at level 2.
Pain/discomfort had the greatest relative importance, followed by feeling worried, sad, or unhappy and usual activities; looking after oneself had the least importance.
After quality control, 972 DCE respondents contributed 14,580 choices and 200 cTTO respondents contributed included valuations; the included cTTO data met all quality-control criteria.
The final Belgian EQ-5D-Y-3L value set covered all 243 health states and had an approximate utility range from -0.475 to 0.954.
Across all cTTO valuations, 22.4% were worse than dead.

outcome: Candidate-model logical consistency, coefficient significance, fit, and prediction error
statement: The hybrid model that corrected for heteroskedasticity and omitted a constant was selected as the final value-set model because it produced logical and significant coefficients and predicted most valued health states well.

outcome: Pakistani EQ-5D-3L utility decrements and health-state values
statement: In the final model, severe problems with usual activities received the largest decrement, followed closely by severe mobility problems; severe self-care, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression problems had smaller decrements.

outcome: Pakistani EQ-5D-3L utility decrements and health-state values
statement: The final Pakistani EQ-5D-3L value set ranged from 1 for state 11111 to -0.171 for state 33333, and 1.23% of all health-state values were negative.
Four respondents did not trade any life-years for any cTTO health state, but they remained in the modeling sample.

outcome: Candidate-model logical consistency, coefficient significance, fit, and prediction error
statement: Models that corrected for heteroskedasticity had substantially lower mean absolute error for the 28 cTTO states than models without that correction, although they predicted state 33333 less well.

outcome: Pakistani EQ-5D-3L utility decrements and health-state values
statement: The final scoring function subtracts ten dimension-level decrements from 1.

outcome: Pakistani EQ-5D-3L utility decrements and health-state values
statement: The Pakistani preference pattern differed from the reported Tunisian and Malaysian EQ-5D-3L value sets: usual activities had the largest severe-level decrement in Pakistan, whereas mobility had the largest weight in those two countries.
The analyzed sample contained 122 patients with rheumatic diseases and was predominantly female.

outcome: Participant EQ-5D-5L health and EQ VAS scores
statement: Participants had substantial health problems: pain/discomfort was most often affected, and the mean EQ VAS was about 61.

outcome: Personal and aggregate EQ-5D-5L utility functions and health-state values
statement: Pain/discomfort received the highest mean dimension weight and anxiety/depression the lowest; mean ratings for slight, moderate, and severe problems were about 75, 50, and 22.

outcome: Personal and aggregate EQ-5D-5L utility functions and health-state values
statement: Most participants judged the worst EQ-5D-5L state as worse than dead, and the mean value for state 55555 was negative.

outcome: Personal and aggregate EQ-5D-5L utility functions and health-state values
statement: The aggregate patient-based model generated values for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states, with monotonic mean coefficients across levels in every dimension.

outcome: Ability to derive complete personal and group value sets from a small patient sample
statement: A personal EQ-5D-5L utility function was constructed for every participant. Mean coefficients had high precision, although personal value sets were heterogeneous.

outcome: Precision, internal consistency, level-rating errors, and DCE hold-out predictive accuracy
statement: Level-rating responses indicated high task engagement and understanding for most participants.

outcome: Precision, internal consistency, level-rating errors, and DCE hold-out predictive accuracy
statement: Personal utility functions predicted about two thirds of DCE hold-out choices and performed better for easy choices than for hard or moderate choices.

outcome: Completion time and participant feedback on the OPUF survey
statement: The survey was usually completed in under 20 minutes and was generally well received, but participants reported some navigation, instruction, slider-handling, and implausible-state problems.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index (utility) normative values scored with the US value set
statement: In the face-to-face sample the mean EQ-5D-5L utility was 0.851 and the mean EQ VAS was 80.4, and 31.2% of respondents reported no problems on any dimension (state 11111).

outcome: Difference in normative values between face-to-face and online modes of data collection, and sample representativeness
statement: Both samples were more educated than the US general population, and face-to-face respondents aged 65 and older matched the US population more closely than online respondents of the same age; the face-to-face older sample was healthier than MEPS respondents.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index (utility) normative values scored with the US value set
statement: Mean utility differed across age bands and did not decrease monotonically: it fell until age 45-54 and then plateaued or rose slightly in older bands.

outcome: EQ VAS normative values
statement: Mean EQ VAS reached a nadir at age 45-54 and then increased across the older age bands.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index (utility) normative values scored with the US value set
statement: Mean utility and EQ VAS did not differ significantly by gender, race or Hispanic ethnicity, but decreased strongly with worse self-rated general health, more regular prescription medications and experience of serious illness.

outcome: Reported problems by EQ-5D-5L dimension and level, and frequency of self-reported health states
statement: Problems were least frequent on self-care and most frequent on pain/discomfort; the prevalence of problems rose with age on all dimensions except anxiety/depression, which fell with age.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index (utility) normative values scored with the US value set
statement: Among self-reported conditions, depression, arthritis and sinusitis had the lowest mean utility, and hypertension, diabetes and hay fever the highest.

outcome: Difference in normative values between face-to-face and online modes of data collection, and sample representativeness
statement: Online respondents reported worse health than face-to-face respondents: overall mean utility 0.800 and mean EQ VAS 74.6 versus 0.851 and 80.4 face-to-face, with only 23.9% reporting state 11111.

outcome: Difference in normative values between face-to-face and online modes of data collection, and sample representativeness
statement: After controlling for age, race, gender, ethnicity and general health status, online respondents had index values 0.027 lower and EQ VAS values 3.0 units lower than face-to-face respondents.

outcome: Difference in normative values between face-to-face and online modes of data collection, and sample representativeness
statement: The online sample was less representative of the US general population, with White respondents overrepresented (77.8% versus 65.5% in the US adult population) and few respondents aged 75 or older (1.9%).

A search of MEDLINE, Embase and the EuroQol EQ-5D publications database on June 13, 2021 retrieved 1339 references, of which 134 were assessed in full text and 47 studies were included, covering 45 310 children and 2690 proxy respondents from 15 countries; 40 studies used the EQ-5D-Y-3L only, 7 the EQ-5D-Y-5L and 4 both versions.

outcome: Known-groups and convergent validity of the EQ-5D-Y dimensions, EQ VAS and EQ index
statement: Convergent validity was investigated in 21 articles: the pooled correlation of the EQ index was strongest with other global measures of health and weakest with clinical or biological measures and with measures of school functioning, and the EQ VAS correlated most strongly with activities of daily living instruments and least with school functioning.

outcome: Responsiveness of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L (effect size, standardized effect size, standardized response mean)
statement: Responsiveness evidence was scarce, with 4 studies for the EQ-5D-Y-3L and 1 for the EQ-5D-Y-5L; children with type 1 diabetes who improved over 9 months showed moderate responsiveness for the EQ VAS and the EQ summary score, and children with idiopathic scoliosis who deteriorated over 3 months showed at least moderate responsiveness for both indices.

Only 12 of the 47 included studies (26%) reported an EQ index, and all of these used adult value sets (half the UK MVH A1 EQ-5D-3L value set); no included study used a value set developed specifically for the EQ-5D-Y.

outcome: Content validity and acceptability of the EQ-5D-Y-5L reported in a qualitative study of child and adolescent psychiatric inpatients
statement: A single qualitative study found that children and adolescents in psychiatric inpatient care could in general self-report their health meaningfully with the EQ-5D-Y-5L and valued its physical dimensions and generic character, although some patients considered the descriptive system too generic.

Substantial statistical heterogeneity was present in most pooled analyses, reflecting differences in population age, country, clinical area, disease severity and the comparator quality-of-life instrument used.

Included studies were mostly cross-sectional (80.9%), used convenience samples (83.0%) and the paper-and-pencil version (74.5%); Sweden contributed most studies (n = 10), followed by Spain and the United Kingdom (n = 7 each) and South Africa (n = 6), and the most represented areas were school populations and musculoskeletal diseases and orthopedics.

outcome: Methodological quality of the included psychometric studies scored with the modified Downs and Black quality index (maximum 14 points)
statement: Methodological quality was high (modified Downs and Black quality index mean 11.8, SD 1.5 of a maximum 14 points; only 3 studies, 6.7%, scored below 10), with the weakest domains being sample size or power calculation (present in 21.3% of articles) and clear description of hypotheses (51.1%).

outcome: Feasibility of the EQ-5D-Y: time to complete and proportion of missing values in the profile, dimensions and EQ VAS
statement: Feasibility was high: completion time ranged from 1.3 to 1.8 minutes in school children, was under 5 minutes in psychiatric and mixed populations and about 8 minutes in children with cerebral palsy, and pooled missing values were 0% for the EQ-5D-Y-3L profile, 1% for the EQ-5D-Y-5L profile and 1% for the EQ VAS.

outcome: Distributional properties: proportion reporting the best health state 11111 (ceiling) and the worst state 33333/55555 (floor)
statement: A substantial ceiling effect was found: the pooled proportion reporting the 11111 profile was 55% for the EQ-5D-Y-3L (highest in general populations, lowest in hematological diseases) and 20% for the EQ-5D-Y-5L, whereas the worst state 33333 was pooled at 0.04% and no study reported the 55555 state.

outcome: Test-retest, interrater (child versus proxy) and intermodal (paper versus web) reliability
statement: Ten articles assessed test-retest reliability in 21 subpopulations with intervals of 12 hours to 9 months: EQ VAS intraclass correlation was excellent in 8 of 12 subpopulations and poor in the one subpopulation using proxy respondents, whereas dimension-level kappas ranged from poor to excellent for mobility, self-care and usual activities and only poor to fair for pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression.

outcome: Test-retest, interrater (child versus proxy) and intermodal (paper versus web) reliability
statement: Ten studies assessed interrater (child versus parent proxy) reliability; agreement measured with kappa tended to be higher for mobility (0.04-0.71) than for self-care (0.04-0.36), usual activities (0.01-0.44), pain/discomfort (0.07-0.41) and anxiety/depression (0.02-0.42).

outcome: Test-retest, interrater (child versus proxy) and intermodal (paper versus web) reliability
statement: Intermodal reliability was addressed in a single study of 713 pupils completing paper-and-pencil and web-based EQ-5D-Y-3L versions at least 2 hours apart, showing excellent agreement for EQ VAS and mobility, good agreement for self-care, pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression, and fair agreement for usual activities.

outcome: Known-groups and convergent validity of the EQ-5D-Y dimensions, EQ VAS and EQ index
statement: Known-groups validity was assessed in 27 studies and the EQ-5D-Y generally distinguished age groups, school grades, boys and girls, general population from patients and levels of disease severity, but only 9 articles stated formal hypotheses on the direction of group differences.

outcome: Associations of demographic, socioeconomic, regional, and health factors with HRQoL
statement: Nearly one-third of participants reported a health complaint on the survey date.

outcome: Correlations between EQ-5D-Y-3L values, EQ VAS, and PedsQL Total Score
statement: EQ-5D-Y-3L values had moderate positive correlations with EQ VAS and PedsQL Total Score.

outcome: Associations of demographic, socioeconomic, regional, and health factors with HRQoL

outcome: Associations of demographic, socioeconomic, regional, and health factors with HRQoL

outcome: Population distributions and reference scores for EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, EQ VAS, and PedsQL
statement: The study established overall reference means for EQ VAS, EQ-5D-Y-3L values, and PedsQL total, psychosocial, and physical scores.

outcome: Population distributions and reference scores for EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, EQ VAS, and PedsQL
statement: Reported HRQoL problems were common and differed by instrument: 43.35% for EQ-5D-Y-3L, 44.10% for EQ-5D-Y-5L, and 94.93% for PedsQL Generic.

outcome: Representativeness against Indonesian census benchmarks
statement: The sample matched the target Indonesian youth population closely: differences in residence, age, gender, and geographic quotas were less than 4 percentage points.

outcome: Population distributions and reference scores for EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, EQ VAS, and PedsQL
statement: Participants reported 33 of the 243 possible EQ-5D-Y-3L health states; the lowest reported state was 12332.

outcome: Associations of demographic, socioeconomic, regional, and health factors with HRQoL
statement: Among reported complaints, stress had the largest adverse association with EQ-5D-Y-3L values, EQ VAS, and PedsQL Total Score.
Time preferences were nonlinear: the exponential discount parameter was clearly above zero.
When utilities were anchored on duration, immediate death had utility below zero under both specifications, although nonlinear time preferences moved it much closer to zero.
The estimated utility of the worst EQ-5D-5L state varied substantially across the four combinations of anchor and time-preference specification.
Nonlinear time preferences anchored on duration gave the closest correspondence with the Trinidad and Tobago cTTO tariff, both in range and at individual health-state level.
Anchoring on immediate death produced smaller disutilities than anchoring on zero duration, and assuming linear time preferences produced implausible utility scales.
A priori convergent-validity hypotheses were supported: conceptually similar EQ-HWB-9 and comparator items had strong correlations, especially for physical and emotional constructs.
