Weak correlations between theoretically distinct constructs supported discriminant validity; ASCOT-Carer personal safety and CarerQoL support were notably distinct from EQ-HWB-9 content.
Parallel analysis supported a four-factor exploratory solution that explained 100% of common variance, with minimal cross-loading.

The four factors represented mental and emotional well-being, social care-related quality of life, physical functioning, and care-related burden. EQ-HWB-9 items grouped mainly with EQ-5D-5L items, while ASCOT-Carer and CarerQoL items mainly defined distinct caregiver-specific factors.

CarerQoL mental health was the only item with meaningful cross-loading on two factors; ASCOT-Carer personal safety, CarerQoL fulfilment in caregiving, and CarerQoL support did not load at or above 0.30 on any factor.
Thirteen studies passed the MMAT quality threshold and entered the synthesis; seven assessed visualization preference and seven assessed comprehension, with overlap between these groups.

For individual-level PROM data, bar charts were preferred over line graphs in three studies, while one study preferred heat maps; for group-level data, two studies preferred pie charts over bar charts and icon arrays.

Bar charts and line graphs were generally well understood. Reported interpretation accuracy for individual-level displays ranged from 49% to 100% among patients and from 90% to 100% among clinicians; group-level pie charts were correctly interpreted by 52% to 95% of respondents.
Color, labels, score direction indicators, emojis, and other visual cues affected preferences, but their effects on comprehension were inconsistent and often small.

Clinicians generally preferred graphs that included statistical uncertainty or detail, such as confidence intervals or p-values, whereas patients generally preferred displays without these statistical measures.

Only one included study evaluated predicted PROM presentation, using text or a table; 51.6% of patients and 74.4% of parents chose not to view the predictions because they found them too complicated or unclear, and no included study assessed comprehension of predicted PROMs.

Lower comprehension was associated in some studies with older age, lower cognitive assessment scores, lower financial resources, or lower education, although one study found no significant association with education.

The evidence base was clinically heterogeneous: eight of 13 studies were in oncology, while the remaining studies covered pediatrics and inflammatory or immune, respiratory, neurological, and cardiovascular conditions.

Preference was measured with ranking tasks or selection among options, while comprehension was measured with objective interpretation questions in some studies and subjective clarity ratings in others.

outcome: Mean and median composite TTO values for the 10 EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Mean composite TTO values decreased with increasing health state severity, ranging from 0.81 for the mildest state 21111 to 0.19 for the worst state 55555.

outcome: Data quality and face validity indicators: worse-than-dead frequency, value clustering, dominance-task failure, task completion times, interviewer protocol compliance
statement: Health states were rarely valued as worse than dead, and most respondents never gave a worse-than-dead value.

outcome: Data quality and face validity indicators: worse-than-dead frequency, value clustering, dominance-task failure, task completion times, interviewer protocol compliance
statement: Female respondents were significantly more likely than male respondents to give at least one worse-than-dead value, while age group was not associated with this propensity.

outcome: Proportion of respondents choosing the lower level sum score state in each DCE pair
statement: DCE data showed good face validity: respondents tended to choose the lower level sum score state, and almost all chose the dominant option in the rationality check task.

outcome: Data quality and face validity indicators: worse-than-dead frequency, value clustering, dominance-task failure, task completion times, interviewer protocol compliance
statement: Interviewer protocol compliance was poor: 120 of 320 interviews were discarded, all interviewers omitted elements of the lead-time TTO warm-up at least once, and the worse-than-dead rate varied widely across interviewers.

outcome: Respondent feedback on task comprehension, instructions, screen presentation and cultural or religious acceptability of the valuation tasks
statement: Respondents found the questions easy to understand but were highly dissatisfied with the instructions and the computer-based presentation of the tasks.

outcome: Ranked relative importance of the five EQ-5D dimensions
statement: Mobility was ranked the most important EQ-5D dimension and pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression the least important, with younger respondents ranking anxiety/depression higher than older respondents.

outcome: Respondent feedback on task comprehension, instructions, screen presentation and cultural or religious acceptability of the valuation tasks
statement: Most respondents reported that their religious or spiritual beliefs influenced their valuation responses, frequently invoking destiny and God's power over health, life and death; some found it uncomfortable to think about death and illness or rejected giving up time.

outcome: Data quality and face validity indicators: worse-than-dead frequency, value clustering, dominance-task failure, task completion times, interviewer protocol compliance
statement: Task completion times fell as respondents progressed through the exercise, more strongly for TTO than for DCE.
Appetite, sleep, and energy were the most frequently mentioned facets in both frameworks.
The review included 31 studies: 14 addressed general HRQoL definitions, 11 addressed HRQoL frameworks, and 6 addressed both.

Although the TCM framework emphasized holistic unity of body and spirit, instruments based on it did not always operationalize that unity; for example, CQ-11D measured body and mind as separate dimensions.

The synthesized modern medicine framework comprised physical, mental, social, and environmental health, with physical function and senses, emotional and cognitive aspects, interpersonal and work or school aspects, economic conditions, and adaptation to weather and living conditions.
Of 59 unique HRQoL facets, 28 occurred in both TCM and modern medicine frameworks, 9 were specific to TCM, and 22 were specific to modern medicine.
The TCM literature commonly described Yin-Yang as a foundational theory and also identified Ping ren and He as principles of health, with health understood through balance and harmony.
The synthesized TCM framework centered on Xing Shen Tong Yi (unity of body and spirit), Tian Ren He Yi (harmony between humans and nature), and Qi Qing (seven emotional forms).
TCM included distinctive facets such as urination, stool, and spirit of the eyes, whereas modern medicine included facets such as body weight, medication dependence, and burden to others.

outcome: Value of quality-adjusted life span on a QALY scale (27 life span coefficients)
statement: The results reject constant proportionality and support a power relationship between life span and value (value = preference weight x life span^beta).

outcome: Fit of alternative value functions and test of the constant proportionality assumption
statement: The estimated power increases with the temporal unit used to express time.

outcome: Value of quality-adjusted life span on a QALY scale (27 life span coefficients)
statement: Life span coefficients from the saturated model show decreasing marginal value of life span and a log-log linear relationship between time and value, which rejects the constant, discount and logarithmic functions.

outcome: Value of 90 health problems of varying duration and severity on a QALY scale
statement: Living with extreme problems is worse than immediate death at any duration, whereas the value of severe problems is nonmonotonic with duration.

outcome: Value of 90 health problems of varying duration and severity on a QALY scale
statement: The first day of any health problem imposes only a small burden for moderate problems but a substantial loss for severe or extreme problems.
A substantial minority of respondents did not vary their choices across life span or health problem attributes, and dropouts differed demographically from completers.

outcome: Implausibility score per health state and its effect on model fit and prediction accuracy
statement: About 30% of the 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states were judged implausible by at least half the respondents, and no state was judged implausible by everyone.

outcome: Implausibility score per health state and its effect on model fit and prediction accuracy
statement: Implausibility increased with the variance between dimension levels within a state, and moderately impaired states on the misery index were most often judged implausible.

outcome: EQ-VAS values of EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: States rated implausible received lower EQ-VAS values, with further reductions when the state included extreme problems in self-care or anxiety/depression.

outcome: Implausibility score per health state and its effect on model fit and prediction accuracy
statement: Adding the implausibility variable changed model performance only marginally.

outcome: Themes on reasons, difficulties, strategies and values relating to implausible states
statement: Respondents judged states implausible mainly because of perceived logical conflict between dimensions, described as mutual inclusiveness, causality or close relatedness between dimensions.

outcome: Themes on reasons, difficulties, strategies and values relating to implausible states
statement: Implausible states caused reluctance to engage and difficulty imagining consequences; respondents coped by focusing on the most severe dimension, referring to a similar state, or rewriting the state to make it plausible, and felt the values they gave were vague and low.

outcome: EQ-VAS values of EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: EQ-VAS values showed face validity, decreasing monotonically with the misery index.

outcome: Face validity of the Traditional Chinese EQ-HWB in Hong Kong
statement: Participants generally found the EQ-HWB clear, meaningful, relevant, and appropriate, which supported strong overall face validity in Hong Kong; self-care, trouble remembering, and feeling good about yourself received no problem feedback.

outcome: Item clarity, comprehensibility, conceptual meaning, relevance, and appropriateness
statement: The items that generated the most concern were inability to cope with day-to-day life, accepted by others, no control over day-to-day life, and feeling unsafe; concerns mainly involved wording clarity, conceptual meaning, labels, and examples.

outcome: Item clarity, comprehensibility, conceptual meaning, relevance, and appropriateness
statement: Linguistic and conceptual problems included an unfamiliar Chinese idiom for exhausted, broad or misleading day-to-day activity examples, uncertainty about the meaning of unsafe and control, and perceived overlap among emotional and social items.

outcome: Interpretability of frequency and severity response scales
statement: Participants had difficulty distinguishing frequency from severity response scales and differentiating translated categories such as occasionally versus sometimes and slight versus some difficulty; some preferred numerical scales or specified numbers of days.

outcome: Item clarity, comprehensibility, conceptual meaning, relevance, and appropriateness
statement: Participants repeatedly confused no support from others with accepted by others, and they also saw overlap between pain and discomfort and among anxiety, frustration, sadness, and depression.

outcome: Embarrassment, social desirability, and willingness to answer honestly
statement: Almost all participants reported no embarrassment, and no item was identified as producing social desirability bias; participants nevertheless stressed confidentiality and self-report for emotionally sensitive items.

outcome: Face validity of the Traditional Chinese EQ-HWB in Hong Kong
statement: Participants considered the instrument broadly comprehensive but suggested locally relevant coverage of work satisfaction, physical activity and healthy diet, financial difficulties, and social relationships.
Although tasks instructed participants to assume no long-term consequences and equal costs and carer effects, some participants still drew on real-world expectations of long-term effects.

Differences between attitudinal and PTO responses often arose because the attitudinal questions used broad child and adult categories and prompted concern about equal access and insufficient health-care resources. Participants proposed equality, largest health gain, or other fairness criteria such as ability to pay.

Participants often considered effects beyond the patient, including a parent's caregiving role, effects of a child's illness or death on family, productive work, taxation, and wider social contribution. These considerations could favor either younger people or adults.

PTO choices drew on personal experience, emotional responses, anticipated life experiences, age after treatment, proportional gain, and fair-innings reasoning. Participants who used fair-innings reasoning tended to favor younger people because older adults had already had more opportunities.

Some participants found PTO tasks difficult or uncomfortable. They questioned unspecified severity, had difficulty imagining mental illness in very young children, or regarded age-based trade-offs as socially undesirable.

The qualitative accounts supplied plausible explanations for patterns from the wider quantitative PTO study: difficulty conceptualizing infant mental health, strong emotional reactions to child pain, greater use of fair-innings reasoning when adults were aged 55 rather than 40, and a greater tendency for younger respondents to prioritize younger recipients.

Participants treated identical calendar-time or quality-of-life gains as having different meaning at different ages. Their judgments reflected expected life experiences, usual activities, ability to cope or adapt, ability to understand the condition, and age-specific social expectations.

Among participants who could select no preference, some refused age-based prioritization. Four selected no preference for every PTO task and one did so for all life-extension tasks; all five were older than 40 years.
The researchers judged that thematic saturation was reached after the 38th interview, when new interviews no longer added information relevant to the study objectives.

Adolescents tended to prioritize younger people and focused on school, sport, travel, coping, and the opportunities that older people had already experienced. Parents and older participants more often raised adult caregiving, family, work, and social roles, although views within parent groups were mixed.
The analysis produced nine themes in two broad categories: decision-making processes for PTO questions and decision-making processes for attitudinal questions.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility score
statement: In the full sample, Roma respondents had lower mean EQ-5D-5L utility than general-population respondents.

outcome: EQ VAS score
statement: In the full sample, Roma respondents had lower mean EQ VAS scores than general-population respondents.

outcome: Severity of problems in the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: Roma respondents had significantly higher odds of worse self-care, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression levels; estimates for mobility and usual activities were smaller and more uncertain.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L completion in the Roma-community survey
statement: The high EQ-5D-5L completion rate in the Roma sample showed that face-to-face use was feasible in this population.

outcome: Covariate balance and matched-sample retention
statement: Coarsened exact matching improved joint covariate balance while retaining 70% of the original sample.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility score
statement: After coarsened exact matching and age adjustment, all primary regression models estimated lower EQ-5D-5L utility for Roma respondents.

outcome: EQ VAS score
statement: After coarsened exact matching and age adjustment, both EQ VAS models estimated lower scores for Roma respondents.
Propensity-score-matching sensitivity analyses produced similar utility and EQ VAS differences.

Most respondents did not rate their current health at 100, most thought they could have been at 100 in the past, and most thought they would not be at 100 in the future. A minority in each country considered 100 impossible for any human to attain.

Interpretations of 100 or Best Imaginable Health covered physical health, mental well-being, social relationships, medical conditions and treatment, and health-promotion knowledge and behaviors. Respondents usually combined themes, and Japanese respondents did not describe 100 in terms of social relationships.

Respondents linked a 5- to 10-point EQ-VAS change to physical health, mental well-being, social relationships, medical conditions and treatment, and health-promotion behaviors. Some Japanese and Singaporean respondents considered a 5-point change insignificant.

The most frequent criticisms were excessive granularity and vague labels and numeric points that were open to interpretation. Respondents suggested a shorter scale and explanatory labels or examples; other concerns included reducing complex health to one number, long instructions, and vertical orientation.

Broad patterns were similar across China, Japan, and Singapore, but there was considerable variation between respondents in how they understood anchors, score increments, and the achievability of 100.

All Japanese respondents and almost all Chinese and Singaporean respondents selected an EQ-VAS score that was a multiple of 5. Respondents said that one-point precision was cognitively difficult, differences below 5 points were not meaningful, and printed scale numbers acted as visual cues.
One Chinese and one Singaporean respondent could not complete the EQ-VAS because they had difficulty summarizing health in a single number.
Most respondents had a positive view of the EQ-VAS and found it relatively easy to understand. Some valued it as a prompt to reflect on health, and a few valued its high granularity.

Respondents interpreted 0 or Worst Imaginable Health through three main themes: death or near death, serious or advanced disease, and disability such as dependence, paralysis, wheelchair use, or being bedridden.

outcome: Mean and distribution of EQ-5D utility values
statement: Clinically relevant baseline utility differences varied by scoring direction and country. They were absent for Japanese comparisons but occurred most often for United States comparisons.

outcome: Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio
statement: In scenario 1, the ICER for the Japanese EQ-5D-3L to EQ-5D-5L crosswalk was EUR 11,063 per QALY, compared with EUR 855,681 per QALY for the Japanese EQ-5D-3L value set.

outcome: Incremental QALYs
statement: The largest observed incremental-QALY difference was 0.06 for Dutch EQ-5D-3L scoring comparisons and 0.08 for United States EQ-5D-5L scoring comparisons.

outcome: Probability of cost-effectiveness
statement: At a willingness-to-pay threshold of EUR 20,000 per QALY, the largest scoring-method differences in probability of cost-effectiveness for small treatment effects were 0.42 for mild depression with Japanese 3L scoring and 0.63 for moderate cancer with Japanese 5L scoring. Differences were much smaller for medium and large effects.

outcome: QALYs
statement: QALYs differed statistically significantly between value sets and crosswalks in all 36 scenarios for all three countries; differences ranged from -0.18 to 0.13.

outcome: Mean and distribution of EQ-5D utility values
statement: Across all scenarios and countries, crosswalk-based baseline utility distributions differed from value-set distributions. Mean utility differences ranged from -0.33 to 0.13 and were statistically significant in almost all condition-severity-country comparisons.

The final analysis sample of 1054 respondents closely matched the Indonesian general population on residence, gender and religion, with statistically significant but small (<4%) deviations in some age, education and ethnicity groups.

outcome: Self-reported health on the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system and EQ VAS
statement: Self-reported problems were most frequent in pain/discomfort and least frequent in self-care, and 44.02% of respondents reported full health (11111).

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state values for all 3125 states
statement: The hybrid value set ranges from 1.000 for full health to -0.865 for the worst state 55555, with 11112 valued at 0.921 and 35.46% of the 3125 states having negative values.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state values for all 3125 states
statement: Mobility had the largest influence on values and pain/discomfort the smallest, in all three models.
Predicted values from the C-TTO, rescaled DCE and hybrid models were highly correlated, indicating convergent validity between the elicitation methods.

outcome: Interview data quality and consistency of valuation responses
statement: Quality control led to exclusion of the first 102 interviews and interviewer retraining; afterwards no interviewer had to be removed and the models were logically consistent.

Looking after Myself had the greatest age-group variability and the highest problem frequency. Across ages, only 48% to 63% reported no problem on this dimension, whereas no-problem responses on the other dimensions ranged from 64% to 75%; there was no progressive age gradient.
Mean EQ-5D-Y latent, EQ VAS, Dolan-tariff, and PedsQL total scores did not differ significantly among the 3-, 4-, and 5-year age groups.

Dimension-level test-retest stability was weaker for less directly observable states. Pain or Discomfort and Worried, Sad or Unhappy were unstable in the 3-year group; Usual Activities and Pain or Discomfort showed problems in the small 4-year group; Worried, Sad or Unhappy had poor agreement in the 5-year group.

EQ VAS and Dolan-tariff scores generally had good 24-hour test-retest agreement, although the Dolan ICC was lower in the 4-year subgroup. Latent-score ICCs were below the prespecified 0.70 reliability threshold in all three age groups and were lowest in the 4-year subgroup.

EQ-5D-Y latent, Dolan, and EQ VAS scores had small to moderate correlations with PedsQL total score, except that EQ VAS was not significantly correlated with PedsQL total in 4-year-olds. There was no systematic weakening of composite-level concurrent validity at younger ages.

Known-groups validity was demonstrated: children with an acute or chronic health condition had significantly worse latent, Dolan-tariff, and EQ VAS scores than the general-population group, with no interaction between health-condition status and age group.

Caregivers most often judged Looking after Myself unsuitable for the child's age: 27% for 3-year-olds, 14% for 4-year-olds, and 13% for 5-year-olds. Explanations consistently referred to normal age-related dependence for washing and dressing.

At dimension level, Mobility showed logically ordered, large concurrent-validity effects against PedsQL Physical scores in all age groups. Usual Activities did not show logical ordering against PedsQL Social scores in 5-year-olds, and Worried, Sad or Unhappy did not show logical ordering against PedsQL Emotional scores in the 3- and 5-year groups.

outcome: Prediction-model fit, discrimination, calibration, optimism, and shrinkage
statement: The model had moderate discrimination and good calibration. Bootstrap validation reduced the expected discrimination and model fit only modestly.

outcome: Post-COVID-19 condition at two years: at least one new or worsened post-COVID symptom rated 3 or higher on a five-point severity scale
statement: The final model retained 12 predictors: female sex, body mass index, ward admission, intensive care admission, arrhythmia or palpitations, chronic bronchitis, asthma, angina pectoris, previous stroke, hernia or severe back problems, osteoarthritis, and chronic rheumatoid arthritis.

outcome: Post-COVID-19 condition at two years: at least one new or worsened post-COVID symptom rated 3 or higher on a five-point severity scale
statement: At two years after infection, 551 of 904 participants met the study definition of post-COVID-19 condition. Among affected participants, the median number of complaints was two.

outcome: Post-COVID-19 condition at two years: at least one new or worsened post-COVID symptom rated 3 or higher on a five-point severity scale
statement: The most frequent qualifying symptoms were fatigue, muscle weakness or pain, sleep problems, shortness of breath, and cognitive problems.
All 24 older adolescents completed both valuation surveys and could value health states, including identification of states worse than dead; the tasks were feasible and acceptable.
Mean preference-weight differences between EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-5L were less than 0.01, with no evidence of a meaningful difference; dimension rankings were almost identical.

Agreement between instrument-specific dimension weights was reasonable, with small Bland-Altman differences and intraclass correlation coefficients from 0.49 to 0.79, although confidence intervals were wide.
Before rescaling to dead equals zero, the mean dead values were similar for EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-5L.
The EQ-5D-Y-5L worst-state value was less negative and produced fewer states worse than dead than EQ-5D-5L.
Most participants answered both repeated consistency questions correctly for each instrument.
Participants generally found the introductory video helpful and the surveys straightforward; some found the DCE and binary-search questions difficult or thought-provoking.
Most participants did not notice the wording differences. When prompted, many viewed EQ-5D-5L anxiety and severity wording as more clinical or serious and generally preferred EQ-5D-5L wording.
Participants reported that interviewer presence encouraged more careful completion, and the authors judged that the supportive environment enhanced data quality.

outcome: Correlation between respondent-level random effects for TTO and DCE data, by EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: Joint modelling showed mostly positive but generally modest correlation between respondent-level TTO and DCE random effects; only pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression at level 4 or 5 had a high posterior probability of at least moderate to strong correlation.

outcome: Agreement (Cohen's kappa) in latent class membership between TTO and DCE tasks
statement: Agreement in latent class membership between the TTO and DCE tasks was poor.

outcome: Regression coefficients (disutilities) for EQ-5D-5L dimensions from TTO and DCE models
statement: Class phenotypes were consistent between TTO and DCE data, with one class showing large disutility for pain/discomfort, one for anxiety/depression, and a residual class containing most respondents; class sizes differed substantially between tasks.

outcome: Association (odds ratios) between TTO and DCE latent class membership
statement: Latent class membership was associated across tasks: respondents in a given TTO class were more likely to be in the corresponding DCE class.

outcome: Agreement (Cohen's kappa) in latent class membership between TTO and DCE tasks
statement: Results with 4 latent classes were qualitatively similar to the 3-class solution, adding a class with large disutility for self-care.

outcome: Regression coefficients (disutilities) for EQ-5D-5L dimensions from TTO and DCE models
statement: Regression coefficients and standard errors changed little when moving from independent to joint modelling of the TTO and DCE data, and pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression showed the most between-respondent variation in both data types.

outcome: Model fit: AIC, BIC and posterior predictive tail-area probabilities
statement: Posterior predictive assessment showed good fit of both models to the TTO data, while the mixed model fitted the DCE data better than the latent class model.

outcome: Model fit: AIC, BIC and posterior predictive tail-area probabilities
statement: Information criteria for the number of latent classes differed by task: for the TTO data AIC and BIC continued to decrease with more classes, while for the DCE data the BIC increased beyond 3 classes.
Across all participants, mean EQ-5D-5L health-state utility and EQ VAS scores indicated lower HRQoL than reported Ethiopian general-population values.
Reported problems were most frequent in the EQ-5D-5L anxiety/depression and pain/discomfort dimensions, while mobility and self-care problems were least frequent.
Participants with both anxiety and depression had significantly lower utility and EQ VAS scores than participants with anxiety only or depression only; effect sizes were small to moderate.
HRQoL decreased with greater anxiety or depression symptom severity; older participants also reported lower utility and EQ VAS scores than younger participants.
In the final hierarchical regression model, older age, higher PHQ-9 scores, comorbid hypertension, and multiple medication use were associated with lower utility values.

In the final EQ VAS model, female sex, higher PHQ-9 scores, comorbid hypertension, multiple medication use, and frequent alcohol consumption were associated with lower scores, while more-than-enough income was associated with a higher score.
The EQ-5D-5L, PHQ-9, and GAD-7 showed acceptable to strong internal consistency in this sample.

outcome: Self-rated health on the EQ-VAS
statement: Unadjusted mean EQ-VAS scores differed markedly by attitudinal segment, with unconfident fatalists more than 20 points lower than health conscious realists.

outcome: Self-rated health on the EQ-VAS
statement: After adjustment for EQ-5D health status, age, gender and household income, self-rated health still differed by attitudinal segment.

outcome: Low and complete life-satisfaction
statement: Attitudinal segment predicted life-satisfaction, with unconfident fatalists much more likely to report low life-satisfaction and much less likely to report complete satisfaction.

outcome: Reported problems on EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: Unconfident fatalists reported the highest proportion of problems on every EQ-5D-5L dimension, including the most severe levels, and the lowest proportion in full health.

outcome: Self-rated health on the EQ-VAS
statement: Results were robust to sensitivity analyses that adjusted for health using the single-item general health question or self-reported comorbidities.
Both EQ-5D-Y versions were feasible on self-completion, with 2% or fewer missing responses per dimension, far fewer than the PedsQL.
Median level sum scores and EQ VAS were reported for the sample.
Reporting of no problems fell markedly for Mobility when moving from the Y-3L to the Y-5L, while the full-health (11111) ceiling was already low on both versions.
Floor effects (most severe level) fell on the Y-5L for all dimensions except Looking After Myself, where reporting of the most severe level increased.
Informativity improved on the Y-5L across all dimensions, by an average Shannon H' of 0.27, with similar evenness; Worried, Sad or Unhappy discriminated poorly on both versions.

Inconsistent paired responses when moving from the Y-3L to the Y-5L ranged from 6% (Looking After Myself) to 14% (Usual Activities), and most inconsistency came from respondents moving from some problems on the Y-3L to no problems on the Y-5L.
Convergent validity of paired Y-3L and Y-5L dimension responses was high.
The Y-3L and Y-5L level sum scores had moderate to high associations with the PedsQL total and physical summary scores, while the EQ VAS showed no association with the PedsQL.

The physical dimensions Mobility, Looking After Myself and Usual Activities correlated significantly with GMFCS level, with higher correlations for the Y-5L than the Y-3L, whereas Pain or Discomfort, Worried Sad or Unhappy and the VAS did not differ across GMFCS levels.
Both level sum scores separated GMFCS level 4-5 from less severe levels, but neither separated GMFCS level 1 from levels 2-3.

outcome: Intra-individual agreement between EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-Y-5L
statement: Agreement was lower at domain level, and no domain met the predefined equivalence threshold.

outcome: Intra-individual agreement between EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-Y-5L
statement: Agreement between the adult and youth EQ-5D level sum scores did not meet the predefined threshold for equivalence.

outcome: Between-version measurement error and limits of agreement
statement: Between-version disagreement was mainly random; most level-sum-score differences were within about three points in either direction.

outcome: Score distributions, ceiling effects, and floor effects
statement: Ceiling effects were similar for most scores, but the adult EQ-5D-5L had a significantly larger ceiling in anxiety/depression.

outcome: Test-retest reliability of each EQ-5D version
statement: Test-retest reliability point estimates were slightly higher for the adult EQ-5D-5L level sum score, but the difference between versions was not statistically significant.

outcome: Intra-individual agreement between EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-Y-5L
statement: In sensitivity analyses, inter-version agreement was higher in subgroups with more severe scoliosis and lower in less affected patients; age and education did not appear to affect agreement.

outcome: Convergent construct validity against SRS-22r
statement: Both EQ-5D versions met the same number of prespecified convergent-validity hypotheses against the SRS-22r.

outcome: Feasibility of telephone follow-up: follow-up rate, number of contact attempts, and phone ownership
statement: Excluding patients known to have died, 95% of discharged patients were successfully followed up to 3 months by telephone.

outcome: Feasibility of telephone follow-up: follow-up rate, number of contact attempts, and phone ownership
statement: Contact by telephone often required repeated attempts, but no contacted patient refused the interview.

outcome: Feasibility of telephone follow-up: follow-up rate, number of contact attempts, and phone ownership
statement: Almost all patients had a regular mobile phone; only one had a smart phone allowing a video call interview.

outcome: Patient acceptability of telephone follow-up interviews
statement: Patients found telephone follow-up acceptable; at the 3-month interview all said they were happy to participate, mainly because they felt supported.

outcome: Pre-admission and post-discharge care pathways, referral source, and follow-up consultations
statement: Two-thirds of patients reached the hospital by referral from another hospital, and the emergency department was the most common first point of contact.

outcome: Pre-admission and post-discharge care pathways, referral source, and follow-up consultations
statement: Time to first health professional contact differed sharply between injury and illness admissions.

outcome: Pre-admission and post-discharge care pathways, referral source, and follow-up consultations
statement: Most patients returned to their pre-admission residence, usually more than one hour from the referral hospital, with family as primary caregivers.

outcome: Pre-admission and post-discharge care pathways, referral source, and follow-up consultations
statement: Post-discharge consultation with a health professional was common in the first month and declined thereafter.

outcome: Known-groups validity by age group and EQ VAS-defined severity group
statement: EQ-TIPS-3L scores did not differ significantly by age group. PedsQL social functioning, cognitive or school functioning, and total scores indicated fewer problems in the younger group.

In children aged 2 to 4 years, DeLuca PedsUtil and Kwon PedsQL GCS total scores were strongly associated with the PedsQL total score and with each other; each had at least a moderate association with EQ-TIPS-3L level sum score.

outcome: EQ-TIPS-3L and PedsQL response distributions, ceiling and floor patterns, and missing data
statement: Across both age groups, EQ-TIPS-3L most often identified problems with eating and pain, and EQ-TIPS-3L missing data were minimal.

outcome: Concurrent validity from hypothesized item, dimension, subscore, and total-score correlations
statement: Most prespecified item correlations met the moderate-to-strong criterion. The paper reports 11 of 12 hypotheses met in the 2-to-4-year group, but it gives inconsistent counts for the 0-to-24-month group.

outcome: EQ-TIPS-3L and PedsQL response distributions, ceiling and floor patterns, and missing data
statement: Among children aged 2 to 4 years, common PedsQL problems included pain, fear, sadness, anger, and missing school; all three school-functioning items had substantial missing data because many children did not attend school.

outcome: EQ-TIPS-3L and PedsQL response distributions, ceiling and floor patterns, and missing data
statement: Among children aged 0 to 24 months, the most common PedsQL problems were tiredness, resting a lot, crying or fussing when left alone, and difficulty being soothed when upset.
The analysis included 260 children after 3 of 263 available participant records were excluded because more than half of PedsQL responses were missing.

outcome: Concurrent validity from hypothesized item, dimension, subscore, and total-score correlations
statement: EQ-TIPS-3L level sum score had moderate-to-strong correlations with all PedsQL subtotal and total scores except cognitive functioning in children aged 0 to 24 months and school functioning in children aged 2 to 4 years.

outcome: Known-groups validity by age group and EQ VAS-defined severity group
statement: EQ-TIPS-3L level sum score, PedsQL total score, DeLuca PedsUtil total score, and Kwon PedsQL GCS total score each differentiated groups defined by EQ VAS score at least 80.
Discounting was present when nonlinear time preferences were modeled in almost all arms; only the Danish fullhealth_gen estimate had a 95% credible interval that included zero.
The immediate-death arms produced higher estimated discount rates than the full-health arms in both countries, and the full-health estimates had better face validity.
The full-health anchor produced wider utility ranges, worse values for severe states, and more health states valued below zero than the immediate-death anchor.

Generator-developed designs tended to produce the highest and lowest utilities for a given health state; efficient designs produced more consistent results, but neither construction method had consistently better mean absolute error.
Milder health-state utilities were relatively stable, whereas severe health-state utilities were sensitive to both the anchor and the choice-set construction method.
The Peruvian data produced more non-significant or inconsistent parameters and much more variable discount rates than the Danish data.
The experimental Peruvian utilities differed substantially from the published Peruvian value set, while the Danish experimental utilities were more consistent with the published Danish value set.
The sensitivity analysis generally supported representing immediate death as zero years: the death-dummy 95% credible interval included zero in all arms except Peru death_gen.

outcome: Composite TTO utility values for EQ-5D health states by perspective
statement: Composite TTO utility values were significantly higher when the same EQ-5D health state was valued for an 8-year-old child than for a 40-year-old adult, at all four severity levels, and the difference grew with severity.

outcome: VAS ratings of EQ-5D health states by perspective
statement: VAS ratings were also higher for child health states, but the differences were smaller and reached significance only for the two most severe states.

outcome: Composite TTO utility values for EQ-5D health states by perspective
statement: The two most severe states were valued as worse than dead for adults, while only the worst state was worse than dead for children, so the child value range was compressed by about 20%.

outcome: Themes and nodes describing reasons for valuing child and adult health states
statement: Five themes, grouped into the meta-themes "general principles on the value of life" and "conversion factors", were identified in 274 coded statements from 32 think-aloud interviews; four of the five themes were interpreted differently for children and adults.

outcome: VAS ratings of EQ-5D health states by perspective
statement: Respondents with parenting experience gave significantly higher VAS values to child health states than respondents without children, whereas parenting experience had no effect on TTO utility values, and no country effect was found in either analysis.

outcome: Concordance between qualitative statements and quantitative TTO valuations
statement: Comparison of respondents' statements about childhood being the foundation years and about adults' caretaking role with the same respondents' traded life-years showed generally good concordance between qualitative and quantitative results.

outcome: Themes and nodes describing reasons for valuing child and adult health states
statement: The theme "all lives are precious" was the only theme with the same interpretation for children and adults; respondents reported difficulty in giving up life-years for either, but were willing to trade many life-years when health states caused severe suffering.

outcome: Estimated EQ-5D-3L health state values from main-effects and interaction-effects value functions
statement: All main effects were logically ordered and statistically significant in both the main-effects and the interaction-effects conditional logit models.

outcome: Model fit and prediction accuracy (pseudo R-squared, AIC, likelihood ratio, MAE, RMSE)
statement: Adding all 40 second-order interaction terms significantly improved model fit, and all 10 pairwise attribute interactions were significant, but the gain in explained variance was small.
The interaction between mobility and self-care was the most salient, and the interaction between mobility and anxiety/depression the least.

outcome: Estimated EQ-5D-3L health state values from main-effects and interaction-effects value functions
statement: The interaction-effects model produced systematically lower values than the main-effects model across the whole range of the 243 EQ-5D-3L health states (values rescaled 0 to 1).

outcome: Responsiveness of the EQ-5D index score, expressed as effect size, standardized response mean, and Guyatt's Responsiveness Index within WOMAC-anchored change groups
statement: For patients with a "small but important" improvement on the WOMAC anchor, the EQ-5D-5L was consistently more responsive than the EQ-5D-3L in both THR and TKR patients.
The EQ-5D-5L also had larger effect size, standardized response mean, and Guyatt's Responsiveness Index than the EQ-5D-3L in the moderate and large improvement groups for both THR and TKR.
For the "very mild improvement" groups, all three responsiveness coefficients were small for both EQ-5D versions in both THR and TKR samples.

outcome: Spearman correlation between change in EQ-5D index score and change in WOMAC overall score (anchor validity)
statement: Change in the EQ-5D index score correlated at least moderately with change in the WOMAC overall score for both versions and both joints, meeting the a priori anchor criterion.

outcome: Ceiling and floor effects at health state and dimension level at baseline
statement: Ceiling and floor effects at the health state level were negligible for both versions (all < 0.3%), but the EQ-5D-3L had larger ceiling effects on self-care and anxiety/depression and larger floor effects on usual activities and pain/discomfort than the EQ-5D-5L; for mobility on the 3L more than 94% of patients selected level 2.

outcome: EQ-5D index score at baseline and 3 months and its change
statement: Baseline EQ-5D index scores were lower in the 5L samples than the 3L samples, and lower for THR than TKR patients.
A sensitivity analysis using a simpler WOMAC overall score classified more than 98% of patients into the same change subgroup and gave extremely similar correlations and responsiveness statistics.
The selected censored heteroskedastic hybrid model produced Romanian EQ-5D-5L utilities from full health at 1.000 to the worst state at -0.323; 1.3% of modeled health-state values were negative.
Pain/discomfort had the largest level-5 utility decrement, followed by mobility.
The hybrid models were logically consistent, and cTTO and rescaled DCE predictions had very strong correlations above 0.9, which supported joint estimation.
Of 1,674 completed interviews, 1,493 respondents were included in the analysis after the prespecified quality exclusions.
The feedback module reduced respondents with logically inconsistent cTTO responses from 311 to 247 and removed 1,152 cTTO values marked as incorrect.
Romanian observed cTTO values were higher than Hungarian values for 91.4% of common-state comparisons; Romanian values were lower than Polish values in 61.3% of statistically significant comparisons.

The Romanian EQ-5D-5L value set showed good agreement with the Romanian EQ-5D-3L value set for matched states, but it had fewer negative values and pain/discomfort replaced mobility as the most important dimension.
Survey weighting improved demographic representativeness but made the slight and moderate self-care coefficients logically inconsistent.
The analyzed sample had a mean EQ VAS of 82.5, and 52.4% reported full health on EQ-5D-5L.
Cross-country differences persisted when the analysis was restricted to original EQ-5D-3L value sets, so crosswalk conversion did not meaningfully explain the main result.
Country value sets were highly correlated, but their utility values differed significantly both overall and in every pairwise comparison.
The importance and decrement of EQ-5D domains differed by country and by severity. Pain/discomfort was most important in Peru and the United States, while mobility was most important in Uruguay.
The largest median pairwise discrepancy was between Ecuador and Peru; the maximum state-level difference for this pair occurred for health state 43455.
Applying the country value sets to the chronic hepatitis C cohort produced materially different QALY weights, which were significantly different in most pairwise country comparisons.
Value-set ranges and central values varied greatly. Peru had the widest range and lowest median utility, while Ecuador had the highest median utility.
Differences of at least 0.05 affected large proportions of health states in most comparisons; even the least discrepant pair, Ecuador and Uruguay, differed for 38.2% of states.
The prevalence of health states valued worse than dead varied sharply, with the highest proportion in Peru and the lowest in Uruguay.
In the primary random-effects Tobit model, Polish migrants assigned significantly greater disutility to a given EQ-5D-5L health state than matched Irish natives.
Polish migrants were significantly more likely than matched Irish natives to assign a negative, worse-than-dead value to a given health state.

After one-to-one propensity-score matching, the Polish and Irish groups had no statistically significant differences in the observed matching variables, and their propensity-score distributions were almost identical.
Length of residence in Ireland, which averaged nine and a half years among Polish migrants, had no significant association with health-preference valuation.

Sensitivity analyses with alternative calipers produced identical results; one-to-three matching produced smaller estimates, while exact matching on gender and urban location produced a smaller, non-significant group difference but worsened age balance.
The extended Tobit sensitivity model that added all propensity-score covariates retained the Polish-status association only at the p<0.1 level; the authors attributed the change to multicollinearity.
More than one-third of respondents received a COVID-19 vaccine during pregnancy.
Belief that COVID-19 was a serious disease and concern about giving birth during the pandemic were associated with greater odds of vaccination during pregnancy.
Protection of the baby and protection of oneself were the most commonly reported reasons for vaccination.
Among unvaccinated respondents, planned vaccination timing and intention varied, and more than one-quarter did not intend to receive a vaccine.
Concern about side effects was the most common reason among respondents who never planned to vaccinate.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state utility decrements and index values
statement: The preferred hybrid model with heteroskedastic error terms produced logically consistent, significant parameter estimates and a value set spanning -0.661 to 1 for the 3125 EQ-5D-5L states.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state utility decrements and index values
statement: The relative importance ranking of dimensions was consistent across all four models, with pain/discomfort most important, followed by anxiety/depression, self-care, mobility and usual activities.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state utility decrements and index values
statement: cTTO-only and DCE-only models each showed one inconsistency between levels 2 and 3, but their predictions agreed closely, supporting combination of both data types.

outcome: Data quality indicators: flagged interviews, inconsistencies before and after the feedback module, clustering of values
statement: The feedback module reduced inconsistencies in cTTO responses; respondents removed 6.16% of cTTO observations from the rank ordering.

outcome: Data quality indicators: flagged interviews, inconsistencies before and after the feedback module, clustering of values
statement: Data quality under the EQ-VT 2.0 quality control process was high: only 7.17% of interviews were flagged, clustering at 0 was low, and observed mean cTTO values ranged from -0.461 (55555) to 0.973 (21111).

outcome: Self-reported health of respondents (EQ-5D-5L profile and EQ VAS)
statement: The sample matched German general population quotas for age, sex, education and employment status, with 36.4% reporting full health 11111 and a mean EQ VAS of 79.45.
The EQ-5D-5L value set distribution was left-skewed and covered a larger evaluation space than the bimodal German EQ-5D-3L value set and the crosswalk.
Within respondents, valuations differed substantially across perspectives, but overall mean differences were generally small or absent and their direction depended on the health state and respondent.
Perspective changes could change the classification of a health state between better than dead and worse than dead.

The effect of valuing health for children rather than adults was heterogeneous in direction but showed within-respondent consistency for VAS and TTO; the self-versus-other effect showed weak consistency for TTO and none for VAS.

When models controlled for health-state indicators, valuing for another person produced slightly higher TTO utilities than valuing for oneself; this effect was not present when severity was controlled with the level sum score.
The main results state that VAS variance was higher for adult perspectives than for child perspectives.
TTO variance was lower when respondents valued health states for other people than when they valued health states for themselves.

Dominance violations occurred more often for child perspectives, especially the other-child perspective; VAS endpoint use was more common for child perspectives, and TTO non-trading differed across perspectives.
Most follow-up patients reported no change in global health over 3 months, with small minorities reporting improvement or worsening.

outcome: Floor and ceiling effects of the EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-Y-3L utility scores at baseline
statement: Baseline utility scores were high for both versions, with no floor effect and a large ceiling effect that was slightly smaller for the EQ-5D-Y-5L.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-Y-3L utility scores derived from the Chinese adult value sets
statement: Mean changes in utility score from baseline to 3-month follow-up were not statistically significant for either version in the whole follow-up sample.

outcome: Responsiveness of EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-Y-3L utility scores to self-perceived change in global health (mean change, standardized effect size, standardized response mean, responsiveness statistic, area under the ROC curve)
statement: Both versions moved in the expected direction with self-reported change in global health: scores fell in the worsened group and rose in the improved group, with the largest effect sizes seen in the worsened group.

outcome: Agreement of dimension-level responses between baseline and 3-month follow-up among patients reporting unchanged health (percentage agreement and Gwet agreement coefficient)
statement: Among patients reporting unchanged global health, dimension-level agreement between baseline and follow-up was very good for Mobility, Looking after myself and Usual activities, and good for Pain/discomfort and Feeling worried/sad/unhappy, for both versions.

outcome: Agreement of dimension-level responses between baseline and 3-month follow-up among patients reporting unchanged health (percentage agreement and Gwet agreement coefficient)
statement: The 5LY had a lower percentage of consistent response pairs than the 3LY, most markedly in Pain/discomfort and Feeling worried/sad/unhappy, although the differences were not statistically significant.

outcome: Responsiveness of EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-Y-3L utility scores to self-perceived change in global health (mean change, standardized effect size, standardized response mean, responsiveness statistic, area under the ROC curve)
statement: Discrimination between patients reporting unchanged and worsened health reached the adequate-responsiveness threshold for the 5LY, while discrimination between improved and unchanged health was weak for both versions.

outcome: Responsiveness of EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-Y-3L utility scores to self-perceived change in global health (mean change, standardized effect size, standardized response mean, responsiveness statistic, area under the ROC curve)
statement: Among treatment-modality change groups, the largest score reduction was in patients who started bracing.
Characteristics of patients who completed and did not complete the follow-up interview did not differ statistically.

outcome: Loss aversion coefficient lambda
statement: Most respondents were loss averse for life duration, and the loss aversion estimate did not differ significantly between the 10-year and 20-year reference-points.

outcome: Loss aversion coefficient lambda
statement: Loss aversion was not systematically associated with demographics or with discounting, whereas more concave utility of life duration was associated with older age and higher education, and religious respondents had more convex utility of life duration.

outcome: Shape of the utility function for life duration (AUC) and exponential discount rate rho
statement: At aggregate level there was little discounting, but large heterogeneity existed, with concave, linear and convex utility of life duration all common.

outcome: Corrected composite TTO utilities under the constant alternative and maximum BTD specifications
statement: Corrected cTTO utilities were generally significantly lower than both elicited and confirmed utilities, with the exception of state 35332 under constant alternative correction.

outcome: Confirmed composite TTO utilities after respondent reflection and adjustment
statement: Confirmed cTTO utilities were significantly lower than elicited utilities for all health states except 24443, and changes made by respondents were more often downward than upward.

outcome: Agreement between the direction of respondents own adjustments and the direction predicted by the corrective approach
statement: The majority of adjustments respondents made in the validation task were in the direction predicted by the corrective approach, significantly so for 4 of 6 health states.

outcome: Corrected composite TTO utilities under the constant alternative and maximum BTD specifications
statement: The two assumed reference-points for lead-time TTO gave the same qualitative results, but constant alternative correction produced significantly lower utilities for the severe states 24443 and 55555.

outcome: Data quality indicators including non-trading, all-in-trading and inconsistent responses, compared between personal and digital interviews
statement: No differences in data quality or in cTTO utilities were found between personal and digital interviews, but non-trading and all-in-trading responses were frequent.

outcome: Corrected composite TTO utilities under the constant alternative and maximum BTD specifications
statement: When correcting for loss aversion only or discounting only, the downward effect of correction on cTTO utilities was driven exclusively by loss aversion.

outcome: Corrected composite TTO utilities under the constant alternative and maximum BTD specifications
statement: For several states the difference between confirmed and corrected utilities was larger than the difference between elicited and confirmed utilities, suggesting possible overcorrection.

The New Zealand population norms had a mean personal EQ-5D-5L utility value of 0.847 and a mean EQ VAS score of 74.8. The 25 most common profiles covered 78% of participants, and full health (11111) was the most common profile.
Pain or discomfort was the most frequently reported EQ-5D-5L problem, followed by anxiety or depression, usual activities, mobility, and self-care.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension responses and health profiles
statement: Participants with chronic disease had higher odds of problems on every EQ-5D-5L dimension and lower personal utility values and EQ VAS scores than participants without chronic disease.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension responses and health profiles
statement: Participants with long-term disability had higher odds of problems on every EQ-5D-5L dimension and lower personal utility values and EQ VAS scores than participants without long-term disability.

Anxiety or depression problems were greatest among participants aged 18 to 24 years and decreased with age. Older groups generally had higher adjusted utility and EQ VAS scores than the youngest group.
A small subgroup had negative personal utility values, which classified their current health state as worse than dead.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health profile: reported level of problems on mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression
statement: Pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression were the EQ-5D dimensions in which most breast cancer patients and survivors reported problems, while self-care was least affected.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health profile: reported level of problems on mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression
statement: Current patients reported significantly more problems than survivors on mobility, self-care, usual activities, and anxiety/depression, with no significant difference on pain/discomfort.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health profile: reported level of problems on mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression
statement: Compared with age-matched women from the general population, breast cancer patients and survivors reported significantly more problems on all five EQ-5D dimensions, with the largest gaps on anxiety/depression.

outcome: Self-rated overall health status on the EQ VAS (0-100)
statement: Mean EQ VAS and utility scores followed a consistent hierarchy: patients lowest, then survivors, then age-matched general-population women.

outcome: Self-rated overall health status on the EQ VAS (0-100)
statement: In Tobit models, survivor status was independently associated with higher EQ VAS and utility scores after adjustment for sociodemographic characteristics.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility score derived with the Vietnamese value set
statement: Age 60 and over was associated with lower EQ VAS and utility scores, while higher education and higher household monthly income were associated with higher scores; marital status and urban/rural residence were not significantly associated.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility score derived with the Vietnamese value set
statement: Among patients, the lowest HRQoL was reported just after mastectomy and during chemotherapy, and the highest after lumpectomy or breast reconstruction surgery, but differences across treatment stages were not statistically significant.
Regional variation was statistically significant in all EQ-5D-5L domains except Pain/Discomfort in spring 2020, Mobility in summer 2020, and Anxiety/Depression in winter 2021.
Anxiety/Depression was the most frequently reported problem across all regions and waves, and problems were more common in winter 2021 than in spring 2020 in several regions.

East South Central often had the poorest HRQoL. It had the lowest adjusted utility and EQ VAS in spring 2020 and winter 2021, and the highest winter 2021 prevalence of Mobility, Self-Care, and Pain/Discomfort problems.

Mean utility declined from spring 2020 through winter 2021, while mean EQ VAS first increased in summer 2020 and then declined in winter 2021. The two measures often showed different regional and temporal trends.
Respondents generally reported more problems with Anxiety/Depression and Usual Activities than with Mobility, Self-Care, and Pain/Discomfort.

Region-division pairwise differences in adjusted utility and EQ VAS generally fell in the central range of state-level pairwise differences, but long tails and some direction reversals showed substantial state-level variation within regions.

outcome: Dominant-task failures, missing choices, and choice randomness
statement: Adolescents failed the dominant choice task more often than adults, and failure generally decreased with adolescent age.

outcome: Reported difficulty and feasibility of adolescent DCE preference elicitation
statement: Adolescents reported more difficulty completing the DCE and differentiating health states than adults; difficulty imagining the described problems was also more common among adolescents.

outcome: Difference between adolescent own-perspective and adult child-perspective preference weights
statement: In the pooled mixed logit model, adolescent interaction coefficients were significantly above zero for all dimension levels except mobility level 2 and self-care levels 2 and 3, which indicates smaller latent-utility decrements for adolescents for most levels.

outcome: Dominant-task failures, missing choices, and choice randomness
statement: Missing DCE choices were more frequent in the adolescent sample than in the adult sample.
The mixed logit model fit both samples better than the multinomial logit model, based on higher log-likelihood and lower Bayesian Information Criterion.

outcome: Dominant-task failures, missing choices, and choice randomness
statement: Adolescent predicted and observed choice probabilities were more centered near 0.5, which indicates greater choice randomness and less decisive preferences than in adults.

outcome: Relative importance of EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions and levels on the latent DCE scale
statement: Both groups ranked the dimensions in the same order: pain/discomfort, worried/sad/unhappy, usual activities, mobility, and looking after oneself.

outcome: Difference between adolescent own-perspective and adult child-perspective preference weights
statement: Relative-importance weights differed between groups. Adolescents assigned more weight to mobility and self-care and less weight to usual activities and pain/discomfort than adults.
Children with COVID-19 had lower HRQoL and reported more problems than non-infected children on both instruments; full-health profiles were less frequent in infected groups.

The EQ-TIPS, self-complete EQ-5D-Y-3L, and proxy EQ-5D-Y-3L distinguished groups defined by infection, disease severity, symptom burden, and OHA, with mostly moderate-to-large known-groups effect sizes.
The EQ-TIPS LSS did not distinguish mild from moderate COVID-19, and its communication dimension had the highest ceiling effect among infected young children.

Child-parent agreement for EQ-5D-Y-3L was moderate to good for dimensions and good for the index and EQ VAS; agreement was poorer for pain or discomfort and feeling worried, sad, or unhappy than for physical dimensions.
Parents tended to report more severe EQ-5D-Y-3L problems and lower index and EQ VAS scores than children, but changes between disease categories were similar across self and proxy modes.
EQ-TIPS LSS, EQ-5D-Y-3L index scores, and EQ VAS were strongly responsive to clinical recovery and improved OHA; the proportion reporting no problems improved on every EQ-TIPS dimension.
The newly published Chinese EQ-5D-Y-3L value set produced index scores that discriminated well between relevant COVID-19 disease groups.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L Index
statement: Patients with migraine had worse HRQoL than matched general-population controls on EQ-5D-5L dimensions, the EQ-5D-5L Index, and EQ VAS.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L Index
statement: The HRQoL deficit was substantially larger for chronic migraine than for episodic migraine.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension-level health problems
statement: Migraine had the largest dimension-level impact on pain/discomfort, followed by anxiety/depression and usual activities; mobility and self-care showed no visually important differences.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L Index
statement: For episodic migraine, EQ VAS was significantly lower than in matched controls, while the EQ-5D-5L Index difference showed only a statistical tendency.

Using the 8-parameter multiplicative model with the 5 mildest states added to the small designs, the EQ-VT design had the lowest root mean square error across all EQ-5D-5L states, while the two small 30-state designs had modestly higher errors.

Adding the 5 mildest health states lowered the overall RMSE substantially for the D-efficient design but not for the orthogonal design, and the choice of model specification and of homoscedastic versus heteroscedastic standard errors had little impact on RMSE.
The small designs predicted the values of their own empirical state set better than the EQ-VT design did, but performed worse on the validation state set.

Some model coefficients differed between designs: 95% confidence intervals did not overlap for the mobility parameter (EQ-VT vs orthogonal), for the anxiety/depression parameter (D-efficient vs orthogonal and EQ-VT) and for the level 4 parameter (orthogonal vs EQ-VT and D-efficient); the D-efficient design had the largest and the orthogonal design the smallest level parameters.

Prediction errors varied with health-state severity: all designs performed similarly for mild states (misery index up to 13), the orthogonal design performed worse in misery index groups 14 and 17, and the D-efficient design performed poorly for severe states (misery index above 20); the EQ-VT design mispredicted state 55535.

Observed mean cTTO values covered the whole valuation space, with the highest value for state 12111 and the lowest for state 55555, and larger standard deviations for more severe states; the D-efficient design had fewer observations clustered at -1 and more at 0.95 than the other designs, and digit preference produced clustering at round values such as 1 and 0.5.

In the 20-parameter additive model the coefficients of all five level-2 dummy variables were not significant for the two small designs, and the level 2 parameter of the 8-parameter multiplicative model remained non-significant for the orthogonal design.

Data collection was feasible despite the increased burden: interviews lasted on average 46 minutes, respondents made on average 7.89 moves per state and took 56.9 seconds per non-practice TTO task, and quality control led to dropping and repeating the first 32 interviews of one interviewer.
The authors generated an interim Jordanian EQ-5D-5L crosswalk value set from the new EQ-5D-3L value set using the published Van Hout mapping method.
Mean EQ VAS was 81.24; 40 respondents reported profile 11111, and pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression were the most commonly reported problem dimensions.

All cTTO, DCE, and hybrid model types were statistically significant and logically consistent. The hybrid model corrected for heteroskedasticity had the best hybrid-model fit and lowest mean absolute error and was selected for the value set.
Observed cTTO values clustered at the scale endpoints; the mean across the 28 valued states was 0.290, the observed mean for state 33333 was -0.541, and six respondents were non-traders.
The study completed 301 virtual valuation interviews; 300 respondents passed all four quality-control criteria, and only one interview was flagged.

The analyzed sample closely matched the Jordanian population for governorate, gender, age, and area type, although urban residents were overrepresented by 5 percentage points and highly educated respondents made up about half of the sample.
Removing feedback-flagged states or the six non-traders did not change selection of the random-intercept cTTO model or the heteroskedastic hybrid model.

The selected value set predicted -0.563 for state 33333. Severe mobility problems had the largest utility decrement, followed by severe anxiety/depression, while severe usual-activity problems had the smallest decrement.

outcome: TTO health state values (uncensored and censored at 0)
statement: Mean uncensored TTO values differed significantly across the three dimension orderings, with the standard order producing the lowest overall mean value.

outcome: TTO health state values (uncensored and censored at 0)
statement: Differences across orders were significant for two moderate states, but disappeared when negative values were censored at 0, indicating the differences relate to worse-than-dead response behaviour.

outcome: TTO health state values (uncensored and censored at 0)
statement: There was no interaction between dimension order and the Life A comparator, and no interaction between interviewer and order, although interviewer effects were present overall.

outcome: TTO health state values (uncensored and censored at 0)
statement: In the TTO regression models the dimension order dummy approached but did not reach significance; self-care and pain/discomfort had the largest decrements and mobility the smallest in all three order arms.

outcome: DCE choice proportions and modelled dimension coefficients
statement: For the DCE, choice proportions differed across orders for only one of seven state pairs, but the likelihood-ratio test rejected homogeneity of preferences across orders; anxiety/depression consistently had the largest decrement.

outcome: Task feasibility and respondent feedback (ease of understanding, difficulty of deciding), interview duration and interviewer effects
statement: Both tasks were reported as feasible and no order was rated as more difficult than another.
Both instruments had very low item missingness and similar acceptability.
Conceptually overlapping EQ-5D-5L and preliminary EQ-HWB-S items had moderate to strong correlations, with all reported coefficients statistically significant.
The preliminary EQ-HWB-S had fewer instrument-level ceiling effects than EQ-5D-5L.
Among respondents who reported full health on EQ-5D-5L, the preliminary EQ-HWB-S detected problems most often for exhaustion, concentration, and sadness.

Both instruments discriminated respondents with and without physical and mental conditions, but only preliminary EQ-HWB-S items distinguished caregiving status and caregiver burden in the reported comparisons.

Screening a pool of 2197 existing items against the selection criteria produced 687 candidate items mapped to 32 subdomains within 7 domains; 458 came from generic preference and non-preference-based health, social care, and wellbeing measures and 229 from item banks and other measures.

Physical sensations items performed well with only 1 of 8 dropped; the word "physical" was added to pain and discomfort items to separate them from mental health aspects, since discomfort was often read as including mild pain.

Relationship items largely performed well, but "support" and "other people" were ambiguous, "disagreements and conflict" covered two issues and was read positively by some UK and Australian respondents, "got on" was colloquial and translated poorly, and "judged" was not always negative.

Self-identity items performed worst: 6 of 10 items were dropped and the dignity/respect subdomain was removed, because dignity was linked to respondents own behaviour, respect to manners or single incidents, and "valued" or "useful" were read by older people as doing tasks or being paid.

Common findings across countries were that examples of the construct and contextual information were valued, simpler layouts were preferred, response option preferences were mixed and often unexplained, and completion instructions including the recall period at the top of the page were often ignored or forgotten.

Detailed team review against the criteria dropped 598 items, mainly for duplication of concepts, double-barrelled content such as the impact of pain on functioning, or overlap between subdomains; 89 items went to stakeholder review and 97 items were taken forward into face validation.

Some subdomains were not carried forward or were restructured: social engagement, autonomy, and thinking clearly overlapped with other items, self-worth/respect was split into confidence and self-worth, and guilt/shame and burden were dropped over social desirability concerns.

A default 5-level response scale and a default 7-day recall period were adopted, with the recall period judged item by item; longer recall was considered necessary for constructs such as coping and control but problematic for tracking change after acute events.

Face validation of 97 draft items and 4 response scales in 170 interviews across 6 countries retained 47 items, modified 14, added 3 new items, and eliminated 36, giving a 64-item set for the psychometric survey.

Activity domain items showed ambiguity: "communicate" was read as mode or effectiveness of communication rather than hearing and speech, "self-care" was read by mental health respondents as wellbeing activities rather than washing and dressing, and items about receiving help created ambiguity for respondents without care.
In the autonomy domain respondents preferred items with more context, for example coping with day-to-day life rather than coping alone, and an item that defined control was found helpful.

Cognition items were generally understood, but memory was seen as a long-term issue that did not fit a 7-day recall, and some respondents linked memory items to dementia and doubted they could report their own memory loss.

In feelings and emotions, top levels of "happy" and "enjoyed life" were seen as unrealistic, "depressed" was read as a clinical diagnosis, "life not worth living" was considered very negative, and "safe", "secure", and "relaxed" were ambiguous or read as a physical state.

outcome: Face validity of the EQ-HWB-9: acceptability, ease of completion, suitability of dimensions and missing content
statement: Most caregivers rated the EQ-HWB-9 as an acceptable proxy measure of the health and wellbeing of the person with dementia, with no difference between recall groups.

outcome: Face validity of the EQ-HWB-9: acceptability, ease of completion, suitability of dimensions and missing content
statement: Most caregivers found the items easy to answer, but a substantial minority reported moderate or high difficulty, citing the inherent difficulty of rating another person and vague distinctions between response options such as 'only occasionally' and 'sometimes'.

outcome: Face validity of the EQ-HWB-9: acceptability, ease of completion, suitability of dimensions and missing content
statement: Caregivers judged observable dimensions as more suitable for describing the health status of the person with dementia than internal states, which required interpretation of facial expressions, gestures and behaviour.

outcome: Face validity of the EQ-HWB-9: acceptability, ease of completion, suitability of dimensions and missing content
statement: Over half of caregivers reported no missing dimensions; those who did most often named sleep, communication and the occurrence of events. Loneliness, pain and sadness/depression were the items most often reported as difficult to answer.

outcome: Adherence to the assigned recall period and preferred recall period
statement: Self-reported adherence was lower in the 7-day recall group than in the 'today' recall group, with more frequent deviations from the instructed recall period.

outcome: Adherence to the assigned recall period and preferred recall period
statement: Caregivers most often preferred a seven-day recall period, and generally preferred the recall period to which they had been assigned; recall periods longer than seven days were regarded as inappropriate.

outcome: Adherence to the proxy-proxy perspective and response certainty
statement: Caregivers generally understood and followed the instructed proxy-proxy perspective, but described tension between their own view and an accurate depiction of the care recipient, and reported uncertainty in selecting response options, particularly for pain, sadness/depression and anxiety when communication was impaired. Relationship closeness affected perceived difficulty.

outcome: Preferred frequency of administration of the EQ-HWB-9
statement: Preferences for administration frequency were heterogeneous, with weekly administration the most common preference.

Many caregivers reported health changes in the care recipient during the study period and described fluctuating good and bad days as typical, with events such as visits or medical appointments influencing behaviour.

outcome: Number of main-effects coefficients differing statistically between two studies
statement: In pairwise pooled models with study interaction terms, the number of the 20 main-effects coefficients that differed statistically between two studies ranged from 2 to 16 (mean 9.3); Malaysia versus Singapore differed most and Malaysia versus Taiwan least.

outcome: Latent-scale DCE main-effects coefficients (20 dummy variables) per study
statement: In the study-specific mixed logit models, all coefficients were significant at the 0.05 level except level 2 of usual activities in Taiwan, and three coefficients were logically inconsistent (one in Vietnam, two in the Philippines) at level 3 of self-care, mobility and usual activities; standard errors generally increased with severity.

outcome: Relative importance of the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions
