statement: Mobility was the most important dimension in every study except Vietnam, where pain/discomfort was most important; the least important dimension was usual activities in 6 studies, self-care in 3 and anxiety/depression in 2, so no universal rank order existed across the 11 Asian populations.

outcome: Relative importance of the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: The sum of the relative importance of the three functional dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities) exceeded the sum of the two symptom dimensions (pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) in all 11 studies, and pain/discomfort was valued higher than or equal to anxiety/depression in all studies except Thailand.

outcome: Relative importance of EQ-5D-5L severity levels 2, 3 and 4 relative to level 5
statement: Relative importance of severity levels was more comparable across studies than dimension importance: on average level 2 accounted for about 20%, level 3 about 30% and level 4 about 70% of the weight of level 5.

outcome: Relative importance of the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: Only Hong Kong, Malaysia and Taiwan shared the same dimension rank order (mobility > pain/discomfort > anxiety/depression > self-care > usual activities).

outcome: Latent-scale DCE main-effects coefficients (20 dummy variables) per study
statement: The heteroscedastic conditional logit model removed the non-significant Taiwanese coefficient but did not remove the inconsistencies for the Philippines and Vietnam, and introduced one non-significant coefficient for South Korea and one inconsistency for Thailand.

Of 95 unique studies identified, only nine investigated the relationship between PROMIS-29 and EQ-5D; six of these used EQ-5D-5L, seven were from the United States and five were published in 2020 or 2021.

Four of the six relationship categories had been addressed for PROMIS-29 and EQ-5D-3L and three for PROMIS-29 and EQ-5D-5L; no study performed response mapping or compared the characteristics of the value sets for either EQ-5D version.
In a US general-population sample, PROMIS-29 described far more distinct health states than EQ-5D-3L, indicating a large EQ-5D-3L ceiling effect and limited sensitivity to mild problems.

Mapping PROMIS-29 domain scores to EQ-5D utilities is feasible: the Revicki linear model explained 57% of the variance in EQ-5D-3L utility with all five domain coefficients significant, but overestimated EQ-5D scores below 0.40.

Klapproth and colleagues found that applying the US Revicki model to European data systematically underestimated the EQ-5D-5L crosswalk value for the UK and France but not Germany, and concluded that mapping algorithms should not be generalised across countries.

PROMIS-29 and EQ-5D utility scores were highly correlated but PROMIS-29 utilities were much lower, had a wider and more granular range and showed no ceiling effect, whereas EQ-5D utilities showed discontinuities and ceiling effects.
Hartman and Craig developed the only scale transformation, a non-linear power function converting PROMIS-29 utility loss to EQ-5D-3L utility loss; no study has since validated it.

Both EQ-5D-5L (crosswalk) values and PROPr distinguished socio-demographic groups and the presence of self-reported chronic conditions, but the two systems produced different utility estimates across those groups.

Five studies collected both instruments in patient groups and reported known-group validity or responsiveness, with instances of significant differences on one instrument and not the other (for example physical function on PROMIS-29 but not mobility on EQ-5D-5L in systemic sclerosis).
Restricting analysis to online respondents who agreed that the TTO was easy to understand did not yield different TTO values from the other online respondents.
Online respondents showed lower task engagement: more completed all tasks in three trade-offs or fewer and the mean number of trade-offs per task was lower.
Online respondents produced substantially more logical inconsistencies, including failure to assign profile 55555 the lowest value.
Adjustment for measured respondent characteristics did not materially remove the higher valuations associated with online administration.
The online modeled value set had eight insignificant dimension-level decrements and two preference inversions, while each main face-to-face model had one significant inversion.
The online random-intercept value model had compressed decrements and no modeled worse-than-dead health states; its value for 55555 was positive, unlike both face-to-face models.
Online respondents gave higher mean raw cTTO values than both face-to-face comparator samples.
Online respondents supplied far fewer raw worse-than-dead valuations than face-to-face respondents, although similar proportions entered the lead-time TTO section.

Caregivers of children with a health condition most often selected TANDI as the best description of the child's health, whereas caregivers in the preschool comparison group most often selected PedsQL.
The best TANDI profile 111111 was reported for 70 children overall and was more common in the preschool comparison group than in the health-condition group.

TANDI Movement, Play, and Pain had strong expected associations with EQ-5D-Y Proxy Mobility, Usual Activities, and Pain or Discomfort. TANDI also had moderate-to-strong associations with similar PedsQL content, although Relationships had only a weak association with PedsQL social functioning.

TANDI LSS and VAS scores differentiated children with a health condition from the preschool comparison group; dimension responses differed except for Communication, but Relationships and Eating showed unexpected patterns.
TANDI had no missing responses, and no child was reported in the worst possible health state, so no floor effect was evident.
Children with a health condition had more unique TANDI health profiles than preschool children in the comparison group.

TANDI LSS correlated strongly with the PedsQL total score and the EQ-5D-Y Proxy preference-based score. The TANDI VAS association was low with PedsQL total and moderate with the EQ-5D-Y preference-based score.

TANDI LSS and VAS differed across clinician-rated mild, moderate, and severe health states. LSS separated mild from moderate and severe states, but neither score separated moderate from severe states.

outcome: Mean observed composite time trade-off values for EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-Y health states by study arm
statement: Multivariate analysis of variance showed a statistically significant interaction between instrument wording and perspective for composite time trade-off responses in both blocks, so wording and perspective could not be analyzed as independent factors.

outcome: Mean observed composite time trade-off values for EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-Y health states by study arm
statement: Post hoc paired comparisons showed significant differences between three arm pairs: EQ-5D-3L adult versus EQ-5D-3L child, EQ-5D-3L adult versus EQ-5D-Y adult, and EQ-5D-3L adult versus EQ-5D-Y child.

outcome: Mean observed composite time trade-off values for EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-Y health states by study arm
statement: Values elicited from the child perspective were generally higher than those from the adult perspective, and EQ-5D-3L states received generally lower values than the corresponding EQ-5D-Y states.

outcome: Mean observed composite time trade-off values for EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-Y health states by study arm
statement: Values for the worst state 33333 did not differ significantly across the four study arms, either overall or by country.

outcome: Choice probabilities in DCE pairs and in comparisons with immediate death by study arm
statement: In the DCE with death, immediate death was chosen less often in the child perspective arms, so health states were more often preferred to death when valued for a child.

outcome: Mean observed composite time trade-off values for EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-Y health states by study arm
statement: Mild states at the top of the scale and the severest state 33333 showed no significant differences between arms; differences were concentrated in states with level 3 problems in mobility, self-care or usual activities.

outcome: Mean observed composite time trade-off values for EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-Y health states by study arm
statement: In the Netherlands values tended to be higher from the adult perspective than the child perspective, the opposite of the pattern in the other three countries.

The research programme showed that values for EQ-5D-Y-3L child health states differ from values for EQ-5D-3L adult health states and that instrument wording and perspective interact; EQ-5D-3L value sets must not be applied to EQ-5D-Y-3L states.
For health state 33333, cTTO values were higher under the child perspective than under the adult perspective.
DCE with duration and QALY-composition results were similar for people aged 10, 15, and 40 years, except that respondents accepted larger time trade-offs to avoid pain or discomfort in children.
All tested models gave similar relative importance for dimensions, and the DCE was feasible for estimating latent-scale relative dimension and level importance.
All four anchoring techniques gave lower values for the adult perspective than for the child perspective for health state 33333.
The final protocol uses an online DCE to estimate relative dimension and level importance and a separate face-to-face cTTO sample to anchor values at full health = 1 and dead = 0.
The DCE design contains 150 pairs in ten blocks, with 15 forced choices per respondent; the cTTO design contains one block of ten states and must include the worst state, 33333.
The recommended samples are 1000 adults for online DCE and 200 adults for face-to-face cTTO, with both samples selected to be as representative of the relevant country as possible.

outcome: Unique values and standardized response mean for dominant/dominated pairs
statement: pTTO produced slightly more unique values per respondent and substantially better discrimination for the severe health-state pair, but slightly lower standardized response means for mild and moderate pairs.

outcome: Value distribution, gaps, and clustering
statement: pTTO values had a smoother and more continuous distribution than cTTO values, although pTTO had its own midpoint cluster.

outcome: Interviewer-rated task-completing difficulty
statement: pTTO and cTTO had similar interviewer-rated feasibility, but respondents found pTTO somewhat less acceptable and more difficult overall.

outcome: Stringent and less stringent logical consistency
statement: pTTO greatly improved logical consistency for the severe dominant/dominated pair, while cTTO performed slightly better for the mild and moderate pairs.

outcome: pTTO and cTTO values for selected EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: For all six target health states, mean pTTO values were higher and their standard deviations were smaller than the corresponding original and converted cTTO values.

outcome: Ordering effects
statement: There was no statistically significant difference in TTO values between participants who completed cTTO first and those who completed pTTO first.
Mobility had the largest effect on preferences; the preferred-model dimension ranking was mobility, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression, self-care, then usual activities.
The feedback module reduced participants with at least one incorrectly ranked cTTO state from 26% to 12.5%; model performance worsened when flagged states were re-included.
In the analyzed sample, anxiety/depression was the most common EQ-5D-5L problem and self-care was the least common; mean EQ VAS was 76.9.

The constrained heteroskedastic model based on cTTO data was selected because it was logically consistent, handled heteroskedasticity, had statistically significant monotonic parameters, and had better prediction accuracy than the other tested models.

The pilot found that the wheelchair practice state was often judged worse than dead, so the study replaced it with a migraine example and used graphics and traffic-light color cards to support illiterate participants.
The preferred value set ranged from full health at 1 to -0.964 for state 55555; state 11211 had the highest predicted impaired-state value of 0.948.
The analyzed sample represented age, sex, and geographic distribution reasonably well, but rural residents, illiterate adults, and adults aged 65 years or older were underrepresented.
Of 1378 conducted interviews, 75 were incomplete, 113 were removed with three interviewers for poor protocol compliance, 216 were pilot interviews, and 974 entered the final analysis.
A large share of observed valuations and predicted health states were worse than dead.
Most residents with MMSE scores of 24 or above received green grades and showed sufficient cognitive capacity to reliably self-complete the EQ-5D-5L.
In the think-aloud cohort, every resident with an MMSE score of 23 or below received an amber or red overall traffic light grade.
In the think-aloud cohort, 21 of 33 residents with an MMSE score of 24 or above received a green overall traffic light grade.
In the eye-tracking cohort, 14 of 16 residents with an MMSE score of 23 or below received an amber or red overall traffic light grade.
In the eye-tracking cohort, 15 of 22 residents with an MMSE score of 24 or above received a green overall traffic light grade.
All enrolled residents could complete the EQ-5D-5L task, but the mixed-methods evidence showed that only a proportion completed it reliably.
Seven of 45 randomized eye-tracking participants were excluded because recordings were incomplete or insufficient for heat-map and gaze-plot analysis.

outcome: Low personal wellbeing at 24 months post-injury (Personal Wellbeing Index below 70)
statement: Two years after injury, about a quarter of participants had a low level of personal wellbeing, well below the normative range for western populations.

outcome: Low personal wellbeing at 24 months post-injury (Personal Wellbeing Index below 70)
statement: Anatomical injury severity and hospitalisation did not predict low personal wellbeing after adjustment for pre-injury characteristics; if anything, higher severity and hospitalisation were associated with lower risk.

outcome: Low personal wellbeing at 24 months post-injury (Personal Wellbeing Index below 70)
statement: Injury caused by intentional assault increased the risk of low personal wellbeing at 24 months compared with accidental injury.

outcome: Low personal wellbeing at 24 months post-injury (Personal Wellbeing Index below 70)
statement: Among the EQ-5D dimensions, problems with anxiety/depression at 3 months and problems on the additional cognitive functioning item were the strongest predictors of low personal wellbeing at 24 months; self-care problems became significant only after adjustment for pre-injury characteristics, while mobility, usual activities and pain/discomfort were not predictive.

outcome: Low personal wellbeing at 24 months post-injury (Personal Wellbeing Index below 70)
statement: Pre-injury life satisfaction, measured by a single question, correlated moderately strongly with the 24-month Personal Wellbeing Index, and adjusting for it did not change the results.

outcome: Sensitivity of cTTO utility to EQ-5D-5L severity measured by level sum score
statement: For negative utilities, arm A replicated the absence of a significant association between level sum score and utility. Only arm B had a statistically significant negative association; arms C and D did not.

outcome: Distribution and sign of elicited EQ-5D-5L utilities
statement: Compared with standard cTTO, removing the immediate-death sorting question in arm B increased the proportion of pooled valuations classified as worse than dead and made the mean utility among worse-than-dead valuations less negative.

outcome: Floor effects and censoring of negative utility values
statement: Arm B reduced the floor at utility -1 relative to arm A for pooled states and for state 55555.

outcome: Floor effects and censoring of negative utility values
statement: Extending LT-TTO below -1 produced many very low values and moved censoring to -10; 10.1% of pooled observations were below -1, and 66% of observations below -1 were equal to -10.

outcome: Sensitivity of cTTO utility to EQ-5D-5L severity measured by level sum score
statement: Randomizing the first negative LT-TTO value slightly reduced the spike at -0.5 but did not improve the utility distribution or produce a significant severity association.

outcome: Logical consistency of within-respondent utilities for Pareto-ordered health states
statement: For pairs of worse-than-dead states, strict agreement with Pareto ordering was higher in arm B than in arm A, although censoring contributed to this difference.

outcome: Distribution and sign of elicited EQ-5D-5L utilities
statement: In the supplementary illustrative value-set analysis, the estimated value of state 55555 was lower in arm B than in arm A; the study was not designed to produce a complete value set.

outcome: Perceived task difficulty
statement: The four arms did not differ substantially in perceived difficulty.

EQ-5D-5L utility values and EQ VAS scores followed a rise-and-fall pattern: both improved in the early heatwave period, then declined during the peak heatwave period; recovery after the heatwave was incomplete.
Pain/discomfort was the EQ-5D-5L dimension most affected at peak heatwave, while self-care and anxiety/depression remained stable and mobility and usual activities changed less.

Older age predicted lower utility values and EQ VAS scores. Underweight participants had lower utility values, obese participants had lower EQ VAS scores, and lower education was associated with greater vulnerability.

Temperature had nonlinear associations with HRQoL. Utility values declined across same-day maximum temperatures of 27 to 33 degrees Celsius, minimum temperatures of 19 to 22 degrees Celsius, and average temperatures of 22 to 29 degrees Celsius.

Same-day humidity was negatively associated with utility values and EQ VAS scores. Seven-day average humidity had a nonlinear association with EQ VAS, with scores increasing above 78% humidity and decreasing as humidity rose below that threshold.

The support-vector machine model performed better than the XGBoost, random forest, and K-nearest neighbors models. BMI was the most important utility-value predictor, and age was the most important EQ VAS predictor.
Humid heatwaves had a more pronounced negative effect on HRQoL than dry heatwaves.

outcome: Ceiling and floor effects
statement: The Y-5L reduced the overall ceiling effect compared with Y-3L, with larger relative reductions in the acute and chronic groups than in the general population.

outcome: Convergent validity
statement: Correlations of dimensions with EQ VAS were similar and weak to moderate for both versions, while paired Y-3L and Y-5L dimensions showed strong convergence.

outcome: Absolute and relative informativity of dimensions
statement: Absolute informativity improved across all dimensions on Y-5L, while response-distribution evenness was broadly retained.

outcome: Known-group validity
statement: Both versions discriminated known health-condition groups and showed significant differences in VAS and level-sum scores among acute, chronic, and general-population groups.

outcome: Missing responses and completion feasibility
statement: Missing dimension responses were low for both instruments but were more frequent for Y-5L than Y-3L.

outcome: Consistency of response redistribution from Y-3L to Y-5L
statement: Only a small proportion of paired dimension responses were inconsistent when responses moved from Y-3L to Y-5L.

outcome: Test-retest reliability
statement: Both versions had moderate to substantial test-retest agreement in the stable chronic-condition group; agreement was generally lower in the general-population group, with fair agreement for Looking After Myself and Usual Activities.

outcome: Importance and relevance of cognitive-function components and candidate items
statement: Literature and target-population input identified school performance, concentration, memory, and learning ability as the most important cognitive components; the pilot bolt-on retained four items for general cognitive abilities, concentration, memory, and school performance, with learning ability represented in examples.

outcome: Factor structure and item-reduction performance
statement: Factor and regression analyses supported reduction to one or two cognitive items. Memory was the best single item, and concentration plus memory was the best two-item combination for EQ VAS model fit and explanatory power.

Participants with rheumatic disorders reported more mobility, usual-activity, and pain or discomfort problems than those with type 1 diabetes, but the disease groups did not differ significantly on the cognitive items.

outcome: Self-rated overall health on EQ VAS
statement: EQ VAS and standard EQ-5D-Y dimension responses did not differ significantly between the two questionnaire versions.

outcome: Explanatory power for EQ VAS
statement: Some regression coefficients for severe concentration and memory problems had counter-intuitive positive signs.

outcome: Comprehensibility, clarity, and interpretation of cognitive bolt-on items
statement: The bolt-on was relevant, clear, easily understood, and well accepted; all participants completed it without assistance or clarification, and no item was deleted, merged, or added. Appointments was added as an example for memory.
Younger participants required more completion time than older participants, and the pilot items detected cognitive impairment in a minority of participants.

outcome: Completion and missing-item performance
statement: The extended instrument was feasible: most respondents completed all descriptive items, item-level missingness was low, and memory had the highest missingness among the bolt-on items.

outcome: Absolute and relative informativity
statement: The bolt-on items detected more reported problems and had a lower ceiling than the standard EQ-5D-Y items.

outcome: Explanatory power for EQ VAS
statement: Adding all four cognitive items increased the variance in EQ VAS explained by the item-level linear regression model. The increase occurred in both disease groups.

outcome: Absolute and relative informativity
statement: The cognitive bolt-on items had higher relative informativity than the standard EQ-5D-Y items.

outcome: Convergent validity with KIDSCREEN-27
statement: Concentration and school-performance items had moderate-to-strong correlations with similar KIDSCREEN-27 items, which supported convergent validity.

outcome: Internal consistency of cognitive bolt-on items
statement: The four-item bolt-on had acceptable internal consistency; removal of memory produced only a small increase in Cronbach’s alpha.
After the study applied its time and logical-consistency criteria, 3109 adults and 2129 adolescents were included in the analysis.
Adult and adolescent preference coefficients differed overall in Germany, Slovenia, and Spain; the Wald and likelihood-ratio tests were significant at the 1% level in each country.

Relative attribute importance was broadly similar between groups. Adolescents generally gave more importance to mobility and self-care and less importance to pain or discomfort than adults in Slovenia and Spain; differences were not significant in Germany or for anxiety or depression in any country.

The implied dimension-level rank order differed slightly between adults and adolescents in all countries: AD2 and PD2 reversed in Germany; mobility and usual-activity levels reversed in Slovenia; and severe mobility versus anxiety or depression and level-2 usual activities versus anxiety or depression reversed in Spain.
Adolescents completed the DCE more quickly and made fewer dominant-pair inconsistencies overall than adults, although the country-specific inconsistency pattern was not uniform.
All adult mixed-logit coefficients were logically consistent and statistically significant at the 1% level.
Of 46 registries licensed to use EQ-5D, 41 reported collecting EQ-5D data; collection was most common in musculoskeletal registries but occurred across many disease areas.

The registries used several EQ-5D versions: 23 collected EQ-5D-3L, 16 collected EQ-5D-5L, one collected EQ-5D-Y, and one collected both EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-Y; seven 5L registries had changed from 3L in 2017 or 2018.

Measurement schedules and administration modes varied substantially; paper-only questionnaires were most common, and measurements ranged from about 60 individuals in two registries to more than 440,000 measurements in the Swedish Hip Arthroplasty Registry.

Thirty-six registries provided EQ-5D results to patients, clinicians, or other decision-makers, most often as aggregate results in annual reports or websites; five reported no communication of EQ-5D data through any channel.

Twenty-two registries reported use of EQ-5D data. The most frequent uses were intervention assessment and quality indicators, with additional use in health-economic studies, benchmarking, quality improvement, and individual consultations.
Reported use was more common among intervention registries than diagnosis registries: 10 of 15 intervention registries and 12 of 26 diagnosis registries reported use.
Representatives from 19 registries reported that EQ-5D data were not used or that they did not know whether the data were used; active use in quality improvement was reported by only six registries.
Median HADS-A anxiety score decreased significantly after ozone therapy.
Median HADS-D depression score decreased significantly after ozone therapy.
The EQ-5D-5L anxiety/depression dimension improved significantly after ozone therapy.
EQ VAS self-perceived general health improved significantly after ozone therapy.
The proportions with mild or greater anxiety and depression both decreased after therapy, but neither paired proportion comparison reached statistical significance.
Before and after therapy, HADS-A and HADS-D correlated positively with the EQ-5D-5L anxiety/depression dimension and inversely with EQ VAS.
In the 13 cancer survivors, HADS-A and EQ VAS improved significantly; changes in HADS-D and the EQ-5D-5L anxiety/depression dimension were not statistically significant.
Nine of 16 patients were taking anxiolytic and/or antidepressant treatment before ozone therapy, and these treatments were not prescribed or modified during ozone therapy.

outcome: Prevalence of reported problems on the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: Overall self-reported health was high: 54% of the sample reported full health (11111), and mean EQ VAS and EQ index scores were 86.0 and 0.957.

outcome: Prevalence of reported problems on the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: Problems were far more common in pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression than in mobility, self-care and usual activities.

outcome: Prevalence of reported problems on the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: Problems in mobility, self-care and pain/discomfort increased with age, while anxiety/depression problems were more prevalent in younger age groups.

outcome: EQ VAS score
statement: Mean EQ VAS and EQ index scores declined with age, ranging across age and gender groups from 82.9 to 88.3 for EQ VAS and 0.912 to 0.971 for the index.

outcome: EQ VAS score
statement: Contrary to most population norm studies, females reported higher EQ VAS scores than males in every age group except 20-29 years, and males had significantly lower adjusted EQ VAS scores.

outcome: Prevalence of reported problems on the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: Lower socio-economic status was associated with poorer self-reported health: lower education and being retired or unemployed predicted more problems and lower EQ VAS and index scores, while having health insurance predicted a higher EQ VAS.

outcome: Prevalence of reported problems on the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: Self-reported health differed between the five cities, with Beijing reporting the highest EQ VAS and index scores; pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression also differed significantly across cities.

outcome: Prevalence of reported problems on the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: Compared with the 2008 Chinese EQ-5D-3L norms, more problems were reported on pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression with the 5L version.
Mortality became a larger driver at age 65, and the HRQoL share of QALE inequality fell for both sexes.

Atkinson-index calculations gave greater implied weight to an identical health gain in the most deprived quintile than in the least deprived quintile, with the ratio increasing with inequality aversion.
At birth, the least deprived fifth had substantially higher life expectancy and QALE than the most deprived fifth.
Mortality explained most of the combined-sex QALE inequality at birth; pain/discomfort was the largest EQ-5D-5L dimension contributor and usual activities was the smallest.
Combined-sex QALE at birth increased monotonically from the most deprived to the least deprived quintile.
The complete-case HRQoL analysis included 14,412 of 16,175 HSE participants aged 16 years or older after exclusion of participants with incomplete EQ-5D-5L profiles.
The dimension pattern differed by sex: pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression contributed more for females, while mobility was relatively more influential for males.
Adjustment for HRQoL largely removed the female advantage in life expectancy at birth.
HRQoL explained a much larger share of QALE inequality for females than for males.

outcome: Participant-reported ease of understanding the instructions and difficulty of the choice tasks; agreement of the DCE-derived dimension ranking with expectation
statement: In the think-aloud sessions most participants found a binary better-than-dead / worse-than-dead assessment more challenging than moving a VAS slider, but their binary answers reflected their thoughts more accurately, so the binary search algorithm was adopted for the tool and the VAS was dropped.

outcome: Mean DCE weights and social disutility coefficients for EQ-5D-5L levels, and the resulting 3125 health state values
statement: Robustness checks using stricter speed thresholds (median 8 s and 10 s per answer) produced very similar value sets, with Pearson correlations of 1.000 and mean values for dead of 0.338, 0.337 and 0.333.

outcome: Mean DCE weights and social disutility coefficients for EQ-5D-5L levels, and the resulting 3125 health state values
statement: The New Zealand value set correlated highly with 13 other countries' EQ-5D-5L value sets (Spearman 0.895–0.970), but only Hong Kong, Indonesia and Ireland had more health states worse than dead than New Zealand.

outcome: Data quality: consistency of repeated DCE answers, response times, and exclusion rates
statement: Of the 5112 people who completed the survey, 2644 (51.6%) were excluded by the data quality checks, leaving a high-quality sub-sample of 2468: 3 reported invalid responses, others valued dead at unity, answered the two repeated DCE questions inconsistently, or answered implausibly fast (median under 6 s per answer).

outcome: Data quality: consistency of repeated DCE answers, response times, and exclusion rates
statement: Participants who took longer per decision were more consistent, supporting the 6 s median threshold; of the 2256 inconsistent participants, 683 were also implausibly fast.

outcome: Data quality: consistency of repeated DCE answers, response times, and exclusion rates
statement: Always clicking the same button was much more common among excluded participants (225, 9%, mostly "they are equal") than in the high-quality sub-sample (132, 5%, all "they are equal"), and the retained always-equal participants showed no other sign of poor data quality.

The high-quality sub-sample was generally representative of the New Zealand adult population on age, gender, ethnicity and long-term disability, although it was more educated and higher-income than the census population.

outcome: Feasibility of the online valuation tool, including completion time and number of questions asked
statement: Participants answered 20 DCE questions on average with a median of 12.6 s per answer, and the whole tool typically took 5–10 minutes to complete.

outcome: Participant-reported ease of understanding the instructions and difficulty of the choice tasks; agreement of the DCE-derived dimension ranking with expectation
statement: Feedback was mostly positive: 63.7% found the instructions and design easy to understand, 49.1% found choosing between two health states difficult, and 87.0% said the DCE-derived ranking of the five dimensions was as they expected.

outcome: Mean DCE weights and social disutility coefficients for EQ-5D-5L levels, and the resulting 3125 health state values
statement: Anxiety/Depression was on average the most important dimension, followed by Pain/Discomfort, Self-Care, Mobility and, least important, Usual Activities, with disutility increasing monotonically across levels on every dimension.

outcome: Mean DCE weights and social disutility coefficients for EQ-5D-5L levels, and the resulting 3125 health state values
statement: The New Zealand social value set ranges from 1 for 11111 to −0.830 for 55555, and 780 of the 3125 states (25%) are worse than dead.
Adding the respiratory dimension reduced the proportion of respondents who reported no problems on all dimensions.

The respiratory bolt-on utility correlated slightly more strongly with almost all respiratory-related clinical parameters than the standard EQ-5D-5L utility; correlations with CAT and MRC were strong.

Normal-distribution generalized linear models had the best fit. Clinical-parameter coefficients were generally larger for respiratory bolt-on utility, but only the CAT coefficient differed beyond the confidence interval of the standard EQ-5D-5L estimate.
Both instruments discriminated between the prespecified clinical groups, but absolute utility differences were consistently larger with the respiratory bolt-on.
Respiratory bolt-on responses covered all five severity levels, with most respondents reporting slight or moderate breathing problems.

After utility scales were normalized, subgroup differences became smaller and were no longer significantly different between instruments, which showed that scale length contributed to the apparent gain in discrimination.

Worse respiratory-dimension levels were associated with worse deprivation, smoking, comorbidity, lung function, physical activity, disease-specific quality of life, dyspnea, exacerbation, and performance-test measures.
Mean utility was slightly lower and its scale was wider for the EQ-5D-5L plus respiratory bolt-on than for the standard EQ-5D-5L.

Both instruments were acceptable and quick to complete. More than 70% of adolescents rated each as somewhat or very easy, and the overall difference in reported difficulty was not statistically significant.
The EQ-5D-Y-5L took longer on average to complete than the EQ-5D-5L, but completion time did not differ significantly by special healthcare needs, mental health concerns, or age group.

The EQ-5D-Y-5L identified more self-reported problems than the EQ-5D-5L in every corresponding dimension, with the largest differences in usual activities, pain/discomfort, and worried/sad/unhappy versus anxiety/depression.
A ceiling effect occurred for EQ-5D-5L in adolescents with special healthcare needs, whereas EQ-5D-Y-5L was below the prespecified threshold; neither instrument had floor effects.
Corresponding dimensions and level sum scores showed strong convergent validity overall, and subgroup analyses showed similar patterns.

EQ-5D-5L had better test-retest reliability at the level-sum-score level than EQ-5D-Y-5L in the full sample and among adolescents with special healthcare needs and mental health concerns; dimension-level agreement was at most moderate overall.
Both instruments distinguished adolescents with and without special healthcare needs and mental health concerns, but EQ-5D-Y-5L produced larger known-group effect sizes overall and across age groups.

In the authors' summary against four prespecified psychometric cutoffs, EQ-5D-Y-5L met three cutoffs and EQ-5D-5L met two in the full sample; the youth instrument performed better for ceiling effects and known-group validity, while the adult instrument performed better for test-retest reliability.

outcome: Reporting any health problem at 30 days (low utility score group, utility below 1)
statement: After full adjustment for pre-PCI, PCI and post-PCI characteristics, patients with prior CABG were more likely than those without prior CABG to report any health problem at 30 days after PCI.

outcome: Problems on the EQ-5D-3L mobility dimension at 30 days
statement: Prior CABG was associated with a higher likelihood of reporting problems on every EQ-5D-3L dimension at 30 days in the fully adjusted model.

outcome: Reporting any health problem at 30 days (low utility score group, utility below 1)
statement: About one third of included patients reported a health problem at 30 days; mobility, usual activities, pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression problems were each reported by roughly 15% of patients, and personal-care problems by about 5%.

outcome: Reporting any health problem at 30 days (low utility score group, utility below 1)
statement: The association between prior CABG and reported problems differed by ejection fraction: it was present in patients with EF at or above 50% and absent or reversed in patients with EF below 50%, with significant interaction for the overall problem, mobility, personal care and usual activity outcomes but not for pain/discomfort or anxiety/depression.

Patients with prior CABG had a higher cardiovascular risk profile at baseline, were older, waited longer from admission to PCI, and more often had femoral access and lesions in the left main, left circumflex or a graft.

outcome: Likelihood of completing the 30-day EQ-5D questionnaire
statement: Completion of the 30-day EQ-5D questionnaire was not random: acute coronary syndrome presentation, lower ejection fraction, diabetes, cerebrovascular disease, later data-collection year, longer stent length, in-hospital renal impairment and use of ticagrelor, beta-blockers, aspirin or oral anticoagulants reduced the likelihood of completion.
Major in-hospital complications after PCI did not differ between the prior CABG and no prior CABG groups.

All participants found the modified questionnaire easy to understand; all items were judged relevant, acceptable, and supported by appropriate response options. Most items were interpreted as intended.

Control over day-to-day life was the most difficult item: three participants misinterpreted it or did not understand it. Interpretations of anxiety varied, and participants often distinguished temporary sadness from clinical depression.

Participants identified possible missing content, chiefly leisure or free-time activities and explicit social interaction; smaller numbers mentioned financial autonomy, access to medication, environmental conditions, and more positive framing.

The detailed findings did not show a clear overall preference between the modified and earlier experimental versions, although the modified autonomy wording received stronger support and the changes generally improved local-language alignment.

Twelve participants reproduced the intended five-label frequency order exactly. Four did not place one or both anchor labels in the expected positions, while the other deviations were minor reversals among intermediate labels.
Across 100 card placements, 23 were not in the expected position. Agreement was highest for the two anchors and lower for the two middle response labels.

The earlier label "Only occasionally" had no single stable placement: it was most often paired with "Sometimes", but participants also associated it with "A little of the time", "Often", or "None of the time".

outcome: Within-person change in EQ-5D-5L utility (Dutch value set) between 2 and 3 years
statement: Mean within-person change in EQ-5D-5L utility and EQ VAS between 2 and 3 years after infection was not significantly different from zero.

outcome: Within-person change in EQ-5D-5L utility (Dutch value set) between 2 and 3 years
statement: Individual change scores varied widely in both directions: about 30% declined, 32% improved and 37% showed no change in utility, with a similar spread for EQ VAS.

outcome: Within-person change in EQ-5D-5L utility (Dutch value set) between 2 and 3 years
statement: In the multivariable model, female sex was associated with lower (declining) utility change scores, with a significant positive interaction for women aged 67 years or older.

outcome: Within-person change in EQ-5D-5L utility (Dutch value set) between 2 and 3 years
statement: Participants reporting social participation problems at 2 years had higher subsequent change scores on both EQ utility and EQ VAS.

outcome: Within-person change in EQ-5D-5L utility (Dutch value set) between 2 and 3 years
statement: Median EQ-5D-5L utility and EQ VAS levels were similar at 2 and 3 years, and most participants still met the post COVID-19 condition definition at 3 years.

outcome: Within-person change in EQ-5D-5L utility (Dutch value set) between 2 and 3 years
statement: Direction of change depended on initial HRQoL: participants with low initial utility tended to improve, while those with high initial utility most often showed no change.

outcome: Within-person change in EQ VAS between 2 and 3 years
statement: The most frequent post COVID-19 symptoms at the 2-year follow-up were fatigue, muscle pain or weakness, and sleeping problems, and the sex association seen for utility was not seen for EQ VAS.

outcome: Prevalence of C-TTO response path patterns and external agreement (Lin's CCC) between models and the follow-up study
statement: C-TTO response paths were dominated by satisficing and straight-lining patterns, with fewer circling and wandering paths.

outcome: Prevalence of C-TTO response path patterns and external agreement (Lin's CCC) between models and the follow-up study
statement: Protocol violations were far more frequent in the original valuation study than in the follow-up study.

outcome: Prevalence of C-TTO response path patterns and external agreement (Lin's CCC) between models and the follow-up study
statement: Stepwise relaxation of assumptions about C-TTO responses progressively improved agreement with the follow-up (external validation) model across all 3125 EQ-5D-5L states.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state values (20 main-effect coefficients and predicted values for 3125 states)
statement: Accounting for protocol violations widened the predicted value range, lowering the value of the worst state 55555 and raising values of mild states; all 20 main-effect coefficients were logically consistent and 16 of 20 were statistically significant in model 3.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state values (20 main-effect coefficients and predicted values for 3125 states)
statement: In the recommended Spanish EQ-5D-5L value set, anxiety/depression and pain/discomfort carried the largest decrements, contrasting with the earlier Spanish EQ-5D-3L value set where mobility had the largest decrement; the model 3 distribution overlapped the crosswalk distribution but not the EQ-5D-3L distribution.

outcome: Prevalence of C-TTO response path patterns and external agreement (Lin's CCC) between models and the follow-up study
statement: C-TTO intervals derived from response paths were asymmetric around the observed mean value, with a larger distance to the upper bound than to the lower bound, especially for more severe states.

outcome: Conventional change in EQ-5D-3L summary score and EQ VAS from T1 to T2
statement: Mean current HRQL improved between one week and three months after injury on both EQ-5D-3L and EQ VAS.

outcome: Retrospective change in EQ-5D-3L summary score and EQ VAS from then-test T1 to T2
statement: Retrospective change was significantly greater than conventional change for both EQ-5D-3L and EQ VAS.

outcome: Agreement between conventional and retrospective HRQL change
statement: Individual agreement between conventional and retrospective change was fair and nearly identical for EQ-5D-3L and EQ VAS.

outcome: Response shift in EQ-5D-3L summary score and EQ VAS
statement: For EQ-5D-3L, response shift was significantly larger in magnitude than recall bias.

outcome: Response shift in EQ-5D-3L summary score and EQ VAS
statement: For EQ VAS, response shift was larger in magnitude than recall bias, but the difference was not statistically significant.

outcome: Recall bias in EQ-5D-3L summary score and EQ VAS
statement: Increasing PTSD symptoms predicted worse recalled T1 EQ-5D-3L and greater response shift in the multivariable analyses.

outcome: Recall bias in EQ-5D-3L summary score and EQ VAS
statement: Traumatic brain injury and increasing PTSD symptoms predicted both recall bias and response shift on EQ VAS.
Response shift was greatest in important trauma subgroups, including patients with severe injury, traumatic brain injury, or PTSD symptoms.

outcome: Latent-scale DCE values for EQ-5D-Y-3L dimension levels
statement: The mixed-logit DCE model produced logically ordered, statistically significant coefficients; pain/discomfort carried the largest weight and self-care the smallest, with wide preference heterogeneity across respondents.

outcome: Mean observed composite time trade-off values for 23 EQ-5D-Y-3L states
statement: The 222 cTTO respondents provided 2664 observations; mean observed values ranged from -0.185 for state 33333 to 0.939 for state 11121, and 8.9% of values were negative, with 76% of negative values concentrated in states 33332 and 33333.

outcome: Mean observed composite time trade-off values for 23 EQ-5D-Y-3L states
statement: The distribution of mean cTTO values was non-linear: values for the two worst states were far lower than a linear main-effects model over all cTTO data predicted.

outcome: Fit of alternative anchoring functions (R-squared, mean absolute error, logical consistency)
statement: Non-linear (power) mapping functions outperformed linear mapping in fit and accuracy; the power model with a constant fitted best statistically but mispredicted mild states, so the power model without a constant was preferred.

The final Indonesian EQ-5D-Y-3L value set applies a rescaling coefficient of 0.1048 and a power of 1.9013 and ranges from 1.000 for full health (11111) to -0.086 for the worst state (33333), with pain/discomfort the most and self-care the least important dimension.

Hybrid modelling was not viable because DCE observations (16,080) far outnumbered cTTO observations (2220), so the hybrid estimates almost entirely reproduced the DCE model and did not reflect respondents' cTTO scale use.

Compared with the adult Indonesian EQ-5D-5L valuation, far fewer cTTO observations were negative in the youth valuation (2.5% versus 35.4%), and dimension importance differed, with pain/discomfort most important for children but least important for adults.

The analysed DCE sample matched the Indonesian general population on residence, sex, age, education, island of residence and religion within an absolute difference of about 5%, while the cTTO sample came entirely from Java and over-represented middle education levels.

outcome: Prevalence of disability (any reported difficulty on the Washington Group Short Set)
statement: The overall prevalence of any disability across the two sites was 9.7%, higher than the 2011 National Census estimate for South Africa and than the Western Cape provincial rate of 5.4%.

outcome: Prevalence of disability (any reported difficulty on the Washington Group Short Set)
statement: Disability prevalence differed significantly between the two under-resourced sites, being about twice as high in the urban informal settlement of Nyanga as in the semi-rural town of Oudtshoorn.

outcome: Distribution of disability severity levels (some difficulty, severe difficulty, unable to do)
statement: The pattern of severity differed by site: Nyanga had more people with some or severe difficulty, while Oudtshoorn had about three times the proportion reported as unable to perform a function.

outcome: Demographic and socio-economic patterns of disability (age, gender, employment, household income)
statement: People screening positive for disability were older, more often women, more often unemployed and lived in lower-income households than people without disability.

outcome: Demographic and socio-economic patterns of disability (age, gender, employment, household income)
statement: Among people with disability, the age distribution differed by site: Oudtshoorn had a higher proportion of elderly and Nyanga a higher proportion of working-age adults.

outcome: Demographic and socio-economic patterns of disability (age, gender, employment, household income)
statement: People with disability in Oudtshoorn were older on average and reported lower median household income than their counterparts in Nyanga.

outcome: Demographic and socio-economic patterns of disability (age, gender, employment, household income)
statement: The two sites differed socio-economically: Oudtshoorn had lower employment and lower reported household income, an older informant profile, larger households and a care dependency ratio almost twice that of Nyanga.

outcome: Ceiling effect
statement: Adding cognition items reduced the EQ-5D-5L ceiling effect. Larger compound items produced the lowest ceiling effects.

outcome: Response informativity
statement: Response informativity generally increased as a bolt-on covered more cognitive functions. Learning was the most informative single-aspect item, and the item that covered all four functions was the most informative compound item.

outcome: Convergent validity against MMSE scores
statement: Calculation had strong convergence with the MMSE attention and calculation subscale, memory had moderate convergence with the MMSE recall subscale, and concentration had weak convergence. Compound items had the strongest correlations with the MMSE total score.

outcome: Discrimination between participants with and without MMSE-defined MCI
statement: Calculation had the greatest discriminatory power among the single-aspect items. The memory, calculation, and learning compound item had the highest ANOVA F-statistic, and it shared the highest AUC with the four-function compound item.

outcome: Additional explanatory power for EQ VAS
statement: Each cognition bolt-on explained additional variance in EQ VAS after adjustment for the five EQ-5D dimensions. Items that covered learning gave the largest additional explanatory contribution.
Adding cognition to the rescaled EQ-5D-5L level sum score improved convergence with MMSE and discrimination of MMSE-defined MCI compared with the core EQ-5D-5L level sum score.
The EQ-5D-3L analyses showed similar overall trends for ceiling effects, convergent validity, discriminatory power, and explanatory power.

Bland-Altman plots showed nearly no observations outside the 95% limits of agreement, which the authors interpreted as acceptable overall agreement; EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L agreement was slightly weaker at the lower end of the scale.

All prespecified convergent-validity hypotheses against WHODAS-12 were supported. EQ-5D-5L dimensions and utility score had stronger correlations with corresponding WHODAS-12 domains and the sum score than EQ-5D-3L and SF-6Dv2.

At the dimension level, all EQ-5D-3L dimensions had notable ceiling proportions, EQ-5D-5L self-care had a moderate ceiling effect, and no SF-6Dv2 dimension had a ceiling effect. At the full-profile level, none of the three measures showed a significant ceiling or floor effect, and full health was less frequent with EQ-5D-5L and SF-6Dv2 than with EQ-5D-3L.
Related EQ-5D-3L, EQ-5D-5L, and SF-6Dv2 dimensions and utility scores were strongly correlated, and each utility score was significantly associated with EQ VAS.

Utility scores declined in participants with symptoms or disability. EQ-5D-5L had greater discriminatory power than EQ-5D-3L for every reported condition and than SF-6Dv2 for most conditions; SF-6Dv2 was slightly more efficient for unstable walking or falls and difficulty breathing.
The baseline survey had no missing data because all questions required a response, and the mean completion time was approximately 15 minutes.

All three utility scores had good one-week test-retest reliability. Dimension agreement was generally strongest for EQ-5D-3L; the authors reported that four of its five dimensions had very good agreement, while EQ-5D-5L and SF-6Dv2 dimensions had moderate to good agreement.

The largest dimension improvements were usual activities and mobility in pulmonary rehabilitation, mobility and usual activities in community exercise, and usual activities, pain/discomfort, and mobility in physiotherapy.
Group-based community exercise produced small-to-moderate mean improvements; the index change reached the minimally important difference threshold, but the EQ VAS change did not.
About half of community exercise patients improved on the index and EQ VAS, and more than half improved on the level sum score.

Patients with anxiety/depression problems at intake were more likely to improve than those without such problems in all three programs. Older age was associated with EQ VAS change in pulmonary rehabilitation, and urban region was associated with greater level sum score improvement in community exercise. Gender was not associated with change.

At intake, patients in all three programs had poorer EQ-5D-5L health than the Alberta general population. Health improved by end of rehabilitation; pulmonary rehabilitation and community exercise remained below population norms, whereas aggregate physiotherapy index and EQ VAS scores surpassed the norms.
Physiotherapy produced moderate-to-large mean improvements, and both the index and EQ VAS changes reached their minimally important difference thresholds.
Most physiotherapy patients improved, with the largest improvement proportions of the three programs.
Pulmonary rehabilitation produced small mean improvements. The mean index and EQ VAS changes did not reach their minimally important difference thresholds.
Fewer than half of pulmonary rehabilitation patients improved on each summary score, and the pulmonary program had the smallest improvement proportions among the three programs.

Forward-group increases in core-dimension importance were usually measurement based, while decreases were usually relative preference based. Backward-group increases were usually relative preference based, and decreases were rare.

Two authors independently applied the final reasoning framework with 87.7% agreement; discrepancies were resolved by team consensus, and no substantively new themes appeared after the sixth to seventh interview within subgroups.

Some backward-group participants continued to consider removed bolt-ons and inferred their severity from remaining dimensions. Usual activities was used most often; frequent links included usual activities with vision or cognition, mobility with social relationships, and anxiety/depression with cognition.

In the forward group, shifts were mainly measurement reasoning (56%) or relative preference reasoning (29%). In the backward group, relative preference reasoning (53%) was most common, followed by measurement reasoning (31%). Absolute preference reasoning was least common in both groups.

All forward-group participants said that adding bolt-ons made health states seem more severe, and all backward-group participants said that removing bolt-ons made health states seem less severe. Most participants also reconsidered core dimensions after key additions or removals.

Bolt-on addition produced 80 coded shifts in perceived core-dimension importance, compared with 36 shifts after bolt-on removal. Most shifts occurred at the first presented bolt-on transition rather than the next transition.

Cognition generated the most shifts in the forward group, while vision generated the most shifts in the backward group. Effects varied across the three bolt-on dyads and the direction of presentation.

The anxiety/depression domain showed cut-point shift for present-hedonistic and future time perspective. Higher scores had stronger negative associations with moderate-to-extreme problems versus no or slight problems than with slight-to-extreme problems versus no problems.

After adjustment for socio-demographic characteristics and chronic conditions, higher past-negative and present-fatalistic scores and lower present-hedonistic and future scores were associated with more problems in at least one EQ-5D-5L domain. Significant associations occurred for usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression; mobility was not associated with time perspective.
The final sample reported generally good health: mean EQ VAS was 78.03, mean EQ-5D-5L index was 0.919, and 38% reported full health (11111).

In the adjusted EQ-5D-5L index model, present-fatalistic scores were associated with lower index values and future scores with higher index values. Adding time perspective increased explained variance from 30.9% to 32.6%.

In the adjusted EQ VAS model, past-negative and present-fatalistic scores were associated with lower EQ VAS, while future and present-hedonistic scores were associated with higher EQ VAS. Adding all time-perspective subscales increased explained variance from 26.6% to 30.2%.

outcome: Composite TTO utility value of EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Pooling all 10 health states, heart disease patients gave lower mean utility values than the general population, while the cancer patient difference was not significant.

outcome: Composite TTO utility value of EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: After adjustment for sociodemographic characteristics, the only significant difference remaining was that heart disease patients valued mild health states higher than the general population.

outcome: Composite TTO utility value of EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Unadjusted values for severe health states were markedly lower among heart disease patients than the general population, but the difference disappeared after adjustment.

outcome: Difference in utility values between pairs of health states (approximating utility gain from transitions)
statement: Differences in utility between pairs of health states were larger for heart disease patients than for the general population, while cancer patients and the general population were similar.

outcome: Composite TTO utility value of EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Among adjustment covariates, age had the strongest association with utility values, with older age associated with lower values.
EQ-5D-Y-5L had lower ceiling effects than EQ-5D-Y-3L in the combined proxy and self-report samples, although ceiling effects remained and were especially evident for asthma and dental-problem groups.

Responses redistributed across the added EQ-5D-Y-5L severity levels with relatively low inconsistency; inconsistency was highest for feeling worried, sad or unhappy and lowest for mobility in both reporting samples.
Corresponding EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L domains had high Spearman correlations in both reporting samples, which supported criterion validity.
The Shannon index was higher for EQ-5D-Y-5L in every domain, which indicated greater absolute informativity and discriminatory power; Shannon evenness was comparable but marginally lower.

Test-retest agreement varied by domain and reporting sample; mobility had the highest agreement in both groups. Categorized EQ VAS agreement was substantial for proxy reports and moderate for self-reports.
The feeling worried, sad or unhappy domain showed the greatest redistribution and information gain, while mobility had the highest proportion of no-problem responses.

outcome: Self-reported change in alcohol consumption since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic
statement: Most respondents reported no change in alcohol consumption; decreases were more common than increases.

outcome: Weekly alcohol-consumption category before and during the pandemic
statement: The distribution of weekly alcoholic beverages differed between the recalled pre-pandemic period and the pandemic period.

outcome: Self-reported change in alcohol consumption since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic
statement: Excessive drinking before the pandemic and job loss due to COVID-19 were the strongest reported predictors of both decreased and increased alcohol consumption, with larger associations for increased consumption.

outcome: Self-reported change in alcohol consumption since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic
statement: Moderate-to-severe depression symptoms predicted both decreased and increased alcohol consumption, but moderate-to-severe anxiety symptoms did not remain independently associated in the multinomial model.
Additional predictors of decreased consumption were age 18-34 years, male gender, residence in Greece, Italy, Sweden, or the United Kingdom, and one or more chronic diseases.
Additional predictors of increased consumption were age 35-54 years, male gender, high education, and no change in general health.
The multinomial logistic regression model had limited explanatory power despite a statistically significant fit.

Seven of ten children, all aged 8 to 10 years, initially tended to tick every response box and needed the interviewer to read and explain the self-completion instructions; after explanation, they selected one level per dimension without response assistance.

Health, pain or discomfort, and looking after myself caused important conceptual problems: some children conflated health, healthy, and life; some interpreted pain or discomfort emotionally; and two treated lack of soap or water as a self-care limitation rather than inability to wash or dress.
Most children supplied appropriate examples for the severity levels and dimensions, and they proposed no further meaningful wording changes at the end of the interviews.

All seven healthy questionnaire completers reported the 11111 descriptive profile and high EQ VAS scores, whereas all three acutely ill completers reported suboptimal profiles; two sick children had EQ VAS scores that appeared inconsistent with their descriptive profiles.

The adaptation produced a final beta Chichewa EQ-5D-Y-5L with acceptable overall linguistic and conceptual equivalence to the UK English version, although comprehension remained mixed for looking after myself and pain or discomfort.
Successive wording changes resolved the level 2 versus 3 inversion and then the level 4 versus 5 inversion; the final round established the intended hierarchical severity ordering.

In round 1, 52 of 120 severity-card placements were incorrect; most incorrect placements reflected inversion between the translated levels for “a little bit” and “some,” with a smaller share reflecting inversion between “a lot” and “extreme.”
At 5-7 years after injury, 118 of 243 participants reported itching; mean EQ-5D-5L utility was 0.87 and mean EQ VAS was 81.6.
Adding the itching item reduced the full-health ceiling from 46.5% to 32.1% and increased the observed number of distinct profiles from 59 to 86.
The extended measure had higher absolute and relative informativity than EQ-5D-5L alone.
Convergent validity against EQ VAS was weaker for the extended level-sum score than for the standard EQ-5D-5L level-sum score.
Severe or extreme itching with no problems on another EQ-5D-5L dimension was more common than the reverse pattern, so all standard dimensions were dominant over itching.
Adding itching produced almost no gain in explained EQ VAS variance; itching levels were not statistically significant, and backward selection excluded itching from the final model.
Mean EQ VAS was lower for moderate-to-extreme itching than for no or slight itching, but the pattern was not monotonic across the three higher itching levels.

outcome: Coverage of the severity range by health states selected into the design
statement: The unstratified efficient design for DCE-duration selected a skewed, relatively mild set of health states, while the severity-stratified design spread selected states across the severity range.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state values on the QALY scale (DCE-death, DCE-duration) or latent utility scale (standard DCE)
statement: For the standard DCE and DCE-death formats, severity stratification had little effect on the selected states or on estimated values, with overlapping 95% credible intervals across designs.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state values on the QALY scale (DCE-death, DCE-duration) or latent utility scale (standard DCE)
statement: In DCE-duration, values from the severity-stratified design were higher than those from the unstratified design, particularly for states worse than dead, and fewer states were classified as worse than dead.

outcome: Mean signed errors of predicted choice probabilities (in-sample and out-of-sample)
statement: For DCE-duration, the unstratified design produced significant negative mean errors for bad health states, especially on the B-C tasks, while errors of the severity-stratified design were not significant, indicating that the unstratified design overestimated willingness to trade off life years to avoid bad states.

outcome: Quality-adjusted life expectancy by single year of age and sex, undiscounted and discounted at 1.5% and 3.5%
statement: Undiscounted quality-adjusted life expectancy at birth is about 68.2 QALYs for both sexes; Table 2 reports 68.24 QALYs for women and 68.21 QALYs for men, while the abstract assigns 68.24 to men and 68.21 to women.

outcome: Period life expectancy by single year of age and sex
statement: Life expectancy at birth is higher for women than for men, but quality-adjusted life expectancy at birth is almost equal, because women report lower health-related quality of life at most ages.

outcome: Quality-adjusted life expectancy by single year of age and sex, undiscounted and discounted at 1.5% and 3.5%
statement: Discounting reduces quality-adjusted life expectancy at birth substantially, and the sex difference reverses slightly in favour of men after discounting.

outcome: Mean EQ-5D-5L utility score by age band and sex, crosswalked to the UK EQ-5D-3L value set
statement: Mean EQ-5D-5L utility declines with age in both sexes and is lower for women than for men in nearly every age band.

outcome: Quality-adjusted life expectancy by single year of age and sex, undiscounted and discounted at 1.5% and 3.5%
statement: Quality-adjusted life expectancy estimates based on the 1993 MVH EQ-5D-3L population norms are considerably higher than those based on the EQ-5D-5L crosswalk data, especially for women.

outcome: Quality-adjusted life expectancy by single year of age and sex, undiscounted and discounted at 1.5% and 3.5%
statement: The two crosswalk methods, Hernández Alava et al and van Hout et al, generate very similar quality-adjusted life expectancy estimates.

outcome: Quality-adjusted life expectancy by single year of age and sex, undiscounted and discounted at 1.5% and 3.5%
statement: At age 60 years, women can expect 1.07 more undiscounted QALYs than men.
Item nonresponse for the EQ-5D-5L in the Health Survey for England was 10.9% of participants.
The study found no statistically significant baseline characteristics.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension levels and health profiles
statement: At baseline, pain or discomfort was the most common EQ-5D-5L problem in the exercise and active living cohort; mean index and EQ VAS scores were below the Alberta norms.

outcome: Canadian EQ-5D-5L index score and change
statement: Average index and EQ VAS changes were small and did not reach the stated minimally important differences; usual activities had the largest dimension improvement and pain or discomfort had the largest deterioration.

outcome: Paretian classification of health change
statement: Among participants with repeated measures, Paretian classification showed more improvement than deterioration, but mixed and unchanged profiles were also common.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension levels and health profiles
statement: In both programs, health status remained lower than age- and sex-matched Alberta general population norms after the slight post-program improvements.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension levels and health profiles
statement: At baseline, pain or discomfort was the most common EQ-5D-5L problem in the nutrition cohort; mean index and EQ VAS scores were below the Alberta norms.

outcome: Canadian EQ-5D-5L index score and change
statement: Average index and EQ VAS changes were small and did not reach the stated minimally important differences; anxiety or depression had the largest dimension improvement and pain or discomfort had the largest deterioration.

outcome: Paretian classification of health change
statement: Among nutrition participants with repeated measures, Paretian classification showed more improvement than deterioration, but mixed and unchanged profiles were also common.

P2 had lower ceiling effects than P1 for both EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L, but neither between-perspective difference was statistically significant. Proxy-reported full health was more frequent than child-reported full health, with significant differences for EQ-5D-Y-3L.
Dimension-level agreement was good or very good for EQ-5D-Y-3L and very good for EQ-5D-Y-5L for both perspectives; P2 appeared somewhat better overall, but performance varied by dimension.
Neither proxy version showed clear overall superiority across ceiling effect, known-groups validity, responsiveness, and patient-proxy agreement.

Both proxy perspectives generally reported better HRQoL than the children reported. All P1 score differences were statistically significant; for P2, only the Y-3L index difference was statistically significant.

All P1 and P2 index or level-sum scores changed in the direction of improved health among proxies reporting an EQ VAS improvement greater than 5 points. Responsiveness was mostly small; the P1 Y-3L index and P2 Y-5L level sum changes were statistically significant.
Agreement between child-reported and proxy-reported 3L index, 5L level sum, and EQ VAS scores was low for both proxy perspectives.

All P1 scores differed in the hypothesized direction across GINA or vIGA-AD known groups. All P2 comparisons except the EQ-5D-Y-3L index comparison between asthma-control groups had the hypothesized direction; only selected comparisons were statistically significant.
No statistically significant difference in relative attribute importance was found between adult-own and child perspectives for any EQ-5D-Y-3L dimension.

Both perspectives produced the same dimension ranking from most to least important: having pain or discomfort, doing usual activities, feeling worried, sad or unhappy, mobility, and looking after myself.
Most DCE choice pairs did not differ by perspective, and the pooled level-sum-score model found no overall perspective effect.
DCE responses showed high attentiveness and logical consistency; exclusion of respondents who failed the dominance test did not change the relative-importance results.
Child-perspective cTTO values covered positive and worse-than-dead states; the worst EQ-5D-Y-3L state had a negative mean value.
Worst-state-rescaled utilities for all 243 EQ-5D-Y-3L states showed no large difference between adult-own and child perspectives.
The pooled attribute model found differences for pain/discomfort level 2 and level 3, but not for most other attributes.

None of the three legacy valuation samples accurately represented its national population at the time of original data collection, and all three national populations became significantly older over the subsequent two decades.

Modeled EQ-5D-3L preferences differed by respondent age and sex: demographic-specific scale parameters differed from 1 for all five dimensions in the United Kingdom, all dimensions except mobility in the United States, and pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression in Japan.

Original and 2022 age-and-sex-reweighted value-set decrements were almost identical: most differences were 0.00 or smaller in magnitude, the maximum reported difference was 0.01, and every 95% credible interval for a difference included 0.

A sensitivity analysis that also accounted for changes in United States race and ethnicity composition did not change the conclusion that demographic change had no material effect on value-set validity.
OPUF produced plausible, well-ordered aggregate EQ-HWB-S value sets in all four samples; the aggregate utility assigned to state 555555555 ranged from 0.00 to -0.17.

Between 5% and 10% of recruited respondents in each main sample were excluded because they placed being dead or state 555555555 at the top anchor of 100, which prevents construction of a meaningful personal utility function.
Most analyzed respondents gave no illogical within-dimension level ratings, although suspect patterns such as zero weights, all-100 weights, and illogical ratings occurred.

Free-text feedback commonly described the survey as interesting or thought-provoking, but several respondents called questions difficult, confusing, complex, or complicated; one reported sensitive sliders.
Despite analysis samples of 99 to 311 respondents, confidence-interval precision was comparable to the published EQ-VT pilot study based on 520 respondents.
Own-state health and wellbeing were broadly similar across samples except that the rheumatic-disease sample reported consistently more severe problems and a lower median adapted EQ VAS score.

Physical pain, mobility, and day-to-day activities were the three most important dimensions in all four samples; physical pain was the highest-ranked dimension in each sample, tied with mobility in the diabetes sample.

The United Kingdom OPUF value set differed from the published United Kingdom EQ-VT pilot value set in relative dimension weights, intermediate-level positions, and overall scale; 17 of 36 coefficients differed significantly.
The four OPUF value sets were fairly consistent across samples, with only a few statistically significant coefficient differences.
The proportion that preferred the worst EQ-HWB-S state over being dead varied across samples and was highest in the rheumatic-disease sample.
The anchoring task produced very negative outliers; values below -1 occurred in every sample, so the analyses censored anchor values at -1.
Median survey completion time was about 11 minutes in both general-population samples and about 16 minutes in both patient samples.

Completion was about 98% in the United Kingdom Prolific sample but 24% to 33% in the three Bilendi samples; the study did not record where or why those participants discontinued or failed eligibility and quality checks.
Most respondents reported that the survey was easy to understand and answer, and about 87% to 89% judged its duration exactly right.

outcome: Latent-scale coefficient decrements for each level of the 13 EQ-5D-5L and ASCOT dimensions
statement: Respondents traded across health and social care dimensions: in the pooled conditional logit model (Model 1) the dimensions with the largest disutility at the worst level were four EQ-5D-5L dimensions (pain/discomfort, mobility, anxiety/depression, self-care) and the ASCOT control dimension, while ASCOT social participation, dignity and accommodation had the smallest coefficients.

outcome: Monotonicity of level coefficients and effect of instrument presentation order on scale and preferences
statement: Coefficients increased significantly between EQ-5D-5L levels 3 and 4 for all five EQ-5D-5L dimensions, and between ASCOT levels 3 and 4 for all eight ASCOT dimensions, but some non-significant disordering appeared for usual activities levels 4 and 5, pain/discomfort levels 2 and 3, and accommodation levels 1 and 2.

outcome: Monotonicity of level coefficients and effect of instrument presentation order on scale and preferences
statement: The order in which the instruments were presented affected the estimates: EQ-5D-5L dimensions had larger decrements when presented first, ASCOT control gained weight when ASCOT was presented first, non-monotonicity increased in the ASCOT-first model, and the scale test rejected preference homogeneity across the two orders.

outcome: Relative magnitude and rank of dimensions across the two instruments
statement: Ten of the 13 dimensions had the same rank in both order-specific conditional logit models, and dimensions ranked one to five, six to eight and nine to 12 stayed within the same rank bands.

outcome: Preference heterogeneity, expressed as latent class shares and random parameter standard deviations
statement: The two-class latent class model fitted best; class 1 (55% of the sample) showed strong ordered preferences across most EQ-5D-5L and ASCOT dimensions while class 2 (45%) showed a less clear pattern with disordering, and class 1 members were more likely to be aged over 60 and to have a long-term condition.

outcome: Preference heterogeneity, expressed as latent class shares and random parameter standard deviations
statement: The mixed logit model found significant preference heterogeneity at the more severe levels of all five EQ-5D-5L dimensions and of seven of the eight ASCOT dimensions, with food and drink showing heterogeneity only at level 2.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-5L and ASCOT utility scores and dimension level distributions in the sample
statement: The sample of 975 respondents was broadly representative of the Australian population for age, gender and income but was more highly educated and more likely to be born in Australia; self-reported ASCOT utility was higher than EQ-5D-5L utility.

outcome: Self-reported difficulty of the choice tasks and survey completion times
statement: The choice task format was acceptable in the pilot launch: only a minority of the 118 pilot respondents reported the task difficult, and median completion time in the full sample was 22 minutes 12 seconds.
An initial list of 35 items derived from a systematic review of EQ-5D valuation studies was refined by the expert panel to 26 candidate items, which were then surveyed.

outcome: Importance rating and consensus status of candidate reporting items
statement: Sixteen EuroQol Research Foundation members from eight countries responded to the email survey; 22 items were rated as required by more than 50% of participants, and consensus was high.

The item requiring description of the attributes and levels of the health states valued was dropped during deliberation because a neighbouring item on health-state selection provides sufficient detail for replication, giving a final checklist of 21 items in seven sections: descriptive system, health states valued, sampling, preference data collection, study sample, modeling, and scoring algorithm.

The optimal scaling model without interactions is an exact reparameterization of the standard dummy-coded main-effects model, and predicted health state values of the two specifications lie on or very close to the diagonal in all three applications.

outcome: Number of model parameters required relative to a full set of level-by-level 2-way interactions
