statement: The optimal scaling interaction specification reduced the number of model parameters substantially relative to a full set of level interactions.

outcome: Domain importance parameters, optimal scale positions of intermediate levels, and 2-way interaction parameters between health domains
statement: The heteroskedasticity polynomials showed that the standard deviation of cTTO predictions fell from about 0.55 for health states with predicted values below 0.4 to about 0.25 for values above 0.8, and the 4-parameters positioning level 2 ranged from 0.12 to 0.63, being largest for self-care and anxiety/depression.

outcome: Domain importance parameters, optimal scale positions of intermediate levels, and 2-way interaction parameters between health domains
statement: A major difference between the two DCE samples was the relative importance of mobility: mobility (level 3, confined to bed) was the most important attribute in the EQ-5D-3L sample, whereas mobility was among the least important attributes in the EQ-5D-5L sample.

A supplementary model with separate optimal scales for main and interaction effects showed that intermediate levels of mobility, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression affect the interaction effects more strongly than the main effects, improving the Watanabe-Akaike information criterion to 54 664.

outcome: Statistical model fit measured by the Watanabe-Akaike information criterion
statement: In the Australian cTTO application the optimal scaling model with a full set of 2-way interactions between domains had the best Watanabe-Akaike information criterion, better than the model with an N3 term and the main-effects model.

outcome: Domain importance parameters, optimal scale positions of intermediate levels, and 2-way interaction parameters between health domains
statement: Almost all cTTO interaction parameters were positive and half were significant; only the self-care by usual activities interaction was negative and significant.

outcome: Domain importance parameters, optimal scale positions of intermediate levels, and 2-way interaction parameters between health domains
statement: In the cTTO application, main-effects estimates indicated pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression as most important, followed by mobility, with self-care and usual activities least important.

outcome: Estimated EQ-5D health state values, including the value of the worst health state (pits) on the QALY scale
statement: Including interactions raised the cTTO-based value of the worst EQ-5D-3L health state (33333) from -0.39 in the main-effects model to -0.23 in the interaction model.

outcome: Statistical model fit measured by the Watanabe-Akaike information criterion
statement: In the Dutch latent-scale DCE application the mixed logit optimal scaling model with all 2-way interactions had the best Watanabe-Akaike information criterion, and all interaction parameters were positive and significant except the usual activities by anxiety/depression interaction.

outcome: Statistical model fit measured by the Watanabe-Akaike information criterion
statement: In the Dutch EQ-5D-5L DCE with duration application the model with all 2-way interactions had the best Watanabe-Akaike information criterion, and all interactions were positive and significant except pain/discomfort by anxiety/depression.

outcome: Estimated EQ-5D health state values, including the value of the worst health state (pits) on the QALY scale
statement: Including interactions raised the QALY-anchored value of the worst EQ-5D-5L health state (55555) from -1.34 in the main-effects specification to -0.10 in the interaction model, and lowered the estimated discount rate from 0.043 to 0.019.

outcome: Statistical model fit measured by the Watanabe-Akaike information criterion
statement: Adding N3 or N45 terms improved model fit relative to main effects but captured decreasing marginal effects less well than the full set of 2-way interactions between optimal scales.

Participants reported substantial within-day and day-to-day fluctuation across EQ-5D-5L items and preferred retrospective coverage from the prior assessment, three daily assessments for seven days, and item-specific assessment frequencies.

The final EQ-5D-AA used three individually timed daily alerts over nine full days; the first two days were a familiarisation phase and days 3-9 supplied the one-week analysis period. Mobility, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression were assessed three times daily; usual activities twice daily; self-care and EQ VAS once daily.

Four waves were sufficient for iterative refinement. The first three waves led to substantive changes, including increasing anxiety/depression assessment to three times daily and adding options to bring alerts forward; the fourth wave led only to a minor greeting-page change.
Most participants described the EQ-5D-AA as short, easy, comprehensible, and manageable, although alerts sometimes interrupted activities and occasional technical problems occurred.
Seven participants responded to every alert; ten missed between one and ten alerts. Missing responses averaged 7.4% per person, and all items were complete whenever an alert was answered.

Thirteen of 17 participants judged the EQ-5D-AA better than the two standard EQ-5D-5L assessments for representing their health, mainly because it was more informative or precise and captured fluctuations across more times and days.

Most participants varied over time on every EQ-5D-AA item, but stable and highly fluctuating response patterns both occurred. Mean no-problem responses exceeded 50% for each descriptive-system item, and individual EQ VAS variability ranged widely.
Agreement between the standard baseline EQ-5D-5L and averaged EQ-5D-AA scores was high: ICC 0.833 for index scores and 0.896 for EQ VAS.
At group level, the standard EQ-5D-5L produced slightly more severe descriptive-system ratings than the EQ-5D-AA and a slightly lower mean index score and EQ VAS.

outcome: Attribute-level main-effect estimates from kaizen preference paths
statement: Only 12 of 21 CSOR conditional-logit estimates were positive and significant; the fixed attribute order can have contributed to this result. Emergency major operations were the most important attribute.

outcome: Attribute-level main-effect estimates from kaizen preference paths
statement: The CVP design lacked multi-level improvements, so conditional-logit main effects could not be estimated directly; ZBT estimates were positive and significant, and vaccination effectiveness had the largest main effect.

outcome: Association and agreement between kaizen and paired-comparison results
statement: Conditional-logit and ZBT estimates were highly correlated within each source study.

outcome: Task completion time, button use, and positional response behavior
statement: Vertical response patterns were less frequent in Y-3L, which used one hold-out, than in CVP, which used no hold-outs; the authors inferred that one hold-out can reduce positional behavior by about half.

outcome: Association and agreement between kaizen and paired-comparison results
statement: Y-3L kaizen predictions had high correlation and strong agreement with paired-comparison probabilities, which supports predictive validity.

outcome: Standard errors and simulated small-sample precision
statement: With 631 respondents and ten kaizen tasks, median standard errors were smaller than or similar to those from paired comparisons.

outcome: Standard errors and simulated small-sample precision
statement: Bootstrap simulation suggested that 60 respondents who each complete 20 kaizen tasks can achieve median standard errors of 0.100 for conditional logit and 0.010 for ZBT.

outcome: Task completion time, button use, and positional response behavior

outcome: Task completion time, button use, and positional response behavior
statement: In all three surveys, warm-up kaizen tasks took longer and prompted more information-button and reset-button use than later tasks.

outcome: Attribute-level main-effect estimates from kaizen preference paths

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state values elicited by each TTO specification

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state values elicited by each TTO specification
statement: Classic TTO values with transformed negative values were closest to lag-time TTO in the 20-year time frame in terms of mean absolute difference.

outcome: Relative importance of EQ-5D dimensions by TTO specification and duration
statement: The relative importance of EQ-5D dimensions depended on health-state duration rather than on the choice between lead-time and lag-time TTO: anxiety/depression had the largest decrement with 10-year duration, pain/discomfort with 5-year duration.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state values elicited by each TTO specification
statement: The range of values produced by all online TTO variants was narrower than expected from mapped EQ-5D-5L estimates and from previous Dutch face-to-face EQ-5D-3L valuation studies; classic TTO produced no negative mean health-state values.

outcome: Task engagement and response characteristics: variance of values, non-trading, number of iterations, lack of differentiation

outcome: Task engagement and response characteristics: variance of values, non-trading, number of iterations, lack of differentiation
statement: Task engagement in the online setting was low: the median number of iterations was three in all specifications, about two-thirds of respondents used four or fewer iterations, and around one third valued health states at 1 (non-trading).

outcome: Self-reported feasibility and clarity of the TTO tasks
statement: Feasibility ratings were broadly similar across specifications, with lead-time TTO in the 20-year time frame rated systematically slightly more difficult; difficulty in locating the indifference point did not differ between tasks.

outcome: Task engagement and response characteristics: variance of values, non-trading, number of iterations, lack of differentiation
statement: An ordering effect was present: respondents used fewer iterations for health states presented later in the sequence.

outcome: Completion of initial and follow-up EQ-5D-3L collection
statement: A majority of enrolled patients completed at least one follow-up EQ-5D-3L questionnaire.

outcome: Willingness to complete EQ-5D-3L at subsequent clinic visits
statement: Among 160 feasibility-questionnaire respondents, most were willing to complete EQ-5D-3L at subsequent clinic visits.

outcome: Ease of understanding and completion, question acceptability, and questionnaire length
statement: Questionnaire respondents generally rated the EQ-5D-3L as easy to understand, easy to complete, acceptable, and acceptable in length.

outcome: Patient experiences and recommendations for routine EQ-5D collection
statement: Interview participants described the EQ-5D-3L as simple, short, and feasible in the chemotherapy unit, but some thought it oversimplified their cancer and treatment experience and was sensitive to moment-to-moment treatment effects.

outcome: Patient experiences and recommendations for routine EQ-5D collection
statement: Patients differed in their preferred administration mode and timing: some preferred paper and access to staff for clarification, while others preferred an electronic questionnaire completed on their own device or at a flexible time; suggested schedules ranged from every visit to selected points across treatment.

outcome: Completion of initial and follow-up EQ-5D-3L collection
statement: Operational barriers included cancelled appointments, missed patients, patients being busy or asleep, short treatment durations, language barriers, and high coordinator burden.
Of 3206 contacted individuals, 1085 completed interviews and 1080 were used for modeling after excluding 5 respondents who gave identical answers to all cTTO states.

outcome: cTTO-based quality weights for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: The model with 20 dimension-level dummies plus the N4 term (any dimension at level 4 or 5) was selected as the final model on goodness of fit, consistency and parsimony; all coefficients were statistically significant and logically consistent.

outcome: cTTO-based quality weights for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Applying the final model to all 3125 EQ-5D-5L states, values ranged from 0.883 for state 11211 to -0.066 for state 55555, with 4 states taking negative values.

outcome: cTTO-based quality weights for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Observed cTTO values decreased with misery score, from 0.88 at a misery score of 6 to -0.07 for the 55555 state, and mobility had the largest influence on utility estimates.

outcome: Feasibility of cTTO and DCE: administration time, logical inconsistency, self-reported difficulty
statement: Computer-assisted cTTO was feasible: mean administration time was 13.6 minutes for 10 cTTO tasks and 4.4 minutes for 7 DCE tasks, and 66.4 % of respondents showed no logical inconsistency.
DCE estimates were largely logically inconsistent, so the value set was modeled from cTTO data alone.

Sample characteristics matched census distributions except for education, with fewer respondents having elementary education or less (4.6 % vs 13.2 %); age, sex and education were not significant in modeling.

outcome: Under-reporting of problems in the composite domains relative to the individual subdomains
statement: For current health, fewer respondents reported problems in the pain/discomfort composite than in either individual subdomain, while for anxiety/depression the difference was not significant; for worst recalled health both composites showed significantly fewer problems than the subdomains.

outcome: Content categories of the meaning and experience of discomfort
statement: A substantial minority of respondents reporting pain described psychological pain.

outcome: Under-reporting of problems in the composite domains relative to the individual subdomains
statement: In the composite domains respondents under-reported discomfort more often than pain for current health, and under-reported anxiety more often than depression for both recall periods.

outcome: Response behaviour type in the composite domains (uniform, most severe, least severe, average, synergistic, inconsistent)
statement: Six response behaviours were identified in the composites, with uniform, most severe and least severe responses most common and inconsistent responses present in 13%-17% of respondents.

outcome: Ordering effect: composite response driven by first vs second subdomain
statement: Among respondents scoring different levels in the two subdomains, responses in the composite were mainly driven by the first mentioned subdomain (pain or anxiety).

outcome: Content categories of the meaning and experience of discomfort
statement: Content analysis of 10 428 examples produced 108 subcategories under three main categories: physical discomfort due to pain, nonpain physical discomfort and psychological discomfort; more than 100 different forms of discomfort were captured.

outcome: Association of respondent characteristics with the interpretation of discomfort
statement: Women, respondents aged 55 years or older, and those in worse self-perceived health or with chronic conditions more often considered discomfort as pain, whereas education, marital and employment status, region and place of residence had no significant effect.

outcome: Under-reporting of problems in the composite domains relative to the individual subdomains
statement: Respondents with nonpain physical discomfort or psychological discomfort more frequently under-reported their current health problems in the pain/discomfort composite than respondents with discomfort due to pain.

outcome: Spearman correlations among EQ-5D-5L domains, individual subdomains and EQ VAS
statement: Correlation between the individual pain and discomfort subdomains was only moderate; discomfort correlated more strongly with anxiety than with pain, and pain correlated more strongly than discomfort with the pain/discomfort composite.

outcome: Spearman correlations among EQ-5D-5L domains, individual subdomains and EQ VAS
statement: The individual discomfort subdomain showed the strongest correlation with EQ VAS among all domains and subdomains for current health.

No reported secondary outcome differed significantly between the individualized decision aid and routine care at the final assessment; effect directions were generally compatible with benefit from the decision aid.
Among participants who underwent surgery and reported having expectations, most in both arms said that their expectations were met, with no significant between-arm difference.

Most participants in both arms reported little decisional regret: more than 80% endorsed making the right or wise decision and rejected regret or harm; none of the item-level odds ratios differed significantly by arm.
Most surgical participants were satisfied with knee replacement results, with a nonsignificant higher odds of satisfaction in the intervention arm.
EQ-5D-5L index improved and WOMAC and PHQ-9 scores decreased in both arms, but changes in health-related quality of life and depressive symptoms did not differ significantly by trial arm.
Participants who underwent surgery had a significantly larger EQ-5D-5L improvement than participants who did not undergo surgery, regardless of trial arm.
Patient and surgeon most often agreed that the expected benefits of joint replacement outweighed its risks in both trial arms.

outcome: Presence, number and composition of clusters in the distribution of EQ-5D-5L values
statement: Partitioning all 3125 EQ-5D-5L profiles by the presence of severe levels showed large overlaps in value ranges, so the classification system alone does not create distinct clusters of values.
Differences between adjacent ranked profile values revealed only a few small gaps, mostly at the extremes of the distribution, with the largest gap between full health and the next best profile.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index values based on the English value set and on the mapped value set
statement: Patient groups differed in self-reported health, with community rehabilitation patients oldest and worst off, and mean index values were consistently higher under the English value set than the mapped value set.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension level responses, reported profiles and EQ VAS scores
statement: Patients used a wide spread of EQ-5D-5L profiles, and the most frequently reported profile differed by group.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension level responses, reported profiles and EQ VAS scores
statement: Dimension level responses varied markedly across services; community rehabilitation patients reported extreme problems with usual activities far more often, which the authors read as evidence of face validity.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index values based on the English value set and on the mapped value set
statement: All observed value distributions were significantly negatively skewed; the mapped value set produced a visible gap below full health and, for community rehabilitation patients, a possible two-group shape, whereas the English value set distributions did not.

outcome: Presence, number and composition of clusters in the distribution of EQ-5D-5L values
statement: Cluster analysis gave inconsistent and judgement-dependent results, but again indicated two clusters for the mapped value set, while clusters found for the English value set differed in number between patient groups and were very different from the mapped value set clusters.

outcome: Test-retest reliability (agreement coefficients, ICC, CCC, limits of agreement)
statement: The EQ-5D-5L descriptive system showed almost perfect test-retest agreement across the five dimensions.

outcome: Test-retest reliability (agreement coefficients, ICC, CCC, limits of agreement)
statement: Agreement between test and retest was poor for the EQ VAS and the EQ-5D-5L index score; data transformation changed the ICCs only slightly and concordance coefficients were similar.

outcome: Test-retest reliability (agreement coefficients, ICC, CCC, limits of agreement)
statement: WHOQOL-BREF showed almost perfect agreement for the two global items and moderate to good agreement for the four domains.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L self-reported health profiles and EQ VAS scores by socio-demographic subgroup
statement: Indonesian general population norms: mean EQ VAS 79.39 and mean EQ-5D-5L index 0.91, with most reported problems in pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression and fewest in self-care; 44.07% reported full health '11111' and only 33 of the 3125 possible health states occurred.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L self-reported health profiles and EQ VAS scores by socio-demographic subgroup
statement: EQ-5D-5L scores varied by socio-demographic group: female and older respondents had lower index scores, while rural, younger and higher-educated respondents had higher EQ VAS scores.

outcome: WHOQOL-BREF domain scores, overall quality of life and general health satisfaction
statement: WHOQOL-BREF norms showed domain means between 58.5 and 69.2, with higher scores for men, younger, higher-educated and higher-income respondents.
The achieved sample matched the national distribution closely, with all deviations from the Bureau of Statistics targets below 4%.

The consensus process produced 50 recommendations organised into 11 topics: Transparency and Reliability, Model Design, Conditions Under Which Generic Questionnaires Are Not Sensible or Valid, Utility Evidence Hierarchy, Utility Data Searching, Modeling Utility Values, Extrapolating QALYs for Models With Lifetime Horizons, Caregiver Utility, Utility Data Synthesis, Quality/Certainty of the Evidence, and Utility Estimates in End-of-Life Conditions.

The Brazilian consensus diverged from other international guidelines on two items: it kept the possibility of using outcomes other than the QALY, for example cost-minimisation, and it declined to recommend specific end-of-life criteria.

The panel recommends the EQ-5D-3L as the preferred instrument for collecting health state values, with the same instrument used for all utility inputs in a model; the SF-6D is an acceptable option because it also has Brazilian value sets, and mixing instruments within one model is considered inadequate.

A six-level hierarchy for utility parameters was agreed, ranking Brazilian social preferences from EQ-5D-3L data highest, then nonstandard generic instruments weighted with Brazilian and then non-Brazilian preferences, mapping from condition-specific instruments to the EQ-5D-3L, direct patient preference measurement by time trade-off or VAS, published utilities with fully documented elicitation, and expert elicitation lowest.

Preference weights should come from the general population rather than from patients, while patients experiencing the condition should describe the health states; Brazilian value sets are preferred for calculating the weights.

Caregiver utility should enter a model only when the quality of life of close relatives is clearly affected, only as a scenario analysis added to patient utility, and the impact on health state utility values of professional caregivers should not be included.

No recommendation was made for differential weights in end-of-life health conditions, because the panel judged that the EQ-5D-3L lacks dimensions essential for evaluating palliative care and that the supporting evidence is not robust.

Modeling recommendations include never setting baseline mean utility to full health, using age-specific Brazilian population norms when age-specific utility data are missing, using the multiplicative method for concurrent clinical events, including utility estimates in deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analyses, and discounting utility data at the official Brazilian rate.
Mapping is accepted only as an alternative when an extensive search finds no generic preference-based data, and model performance must be demonstrated whenever a mapping model is applied.

Meta-analysis of utility values should be conducted only when studies have similar populations, the same measurement instrument and the same preference weights, with random-effects models preferred; data quality should be appraised with tools such as RoB 2 for trials and ROBINS-I for cohorts.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index
statement: The EQ-5D-5L index improved significantly after ozone treatment; 18 of 26 participants improved, five were unchanged, and three worsened.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension severity
statement: All five EQ-5D-5L dimensions improved significantly in the full sample, with improvement among participants who had baseline impairment ranging from 60% for mobility to 79% for anxiety or depression.

outcome: EQ VAS self-rated health
statement: EQ VAS self-rated health improved significantly after ozone treatment, and 21 of 26 participants reported improvement.

outcome: Cancer-treatment toxicity grade
statement: Cancer-treatment toxicity decreased after ozone treatment; 14 of 26 participants had a lower CTCAE grade and 18 of 26 reported at least 50% improvement in treated symptoms.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension severity
statement: Participants with chemotherapy-induced side effects improved significantly in all EQ-5D-5L dimensions, whereas dimension changes were not significant in the smaller radiotherapy subgroup; EQ VAS and toxicity grade improved significantly in both subgroups.

outcome: Adverse effects of ozone treatment
statement: Reported ozone-treatment adverse effects were generally transient: meteorism or bowel bloating with rectal insufflation, pruritus with local application, and headache in one participant.
For 38.5% of respondents, a lead-time of 50 years or less was insufficient to elicit the true preference for at least one assigned health state.

The relative dimension ranking changed from mobility, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression, usual activities, self-care under GLS and Tobit-GLS to pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression, self-care, mobility, usual activities under IR-GLS with alternative lead-time.
The IR-GLS alternative-lead-time model gave lower predicted utilities for most states; 11 of the 86 tested states had predicted values below -1, while the GLS and Tobit-GLS minima were above -1.
The IR-GLS alternative-lead-time model distinguished point, interval, and left-censored observations and retained more uncensored observations than Tobit-GLS.
Most changes in pairwise utility differences had an absolute magnitude greater than 0.1 and no more than 1.

Relative to Tobit-GLS, IR-GLS with alternative lead-time enlarged most ordered state-pair utility differences, reduced a smaller share, and reversed the sign for 9%; the analysis restricted to 319 plausible states showed a similar pattern.
The alternative-lead-time interval-regression model produced a much wider predicted utility range than the conventional GLS and Tobit-GLS models.
Most respondents reported at least one worse-than-dead state, and 421 exhausted the standard 10-year lead-time at least once.

outcome: Weighted Romanian norms for EQ-5D dimension levels and health-state profiles
statement: Pain/discomfort had the highest reported problem frequency for both EQ-5D versions; the proportion reporting no problems was lower in rural than urban respondents across every dimension of both versions.

outcome: Weighted Romanian norms for EQ-5D dimension levels and health-state profiles
statement: The most frequent profiles were 11111 and 11121 for both versions, and full health was more frequent with EQ-5D-3L than with EQ-5D-5L.

outcome: Weighted Romanian EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-3L index norms
statement: Mean index health declined substantially with age for both EQ-5D versions, from the 18–24-year group to the group aged 75 years or older.

outcome: Weighted Romanian EQ VAS norms
statement: EQ VAS health declined from age 35 onward; the mean score was 90.3 in the youngest group and 60.4 in the oldest group for the first administration used to produce the norms.

outcome: Weighted Romanian norms for EQ-5D dimension levels and health-state profiles
statement: Women aged 65 years or older generally reported poorer health than men; the largest sex difference in EQ-5D indexes occurred in the group aged 75 years or older.

outcome: Difference between the two EQ VAS administrations
statement: Almost one third of respondents changed their EQ VAS score between administrations, and older respondents accounted for most differences of 5 or 10 points.

outcome: Weighted Romanian norms for EQ-5D dimension levels and health-state profiles
statement: Anxiety/depression was the only EQ-5D dimension with a comparatively high problem frequency among the youngest respondents rather than a pattern that mainly increased with age.
The median EQ-HWB-9 index increased significantly during six months, and its approximate absolute increase of 0.168 was the largest change among the EQ-based scores.
The median EQ-5D-5L index increased significantly from baseline to six months.
The median EQ VAS increased by 10 points, but the change was not statistically significant.
EQ-HWB-9 responses shifted toward lower severity across most domains, and EQ-5D-5L responses showed a greater proportion with no problems in all five dimensions at six months.
At six months, EQ-HWB-9 and EQ-5D-5L distinguished participants with high versus low perceived change; participants with higher perceived change had higher index scores.
Income-generation groups did not differ significantly on either index, and participants who did not report income had numerically higher scores.

Participants reporting two or more improved Dara areas did not have higher global health scores: EQ-HWB-9 did not differ significantly, while EQ-5D-5L significantly favored those with zero or one improved area.

Perceived Change Scale results showed positive changes in optimism, autonomy, problem solving, decision making, clear thinking, and social connection, while interest in other people had the highest proportion of never responses.

Participants were predominantly women and single mothers with low socioeconomic status and education; 44.2% had children living with chronic disease, and 95.1% reported no current income generation at baseline.

outcome: Feasibility measured as the number and percentage of missing responses per measure and per item
statement: Missing responses were far fewer on the EQ-5D-Y measures than on the longer PedsQL: 1% on the EQ-5D-Y-3L and 3.5% on the EQ-5D-Y-5L dimensions compared with 19% across the 23 PedsQL items among those who completed it, and 16 children completed no PedsQL item at all.

outcome: Concurrent and convergent validity: Spearman correlations of EQ-5D-Y dimensions with PedsQL items and sub-scales, and Pearson correlations of EQ-5D-Y level sum scores and VAS with PedsQL scores and Self-Rated Health
statement: EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions correlated highly with conceptually similar PedsQL items (Spearman > 0.5) and moderately with related items (around 0.3), with no systematic advantage for the five-level version.

outcome: Concurrent and convergent validity: Spearman correlations of EQ-5D-Y dimensions with PedsQL items and sub-scales, and Pearson correlations of EQ-5D-Y level sum scores and VAS with PedsQL scores and Self-Rated Health
statement: EQ-5D-Y level sum scores correlated moderately to strongly with the PedsQL total and Physical Health Summary scores, while correlations with psychosocial scores were weaker, especially in the acute and chronic groups.

outcome: Concurrent and convergent validity: Spearman correlations of EQ-5D-Y dimensions with PedsQL items and sub-scales, and Pearson correlations of EQ-5D-Y level sum scores and VAS with PedsQL scores and Self-Rated Health
statement: The EQ-5D-Y-5L VAS was not significantly correlated with PedsQL scores in the acute group, whereas both EQ-5D-Y level sum scores were.

outcome: Concurrent and convergent validity: Spearman correlations of EQ-5D-Y dimensions with PedsQL items and sub-scales, and Pearson correlations of EQ-5D-Y level sum scores and VAS with PedsQL scores and Self-Rated Health
statement: The Self-Rated Health question correlated more strongly with the EQ VAS than with PedsQL scores, and its correlation with the VAS was strongest in the general population group.

outcome: Known-group validity across acute, chronic and general population groups by ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests
statement: Known-group validity: EQ-5D-Y-5L level sum score and VAS and EQ-5D-Y-3L level sum score discriminated between all three health groups, while the PedsQL psychosocial summary and total scores did not distinguish acute from chronic illness.

outcome: Known-group validity across acute, chronic and general population groups by ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests
statement: The Self-Rated Health question did not distinguish the acute from the chronic group (p = 0.386) but did distinguish both from the general population.
Psychometric performance was similar for children aged 2 and 3 years, with no material age-related difference in HRQoL scores.
EQ-TIPS had a ceiling effect among children with special health care needs, but not among children reported to have fair or poor health; PedsQL showed no ceiling effect under the study threshold.
EQ-TIPS level sum score and PedsQL total score were strongly correlated, and all prespecified related item pairs had moderate-to-strong correlations.
EQ-TIPS required less completion time and was rated easy by more caregivers than PedsQL.

Both instruments distinguished general-health and special-health-care-needs groups, while EQ-TIPS had larger effect sizes than PedsQL for sleep problems, atopy, and neurological conditions compared with the healthy reference group.
Both instruments had good psychometric stability, with stronger four-week test-retest agreement for the EQ-TIPS level sum score than for the PedsQL total score.

Changes in both instruments were in the expected direction, but EQ-TIPS changes were not statistically significant; PedsQL detected improvement in the main health condition and reached its proxy-report minimal clinically important difference.
Neither EQ-TIPS nor PedsQL had an available preference-weighted scoring algorithm for use as HRQoL values in economic evaluation; EQ-TIPS analyses therefore used an unweighted level sum score.

outcome: Feasibility of the two EQ-5D-Y-3L versions: missing dimension responses and completion time
statement: The interviewer-administered version had no missing dimension responses, while 22 children left responses missing on the self-complete version; the proportion of missing responses was significantly higher in 8-year-olds than in 9- or 10-year-olds.

outcome: Feasibility of the two EQ-5D-Y-3L versions: missing dimension responses and completion time
statement: The interviewer-administered version took less time to complete than the self-complete version, and 8-year-olds took the longest with both versions.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L dimension responses, ceiling effect and EQ VAS score
statement: Dimension responses, utility scores, EQ VAS scores and the ceiling effect did not differ significantly between the two versions, although more problems were reported on the interviewer-administered version for Looking After Myself, Pain or Discomfort and Worried, Sad or Unhappy.

outcome: Inconsistency of paired dimension responses between the interviewer-administered and self-complete versions
statement: Between 22% and 31% of paired dimension responses were inconsistent between versions, with the highest inconsistency in Pain or Discomfort; inconsistency did not differ by sex, age or health condition.

outcome: Known-group validity of dimension, utility and VAS scores across health condition, age and sex
statement: Known-group validity by dimension rank order showed no differences for age, sex or health condition on either version, while utility scores differed significantly across health condition groups on both versions and EQ VAS scores differed only on the self-complete version.

outcome: Concurrent validity: correlation between EQ-5D-Y-3L utility score and EQ VAS score for each version
statement: Concurrent validity between the utility score and the EQ VAS score was significant for both versions and did not differ significantly between them.

outcome: Convergent validity between versions and with corresponding WeeFIM, FPS-R and MFQ items
statement: Gamma correlations between matching dimensions of the two versions were high and significant, and were lower in 8- and 9-year-olds than in 10-year-olds for several dimensions.

outcome: Convergent validity between versions and with corresponding WeeFIM, FPS-R and MFQ items
statement: Both versions showed low to moderate convergent validity with corresponding items of the WeeFIM, FPS-R and MFQ, with significantly higher correlations for the interviewer-administered Mobility and Looking After Myself dimensions against the WeeFIM motor and self-care totals; Usual Activities showed no association with WeeFIM social interaction.

outcome: Child preference for the interviewer-administered or self-complete version and stated reasons
statement: Most children preferred the interviewer-administered version, and literacy skills were the most frequent stated reason, decreasing with age.
Barriers to full electronic uptake included unreliable internet access, email spam filtering, and the staff time needed for reminders and patient explanation.
Eight epileptologists currently used the PROM and PREM workflow, and three others had used it previously.
Before electronic implementation, 2019 completion rates ranged from 65% for QOLIE-10 to 82% for GASE and GAD; the authors attributed the difference partly to respondent burden.
REDCap generates a one-page summary of demographic, clinical, and PRM data for each visit and can send immediate alerts, including for NDDI-E scores above 13 and high-risk suicidal ideation.

The COVID-19 response accelerated tablet and emailed REDCap survey use. The authors believed electronic forms increased completion because questions could not be skipped, but they had not formally evaluated this effect.
The program registry began in 2007, contains longitudinal PROM and PREM data for almost 6000 people, and collects seven PROMs plus one PREM at every clinic visit.
Most patients consented at their first clinic visit to research use of routine registry data.
All patients are invited to complete PRMs before every encounter. Participation is optional, no incentive is offered, and administrative assistants provide reminders by automated email and telephone.

The review identified 10 generic childhood preference-based HRQoL measures; nine were adapted mainly from adult measures, only CHU9D was developed specifically with dimensions generated directly from children, and none was originally developed in sub-Saharan Africa or another resource-constrained setting.
The six included sub-Saharan African studies met most criteria on the CASP case-control checklist and were judged to be of good quality.

Psychometric evidence was mixed: only six measures had at least one adequate item of evidence for both reliability and validity, while conceptual framework, content validity, and convergent validity were the properties assessed most often.
Only Health Utilities Index Mark 3 and EQ-5D-Y had been applied in child or adolescent populations in sub-Saharan Africa; the two application studies were conducted in Uganda and South Africa.
Six studies attempted cross-cultural validation in sub-Saharan Africa: five evaluated EQ-5D-Y in South Africa and one evaluated Health Utilities Index Mark 3 in Uganda.

The Ugandan Health Utilities Index Mark 3 study used forward translation into local languages during family interviews, without reported backward translation or prior cognitive interviews, and assessed only some psychometric properties.

South African EQ-5D-Y studies used the English UK version without translation into a native South African language, and conceptual-equivalence interviews were not conducted in South Africa during development. Across studies, psychometric properties were broadly evaluated except internal consistency.

In the Ugandan application study, Health Utilities Index Mark 3 scores differed little between children with spina bifida and adult proxies, and the child and proxy scores were strongly correlated; child and caregiver visual analog scale scores agreed poorly.

In the South African application study, EQ-5D-Y showed few missing responses, but children with and without disabilities had similar EQ VAS scores and agreement between children and parent proxies was low or absent.
No identified measure had complete, robust evidence of linguistic equivalence, conceptual equivalence, and psychometric validation across diverse sub-Saharan African cultural contexts.

outcome: Reasons for pediatric COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy
statement: Among respondents who were unsure or would refuse vaccination, the most frequent selected reasons were vaccine safety concerns and the belief that children did not need the vaccine.

outcome: Intention or hesitancy to vaccinate children younger than 5 years against COVID-19
statement: Older age and urban residence were associated with less hesitancy, while US birth was associated with more hesitancy. The paper also reported an education association, but it used inconsistent education labels across sections.

outcome: Intention or hesitancy to vaccinate children younger than 5 years against COVID-19
statement: In the adjusted model, greater perceived susceptibility and perceived vaccine benefits were associated with less hesitancy, while perceived barriers about long-term vaccine effects were associated with more hesitancy. The adjusted table did not show statistically significant associations for perceived severity or cues to action.

outcome: Intention or hesitancy to vaccinate children younger than 5 years against COVID-19
statement: Nearly half of respondents were hesitant to vaccinate their children younger than 5 years against COVID-19; the remainder intended to vaccinate.
Sensitivity analyses that defined hesitancy as refusal only or uncertainty only did not materially change the results.

outcome: Reasons for pediatric COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy
statement: The open-ended analysis identified concerns about the vaccine, lack of evidence, the belief that the vaccine was unnecessary, lack of spouse support, and the need for a provider recommendation.
Whether re-analysis can mitigate obsolescence depends on access to the original valuation data, which the authors report is variable.

Required evidence and responses differ by type: normative change may directly require a new aligned value set; method obsolescence can permit re-analysis or a method-comparison study; compositional change can permit reweighting; preference change can require monitoring and new valuation; and instrument change can require a small wording comparison followed by new valuation if needed.
The desktop inventory showed clear growth in valuation studies over time and a large number of older value sets that remain widely used and cited.

The body taxonomy has four numbered types: normative misalignment; outdated or unreliable methods; population change, subdivided into compositional change and preference change; and mismatch after the descriptive instrument changes.

Replacing a value set can change QALYs and ICERs, reduce comparability with historical evidence and thresholds, create opportunities for selective use of competing value sets, and raise questions about reappraising past decisions.

The proposed working definition treats value-set validity as both adequate representation of average preferences in the population of interest and acceptable empirical and theoretical properties for the decision-making context.
Framework analysis produced 20 themes: nine about understanding health states and consequences, four about differences in patient and public responses, and seven about possible solutions.

outcome: Public understanding and interpretation of hypothetical EQ-5D-5L states and their consequences
statement: Most participants found hypothetical states difficult to imagine without relevant experience. Mental-health-aligned problems were generally harder to understand vicariously than observable physical problems.

Participants differed in how they interpreted dimension labels, the 10-year duration, and consequences. Some changed or reimagined the stated health profiles, and prior direct or indirect experience shaped their responses.

outcome: Public views on the accuracy and acceptability of hypothetical general-public versus experienced patient responses
statement: Participants generally viewed experienced patient responses as more accurate than hypothetical public responses, but they also identified possible bias, vested interest, distorted reporting, and adaptation among patients.

outcome: Public views on the accuracy and acceptability of hypothetical general-public versus experienced patient responses
statement: Most participants were surprised that hypothetical general-public values are used for health resource allocation and were critical of relying on a potentially uninformed public. Many preferred patient input or at least some relevant experience.

outcome: Acceptability of proposed ways to resolve differences between hypothetical and experienced responses
statement: Participants generally supported giving the public more factual information about patient experience, but they distinguished informing from emotional influence and did not regard information as equal to direct experience.

outcome: Acceptability of proposed ways to resolve differences between hypothetical and experienced responses
statement: Other acceptable proposals included combining or weighting patient and public responses, including carers, relatives or health professionals, and screening or selectively sampling people with relevant experience.
Participants differed in willingness to revise their own responses after seeing patient results, even though they often described patient responses as more accurate.
No new themes were added in the later focus groups, which the authors interpreted as evidence of data saturation.

outcome: Attribute non-attendance measured by number of revisits per attribute
statement: No EQ-5D-5L attribute was overlooked: revisit frequencies were above zero for all five attributes, so no attribute non-attendance was detected, although Mobility (top) and Anxiety/Depression (bottom) were attended slightly less often than the other attributes.

outcome: Left/right asymmetry in fixation duration and number of fixations
statement: Respondents fixated slightly longer and more often on the left-side health-state description (state A) than on the right-side description (state B), although three respondents showed the opposite pattern.

outcome: Attention paid to each EQ-5D-5L attribute (fixation duration and count)
statement: Attention differed across attributes: Self-care and Usual Activities had the longest fixation durations and most fixations, Pain/Discomfort slightly less, while Mobility and Anxiety/Depression attracted least attention.

outcome: Respondent fatigue indicated by average time spent per task
statement: No increasing or decreasing trend in average time spent per task was observed across the seven discrete choice tasks, so respondent fatigue was not demonstrated; time per task instead tracked task difficulty, with less time spent on easy pairs contrasting a severe with a mild state.

Missing responses were generally low, but both instruments had completion problems in younger children; the EQ-5D-Y-5L had more dimensions at or above the prespecified problematic missingness threshold.

Psychometric tests based on utility values and level sum scores gave no major differences in conclusions; score directions were opposite because higher utility and lower sum scores indicate better health.
Ceiling effects showed a mixed pattern: reductions were more evident in adolescents and in some dimensions, while the complete-state ceiling increased among children.
Response inconsistencies between versions were most frequent for pain or discomfort and were more frequent for looking after myself in children than in adolescents.
The EQ-5D-Y-5L did not improve dimension informativity; the EQ-5D-Y-3L had higher Shannon H values in all dimensions, and response evenness differed only slightly.
Convergent-validity criteria against PedsQL 4.0 GCS were met at the scale level for both EQ-5D-Y versions, but dimension-to-subscale correlations were mixed.
Discriminant validity was supported for gender and age within age groups, but not for school grade among adolescents or across all participants.
Both versions showed known-group validity between healthy and sick participants, but the EQ-5D-Y-3L distinguished these groups better in children and the EQ-5D-Y-5L did so better in adolescents.
In the main empirical-validity analyses, EQ-5D-Y-5L utility scores were less efficient than EQ-5D-Y-3L utility scores at detecting differences in external health-status indicators.
One sensitivity analysis restricted to utility scores from 0 to 1 reversed the principal pattern for one self-rated-health contrast and strongly favored the EQ-5D-Y-5L.
The protocol uses the same respondent for both sequential DCEs, which removes differential sampling between the two DCEs and permits respondent-level agreement assessment.
The wave 2 design compares EQ-5D-5L with no cognition attribute, one composite memory/concentration attribute, and separate memory and concentration attributes to test system effects and overlap.
Fifteen kaizen tasks and five paired comparisons per DCE provide enough planned choice probabilities to make a two-DCE full-block survey feasible with 200 respondents per block.
Wave 1 coma referents define experience scales, while the wave 2 immediate-death referent defines a QALY scale; each DCE therefore has a distinct proportional scale.
Composites had lower ceiling percentages than their component items and generally captured at least as many reported problems, which gave little to no evidence of underreporting on composites.

Composite-component agreement was substantial to almost perfect; the first-listed components showed higher response agreement and stronger correspondence with their composites than the second-listed components.

At the item level, only pain had higher absolute and relative informativity than its composite. At the instrument level, versions that included both components had higher absolute informativity than the original EQ-5D-5L, although relative informativity did not improve consistently.

Composites correlated strongly with their corresponding components. First-listed components correlated more strongly with their composites, and correlations between self-care and its components increased with age.

Exploratory factor analysis identified stable physical functioning, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression factors. Each composite loaded with its corresponding components, and the factor structure remained stable across age groups.

Adding both components produced modest increases in adjusted R-squared for pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression. Models with component-level interaction terms improved explanatory power more and outperformed the standard EQ-5D-5L.

Pain-related problems increased with age, while anxiety- and depression-related problems were more common in younger adults. Pain-by-discomfort interactions added most explanatory power for ages 60-69, and anxiety-by-depression interactions added most for ages 18-29.
Separating washing self and dressing self from self-care gave minimal psychometric improvement in this general population sample.

Maximum simulated-likelihood estimation produced biased mixed logit mean coefficients and variances even when the estimator specification matched the data-generating process; correlations were relatively more accurate but could also be biased.

With correct model specification, willingness-to-pay estimates were relatively accurate despite bias in the underlying coefficients and variance components; average percentage differences in mean willingness to pay were below 1% across the three heterogeneity groups with 500 Halton draws.

Under-specification by fixing a true correlation at zero increased bias in willingness-to-pay means and variances. The effect was especially pronounced when alternative-specific constants were correlated.

Over-specification by allowing a correlation when the true correlation was zero could suggest a spurious correlation and increased willingness-to-pay bias, although it had little substantive effect on mean coefficients and most variance estimates.
The robustness analysis with 3,000 rather than 500 Halton draws did not identify substantive differences in the results.
Across the simulated settings, erroneous restriction or allowance of correlations led to differences of up to about 9% between true and estimated willingness to pay.

The adaptation made minor changes to familiar local phrasing and clarity, including changing mobility to walking, changing self-care wording to showering or wearing clothes, clarifying EQ VAS instructions, and adding understood examples of discomfort such as aches, breathlessness, itching, and feeling like vomiting.
Most children considered the descriptive system sufficient, but suggested missing or underrepresented concepts included social relationships, appetite, sleep, and additional mental-health content.
Spontaneously elicited poor-health concepts fit three overarching domains: physical health, mental well-being, and social relationships; most concepts were physical-health concepts.
All five EQ-5D-Y descriptive-system dimensions were represented in children’s spontaneous accounts of poor health; pain or discomfort and usual activities were discussed most often.
Cognitive-debriefing results supported final Singapore English EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L versions that were comprehensible to local children as young as 8 years.
All five children who tested Y-5L ordered the severity labels as intended for every dimension without difficulty.

Children generally considered each of the five descriptive-system dimensions relevant and important for child health. One child answered usual activities through a non-health lens, and one interpreted pain or discomfort as mental and physical pain while the other children interpreted it as physical.

outcome: Range of the value set and proportion of the 243 health states valued worse than dead
statement: The worst state rescaling value set had the largest range, with the value for the worst state 33333 fixed at the observed Tobit-adjusted mean cTTO value, while linear mapping produced the smallest range.

outcome: Range of the value set and proportion of the 243 health states valued worse than dead
statement: The proportion of the 243 EQ-5D-Y-3L health states valued as worse than dead differed markedly between the anchoring approaches.

outcome: Relative attribute importance scores and dimension rankings of the resulting value sets
statement: Worst state rescaling and linear mapping preserved the relative attribute importance scores and the level and dimension rankings of the DCE exactly, whereas the hybrid model altered them, most notably making mobility the least important dimension instead of looking after myself.

outcome: Alignment of predicted values with Tobit-adjusted mean cTTO values (mean absolute error and root mean squared error)
statement: Compared with the Tobit-adjusted mean cTTO values, the hybrid model value set aligned best and the worst state rescaling value set aligned worst; all three value sets underpredicted most mild health states.

outcome: Relative attribute importance scores and dimension rankings of the resulting value sets
statement: Pain/discomfort was the most important dimension and feeling worried, sad or unhappy the second most important dimension in all three value sets.

outcome: Distribution of EQ-5D studies across countries, publication years and ICD-10 clinical areas
statement: 143 EQ-5D studies published between 2000 and 2015 were identified from eight CEE countries, giving 152 country-specific results and a pooled sample of 81,619 participants, with Poland and Hungary contributing most.

outcome: Distribution of EQ-5D studies across countries, publication years and ICD-10 clinical areas
statement: Uptake lags behind other regions and behind local decision-making volume: the EuroQol database held 628 UK, 234 Spanish, 230 US, 228 Dutch, 155 German and 98 Canadian studies in August 2015, while only about 75 EQ-5D studies accompanied more than 2500 reimbursement decisions made in selected CEE countries up to the end of 2013.

outcome: Distribution of EQ-5D studies across countries, publication years and ICD-10 clinical areas
statement: The number of EQ-5D publications increased steadily over the 15-year period, with the first studies appearing in Slovenia (2000), Hungary (2001), Austria and Poland (2003), Slovakia (2004), the Czech Republic (2007), Romania (2013) and Bulgaria (2014); growth was most marked in Hungary and Poland after 2007.

outcome: Distribution of EQ-5D studies across countries, publication years and ICD-10 clinical areas
statement: Cardiovascular, neurological, musculoskeletal and endocrine/nutritional/metabolic diseases were the most studied clinical areas; only four oncology studies and only four studies of caregivers were found.

outcome: Completeness and correctness of EQ-5D reporting (index score, EQ VAS, dimension percentages, tariff specification, study period, funding disclosure)
statement: Reporting practice was heterogeneous: 112 (78 %) studies reported EQ VAS results, 104 (73 %) reported descriptive system results, 86 (60 %) calculated an EQ-5D index score, and 27 (31 % of those calculating an index) did not specify the tariff used.

outcome: Completeness and correctness of EQ-5D reporting (index score, EQ VAS, dimension percentages, tariff specification, study period, funding disclosure)
statement: Additional methodological deficiencies were found, including treating the ordinal EQ-5D level labels as cardinal summable values, modifying the EQ VAS range to 0-10, expressing the index score as a percentage, and failing to state the study period (25 %) or the funding source (27 %).

outcome: Availability of national value sets and population norms and alignment of practice with national HTA guidance
statement: Representative EQ-5D population norms exist for Hungary, Poland and Slovenia, and only Poland and Slovenia have national value sets; no study reported EQ-5D-Y results because national language validation was completed only in May 2015.

outcome: Completeness and correctness of EQ-5D reporting (index score, EQ VAS, dimension percentages, tariff specification, study period, funding disclosure)
statement: Most studies used on-site paper-based administration and a cross-sectional design; randomised controlled trials were rare compared with the global share of EQ-5D studies registered as RCTs.

outcome: Reported EQ-5D index scores and EQ VAS scores by country and condition
statement: Lowest mean EQ-5D index and EQ VAS scores by country ranged from -0.03 in Polish stroke patients with modified Rankin Scale 5 to 0.75 in Romanian coronary heart disease patients, with the lowest EQ VAS 22.5 in Polish low back or sciatic nerve pain patients.

outcome: Distribution of EQ-5D studies across countries, publication years and ICD-10 clinical areas
statement: Funding patterns partly explain the clinical focus: in Hungary 75 % of neurological EQ-5D studies were at least partly government funded, and in the Czech Republic 57 % of circulatory system studies received government funding, while EU and EuroQol Group funding mainly supported population norm data collection and methodological research.
Fatigue was common in the analytic sample.
Mean EQ-5D utility scores were similar for the 3L and 5L descriptive systems.
Fatigue had moderate correlations with pain/discomfort, usual activities, and anxiety/depression for both EQ-5D versions; the 5L correlations were generally stronger and also moderate for mobility.
EQ-5D domains explained a minority of the variance in RPQ fatigue; participant characteristics added only a small amount of explained variance.
Participants with one or more chronic health conditions reported substantially worse fatigue and EQ-5D outcomes than participants without a chronic health condition.
Across head-to-head comparisons, many respondents reported fatigue without a problem on the corresponding EQ-5D domain; the 5L generally produced more corresponding responses than the 3L.

outcome: Self-reported health on a 5-point scale
statement: Within countries, the survival/self-expression dimension was positively associated with self-reported health, while the traditional/rational-secular dimension was negatively associated with it.

outcome: Self-reported health on a 5-point scale
statement: In multilevel mixed models, fixed effects confirmed a negative association for traditional/rational-secular values and a positive association for survival/self-expression values with self-reported health; adding socio-demographic and macroeconomic controls did not change the direction of these associations.
Random effects for both cultural dimensions and for the intercept were significant, showing that mean self-reported health and the strength of the cultural associations differ between countries.

outcome: Self-reported health on a 5-point scale
statement: The between-country regression produced coefficients similar to the within-country and mixed model estimates, and the between-country effect of cultural values corresponded to a difference of about 0.75 points on the 5-point self-reported health scale.
Mean TTO utilities were similar under the adult and child perspectives for all four health states; none of the paired differences was statistically significant (all P > .25).

Respondents showed a substantial preference for treating children rather than adults: 56% gave more weight to children in all five PTO tasks, whereas 3.3% gave more weight to adults in all five tasks.

For every PTO question, the transformed equity weight for children was greater than the corresponding weight for adults (all P < .01). Unadjusted child priority ratios ranged from 0.61 to 0.70, and TTO-adjusted child equity weights ranged from 0.55 to 0.70 across tasks.

Adjustment for perspective-dependent TTO utilities did not change the priority estimate significantly for PTO2, but it did change the estimate for PTO1 and PTO3; adult-child utility differences therefore explained part of priority setting in two of the three quality-of-life tasks.
Equity weights differed by health-state transition and were higher for the lifesaving PTO task than for each quality-of-life-improvement task.

In mixed-effects regressions, older and more educated respondents gave more weight to treating children. Adult and child utilities for state 32323 were significant in opposite directions, but those directions were contrary to the theoretical model prediction.

outcome: Model performance: coefficient sign, significance, level ordering and the gap between values for 22222 and 55555
statement: Non-iterative TTO with or without lead time is feasible: over 90% of respondents in every variant passed the logical consistency task and all models produced a significant positive duration coefficient.

outcome: Data quality indicators: logical consistency pass rate, non-trading, task completion time and stability across task blocks
statement: NI(LT)TTO tasks took less time and were reported as less difficult than DCE with duration tasks, and within the NI(LT)TTO types the tabulated mode was quicker and clearer than the visual aid mode.

outcome: Predicted health state values for EQ-5D-5L states 22222, 33333, 44444 and 55555 by variant
statement: Predicted values for the milder states were implausibly low in several NI(LT)TTO variants, including a negative predicted value for state 22222 in the visual single-stage lead time variant.

outcome: Predicted health state values for EQ-5D-5L states 22222, 33333, 44444 and 55555 by variant
statement: The range between the predicted values of states 22222 and 55555 was narrower for the visual lead time variants than for DCE with duration and than in an earlier DCE-TTO study.

outcome: Data quality indicators: logical consistency pass rate, non-trading, task completion time and stability across task blocks
statement: Non-trading was common in the NI(LT)TTO variants, where many respondents always chose the shorter time in full health, whereas it was rare in the DCE with duration variants; excluding non-traders raised predicted values only slightly.

outcome: Data quality indicators: logical consistency pass rate, non-trading, task completion time and stability across task blocks
statement: Preferences were stable across the 12 NI(LT)TTO tasks, whereas the DCE with duration data deteriorated between early, middle and late task blocks, suggesting 12 DCE-TTO tasks may be too demanding.

outcome: Predicted health state values for EQ-5D-5L states 22222, 33333, 44444 and 55555 by variant
statement: Latent class analysis showed substantial preference heterogeneity, with some classes implying no state worse than dead and others implying all four selected states worse than dead, which lacks face validity.

outcome: Respondent assessment of task clarity, difficulty, confidence and willingness to answer more tasks
statement: Free text comments were mostly positive and reinforced the quantitative findings: comments in NI(LT)TTO variants focused on trading quality of life against survival rather than between dimensions, and difficulty comments were more frequent in DCE-TTO and in visual variants.

outcome: EQ-5D index scores by Type 2 diabetes complication, study population, age, number of co-morbidities, BMI and diabetes duration
statement: Of 95 identified articles, 59 met the selection criteria; 54 reported EQ-5D index, VAS or dimension results and 39 reported measurement property evidence. Most included studies were cross-sectional and most used the UK value set.

outcome: EQ-5D index scores by Type 2 diabetes complication, study population, age, number of co-morbidities, BMI and diabetes duration
statement: EQ-5D index scores across included studies ranged from 0.20 for severe diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain to 0.88 for a general population subgroup with good HbA1c; EQ VAS scores ranged from 45 to 80.

outcome: EQ-5D index scores by Type 2 diabetes complication, study population, age, number of co-morbidities, BMI and diabetes duration
statement: Pooled mean EQ-5D index scores using the UK value set were calculated for six Type 2 diabetes subgroups.

outcome: Validity, reliability and responsiveness of the EQ-5D in Type 2 diabetes
statement: Construct validity was examined in 16 studies and the EQ-5D index and VAS generally discriminated between demographic groups and disease-specific variables such as HbA1c, disease duration, BMI and number of complications; convergent and discriminant validity were confirmed in all 14 studies examining them, and predictive validity for vascular events and visual acuity was reported.

outcome: Validity, reliability and responsiveness of the EQ-5D in Type 2 diabetes
statement: Test-retest reliability was reported in two studies and interpreted as good to excellent; responsiveness was reported in seven studies and was acceptable in all but one study of long-term management of diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain.

outcome: Validity, reliability and responsiveness of the EQ-5D in Type 2 diabetes
statement: Several studies reported a ceiling effect for the three-level EQ-5D relative to more comprehensive instruments such as the SF-12 and SF-6D, and two studies indicated the EQ-5D could not capture further deterioration in people with multiple complications.

outcome: EQ-5D index scores by Type 2 diabetes complication, study population, age, number of co-morbidities, BMI and diabetes duration
statement: Choice of country value set produced substantial differences in index scores, with the US value set giving higher scores than the UK value set and the Japanese value set giving much higher scores for more severe states.

outcome: EQ VAS scores and EQ-5D dimension response distributions
statement: Across 24 studies reporting dimension responses, problems were most frequently reported for Mobility, Pain/Discomfort and Anxiety/Depression, while Self-Care was the least affected dimension; patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain reported problems with pain most often.

outcome: Consensus endorsement of emerging good practice recommendations for incorporating family and caregiver health spillovers
statement: The task force reached consensus on 11 recommendations for emerging good practice and on 12 prioritised future research recommendations, from 14 good practice and 11 future research items put to the first-round vote.

Patient and caregiver contributors favoured inclusion of health spillovers in economic evaluations and particularly endorsed a time horizon long enough to capture impacts occurring remote to the caregiving experience, and additive summation across the family network.

SHEER recommends that family and caregiver health spillovers be included in economic evaluations conducted from a healthcare/health payer perspective as well as from more inclusive societal or public sector perspectives.

The recommended aggregation procedure is stepwise: estimate spillovers among specified caregivers and family members or for the closest and second closest network members; report patient and caregiver/family QALY gains and losses separately; aggregate spillovers with patient effects by additive summation; and supplement the reference case with sensitivity analysis using wider or narrower networks.

Equal weighting should be applied to patient and family/caregiver health impacts unless empirical evidence shows that the decision maker or society values them differently in the context under investigation.

Collection of primary spillover data is currently preferred, with clear justification required when secondary data are used; the evidence review found trial-based evaluations more often used primary data while models relied on secondary data.

Outcome measurement should follow the jurisdiction's health technology assessment guidelines unless another method is empirically shown to be more appropriate, should ideally use the same measure for patients and spillover recipients when outcomes are to be aggregated, and should otherwise consider cost-consequence analysis.

outcome: Consensus endorsement of emerging good practice recommendations for incorporating family and caregiver health spillovers
statement: Consensus was not reached on two proposed recommendations: using empirical exchange rates to convert care-related quality of life measures such as the Carer Experience Scale or CarerQol into health-related quality of life outcomes such as EQ-5D, and presenting spillover and patient effects as a multiplier applied to the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio; no proposed recommendation was judged inappropriate.

outcome: Priority ranking of proposed future research avenues
statement: The highest priority future research avenues were exploring the distributional consequences of spillovers, adopting longitudinal study designs, and examining joint patient-caregiver utility elicitation methods; the lowest ranked were reporting bias and elicitation of social value weights.

Analysts should consider and discuss the risk of double counting given the measurement technique used, flagging it as a source of uncertainty or bias, and should characterise and present uncertainty around spillover estimates, preferably by applying probability distributions to model parameters such as caregiver utility within probabilistic sensitivity analysis.

No individual one of the 10 cTTO health-state means differed significantly between 2019 and 2024, with or without Bonferroni correction; the overall cTTO mean was slightly higher in 2024 and differed significantly.

The ordering of the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions was unchanged, but 2024 respondents placed more relative importance on mobility and self-care and less on pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression; usual activities did not differ.

Comparisons of anchored DCE estimates showed small differences for mild and moderate states and larger differences for severe states; 2024 values were higher for severe states and lower for moderate states.
DCE choice consistency depended on task design: it was lower for the 2024 standard 7-pair design, higher for the 12-pair Bailey design, and not different from 2019 when all 19 pairs were combined.
The online survey quality-control process retained 1003 of the 1063 complete responses after excluding speeders and potential bots.
Respondents considered all 97 candidate items relevant and most were well understood and accepted; no item was considered embarrassing or stressful and no missing content was identified.
EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L gave similar proportions of full health and of severe problems, and their misery indices correlated strongly.
The EQ-HWB summative score correlated only moderately with the EQ VAS, although a good correlation was expected because both assess quality of life.

Argentina contributed 24 of 168 international face validity interviews and 497 of 4830 psychometric surveys, and the Argentina team recommended or strongly recommended 23 of the 25 final EQ-HWB items.

Face validity interviews identified specific Argentine Spanish wording problems: "personal needs" was open to more than one interpretation and was replaced by explicit self-care examples, "to cope" was hard to translate (respondents preferred "hacer frente" over "arreglarmelas"), "unhappy" carries an insulting connotation in Argentinean culture, a literal translation of "unsafe" was read as lack of self-confidence, and getting around outside the home was read as street infrastructure problems, prompting "desplazar" instead of "trasladar".
Based on the international face validity findings across countries, 64 candidate items were taken forward to psychometric testing, including 14 modified items and 3 new items.

Among the 27 items that fed the final long measure, 14 showed a relevant floor effect and only 1 (hearing) showed a ceiling effect; floor effects were concentrated in the activity domain (all items) and in 2 of 3 cognition items.

All items detected differences between people with physical or mental conditions and healthy comparators with moderate to large effect sizes, but items discriminated less well for carers, performed worse when hours of care were considered, and 10 items could not detect differences for social care users.

Most items correlated as expected within their subdomain, but 18 of 27 items showed poor within-subdomain correlation (rho < 0.5) in Argentina, compared with 2 items in the United Kingdom and 3 in Germany, and almost half of the items correlated strongly with items in other subdomains.

Item response theory analysis indicated only 1 disordered item ("I was able to look after myself") and differential item functioning in 2 activity-domain items ("How well were you able to get around inside your home" and "How difficult is it for you to look after yourself").
The United Kingdom confirmatory factor analysis model fitted the Argentine data well when mobility was merged with self-care, energy was removed and self-worth was merged with coping.
Sample health scores were EQ-5D-3L index 0.573 (Argentine value set), EQ-5D-5L index 0.879 (Uruguayan value set), EQ VAS mean 68 and SWEMWBS mean 24.2.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L health state values on the QALY scale for the Netherlands
statement: The final Dutch EQ-5D-Y-3L value function is U = 1 - 0.036*MO2 - 0.191*MO3 - 0.028*SC2 - 0.139*SC3 - 0.058*UA2 - 0.211*UA3 - 0.111*PD2 - 0.363*PD3 - 0.096*AD2 - 0.314*AD3, derived from the mixed-logit DCE model rescaled by 0.0606.

outcome: Model fit (AIC) and data-quality exclusions
statement: Including the 341 excluded DCE respondents produced a much larger relative worsening in AIC than the relative gain in sample size, indicating noisier responses among excluded respondents.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L health state values on the QALY scale for the Netherlands
statement: Compared with other EQ-5D-Y-3L value sets, the dimension ordering was similar across the Netherlands, Slovenia, Germany, Spain and Japan, and the Dutch set was most similar to the German set; the Dutch ratio of the largest to smallest level 3 weight was 2.62.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L health state values on the QALY scale for the Netherlands
statement: Compared with the Dutch EQ-5D-5L value set, dimension importance was similar but the worst state value was higher (-0.218 for 33333 versus -0.446 for 55555) and fewer states were worse than dead (3.3% versus 15.5%).

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L health state values on the QALY scale for the Netherlands
statement: In the DCE-based value set, pain/discomfort received the largest level 3 weight, followed by feeling worried, sad or unhappy, usual activities, mobility and looking after myself.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L health state values on the QALY scale for the Netherlands
statement: Predicted values ranged from -0.218 (state 33333) to 1, and 8 of 243 health states (3.3%) had negative values.

outcome: Mean observed cTTO values per health state
statement: In the cTTO data, 16.3% of responses were negative, the mean value for state 33333 was -0.372, and only state 13133 had another negative mean (-0.038); other state means ranged from 0.968 (12111) to 0.054 (22333).

outcome: Model fit (AIC) and data-quality exclusions
statement: In cTTO models, feeling worried, sad or unhappy received the largest weight followed by pain/discomfort; the random intercept model produced logically inconsistent and insignificant level 2 estimates, while the two heteroskedastic models (AIC 1545 versus 2160) were logically consistent.

outcome: Model fit (AIC) and data-quality exclusions
statement: The mixed-logit model outperformed the conditional logit model (AIC 8202 versus 9579) and was selected for the value set.

outcome: Prediction accuracy of anchoring strategies (R-squared, MAE, RMSE)
statement: Linear mapping without a constant gave the highest R-squared (95.38%) and the smallest errors for mild health states, and was selected over linear mapping with a constant and over direct rescaling on the mean cTTO value of state 33333.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L health state values on the QALY scale for the Netherlands
statement: Values generated from cTTO data alone and from the rescaled DCE model differed substantially, with a maximum difference of more than 0.3.

Samples: 197 respondents completed cTTO tasks (57.4% female, mean age 41.9 years, few elderly) and 959 of 1300 DCE respondents passed quality control, the DCE sample being representative for Dutch age and sex but over-sampling lower-middle and upper-middle educated respondents.
Self-reported problems on the EQ-5D-3L dimensions increased and EQ-VAS scores decreased with increasing age, and were worse for women than for men.

Self-care could hardly discriminate between respondents below 80 years, with over 88% reporting no problems in each such age group; for pain & discomfort the distribution reversed after about age 70, when more people reported moderate problems than none.
