The percentage of respondents at full health declined over the lifespan at country-specific rates; some countries showed a continuous decline while others showed a plateau until age 70 or 75.
EQ-VAS responses clustered on multiples of 10; the modal range was 78 to 82, with a second peak at 58 to 62 in the oldest age group.
No systematic relationship between education and self-reported health was observed in the sample.
Pain & discomfort was the most frequently reported problem dimension across all age groups, and self-care the least frequent.
Mean EQ-VAS across the total sample was 71.2 and the mean European VAS index value was 0.79.
Mean EQ-VAS declined with age and was lower in women; ranges by age group differed between men and women.
European-VAS-derived EQ-5D index values showed a less pronounced age gradient than EQ-VAS, especially in men.
Countries differed markedly in the level of reported problems, with Denmark, Switzerland and the Netherlands reporting the highest average proportion of "no problems".
Men were more likely than women to report full health (11111) in every country, with the sex gap largest in Portugal and Italy and smallest in Germany.
Extreme problems (level 3) were rare, averaging 0.95% in Switzerland to 4.47% in Hungary across dimensions.
Between-country differences in reporting any problems were large on all five dimensions.

outcome: Self-reported ease or difficulty of instrument completion
statement: Acceptability was similar across instruments, but EQ-5D-Y-5L had the largest proportion rated easy or very easy and KIDSCREEN-27 had the smallest proportion.

outcome: Four-week test-retest reliability
statement: Across the assessed properties and subgroups, PedsQL and EQ-5D-Y-5L were the strongest-performing instruments.

outcome: Instrument completion time
statement: Median completion time ranged from EQ-5D-Y-5L as the shortest instrument to KIDSCREEN-27 as the longest, with little variation between reporter, age, or gender subgroups.

outcome: Four-week test-retest reliability
statement: PedsQL, EQ-5D-Y-5L, and EQ-5D-Y-3L had moderate test-retest reliability in the total sample, while CHU9D had poor reliability.

outcome: Floor and ceiling effects
statement: No instrument had a floor or ceiling effect in the total sample, but EQ-5D-Y-3L had ceiling effects in three subgroups; no floor effects occurred in any subgroup.

outcome: Convergent validity against PedsQL
statement: All four instruments compared with PedsQL had strong convergent validity in the total sample and the same pattern occurred in all subgroups.

outcome: Known-groups validity by school setting, special health care needs, and SDQ classification
statement: For school setting as a proxy for autism severity, only EQ-5D-Y-5L met the study criterion for known-groups validity with a moderate effect; PedsQL, EQ-5D-Y-3L, and CHU9D had small significant effects, and KIDSCREEN-27 did not distinguish the groups.

outcome: Known-groups validity by school setting, special health care needs, and SDQ classification
statement: For special health care needs, PedsQL and CHU9D met the known-groups criterion with moderate effects, while EQ-5D-Y-5L, EQ-5D-Y-3L, and KIDSCREEN-27 had significant but small effects.

outcome: Known-groups validity by school setting, special health care needs, and SDQ classification
statement: All five instruments distinguished children with normal versus abnormal or concerning SDQ behavioral-difficulty classifications with large effects.

outcome: Four-week test-retest reliability
statement: Sensitivity analyses based on utility scores for EQ-5D-Y-3L and CHU9D were largely consistent with analyses based on level sum scores.
Bot exclusions averaged 3.0% and peaked in China, speeding was uncommon, and duplicate records were rare.
Agreement on repeated marital-status and age questions was high across countries.
Across 15 countries, survey-link click rates were generally high, but completion varied substantially by country.

Missingness varied markedly by country and item; Japan and Spain had the lowest ranges, while Australia had very high missingness for height and weight, and EQ VAS, vignette EQ VAS, and household size were often among the most-missing variables.
Only small proportions of extreme high height and weight values were observed in the main data, although low height and weight values were more frequent in some countries.

Pilot results led to one moderate, gender-neutral response-heterogeneity vignette; non-mandatory questions without a prefer-not-to-answer option; earlier placement of sociodemographic questions; bounded numeric response options; shorter mental-health modules; explanatory icons for sensitive items; and removal of political affiliation.

Repeated education responses had high agreement, but repeated 1-item self-rated health responses were less consistent, which led the study to use date of birth and marital status for final consistency checks.
Of 4,538 people sent the pilot survey, 3,406 consented and 3,012 completed it; completed pilot data informed the final survey design.
Mean country completion times ranged from 18.3 to 31.4 minutes, while average proportional quota achievement ranged from 68.7% to 98.6% across countries.
Of 1,073 recruited participants (excluding pilot), 1,000 completed the valuation and were retained for modelling, giving 10,000 C-TTO and 7,000 DCE observations.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state utility values for the Taiwanese general population
statement: The distribution of observed C-TTO values showed a large share of worse-than-dead valuations and a spike at -1.
C-TTO value distributions did not differ significantly between the full sample, the sample without quality-control flags and the education-matched subsample, so all 1,000 respondents were retained.

outcome: Model performance: logical consistency, goodness of fit and distribution of predicted values
statement: The hybrid model with C-TTO left-censored at -1, without heteroscedasticity and without a constant, was selected as the preferred model; all 20 main-effect coefficients were logically consistent (monotonic).

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state utility values for the Taiwanese general population
statement: Predicted utilities from the preferred value set: full health 11111 = 1, health state 11112 = 0.9363, state 21111 = 0.8924, state 12345 = 0.0395 and the worst state 55555 = -1.0259.
Dimension importance in Taiwan was more evenly spread than in other Asian value sets: total disutility was similar for mobility, pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression.
Alternative model specifications produced different lower bounds for predicted utility than the preferred hybrid model.
The sample matched the Taiwanese adult population on sex, age group and living area but was substantially more educated.

Practice-level EQ-5D-5L had small positive bivariate correlations with current clinical quality, satisfaction with access, and satisfaction with general practitioner consultations; all three correlations had P < .001.
At the sample means, the preferred fixed-effects estimates implied small elasticities for current clinical quality and lagged patient-reported access and consultation satisfaction.

In the preferred practice fixed-effects model, current clinical quality and 1-year lagged satisfaction with access and consultations had positive statistically significant associations with the EQ-5D-5L index, but the estimated effects were small.
Across the five-year period, the mean practice-level EQ-5D-5L index was 0.844, slightly below the reported English population norm of 0.876.

The auxiliary regression test rejected the random-effects assumption that time-varying explanatory variables were uncorrelated with unobserved time-invariant practice factors, so the authors preferred the fixed-effects estimator.
Crosswalk and rescaled level-sum health measures were very highly correlated with the baseline EQ-5D-5L index, and sensitivity regressions gave similar conclusions.

Self-reported health and each practice quality measure varied more between practices than within practices over time; the between-practice standard deviation of the EQ-5D-5L index was approximately twice the within-practice standard deviation.
cTTO values clustered at zero with few values between 0 and -0.5, while tTTO produced fewer zeros and more values between -0.5 and 0; distributions of positive values were similar.
For states valued worse than dead, cTTO values were higher (less negative) than tTTO values; overall tTTO values lay more towards the negative side of the scale.
Mean differences between cTTO and tTTO values across the 18 severe states ranged from 0.020 to 0.213, exceeding 0.05 for 16 states and 0.1 for 8 states.
Agreement between the two techniques was better for positive tTTO values; disagreement concentrated where tTTO values fell between -1 and 0.

Participants who did not agree that the cTTO questions were easy to understand were more likely to shift from positive or zero cTTO values to zero or negative tTTO values; no demographic variable was significant.

outcome: Interviewer engagement: time spent on each wheelchair example
statement: Interviewer engagement, measured as time spent on the wheelchair examples and the number of iteration moves shown, was similar to or higher in videoconference interviews than in subsequent face-to-face interviews in both countries, with almost no statistically significant differences.

outcome: Interviewer engagement: time spent on each wheelchair example
statement: Interviewer learning effects were evident in both countries, since several engagement metrics differed significantly between the first 20 face-to-face interviews per interviewer and the subsequent face-to-face interviews.

outcome: Respondent engagement: proportion of values on specific responses (1, 0.5, 0, -0.5) and proportion of half-year unit responses
statement: Respondent engagement, measured as the proportion of values on specific responses and the proportion of half-year unit responses, was not significantly affected by the mode of administration in either country, although these proportions varied more in Spain than in Belgium.

outcome: Respondent engagement: time taken per main cTTO task
statement: The observed time per main cTTO task was higher in videoconference than in subsequent face-to-face interviews in Spain, while in Belgium task duration remained essentially unchanged.

outcome: Total interview duration as a combined interviewer and respondent engagement measure
statement: Total interview duration was longer for videoconference interviews in both countries, and the difference was statistically significant only in Spain.

outcome: Distribution of cTTO values, including the proportion of negative (worse-than-dead) values
statement: The proportion of negative (worse-than-dead) cTTO values increased in videoconference interviews in both Spain and Belgium, but neither increase was statistically significant.

outcome: Face validity: proportion of respondents with inconsistent cTTO values under strict and weak criteria, before and after the feedback module, and proportion of flagged health states
statement: The proportion of respondents giving inconsistent cTTO values was lower for videoconference interviews in Spain and higher for videoconference interviews in Belgium, and these observed differences were not statistically significant overall, except for the weak-criterion inconsistency after the feedback module in Spain.

Because the recruitment quotas were designed for national representativeness and not for the mode-of-administration subgroups, the comparison groups differed in composition: fewer university-educated respondents in the Spanish videoconference group and more women in the Belgian videoconference group.

outcome: Self-rated health today on the EQ VAS (0-100)
statement: Unadjusted mean EQ VAS scores did not differ between the 2017 and 2002 US general population samples.

outcome: Adjusted mean difference in EQ VAS score between 2017 and 2002
statement: No difference in mean EQ VAS was observed after adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics (Model 1) or additionally for history of illness (Model 2).

outcome: Adjusted mean difference in EQ VAS score between 2017 and 2002
statement: After further adjustment for any reported problems on the EQ-5D-3L dimensions (Model 3), mean EQ VAS was significantly higher in 2017 than in 2002.

outcome: Adjusted mean difference in EQ VAS score between 2017 and 2002
statement: In the interaction model (Model 4), the EQ VAS decrement associated with problems in usual activities and in pain/discomfort was smaller in 2017 than in 2002.

outcome: Reported problems on each EQ-5D-3L dimension
statement: Compared with 2002, the 2017 sample was older, more Hispanic and more educated, and reported problems more frequently on mobility, self-care and usual activities.

outcome: Adjusted mean difference in EQ VAS score between 2017 and 2002
statement: A sensitivity analysis using a generalized linear model with a beta distribution produced only marginal differences from the ordinary least squares base case.

outcome: Adjusted mean difference in EQ VAS score between 2017 and 2002
statement: Model 3 explained substantially more variance in EQ VAS than the earlier model specifications.
Participants reported a narrow concentration of EQ-5D-5L states: 106 of 3125 possible states occurred, and full health was the most frequent state.
Anxiety/depression was the most notable dimension pattern: 41.2% reported any problems, with higher frequencies among adults aged 18–24 years and women.
The overall mean EQ-5D-5L index value was 0.927 and the mean EQ VAS score was 81.83.
Both EQ-5D-5L index values and EQ VAS scores decreased with age.

In adjusted analyses, chronic conditions were associated with lower EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS values; female sex and social assistance recipiency were also associated with a lower index, while higher income was associated with better results.
Italian mean EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS results were higher than those reported in most European comparator populations.
The study completed remote videoconference interviews with 1182 adults and reported this administration mode as feasible.
All analyzed MIC profiles showed a consistent education gradient in the differently framed VAS, which supported the main Tromsø pattern across six countries.
Fractional logit and robust M-estimation analyses produced results similar to the primary linear regressions.
Higher education was associated with better social relationships in the Tromsø data.
Within EQ-5D-5L profile 11121, adjusted EQ VAS increased at each education level relative to primary education.

The education effects were generally small, but eight of ten profiles exceeded the cited lower EQ VAS minimally important difference of 0.96; profile 21231 had the largest explained variance and a large Cohen f effect size.

In nine of ten selected EQ-5D-5L profiles, mean EQ VAS was highest for the highest education level and lowest for the lowest education level; profile 11132 showed no significant difference and had a small sample.
The two most prevalent profiles had similar education gradients in men and women, but less prevalent profiles suggested stronger gradients in women.
Education had statistically significant but weak positive associations with vitality in the MIC data.

The physical EQ-HWB items for seeing, hearing, mobility, activities, personal care, and feeling unsafe had more responses at the lowest problem level than other items, while exhaustion, sleep problems, and anxiety were common.

The EQ-HWB sum score and the EQ-HWB-S sum and index scores distinguished all tested known groups across caregiver health, contribution, work, finance, support, child mental health, and child health-related quality of life, and generally produced larger effects than EQ-5D-5L and CarerQoL-7D.
All nine prespecified moderate correlations between EQ-HWB and EQ-5D-5L were supported; 26 of 31 prespecified moderate correlations between EQ-HWB and CarerQoL-7D were supported.
Whole-instrument two-day test-retest reliability was good for EQ-HWB and for EQ-HWB-S raw scores.
Item-level weighted kappa values showed fair to substantial two-day agreement, with the lowest agreement for the first three items.
Mean EQ-HWB completion time was shorter at follow-up than at baseline.
The survey contained no missing data because participants had to complete every item before they could continue.
Ten or eleven baseline respondents appear to have reversed the response options for seeing, hearing, and mobility; their responses were retained, and the anomaly did not occur at follow-up.
All three EQ-HWB scoring approaches showed large discrimination for financial problems and concern about meeting costs, despite the absence of a specific finance item in EQ-HWB.

outcome: Modelled utility coefficients per EQ-5D-5L dimension level in the hybrid model
statement: The censored heteroskedastic hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data produced consistent and statistically significant parameters for all 20 EQ-5D-5L dimension levels.

outcome: Modelled utility coefficients per EQ-5D-5L dimension level in the hybrid model
statement: Scatter plots of DCE against cTTO estimated values showed a strong, close to proportional relationship, supporting the assumption behind the hybrid model.

outcome: Range of the Portuguese EQ-5D-5L value set
statement: The derived Portuguese EQ-5D-5L values ranged from -0.603 for the worst state to 1 for full health.

outcome: Modelled utility coefficients per EQ-5D-5L dimension level in the hybrid model
statement: Pain/discomfort and mobility carried the largest decrements in the hybrid model, while usual activities and anxiety/depression carried the smallest.

outcome: cTTO values for 86 EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Observed mean cTTO values ranged from -0.45 for the pits state 55555 to 0.95 for state 11112.

outcome: Range of the Portuguese EQ-5D-5L value set
statement: The Portuguese value set correlated very strongly with the Spanish hybrid value set and slightly less with the Irish one, with Irish respondents valuing health states lower in general.

outcome: Interviewer protocol compliance and valuation data quality
statement: 1119 of 14,510 cTTO valuations were flagged by respondents in the feedback module and excluded, and one respondent was excluded for a positive slope of values against the misery index; no exclusion criteria were applied to DCE data.

outcome: Interviewer protocol compliance and valuation data quality
statement: Interviewers complied with the quality control protocol, with a maximum of 9% of interviews flagged as poor quality among the 28 retained interviewers, and no clustering of responses around specific values.

outcome: Robustness of model parameters to exclusion of feedback-module flagged responses
statement: In the sensitivity analysis without exclusions, the cTTO model showed no inconsistencies other than a negative mo2 coefficient, and more parameters lost statistical significance than in the main analysis.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-5L profile and EQ VAS of the general population sample
statement: The self-reported health of the sample gave a mean EQ VAS of 78.9, and 32.9% of respondents reported a disease diagnosed by a health professional.
Most respondents said that their answers might differ if the imagined child had a different age.
Most respondents were not internally consistent across VAS, TTO, and location-of-dead tasks because they classified 33333 as better than dead by one method but not by another.

outcome: Anchored value of health state 33333 relative to dead and full health
statement: Every reported DCE-with-duration model predicted a negative value for 33333 under the adult perspective and a positive value under the child perspective.

outcome: Logical consistency and duration sensitivity of DCE-with-duration models
statement: Child-perspective DCE-with-duration models were logically inconsistent because respondents focused strongly on longer life duration; they generally avoided shorter duration and pain or discomfort for the child, but focused on mobility and pain or discomfort for themselves.

outcome: Difficulty and acceptability of adult and child perspective tasks
statement: Most respondents found the child-perspective questions more difficult than questions about their own health, and more than half found it somewhat or very difficult to imagine a 10-year-old child's health.
One main-study respondent and one pilot respondent found the subject matter distressing and their interviews were terminated.

outcome: Feasibility of candidate anchoring methods
statement: The tested stated-preference methods were mostly feasible and produced plausible anchors, but location-of-dead could not quantify cases in which dead was considered worse than 33333.

outcome: Anchored value of health state 33333 relative to dead and full health
statement: The location-of-dead method placed dead among more severe states and produced higher rescaled values for 33333 under the child perspective than under the adult perspective.
When respondents could imagine states worse than dead despite choosing 33333 over death, their descriptions most often concerned vegetative states or severe brain damage.

Across all four methods, health state 33333 received a higher value under the 10-year-old child perspective than under the respondent's own adult perspective, although the size and form of the difference varied by method.
Most respondents favored equal treatment priority for adults and children; the remainder almost entirely favored priority for children.

Anxiety or depression was the most important dimension on average for the child perspective, usual activities was most important for the adult perspective, and mobility was least important under both perspectives.

outcome: Anchored value of health state 33333 relative to dead and full health
statement: Lag-time TTO placed the mean value of 33333 close to dead for the child perspective and clearly below dead for the adult perspective; most respondents gave the child-perspective state a higher value.

outcome: Anchored value of health state 33333 relative to dead and full health
statement: Rescaled VAS values for 33333 were higher under the child perspective, and respondents more often classified the state as better than dead for a child than for an adult.
There is no consensus on what health state valuation exercises are attempting to elicit, for adults as well as for children.
Many HTA agencies recommend that the public be involved in utility generation exercises, but some criteria for defining a member of the public exclude children.
Of the many candidate sample types, perspectives and valuation methodologies considered, only a few were judged relevant, acceptable and feasible for use in the child health context.
Views diverged on whether adult and child value sets with different properties can be compared and integrated.
Most adults judged that each measure could capture their quality of life, with the highest support for EQ-HWB and the lowest support for EQ-5D-5L.

Adults who judged measures inadequate described insufficient depth, limited condition and rarity relevance, adaptation of usual activities, and recall periods that were too short for fluctuating conditions.
Carers most often judged ASCOT-Carer to capture their own quality of life; support was lower for EQ-HWB and substantially lower for EQ-5D-5L.

Carers described insufficient depth and caring relevance, adaptation of usual activities around caring, and short recall periods; for EQ-5D-Y-5L, communication difficulties also made proxy completion uncertain.
Most parent proxy respondents judged that EQ-5D-Y-5L captured their child's quality of life.
Observed response-process error rates were low across all measures, with no clear pattern; the highest domain-specific rate was 8% for EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort.

Adults identified 17 domains that were not adequately captured. Seven recurred across all instruments: treatment availability, professional opportunities, information and uncertainty, medication or treatment burden, worry about passing on the condition, relationships, and experience with the healthcare system.

Carers identified 17 domains that were not adequately captured. Seven recurred across all three own-QoL instruments: carer burden, financial impact, condition severity, information and uncertainty, support, social engagement, and treatment availability.
For children, parents identified six domains not adequately addressed by EQ-5D-Y-5L: community access, frustration, future issues, social engagement, support, and treatment burden.
EQ-HWB was the most preferred measure in both participant groups; the relevant ASCOT measure ranked second.

outcome: Minimally important difference of the EQ-5D-5L index score
statement: Instrument-defined MID estimates of the EQ-5D-5L index score were 0.049 for all change, 0.043 for improvement and 0.053 for deterioration (0.037-0.038 when maximum-valued scoring parameters were excluded).

outcome: Minimally important difference of the EQ-5D-5L index score
statement: Pooled anchor-based MID estimates were 0.042 for all change, 0.035 for improvement and 0.049 for deterioration, with individual anchor estimates ranging from 0.021 to 0.060.

outcome: Minimally important difference of the EQ-5D-5L index score
statement: MID estimates varied with baseline index score: with all single-level transitions included, the instrument-defined MID was larger at lower or intermediate baseline index scores and declined to about 0.037 as baseline scores approached the upper limit, while excluding maximum-valued scoring parameters gave a near-constant MID of about 0.037.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index score and its 1-year change
statement: Correlations between change in anchor score and change in EQ-5D-5L index score were modest and varied by anchor, and a large proportion of health state changes were ambiguous under the Paretian classification.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index score and its 1-year change
statement: A ceiling effect was observed, with 14.3% to 17.3% of respondents reporting full health (11111), and anchor-based improvement MID estimates became negative at the upper limit of baseline index scores.

outcome: Minimally important difference of the EQ-5D-5L index score
statement: MID estimates were similar across subgroups defined by sex, age, diabetes duration and number of comorbidities.

outcome: Feasibility and acceptability of the EQ-5D-Y: missing and inappropriate responses
statement: The EQ-5D-Y was feasible: complete valid data were provided by 91-100% of respondents, with missing or inappropriate responses of 0-2% on the descriptive system and 0-9% on the VAS.

outcome: Distribution of reported problems on EQ-5D-Y dimensions by country
statement: Reported problems were most frequent on 'having pain or discomfort' and 'feeling worried, sad or unhappy' and least frequent on 'looking after myself'; large ceiling effects were seen in all dimensions, with the fewest problems in Sweden and the most in South Africa and Italy.

outcome: Test-retest reliability of EQ-5D-Y dimensions and VAS
statement: Test-retest agreement after 7-10 days was 69.8-93.8% in Italy and 86.2-99.7% in Spain, with kappa coefficients up to 0.67 and VAS intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.82 (Italy) and 0.83 (Spain); high ceiling effects limited kappa estimation, and no kappa could be computed for self-care in Italy.

outcome: Convergent validity of EQ-5D-Y with KIDSCREEN, PedsQL, general health item and life satisfaction ladder
statement: Convergent validity was supported for the psychological dimension and the VAS: 'feeling worried, sad or unhappy' correlated moderately to highly with KIDSCREEN-27 psychological well-being and with PedsQL emotional functioning, and the VAS correlated moderately to highly with the KIDSCREEN-10 index, self-rated general health and the life satisfaction ladder.

outcome: Convergent validity of EQ-5D-Y with KIDSCREEN, PedsQL, general health item and life satisfaction ladder
statement: Convergent validity was not supported for the mobility, 'looking after myself' and 'doing usual activities' dimensions, which correlated weakly (below the expected 0.3 threshold) or not at all with KIDSCREEN-27 physical well-being, PedsQL physical functioning, the general health item and the life satisfaction ladder.

outcome: Known-groups validity of EQ-5D-Y dimensions
statement: Known-groups validity was partly supported: respondents with a medicated chronic condition, with fair or poor self-rated health, or with borderline or abnormal SDQ scores reported significantly more problems on several EQ-5D-Y dimensions, but no dimension differed significantly across all five countries and 'looking after myself' discriminated least.

outcome: Proportion of respondents preferring Level 5 over Level 4 (preference inversion rate)
statement: Among U.S. English-speaking respondents, substantial preference inversion was observed only in the anxiety/depression dimension.

outcome: Proportion of respondents preferring Level 5 over Level 4 (preference inversion rate)
statement: Preference inversions were more common among Brazilian Portuguese-speaking respondents, and indifference between Levels 4 and 5 could not be rejected for pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression.

outcome: Proportion of respondents preferring Level 5 over Level 4 (preference inversion rate)
statement: Brazilian respondents preferred 'extremamente' over 'gravemente ansioso(a) ou deprimido(a)' in the anxiety/depression item.

outcome: Proportion of respondents preferring Level 5 over Level 4 (preference inversion rate)
statement: Separating anxiety from depression did not mitigate inversion, whereas replacing 'or' with 'and' shifted U.S. preferences away from indifference.

outcome: Patient interpretation of the Portuguese labels 'grave' and 'extremo'
statement: In cognitive interviews, most Brazilian patients said 'grave' (severe) is worse than 'extremo' (extreme), because 'extremo' suggests a transitory condition while 'grave' suggests a long-lasting disease.

Following presentation of this evidence at the 2015 EuroQol Plenary Meeting, an external translation review changed the Brazilian Portuguese Level 4 wording for pain/discomfort (graves to fortes) and anxiety/depression (gravemente to muito), and the EuroQol version management taskforce adopted these changes.

outcome: Self-reported health on the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system and EQ VAS
statement: Self-reported health was broadly similar between sites, with 21% of U.S. and 16% of Brazilian respondents reporting no problems on all five EQ-5D-5L domains and median EQ VAS of 75 and 80 respectively.

Each bolt-on reduced the EQ-5D-5L ceiling; sleep, tiredness, vision, and self-confidence produced the largest single-item reductions. Problems on at least one bolt-on were reported by most respondents with an EQ-5D-5L 11111 profile.
The number and diversity of observed health profiles increased as bolt-ons were added, while the concentration in the 20 most frequent profiles decreased.

Breathing, hearing, and vision correlated only weakly with all EQ-5D-5L core dimensions. Tiredness correlated moderately with pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression, while cognition, self-confidence, and social relationships correlated moderately with anxiety/depression.

Self-confidence, sleep, and tiredness showed moderate or strong correlations with corresponding PROMIS and SF-6D items or domains; cognition and social relationships generally showed weak or moderate correlations.

The final nine-factor CFA had acceptable fit. Seven bolt-ons loaded on factors separate from all EQ-5D-5L core items, while cognition and self-confidence loaded with anxiety/depression on psychological functioning.

Relevant bolt-ons improved discrimination between healthy respondents and respondents with chronic conditions. The sleep bolt-on improved performance in 9 of 13 condition groups; breathing, hearing, skin irritation, and vision improved known-group validity in the corresponding disease groups.

Hearing and vision were especially useful for detecting declining health with age. Vision or vision plus tiredness improved discrimination by health status, physical health, and quality of life, while cognition, self-confidence, social relationships, and tiredness were more useful for mental-health and well-being groups.

Tiredness had the greatest univariable explanatory power for EQ VAS and PROMIS Global Health, and social relationships had the greatest for SWLS. Adding bolt-ons to models with the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions produced only modest gains in adjusted R-squared.
The cognition bolt-on did not meet the authors' psychometric expectations.
Both health outcomes were best in Italy and worst in the United Kingdom.
The EQ-5D-5L transformed level sum score discriminated slightly better between socioeconomic groups than EQ VAS in stratified analyses and produced stronger multivariable models.

In the United Kingdom and the Netherlands, respondents with low education had the worst transformed level sum scores and respondents with middle or high education had better scores; Italy had the best score in the middle-education group. EQ VAS followed the same general pattern with slightly smaller differences.

More chronic health conditions and inability to work were consistent, strong independent predictors of worse transformed level sum score and EQ VAS results. Adjustment largely removed the education effect, except for a small remaining effect in the United Kingdom.
Within specific chronic-condition groups, education-related differences were inconsistent after adjustment; models for respondents without chronic conditions had very low explained variability.
Anxiety/depression problems were most frequent in the two youngest age groups and least frequent at age 65 years or older; mobility and pain/discomfort problems generally increased with age.
More than half of participants had at least one chronic disease and almost one third had two or more; mental illness or distress was the most common disease group.
Mean utility was lower among participants with chronic disease or long-term disability, and it generally decreased as the number of chronic diseases increased.
Pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression were the most frequently reported EQ-5D-5L problems; self-care problems were least frequent.
The full sample had a mean EQ VAS score of 71.6 and a mean participant-specific utility value of 0.83.
Anxiety/depression had the highest mean preference weight and usual activities had the lowest mean preference weight.

outcome: Lead-time TTO values for EQ-5D-5L health states, calculated as (T − lead time)/unhealthy time
statement: Values from the arm using a 10-year lead time were slightly lower than those from the arm using a 5-year lead time, both overall and for each of the ten health states, though only one state differed significantly.

outcome: Lead-time TTO values for EQ-5D-5L health states, calculated as (T − lead time)/unhealthy time
statement: At the aggregate level the difference in mean health-state values between the two lead-time arms was not statistically significant.

outcome: Valuation behaviour: number of iteration questions per task, time taken per task, exhaustion of tradable time, proportion of states rated better than dead
statement: Exhaustion of tradable time occurred only in the shorter lead-time arm, and at a very low rate; the arms did not differ in number of questions or time per task.

outcome: Lead-time TTO values for EQ-5D-5L health states, calculated as (T − lead time)/unhealthy time
statement: The raised-bar visual aid did not change the TTO values or their distribution compared with the standard aligned-bar display.

outcome: Valuation behaviour: number of iteration questions per task, time taken per task, exhaustion of tradable time, proportion of states rated better than dead
statement: With the visual aid highlighting the end of lead time, respondents used more iteration questions and spent more time on tasks that resulted in values close to zero.

Thirty-one eligible studies described in 41 publications were included; all but two assessed pre-injury HRQL retrospectively by asking patients to recall their health before the injury, and only two used prospectively collected pre-injury data from longitudinal cohorts.
The SF-36 was the most frequently used instrument, followed by the EQ-5D, the SF-12 and the PedsQL; pre-injury HRQL was most often assessed by questionnaire or face-to-face interview.

outcome: Difference between reported pre-injury HRQL and age- and gender-adjusted population norms as an indicator of bias in retrospective assessment
statement: Recalled pre-injury HRQL scores consistently exceeded the calculated age- and gender-adjusted general population norms on the EQ-5D, SF-36 and SF-12, with exceptions in injuries of higher severity such as hip fracture in patients aged 80 years and older, motor vehicle injury, vertebral fracture and traumatic brain injury.

outcome: Pre- and post-injury EQ-5D utility index scores
statement: Pre-injury EQ-5D scores were lowest in hip fracture populations and highest in populations with traumatic brain injury, major trauma, unintentional injury, or wrist or vertebral fracture, and decreased with increasing mean age of the sample.

outcome: Change from pre-injury to post-injury HRQL and extent of recovery
statement: All studies reported reduced post-injury HRQL compared with pre-injury levels; on the EQ-5D only one of twelve studies showed full recovery to pre-injury levels one year after injury, and on the SF-36 and SF-12 the physical component was reduced far more than the mental component at the first post-injury assessment.

outcome: Change from pre-injury to post-injury HRQL and extent of recovery
statement: The two studies with prospectively assessed pre-injury HRQL reported the lowest pre-injury mental component scores of all included studies and showed full recovery of mental health and almost full recovery of physical health at final follow-up, whereas all but one retrospective study reported that patients had not returned to their recalled pre-injury levels even years after injury.

outcome: Reported pre-injury health-related quality of life scores
statement: Reported pre-injury SF-36 and SF-12 component scores were similar across studies with low statistical heterogeneity, and pre-injury physical component scores were on average slightly higher than mental component scores.

The timing and reference period of pre-injury assessment were poorly standardised: the recall period was undefined in 15 studies and unreported in 2, while assessments took place from the day of injury up to several years afterwards, and measuring pre-injury HRQL was a primary aim in only four studies.
EQ-5D-5L retains the five EQ-5D dimensions, expands each to five levels, improves granularity and psychometric performance, and accounted for most requests for adult EuroQol instruments in 2023/24.

EQ-TIPS, EQ-HWB, and proposed bolt-ons have experimental status and are selectively available for research until evidence on psychometric performance, translatability, and language availability is sufficient.

The planned EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox will curate bolt-ons with compelling psychometric evidence for specific populations, but the evidence base and methods for valuing interacting bolt-on and core dimensions remain incomplete.
EQ-DAPHNIE has established infrastructure for population-health description and instrument comparison. Data collection started in five countries in 2024 and was continuing in ten more.

Early DCE-with-duration studies produced variable and often lower-than-expected utilities. Research identified time preference, task design, format, and model specification as important, and the Foundation is preparing an experimental DCE-based valuation protocol.
EQ-5D Deep Dive is testing modules that add detail within existing EQ-5D dimensions while retaining links to the core descriptive system and value sets; pilot work is at an early stage.

EQ-HWB broadens measurement beyond health for health and social care. It has a 25-item long version and a nine-item short version, with ongoing validation and a UK pilot value set for the short version.
EuroQol supports adult and child EQ-5D instruments with extensive translations and a large set of country-specific value sets; the paper identifies EQ-5D-5L as the flagship adult instrument.
EQ-TIPS version 3.0 is a de novo seven-dimension, parent- or caregiver-completed measure for ages 0–3 and is undergoing multinational validation in healthy and paediatric populations.
EQ-5D-Y-3L has country-specific value sets, whereas EQ-5D-Y-5L had no value set; research is developing mapping functions and a dedicated EQ-5D-Y-5L valuation protocol.
Adult dengue inpatients reported most problems in the pain/discomfort and usual activities dimensions of the EQ-5D-5L, while mobility was largely unaffected.
Mean EQ VAS in adult dengue inpatients was 67 and the mean EQ-5D-5L utility score was 0.572.
All child dengue inpatients reported pain on the EQ-5D-Y, and half reported many problems with anxiety.
Mean EQ VAS in child dengue inpatients was 54.375.
The sample of 18 dengue inpatients was mostly male, mostly educated to high school level or below, and 61.11% reported a history of dengue in themselves or their family.

Neither instrument distinguished healthy caregivers from matched healthy non-caregivers at the instrument level. At item level, EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression and EQ-HWB discomfort severity and pain severity detected caregiving effects.

EQ-5D-5L had an instrument-level ceiling effect, while the preliminary EQ-HWB did not meet the instrument-level ceiling-effect criterion. Several items in both instruments had item-level ceiling effects.

Items with similar physical content had strong correlations across the instruments: EQ-HWB mobility, day-to-day activities, self-care, and pain severity aligned with the corresponding EQ-5D-5L dimensions.

Both instruments distinguished healthy respondents from patient groups at the instrument level with large effect sizes. EQ-HWB items across several health and well-being domains were especially sensitive to depression and generalized anxiety disorder.

EQ-HWB activity items aligned most with EQ-5D-5L mobility, self-care, and usual activities; EQ-HWB physical-sensation items aligned most with pain/discomfort; and its self-identity, cognition, autonomy, feelings and emotions, and relationship domains aligned most with anxiety/depression.

Exploratory factor analysis supported five preliminary EQ-HWB factors: cognition, physical activity, feelings and emotions, positively framed items, and physical sensation. EQ-5D-5L showed three factors.

outcome: Model performance and compatibility of cTTO and DCE data (logical ordering, statistical significance, parsimony, agreement)
statement: The heteroscedastic Tobit model of cTTO data, censored at -1 and with a respondent-level random effect, was selected as the preferred model; it produced logically ordered, statistically significant coefficients for all dimension levels.

outcome: Modelled utility decrements for each EQ-5D-5L dimension level and predicted values for all 3125 health states
statement: Predicted values from the preferred model ranged from -0.573 for the worst state 55555 to 1 for 11111, and 624 of 3125 states (20.0%) were worse than dead.

outcome: Modelled utility decrements for each EQ-5D-5L dimension level and predicted values for all 3125 health states
statement: The largest utility decrement was for pain/discomfort level 5 and the smallest for usual activities level 2; the dimension importance ranking in the preferred Tobit model was pain/discomfort, mobility, anxiety/depression, self-care, usual activities.

outcome: Model performance and compatibility of cTTO and DCE data (logical ordering, statistical significance, parsimony, agreement)
statement: The mixed logit DCE model had 2 disordered parameters while the Tobit and hybrid models had none; the hybrid model was in agreement with its component models.

outcome: Observed composite time trade-off values for EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Observed mean cTTO values ranged from -0.366 for 55555 to 0.965 for 11121, and 24.0% of included cTTO responses were worse than dead, with values clustered at 1, 0 and -1 in 20.5%, 5.1% and 14.7% of responses.

outcome: Data quality indicators: logical inconsistency rates, respondent-flagged responses, task comprehension and interviewer effects
statement: Logical inconsistency was present in 30.5% of respondents before the feedback module and in 16.2% after; overall 5.6% of eligible cTTO responses were inconsistent, falling to 2.2% after the feedback module.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-5L health profile and EQ VAS score of respondents
statement: The full and analytic samples closely matched the 2015 US Census and national health statistics for age, sex, race, ethnicity, chronic conditions and general health status.

outcome: Proportion of EQ-5D-5L health states valued worse than dead
statement: The EQ-5D-5L value set gave a wider range of scale and a more symmetric unimodal distribution than the US EQ-5D-3L value set and the crosswalk, which had 4.1% and 1.2% of states worse than dead respectively.

outcome: Data quality indicators: logical inconsistency rates, respondent-flagged responses, task comprehension and interviewer effects
statement: Sensitivity analyses that re-included flagged cTTO responses and all respondents produced only marginal differences in model estimates, and no significant interviewer effect was observed.

Formative research combining reviews of four paediatric core outcome sets, epidemiological cohort data, parent group discussions, surgeon consultation and think-aloud interviews produced a descriptive framework of seven attributes: four operation-count attributes (planned major, planned minor, emergency major, emergency minor), infections treated in hospital, child quality of life (good, fair, poor) and survival after diagnosis (six levels from 1 month to more than 20 years).

Survival, quality of life and adverse events were the three outcome categories common to all four relevant core outcome sets, and the Parent Advisory Group concluded that condition-specific outcomes could be represented by the overarching quality of life attribute.

A preliminary D-efficient design generated in Ngene, with attribute-level overlap in three attributes and four classes of implausible scenario excluded, produced 45 choice tasks in five blocks of nine, plus one palliative anchor task added to every block; the kaizen task design was constructed directly from those pairs using the worst attributes as the starting profile and the best attributes as the four possible improvements.

The 20 included articles represented 8145 residents; 17 were validation articles and 3 were nonvalidation articles. Most studies were European, and nursing staff were the proxy respondents in 75% of articles.

outcome: Missing data rates for EQ-5D dimensions, EQ-5D index, and EQ VAS
statement: Feasibility was better for the EQ-5D descriptive system and index than for EQ VAS: pooled missingness was 5% for each EQ-5D dimension and the index, compared with 26% for EQ VAS.

outcome: Construct validity of proxy-reported EQ-5D index and EQ VAS
statement: Construct-validity evidence for the EQ-5D index was inconsistent with moderate certainty, whereas the EQ VAS had sufficient construct validity with high-certainty evidence.

outcome: Responsiveness of the proxy-reported EQ-5D index
statement: Only one third of responsiveness tests for the EQ-5D index were positive, and the certainty of responsiveness evidence was low.

outcome: Proxy-resident agreement for EQ-5D dimensions, index, and EQ VAS
statement: At baseline, proxy-resident agreement was generally poor to moderate for the EQ-5D dimensions, index, and EQ VAS; staff-only proxies and the proxy-proxy perspective generally showed the poorest agreement.

outcome: Proxy-resident agreement for EQ-5D dimensions, index, and EQ VAS
statement: After repeated administration, agreement became sufficient only for mobility and increased for usual activities, but agreement for the index, EQ VAS, self-care, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression remained insufficient.

outcome: Difference between proxy-reported and resident self-reported EQ-5D scores
statement: Proxy reports produced lower EQ-5D index scores than resident self-reports. EQ VAS scores were also lower when staff or relatives served as proxies.

outcome: Test-retest reliability evidence for proxy-reported EQ-5D
statement: No included study assessed EQ-5D test-retest reliability with appropriate reproducibility statistics.
Construct-validity tests based on validation articles were less likely to be positive than tests based on nonvalidation articles after adjustment for clustering.
Pain, communication, the 111111 profile, and level sum score differed across some age groups, but age and health-care group were strongly associated.
All hypothesized concurrent-validity relationships were significant and weak to moderate; the strongest highlighted relationship was between EQ-TIPS pain and FLACC pain.
Pain, the 111111 ceiling profile, and level sum score distinguished health-care groups; EQ VAS did not distinguish general health across health-care groups.
The EQ-TIPS descriptive system had little missing data and no floor effects in inpatient or outpatient children, but EQ VAS responses were more often missing.
Movement, play, pain, and eating had significant fair-to-moderate one-week agreement; EQ VAS was reliable, but relationships, communication, and level sum score were not reliable in this sample.
The 10 cognitive-interview participants reported no comprehension problems, so the investigators made no changes to the isiXhosa consensus version.
EQ-TIPS dimension levels explained little variance in EQ VAS general-health ratings, and no dimension coefficient was statistically significant.
EQ-5D index and EQ VAS scores did not significantly differ by care setting, while selected WHOQOL-OLD scores differed between home and institutional care and between formal and informal care.
All three instruments had high score completion, and missing responses for every EQ-5D dimension were below 4%; however, EQ VAS response errors and the need for assistance were common.

EQ-5D indices, EQ VAS, and most WHOQOL-OLD scores differentiated care levels and general-health groups, with worse care needs and health associated with lower scores; most gender and education differences were not significant.

EQ-5D and WHOQOL-OLD showed poor-to-moderate relationships and captured partly overlapping but distinct constructs; WHOQOL-OLD facets on intimacy, death and dying, and sensory abilities were weakly related to most EQ-5D components.
EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L showed good to excellent index test-retest reliability, while EQ VAS reliability was moderate; WHOQOL-OLD total-score reliability was good but facet reliability varied.
Neither EQ-5D version was clearly superior, although EQ-5D-5L had a higher index ICC and generally stronger correlations with WHOQOL-OLD facets.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L values on a QALY scale for US adults
statement: The estimated US EQ-5D-5L values on a QALY scale ranged from -0.287 for state 55555 to 0.992 for state 11121.
All 20 effect-coded coefficients were positive; pain/discomfort was the most valuable domain and the shift from moderate to severe pain/discomfort was the largest single parameter.
The lifespan power parameters were all below 1 and increased with the temporal unit, rejecting the constant proportionality assumption.
Level counts contributed significantly, so the published value set is based on the 28-parameter model.

outcome: Discrimination (sensitivity, specificity) and convergent validity of EQ-5D-5L versus EQ-5D-3L values
statement: EQ-5D-5L values discriminated between fair and poor self-reported health slightly better than EQ-5D-3L values and correlated slightly better with the VAS.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L values on a QALY scale for US adults
statement: On the 72 descriptions common to both instruments the US EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-3L values were highly correlated, but the EQ-5D-3L values had a shorter range and a large gap near full health.

After adjusting for ceiling effects and descriptive system bias, US EQ-5D-5L values agreed most closely with those of England, exceeding the agreement among three countries that used the same interview-based TTO protocol.

outcome: Model logical consistency, goodness of fit and predictive accuracy used for model selection
statement: The preferred specification was a hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data, multiplicative with eight coefficients, an intercept for the cTTO data, respondent-level intercept random effects and a correction for heteroskedasticity; data were not treated as censored.

outcome: Composite time trade-off values for 86 EQ-5D-5L health states and the unconscious state
statement: Inter-interviewer variation was observed in the fraction of cTTO responses clustered at -1 and in the fraction of negatively valued states.

outcome: Model logical consistency, goodness of fit and predictive accuracy used for model selection
statement: The additive 20-coefficient cTTO-only model had the best fit but was rejected because of logical inconsistencies in the usual activities, self-care and pain/discomfort dimensions; the multiplicative eight- and nine-coefficient models performed best on predictive accuracy, and MULT8 was preferred because the additional MULT9 coefficient was statistically insignificant.

outcome: Modelled utility values for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states (Belgian value set)
statement: Estimated coefficients of the preferred model: intercept 0.038 and level-5 dimension decrements of 0.482 for pain/discomfort, 0.439 for anxiety/depression, 0.227 for mobility, 0.181 for usual activities and 0.166 for self-care, with severity-level rescaling factors of 0, 0.139, 0.258, 0.788 and 1 for levels 1 to 5.

outcome: Modelled utility values for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states (Belgian value set)
statement: The resulting Belgian EQ-5D-5L value set ranges from -0.532 for state 55555 to 1 for full health, with a maximum non-full-health value of 0.939 for state 12111, and 15.0% of the 3125 health states valued worse than dead.

outcome: Composite time trade-off values for 86 EQ-5D-5L health states and the unconscious state
statement: A utility value of -0.454 was obtained directly from survey responses for the unconscious state, which was added as an 11th cTTO state in two blocks; only five EQ-5D-5L states in the new value set are valued lower.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-5L health profile and EQ VAS score of the respondents
statement: The final sample of 892 respondents was representative of the Belgian adult population in age, sex, region of residence, educational attainment, labour market status, self-assessed health and HRQoL, although the targeted 1000 valid interviews was not reached.

outcome: Composite time trade-off values for 86 EQ-5D-5L health states and the unconscious state
statement: The cTTO data covered the full value range with clustering at key values and showed increasing variability as health states worsened, supporting face validity and indicating heteroskedasticity; DCE choices favoured the state with the lower level sum score, more strongly as the difference widened.

outcome: Model logical consistency, goodness of fit and predictive accuracy used for model selection
statement: Results were robust to sample choices: re-estimation without exclusions for implausible response patterns, restricted to pre-COVID interviews, or excluding observations flagged in the feedback module gave small average absolute coefficient differences and an identical preference ranking of dimensions.

outcome: Modelled utility values for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states (Belgian value set)
statement: Compared with the existing Belgian EQ-5D-3L value set, the new EQ-5D-5L value set covers a wider value range, values more states worse than dead, values mild states higher, and reorders the dimensions, with pain/discomfort rather than anxiety/depression carrying the largest utility loss.

The EuroQol instrument was developed between 1987 and 1991 by an interdisciplinary five-country group; an initial six-dimension version was published in 1990 and was refined to five dimensions with three levels, formally designated EQ-5D in 1995 and defining 243 health states.

The EQ-5D-3L descriptive system has remained essentially unchanged since 1990, while a five-level version (EQ-5D-5L, approved 2009, with 'confined to bed' replaced by 'unable to walk about') and a youth version (EQ-5D-Y, approved 2009) were added.
By 2015/2016 the instrument family was widely available and heavily used, as recorded by the EuroQol Executive Office.

outcome: Uptake, availability and use of EQ-5D instruments and value sets
statement: Registered EQ-5D studies in the top 25 clinical areas were distributed across study types.

Valuation methodology progressed from ad hoc adaptations of the UK MVH time trade-off design to standardised protocols: the Paris protocol for EQ-5D-3L in 2009 and an international EQ-5D-5L valuation protocol implemented in the EQ-VT computer-assisted personal interview software, with valuation studies starting in England, the Netherlands, Spain and Canada in 2012.

The EuroQol Group formalised as an Association and Foundation under Dutch law in 1995 with a not-for-profit business model: commercial users pay licence fees, academic users use the instruments free of charge, and revenue funds the Group's research; membership grew to about 80 international members.

A 2014 scientific strategy process produced six working groups: descriptive systems, valuation, large-scale applications, EQ-5D in younger populations, interface development, and education and outreach, including a fundamental programme of research on the core descriptive system and on bolt-on and bolt-off dimensions.

EQ-5D is increasingly embedded in routine administrative outcome measurement, such as the NHS England PROMs programme begun in 2009 for hip and knee replacement, varicose vein and hernia surgery, and similar programmes in Sweden, Alberta and New Zealand private insurance.

outcome: Model predictive accuracy: mean absolute error, intraclass correlation, and logical consistency (monotonicity)
statement: In cross-validation, the multiplicative models produced the lowest mean absolute error, outperforming the additive 20-parameter models.

All three sets of interaction terms (N5, extended D1, and the square-root city block-metric) were rejected because they produced logically inconsistent models or substantially impaired predictive accuracy.
Bootstrap standard errors were smaller for the multiplicative models than for the additive models, and the estimated intercept was similar across models.
Using the selected rescaled 8-parameter multiplicative model, values were generated for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states.
The new EQ-5D-5L values show face validity against the Chinese EQ-5D-3L value set in dimension rank order, but the mildest and worst state values differ markedly between the two value sets.
The six TANDI dimensions had good internal consistency; pain and eating had lower item-rest correlations and would increase reliability if removed.
Rotated factor analysis supported two dimensions of HRQoL: activity and participation explained most variance, while pain and eating formed a body-functions factor.
Concurrent validity was strongest for movement, play, communication, and eating against related comparator domains; pain had a moderate association with FLACC or NIPS.

Known-groups results distinguished general-population children from the acute- and chronic-illness groups across most dimensions and on general-health VAS; acute and chronic groups differed significantly only for pain.
TANDI dimension performance and general-health VAS did not show statistically significant differences across the three age groups.

Dimension severity was logically associated with lower general-health VAS; the regression model explained 45% of variance after nine outliers were excluded, and severe eating problems had the largest decrement.
The small general-population retest sample showed high dimension agreement and reliable one-week VAS scores, although there was little response variance.
There were no missing TANDI dimension or VAS responses; all comparator measures were complete except seven FLACC pain-scale forms.

outcome: Unanchored and anchored DCE-TTO coefficients and utility ranges by presentation approach
statement: Approaches A, B and C produced mainly monotonic coefficients with larger disutility as severity increased, with the exception of usual activities levels 2 and 3, which were disordered in all models (significant only for Approach C).

outcome: Unanchored and anchored DCE-TTO coefficients and utility ranges by presentation approach
statement: Approach D (level indicator) had further non-significant inconsistencies between levels 1 and 2 of pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression, but produced larger ordered differences at levels 4 and 5, and was the only approach that significantly separated severe and extreme anxiety/depression.

outcome: Unanchored and anchored DCE-TTO coefficients and utility ranges by presentation approach
statement: The range of anchored utility values differed by approach, being substantially wider for the level indicator approach.

outcome: Unanchored and anchored DCE-TTO coefficients and utility ranges by presentation approach
statement: The dimension with the largest overall decrement differed: pain/discomfort for the three highlighting approaches and mobility for the level indicator approach; usual activities had the smallest decrement in all four approaches.

outcome: Logical ordering (monotonicity) of dimension level coefficients and scale parameter poolability across approaches
statement: Swait and Louviere testing rejected the null hypothesis that values do not differ across approaches, so data from the four approaches cannot be pooled.

outcome: Respondent reported task difficulty, helpfulness of presentation, ease comparison and 0-10 ratings of each approach
statement: Respondent feedback favoured the level indicator approach and disfavoured the grey highlight approach; about 75% reported considering the whole health state description and around 30% found the tasks difficult.

outcome: Respondent reported task difficulty, helpfulness of presentation, ease comparison and 0-10 ratings of each approach
statement: Survey completion and dropout were similar across versions, with 70.3% of those invited completing and dropout among those reaching the DCE tasks of 13% to 16%.
Missing responses were uncommon: 24 of 323 participants had at least one missing response.
No EQ-HWB item met the study definition of a floor effect, while six items met the definition of a ceiling effect: hearing, mobility, day-to-day activities, self-care, safety, and coping.
EQ VAS correlated similarly with the level sum scores of EQ-HWB, EQ-HWB-S, and EQ-5D-5L.
Conceptually similar EQ-HWB and EQ-5D-5L items showed moderate to strong convergence, with variation across concepts.
Parallel analysis supported five factors when EQ-HWB was analyzed with EQ-5D-5L; three factors were shared health-related constructs, and two additional factors were captured by the long EQ-HWB.
Parallel analysis supported three factors when derived EQ-HWB-S was analyzed with EQ-5D-5L.

Patients had worse outcomes than carers and the general public. EQ-5D-5L showed the largest effects in comparisons that included patients, but it did not distinguish carers from the general public. EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S performed better when carers were part of the comparison.
Participants with EQ VAS below 80 and participants aged 60 years or older had significantly worse outcomes on all three measures than their comparison groups.

outcome: Raw composite TTO values (range 1 to -1) for EQ-5D-5L hypothetical health states
statement: In the multivariable censored regression adjusted for health state severity, respondents aged 31-45 years and over 60 years gave lower cTTO values than respondents aged 18-30 years.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-5L health state and EQ VAS score of respondents
statement: Sample characteristics: mean age 36.9 years, 47.7% female, 69.7% reported previous illness experience, mean EQ VAS 77.0, and 95% reported that the valuation tasks caused no conflict with their religious beliefs.

outcome: Raw composite TTO values (range 1 to -1) for EQ-5D-5L hypothetical health states
statement: Female respondents gave lower cTTO values than male respondents in both univariate and multivariable models.

outcome: Raw composite TTO values (range 1 to -1) for EQ-5D-5L hypothetical health states
statement: Married respondents gave higher cTTO values than single respondents in the multivariable model, while divorced or widowed respondents gave lower values than single respondents in the univariate model.

outcome: Raw composite TTO values (range 1 to -1) for EQ-5D-5L hypothetical health states
statement: Literate respondents at every educational level gave higher cTTO values than illiterate respondents.

outcome: Raw composite TTO values (range 1 to -1) for EQ-5D-5L hypothetical health states
statement: Respondents from Alexandria, Delta, North Upper Egypt and South Upper Egypt gave lower cTTO values than respondents from Greater Cairo in the multivariable model, and urban respondents gave lower values than rural respondents.

outcome: Raw composite TTO values (range 1 to -1) for EQ-5D-5L hypothetical health states
statement: Respondents with full or partial health insurance and respondents with two or more comorbid chronic conditions gave lower cTTO values.

outcome: Raw composite TTO values (range 1 to -1) for EQ-5D-5L hypothetical health states
statement: Respondents who preferred quantity of life over quality of life, and undecided respondents, gave substantially higher cTTO values than respondents who preferred quality of life.

outcome: Raw composite TTO values (range 1 to -1) for EQ-5D-5L hypothetical health states
statement: Employment status, number of people in the household, religion and previous experience with illness were not significantly associated with health state values in either the univariate or the multivariable model.

outcome: Raw composite TTO values (range 1 to -1) for EQ-5D-5L hypothetical health states
statement: The multivariable model explained about 54% of variance, computed as the R-squared between predicted and observed values.
Utility deterioration was significant in all studied countries except China, and Uganda had the largest reported mean decrement.
Anxiety/depression was the EQ-5D-5L domain that most often worsened, while self-care worsened least often.
Income loss, long-term health conditions, and most direct or indirect experiences of COVID-19 were associated with higher odds of worsened health across genders.

National government-response and pandemic-severity associations differed by gender: there were no significant associations for females and other genders for most indicators, while several significant and directionally mixed associations were present in males.
Across countries, perceived health was unchanged for about 48% of respondents and worsened for more than one-third under the Paretian classification.
For the median country other than China, estimated QALY loss associated with morbidity was several times greater than QALY loss from premature mortality.
The overall pattern of HRQoL deterioration remained consistent when United States and Indian EQ-5D-5L value sets were used in sensitivity analyses.

Health deterioration, especially anxiety/depression, was more frequent in younger people; anxiety/depression deterioration was also more frequent in females and respondents of other genders than in males.
Using the United Kingdom value set, mean EQ-5D-5L utility fell significantly from the recalled prepandemic period to the survey period.

outcome: Coverage of the conceptual models by generic patient-reported outcome measures
statement: Generic patient-reported outcome measures covered more of the HRQoL and QoL models than the well-being model; EQ-HWB had the broadest reported HRQoL and well-being coverage.
The review retrieved hundreds of first-, second-, and third-level domains and curated them into 118 unique entities.
The review included 35 studies and 36 conceptual frameworks from 14,114 identified papers.

outcome: Conceptual domains, overlap, and final models for HRQoL, QoL, and well-being
statement: The final conceptual models contained 18 HRQoL dimensions, 22 QoL dimensions, and 10 well-being dimensions.

outcome: Conceptual domains, overlap, and final models for HRQoL, QoL, and well-being
statement: The three concepts shared substantial content but also had concept-specific dimensions.

outcome: TTO score for each valued EQ-5D-5L health state (range -1.0 to 1.0)
statement: In the multivariable random-effects model adjusted for health state severity and inconsistency, older age, male sex, being married and urban dwelling were significantly associated with TTO scores.

outcome: TTO score for each valued EQ-5D-5L health state (range -1.0 to 1.0)
statement: Respondents in the two western Canadian cities gave significantly lower TTO scores than those in Montreal, while Hamilton did not differ from Montreal.

outcome: TTO score for each valued EQ-5D-5L health state (range -1.0 to 1.0)
statement: Education, employment, income, ethnicity, country of birth, health literacy, multimorbidity, previous illness experience and self-rated health were not significantly associated with health state values in the multivariable model.

outcome: Inconsistency in TTO valuations
statement: About 11% of respondents had inconsistent TTO valuations; they were older, less educated, poorer, more often Aboriginal, had inadequate health literacy, more comorbidities and lower self-rated health, and inconsistency was strongly associated with higher TTO scores.
Sample characteristics: mean age 47.6 years, 45% male, 53% married, 63% above high school education, 82% urban, 75% born in Canada, mean EQ VAS 82.3.

Convergent validity was strong at item and scale levels, especially between EQ-HWB mental-health content and the PHQ-9, GAD-7, and ReQoL-10. Physical, pain, social, and wellbeing items also correlated with conceptually related comparator items.

Exploratory cross-instrument analysis supported five components: mental health and cognition, positive wellbeing, physical health, pain and discomfort, and social relationships. Modified EQ-HWB items loaded across all five components.

The modified EQ-HWB and derived EQ-HWB-9 had no instrument-level floor or ceiling effects, although personal care and getting around inside or outside had item-level ceilings above the prespecified 70% threshold.
The 900 baseline participants completed the fixed-order questionnaire in a mean of 10.7 minutes, and the reported response rate was 81%.

The modified and experimental items had broadly similar relative informativity, although several experimental items performed slightly better; the largest absolute-informativity difference concerned enjoyable activities.

The modified EQ-HWB discriminated across all seven predefined known-group factors and had large effects for six. Scores decreased as anxiety and depression severity increased; EQ-HWB-9 performance was comparable to the long form.

Among 132 participants with unchanged general health, modified EQ-HWB item agreement ranged from substantial to almost perfect, and scale-level reliability met the prespecified acceptable threshold for both the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-9.

Across the 12 differing items, the modified version produced a mixed pattern of higher, lower, and unchanged ceilings and floors. The largest distribution changes occurred when three positively framed experimental items were changed to negative framing.

outcome: Attainment of preference indifference in the tWTA question
statement: The conditional tWTA question was triggered often, but most triggered tasks still did not reach preference indifference.

outcome: Distribution and range of censored and uncensored health-state values
statement: Adding tWTA responses reduced clustering at -1 but moved substantial clustering to the assigned lower bound of -6.5, so censoring remained.

outcome: Sensitivity of negative values to EQ-5D-5L health-state severity
statement: Uncensored negative values did not improve sensitivity to EQ-5D-5L health-state severity compared with censored values.

outcome: Logical consistency of censored and uncensored values
statement: Uncensored values had more logically inconsistent health-state pairs than censored values.

outcome: Value-set model performance, uncertainty, and predictions
statement: The preferred uncensored-data GLS model produced much lower predictions and more statistically insignificant coefficients than the preferred censored-data Tobit-GLS model.

outcome: Compatibility of censored and uncensored cTTO data with DCE data
statement: Heteroscedasticity-corrected standard hybrid models were preferred for both datasets; performance was broadly comparable, but uncensored TTO data were slightly less compatible with DCE data.
Respondents who received the tWTA question were older and more likely to have illness experience; in adjusted analysis, only age and illness experience were associated with receiving it.

outcome: Value-set model performance, uncertainty, and predictions
statement: Sensitivity analyses that assigned -7.0 or -11.0 to the lowest uncensored response produced similar modelling patterns.

outcome: Difference in utilities between adult and child perspectives
statement: Utilities elicited from a child perspective were generally higher than utilities elicited from an adult perspective for the same health states, although some studies found no difference and one early VAS study found lower child-perspective values.

outcome: Stakeholder support for child-perspective valuation
statement: Stakeholder studies showed near consensus against relying only on adults using a child perspective and favored direct involvement of children and adolescents, while often retaining some adult input.

outcome: Advantages, disadvantages, and research needs for alternative valuation approaches
statement: Mapping or blinded age-invariant valuation could improve comparability with adult evaluations, but could miss child-specific dimension importance and had limited stakeholder support when adults were unaware of pediatric use.

outcome: Advantages, disadvantages, and research needs for alternative valuation approaches
statement: Direct child involvement was supported by stakeholders and was feasible for adolescents in several preference tasks, but ethical, reliability, and validity concerns remained, especially for tasks involving death or life-duration trade-offs.

outcome: Advantages, disadvantages, and research needs for alternative valuation approaches
statement: Group-based deliberative valuation could combine adult, child, and expert input, but pediatric applications were absent and valid QALY-scale value-set generation, representativeness, and reproducibility remained unresolved.

outcome: Relative importance of EQ-5D dimensions
statement: Valuation perspective could change the relative importance of dimensions: pain/discomfort often received greater priority for children, while self-care was less important for children and more important for adults.
Evidence on the age of the imagined child was mixed and varied by country and dimension; age differences were found in some countries and health states but not in others.

outcome: Non-severity-related influences and potential systematic bias
statement: Adults were more reluctant to choose immediate death or trade life-years when valuing for children, and fewer child-perspective states were classified as worse than dead, especially when duration was explicit.

Evidence did not consistently show that adult and child perspectives assign different values to life-years: discounting differences were small or inconsistent, and no perspective difference in loss aversion was found.

outcome: Non-severity-related influences and potential systematic bias
statement: Child-perspective tasks increased psychological distance because adults decided for another person, but evidence about the direction and size of its effect on utilities was mixed.

outcome: Non-severity-related influences and potential systematic bias
statement: Adults found child-perspective valuation more cognitively and emotionally difficult, especially when tasks required them to shorten or end a child’s life.
Adults used different external goals when valuing for children, including finishing school or reaching age 18; the magnitude and effect of these considerations on utilities remained unclear.

outcome: Stakeholder support for child-perspective valuation
statement: Differences between adult- and child-perspective utilities did not reliably reproduce societal priority-setting preferences, including preferences to prioritize quality-of-life gains for children.

outcome: Distributional characteristics and ceiling and floor effects
statement: Neither the modified EQ-HWB nor the derived EQ-HWB-S had a scale-level ceiling or floor effect under the prespecified 15% threshold. Four EQ-HWB items had a ceiling effect, and no EQ-HWB item had a floor effect.

outcome: Distributional characteristics and ceiling and floor effects
statement: The three items changed from positive to negative framing had response distributions within the range of the other EQ-HWB items.

outcome: Convergent validity at item and instrument levels
statement: Several expected item-level associations were only moderate: getting around inside or outside with EQ-5D-5L mobility, and day-to-day activities and enjoyable activities with EQ-5D-5L usual activities.

outcome: Convergent validity at item and instrument levels
statement: The EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S level sum scores had strong correlations with every comparator outcome measure, but WHO-5, ICECAP-A, and SWEMWBS correlated more strongly with each other than with either EQ-HWB version.

outcome: Known-group validity and effect sizes
statement: The EQ-HWB differentiated five of nine known-group comparisons with large effect sizes, whereas EQ-HWB-S differentiated three. EQ-HWB had a larger effect size than EQ-HWB-S for every known group.

outcome: Structural validity and component structure
statement: Principal component analysis supported four components that explained 55% of total variance: psychological health and well-being; daily activities and sensory functioning; pain, discomfort, and related functional limitations; and positive well-being. EQ-HWB items mainly loaded on separate factors from ICECAP-A, SWEMWBS, and WHO-5 items.

outcome: Distributional characteristics and ceiling and floor effects
statement: Mean level sum scores were 80.7 for EQ-HWB and 80.0 for EQ-HWB-S on the 0-to-100 scale.

outcome: Change in national EQ-5D-5L health measures from 2012 to 2022-2023
