statement: EQ-5D-5L index values, EQ VAS scores, and ceilings were lower in 2022-2023 than in 2012 across all compared demographic groups, and the EQ VAS Kakwani index increased.

outcome: Health inequality in EQ-5D-5L index values, EQ VAS scores, and dimension problems
statement: Health measures were generally more favorable for younger respondents, males, people with private insurance, higher-income groups, and employed respondents; females, lower-income groups, and older groups generally had higher odds of level 3-5 problems, with anxiety/depression showing a different age pattern.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index, EQ VAS, ceiling, health-state, and dimension-level population norms
statement: Pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression had the highest proportions of respondents reporting any problem.

outcome: Health inequality in EQ-5D-5L index values, EQ VAS scores, and dimension problems
statement: The modified Kakwani index showed inequality in EQ VAS and index values; sex had the largest relative demographic contribution to both measures.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index, EQ VAS, ceiling, health-state, and dimension-level population norms
statement: Among 2,989 respondents in 2022-2023, the mean EQ-5D-5L index value was 0.921, the mean EQ VAS score was 79.6, and 31.5% reported the 11111 ceiling state.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index, EQ VAS, ceiling, health-state, and dimension-level population norms
statement: The combined 2022-2023 sample was representative of the national population by age, sex, and region, and all respondents had complete EQ-5D-5L and EQ VAS data.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index, EQ VAS, ceiling, health-state, and dimension-level population norms
statement: The most common state was 11111, and the other most common states mainly contained mild-to-moderate pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression problems.
For each of the four health states, mean TTO utility was lower than mean SG utility; paired comparisons were significant for all states (all p<0.006).

Both methods gave the same utility ordering: depression was lowest, followed by arthritis, wheelchair, and diabetes as highest. This ordering also matched the England EQ-5D-5L value-set ordering for the vignette profiles.

Attention was approximately balanced between health state and duration in TTO. In SG, attention favored health state and probability over duration. Duration received more relative attention in TTO than in SG, and health state received more relative attention in SG than in TTO (both p<0.001).

Greater attention to the task-specific trade-off attribute was associated with higher health-state utility: TTO duration attention was positively associated with TTO utility, SG probability attention was positively associated with SG utility, and SG health-state attention was negatively associated with SG utility.

A larger shift toward health-state attention in SG relative to TTO was associated with a smaller SG-minus-TTO utility gap; the duration-attention difference was not significantly associated with the gap.
Monotonicity violations were more frequent in SG than TTO, but violation counts were not correlated with the attention-allocation indices.
Attribute acquisitions became shorter and less frequent across later trials in both tasks; results around scheduled breaks suggested familiarization rather than increasing fatigue.

outcome: Discriminatory performance of EQ-5D-5L Anxiety/Depression level against anxiety, depression, and co-morbid symptom classifications
statement: Discriminatory performance was significantly poorer in the two younger age groups than in the two older age groups.

outcome: Discriminatory performance of EQ-5D-5L Anxiety/Depression level against anxiety, depression, and co-morbid symptom classifications
statement: Among participants with exactly one chronic condition, performance was significantly poorer for those who reported an anxiety or depression disorder than for those who reported another chronic condition.

outcome: Subgroup-specific optimal EQ-5D-5L Anxiety/Depression cut-off
statement: Youden-index analyses indicated different preferred Anxiety/Depression cut-offs by age and type of singular chronic condition.
The mutually exclusive symptom groups comprised 72.0% with neither anxiety nor depression, 6.8% with anxiety only, 4.3% with depression only, and 16.9% with both.
Performance did not differ significantly by gender, education, or presence of chronic conditions, except for marginally poorer performance in the highly educated group in two diagnostic comparisons.

outcome: Prevalence of EQ-5D-5L Anxiety/Depression problems and GAD-7/PHQ-9 symptoms
statement: In the analyzed sample, 50.5% reported slight-to-extreme problems on the EQ-5D-5L Anxiety/Depression dimension, 23.7% met the GAD-7 anxiety threshold, and 21.2% met the PHQ-9 depression threshold.
Non-parametric ROC analyses gave lower AUROC values and higher GAD-7/PHQ-9 thresholds gave higher AUROC values, but the main subgroup differences and conclusions largely remained.

outcome: Discriminatory performance of EQ-5D-5L Anxiety/Depression level against anxiety, depression, and co-morbid symptom classifications
statement: The EQ-5D-5L Anxiety/Depression dimension had good discriminatory performance in the total sample, and performance did not differ significantly among anxiety, depression, and co-morbid anxiety/depression classifications.

outcome: Clarity, comprehensiveness and relevance of the candidate respiratory bolt-on items and their overlap with existing EQ-5D dimensions
statement: The content review showed that all six disease-specific asthma and COPD questionnaires ask about the impact of asthma or breathlessness on physical activities and five address disease-specific symptoms, whereas the EQ-5D covers physical activities only through mobility and symptoms only through pain/discomfort; impact on sleep and use of medication appear in several disease-specific questionnaires but not in the EQ-5D.

outcome: Logical inconsistency of estimated dimension-level coefficients and quality of the valuation interviews
statement: The hybrid model with intercept produced a non-significant intercept and 2 logically inconsistent parameters for R1 against 6 for R2, almost all at levels 2 or 3 and not significantly different from zero.

outcome: Additional variance in EQ VAS scores explained by respiratory items added to the EQ-5D dimension scores
statement: In the post hoc regression analyses the explained variance of EQ VAS scores increased most when items on the impact of asthma or breathlessness on physical activities from the ACQ, AQLQ, CCQ or mMRC were added to the EQ-5D dimension scores, while for the SGRQ items about problems caused by the chest condition gave the largest increase.

outcome: Additional variance in EQ VAS scores explained by respiratory items added to the EQ-5D dimension scores
statement: The principal component analyses identified constructs on which no EQ-5D item loaded, relating either to respiratory symptoms or to the impact of breathlessness on activities, and respiratory symptom items did not load on the same construct as the EQ-5D pain/discomfort item.

outcome: Clarity, comprehensiveness and relevance of the candidate respiratory bolt-on items and their overlap with existing EQ-5D dimensions
statement: In think-aloud sessions patients judged an item on the impact of shortness of breath on physical activities highly relevant but of limited added value over the existing EQ-5D items, whereas an item on symptoms was judged less important but without overlap with the existing EQ-5D items, so both candidates were carried into the valuation study.

outcome: Logical inconsistency of estimated dimension-level coefficients and quality of the valuation interviews
statement: Slightly more than 200 valuation interviews were completed for each bolt-on candidate; respondent characteristics did not differ significantly between arms and were comparable to the Dutch EQ-5D-5L valuation study, and the quality-control report rated interview quality as good by EQ-VT standards.

outcome: Mean composite TTO values for EQ-5D-5L+R health states
statement: Mean TTO values for very mild health states with no problems on the respiratory dimension were higher than the reference values from the Dutch EQ-5D-5L valuation study, while health states with level 4 or 5 on the respiratory dimension received significantly lower values.

outcome: Choice probabilities for pairs of EQ-5D-5L+R health states in the DCE
statement: DCE choice probabilities followed the same pattern: states with level 1 on the respiratory dimension were more often chosen as the better state than the corresponding reference states, and states with level 4 or 5 were chosen less often, more markedly for bolt-on R2.

outcome: Utility decrements of the respiratory bolt-on levels estimated in the hybrid model
statement: In the hybrid models the utility decrements of the respiratory dimension were statistically significant at levels 3, 4 and 5 for both candidates and were larger for R2 (breathing problems) than for R1; only for R2 was each decrement significantly greater than that of the previous level from level 3 onward.

outcome: Mean composite TTO values for EQ-5D-5L+R health states
statement: TTO values differed little between the two bolt-on candidates except for health states with level 5 on the respiratory dimension, where values were significantly lower for R2, and R2 produced a wider range of values than R1 apart from the worst state 555555.
Adding the skin irritation bolt-on produced the largest ceiling reduction in both disease groups.

Skin irritation showed the expected convergent relationships with skin-specific measures, while self-confidence was strongly related to the EQ-5D-5L anxiety/depression dimension; most other relationships with EQ-5D-5L dimensions were weak.
In atopic dermatitis, skin irritation provided the largest gain in explanatory power for the Patient-Oriented Eczema Measure, and other bolt-ons added little further improvement.
In psoriasis, skin irritation provided large gains in explanatory power for Psoriasis Symptoms and Signs Diary outcomes, and other bolt-ons added little further improvement.
Many patients who reported no EQ-5D-5L pain or discomfort still reported skin irritation problems.

Adding skin irritation improved known-groups validity in both conditions across DLQI and the relevant condition-specific symptom groups; adding self-confidence helped further in atopic dermatitis, while skin irritation plus feeling connected performed best in psoriasis.
The instruments used recall periods ranging from today to the past month, which the authors identified as a possible source of reduced comparability.

The social bolt-ons had limited psychometric impact compared with skin irritation, partly overlapped with anxiety/depression, and social relationships and social participation did not differ meaningfully in performance.

outcome: Distribution of self-reported levels on each EQ-5D dimension by survey variant
statement: Self-reported EQ-5D-5L level distributions deviated somewhat across the 4 reordered subtypes, but none of the variation was explained by a dimension appearing first or last, so the null hypothesis a1 could not be rejected.

outcome: Anchored dimension-level decrements (health state values on a scale where 1 is full health and 0 is dead) estimated from DCE-TTO conditional logit models
statement: Anchored dimension decrements varied across the 4 orderings without a serial position pattern; the largest decrements often occurred when duration was presented first (type IIId) and never when the dimension appeared first, so hypothesis a2 could not be rejected.

outcome: Statistical significance of interactions between survey variant and dimension-level or duration parameters in pooled choice models
statement: In the pooled model with design interactions, the mobility level 5 coefficient was the parameter most sensitive to reordering, while the duration coefficient showed no consistent design effect.

outcome: Distribution of self-reported levels on each EQ-5D dimension by survey variant
statement: The proportion self-reporting no problems on the composite dimension exceeded the proportion reporting no problems on both split subdimensions for anxiety or depression but not for pain or discomfort, so hypothesis b1 was rejected for anxiety or depression only.

outcome: Anchored dimension-level decrements (health state values on a scale where 1 is full health and 0 is dead) estimated from DCE-TTO conditional logit models
statement: At level 5 the composite dimension decrement was significantly larger in magnitude than the corresponding split subdimension decrement for pain or discomfort and for anxiety or depression, so hypothesis b2 was rejected for the level 5 coefficients but not for any level 3 coefficient.

outcome: Anchored dimension-level decrements (health state values on a scale where 1 is full health and 0 is dead) estimated from DCE-TTO conditional logit models
statement: Predicted values for the all-extreme-problems state differed substantially between the standard and the split descriptive systems, by amounts an order of magnitude larger than published minimally important differences for EQ-5D-5L index scores (0.037 to 0.069).

outcome: Distribution of self-reported levels on each EQ-5D dimension by survey variant
statement: Variation in self-reported EQ-5D-5L problems across the 5 bolt-off subtypes was not statistically significant relative to type III, so hypothesis c1 could not be rejected.

outcome: Anchored dimension-level decrements (health state values on a scale where 1 is full health and 0 is dead) estimated from DCE-TTO conditional logit models
statement: Bolting off a dimension increased the estimated disutility of the remaining dimensions: 33 of the 36 significant anchored coefficients in the 5 bolt-off models were larger than the corresponding type III coefficient, and hypothesis c2 was rejected for all dimensions except mobility, while duration was unaffected.

outcome: Anchored dimension-level decrements (health state values on a scale where 1 is full health and 0 is dead) estimated from DCE-TTO conditional logit models
statement: With the exception of type Vd (pain or discomfort dropped), the worst state of a bolt-off instrument (4 extreme dimensions) had a predicted value worse than the corresponding EQ-5D-3/5L prediction and worse than the value of state 55555 in type III.

outcome: Feasibility measured as number of missing values in the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L
statement: Both the Spanish EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L were fully feasible in children with cancer: there were no missing answers for either version.

outcome: Ceiling effect: proportion of "no problems" responses per dimension and for the overall system, with absolute and relative reduction
statement: The EQ-5D-Y-5L reduced the ceiling effect relative to the EQ-5D-Y-3L in every dimension and for the overall health state 11111.

outcome: Redistribution of EQ-5D-Y-3L responses across EQ-5D-Y-5L levels and proportion of inconsistent response pairs
statement: Many children who reported level 1 on the EQ-5D-Y-3L moved to level 2 ("a little bit of a problem") on the EQ-5D-Y-5L, and level 2 responses spread over levels 2 to 4.

outcome: Redistribution of EQ-5D-Y-3L responses across EQ-5D-Y-5L levels and proportion of inconsistent response pairs
statement: Inconsistent 3L-5L response pairs were scarce, ranging from 1.4% to 4.1% of children by dimension.

outcome: Absolute informativity (Shannon index H') and relative informativity (Shannon evenness index J') per dimension and overall
statement: Absolute informativity (Shannon index H') did not differ significantly between the 3L and 5L versions in any dimension or for the overall system, and relative informativity (J') showed hardly any difference.

outcome: EQ VAS self-rated health today by redistribution subgroup
statement: Mean and median EQ VAS values generally fell as the redistribution subgroup moved to worse 3L-5L response pairs, for example in mobility from 85.3 (g1.1) to 59.0 (g2.4).

Diseased respondents had lower EQ-5D-5L and WHO-5 scores than healthy respondents. Younger respondents had lower WHO-5 scores than older respondents, and this age pattern was stronger in the diseased group.
In adjusted pooled models, higher government-response stringency was positively associated with the EQ-5D-5L index, with a larger coefficient in diseased than healthy respondents.

In adjusted pooled models, higher government-response stringency was positively associated with EQ VAS; the association was statistically significant for diseased respondents but not for healthy respondents.
In adjusted pooled models, higher government-response stringency was negatively associated with WHO-5 mental well-being in both healthy and diseased respondents.

The largest adverse associations included inability to work, feeling insufficiently protected against COVID-19, poor experience of health-care access, and, among diseased respondents, a greater number of chronic conditions.

Country patterns differed: South Africa had the highest median EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS, Russia had the lowest median EQ-5D-5L index, the Netherlands had the highest median WHO-5 index, and South Africa had the lowest median WHO-5 index.
The selected classification system contained 13 attributes: all nine EQ-HWB-9 items and four additional EQ-HWB items.

outcome: Similarity of United Kingdom and Australian preferences
statement: United Kingdom and Australian health-state preferences were highly similar. Both samples prioritized vision, hearing, mobility, and pain severity; less than 5% of variance was attributed to sample preference differences and the cross-country Pearson correlation was 0.96.

outcome: Feasibility of DCE with duration for a long health and wellbeing measure
statement: Most respondents understood the task and thought that the amount of information and the number of tasks were suitable, but more than one quarter met the study definition of a potential speeder and about 15% reported difficulty distinguishing options or choosing.

outcome: Completion speed, attention checks, coefficient significance, and logical consistency
statement: Most severe attribute levels had increasing disutility and most coefficients were significant and monotonic. Non-significance and non-monotonicity occurred more often for mild levels and wellbeing attributes.

outcome: Attribute presentation-order effects on preferences and utility distributions
statement: Evidence for an attribute-order effect was mixed. Four of 78 level-coefficient comparisons differed at the 5% level, pooled models found several small order interactions, and order changed utility distributions, but the Swait-Louviere test found no significant scale heterogeneity.

outcome: Feasibility of DCE with duration for a long health and wellbeing measure
statement: The pilot collected 100 responses, of which 97 were valid. Mean time per DCE-with-duration question was 20 seconds, the survey functioned effectively, and the team made no changes after the pilot.

outcome: Respondent understanding, confidence, difficulty, and task burden
statement: The 11 qualitative participants found the EQ-HWB information interpretable and could complete the DCE-with-duration tasks independently; their feedback changed the attribute introduction but not the item or level wording.

outcome: Anchored utility values and relative attribute importance
statement: Physical health attributes had the largest disutilities. Pain severity, vision, daily activity, and mobility were among the five most important attributes across all models, and modeled and stated rankings were highly consistent.

outcome: Anchored utility values and relative attribute importance
statement: The health-first value range was 1 to -0.634 in the United Kingdom and 1 to -0.588 in Australia. The wellbeing-first worst-state values were -0.791 and -0.539, respectively.
Worse-than-dead valuations were common: 33.0% of participants assigned at least one WTD value, and the reported mean number of WTD ratings was 6.60 (SD 5.48).
Extreme lower-bound valuations were also common: 16.1% of participants assigned at least one -1 value, and the reported mean number of -1 ratings was 3.22 (SD 4.57).

Participant socio-demographic associations were not robust after adjustment. Non-tertiary education had a borderline association with more WTD ratings among WTD raters, and caregiving experience had a borderline association with assigning at least one -1 rating. Adjusted tables also reported interviewer effects.
The most common closed-ended considerations were physical burden, mental burden, financial burden, medical costs, and increased living costs.

Priorities differed by age: younger adults cited medical and living costs less often, job or income loss and loss of enjoyment more often, while the 45-64-year group was least likely to say that living in poor health was better than death.

Avoiding physical and mental burdens on family was a central reason for preferring death over poor health across age groups. Younger adults also emphasized pain, enjoyment, and dignity; middle-aged adults emphasized family and financial burden; older adults emphasized pain, mobility, autonomy, and dependency.
Most participants reported a preference for death rather than life with severely impaired health.

outcome: Survey dropout rate during the DCE choice tasks, by study arm
statement: Dropout during the DCE was highest in the base case arm without overlap or color coding and significantly lower in every experimental arm, with the combination of overlap and color coding lowest.

outcome: Relative choice consistency between study arms (scale parameter gamma)
statement: Level overlap raised relative choice consistency by about one third as a stand-alone strategy, color coding alone had no effect on choice consistency, and the combination of overlap with highlighting or intensity color coding raised choice consistency by roughly two thirds.

outcome: Cognitive debriefing scores on clarity, ease of identifying differences, ease of choosing, number of choice tasks, and topic interest (7-point Likert)
statement: Cognitive debriefing scores improved with level overlap: questions were clearer, differences between health states were easier to identify, choosing was easier, and agreement that there were too many choice tasks fell; color coding mainly improved identification of differences and overall survey interest.

outcome: Relative choice consistency over the course of the 21 choice tasks (scale parameter delta): warm-up, learning, and fatigue effects
statement: No respondent fatigue was observed in any study arm over the 21 choice tasks, but the arms without level overlap showed a significant warm-up or learning effect in the first three choice tasks that was absent in the arms with overlap.

outcome: Respondent ranking of the preferred visual presentation format
statement: Respondents who completed the ranking task preferred color coded formats over the format without color.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L level decrements (population mean and standard deviation of preference weights)
statement: All EQ-5D-5L level decrements were logically consistent, had the expected sign, and had 95% credible intervals excluding zero, with the largest decrements for the most severe anxiety/depression and pain/discomfort levels.

outcome: Survey dropout rate during the DCE choice tasks, by study arm
statement: Respondents who dropped out were on average older and lower educated than completes, while background characteristics were balanced across study arms, confirming adequate randomization.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L level decrements (population mean and standard deviation of preference weights)
statement: Sensitivity analyses reported in the supporting information showed that level overlap reduced the extra emphasis on the first and last attribute, that intensity color coding increased the distance between slight and moderate problem levels, and that highlighting shifted emphasis from moderate to more extreme levels; relaxing the assumption of an identical preference structure did not change the conclusions.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index score (Canadian value set)
statement: Mean EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS scores in the analyzed Alberta sample were 0.85 (SD 0.14) and 79.6 (SD 17.7), and 30.6% of respondents reported full health (11111).

outcome: Reporting of problems in each EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: Most respondents reported no problems with mobility, self-care and usual activities, while pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression were the dimensions most often reporting problems.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index score (Canadian value set)
statement: Mean EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS scores fell steadily as deprivation increased on both the CDI and the ODI, and all differences were statistically significant (p < 0.001).

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index score (Canadian value set)
statement: The difference in mean EQ-5D-5L index score between the least well-off and the most well-off was 0.17 on both indices, a large difference (effect size 1.21) that exceeds the reported minimally important difference of 0.04.
Correlations between the deprivation indices and the EQ-5D-5L dimensions, index and VAS scores were absent to poor.

outcome: Reporting of problems in each EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: In adjusted logistic regression, the least well-off respondents had a higher likelihood of reporting problems in every EQ-5D-5L dimension, with the largest odds ratio for mobility and the smallest for anxiety/depression on the CDI.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index score (Canadian value set)
statement: In adjusted linear regression, the least well-off had lower EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS scores than the most well-off on both deprivation indices.

outcome: Quality-control indicators: flagged interviews, nontraders, inconsistency and TTO task duration by literacy level
statement: Both literate and illiterate respondents completed the cTTO and DCE tasks, and quality-control indicators were similar between the two groups, with a lower percentage of flagged interviews among illiterate respondents.

outcome: Respondent experience of the TTO and DCE tasks and of the graphical illustrations
statement: Illiterate respondents found the graphical illustrations useful but time consuming, and suggested displaying them on the computer screen within the EQ-PVT platform rather than in a printed booklet.

outcome: Quality-control indicators: flagged interviews, nontraders, inconsistency and TTO task duration by literacy level
statement: The number of nontraders was slightly higher among illiterate respondents but the difference was not significant, and the percentage of health states valued as worse than dead was lower among illiterate respondents.

outcome: TTO values and their distribution, including states valued as worse than dead
statement: The range and distribution of TTO values were similar for the two literacy groups.

outcome: Conditional logit DCE coefficients and odds ratios for EQ-5D-3L dimension levels
statement: In the conditional logit DCE models, usual activities had the highest impact on choice, followed by self-care and then anxiety/depression and mobility, with similar patterns but larger coefficient magnitudes among illiterate respondents.

outcome: Conditional logit DCE coefficients and odds ratios for EQ-5D-3L dimension levels
statement: Odds ratios showed that severe problems in the EQ-5D dimensions strongly reduced the odds of choosing a health state, with the strongest effects for level 3 usual activities and level 3 mobility, and, among illiterate respondents, also for self-care problems.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L response distributions and EQ VAS scores
statement: Responses were better distributed across levels on the EQ-5D-5L than on the EQ-5D-3L, especially for mobility, pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression, while EQ VAS scores did not differ between the two versions.
Illiterate respondents were older, more often unemployed and rural, had lower education, income and self-reported health, and lived in larger households with fewer earners than literate respondents.

outcome: Themes on religious, cultural and family considerations influencing trade-off choices
statement: Most literate and illiterate respondents reported that religion had no impact on their responses, whereas most illiterate respondents reported that cultural norms affected their answers, especially for self-care.

outcome: Themes on religious, cultural and family considerations influencing trade-off choices
statement: Literate respondents said they thought first about themselves and then about family and the healthcare system when trading life-years, whereas illiterate respondents thought first about their family.

The adapted EQ-VT 2.0 protocol was feasible for valuing EQ-HWB-S with cTTO and DCE by online videoconference. Participants generally understood the tasks and health states, and interviewers reported high understanding and engagement.
cTTO values covered the full permitted range and decreased as EQ-HWB-S state severity increased; negative values were common for severe states.

No interviewer reached the protocol threshold for retraining or data removal. There were few nontraders and few DCE response patterns that suggested poor engagement, although 40 participants had an inconsistency involving the worst state.

Predictions from the heteroskedastic Tobit cTTO model and heteroskedastic probit DCE model showed strong concordance, although dimension coefficients differed and several candidate models had disordered severity coefficients.

The selected pilot value set used a hybrid heteroskedastic Tobit model with constrained ordered coefficients. Pain, mobility, daily activities, and sadness or depression had the largest disutilities, followed by loneliness, anxiety, exhaustion, control, and cognition.
The achieved sample was broadly similar to the UK general population for age, sex, and ethnicity, but it was more highly educated and the recruitment target was not met.
cTTO tasks took longer than the EQ-VT 2.0 minimum benchmark, but participants reported that the tasks were easy to understand even though decisions were difficult.

outcome: Self-reported EQ VAS rating of own health (0-100) and EQ-5D-Y-3L dimension level distribution
statement: Of the 243 possible EQ-5D-Y-3L health states, 92 were reported by the 6,468 adolescent respondents, and the mean EQ VAS score was 75.4.

outcome: Self-reported EQ VAS rating of own health (0-100) and EQ-5D-Y-3L dimension level distribution
statement: Problems were most often reported in the dimension feeling worried, sad or unhappy, followed by having pain or discomfort; fewer than 5% reported any problems in mobility or looking after myself.

outcome: Predicted experience-based EQ VAS values for EQ-5D-Y-3L health states, and rescaled values on a 0-1 scale
statement: In the preferred OLS main-effect model (Model 1) the largest VAS decrements were for feeling worried, sad or unhappy, followed by doing usual activities; monotonic consistency held across all dimensions.

outcome: Predicted experience-based EQ VAS values for EQ-5D-Y-3L health states, and rescaled values on a 0-1 scale
statement: Coefficients for moving from level 2 to level 3 in mobility, looking after myself and doing usual activities were not statistically significant in the OLS models, and the added N2 interaction term was small but significant.

outcome: Model performance: monotonic consistency, adjusted R-squared, AIC/BIC, MAE, RMSE and Spearman correlation between observed and predicted VAS values
statement: All four models (two OLS, two GLM) performed similarly on goodness of fit and prediction accuracy, so the simpler and more understandable OLS main-effect model was selected, and its performance held in a randomly split half sample.

outcome: Predicted experience-based EQ VAS values for EQ-5D-Y-3L health states, and rescaled values on a 0-1 scale
statement: Anchoring the predicted values at the worst and best EQ-5D-Y-3L states gave a rescaled value for health state 33333 of 0.24, close to the Japanese value set (0.29) and to Wu et al. (0.38), while the Slovenian value set gave a negative value (-0.69).
The Spanish EQ-5D-Y-5L had few missing responses, which the authors judged acceptable feasibility.

Both youth versions had high and similar ceiling effects in this healthy sample. The five-level version had only small reductions by dimension and for full health, with no reduction for usual activities.

Absolute informativity was higher for EQ-5D-Y-5L in every dimension and for the overall system, but statistically significant differences were limited to feeling worried, sad, or unhappy and the overall system. Relative informativity decreased for most dimensions and increased for looking after myself.
Most paired 3L-to-5L responses were consistent. Pain or discomfort had the largest reported inconsistency, and EQ VAS values decreased significantly as paired dimension severity increased.

Correlations of both EQ-5D-Y versions with KIDSCREEN and the Cantril life satisfaction ladder were usually statistically significant but low, which left convergent validity in doubt. Corresponding 3L and 5L dimensions had moderate or high agreement.

Test-retest agreement for EQ-5D-Y-5L was perfect for mobility and looking after myself, substantial for usual activities, moderate for pain or discomfort, and moderate for feeling worried, sad, or unhappy.
Most respondents reported full health. The highest prevalence of problems was in pain or discomfort and feeling worried, sad, or unhappy, while severe problems were rare.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility score calculated with the German value set
statement: The 433 analyzed patients had a mean German-value-set EQ-5D-5L utility score of 0.82.

Excluded patients tended to be older, to have more metastatic sites, and to receive fluoropyrimidine monotherapy more often than included patients, which indicated selective missingness among older or more severely ill patients.

The study successfully added the EQ-5D-5L to an ongoing registry questionnaire and linked the responses to clinical registry data, which demonstrated that this form of additional data collection was feasible.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L visual analogue scale score
statement: The 433 analyzed patients had a mean EQ VAS score of 62.05.

outcome: EORTC QLQ-C30 global health status/QoL score
statement: The 433 analyzed patients had a mean EORTC QLQ-C30 global health status/QoL score of 56.66.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension-level problem distribution
statement: Dimension responses showed substantial burden: pain or discomfort was reported by 60.5%, anxiety or depression by 56.4%, and problems with walking by about half; only 16.9% reported no problem in any EQ-5D-5L dimension.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility score calculated with the German value set
statement: EQ-5D-5L utility, EQ VAS, and EORTC global health status/QoL scores were significantly correlated, but EQ VAS and EORTC scores had wider distributions than utility scores.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility score calculated with the German value set
statement: In the Tobit model, hypertension, fatigue, and pain had statistically significant negative associations with EQ-5D-5L utility; marginal effects at the sample mean were small.

Fatigue and pain had negative associations in all three regression models. Most demographic characteristics, including age and sex, and most clinical characteristics did not have significant associations with HRQoL.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L visual analogue scale score
statement: In the EQ VAS OLS model, second-line or later treatment, chronic gastric or bowel disease, fatigue, and pain had negative associations; questionnaire completion at 12 or 24 months and one prior progression had positive associations.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility score calculated with the German value set
statement: Patients had lower HRQoL than published German general-population references, with a smaller difference for EQ-5D-5L utility than for EQ VAS.

The best fitting country-specific transformation function varied across countries: Canada, the UK, Korea and Japan were best fitted by a square-root term of the latent utility, Spain, China and Thailand by a simple linear form, and the Netherlands by a linear plus cubic term.

outcome: Predictive precision of transformation functions (mean absolute error, adjusted R-squared)
statement: The western regional generic transformation function fitted well and added little predictive error, whereas the eastern regional function fitted poorly and exceeded the acceptability threshold in all eastern countries except Korea.

outcome: Predictive precision of transformation functions (mean absolute error, adjusted R-squared)
statement: A single global generic transformation function was not acceptable: only the UK had an incremental mean absolute error below 0.02, Canada and China fell between 0.02 and 0.04, and all other countries exceeded 0.04.

outcome: TTO-derived mean health utilities for 86 EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Scatterplots of mean observed TTO health utilities against mean predicted latent utilities for the 86 valued states diverged across countries; the four western countries were similar to each other and Japan was closer to the western countries than to its Asian neighbours.

outcome: Prevalence of suspicious DCE response patterns and clustering of cTTO responses at key values
statement: Response distributions differed by region: more cTTO values equal to 1 and equal to 0 in western countries, the Netherlands had 11% of cTTO scores at the minimum of -1, self-reported utilities were higher in eastern countries, and the prevalence of suspicious DCE response patterns was similar across countries.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility index
statement: Mean EQ-5D-5L utility was significantly lower in the QALY-MICI sample than in the French general population.

outcome: SIBDQ inflammatory bowel disease-specific quality-of-life score
statement: SIBDQ scores did not differ by IBD subtype, but men reported higher SIBDQ scores than women after age adjustment.

outcome: EQ VAS score
statement: Mean EQ VAS was significantly lower in the QALY-MICI sample than in the French general population.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension levels and health-state profiles
statement: Compared with French population norms, usual activities and anxiety/depression were the most affected EQ-5D-5L dimensions; pain/discomfort was also affected but its difference was not statistically significant.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility index
statement: Utility and EQ VAS were higher for men than for women, but neither outcome differed significantly between Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility index
statement: Utility was strongly positively correlated with EQ VAS and SIBDQ and was negatively correlated with HBI and SCCAI disease-activity scores.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility index
statement: Utility declined as disease activity increased in both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis; patients with quiescent disease had values close to the general population.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility index
statement: In adjusted Tobit models, SIBDQ and disease activity were the main predictors of utility; SIBDQ, age, surgery history, and disease activity predicted EQ VAS, with a gender-by-SIBDQ interaction for EQ VAS.

outcome: Sample representativeness and effect of demographic weighting
statement: The sample over-represented younger adults and women and under-represented adults aged 55 years or older; weighting to the EPIMAD age, gender, and IBD distribution increased overall utility only slightly.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L dimension levels and health-state profiles
statement: The study observed 306 of 3,125 possible EQ-5D-5L health states; the full-health profile 11111 was less common than in the French general population.

The wheelchair familiarisation example failed to function as the intended better-than-dead state for many early pilot participants, so the team replaced it with a migraine example while preserving the task sequence and quality-control criteria.
The adapted EQ-VT 2.1 interview process was feasible and culturally acceptable in the Egyptian sample while retaining the protocol structure and quality-control process.

The authors reported that the four-stage interviewer training process, including interviews with interviewers before formal training, had a positive effect on training and the subsequent interview process.

Ambiguous Arabic wording made levels 4 and 5 difficult to distinguish in the pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression dimensions; traffic-light colour coding was used to identify all five severity levels.
Pictorial dimension representations and coloured severity cards enabled interviewer-assisted cTTO and DCE tasks for participants who could not read the text-based states.
Most participants reported no conflict between the valuation tasks and their religious beliefs and reported that religion did not influence their valuation responses.
Most participants preferred a healthy life regardless of length to a long life regardless of quality; becoming a burden on family or friends was the most frequent concern about serious illness.
Mobility was most often ranked as the most important EQ-5D dimension, ahead of anxiety/depression, usual activities, self-care, and pain/discomfort.
Incomplete interviews were most often attributed to religious beliefs, inability to understand the tasks, or interview length.
The study observed a relatively high share of worse-than-dead responses in Egypt, but the authors found religious objection was not a major concern for most participants.
The sample differed from national statistics for several background characteristics, but it retained the demographic diversity required by the researchers.

outcome: Agreement between DCE-TTO values and TTO values estimated from identical preference data
statement: DCE-TTO and TTO values agreed well at the severe end of the QALY scale but diverged upward from about 0.5, with DCE-TTO values increasingly higher than TTO values as health states became milder.

outcome: Agreement between DCE-TTO values and TTO values estimated from identical preference data
statement: The largest discrepancy was for the mildest state 12111, where the DCE-TTO value exceeded the mean TTO value by 0.37; DCE-TTO values exceeded 1 for the two mildest states.

outcome: Mean TTO values for 10 EQ-5D health states, with and without censored regression at -1 and +1
statement: Mean TTO values ranged from 0.9249 for 12111 to -0.3265 for the pits state 55555, and were largely concordant with observed composite TTO values from a recent Dutch study.

outcome: Mean TTO values for 10 EQ-5D health states, with and without censored regression at -1 and +1
statement: Censored regression at -1 lowered TTO estimates for severe states, worsening agreement with DCE-TTO at the bottom of the scale, and left mild-state estimates essentially unchanged.

outcome: Mean TTO values for 10 EQ-5D health states, with and without censored regression at -1 and +1
statement: Censored regression at both -1 and +1 reduced the discrepancy for mild states, cutting the difference for 12111 from 0.37 to 0.14, but produced TTO values above 1 (1.1519 for 12111 and 1.0680 for 11122).

outcome: Distributional behaviour of individual TTO responses: proportion of nontraders, proportion censored at -1, and variance by health state
statement: Mild health states showed high proportions of nontraders and narrow, left-skewed TTO value distributions, while severe states showed many respondents exhausting the lead time, right-skewed distributions and substantially larger standard deviations.

outcome: DCE-TTO health state values estimated from strict pairwise preferences and normalized on the QALY scale
statement: Bootstrap DCE-TTO values were within 0.001 of the values from the full sample, but the bootstrap produced substantially wider confidence intervals; bootstrap TTO values reproduced the full-sample TTO values and confidence intervals faithfully.

outcome: DCE face validity based on preference patterns by level sum score difference
statement: Online and face-to-face data showed similar face-validity patterns when choice probability was assessed against the difference in level sum scores, but preferences differed for individual health-state pairs.

outcome: Potentially suspicious choice patterns and attribute dominance
statement: Potentially suspicious flatlining or alternating choice patterns were more common online than in the screened face-to-face sample.

outcome: Respondent-reported DCE comprehension and decision difficulty
statement: Online respondents less often strongly agreed that the DCE questions were easy to understand, but they reported greater certainty in their choices and did not differ in their reported ability to distinguish alternatives.

outcome: Modeled EQ-5D-5L dimension-level preferences and relative importance
statement: The primary multinomial logit analysis showed that online and screened face-to-face preferences differed by more than a scale parameter.

outcome: Modeled EQ-5D-5L dimension-level preferences and relative importance
statement: Compared with screened face-to-face respondents, online respondents gave more relative importance to Mobility and less relative importance to Anxiety/Depression.

outcome: Respondent self-reported health, EQ-5D-5L profile, and EQ VAS
statement: Online respondents reported poorer health than screened face-to-face respondents, including a lower mean EQ VAS and more problems on all EQ-5D-5L dimensions except Mobility.

outcome: Potentially suspicious choice patterns and attribute dominance
statement: Attribute dominance did not differ significantly between comparators, and the overall prevalence of potentially suspicious patterns remained low in both groups.

Linear mapping without an intercept was selected because it had the highest R-squared and the smallest mean absolute error for mild states, which the authors prioritized because mild states are more prevalent.

The 268 respondents supplied 3,752 cTTO observations. After 685 respondent-flagged responses were removed, 3,067 remained; 197 of these were negative. Raw mean values across the 52 states ranged from 0.099 for 33333 to 0.933 for 12211.
All DCE coefficients were negative and monotonically ordered. At level 3, dimension importance was pain/discomfort, worried/sad/unhappy, usual activities, looking after myself, then mobility.

The garbage-class mixed logit model estimated a 35.4% garbage-class share. Compared with a standard mixed logit sensitivity model, dimension importance changed little, but the garbage-class model increased the scale length by 65%.
The preferred value set assigned values from 0.142 for state 33333 to 1 for state 11111; the second-worst state 23333 had value 0.188 and the mildest impaired state 12111 had value 0.977.
A robustness analysis that retained all feedback-flagged cTTO responses gave similar overall results and a minimum value of 0.174.

outcome: Health-related quality of life measured by EQ-5D index and EQ VAS
statement: Poor overall scores on EQ VAS, the EQ-5D index, GHQ-12 and WEMWBS all indicated a need for social care.

outcome: Association (construct validity) between EQ-5D, wellbeing measures and social care need
statement: At dimension level, the EQ-5D self-care and pain/discomfort dimensions were significantly associated with need for social care; people with extreme anxiety/depression and people unable to perform usual activities were more likely to report need for social care.

outcome: Association (construct validity) between EQ-5D, wellbeing measures and social care need
statement: No GHQ-12 dimension was significantly associated with the Barthel Index, while two WEMWBS dimensions ('been feeling useful' and 'had energy to spare') were associated with it.

outcome: Overall survival time (median survival, survival curves) after palliative radiotherapy
statement: The EQ-5D-3L self-care dimension was the single most predictive dimension of survival and replaced clinician-assessed performance status with similar model discrimination.

outcome: Overall survival time (median survival, survival curves) after palliative radiotherapy
statement: Prognostic groups defined by the self-care based model had median survival of 86, 174 and 483 days, compared with 95, 210 and 515 days for the performance-status baseline model.

outcome: Model discrimination measured by Harrell C-index
statement: C-index values were similar across all model specifications, with no statistically significant differences.

outcome: Model discrimination measured by Harrell C-index
statement: Adding clinician-assessed performance status to EQ-5D based models produced only a marginal, non-significant improvement in discrimination.

outcome: Separation between three prognostic groups measured by the Altman-Royston index of separation at 50-day intervals
statement: Altman-Royston separation was limited at early time points; dimension-based models separated best within the first six months, while EQ VAS based models separated better at longer follow-up, though no difference was statistically significant.

outcome: Overall survival time (median survival, survival curves) after palliative radiotherapy
statement: In the model with all EQ-5D-3L dimensions plus EQ VAS, only self-care and usual activities were consistently significant, with hazard ratios in the expected direction; primary diagnosis and non-bone metastases remained strong predictors in all models.

outcome: Thoughts and feelings when valuing children's health states, including discomfort with the TTO task
statement: Two main categories emerged: 'Thoughts and feelings when valuing children's health states' and 'Strategies when valuing children's health states'; the categories were intertwined because thoughts and feelings shaped the strategies used and vice versa.

outcome: Feasibility of adolescents from 16 years completing TTO and DCE valuation tasks
statement: Participants generally grasped quickly that the TTO task requires trading quantity against quality of life, and no difference in task understanding was observed between adolescents and adults.

outcome: Thoughts and feelings when valuing children's health states, including discomfort with the TTO task
statement: Participants found the TTO task offensive and uncomfortable, describing feelings of doubt, awfulness, being grotesque and responsibility, especially the confirmation box stating how many life years they were willing to give up for a 10-year-old child; the DCE task was seen as easier, more theoretical and more straightforward because it required no shortening of life.

outcome: Thoughts and feelings when valuing children's health states, including discomfort with the TTO task
statement: Initial reluctance to trade off life years did not necessarily produce non-trader behaviour: a majority nevertheless traded life years for the more severe health states, motivated mainly by the wish to avoid suffering for the child.

outcome: Thoughts and feelings when valuing children's health states, including discomfort with the TTO task
statement: Many participants questioned who has the right to value health states for a 10-year-old child and doubted their own standing because they had not experienced the described states; several would have preferred to value their own health or to ask the child.

outcome: Perceived relevance and comprehensiveness of the EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions for describing a child's health
statement: Valuing states described by the EQ-5D-Y-3L was generally accepted, but most participants prioritised the mental health dimension (feeling worried, sad or unhappy), some exclusively, while pain or discomfort was also stressed; several judged some health states implausible or unrealistic as constant states, and many wanted an explicit social dimension.

outcome: Perceived relevance and comprehensiveness of the EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions for describing a child's health
statement: Participants took the surrounding context of the imagined child into account, arguing that family, social support and school could make some states easier for a 10-year-old than for an adult.

outcome: Strategies used to complete the valuation tasks (own and vicarious experience; adopted point of view)
statement: Two strategies were used to complete the tasks: drawing on own or vicarious experience of health states, and adopting a point of view (most often a parent's), with participants aware that different points of view could yield different values.
The achieved sample was broadly representative of the Hong Kong population for sex, educational attainment, marital status, and most age groups, but under-represented people in paid employment.

outcome: Engagement with the feedback module by participant characteristics
statement: About one third of participants engaged with the feedback module, and only a small share of all C-TTO valuations were excluded through it.

outcome: Number of logically inconsistent C-TTO responses before and after the feedback module
statement: The feedback module reduced logical inconsistencies: most participants who excluded states removed their inconsistencies, while one in five non-users retained an inconsistency in the estimation sample.

outcome: Engagement with the feedback module by participant characteristics
statement: Participants who excluded states during the feedback module were younger, more often held post-secondary or degree qualifications, less often had personal experience of serious illness, and less often lived with a chronic condition.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state values for Hong Kong
statement: The hybrid main-effects model without a constant gave logically consistent utility decrements and was selected as the Hong Kong value set; predicted values ranged from -0.864 for state 55555 to 1 for full health.
Applying the feedback module exclusions changed coefficients and predictions only slightly but gave a marginally better goodness of fit.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state values for Hong Kong
statement: C-TTO responses were heteroscedastic, with greater disagreement for more severe states, and 16% of tasks reached the lowest possible value of -1.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health state values for Hong Kong
statement: Predicted values for the 3125 states were very similar between Hong Kong and Indonesia, and Hong Kong had far more states valued worse than dead than China, Japan, or South Korea.

outcome: Engagement with the feedback module by participant characteristics
statement: The feedback module added about two minutes to the end of the C-TTO task, but the overall length of the C-TTO section was similar for users and non-users, and all interviewers met the minimum quality criteria.

outcome: Out-of-sample predictive accuracy (mean absolute error and root mean squared error) of predicted versus observed cTTO values
statement: In the leave-one-state-out cross-validation the CALE model predicted out-of-sample cTTO values more accurately than the conventional additive main-effects model for all 3 types of health states, and the relative advantage grew with the number of dimensions.

outcome: Out-of-sample predictive accuracy (mean absolute error and root mean squared error) of predicted versus observed cTTO values
statement: The leave-one-block-out cross-validation gave the same ordering, with the CALE model best for every state type; the conventional random-intercept model could not converge for the EQ+VI states.
Adding a random intercept marginally improved CALE model performance in all 4 datasets but gave mixed results for the conventional additive model.

outcome: cTTO values and estimated dimension and level coefficients for EQ-SC, EQ-5D-5L and EQ+VI health states
statement: All CALE coefficients were significant at the 0.05 level, whereas the conventional additive models contained several nonsignificant coefficients, nearly all at level 2, and the level-3 vision coefficient was nonmonotonic.
The conventional model fitted the data better in-sample but predicted worse out-of-sample, which the authors read as overfitting of the 20-parameter specification.

outcome: Interview duration and number of life durations considered before the indifference point
statement: Interview burden was modest and 601 students completed the valuation tasks.
The cTTO value distributions were similar across arms and state types and all showed a spike at -1, suggesting some values would fall below -1 if the procedure allowed it.

Estimated dimension weights differed between the 2 student arms in rank order, but within an arm the CALE and conventional models agreed on the rank order of dimension weights and on level weights; anxiety/depression carried the largest weight and mobility a comparatively low weight.

outcome: Fit of the monotone homogeneity model (manifest monotonicity violations)
statement: All five EQ-5D-5L items showed manifest monotonicity with no violations, so the data fit the monotone homogeneity model and respondents can be ordered by the level summary score.

outcome: Item and scale scalability of the EQ-5D-5L (Loevinger H_ij, H_i, H_s)
statement: The full five-item EQ-5D-5L formed a strong Mokken scale with good reliability, but the anxiety/depression item had clearly weaker item scalability than the other items.

outcome: Item and scale scalability of the EQ-5D-5L (Loevinger H_ij, H_i, H_s)
statement: Removing the anxiety/depression item raised scale scalability and reliability substantially.

outcome: Item and scale scalability of the EQ-5D-5L (Loevinger H_ij, H_i, H_s)
statement: The automated item selection procedure kept all five items on one scale at the conventional lower bound of 0.3, and identified the order in which items dropped out as the bound was raised.

outcome: Accuracy of manifest invariant item ordering (H^T) and MIIO violations
statement: Manifest invariant item ordering was moderately accurate for the full scale, with the only violations involving anxiety/depression paired with mobility and with usual activities; excluding anxiety/depression removed all violations and gave highly accurate ordering.

outcome: Interpretability of the EQ-5D-5L level summary score from item ordering
statement: Items ordered by mean item score from easiest to hardest to endorse: pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression, usual activities, mobility, self-care.

outcome: Item and scale scalability of the EQ-5D-5L (Loevinger H_ij, H_i, H_s)
statement: Results were largely consistent across disease and country subgroups, but the scale was weak in the healthy subsample and item-ordering accuracy varied by subgroup.

outcome: Item and scale scalability of the EQ-5D-5L (Loevinger H_ij, H_i, H_s)
statement: Anxiety/depression was more strongly related to usual activities and pain/discomfort than to mobility and self-care, and its item-pair scalability was especially low in the healthy subsample.

outcome: Extent and characteristics of cognition bolt-on evidence
statement: The review included 181 publications from 1997 through 2023 that represented 137 distinct studies, and publication activity increased markedly after 2010.

outcome: Valuation and disability-weight evidence for cognition bolt-ons
statement: No included study developed a complete value set for EQ-5D plus a cognition bolt-on. One Australian burden-of-disease study used a multiplicative regression model based on Dutch disability weights to estimate weights for any EQ-5D-3L plus cognition state.

outcome: Methodological quality of cognition bolt-on item development
statement: The review team obtained exact bolt-on wording for about two thirds of the underlying studies; wording remained unavailable when materials were lost, authors declined to share it, or the team could not identify it.

outcome: Extent and characteristics of cognition bolt-on evidence
statement: The evidence covered cognition bolt-on development, use or psychometric testing, and valuation or disability-weight estimation; categories could overlap within a study.

outcome: Extent and characteristics of cognition bolt-on evidence
statement: Most studies used EQ-5D-3L with a three-level cognition bolt-on, while about one quarter used EQ-5D-5L with a five-level cognition bolt-on.

outcome: Extent and characteristics of cognition bolt-on evidence
statement: Cognition bolt-on content was highly heterogeneous: the authors identified 52 distinct wordings, with cognition and thinking ability as the most common dimension titles and concentrating, memory, and remembering as common examples.

outcome: Methodological quality of cognition bolt-on item development
statement: Methodological quality varied. Only 12 of 52 items scored 11 or 12 on the review checklist, all of these high-scoring items were five-level versions, and common weaknesses were little qualitative input, no translatability evidence, ambiguous wording, and inadequate examples.

outcome: Methodological quality of cognition bolt-on item development
statement: Only six development studies used qualitative methods. These studies used expert panels, focus groups, or individual interviews with experts, clinicians, general-population members, patients, and caregivers to develop 18 items.

outcome: Extent and characteristics of cognition bolt-on evidence
statement: The evidence came from 24 countries and used cognition bolt-ons in 28 languages, but nearly two thirds of studies came from the Netherlands and Dutch was the most common instrument language.

outcome: Use and administration of cognition bolt-ons
statement: Among 120 studies that administered cognition bolt-ons, most involved patient populations. Cross-sectional and longitudinal cohort designs were most common, face-to-face and mail were the leading modes, self-report predominated, and a minority used proxy reporting.

outcome: Valuation and disability-weight evidence for cognition bolt-ons
statement: In the 27 valuation or disability-weight studies, visual analogue scale and time trade-off were the most common elicitation methods. Many studies supplemented EQ-5D plus cognition descriptions with disease labels, symptoms, or images.

outcome: Adult-child perspective difference in cTTO utility
statement: In the mixed-effects regression, uncorrected cTTO utilities were significantly higher for the child perspective than for the adult own perspective.

outcome: Adult-child perspective difference in cTTO utility
statement: After correction for perspective-specific time preference, the child-perspective coefficient was close to zero and was not significant.

outcome: Uncorrected and time-preference-corrected cTTO health-state utilities
statement: Changing the cTTO gauge duration from 10 to 20 years did not have a significant overall effect on utility in either the uncorrected or corrected mixed-effects model.

outcome: Perspective-specific time preference measured by discount-function area under the curve
statement: Average time preference was close to zero for both perspectives; child-perspective AUC was slightly lower than adult-perspective AUC, but the difference was not significant and individual preferences were heterogeneous.

outcome: Adult-child perspective difference in cTTO utility
statement: Time-preference correction reduced the adult-child gap in all eight health-state-by-duration comparisons; this reduction was significant for state 32223 at 10 years and for all four states at 20 years.

For every health state and both durations, mean uncorrected utility was higher under the child perspective, but none of the individual paired comparisons was significant; corrected comparisons were also not significant.

outcome: cTTO response quality, trading patterns, and dominance violations
statement: Longer duration did not materially change trading behavior or response quality; the main observed perspective difference was more non-trading for children in the 10-year condition.
The exploratory bivariate mixed-logit model found statistically significant heterogeneity in both scale and discount rate and a strong positive correlation between them.
The confirmatory bivariate mixed-logit model found statistically significant heterogeneity in both scale and discount rate and a strong positive correlation between them.

In the exploratory analysis, the conditional-logit model had four incremental effects with p-values above 0.05, while all 20 effects in the bivariate mixed-logit model were positive and statistically significant.

In the confirmatory analysis, allowing correlated scale and rate heterogeneity reduced the number of insignificant incremental effects from six under conditional logit to two under bivariate mixed logit.
The 20 confirmatory incremental-effect estimates from conditional logit and bivariate mixed logit remained highly correlated and concordant.
Both models valued EQ-5D-5L health state 55555 as worse than immediate death for one year, but the bivariate model produced a value closer to zero than conditional logit.
Both models valued EQ-5D-5L health state 55555 as worse than immediate death for one year, but the bivariate model raised its estimated value from -0.545 to -0.191.
The two remaining insignificant confirmatory bivariate effects were the change from no to slight pain or discomfort and the change from severe to extreme anxiety or depression.

outcome: Mean EQ-5D-5L utility index score by age group, sex and IMD quintile
statement: Mean EQ-5D-5L utility declined with age for both sexes, and women reported lower mean HRQoL than men in all age groups.

outcome: Mean EQ-5D-5L utility index score by age group, sex and IMD quintile
statement: Mean EQ-5D-5L utility followed a socioeconomic gradient, with lower scores in more deprived IMD quintiles.

outcome: Absolute difference, relative difference and concentration index of EQ-5D-5L utility across deprivation quintiles
statement: Relative inequality between the most and least deprived quintiles was not statistically significant up to age 35-39, reached a maximum around age 60-64, and narrowed again in the oldest age groups.

outcome: Absolute difference, relative difference and concentration index of EQ-5D-5L utility across deprivation quintiles
statement: Absolute gaps in EQ-5D-5L utility between the most and least deprived quintiles exceeded the minimally important difference of 0.063 between ages 40-74 for females and 45-69 for males.

outcome: Absolute difference, relative difference and concentration index of EQ-5D-5L utility across deprivation quintiles
statement: Concentration indices were positive for nearly all age groups, indicating HRQoL concentrated among less deprived quintiles, and peaked at ages 60-64.

outcome: Proportion of respondents reporting no, slight, moderate, severe or extreme problems on each EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: Inequalities were present on all five EQ-5D-5L dimensions; pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression and self-care peaked between ages 55 and 65, whereas mobility inequality increased steadily with age and peaked at ages 75-79.

outcome: Mean EQ-5D-5L utility index score by age group, sex and IMD quintile
statement: Average HRQoL of 45-49 year old males in the most deprived fifth of neighbourhoods was lower than that of 75-79 year old males in the least deprived fifth.

outcome: Proportion of respondents reporting no, slight, moderate, severe or extreme problems on each EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: Severe or extreme mobility problems in the 85+ age group were more frequent in the most deprived than in the least deprived fifth of neighbourhoods.
Greater socioeconomic deprivation was associated with worse preoperative and 12-month PROM scores in THA and TKA patients. Differences were largest before surgery and became smaller by 12 months.

OHS and OKS differences were similar to or larger than EQ-5D differences. EQ VAS differences were smaller, NRS pain differences were comparable to the multi-item measures, and 12-month NRS satisfaction in TKA did not differ between the most and least deprived groups. Hypotheses 1 and 2 were not met, but hypothesis 3 was met.

In the EQ-5D-3L cohorts, usual activities made the largest or one of the largest contributions to socioeconomic score differences, while anxiety/depression made a limited contribution. At 12 months, OHS function contributed most in THA and OKS pain contributed most in TKA.

The EQ-5D-5L cohorts generally showed patterns similar to the EQ-5D-3L cohorts. The preoperative EQ-5D-5L difference in TKA was smaller and not statistically significant, and most 12-month differences were smaller in the 5L cohorts.
No PROM had a ceiling preoperatively. All PROMs had some ceiling at 12 months, with the largest ceiling for NRS pain outcomes and the smallest for EQ VAS.

The socioeconomic difference at 12 months was larger among patients with low preoperative PROM scores than among patients with high preoperative scores. This pattern was less clear for EQ VAS, especially in TKA.
cTTO produced more unique values per respondent; nTTO showed clustering at -1, and oTTO showed more integer responses, spikes, and gaps.
nTTO and oTTO produced more respondents with any logical inconsistency than cTTO, while severe inconsistency frequencies were low and not significantly different.
Overall mean TTO values and percentages of negative values were similar across methods and were not statistically different.
CALE modeling performance ranked cTTO best, nTTO second, and oTTO third by model fit and prediction criteria.
The two non-iterative methods produced acceptable but inferior TTO data compared with cTTO while reducing administration burden.
Both non-iterative methods reduced practice-task and formal-task time, with total interviews about 10 minutes shorter than cTTO.

PedsQL, EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, CHU9D, and PROMIS-25 were reported as easy and quick to complete. EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L were generally the fastest measures, while AQoL-6D and HUI3 were generally the slowest.
Follow-up completion was low and varied by condition, from 27.8% for sleep problems to 50.0% for enuresis.

Ceiling effects above 15% occurred for EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L in asthma, epilepsy, sleep problems, dental problems, type 1 diabetes, and enuresis; PROMIS-25 also had a ceiling effect in asthma under the exploratory total-score method. No instrument had a floor effect.

All measures distinguished the healthy reference group from each condition group and supported known-groups validity; effects were smaller for asthma and dental problems than for other condition groups.
Where sample sizes were adequate, all measures distinguished less severe from more severe disease. Effects were moderate or large except for small effects for EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L in enuresis.

Test-retest reliability varied by condition. PedsQL and EQ-5D-Y-5L were the most consistently reliable: both had moderate reliability in autism and epilepsy and good reliability in enuresis; EQ-5D-Y-5L was the only measure with moderate reliability in asthma, while PedsQL and CHU9D had moderate reliability in dental problems.

In the condition and instrument analyses with adequate samples, no measure detected a statistically significant improvement in total score in the hypothesized direction among children or caregivers who reported improved health. Samples were inadequate for robust responsiveness analysis in most condition groups and for AQoL-6D, HUI3, and PROMIS-25.
All generic measures were strongly correlated with one another, except HUI3 in recurrent abdominal pain, which had moderate correlations with the other measures.

PROMIS-25 results depended on scoring. Domain T-score sensitivity analysis showed ceiling effects in at least two domains in every condition group and weaker ceiling-effect and known-groups performance than the exploratory single total score.

The condition-specific summary favored PedsQL and EQ-5D-Y-5L for autism; PedsQL for asthma, sleep problems, dental problems, and enuresis; PedsQL and CHU9D for eating disorders, epilepsy, and type 1 diabetes; and PedsQL, EQ-5D-Y-5L, and CHU9D for recurrent abdominal pain.
Of 115 valuation respondents, 73 assigned at least one worse-than-dead cTTO value; 19 were interviewed and analyzed.
Eight respondents used simplifying heuristics: attribute nonattendance, affect heuristic, or elimination by aspects; affect and elimination strategies often produced all-in trading for severe states.
Twelve respondents had difficulty identifying an indifference point; lead-time TTO was seen as more cognitively complex and emotionally demanding than conventional TTO.

Worse-than-dead judgments reflected interconnected considerations about health-state severity and duration, personal beliefs and circumstances, and consequences of poor health; being a burden to others was the most frequent reason.
The predefined saturation criterion was met after 16 interviews, and three more interviews were used to validate saturation and improve age and gender heterogeneity.
Some respondents had difficulty imagining hypothetical severe health states, interpreting EQ-5D-5L attribute levels, or estimating their ability to adapt to poor health.
Respondents usually made a cognitively complex, comprehensive trade-off between length and quality of life, but some could not explain the precise indifference point and relied on intuition.
Two respondents were confused by the transition from conventional to lead-time TTO and gave logically inconsistent responses.
In the 19-person qualitative sample, cTTO values covered the full bounded range and a substantial share was negative; some -1 responses did not reach indifference.
The final analysis included 366 adults. Recruitment was difficult, and the sample overrepresented older women and underrepresented men in all age groups.
Bermuda value-set coefficients differed from those reported for other countries, including nearby Trinidad and Tobago and the United States and United Kingdom.
Just over half of respondents reported EQ-5D-3L state 11111. Pain or discomfort was the most common level-2 problem, and the mean EQ VAS score was 80.4.

outcome: Bermuda EQ-5D-3L health-state index values
statement: The study collected 3,660 cTTO responses, and 20.9% of these responses valued a health state as worse than dead.
The bootstrap hybrid model produced logically consistent and statistically significant coefficients. It had the same mean absolute deviation from observed cTTO means as the bootstrap cTTO model.
The hybrid and cTTO bootstrap value sets were similar, and sensitivity analyses that removed feedback-flagged states or retained five excluded interviews did not affect the estimated values.
In the Bermuda EQ-5D-3L value set, pain or discomfort and anxiety or depression had the largest level-2 decrements. Mobility and pain or discomfort had the largest level-3 decrements.
The Bermuda EQ-5D-3L value set contained 34 negative health-state values, and state 33333 had the lowest value.

outcome: EQ-VT interview quality-control flags and protocol compliance
statement: Sixty-eight included interviews had at least one quality-control flag. Two interviewers with continued protocol violations were removed, and their five interviews were excluded.

outcome: Feasibility of online EQ-VT valuation in a small population
statement: The online EQ-VT study was completed successfully, but only 17.6% of recruiting-firm contacts resulted in valuation interviews and 809 prospective respondents refused or ended interviews early.

outcome: Proportion of respondents reporting mild-extreme problems (levels 2-5) in each EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: In the emergency department sample, the proportion reporting mild-extreme problems fell slightly from pre-COVID to wave 2 in mobility, self-care, usual activities and pain/discomfort, and rose marginally in anxiety/depression.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index score scored with the Canadian value set
statement: In the emergency department sample, changes in the EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS scores from pre-COVID to wave 2 were small and below the minimal important difference.

outcome: Proportion of respondents reporting mild-extreme problems (levels 2-5) in each EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: In the primary care sample, the proportion reporting mild-extreme problems increased most in anxiety/depression and in pain/discomfort from pre-COVID to wave 2, while index and VAS changes were not statistically significant.

outcome: Proportion of respondents reporting mild-extreme problems (levels 2-5) in each EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: The proportion of primary care respondents reporting mild-extreme anxiety/depression rose across pandemic periods and was far above the pre-pandemic Alberta general population level.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index score scored with the Canadian value set
statement: EQ-5D-5L index and VAS scores in both the emergency department and primary care samples were lower than in the Alberta general population norms sample in all three pandemic periods.

outcome: Proportion of respondents reporting mild-extreme problems (levels 2-5) in each EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: In the emergency department survey there were no significant variations in pandemic impact on HRQL across age, sex and income subgroups, whereas in the primary care survey younger adults, females and higher-income respondents showed the largest deteriorations.

outcome: Proportion of respondents reporting mild-extreme problems (levels 2-5) in each EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: In the emergency department survey, statistically significant decreases in reporting problems from pre-COVID to wave 2 occurred in specific subgroups for mobility, usual activities and pain/discomfort.

outcome: Proportion of respondents reporting mild-extreme problems (levels 2-5) in each EQ-5D-5L dimension
statement: In the primary care survey, the largest subgroup changes were increases in reporting mild-extreme anxiety/depression, greatest in the youngest age group.

Respondent characteristics were largely stable across pandemic periods, with no differences in the primary care survey and small but statistically significant differences in education and self-reported health in the emergency department survey.
The proposed framework links stronger proximal and distal terror management defenses to a stronger value of prolonging life and therefore to fewer life-years traded in TTO.

outcome: Agreement between framework-predicted and literature-reported directions of TTO associations
statement: In the main results table, framework predictions agreed with the direction of significant characteristics in 32 of 37 studies, more often than expected under random 50% agreement.
Higher-status socioeconomic characteristics, including marriage, employment, children, longer education, and stable housing, were associated with fewer years traded in 19 of 23 studies.
Respondents who favored euthanasia or its legalization traded more years in all three identified studies.
Respondents with higher subjective life expectancy traded fewer years in all three identified studies.
The results table reports that the predicted direction for religiosity was confirmed in 7 of 8 studies; the narrative section gives a different count of 6 of 7.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility score, EQ VAS score, domain problem rates and reported fatigue levels
statement: Just under half of the general population sample reported at least mild fatigue, and fatigue was more frequent and more severe in respondents with a chronic health condition.
