outcome: Ceiling: proportion of respondents in the best profile (11111 vs 111111) and number of unique observed profiles
statement: Adding the fatigue item reduced the ceiling: 37% of respondents were in full health on the EQ-5D-5L versus 25% on the EQ-5D-5L + Fatigue.

outcome: Absolute and relative informativity (Shannon H' and Shannon Evenness J')
statement: Absolute and relative informativity increased when the fatigue item was added, with the largest gain in absolute informativity.

outcome: Convergent validity: Spearman rank correlation of level sum score with EQ VAS
statement: Convergent validity with the EQ VAS increased slightly when the fatigue item was added.

outcome: Domain dependency (dominance) between EQ-5D-5L domains and the fatigue item
statement: Domain dependency analysis showed that all five EQ-5D-5L domains are dominant over the fatigue item: severe fatigue with no problems on another domain was common, while the reverse was rare.

outcome: Explanatory power (R-squared) for EQ VAS of models with and without the fatigue item
statement: Explanatory power for the EQ VAS increased when the fatigue item was added, and the fatigue item added more explanatory power than any single EQ-5D-5L domain it could replace.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L utility score, EQ VAS score, domain problem rates and reported fatigue levels
statement: Mean EQ VAS fell steadily as fatigue severity increased, except within the 11111 profile where the gradient was flat and not statistically significant.

outcome: Explanatory power (R-squared) for EQ VAS of models with and without the fatigue item
statement: Gains from the fatigue item were consistently larger in the subgroup with a chronic health condition than in the subgroup without.
Adding each bolt-on significantly reduced the EQ-5D-5L full-health ceiling, with only small differences between wording variants.
Each bolt-on increased scale-level relative informativity compared with EQ-5D-5L alone.

Fatigue and tiredness correlated moderately to strongly with PROMIS fatigue items, and both sleep variants correlated strongly with PROMIS sleep items; both vision variants had weak correlations with EQ-5D-5L dimensions and EQ VAS.
Responses showed strong agreement within all three bolt-on pairs, and most disagreements were only one response level.
Most bolt-ons modestly increased the adjusted explanatory power of multivariable EQ-5D-5L models for EQ VAS and PROMIS-29+2 level sum scores; vision with aids did not improve the EQ VAS model.
EQ-5D-5L alone and with bolt-ons discriminated known groups with small to moderate effect sizes; bolt-ons improved discrimination in most comparisons without changing effect-size categories.

Between-variant differences were small: tiredness had slightly higher informativity than fatigue; sleep with examples had slightly better ceiling, informativity, and known-groups performance than sleep; and vision with aids had small ceiling and informativity advantages over vision. Fatigue best explained EQ VAS, while tiredness best explained PROMIS-29+2 scores.

Almost all patients considered the two psoriasis-specific bolt-ons relevant areas for describing psoriasis problems, and all patients rated the EQ-PSO better than the EQ-5D-5L for describing their health-related quality of life problems.
Many patients did not apply the stated today recall period and several reported that the recall period may bias responses because their symptoms fluctuate daily or within a day.

Ten patients suggested changes to EQ-5D-5L or EQ-PSO dimensions, including broader mobility descriptors, splitting self-care, pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression, and replacing anxiety with stress or depression with mood disorder.

In the focus group, three of five patients considered itch a form of discomfort and answered the EQ-PSO accordingly, all agreed skin irritation is broader than itching, and the group concluded that self-confidence and anxiety/depression are related but not overlapping constructs.
Most patients interpreted the EQ VAS as a generic health scale, but a few used it as a psoriasis-specific scale and two mixed up the 0 and 100 endpoints.
Only a minority of patients judged the EQ-5D-5L as covering the important aspects of health-related quality of life, and some considered several of its dimensions irrelevant to psoriasis.

Patients reported 35 aspects of the impact of psoriasis grouped into six concepts (triggers, physical symptoms, mental health consequences, HRQoL consequences, searching for a cure, coping); the EQ-PSO covered nearly all of these except skin scaling and lost time due to psoriasis.

More concepts were reported as missing from the EQ-5D-5L than from the EQ-PSO, with social relationships the most frequently named missing concept for both measures and itching named as missing only by one patient for the EQ-5D-5L.
A minor conceptual overlap was identified between skin irritation and pain/discomfort, and between self-confidence and anxiety/depression.

Adding the two bolt-ons substantially changed which dimensions patients ranked as most relevant: skin irritation became the most relevant dimension in the EQ-PSO, followed by self-confidence, while usual activities and anxiety/depression were ranked most relevant in the EQ-5D-5L and self-care least relevant.
Some patients interpreted core dimension wording in a psoriasis-specific way, most prominently reading dressing myself in self-care as a limitation on which clothes they can wear.

Patients agreed on the meaning of skin irritation in terms of itch, but several regarded skin irritation as broader than itch and proposed adding skin scaling, cracking or flaking as supporting examples.
Some patients reframed or struggled with the response levels, using them as a frequency scale or as a level of bother, and reported difficulty in distinguishing adjacent levels.

outcome: Missing values and distributional properties (floor and ceiling effects)
statement: Missing values were negligible and below 5 percent for both versions in the 15 studies reporting them.

outcome: Missing values and distributional properties (floor and ceiling effects)
statement: Floor effects were small for both versions, with the largest mean absolute reduction for the 5L in Pain/Discomfort.

outcome: Missing values and distributional properties (floor and ceiling effects)
statement: All but three of the studies reporting ceiling effects found a lower proportion reporting full health ('11111') with the 5L than with the 3L, and pooled ceiling proportions were lower for the 5L in both patient and population samples.

outcome: Informativity (Shannon's H' and J')
statement: Shannon's H' was always higher for the 5L than the 3L, and Shannon's J' was higher for the 5L in all but five of the 14 studies reporting informativity.

outcome: Inconsistent 3L-5L paired responses
statement: Inconsistent 3L-5L response pairs were generally well below 5 percent, were most frequent for Usual Activities and least frequent for Mobility, and were highest in orthopedic settings.

outcome: Responsiveness to change
statement: Only three studies assessed responsiveness and the evidence was mixed: two found better responsiveness for the 5L with non-parametric statistics, while one found the crosswalk-derived 5L index less responsive than the 3L index.

outcome: Test-retest reliability
statement: Test-retest reliability from six studies showed no clear advantage at dimension level, but index-level intraclass correlations were higher for the 5L, while percentage agreement was equal or higher for the 3L.
The included evidence spanned 24 articles from 18 countries, covering 8 general population and 16 patient samples, with all but two studies using head-to-head administration of both versions.
Of 16,683 respondents who completed the T1 questionnaire, 6765 (41%) completed the T2 questionnaire one year later, with response rates ranging from 32% in the United States to 56% in Italy.
Losing a job and a decreased household income were associated with the greatest mean deterioration in mental well-being.
The average effect of negative recent life events on HRQoL and mental well-being was larger in absolute terms than the effect of positive recent life events.
The multivariable models explained very little of the variance in change scores (R-square 0.002 to 0.017).

Nonresponse analysis showed that respondents who completed the T2 questionnaire were significantly older and reported significantly fewer chronic conditions than the full T1 sample, and differed in education and occupational status.
Most respondents reported the same EQ-5D-5L dimension levels at T1 and T2 (65% to 91% per dimension); change was most frequent in the Anxiety/Depression dimension.
About one third of respondents improved on the HRQoL measures between T1 and T2, while a similar or slightly smaller share deteriorated; EQ VAS showed more deterioration than improvement.

Mental well-being measured by the WHO-5 index improved in 44% of respondents, was unchanged in 16% and deteriorated in 41%, with improvement most frequent in the United States and deterioration most frequent in Greece.
HRQoL improvement was most common among respondents in Greece, whereas deterioration was most prevalent among respondents in the United Kingdom.
In the multivariable models, reported (past) COVID-19 infection at T1 was consistently associated with improved HRQoL and mental well-being relative to respondents not infected at T1.

Low income at baseline was independently associated with greater deterioration in HRQoL, while having one or more chronic conditions at baseline was associated with relative improvement; living alone was associated with deterioration in the univariate analyses.
A low education level was associated with greater deterioration in mental well-being compared with a high education level.
An increase in the number of chronic conditions between waves produced the largest mean deterioration on all four outcome measures, while a decrease produced the largest mean improvement.
Mean EQ-5D-5L utility differed across the three countries in each wave; US values were higher than values in Sweden and Norway in both waves.
Mean rescaled EQ VAS scores differed across countries in each wave; US scores were higher than scores in Sweden and Norway in both waves.
Between waves, Norway had a significant decrease in mean EQ-5D-5L utility, while the United States had a significant increase in mean EQ VAS; Swedish changes were not significant.

Anxiety/depression was the most frequently reported EQ-5D-5L problem in the United States and Sweden in both waves, at more than 50%, while pain/discomfort ranked first in Norway and anxiety/depression ranked second. Younger respondents reported proportionally more anxiety/depression problems than older respondents.
Population QALYs increased between waves in the United States and Sweden but decreased in Norway; all Norwegian age groups except ages 45–54 had estimated QALY losses.

Greater fear about health was associated with lower utility and EQ VAS scores in all three countries. Greater financial fear was negatively associated with both outcomes in the United States and Sweden, and employment was associated with better HRQoL in every country.

Ordinal logistic regression found that greater health and financial fear were associated with worse anxiety/depression, while older age and employment were associated with fewer anxiety/depression problems in all three countries.
The largest level-5 decrement was for mobility, followed by pain/discomfort, self-care, anxiety/depression, and usual activities.
The study produced the first Ghanaian EQ-5D-5L value set based on social preferences.
The Ghanaian value set was developed for use in QALY-based economic evaluation and HTA priority setting.
The preferred value-set model was a constrained hybrid Tobit random-effect heteroskedastic model.
The 300 interviews produced 4,500 cTTO responses and 4,200 DCE responses.
The respondent characteristics were representative of Ghana for religion, education, and marital status.
The predicted value was -0.493 for EQ-5D-5L state 55555 and 0.969 for state 11112, the best state other than full health.

Framework analysis of the 25 interviews produced 28 categories grouped under 5 themes: performing the valuation tasks, perceptions about the person living in the health states, interpreting and assessing the health states, influencing factors, and stating a preference; data saturation was reached after 21 interviews.

Most participants found the valuation tasks more mentally and emotionally straining when performed for a 10-year-old child and a 15-year-old adolescent than for themselves, and some used heuristics such as speeding, straight lining, focusing on or discarding dimensions, or emotional distancing to make the tasks easier.

Participants had a stable self-image, but varied greatly and were often ambiguous about whom they imagined as the 10-year-old child or 15-year-old adolescent, alternating between their own (grand)child, themselves at that age, and an unknown child or adolescent; childhood memories of being 15 were easier to recall than of being 10.

The relative importance of dimensions and levels depended on the perspective: participants judged independence in walking about and looking after myself as more important for a 15-year-old adolescent, judged problems in pain or discomfort and feeling worried, sad, or unhappy as short-lived and less important for a 10-year-old child, and considered being worried, sad, or unhappy as normal in puberty.

Participants believed a 10-year-old child was more flexible, resilient, and better able to cope with impaired health, whereas an adult and a 15-year-old adolescent would understand and therefore suffer more from an impaired health state.

A wide range of nonhealth-related factors influenced stated preferences, including housing and facilities, support systems, notions of normal and acceptable health, anticipated preferences of the child or adolescent and of others, having or not having children, life events and goals, and hope for improvement or new health technology, despite instructions that health states would not change.

Participants gave up relatively few life-years for a 10-year-old child and a 15-year-old adolescent, struggled with the responsibility of inflicting health states on them, sometimes felt not entitled to choose, and reported withholding life-year trades partly for fear of being blamed, resented, or considered a bad parent, with some describing their own preferences as selfish.

Participants believed a 15-year-old adolescent should decide about their own prospective health, and that a 10-year-old child should at least be consulted; some compromised between their own preferences and the anticipated preferences of the child or adolescent.

Conceptually overlapping EQ-HWB and EQ-5D-5L items showed moderate to strong correlations in the full sample, with the strongest reported associations for mobility and anxiety-related content; fewer expected correlations were present in the low-literacy group.
EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-9 level summary scores correlated strongly with EQ-5D-5L level summary scores and inversely with EQ VAS and WEMWBS scores in the relevant full or literate samples.
EQ-HWB had five of 25 items above the 70% ceiling threshold, whereas EQ-HWB-9 had one of nine; no item-level floor effects were found for either instrument.
Interviewer-administered EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-9 were feasible and retained good item-level and acceptable score-level reliability in respondents with low literacy or illiteracy.
The patient group reported the worst mean EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-9 scores, while the low-literacy group reported the most favorable mean EQ-HWB-9 utility.

Both EQ-HWB versions discriminated between patients and nonpatients and between EQ VAS scores below 80 and scores of 80 or above; poorer-health groups had higher level summary scores and lower EQ-HWB-9 utility scores.
Score-level agreement between self-completion and interviewer administration was excellent in the combined literate and patient sample, and item agreement ranged from moderate to almost perfect.

Among 123 respondents reporting stable health, score-level and most item-level test-retest reliability was high across administration modes; low-literacy subgroup score ICCs were lower but remained in the reported acceptable range.
More than 70% of participants rated every assessed instrument as somewhat or very easy; EQ-5D-Y-5L without EQ VAS had the highest ease rating.
Of 5945 eligible participants aged 5-18 years who completed the initial survey, 2346 completed the follow-up survey; the abstract and table report a 39.5% completion rate.
Hospital-recruited participants had substantially higher follow-up completion than online-panel participants.
Eligible participants provided similarly good-quality data across recruitment pathways, with very few extremely inconsistent responses on paired EQ-5D-Y-5L and CHU9D items.
Failure of minimum data-quality eligibility criteria was much more common in online-panel samples than in the hospital sample.
Hospital recruitment cost more per participant and took longer than online-panel recruitment.
At follow-up, participants reported greater ease and completed instruments faster than at the initial survey.
All instruments were completed in less than 3 minutes on average; EQ-5D-Y-5L without EQ VAS was fastest and AQoL-6D was slowest by median completion time.

Younger participants reported greater ease for all instruments except AQoL-6D; general-population panel participants reported greater ease and generally faster completion than condition-group participants.

outcome: TTO data quality
statement: The study completed its target of 1200 interviews and achieved quotas for age, sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic group, and proportional representation across the four United Kingdom nations.
Mixed interview delivery supported inclusion: 1102 interviews were by videoconference and 98 were in person; seven interviews were in Welsh and the rest were in English.

outcome: TTO data quality
statement: After the feedback module, 10 680 of 12 000 TTO responses remained. Data-quality standards were achieved, with high reported understanding, few serious logical inconsistencies, and a low proportion of respondents using only easy-to-reach TTO values.

outcome: Candidate model performance and robustness
statement: The selected value-set model was a random-effects Tobit model censored at -1 with no constant. It was logically consistent, accounted for repeated observations, and performed well under predefined fit, consistency, significance, and robustness criteria.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state utilities and utility decrements
statement: The value set assigns the largest level-5 decrement to pain/discomfort, followed by anxiety/depression, mobility, usual activities, and self-care; the value of state 55555 is -0.567.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state utilities and utility decrements
statement: Compared with the United Kingdom EQ-5D-3L value set, anxiety/depression and usual activities had greater relative impacts. The worst-state value was comparable, but fewer EQ-5D-5L states had values below zero and the least severe impaired state had a higher value.

outcome: Candidate model performance and robustness
statement: Results were largely robust to inclusion of reconsidered TTO values, exclusion of participants whom interviewers judged not to understand or engage, and use of the 102-state versus 86-state design; the extended design reduced logical inconsistency in heteroscedastic Tobit models.

outcome: Participant understanding and views of the interview
statement: Participant understanding was confirmed for most participants by self-report and interviewer report, and participant views of the interview were positive overall.
Forward translation produced initial Arabic paper and digital versions. Back translation led to only one change in the digital missing-item message before the second consensus version was produced.
Children generally understood the intended hierarchy of severity qualifiers: 10 of 160 card rankings were incorrect, with inversions concentrated between adjacent middle levels.

All 11 children described the questionnaire as clear and easy to understand and answer; 10 said it was not too long. Six needed confirmation of their understanding of the general or EQ VAS instructions.
Questionnaire self-completion took a mean of 5.2 minutes, and the complete cognitive-debriefing interview took a mean of 38 minutes.

Initial interviews identified possible emotional interpretations of pain or discomfort, poor understanding of the Arabic word used for digital item, and changes needed in EQ VAS instructions. Three additional interviews supported the revised physical-pain term, the replacement word for item, and the instruction changes; all proposed changes were accepted.
The translation, cognitive testing, and proofreading process produced a final approved Standard Arabic EQ-5D-Y-5L version for Egypt in paper and digital forms.

outcome: DCE task feasibility: completion, time, speeding, patterned responses, and dominant-choice performance
statement: All 36 participants completed the full set of choice tasks.

outcome: Adolescent understanding, technology use, engagement, interpretation, and suggestions for questionnaire improvement
statement: For DCE with duration, the time attribute changed how some participants perceived health states and prioritized health dimensions, but some assumed that health could improve during the period or imagined themselves as older.

outcome: Adolescent understanding, technology use, engagement, interpretation, and suggestions for questionnaire improvement
statement: Across all focus groups, participants reported greater difficulty with the EQ VAS than with DCE or DCE with duration.

outcome: Convergence and divergence between quantitative feasibility indicators and qualitative participant experience
statement: Quantitative and qualitative evidence converged on the feasibility of completing DCE tasks, but qualitative findings showed that participant interpretation varied in ways not visible in the quantitative feasibility indicators.

outcome: Adolescent understanding, technology use, engagement, interpretation, and suggestions for questionnaire improvement
statement: The main problems concerned interpretation: presentation, abstract reasoning, differentiation between severity levels or health states, and framing. Participants sometimes used mental shortcuts, focused on selected dimensions, or imagined a person or time perspective other than the instructed present self.

outcome: DCE task feasibility: completion, time, speeding, patterned responses, and dominant-choice performance
statement: No participant showed speeding at either threshold, patterned responses, or an incorrect answer to the dominant choice task.

outcome: DCE task feasibility: completion, time, speeding, patterned responses, and dominant-choice performance
statement: The average time to complete all DCE tasks was 7 minutes, with a range of 3 to 12 minutes.

outcome: Adolescent understanding, technology use, engagement, interpretation, and suggestions for questionnaire improvement
statement: Participants reported clear instructions and no problems with understanding; technology and engagement problems were minor.

outcome: Response distribution across severity levels, and ceiling and floor effects of the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L
statement: Ceiling and floor effects were small (less than 0.5%) and comparable for both EQ-5D versions in both the THA and TKA samples.

outcome: Response distribution across severity levels, and ceiling and floor effects of the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L
statement: Responses were distributed more evenly across severity levels for the EQ-5D-5L than for the EQ-5D-3L, most markedly for mobility, where more than 90% of patients reported level 2 on the 3L while no 5L level held more than 50% of responses.

outcome: Convergent construct validity: Spearman correlations of EQ-5D dimensions and index with WOMAC domains and overall score
statement: The EQ-5D-5L consistently correlated more strongly with WOMAC overall and domain scores than the EQ-5D-3L at both index and dimension level; the EQ-5D-3L mobility dimension correlated only weakly with WOMAC physical function while the EQ-5D-5L mobility dimension correlated strongly.

outcome: Known-group construct validity: differences in EQ-5D index scores between predefined known groups, with effect sizes
statement: All known-group hypotheses were confirmed for both EQ-5D versions in patients awaiting THA and TKA, with statistically significant index-score differences of small effect size, except the WOMAC physical function grouping, which gave large effect sizes.

outcome: Informativity and discriminatory power: Shannon index and Shannon evenness index per EQ-5D dimension
statement: The EQ-5D-5L had higher Shannon and Shannon evenness indices than the EQ-5D-3L for every dimension, with the largest gain for mobility.

outcome: EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L index scores at baseline before surgery
statement: EQ-5D-5L index scores were consistently lower than the matched EQ-5D-3L index scores in both patient groups, and the difference persisted in a sensitivity analysis that used the US EQ-5D-3L value set.

outcome: Response distribution across severity levels, and ceiling and floor effects of the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L
statement: Level 3 of the EQ-5D-3L mobility dimension (confined to bed) was reported by only 0.8% of patients in the sample.

Propensity score matching balanced the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L samples, leaving no statistically significant differences in age, gender or WOMAC domain scores, although differences in number of preoperative risk factors and mental health history remained.

outcome: Ease, understanding, and respondent preference for kaizen tasks versus paired comparisons
statement: Most respondents reported that kaizen tasks were easier to complete, easier to understand, and preferable to paired comparisons.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L incremental values and profile values on the experience scale
statement: All 10 EQ-5D-Y-3L incremental main effects were statistically significant, and relief of pain or discomfort had the largest estimated value.

outcome: Agreement of new estimates with original and alternative estimates
statement: The new experience-scale main effects correlated strongly with the original United States QALY-scale main effects.

outcome: Scale sensitivity, estimate precision, and robustness
statement: After adjustment for scale differences, confidence intervals for the new main effects were narrower than those from the original survey, although the original survey was more than six times larger.

outcome: Agreement of new estimates with original and alternative estimates
statement: Alternative paired-comparison, block-specific, and mixed-logit specifications largely agreed with the main kaizen conditional-logit estimates.

outcome: Scale sensitivity, estimate precision, and robustness
statement: Kaizen tasks showed greater sensitivity to value differences than the comparisons between an EQ-5D-Y-3L profile and being in a coma.

outcome: Scale sensitivity, estimate precision, and robustness
statement: In Block 1, all effects were significant and had standard errors below 0.05 with 50 respondents.

outcome: Survey and component completion time
statement: Median total survey completion time was about 17 minutes; the kaizen component took a median of 2.6 minutes.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L incremental values and profile values on the experience scale
statement: The worst EQ-5D-Y-3L profile, 33333, had a negative experience-scale value and was worse than being in a coma for one week.
Linear mapping without a constant had the best prediction accuracy across the three anchoring approaches and was selected to produce the final value set.
Among observed cTTO responses, 16.5% were negative and 4.2% were -1. State 33333 had the lowest mean observed value and remained negative after Tobit adjustment.

The mixed logit model with an alternative-specific constant for left-right position had the lowest BIC and highest log-likelihood among the tested DCE models; all dimension-level coefficients were statistically significant at the 0.05 level.
Of the DCE completers, 97.2% passed both dominant-pair checks, and no respondent completed the DCE tasks in less than the 150-second quality threshold.
For non-full-health states, final value-set utilities ranged from 0.981 for state 12111 to -0.200 for state 33333; six states, or 2.5% of all states, had negative utility.
The final value set ranked the dimensions from most to least important as pain or discomfort; feeling worried, sad, or unhappy; doing usual activities; mobility; and looking after oneself.
The analyzed samples matched the 2021 Hong Kong population distribution for age, sex, and geography.

Scores on comparable JAMAR items differed significantly across the three EQ-5D-Y levels for mobility, looking after myself, usual activities and pain, but not for the anxiety item, indicating concurrent validity for most dimensions.
Concurrent validity with the PedsQL Rheumatology Module dimensions was poor except for pain, where the PedsQL pain subtotal differed significantly across EQ-5D-Y pain levels.
The EQ-5D-Y latent value and EQ VAS correlated significantly with the JAMAR HRQoL total and PedsQL total scores, with the latent value showing the stronger correlations.

All measures distinguished between children with mild and moderate JIA severity, with medium to large effect sizes; the PedsQL total gave the largest effect size and the EQ-5D-Y latent value a large effect size, while the EQ VAS gave a medium effect size.
The EQ-5D-Y was the quickest instrument to complete and no outcome measure had missing responses.
Most problems on the EQ-5D-Y were reported in pain or discomfort, then mobility, usual activities and feeling worried, sad or unhappy, with fewest problems in looking after myself.
Reported health worsened with age in females on the EQ VAS, while older males reported fewer problems on the EQ-5D-Y dimensions.
Most recruited children had mild disease according to the JAMAR composite severity score.

outcome: Missing or uninterpretable valuations per health state
statement: Missing or uninterpretable valuations were far less frequent with the scoring questionnaire (version III) than with either lines-to-VAS version, averaging 3.0% versus 10.8% (version I) and 14.2% (version II) across all states.

outcome: Digit preference in raw valuations
statement: Digit preference differed markedly between elicitation formats: scored valuations were far less likely to end in a digit other than 0 or 5, while the inadvertently two-unit-demarcated VAS in version II sharply reduced values ending in 5.

outcome: Missing or uninterpretable valuations per health state
statement: Missing data for the state 'dead' fell sharply with the new two-stage scoring approach.

outcome: Responses excluded under EuroQol Group exclusion criteria
statement: Significantly more version III responses were usable for estimating a social tariff after applying EuroQol Group exclusion criteria.

outcome: Pairwise logical inconsistencies in valuations
statement: Logical inconsistencies were less frequent in the scoring version: nearly half of version III responses had no pairwise inconsistency compared with about a third under both lines-to-VAS versions.

outcome: Raw and rescaled EQ-5D health state values
statement: Mean rescaled health state values were statistically indistinguishable across the three questionnaire versions for all but two states (12111 and 32211), with near-identical rank orderings; 33333 was the only negatively valued state.

outcome: Survey response rate
statement: Response rates did not differ meaningfully between questionnaire versions.

outcome: Respondent-reported understanding, difficulty and descriptive adequacy of EQ-5D
statement: More respondents said they understood the valuation questions under the redesigned versions than under the standard questionnaire, while perceived difficulty and the perceived descriptive adequacy of EQ-5D did not differ.

outcome: Pairwise logical inconsistencies in valuations
statement: The new questions about states worse than dead produced substantial internal inconsistency: most responses that nominated states worse than dead then scored 'dead' at or below those states.

outcome: Responses excluded under EuroQol Group exclusion criteria
statement: Version III also produced more responses excluded because 'dead' was valued at or above full health (11111), partly offsetting its gain in usable responses.

Agreement between each split subdimension and the composite item was fair to moderate; depression generally agreed more closely with the composite item, and agreement was highest for depression among participants with both conditions.
The split depression subdimension had stronger correlations with PHQ-9 and GAD-7 than the composite anxiety/depression dimension and showed minimally better convergent validity.

Adding either split subdimension to EQ-4D-5L produced slightly higher absolute and relative informativity than standard EQ-5D-5L; replacing the composite with both split items gave the highest absolute informativity.

The composite and split dimensions distinguished diagnosis groups and anxiety or depression severity groups, with moderate to large effects for contrasts between mild and severe conditions; the split depression item showed the largest severity effects.

Most participants preferred the split questions. Reasons for either preference concerned question understanding, relevance to the participant's condition, acceptability, and perceived cognitive or interview burden.

Participants reported no problems less often on both split subdimensions than on the composite anxiety/depression item, which indicates that the composite item missed some reported anxiety or depression problems.

outcome: Residual dispersion of cTTO utility
statement: Aggregated psychological distance showed no clear association with residual utility dispersion.

outcome: Mean cTTO utility
statement: Greater aggregated psychological distance was associated with higher cTTO utility; the estimated difference from the lowest to the highest distance level was approximately 0.08 utility units.

outcome: Residual dispersion of cTTO utility
statement: High temporal distance was associated with lower residual dispersion and greater respondent agreement; spatial distance tended toward higher dispersion, while social and hypothetical distance showed no credible association.

outcome: Mean cTTO utility
statement: Distance dimensions had heterogeneous associations with mean utility: hypothetical and temporal distance had clear positive associations, while social and spatial estimates were uncertain.

outcome: Mean cTTO utility
statement: There was no evidence that parental status modified the association between temporal distance and utility.

outcome: cTTO response quality, including extreme trading, clustering, and dominance violations
statement: Psychological distance did not systematically affect extreme trading or other data-quality indicators; strict and weak dominance-violation rates were comparable across conditions and with similar prior work.
The activities item was the most ambiguous. Caregivers variously considered physical or mental limitations, lack of time, transport, housework, and restrictions caused by caring for children.

outcome: Comprehensibility, relevance, and coverage of EQ-HWB-S content
statement: Interviewees generally found EQ-HWB-S clear, relevant, and acceptable, especially the exhaustion, loneliness, cognition, anxiety, sadness or depression, and control items. The instrument was pertinent to parenting, adversity, and caring for children with additional needs.

outcome: Convergent validity against K6 and PWI-A
statement: EQ-HWB-S scores showed strong convergent validity with psychological distress; the sum-score correlation with K6 total exceeded 0.8 and all hypothesized correlations were at least moderate.

outcome: Convergent validity against K6 and PWI-A
statement: EQ-HWB-S scores showed convergent validity with personal wellbeing; the sum-score correlation with PWI-A total exceeded 0.6, while item correlations were weaker for mobility, activities, and pain.

outcome: EQ-HWB-S item response distribution and missingness
statement: EQ-HWB-S missing data were very low and most items had a useful response spread, but mobility was highly skewed toward no difficulty and exhaustion was common.

outcome: Test-retest reliability of the EQ-HWB-S sum-score and items
statement: All individual items had more than 80% agreement; weighted kappa values indicated mainly moderate item-level agreement.

outcome: Known-groups validity and discriminative ability
statement: EQ-HWB-S sum-scores and index scores differed significantly in expected directions across all planned known groups. Differences were largest for caregiver mental distress and were also substantial for child disability and child social-emotional symptoms.
Some caregivers questioned starting the instrument with mobility, and there was moderate support for placing the shorter and more relatable activities item first.

outcome: Responsiveness to change over six months
statement: Over six months, EQ-HWB-S change scores moved in expected directions with changes in psychological distress and global health. Sum-scores also changed with PWI-A, but neither score type was responsive to changes in the simple count of adverse life events.

outcome: Test-retest reliability of the EQ-HWB-S sum-score and items
statement: The EQ-HWB-S sum-score had excellent two-day test-retest reliability in both the full and protocol-conforming samples.
At baseline, the mean EQ-HWB-S level sum-score was 19.6 and the mean pilot UK preference-weighted index score was 0.732.
Sleep was the only omitted EQ-HWB item with near-unanimous support for inclusion in the short form; caregivers generally saw sleep as distinct from exhaustion.
Randomization produced demographically balanced EFT and ERT groups, although the two vividness scores differed significantly between groups.

Most participants in each arm discounted future life years positively. Mean area under the curve was the same in both arms, and EFT did not significantly change discounting classifications or mean time preference.

EFT did not significantly affect unadjusted or time-preference-adjusted cTTO utilities in t-tests or mixed-effects regression. No significant EFT interactions were found for age, current health, vividness, profile 33333, the first task, or profile 55555.

Ex-post direct-method adjustment significantly changed cTTO utilities for most health states within arms. It generally made utilities for severe states more negative, while between-arm distributions remained similar.
cTTO data-quality patterns were similar between arms, with few strong dominance violations and no significant group differences in the reported quality indicators.

Equivalence conclusions depended on the margin. EFT and ERT cTTO utilities were equivalent under the small-effect margin but not under the stricter MID margin; EFT utilities and ex-post-adjusted ERT utilities were not equivalent under either margin.
Self-rated vividness was not significantly associated with cTTO utilities, despite relatively high reported vividness.

Applying the adult individual perspective to EQ-5D-Y valuation may be unsuitable because adult respondents would value states from an instrument not intended to measure their own benefits, while preferences of the children and adolescents for whom the instrument is intended remain excluded.

The child perspective makes respondents value another person's health and may require them to project beliefs, preferences, goals, expectations, time preferences, and loss aversion onto that person, which can change the decision process underlying elicited preferences.

Specifying a 10-year-old beneficiary but no other characteristics or respondent relationship can introduce heterogeneity in the imagined child and raises uncertainty about whether resulting values apply across the full EQ-5D-Y age range.

The limited empirical literature indicates that individual and child perspectives produce different utilities for similar EQ-5D-Y health states; cTTO evidence generally points to higher utilities under the child perspective, while visual analogue scale evidence is ambiguous.

In the illustrative published utility data, the child perspective produced a slightly narrower range between full health and health state 33333 than the individual perspective, which can reduce the maximum incremental HRQoL gain.
Illustrative calculations showed that valuation perspective can change cost per QALY, and that the size and direction of the effect depend on the severity and health-state transition.
Perspective-related utility differences could produce different incremental QALY estimates, ICERs, and reimbursement decisions for children and adolescents compared with adults.

outcome: Self-reported subjective life expectancy for oneself and for a 10-year-old child
statement: Adults expected a 10-year-old child to reach a significantly higher age than they expected for themselves.

outcome: Self-reported subjective life expectancy for oneself and for a 10-year-old child
statement: A majority of respondents expected a child to outlive them, but the opposite or equal expectation was common; own and child subjective life expectancy were moderately correlated and the difference was unrelated to respondent age.

outcome: Self-reported subjective life expectancy for oneself and for a 10-year-old child
statement: Parents tended to expect children to die at a younger age than respondents without children, a difference that was not statistically significant.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L composite TTO utility for a 10-year-old child
statement: In mixed-effects regressions on all TTO utilities, neither own nor child subjective life expectancy, nor any other demographic, was associated with utilities; only health state severity predicted utilities.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L composite TTO utility for a 10-year-old child
statement: For states valued better than or equal to dead, child subjective life expectancy showed only a marginally significant positive association with utilities; for worse-than-dead states, older respondents gave more strongly negative utilities.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L composite TTO utility for a 10-year-old child
statement: Per-state regressions showed only scattered associations: own subjective life expectancy was significant for 1 of 28 states (negative, state 12111) and child subjective life expectancy for 4 of 28 states (positive: 11121, 12111, 21211, 22121), in directions opposite to the most common coefficient sign.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y-3L composite TTO utility for a 10-year-old child
statement: The null result for subjective life expectancy was robust to alternative model specifications, including remaining life expectancy, median splits, single-predictor models, and difference scores.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-Y-3L health profile and EQ VAS of the adult respondents
statement: Respondents were largely in good self-reported health, and there was no correlation between respondent age and own subjective life expectancy.

outcome: Out-of-sample predictive accuracy for mean health state values (mean absolute error, Pearson R, Lin concordance correlation coefficient)
statement: Random-intercept variants of the 8-, 9- and 11-parameter multiplicative models matched or outperformed the additive 20-parameter model in mean absolute error for out-of-sample health state means in all three countries and with both cross-validation methods.

outcome: Out-of-sample predictive accuracy for mean health state values (mean absolute error, Pearson R, Lin concordance correlation coefficient)
statement: Models with random intercepts at the level of individual participants generally predicted health state means more accurately than their fixed-intercept counterparts, with three exceptions in the Spanish data.

outcome: Presence of nonmonotonicity in fitted models
statement: The additive 20-parameter model produced nonmonotonic value sets in the Spanish and Singaporean data, whereas MULT8 was never nonmonotonic; MULT9 and MULT11 were nonmonotonic only in the Singaporean data.

outcome: Out-of-sample predictive accuracy for mean health state values (mean absolute error, Pearson R, Lin concordance correlation coefficient)
statement: Model fit on the complete observed data favoured the 20-parameter model, while cross-validated out-of-sample accuracy favoured the constrained multiplicative models, indicating overfitting of the 20-parameter specification.

outcome: Out-of-sample predictive accuracy for mean health state values (mean absolute error, Pearson R, Lin concordance correlation coefficient)
statement: Predictions of MULT8R and ADD20R were very similar overall, and differences among the multiplicative models were small, with MULT8R tending to predict best.

Seventeen studies met the inclusion criteria; 15 reported on the EQ-5D-3L and only 2 on the EQ-5D-5L, with 13 conducted in patient populations and 4 in general populations, and 16 using a quantitative and 1 a qualitative design.

outcome: Proportion of missing values on the EQ-5D descriptive system dimensions
statement: Missing values per EQ-5D dimension ranged from 0 to 10.7% and were mostly below 7%, with the highest proportions in a sample of cognitively impaired respondents.

outcome: Proportion of missing EQ VAS ratings
statement: Missing EQ VAS ratings ranged from 2.3% to 25.3% and generally exceeded the proportion of missing values on the descriptive system.

outcome: Completion rate, i.e. proportion of computable EQ-5D index values
statement: Completion rates for the EQ-5D-3L were around or above 90% at baseline in most studies, with two studies just above 80%; the single EQ-5D-5L study reported 89.5%, and age-specific rates fell from 94.9% at 65-69 years to 90.9% at 90 years and above.

outcome: Time required to complete the EQ-5D
statement: Completion time was reported in three studies; both EQ-5D versions were usually completed in under five minutes, with means of 265 seconds for the EQ-5D-5L under observation in care homes and 222 seconds in geriatric rehabilitation, and respondents needing assistance took longer than unassisted self-completers.

outcome: Need for interviewer assistance or interviewer-based administration
statement: Interviewer assistance was frequently required: around 50% of one rehabilitation sample needed interviewer administration with the probability rising from 11% at age 65 to 37% at 75 and 73% at 85, and 55% of another sample asked for help or clarification on at least one dimension.

Terminology and operationalisation of feasibility were inconsistent: only 8 studies used the term 'feasibility', 7 used 'completion', and one each 'practicality' and 'acceptability'; feasibility was assessed through missing values (11 studies), completion rates (13), qualitative completion statements (9) and completion time (3).

Qualitative statements described the EQ-5D as brief and easy to use in older respondents, with rare comprehension problems arising from narrow item interpretation or restrictive wording, while the EQ VAS concept caused the most difficulty, affecting 27% of respondents in one study.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state values and dimension-level weights
statement: The nonlinear DCE-with-duration model and all three EQ-VT models gave the same level-5 dimension ordering: pain/discomfort was most important, followed by mobility, anxiety/depression, self-care, and usual activities.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state values and dimension-level weights
statement: The nonlinear DCE-with-duration value for state 55555 was close to the EQ-VT model values, while the linear DCE-with-duration specification produced a much more negative value.

outcome: Agreement between DCE-with-duration and EQ-VT-derived values
statement: Across all 3125 EQ-5D-5L states, nonlinear DCE-with-duration predictions correlated highly with cTTO, rescaled latent-scale DCE, and hybrid EQ-VT predictions.

outcome: Agreement between DCE-with-duration and EQ-VT-derived values
statement: Bland-Altman analyses showed small differences overall. DCE-with-duration predicted slightly higher values, especially in the middle of the scale.

outcome: Agreement between DCE-with-duration and EQ-VT-derived values
statement: The nonlinear DCE-with-duration model predicted the 86 observed mean cTTO values almost as well as the EQ-VT models, although its mean absolute error was larger.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state values and dimension-level weights
statement: Accounting for nonlinear time preferences changed the DCE-with-duration scale substantially; the linear specification generated an implausibly extreme scale.

outcome: Estimated nonlinear time-preference discount rate
statement: The nonlinear DCE-with-duration model estimated a high annual population mean discount rate.

outcome: DCE-with-duration response quality and exclusion robustness
statement: Data quality was poor among fast respondents and respondents recruited in public places. Excluding these data left 970 respondents, and sensitivity analyses with 10-, 12.5-, and 15-second cutoffs changed estimates very little.

outcome: Rate of logically inconsistent cTTO responses, in particular state 55555 not receiving the lowest value
statement: The first wave of EQ-5D-5L valuation studies (England, the Netherlands, China, Canada, Spain) showed high rates of inconsistent responses, clustering of values, low values for mild states and few worse-than-dead responses; roughly 20% of respondents gave at least 1 health state a lower value than the worst state 55555.

outcome: Interviewer effects and protocol compliance during data collection
statement: Analysis of the EQ-VT iteration paths and time stamps showed that some interviewers systematically omitted the explanation of the lead-time part of the cTTO task and elicited no worse-than-dead values, and that very short times were spent on the wheelchair example and on obtaining single cTTO values, indicating satisficing that varied across interviewers.

outcome: Interviewer effects and protocol compliance during data collection
statement: Version 1.1 of the protocol added 3 practice states, confirmatory pop-ups, interviewer performance monitoring and a quality control process with 4 flagging criteria; interviewer effects, clustering and inconsistencies were dramatically reduced in studies that adhered to the updated protocol.

outcome: Proportion of respondents who reconsidered cTTO responses in the feedback module
statement: The feedback module, which shows respondents the rank ordering implied by their cTTO responses and allows them to flag disagreement without deriving new values, led 1 in 3 respondents to reconsider 1 or more initial responses and lowered the number of inconsistencies; it was included in version 2.0.

outcome: Rate of logically inconsistent cTTO responses, in particular state 55555 not receiving the lowest value
statement: The research programme provided no support for the other tested modifications, namely separation of the better-than-dead and worse-than-dead tasks in cTTO, reintroduction of a ranking task for warm-up purposes, relabelling the comparator state in cTTO, and use of a different iteration procedure; these had limited effects on the data, possibly because quality control had already reduced the scope for improvement.

Version 2.1 was released to align the software with the interviewer instructions by adding a dynamic question after the wheelchair example, which asks the respondent to imagine a much better or much worse state so that both parts of the evaluation space are shown.

outcome: Agreement and commensurability between cTTO-derived and DCE-derived values
statement: When modelling DCE data, violations of the logical ordering of dimension severity levels were observed in several countries, particularly for severity levels 2 and 3; an update of the experimental design based on better priors was postponed pending a larger revision of the DCE task.

Value algorithms were built on cTTO data alone in the Netherlands, Canada, South Korea, Uruguay and China, whereas Spain and England adopted hybrid cTTO-DCE models, with the choice driven by local considerations such as availability of software and documentation and properties of the local data.

Preliminary results from ongoing EuroQol-funded research show that DCE-with-duration value estimates are sensitive to model specification and in particular to assumptions about duration preferences, so DCE duration has not been implemented as a substitute for cTTO.

About half of participants agreed that bad living is better than good death, and just over a quarter believed in an afterlife; the distribution of these views did not differ significantly across the five cities.

outcome: Non-trading behaviour (health state valued at 1)
statement: Agreement with 'bad living is better than good death' was strongly associated with more positive valuation behaviour: higher odds of non-trading and of valuing states positively, much lower odds of reaching -1, and a narrower cTTO score range.

outcome: Valuing a health state positively (cTTO value at or above 0)
statement: Belief in an afterlife was associated with higher odds of valuing health states positively, and this effect remained after controlling for the LBD view and other variables.

outcome: Non-trading behaviour (health state valued at 1)
statement: Participants interviewed in Beijing were more likely to be non-traders, more likely to value states positively, far less likely to reach the lowest possible value, and had a narrower score range than participants in the other four cities, after adjustment.

outcome: Non-trading behaviour (health state valued at 1)
statement: College or higher education was associated with more non-trading, more positive valuation and a narrower score range, and experience of serious disease was associated with more positive valuation; men had a narrower score range while age showed no significant effect.
The authors identified 13 arguments for public involvement in health-care decisions and categorized them as input, process, and outcome arguments.

Most public-involvement arguments were judged relevant to involving children in the health-state valuation process; the taxpayer argument was the least directly applicable but could still support involvement in some circumstances.

Children can contribute lived expertise that adults cannot supply, and their involvement can improve the legitimacy, quality, responsiveness, validity, and accuracy of child HRQoL values and related decisions.

Children can participate beyond direct TTO or DCE tasks through age-appropriate qualitative or deliberative work, ranking selected health states or domains, or assessing preferences and values derived from adults.
The appropriate form of involvement and the suitability or modification of conventional valuation methods can differ between age groups.

outcome: Aspects of health considered important but not captured by the five EQ-5D dimensions
statement: A minority of respondents said there are important aspects of health not captured by the five EQ-5D dimensions, and 179 respondents provided free-text descriptions of them.

outcome: Aspects of health considered important but not captured by the five EQ-5D dimensions
statement: Free-text responses were organised into 22 themes; sensory deprivation and mental health were mentioned most often, followed by communication and relationships.
Independent double coding showed high agreement, and all disagreements were resolved by discussion and third-analyst adjudication.

outcome: Perceived differences between EQ-5D-5L state 11111 and 'full health'
statement: Around one third of respondents did not consider EQ-5D-5L state 11111 and 'full health' to be the same; the most common explanation was that the five dimensions are not exhaustive of all conditions.

outcome: Self-reported health profile and EQ VAS score
statement: Most respondents reporting no problems on all five EQ-5D-5L dimensions still rated their own health below the EQ VAS upper anchor.

outcome: Perceived differences between EQ-5D-5L state 11111 and 'full health'
statement: In rating and ranking tasks, 'full health' and 'perfect health' were valued more highly than the EQ-5D-5L state 11111 description.
Respondents who gave text responses about missing aspects of health were similar to other respondents except for being more likely to hold a degree.

outcome: Aspects of health considered important but not captured by the five EQ-5D dimensions
statement: Nearly half of respondents also nominated aspects of quality of life not captured by the EQ-5D dimensions, commonly relationships, loneliness, happiness and living conditions.

Residual diagnostics for EQ-5D utility and EQ VAS showed distributional-assumption problems in all fitted models: QQ plots deviated from their reference distributions and residual-versus-fitted plots showed nonconstant variance. Tobit plots were generally less curved and had more stable variance patterns than linear mixed-effects model plots.
Little's test indicated that all trials except NCT03255382 violated the missing-completely-at-random assumption used for the generalized estimating equations analysis.

outcome: Between-arm change from baseline in EQ-5D utility
statement: For final-visit EQ-5D utility, all four models agreed in statistical-significance classification for all 23 intervention-control comparisons. Linear mixed-effects and generalized estimating equations models agreed fully in clinical-relevance classification, while Tobit and Beta models had lower agreement.

outcome: Between-arm change from baseline in EQ-5D utility
statement: For average EQ-5D utility effects across visits, the models agreed in statistical-significance classification for 22 of 23 comparisons, with one exception involving each model. Clinical-relevance agreement was highest for the linear mixed-effects and generalized estimating equations models and lower for Tobit and Beta models.

outcome: Between-arm change from baseline in EQ VAS
statement: For final-visit EQ VAS, generalized estimating equations and Tobit each showed 95.7% agreement in statistical significance. Clinical-relevance classifications agreed across models except for one linear mixed-effects model result.

outcome: Between-arm change from baseline in EQ VAS
statement: For average EQ VAS effects across visits, the models agreed fully in clinical relevance and generally agreed in statistical significance; one linear mixed-effects model comparison differed from the other models.

Generalized estimating equations produced notable differences when final-visit missingness exceeded 40%, especially in NCT00083889 with 66% missingness. Tobit estimates tended to be larger when ceiling effects differed substantially between treatment arms, while Beta estimates tended to be lower in the same trials.

Across the 13 trials, baseline mean EQ-5D utility and EQ VAS varied substantially. Utility ceiling effects ranged from none to 27% at baseline and exceeded 20% at the last visit in nine trials; final-visit missingness exceeded 40% in three trials.
The search yielded 129 studies. Twenty-two papers met the inclusion criteria and represented approximately 450 participants with varied hearing conditions.

The included evidence covered Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Most studies collected data in one country, and the largest share of these studies was from the United Kingdom or England.

Semi-structured interviews and focus groups were the main data-collection methods. Thematic analysis was the most frequent analytic method, followed by grounded theory and less frequent framework, content, and phenomenological analyses.

The synthesis grouped the effects of hearing conditions into Physical, Mental, and Social categories. Physical themes included sound localization, sound clarity, speech, and physical fatigue. Mental themes included depression, anxiety, listening effort, mental fatigue, fear, and identity. Social themes included relationships, isolation or avoidance, communication, independence, work function, social stigma, confidence, and coping strategies.

The themes were interconnected. Increased listening effort could cause fatigue, which could contribute to anxiety and avoidance of social interactions. Communication was central to many connected effects.

Eight of the 16 synthesis themes mapped to a domain of the Brief ICF Core Set for Hearing Loss. Unmatched themes included several Mental themes, physical fatigue, isolation, and independence. Vestibular functions and sensations in the ICF set had no close synthesis theme.

The EQ-5D captured depression and anxiety. It did not directly capture many important hearing-related Physical and Social themes, including sound localization, sound clarity, speech, communication, isolation, independence, confidence, and coping strategies. Relationships and work function had only partial or broader links to usual activities.

The optimized CASP assessment found that reporting was generally adequate. Researcher-related risk of bias was adequately reported in 11 of 22 studies, and 16 of 22 studies described the analysis process in detail.

In bivariate analyses, utility values differed by age, religion, family type, state, alcohol or tobacco use, ailment status, number of dependents, and administered health-state severity. They did not differ by sex, wealth quintile, rural or urban residence, marital status, education, occupation, or number of earners.
After adjustment for administered health-state severity, older age was associated with a small reduction in the value assigned to the same health state.

Compared with respondents without ailments, respondents with chronic ailments or with both acute and chronic ailments assigned lower values to the same health state; acute ailments alone were not significant.
Compared with no alcohol or tobacco use, alcohol use, tobacco use, and use of both were associated with lower values assigned to the same health state.
Respondents in joint families assigned lower values to the same health state than respondents in nuclear families.
Household income or wealth quintile was not associated with health-state valuation, which did not support the positional-objectivity hypothesis.
Mean TTO utility decreased strongly and monotonically as classified EQ-5D-5L health-state severity increased.
Religion, state of residence, and number of dependent household members remained associated with health-state valuation after adjustment for administered health-state severity.

outcome: Median severity rating (0-100) of each candidate label by dimension and country
statement: Selecting labels closest to the 25th, 50th and 75th centiles of the response scaling continuum produced two alternative 5-level versions in each language rather than a single version.

outcome: Median severity rating (0-100) of each candidate label by dimension and country
statement: Rank ordering and median severity ratings of labels were similar between the UK and Spain and across dimensions, indicating robustness of the response scaling scores.

outcome: Face and content validity, comprehension and acceptability of the alternative 5-level descriptive systems
statement: Focus group participants in both countries found both alternative versions easy to understand and complete, and tended to prefer the wording 'slight-moderate-severe' over 'minor-moderate-major' because it was more colloquial.

outcome: Participant preference between the two alternative label sets
statement: Preferences for labels in the Pain/Discomfort and Anxiety/Depression dimensions were not clear, so the same slight-moderate-severe scaling as in the functional dimensions was retained.

outcome: Plausibility and interpretability of hypothetical EQ-5D-5L health states
statement: Hypothetical health states based on the 5-level systems were well understood, but participants criticised apparent contradictions or lack of realism in some level combinations rather than the label wording.

outcome: Face and content validity, comprehension and acceptability of the alternative 5-level descriptive systems
statement: Participants' explanations of what each label meant showed the labels functioned at the intended level of measurement, with anchors 'no problems' and 'unable to' in the functional dimensions.
Wording was harmonised within the instrument, for example rewording the worst level of Mobility as 'Unable to walk about' instead of 'Confined to bed'.
Acceptability and feasibility were similar across instruments: about 70% of respondents rated each instrument somewhat or very easy, and EQ-5D-Y-5L was most consistently rated easy.
No floor effects occurred for any instrument. PedsQL and CHU9D had no ceiling effects, while EQ-5D-Y-3L had the most ceiling effects and EQ-5D-Y-5L had ceiling effects in selected subgroups.

PedsQL, CHU9D, EQ-5D-Y-3L, and EQ-5D-Y-5L performed almost equally in known-group validity; effects were largest for anxiety and depression severity, followed by general mental-health severity, ADHD severity, and special health care needs.

The four main HRQoL instruments had strong intercorrelations. Associations with mental-health measures were strongest for anxiety and depression, intermediate for mixed internalising and externalising symptoms, and weakest for ADHD symptoms.

The four main instruments detected improvements in general and mental health with small effects, except EQ-5D-Y-5L did not detect improvement in general health; CHU9D and EQ-5D-Y-3L showed the strongest responsiveness patterns.
In the combined sample, CHU9D had good test-retest reliability by the Cicchetti thresholds, while PedsQL, EQ-5D-Y-3L, and EQ-5D-Y-5L had fair reliability; subgroup strengths differed.
Across the psychometric properties, CHU9D and PedsQL had the most consistent overall performance.

AQoL-6D and HUI3 showed good acceptability and feasibility, no floor or ceiling effects, and good convergent validity, but less consistent known-group validity; their responsiveness and test-retest reliability could not be assessed.
Utility-score sensitivity analyses slightly weakened known-group and convergent validity for EQ-5D-Y-3L and CHU9D but slightly improved performance for HUI3 and AQoL-6D.

The adapted version changed mobility level wording from walking about to movement; reframed looking after self as helping look after themselves; added age-appropriate examples for all five dimensions; replaced unsuitable usual-activity examples with playing, socializing, sleeping, and eating; and removed gendered pronouns.

Pain or discomfort and worried, sad, or unhappy examples used unusual, persistent behavior because frequent and rapidly changing emotion is normal at this age and parents often triangulate several behavioral signs.

Rapid changes in independence, communication, and socializing affected how parents interpreted health. Parents of children with health conditions often judged progress against the child's own prior state instead of typical developmental milestones.

Parents agreed that all five broad EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions were relevant to some extent for children aged 2-4 years, but the original proxy wording and examples were not age-appropriate; looking after self was the clearest problem.

Communication, playing, socializing, and eating were raised as possible areas not fully covered by the existing EQ-5D-Y structure, although many parents considered them to fall within existing dimensions.

All five pilot parents considered the adapted examples appropriate and relevant and considered the version clear and easy to complete. One parent remained concerned that the looking-after-themselves wording did not fully reflect the child's lack of independence.
Three analytical themes concerned dimension applicability, differences across ages 2-4 years, and differences between well children and children with health conditions.

outcome: Range of scale of each value set
statement: The US EQ-5D-5L value set had the broadest range of scale, while the US 3L value set and the 5L>3L crosswalk shared a narrower range.

outcome: Number and percent of health states valued worse than dead
statement: The 5L value set classified a much larger share of health states as worse than dead than the 3L value set or the crosswalk.

outcome: Mean single dimension-level utility transition and utility gap between 11111 and the next best state
statement: The crosswalk had the smallest mean single dimension-level transition and the 3L the largest; the 5L had the smallest utility gap between 11111 and the next best health state.

outcome: Distribution shape of index values (kernel density, interval measurement properties)
statement: Scatterplots of mean single-level transitions and kernel density plots indicated the 5L value set had the most consistent transitions and a near-normal single-peaked index distribution, whereas the 3L had multiple local maxima and the crosswalk was skewed.

outcome: Discriminative ability / relative statistical efficiency (ratio of ANOVA F-statistics)
statement: In the US valuation data the 5L value set tended to be more statistically efficient than the crosswalk and the 3L across levels of general health, and it was the most discriminative across EQ VAS strata in both datasets.

outcome: Discriminative ability / relative statistical efficiency (ratio of ANOVA F-statistics)
statement: Within disease groups of the parallel fielding data the 5L was usually the most discriminative, with exceptions where the crosswalk was slightly better.

outcome: Responsiveness of value sets across the EQ VAS spectrum (simulation-based)
statement: In the simulation, the 5L index values changed most steeply with EQ VAS between EQ VAS 25 and 75, while the three scoring approaches gave similar values at low (0-25) and high (75-100) EQ VAS and in the general-population dataset.

outcome: Responsiveness of value sets across the EQ VAS spectrum (simulation-based)
statement: In the parallel fielding dataset the 5L value set produced lower simulated utility values than the 3L and crosswalk value sets across all EQ VAS values for every health condition.
Most cross-instrument items had moderate correlations, while HUI sense items were outliers; pain items showed the strongest cross-instrument correlations in both report groups.
Some items cross-loaded or did not meet the 0.32 loading threshold, and the pattern differed by report source.

PedsQL items alone defined the physical-functioning domains; HUI items defined the senses domains; and EQ-5D-Y-5L physical items mainly clustered within daily activities rather than five distinct EQ-5D-Y-5L domains.
Restricting proxy reports to children aged 7–18 years produced the same six-domain structure, but five items loaded on different domains.
The proxy-report analysis supported six domains: emotional functioning, daily activities, cognition/school functioning, pain, physical functioning, and senses.
The self-report analysis supported seven domains: emotional functioning, daily activities, cognition/school functioning, pain, physical functioning, senses, and social functioning.
In both report groups, emotional functioning, daily activities, and pain contained items from all four instruments.
Social functioning emerged as a separate domain only in self-reports; several peer-social PedsQL items instead loaded with cognition or school activities in proxy reports.
Both response datasets were suitable for exploratory factor analysis: KMO values were high and Bartlett's tests were significant.

outcome: Predictive validity of team predictions measured by chi-square against confirmatory sample proportions
statement: Discreetly Charming Econometricians, led by Michal Jakubczyk, won the competition with the smallest confirmatory chi-square, the fewest rejected predictions and the highest concordance; their approach stratified pairs with and without immediate death and used a Cauchy cumulative density function.

outcome: Predictive validity of team predictions measured by chi-square against confirmatory sample proportions
statement: Bootstrap analysis showed the winning team's advantage was not attributable to chance, and its predictions also beat the average of all models; a perfect model could not have achieved a chi-square near zero.

outcome: Predictive validity of team predictions measured by chi-square against confirmatory sample proportions
statement: Model performance varied systematically by pair type and temporal unit: teams predicted preferences in years worst and weeks best, ratio- or angle-based cumulative density functions (Cauchy, Zermelo-Bradley-Terry) outperformed sigmoidal and linear ones overall, and separate models for immediate-death pairs were advantageous.

outcome: Predictive validity of team predictions measured by chi-square against confirmatory sample proportions
statement: Constant proportionality of the value of life span was rejected by all models that relaxed the assumption, and logit models showed poor predictive validity in health valuation.

outcome: Respondent response behaviour and lexicographic preference patterns
statement: Response behaviour was largely non-degenerate: fewer than 0.5% of respondents always chose the same side, under 2% always chose the shorter life span, and about 5% always chose the longer life span, with slightly more such patterns in the confirmatory sample.

outcome: Respondent descriptions of the survey experience
statement: Most respondents described the survey as interesting and thought-provoking, but a large majority also found it challenging or difficult.

Ten of the 18 registered teams dropped out after receiving the exploratory data, citing poor performance of their intended approach, unexpected complexity of health valuation attributes such as differing temporal units, or personal and work commitments.

Respondents who dropped out were more often female, black or African American, or refused to report household income; the analytical samples had higher educational attainment and household income than the 2010 US Census.
Most respondents completed the surveys on a computer: 84% used a Windows PC, 10% an Apple computer, 4% a tablet and 2% a cell phone, giving more than 900 tablet and cell phone respondents in total.

Estimated level decrements were logically ordered within each domain except for severe versus extreme anxiety or depression in the matched mobile sample, an ordering problem the authors attribute to the wording of the English EQ-5D-5L.

Respondent characteristics differed significantly by device: cell phone respondents were younger, less educated, more racially and ethnically diverse and had lower incomes, while tablet respondents were the oldest, wealthier and the least racially and ethnically diverse group.

Completing the choice tasks took significantly longer on mobile devices, with cell phone users needing more than 90 extra seconds and tablet users 30 to 50 extra seconds compared with computer respondents; matched samples gave the same conclusion.

Cell phone and tablet respondents were more likely to drop out; mobile respondents dropped out significantly more often in the Competition Survey, and tablets had significantly lower completion in the TDL Survey.
Internet connection was related to non-completion for cell phone users, but the adjusted association was not statistically significant.
Device type was not associated with acquiescent behaviour, with describing the survey as difficult or as enjoyable, or with self-reported difficulty of completion.

Heteroskedastic choice models found no significant differences in preference consistency between mobile or tablet respondents and their matched computer control groups, and no association between internet connection and consistency.

Respondents reported on average 2.24 logical inconsistencies in the TDL Survey and 57% were fully consistent; associations between device and inconsistent responding were largely insignificant, although tablet and cell phone estimates were positive, and no relation was found between device and lexicographic preferences.

EQ-5D-5L utility values estimated for matched cell phone and tablet samples did not differ jointly or individually from their computer control groups, apart from extreme anxiety or depression, and mean differences were below 0.06 on the QALY scale for all health states.

For every rater perspective, mean QOL-ACC utility was lower in the mild-to-moderate cognitive impairment subgroup than in the no-impairment subgroup, but none of these between-cognition differences was statistically significant.

Dimension-level agreement was mixed and generally low. Mobility had the strongest agreement in the full sample, proxy-proxy agreement was higher for mobility, pain management, and activities, and proxy-person agreement was higher for emotional well-being, independence, and social connections.

In the full sample, mean resident self-reported QOL-ACC utility was higher than both family-proxy means. Both resident-versus-proxy differences were statistically significant at p < 0.01, while the two proxy-perspective means did not differ significantly (p = 0.10).

Utility-score agreement was moderate and was slightly higher for the proxy-person perspective than for the proxy-proxy perspective in the full sample and both cognition subgroups. Bland-Altman limits of agreement exceeded 0.85 for both proxy comparisons, and most observations outside the limits reflected higher self-report scores.

The Alberta routinely collected PROM database holds health-related quality of life data for over 6000 individuals who have undergone total knee arthroplasty, which allowed the matching algorithms to find more than 50 similar patients per participant by relaxing the sex, age (within 5 years) and body mass index (within 2.5 points) conditions stepwise, and to display pre-surgery comparisons and 3-month post-surgery outcomes for each of the five EQ-5D dimensions.

Preliminary focus group work by the authors found that average outcome information in a decision aid lacked salience and validity for patients, who perceived themselves as different from the average patient and wanted information on how treatment would affect day-to-day life.

Heuristic evaluation and usability testing of existing total knee arthroplasty decision aids identified numerous limitations in navigation and interpretability of information, so a new decision aid was developed for the Alberta context.

About 30% of patients currently complete the routine pre-consultation questionnaire online before arriving at the Edmonton Bone and Joint Centre, with the remainder completing it in the waiting room, which constrains eligibility for the trial.
Semi-structured cognitive interviews were undertaken with 170 participants across the six countries.

Results in China (n = 30) indicated that five items needed major modification or removal because they did not work well in the Chinese context, and some examples included in questions for added context were not considered helpful there.
Other items needed further information or clarification to allow accurate comprehension and completion.
