Internationally, participants preferred simpler layouts of questions but wanted more information on context, and there was no clear preference for any of the tested response options.

outcome: Comprehension, relevance and interpretation of the draft items and proposed domains
statement: Questions related to dignity and communication had varied interpretations that were not always consistent with the target conceptual theme.

outcome: Comprehension, relevance and interpretation of the draft items and proposed domains
statement: Questions related to self-care were difficult for participants, particularly for carers.
Some instructions, such as those regarding recall periods, were frequently ignored.
Paired same-level adult and youth versions had good to very good dimension-level agreement; mental health in the South African three-level comparison had the lowest agreement.

Among adolescents with health conditions, the youth three-level wording reduced the mental-health ceiling relative to both adult versions, and the total 11111 ceiling was lower for EQ-5D-Y-3L than for EQ-5D-5L. No material total-ceiling difference was found between the paired five-level versions.

Discriminatory power was higher for EQ-5D-Y-3L than EQ-5D-3L for pain/discomfort and mental health, higher for the adult EQ-5D-5L than EQ-5D-Y-3L across dimensions because it had more levels, and higher for EQ-5D-Y-5L than EQ-5D-5L across all dimensions.

All EQ-5D version level sum scores differentiated health-condition groups overall. In South Africa, the adult EQ-5D-5L also distinguished diabetes from the general school group when EQ-5D-Y-3L did not; in Ethiopia, both five-level versions distinguished the school group from all condition groups except HIV.
Total paired level sum scores differed significantly between the compared versions, and same-level youth versions had slightly higher mean scores than their adult counterparts.

South African adolescents often had no preference, but those who selected a version generally favored EQ-5D-Y-3L wording. Ethiopian adolescents clearly favored EQ-5D-Y-5L over EQ-5D-5L. Youth versions were commonly described as more personal, relatable, detailed, and easier to understand.
The largest within-person response shifts between youth and adult systems occurred for mental health, followed by pain/discomfort; youth wording more often elicited reported problems.
Both country samples reported generally mild health states, with very few responses at the most severe levels; mental-health dimensions had the most reported problems.

The adult EQ-5D-3L and youth EQ-5D-Y-3L produced similar numbers of unique South African health states, but the experimental EQ-5D-Y-5L produced significantly more unique Ethiopian health states than the adult EQ-5D-5L.

outcome: Instrument-level and item-level floor and ceiling effects
statement: Instrument-level ceiling effects were lowest for EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S, higher for ICECAP-A, and highest for EQ-5D-5L; no instrument had an instrument-level floor effect.

outcome: Convergent and divergent validity
statement: EQ-HWB-S index values correlated strongly with all EQ-5D-5L indices and with ICECAP-A; the selected EQ-5D-5L value set had negligible influence on correlations.

outcome: Dimensionality and factor structure
statement: Exploratory factor analysis identified five factors: psychosocial health, pain and discomfort, sensory and physical functioning, capability wellbeing, and positive psychological states. EQ-HWB and EQ-5D-5L items shared health-related factors, while ICECAP-A items loaded mainly on a distinct capability-wellbeing factor.

outcome: Known-group validity and discrimination
statement: All measures differentiated respondents by health-related known groups, but EQ-5D-5L generally had the largest effect sizes, followed by EQ-HWB-S and then ICECAP-A.

outcome: Instrument index values and EQ-HWB level sum score
statement: Mean index values were 0.755 for EQ-HWB-S, 0.760 to 0.830 across EQ-5D-5L scoring systems, and 0.807 for ICECAP-A.

outcome: Convergent and divergent validity
statement: Item-level correlations between comparable EQ-HWB and ICECAP-A concepts were generally weaker than expected; ICECAP-A stability was the only ICECAP-A item that also loaded on an EQ-HWB factor.

outcome: Test-retest reliability and measurement error
statement: Across the pain and no-pain groups, descriptive-system test-retest reliability was fair to moderate for EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L and poor to moderate for CHU9D; these results were inadequate under the COSMIN threshold.

outcome: Test-retest reliability and measurement error
statement: EQ VAS test-retest reliability was substantial in participants with musculoskeletal pain and moderate in participants without pain for both EQ-5D-Y versions.

outcome: Hypothesis-based construct validity
statement: Against the prespecified COSMIN hypothesis threshold, both EQ-5D-Y versions met the construct-validity threshold versus PedsQL in the pain group but not in the no-pain group; EQ-5D-Y-5L met the threshold versus CHU9D in both groups, while EQ-5D-Y-3L did not. CHU9D did not meet the threshold versus PedsQL in either group.

outcome: Known-groups validity
statement: All three preference-based instruments discriminated participants with musculoskeletal pain from those without pain. For pain severity, both EQ-5D-Y versions discriminated on most dimensions and EQ VAS, while CHU9D discriminated only on worried, pain, and tired dimensions.

outcome: Missing responses and completion rate
statement: All instruments had high completion rates. EQ-5D-Y-3L had the highest completion, while PedsQL had the lowest; the largest item-level missing response was 12.7% for the EQ-5D-Y-5L usual-activities dimension.

outcome: Ceiling and floor effects
statement: Among participants with musculoskeletal pain, the no-problems health-profile ceiling was lower for EQ-5D-Y-5L than for EQ-5D-Y-3L, and was much lower for CHU9D.

outcome: Self-reported health-related quality of life and EQ VAS
statement: Participants with musculoskeletal pain reported worse HRQoL than those without pain, including lower mean EQ VAS and PedsQL total scores and more reported problems on almost all instrument dimensions.
The selected heteroscedastic hybrid model produced EQ-5D-3L utility predictions from −0.796 to 1.0.

All estimated models had logically consistent and statistically significant health-dimension parameter estimates; hybrid Model III had the lowest AIC and the lowest cTTO-based mean absolute error among the hybrid models.
Extreme mobility problems had the largest utility decrement, followed by extreme self-care problems.
Negative cTTO values were common, and a substantial subset of observations was at the lower bound of −1.
Participants selected the health state with the lower misery index in nearly three quarters of DCE responses.
The analyzed sample was broadly representative by age, gender, and region, with slight over-representation of the northeast and men aged 20 to 39 years.
The mean self-reported EQ VAS score was 72.7; 27.7% reported the EQ-5D-3L state 11111.
Forty-three analyzed participants said that religious beliefs affected their valuation responses, but the study recorded only one non-trader.

outcome: Wave-to-wave retention rate of the online panel
statement: Retention fell across waves: 1467 of 2734 wave 1 respondents (53.7%) took part in wave 2 and 964 of 2454 wave 2 respondents (39.3%) took part in wave 3; 940 respondents completed all three waves.

Before adjustment, age and ethnicity differed significantly between wave 1 respondents retained and lost at wave 2, while age, race, ethnicity, education, marital status, region, income, insurance and political affiliation all differed by wave 3 attrition among wave 2 respondents.

outcome: Representativeness of the sample compared with US population and pre-pandemic norms
statement: The sample deviated from the US population: wave 1 was slightly older, more single and more educated with fewer Hispanic and Black respondents and more multiple-race respondents, while wave 2 was younger, less often female and more often married but comparable on race and ethnicity.

outcome: Panel attrition: non-participation in the following survey wave
statement: Younger age consistently predicted dropout at the next wave in both adjusted models, with the effect much stronger for attrition at wave 3 than at wave 2.
Hispanic ethnicity predicted dropout in both periods after adjustment.
Higher self-rated survey difficulty predicted dropout in both periods.

COVID-19 experience predicted dropout in both periods but through different measures: experiencing COVID-19-like symptoms not requiring hospitalisation from wave 1, and a confirmed COVID-19 diagnosis or deferred medical care from wave 2.

From wave 1, health-behaviour, work and HRQoL variables predicted attrition at wave 2, including change of normal diet, average hours of sleep per day, essential-worker status, COVID-19 impact on productivity, and average hours worked per day (inverse association).

From wave 1, VR-12 responses predicted attrition at wave 2: limitation in moderate activity, having a lot of energy only a little or some of the time, and reporting emotional problems much better than one year ago.

From wave 2, ideological, financial, insurance and clinical variables predicted attrition at wave 3, including Republican affiliation, support for social distancing policy, having just enough money to make ends meet, Medicare or no insurance, smoking, underweight BMI, and histories of diabetes or stroke; arthritis and bronchitis were inversely associated.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L VAS score as a correlate of subsequent panel dropout
statement: A higher EQ-5D-5L VAS score at wave 2 was associated with a slightly higher odds of dropping out at wave 3, a counter-intuitive direction relative to earlier literature.
Self-completion produced more missing dimension responses than interviewer administration, especially among children aged 8–12 years.

Agreement across the three versions ranged from moderate to almost perfect by dimension. Agreement was strongest between self-complete and interviewer-administered responses and weaker for comparisons with proxy reports, especially for pain/discomfort and worried/sad/unhappy.

Proxy reports indicated more health problems and a lower proportion of 11111 profiles than child self-complete and interviewer-administered reports, although clinical-group ceiling differences were not statistically significant.
Test-retest reliability was moderate to excellent across all dimensions and excellent for EQ VAS in all three versions; pain/discomfort and worried/sad/unhappy had the lowest dimension reliability.

All three versions differentiated health-condition groups. School participants had the best health, acute conditions had the poorest level sum scores, and self-complete and interviewer-administered scores also differed by Ross heart-failure class and assistive-device use after acute injury.

Self-complete and interviewer-administered level sum scores were responsive to improved and worsened health, while proxy reports showed smaller standardized effects. The unchanged group showed negligible change.

Mode preference was balanced: 47% preferred self-completion. Most respondents found self-completion easy, and more children reported no difficulty with interviewer administration than with self-completion or proxy completion.
Level sum score distributions differed slightly between interviewers, which can indicate an interviewer effect.

outcome: Frequency of internal and statistical validity tests reported in published DCEs, by academic field
statement: Most published DCEs report no internal validity test based on observed choices; use is concentrated in health-related DCEs, where dominant and repeated choice tasks are essentially health-only tests.

outcome: Sensitivity of repeated, dominant and RLH tests to detect simulated bad-quality respondents
statement: Sensitivity analyses using RLH-cleaned benchmark preferences and using the original authors' data instead of the MTurk data produced very similar conclusions.

outcome: Frequency of internal and statistical validity tests reported in published DCEs, by academic field
statement: Dominant (within-set) and repeated choice tasks were the two most frequently used internal validity tests, and DCE completion time was the most common quantitative test in all fields.

outcome: Sensitivity of repeated, dominant and RLH tests to detect simulated bad-quality respondents
statement: Sensitivity and specificity of repeated and dominant choice tasks varied widely with the number of choice options per choice task, the type of incorrect response pattern and the number of validity tasks combined.

outcome: Sensitivity of repeated, dominant and RLH tests to detect simulated bad-quality respondents
statement: Heuristic response patterns were harder to detect than random or flatlining patterns for all tests.

outcome: Specificity of repeated, dominant and RLH tests among simulated good-quality respondents
statement: Chaining two internal validity tasks increased sensitivity but reduced specificity.

outcome: Area under the ROC curve and positive and negative likelihood ratios of the validity tests
statement: The RLH test achieved better specificity at any given sensitivity than repeated and dominant choice tasks, with ROC curves closer to the ideal upper-left corner in all four case studies.

outcome: Area under the ROC curve and positive and negative likelihood ratios of the validity tests
statement: Average likelihood ratios showed the internal validity tests are only slightly more informative than a coin flip, while the RLH test is far more informative.

outcome: Sensitivity of repeated, dominant and RLH tests to detect simulated bad-quality respondents
statement: In the vaccines case study the RLH test could not distinguish flatliners from good-quality respondents unless the position of the opt-out was randomized.

outcome: Convergent validity (Pearson correlations) between the internal validity tests and the RLH test in the MTurk data
statement: Convergent validity with the reference RLH (P > .05) test was much higher for the other RLH cutoffs than for the internal validity tests.
Seventeen participants completed the think-aloud interview; nine were parents or caregivers and eight were non-parents, and mean interview completion time was 54 minutes.

Participants generally understood the DCE tasks, found them feasible, and reported confidence in considering a 3-year-old, although some found poor child health emotionally difficult to imagine and some non-parents struggled because they had limited experience of young children.

Participants simplified choices by focusing on selected domains, overall severity, the number and severity of problems, links between domains, and whether problems could be treated or supported; many gave high priority to pain or discomfort and sadness, worry, or unhappiness.

Age-related assumptions changed health-state interpretation: participants viewed some limitations as normal at age three, sometimes gave less weight to physical domains, and differed in how they understood young children’s emotional awareness, independence, and pain.

Views differed on whose preferences should inform valuation, but most participants favored including parents, caregivers, professionals, or other adults with direct experience of young children; some also supported a representative general-population sample or separate comparison of groups.

Despite the hypothetical-child instruction, most participants imagined a child they knew, including almost all parents imagining their own child. Most expected little difference between ages two and four but expected different preferences for a child aged ten or older.

Participants considered future spillovers, including child development, later education, social life, employment, and lifelong effects, and caregiver spillovers, including practical burden and financial and emotional effects. Caregiver spillovers were reported mainly by parents or caregivers.

Most participants used information outside the stated health-state description, including expected natural improvement, available treatment or support, and beliefs that some problems are typical at age three.
Choice patterns were broadly similar for parents or caregivers and non-parents across the six task pairs; all participants selected the same preferred health state in the first pair.
At the first ECT session, most patients received a pulse width of 0.5 ms; smaller groups received less than 0.5 ms or more than 0.5 ms.
Mean HRQoL improved substantially from before ECT to within one week after ECT on both the EQ-5D index and EQ VAS.

After adjustment for baseline HRQoL, demographic and clinical characteristics, and concurrent medication, pulse width was not significantly associated with EQ-5D index or EQ VAS within one week after ECT.
At six months, the fully adjusted analysis found a lower EQ-5D index for the 0.5 ms group than for the less-than-0.5 ms group, but the corresponding EQ VAS analysis was not significant.
More than 70% of patients improved in at least one EQ-5D dimension within one week after ECT, while about 6% worsened in at least one dimension; the remainder had no change or mixed change.
In the six-month subsamples, the mean improvement seen within one week was maintained on average at six months.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state utility values
statement: Pain/discomfort had the largest effect on health-state preference values, followed by anxiety/depression, mobility, self-care, and usual activities.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D-5L health and EQ VAS
statement: Among respondents, 42.54% reported full health; anxiety/depression was the most common EQ-5D-5L problem and self-care was the least common; mean EQ VAS was 77.25.

outcome: Difference in cTTO value distributions by interview language
statement: The distribution of cTTO values did not differ significantly between interviews in Arabic and French.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state utility values
statement: The preferred value set assigned negative predicted values to 1,271 of the 3,125 EQ-5D-5L health states.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state utility values
statement: Of observed cTTO responses, 62% were positive and 38% were negative; mean values for the 86 valued states ranged from 0.970 for 11211 to -0.940 for 55555.

outcome: Value-set model fit, logical consistency, significance, and prediction accuracy
statement: The hybrid heteroskedastic Tobit model was selected for the Moroccan value set because all coefficients were logically consistent and significant, fit was comparable to the cTTO-only model, and it used both cTTO and DCE data.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state utility values
statement: Predicted utilities from the preferred model ranged from -1.492 for state 55555 to 1 for state 11111; states 11211 and 21111 each had a value of 0.979.
The sample matched the Moroccan general population for age, sex, geographical area, and residence, but illiterate participants were underrepresented.
The study produced the first reported EQ-5D-Y-3L value set in the world at the time of writing.

All mixed-logit coefficients were statistically significant, had the expected negative sign, and ranked pain/discomfort as most important, followed by anxiety/depression, usual activities, mobility, and self-care.
The completed 243-state value set ranged from -0.691 for state 33333 to 1.000 for state 11111.
Fifty of the 243 health states had negative values and were therefore valued as worse than dead.

outcome: Overall and dimension-level ceiling and floor effects
statement: The overall 111111 ceiling decreased only slightly from EQ-TIPS-3L to EQ-TIPS-5L, and there was no overall floor effect on either version.

outcome: Convergent validity between corresponding EQ-TIPS-3L and EQ-TIPS-5L dimensions
statement: Corresponding EQ-TIPS-3L and EQ-TIPS-5L dimensions had strong correlations, although randomized form order affected correlations for Play, Social Interaction, and Movement-related comparisons.

outcome: Absolute and relative informativity of EQ-TIPS dimensions
statement: Shannon H-prime was higher for every EQ-TIPS-5L dimension, with an average improvement of 0.096; relative response spread was generally retained, and Eating had the largest improvement in evenness.

outcome: Known-groups validity by PedsQL and EQ VAS severity groups
statement: Both EQ-TIPS-3L and EQ-TIPS-5L level sum scores significantly distinguished severity groups defined by PedsQL total score and EQ VAS cut-offs.

outcome: Redistribution and inconsistency of paired 3L and 5L dimension responses
statement: Most paired dimension responses redistributed as anticipated; only 15 response pairs were inconsistent, and Eating had no inconsistent responses.
For respondents who selected the most severe EQ-TIPS-3L level, the 5L version permitted some responses to move to the more severe extreme-problems level, especially for Eating and Movement.

outcome: Themes and subthemes of quality of life relevant to patients, social care users and informal carers
statement: Extraction and synthesis of 42 reviews and 24 primary studies produced 7 high-level themes with 32 interrelated subthemes: feelings and emotions; cognition; self-identity; coping, autonomy and control; relationships and social connections; physical sensations; and activity.

outcome: Relevance and applicability of candidate themes across patient, social care user and informal carer groups
statement: Apart from physical sensations, most themes and subthemes recurred across patients, social care users and informal carers, notably feelings and emotions, relationships and social connections, coping, autonomy and control, and activity.

Feelings and emotions covered sadness or depression, anxiety or worry and fear, hope and hopelessness, anger and frustration, vulnerability or safety, and guilt or shame, and these feelings were repeatedly linked to symptoms, loss of usual activities and the caring role.

Cognition, covering concentration, memory, confusion and thinking clearly or decision making, was initially extracted within feelings and emotions but was separated into its own theme after stakeholder discussion because it was judged conceptually different.

The theme originally labelled physical symptoms and functioning was reduced to physical sensations (pain, discomfort, sleep and fatigue), and the remaining functioning subthemes such as mobility, communication, hearing and vision were moved to the activity theme; diverse symptoms such as breathlessness, nausea and diarrhoea were grouped into a single discomfort subtheme.

outcome: Themes and subthemes selected or excluded against predefined criteria for domain selection
statement: Several candidate constructs were excluded as transitional, instrumental to other themes, not relevant to everyone, or ambiguous: loss of normality, reciprocity, dexterity, weight change, disfigurement, menopause symptoms, sensory sensitivity, fertility, sexual function and activity avoidance; work and leisure were reframed as meaningful, valued or enjoyable activity.
The identified themes were broader than the content of commonly used measures specific to health (EQ-5D), social care (ASCOT) or informal care (Carer Experience Scale).

Most included reviews were systematic (39 of 42), included only qualitative studies (32 of 42) and undertook a quality check (30 of 42); included evidence came mainly from the United Kingdom, United States, Canada and other European countries and was mainly restricted to English-language studies.

outcome: Dropout rate during the DCE choice tasks
statement: In the base-case arm without level overlap or color coding, the dropout rate during the choice tasks was 13.9% and respondents attended on average only 2.14 of five attributes.

outcome: Dropout rate during the DCE choice tasks
statement: Introducing color coding alone or level overlap alone each reduced the dropout rate to about 10% and raised attribute attendance to roughly three attributes.

outcome: Dropout rate during the DCE choice tasks
statement: The combination of level overlap and color coding was most effective, lowering the dropout rate to 7.2-8.2% and raising attribute attendance to about four of five attributes.

outcome: Respondent-stated preference ranking of the visual presentation formats
statement: In the debriefing ranking task, most respondents preferred a color-coded presentation over the format without color coding.

outcome: Average number of attributes attended to (attribute non-attendance)
statement: Level overlap cost statistical efficiency: the overlap design needed on average 35 additional respondents under a conditional logit model and six additional respondents under a mixed logit model to obtain significant estimates for all EQ-5D-5L parameters.

The research team and two focus groups assessed the proposed bolt-on wording. Focus-group results were used to modify labels and descriptors when face-validity problems occurred and to select the best wording when variants were tested.

Adjustment for sociodemographic characteristics did not materially change the results, and none of the sociodemographic variables or health-state-pair indicators had a statistically significant effect in the reported combined models.
Of 1581 people who entered the survey, 1040 were included in the final analysis. Each pairwise choice received 167 to 180 responses.

In the adjusted main-effects model across all health-state pairs and levels, every bolt-on reduced preference for the profile to which it was added. Hearing had the largest marginal effect, followed by cognition, relationships, sleep, and energy.

Effects also varied by base health-state pair. Cognition had the largest level 3 effect in all three pairs. Hearing had the largest level 5 effect in all three pairs. Energy had the smallest level 3 effect in two pairs, and sleep had the smallest level 5 effect in two pairs.

Level 1 additions generally had small, non-significant effects. Level 3 and level 5 additions produced negative, usually statistically significant effects, and level 5 effects were larger. At level 3 cognition had the largest effect; at level 5 hearing had the largest effect and sleep had the smallest.
The mean survey completion time was 9.19 minutes and the median was 7.05 minutes.

outcome: Arguments identified in the literature for assigning dead the value 0
statement: The database search identified 3873 records; after removing 1697 duplicates and screening titles and abstracts, 41 full texts were read and 7 papers were included, supplemented by 11 handbooks and 5 PhD theses.

outcome: Arguments identified in the literature for assigning dead the value 0
statement: The reviewed literature offers mainly practical arguments for setting dead at 0, namely that it is done by definition or for convenience, that it makes QALYs comparable to survival analysis, and that it allows utilities to be computed by subtracting disutility from 1; the theoretical argument found is only that assigning 0 to dead is permitted, not required, by the uniqueness properties of the utility function.

outcome: Invariance of QALY indifferences under interval and ratio scale transformations of the duration scale
statement: Adding a constant to the duration scale destroys an indifference between two health episodes: with w(T) = T both episodes yield 17 QALYs, but with w(T) = T + 2 episode A yields 20.4 and episode B 19.8 QALYs, whereas the ratio transformation w(T) = 2T leaves both at 34 QALYs.

outcome: Invariance of QALY indifferences under interval and ratio scale transformations of the duration scale
statement: Given the multiplicative QALY model, the zero condition for duration implies w(0) = 0, and the indifference between being in any health state for zero years and being dead for a nonzero duration implies v(Dead) = 0; both the duration scale and the health-utility scale therefore have ratio scale properties.

outcome: Effect of the position of dead on the relative weighting of life-saving and life-improving treatments in cost-utility analysis
statement: The ordinal position of dead relative to other health states determines how many states are worse than dead and weights life-saving against life-improving gains; a dead anchor close to perfect health emphasises life-improving treatments, and a distant anchor emphasises life-saving treatments.

outcome: Share of respondents classified as using a multiplicative versus a linear additive utility function
statement: In the EQ-5D-5L dataset, 76 percent of respondents were classified as having used a linear additive utility function and only 24 percent the theoretically required multiplicative utility function.

outcome: Share of respondents classified as using a multiplicative versus a linear additive utility function
statement: In the SF-6D dataset, 71 percent of respondents were classified as having used a linear additive utility function and 29 percent the multiplicative utility function.

outcome: Robustness of latent class classification to cut-off values, preference heterogeneity, anchoring, and simulated identification checks
statement: With increasingly stringent cut-off rules the additive share fell (76 to 64 percent for EQ-5D-5L; 71 to 48 percent for SF-6D) and an uncertain category grew, but the additive share always exceeded the multiplicative share.

outcome: QALY weights for EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D dimension levels estimated from the entire sample versus the multiplicative class only
statement: EQ-5D-5L QALY weights estimated from the multiplicative class only were substantially more negative than full-sample weights, with the pits state at -1.40 versus -0.79.

outcome: QALY weights for EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D dimension levels estimated from the entire sample versus the multiplicative class only
statement: SF-6D QALY weights estimated from the multiplicative class only were substantially more negative than full-sample weights, with the pits state at -0.83 versus -0.38.

outcome: Robustness of latent class classification to cut-off values, preference heterogeneity, anchoring, and simulated identification checks
statement: Results were robust to accommodating preference heterogeneity, to anchoring the QALY tariffs on the immediate death parameter, and Monte Carlo simulations confirmed the latent class logit models were identified with sufficient statistical power.

EQ-TIPS responses had a good distribution across dimensions and age groups. Children aged 1–12 months had more reports of no problems with social interaction than older children, but EQ-TIPS level sum and EQ VAS scores did not differ by age.
For EQ-5D-Y-3L, children aged 5–7 years had fewer reported mobility and usual-activity problems, a lower level sum score, and a higher ceiling than older groups.

EQ-TIPS and EQ-5D-Y-3L generally showed moderate-to-strong concurrent associations with PedsQL scores; EQ-TIPS emotional-function associations were weaker, and EQ-5D-Y-3L mobility did not show the expected strong association with PedsQL physical functioning.

EQ-TIPS distinguished prognosis groups, with better proxy-rated HRQoL when long survival and weaning were possible. EQ-5D-Y-3L distinguished breathing-technology and clinical-severity groups, with better HRQoL for tracheostomy only and mild severity.
Neither PedsQL nor PTHSI distinguished the studied clinical indicators, while EQ-TIPS and EQ-5D-Y-3L did.

Caregiver EQ-5D-5L problems were most frequent for pain or discomfort and anxiety or depression; more than half reported that the child's health always limited their own needs, while most reported fulfilment from caregiving.

Caregivers of children who used invasive ventilation had worse PTHSI and EQ-5D-5L level sum scores than caregivers of children with tracheostomy only; greater child clinical severity was also associated with worse caregiver PTHSI scores and higher CarerQoL burden.
Caregiver PTHSI, EQ-5D-5L, and CarerQoL scores were strongly associated with each other, and caregiver-rated child HRQoL generally had moderate associations with caregiver HRQoL and burden.
The 144 children had a median age of 5.9 years; 68.8% used tracheostomy only, 13.2% used invasive ventilation, and 82% had mild clinical workload severity.

outcome: Integration of PPIE into stages of measure development and learning points about running PPIE sessions
statement: Four face-to-face PPIE sessions were held at key project stages with a group of seven members; attendance was 7, 7, 5 and 6, and PPIE was included in 7 of the 11 listed stages of measure development (conceptual model, identifying item content, item reduction, pre-testing, selection of items, design of the measure, dissemination) but not in establishing the need for a measure, item development, or psychometric survey design and analysis.

outcome: PPIE judgements on the relevance and wording of candidate EQ-HWB items and on the coverage of themes and subthemes
statement: In the session 3 card-sorting exercise the group placed items into include, reject or undecided across the activity, autonomy, cognition, feelings and emotions, physical sensations, relationships and self-identity domains; all seven physical-sensation items (pain, discomfort, exhaustion, tiredness, sleep) were placed in include, while most cognition items other than "I found it hard to concentrate" were rejected.

outcome: Integration of PPIE into stages of measure development and learning points about running PPIE sessions
statement: Presenting draft items in session 2 without response options and not in questionnaire format caused considerable confusion and hindered the efficiency of that meeting.

outcome: Integration of PPIE into stages of measure development and learning points about running PPIE sessions
statement: Sessions became more productive as the project progressed and members engaged much more with task-based exercises than with general discussion; early sessions produced frustration and a sense of lack of purpose because the end product was hard to visualise and discussion drifted to issues outside the E-QALY remit.

outcome: PPIE views on questionnaire layout, item order and completion instructions
statement: Session 4 produced concrete design advice: use colour and high-quality production, an easy opening item, final items that minimise leaving respondents with negative emotions, clear instructions on perspective so that carers answer about themselves, and plain language for respondents whose first language is not English; members held mixed views on the exact item order.

outcome: Integration of PPIE into stages of measure development and learning points about running PPIE sessions
statement: Practical and relational factors mattered: accessible meeting rooms, transport links and other facilities required time, several researchers present helped run sessions and build relationships, sessions felt intense and could not cover everything in the scheduled time, and project delays created periods of limited communication that PPIE members noted as a concern.

outcome: Utilities predicted by urban- and rural-specific additive main-effects models
statement: The Bland-Altman comparison of 3,125 urban- and rural-model predictions showed limits of agreement from -0.103 to 0.011, with 151 predictions outside those limits.

outcome: Valuation time and within-person logical consistency
statement: Urban and rural participants had similar TTO task times and within-person logical consistency rates.

outcome: Urban-rural difference in mean EQ-5D-5L health-state value
statement: The joint test of interactions between rural status and health-state characteristics was not significant. Pain/discomfort interaction coefficients were positive, with significant interactions at levels 3 and 5, which suggested greater rural weight on pain/discomfort.

outcome: Utilities predicted by urban- and rural-specific additive main-effects models
statement: Urban- and rural-specific additive models gave the same dimension ranking, but rural-based predictions were generally lower and classified more EQ-5D-5L states as worse than dead.

outcome: Urban-rural difference in mean EQ-5D-5L health-state value
statement: Rural participants assigned lower mean values than urban participants across all health states in both unadjusted and adjusted analyses.

outcome: Urban-rural difference in mean EQ-5D-5L health-state value
statement: The adjusted rural-urban difference was significant for mild and moderate health states, was largest for moderate states, and was not significant for severe states.

outcome: Urban-rural difference in mean EQ-5D-5L health-state value
statement: Seven of 30 individual health states had a statistically significant adjusted urban-rural difference, and 12 of 30 had an adjusted absolute difference at least as large as the 0.058 minimally important difference.
The review included 24 studies represented by 25 papers: 20 predominantly quantitative studies, 3 qualitative studies, and 1 mixed-method study.

outcome: Reporting quality of included studies
statement: The main reporting-quality concern was that most included studies did not report or justify a target sample size; qualitative studies also often did not report whether administration mode affected data quality.

outcome: Difference in mean health-state value between child and adult perspectives
statement: Evidence about health states worse than dead varied by method and study: one analysis found all-in trading patterns in the adult perspective, while one anchored EQ-5D-Y-5L DCE study found more states worse than dead for the 10-year-old child perspective.
Seventeen of 24 studies used EQ-5D-Y-3L, and the source studies used varied valuation methods; 9 studies used mixed valuation methods.

outcome: Difference in mean health-state value between child and adult perspectives
statement: For most severe states, adults acting as proxies for children assigned higher TTO values than adults valuing the same states for themselves, which indicates less willingness to trade children's life years; uncertainty intervals often crossed no difference.

outcome: Difference in mean health-state value between child and adult perspectives
statement: In the multilevel meta-regression, greater health-state severity was associated with larger child-minus-adult mean-value differences, with significant increases at several higher level sum scores, but there was no simple monotonic pattern.

outcome: Difference in mean health-state value between child and adult perspectives
statement: The meta-regression estimated a smaller child-minus-adult mean-value difference for VAS than for TTO, with weak statistical evidence.

outcome: Factors associated with differences between valuation perspectives
statement: The meta-regression found no evidence that the coded perspective comparison itself was associated with the mean-value difference after the other included factors were considered.

outcome: Relative importance and ranking of HRQoL dimensions
statement: Pain or discomfort was usually the most important EQ-5D-Y dimension when adults responded, while adolescent results were mixed; self-care was consistently least important, and adolescents sometimes ranked mobility higher than adults valuing for children.

outcome: Willingness to trade length of life for quality of life
statement: Qualitative evidence showed that respondents could find it difficult to imagine a child in poor health and could become emotional when considering child illness or early death, which could reduce willingness to trade children's life years.

outcome: Factors associated with differences between valuation perspectives
statement: Evidence about parental status and the hypothetical child's age was limited and inconsistent across studies and countries.
EQ-5D-5L produced many more unique observed health profiles than EQ-5D-3L at baseline in both samples.

Differences in responsiveness between value sets were small, including for the US value sets derived from the same sample and protocol, indicating that descriptive system differences rather than value sets drive the 3L-5L difference.

The 3L mobility level 'confined to bed' behaved very differently across samples: it was endorsed once in rehabilitation but by 21% of stroke patients at baseline and 7% at follow-up, producing the largest dimension-level 3L-5L differences in improvement.
Overestimation of health problems by 3L in the improved subsamples increased over time in rehabilitation but decreased slightly in stroke.

EQ-5D-3L consistently overestimated reported health problems relative to EQ-5D-5L on most dimensions (average 14% higher level sum score by dimension), with the largest overestimation in pain/discomfort followed by anxiety/depression and usual activities; underestimation appeared for rehabilitation mobility and self-care and for stroke baseline mobility, and all 3L-5L dimension differences were statistically significant.
Inconsistencies in direction of change between EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L were rare (average 1.0% of dimensions in rehabilitation and 1.1% in stroke).
EQ-5D-5L captured about twice as many level moves per respondent as EQ-5D-3L in both samples, with more change captured in both the improving and the deteriorating direction.
Paretian Classification of Health Change gave mixed results: more patients improved with 5L in rehabilitation but fewer with 5L in stroke.
The probability of superiority showed a clear but modest advantage of EQ-5D-5L over EQ-5D-3L in both samples.

For the improved subsamples all SRM and SES statistics were statistically significant (p < 0.001) and mostly of medium to large magnitude, whereas none of the statistics for the deteriorated subsamples reached significance.

Value responsiveness favoured EQ-5D-5L in the rehabilitation improved subsample for every value set, while in both stroke improved subsamples EQ-5D-3L showed better responsiveness statistics, most clearly for SES.

Relative efficiency (5L/3L ratio) was significant in favour of 5L for SRM in rehabilitation for all value sets except Canada, and only for South Korea and Spain for SES; for stroke, significant ratios favoured 3L (five value sets for mRS-based SES, two value sets for Barthel Index-based SRM and five for Barthel Index-based SES).

outcome: Amount of preference imprecision: length and bounds of equally plausible (epas) and somewhat plausible (spas) answer ranges
statement: Respondents were able to report their own imprecision: only about 20% of the equally plausible answer (epas) ranges had zero length, and the mean epas length was typically two to five times the standard error of the mean of the utility, so imprecision exceeds sampling error even in this smallish sample.

outcome: Point TTO/LT-TTO utility of EQ-5D-3L health states and estimated dimension-level disutilities
statement: Student respondents attached greater disutility to most dimensions/levels than the Polish general population value set, especially for usual activities, with PD3 the exception.

outcome: Point TTO/LT-TTO utility of EQ-5D-3L health states and estimated dimension-level disutilities
statement: Accounting for imprecision changes crisp estimates little: the random-effects panel model, the OLS model, and the fuzzy-crisp least squares models B1, B3 and B4 gave very similar coefficients and nearly identical value sets.

outcome: Point TTO/LT-TTO utility of EQ-5D-3L health states and estimated dimension-level disutilities
statement: The compatibility-maximising fuzzy-crisp model (B2) produced much lower disutilities for all dimensions and levels and much higher utility values in the value set; it behaves like a mode-oriented regression and is unstable and hard to interpret.

outcome: Point TTO/LT-TTO utility of EQ-5D-3L health states and estimated dimension-level disutilities
statement: Median regression yielded lower dimension disutilities and a negative constant, consistent with the negative skewness of health-state utilities (mode < median < mean pattern across B2, A4 and A2).

outcome: Point TTO/LT-TTO utility of EQ-5D-3L health states and estimated dimension-level disutilities
statement: In the fuzzy-fuzzy models, usual activities followed by pain/discomfort accounted for the largest spread of the imprecise disutilities, while absolute disutility was largest for PD3, followed by UA3 and MO3.

outcome: Point TTO/LT-TTO utility of EQ-5D-3L health states and estimated dimension-level disutilities
statement: The naive fuzzy-fuzzy model (C1) produced a parameter reversal: some coefficients for the lower bound exceeded those for the upper bound, so its parameters cannot be interpreted directly as imprecise dimension disutilities, although its value set was still similar to the others.

outcome: Point TTO/LT-TTO utility of EQ-5D-3L health states and estimated dimension-level disutilities
statement: Transporting imprecision into the value set yields a band rather than a line of utilities; with the fuzzy least squares model without intercept (C3) the band narrows to a point for states whose worsened dimensions had degenerate (crisp) parameters.

outcome: Point TTO/LT-TTO utility of EQ-5D-3L health states and estimated dimension-level disutilities
statement: Mean point utilities in the student sample ranged from 0.914 for the mildest state to -0.122 for the most severe state valued, with the proportion of respondents rating a state worse than dead rising to 50% for state 32313, and all state-level utility distributions were negatively skewed.

outcome: Amount of preference imprecision: length and bounds of equally plausible (epas) and somewhat plausible (spas) answer ranges
statement: Respondents distinguished the two range types: in about 30% of cases the epas and spas ranges were equal, and only three respondents said afterwards that providing ranges was difficult (with seven more judged difficult by interviewers).

outcome: Correspondence between values rejected during the TTO titration path and the elicited plausible ranges
statement: Values rejected during the TTO titration path frequently lay inside the ranges the respondent afterwards called plausible, so rejecting a value in TTO is not a valid indicator of clear preference.

outcome: Non-trading in TTO and the proportion of non-trading tasks whose plausible ranges allow trading off life years
statement: Non-trading was frequent for mild states, but in a large share of non-trading tasks the reported ranges extended below full health, indicating imprecision rather than lexicographic preference for longevity.

outcome: Logical (Pareto dominance) inconsistencies in TTO answers and their explanation by imprecision
statement: Logical (Pareto dominance) inconsistencies were rare and partly explained by imprecision: 129 of 3114 comparable pairs (4.1%) were violations, only 15 were serious (utility difference at least 0.5), and in 51 non-serious cases one epas range contained the other utility.

outcome: Amount of preference imprecision: length and bounds of equally plausible (epas) and somewhat plausible (spas) answer ranges
statement: Preferences were rarely so imprecise that a state was uncertain to be better or worse than dead: the ranges included zero utility in only 73 cases (4%) for spas and 35 cases (1.9%) for epas.

outcome: Amount of preference imprecision: length and bounds of equally plausible (epas) and somewhat plausible (spas) answer ranges
statement: Imprecision is driven mainly by the usual activities dimension, followed by anxiety/depression and pain/discomfort, in the regression models of range length.

outcome: Amount of preference imprecision: length and bounds of equally plausible (epas) and somewhat plausible (spas) answer ranges
statement: Health-state severity and internal diversity increase imprecision: a higher maximal level and more dimensions at that maximal level increase range length, a higher minimal level decreases it, and more dimensions at the minimal level (i.e. a more internally diverse state) increase it; overall explanatory power was low (R2 0.023-0.060).

outcome: Amount of preference imprecision: length and bounds of equally plausible (epas) and somewhat plausible (spas) answer ranges
statement: Imprecision is subadditive: the range length for a compound state (e.g. 11133) is smaller than the sum of the lengths for its building states (11131 and 11113).

The previously reported insensitivity was replicated: when negative (worse-than-dead) values were analysed in isolation, the fitted line of value on severity was horizontal, whereas the fitted line for positive values decreased with severity.

At the individual respondent level, cTTO values and severity were negatively related for most respondents, and negative slopes were found within nearly all segments defined by the number of worse-than-dead preferences.

Across segments with more worse-than-dead preferences, the median individual slope became steeper (more negative) while the median intercept stayed similar before dropping in the higher segments, matching the threshold explanation and contradicting the WTD-insensitive explanation.
In the interaction model (Eq. 2), the mean individual slope for negative values was significantly more negative than the mean slope for positive values.
Mean cTTO values decreased monotonically across segments defined by the number of worse-than-dead responses.
Segments with more than 7 worse-than-dead preferences showed a floor effect and contained few respondents (3% of the sample), so they were not shown in the median slope/intercept figure.

outcome: Agreement between paired crosswalk- and EQ-VT-based EQ-5D-5L value sets
statement: Agreement between crosswalk- and EQ-VT-based EQ-5D-5L value sets was generally poor across the 19 pairs.

outcome: Value-set scale, range, mean, state 55555 value, and percentage of states worse than dead
statement: The paired value sets differed substantially in scale and in the proportion of health states valued worse than dead.

outcome: Rank order of the five isolated dimension-severity states and mobility-level pattern
statement: No country preserved the rank order of the five isolated dimension-severity states, and states with mobility at level 5 frequently formed a distinct band in agreement plots.

outcome: Rank order of the five isolated dimension-severity states and mobility-level pattern
statement: The mobility-level band persisted when crosswalk and direct value sets were based on valuation data from the same respondents and also appeared in reverse-crosswalk three-level comparisons.

outcome: Association between elapsed source-study time and value-set correlation
statement: Longer intervals between publication of the 3L and 5L valuation studies tended to be associated with lower agreement.

outcome: Difference in MIC utility scores produced by crosswalk and EQ-VT value sets
statement: Applying all 19 value-set pairs to the MIC data produced significantly different population mean utilities for every pair.

outcome: Difference in MIC utility scores produced by crosswalk and EQ-VT value sets
statement: Differences also persisted in respondents with severe health states and in respondents who reported being unable to walk about.

outcome: Percentage of respondents classified as having a low-quality response pattern by each method
statement: At the sample level, the garbage class mixed logit model and root likelihood selection classified close to identical percentages of respondents as having low-quality response patterns across the 4 datasets and 3 cutoff scenarios.

outcome: Percentage of respondents identically classified by the garbage class mixed logit model and root likelihood selection
statement: At the individual level, about 95% of respondents were identically classified by the two approaches, with slightly lower agreement under the least conservative cutoff scenario.

outcome: Mixed logit preference parameter means and standard deviations of the mixing distribution under each model specification
statement: In the antibiotics dataset, which had the largest share of low-quality respondents, adding a garbage class markedly increased choice consistency: mean preference parameters were about 2.5 times larger and the standard deviations of the mixing distribution became smaller relative to the means.

outcome: Estimated garbage class share as an indicator of discrete choice experiment data quality
statement: The estimated garbage class share provided a direct estimate of the number of low-quality respondents in each dataset, without needing a statistical cutoff value.

outcome: Mixed logit preference parameter means and standard deviations of the mixing distribution under each model specification
statement: Standard mixed logit estimates became progressively more similar to the garbage class mixed logit estimates as more low-quality respondents were excluded by increasingly conservative root likelihood cutoffs, and the same pattern, in smaller magnitude, held in the vaccines, meals and EQ-5D-5L datasets.

outcome: Percentage of respondents identically classified by the garbage class mixed logit model and root likelihood selection
statement: The reference root likelihood classification rule prob(RLH < 1/J) > 0.05 corresponds closely to the garbage class rule prob(class membership probability < 0.5) > 0.75, so the latter can be recommended as the default classification rule.

Correlations between the two measures were moderate: the CDC unhealthy days index correlated -0.56 with the EQ-5D-5L index score and -0.48 with the EQ VAS, while item-level correlations ranged from negligible to moderate (0.15 to 0.67 in absolute value).

Sample scores were skewed towards good health: mean (SD) EQ-5D-5L index 0.849 (0.142), mean EQ VAS 79.5 (17.7), mean unhealthy days index 7.4 (10.5); respondents reported 416 of the 3125 possible EQ-5D-5L health states (13%).
Ceiling effects were larger for the CDC Healthy Days items than for the EQ-5D-5L index, and the EQ-5D-5L index had no floor effect.

Both measures discriminated as hypothesised between subgroups defined by self-rated health, education and material deprivation (all p < 0.001), with larger effect sizes for the EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS than for the unhealthy days index across deprivation levels.

Across age groups the EQ-5D-5L index and EQ VAS declined monotonically with older age, whereas the median unhealthy days index was higher in younger groups and mean values changed non-linearly, implying the counter-intuitive conclusion that health improves with age.
Among respondents who reported 0 unhealthy days, EQ-5D-5L profiles showed substantial problems in older groups, so a score of 0 unhealthy days does not mean full health in older people.
Among respondents who reported 30 unhealthy days, only 2.2% (19 of 873) reported the 11111 EQ-5D-5L health state, and problems in pain/discomfort were widespread.

Among respondents in the 11111 EQ-5D-5L health state, 58.2% reported 0 unhealthy days on the unhealthy days index, so a substantial minority reported some unhealthy days despite reporting no EQ-5D-5L problems.
Both measures showed the same age pattern at item level: physical health worsened and mental or emotional health improved with older age.

outcome: Discriminative ability of negative (worse-than-death) utility values with respect to health state severity
statement: Positive values decreased with severity distance whereas negative values did not, and the correlation with severity was near zero for negative values in most countries.

outcome: Discriminative ability of negative (worse-than-death) utility values with respect to health state severity
statement: In the linear mixed models the effect of severity distance on negative values was trivial compared with its effect on positive values.

outcome: Distinguishability of negative values from random noise in permutation tests
statement: Permutation tests showed that variation of mean values across health states was far larger than chance for positive values but indistinguishable from chance for negative values, except in Thailand.

outcome: Mean composite TTO utility values by severity distance
statement: Negative values clustered at the bottom of the scale, indicating a floor effect, and a large share of respondents rated state 55555 as worse than death.

outcome: Proxy-reported pediatric OI health-related quality of life and EQ-5D-Y health state
statement: Proxy reports showed substantial pediatric OI HRQoL problems, especially mobility, usual activities, and emotional health.

outcome: Proxy-reported pediatric OI health-related quality of life and EQ-5D-Y health state
statement: The most frequent EQ-5D-Y profile was 22222; only about one in ten patients had no problems in all dimensions, and a small proportion had the worst profile 33333.

outcome: Proxy-reported pediatric OI health-related quality of life and EQ-5D-Y health state
statement: Caregivers reported significantly higher eHealth literacy, financial well-being, and mental health when care receivers had no problems with usual activities or emotional health. Financial well-being was also higher when patients had no problems with self-care or pain/discomfort.

outcome: Caregiver eHealth literacy
statement: Caregiver eHealth literacy, financial well-being, and mental well-being were positively and significantly correlated; normalized financial well-being was markedly lower than normalized eHealth literacy and mental well-being.

outcome: Caregiver financial well-being
statement: The structural equation model fit the data well. Financial well-being had a positive direct association with mental health, and eHealth literacy had positive associations with both mental health and financial well-being.

Higher caregiver eHealth literacy and financial well-being were associated with lower pediatric fracture frequency and fewer complications. Caregivers whose family income met daily expenses had higher eHealth literacy, financial well-being, and mental health than caregivers whose income did not.

outcome: Internal consistency reliability of caregiver measures
statement: All three caregiver measures had high internal consistency reliability in this sample.
Most respondents were parents, and nearly two thirds reported that family income could not cover daily expenses.

EQ-HWB-S responses had the expected distribution: mobility and activities were more skewed, while exhaustion, loneliness, cognition, anxiety, sadness or depression, and control had a wider spread. Exhaustion was prominent.

Parents in child health-condition samples had significantly poorer scores than the general-population sample on every EQ-HWB-S item. Mean differences were larger for exhaustion, loneliness, cognition, anxiety, sadness or depression, and control than for mobility, activities, and pain.
Parents in child health-condition samples had poorer preference-weighted scores and level sum-scores than general-population parents, with moderate effect sizes.

All known-group tests based on child health-condition sample membership, special healthcare needs, chronic health condition, and negative COVID-19 impact were significant in the hypothesized direction for preference-weighted and sum-scores. Child-health group effects were moderate, while COVID-19 effects were smaller.

The association between child health-condition sample membership and poorer parent EQ-HWB-S scores remained after adjustment for parent age and gender, household composition, income, education, and healthcare-card status.

Parents of children with autism spectrum disorder, eating disorders, and sleep problems had the poorest mean wellbeing profiles. Autism spectrum disorder, eating disorders, recurrent abdominal pain, and sleep disorder had the largest adjusted condition coefficients; dental problems and asthma had the smallest.
Known-group effect sizes were similar for female and male parents, but they were generally slightly larger for female parents.
For preference-based scores, EQ-5D-3L with the vision bolt-on was more responsive than standard EQ-5D-3L, EQ-5D-5L, and SF-6D; HUI3 was the most responsive measure.
Preference-based mean improvement was larger for EQ-5D-3L with the vision bolt-on than for standard EQ-5D-3L.
For non-preference-based scores, both the three-level and five-level vision bolt-on EQ-5D versions were more responsive than their corresponding standard versions.
Vision bolt-on items showed more frequent postoperative improvement than all standard EQ-5D items and the HUI3 vision item.
Cataract surgery produced substantial objective improvement in visual acuity.
Many patients who reported no problems on standard EQ-5D still reported vision problems on the bolt-on items before surgery.
Statistically significant socio-demographic differences in self-reported health occurred in all countries.
The detailed results gave overall EQ VAS health concentration indices from 0.090 in Korea to 0.173 in Spain.
Age was generally the most important socio-demographic determinant of lower EQ VAS scores and problems in four EQ-5D-3L dimensions; education also had a consistent role, while sex had a smaller role.
Models that combined socio-demographic indicators and the five EQ-5D-3L dimensions explained between 15.4% and 57.7% of the overall health concentration index.
Most income-related odds ratios exceeded 1. The United States had the highest income-related odds ratios on all five dimensions, from 1.21 for pain/discomfort to 1.52 for self-care.
Income-related EQ VAS concentration was not statistically significant in France, Italy, or Spain; the highest significant index was 0.0234 in the United States.

Usual activities and pain/discomfort were the main EQ-5D-3L dimensions that explained inequality in overall EQ VAS health. Usual activities was the strongest contributor in nine countries in the combined analysis and in all four countries with significant income-related concentration; anxiety/depression contributed equally in Belgium in the latter analysis.

outcome: COVID-19 vaccine acceptance during pregnancy, defined as having received at least one dose before or during pregnancy or planning to receive it during pregnancy
statement: Just over half of respondents accepted COVID-19 vaccination around pregnancy, while about one quarter delayed it until after pregnancy and roughly one in six were hesitant or refused.

outcome: COVID-19 vaccine acceptance during pregnancy, defined as having received at least one dose before or during pregnancy or planning to receive it during pregnancy
statement: Attitudes and beliefs about COVID-19 vaccines were the factors most strongly associated with vaccine acceptance during pregnancy.

outcome: COVID-19 vaccine acceptance during pregnancy, defined as having received at least one dose before or during pregnancy or planning to receive it during pregnancy
statement: Care and employment context were independently associated with vaccine acceptance: group prenatal care, prenatal care from a primary care provider, a workplace policy recommending vaccination and a healthcare provider recommendation all increased acceptance, whereas previous COVID-19 infection decreased it.

outcome: Attitudes and beliefs about COVID-19 vaccines and about vaccines in general
statement: Pregnant persons who received a COVID-19 vaccine recommendation from their healthcare provider reported fewer vaccine safety concerns and stronger belief in vaccine benefit.

outcome: Receipt of other recommended maternal vaccines (influenza, Tdap)
statement: Respondents who delayed COVID-19 vaccination until after pregnancy commonly accepted other recommended maternal vaccines, while those who refused COVID-19 vaccination rarely did.

outcome: Self-reported reasons for accepting or refusing COVID-19 vaccination
statement: Concern about side effects was the most common reason for refusing COVID-19 vaccine, and no respondent reported access barriers; protection of self and baby were the main reasons for acceptance.

outcome: COVID-19 vaccine delay, hesitancy and refusal around pregnancy
statement: Vaccine delay and refusal were more common among younger, overseas-born respondents and those with lower educational attainment and household income.

outcome: Decision quality: knowledgeable (3 of 5 knowledge questions correct) and treatment choice concordant with treatment preference
statement: Patients randomized to the decision aid plus surgeon report had higher odds of making a quality decision than patients in routine care.

outcome: Knowledge about benefits and harms of knee replacement and non-surgical treatment
statement: The improvement in decision quality was driven mainly by knowledge: decision aid patients had much higher odds of answering at least 3 of 5 knowledge questions correctly.

outcome: Knowledge about benefits and harms of knee replacement and non-surgical treatment
statement: Knowledge gains were seen for recovery time, need for repeat surgery and serious complications, but not for the individualised question on improvement in pain or discomfort.

outcome: Decision quality: knowledgeable (3 of 5 knowledge questions correct) and treatment choice concordant with treatment preference
statement: Concordance between stated treatment preference and the actual treatment decision did not differ between arms.

outcome: Decisional conflict measured with the 4-item SURE test
statement: Decision aid patients more often reported knowing the benefits and risks of the options on the SURE test, while the overall SURE score and perceived shared decision-making did not differ between arms.

outcome: Treatment decision: undergoing total knee replacement versus non-surgical management
statement: Patients exposed to the decision aid and surgeon report had lower odds of deciding to have surgery within the study timeframe, despite no difference in treatment preference or willingness to have surgery.

outcome: Feasibility of integrating the decision aid into an online routine pre-surgical assessment, including recruitment and survey completion
statement: Recruitment fell well short of the planned sample size, although survey completion among randomized patients was high.
Clustering of patients by surgeon was negligible, so the primary model did not account for clustering.

outcome: Baseline health-related quality of life measured with the EQ-5D-5L (dimension responses and utility)
statement: At baseline, participants had substantially impaired health: mean EQ-5D-5L utility was about 0.47 to 0.48 and most reported moderate to severe problems with mobility, usual activities and pain or discomfort.
Better than dead preferences were expressed in most choices, and a religious life stance and low educational level were associated with more scenarios being preferred to being dead.

outcome: Test-retest agreement of BTD choices (tetrachoric correlation)
statement: Test-retest agreement was good overall but much lower among the fastest responders.

outcome: Feasibility indicators: completion, response time, lexicographic preferences and logical inconsistencies
statement: Feasibility was acceptable: very few respondents dropped out, but responses were fast, 18% were lexicographic, and fast responders produced most inconsistencies.

The random-effects model produced consistent EQ-5D attribute weights, with larger coefficients for level 3 than level 2 for all attributes except mobility level 2, and pain/discomfort carrying the largest weight.
Values depended only weakly on duration, but a small number of maximal endurable time states was detected, fewer than in the earlier interviewer-administered study.
Attribute weights broadly agreed with the previous Dutch valuation study except for anxiety/depression, which received a lower weight here.

outcome: Utilities anchored to full health and dead using duration or immediate-death tasks
statement: Anchored modeling was more coherent for adults than adolescents. For both age groups, DCE with duration performed slightly better than DCE with immediate death on coefficient monotonicity and statistical significance.

outcome: Reported ease of understanding, differentiating, and deciding in DCE tasks
statement: All groups reported that states were relatively easy to understand and differentiate, but choice was harder; children more often reported ease than adolescents and adults.

outcome: Latent EQ-5D-Y-5L dimension-level disutilities and relative dimension importance
statement: Adult latent-DCE coefficients were all monotonic and statistically significant. Children and adolescents had several level-order reversals and some nonsignificant coefficients. Relative dimension rankings differed substantially by age group.

outcome: Coefficient monotonicity, statistical significance, preference heterogeneity, and quality-screening effects
statement: Analysis that retained all survey completers produced notably more logically inconsistent coefficients, which supported exclusion of responses that failed quality checks.
After quality assessment, the analysis included 546 children, 508 adolescents, and 908 adults.

outcome: Latent EQ-5D-Y-5L dimension-level disutilities and relative dimension importance
statement: Adults generally assigned larger disutilities than children and adolescents, especially to level-five pain or discomfort and worried, sad, or unhappy; age-group differences were smaller for several mild levels.

The EQ-5D-5L showed moderate-to-strong convergent relationships with EORTC QLQ-C30 domains; physical and role functioning had strong correlations with the corresponding physical EQ-5D dimensions, index, and EQ VAS.
EQ-5D index and EQ VAS scores discriminated among clinically different groups: scores declined with greater tumor severity and poorer ECOG performance, and differed across treatment modalities.
Across the analyzed sample, EQ-5D index and EQ VAS scores improved significantly from baseline to three months post-treatment.

Responsiveness was small overall for the EQ-5D index and moderate overall for EQ VAS, with larger effects among patients whose EORTC QLQ-C30 global health improved and little or no response in the no-change group.
MCID estimates varied by method. Distribution-based estimates were higher than the average anchor-based estimates for both EQ-5D index and EQ VAS.
The ROC-derived improvement threshold had low sensitivity, high specificity, and limited discrimination between improved and unchanged patients.
MCID-to-MDC ratios were below one at the individual level and above one at the group level, so the estimated MCIDs did not exceed measurement error for individual change but did so for group change.
The source England study achieved a response rate of nearly half of the people identified despite a home interview of about 45 minutes that addressed severe illness and death.
TTO and DCE models gave similar dimension weights and level patterns, despite the quality concerns being limited to TTO data.
The England value set showed broad similarity to value sets for Canada, the Netherlands, and Spain in dimension importance, level decrements, and scale length.

The paper identifies changes in QALY gains, cost-effectiveness estimates, and health technology assessment decisions when value sets change as a transition issue that is separate from statistical quality assurance.
Using all respondents, at least one logical inconsistency occurred less often in the England EQ-5D-5L study than in the MVH EQ-5D-3L study.
Residual distributions for logically consistent responses, inconsistent responses, and all responses were nearly symmetric around zero, with no evidence of a structural directional bias.
Sequential TTO residual pairs produced a nearly flat fitted line and did not support strong sequential dependence.
Probit and logit DCE specifications produced parameter estimates that were identical to three decimal places, and adding the TTO-style variance relationship to DCE data had a negligible effect.
The final hybrid model represented increasing variance at worse health states through respondent heterogeneity in a shape parameter, not through heteroscedastic errors.
For the five mildest EQ-5D-5L states, observed and predicted values did not support the claim that the censoring method biased mild-state estimates upward.
Latent-group membership estimates were robust to different priors and were driven mainly by the data.
Maximum-likelihood and Bayesian heterogeneity models, including multinomial, log-normal, and gamma specifications, produced very similar estimates.

Under uninformative heterogeneity, conditional logit coefficients differed from their true values for many variance specifications. Greater variance, especially in the cost coefficient, reduced coefficient bias, while estimated willingness to pay remained comparatively close to its true value.

Under the Group 4 taste-pattern specifications, all conditional logit coefficient estimates were within three standard errors of the true mean parameters, but the estimated ratios represented ratios of mean coefficients rather than mean individual willingness to pay and could materially underestimate true willingness to pay.
Under substitution-pattern heterogeneity, estimated willingness-to-pay ratios also represented ratios of means but did not accurately represent mean individual willingness to pay.

Conditional logit choice probabilities stayed close to true choice probabilities across the examined variance and correlation structures, even when coefficient and willingness-to-pay estimates were biased.

outcome: Design characteristics of EQ-5D valuation studies (elicitation technique, sampling, survey format, number of states valued)
statement: Thirty-one articles met inclusion criteria: 19 reported TTO-based scoring algorithms, 10 VAS-based, and 2 both, giving 21 TTO-based and 12 VAS-based algorithms; TTO-based algorithms existed for 17 countries as of March 2012.

outcome: Design characteristics of EQ-5D valuation studies (elicitation technique, sampling, survey format, number of states valued)
statement: Valuation study designs varied widely: quota or random sampling of general population respondents predominated, face-to-face interview was standard (one Canadian study used a web survey), total health states valued ranged from 7 to 198 and states per respondent from 1 to 23, and analysed sample sizes ranged from 151 to 3962.

outcome: Utility decrements and model specifications of published TTO- and VAS-based scoring algorithms
statement: Model specifications differed across algorithms: 10 main effects plus an N3 term (MVH structure) were common, some algorithms were main-effects only, Germany dropped three non-significant main effects, and interaction terms were added in the US, Argentina, Chile and Australia; the largest TTO decrements were for level 3 of mobility and pain/discomfort, followed by level 3 self-care.

outcome: Utility decrements and model specifications of published TTO- and VAS-based scoring algorithms
statement: VAS-based value sets were shifted toward the better end of the scale relative to TTO-based value sets, with fewer health states scored below zero, and the largest VAS decrements were for level 3 of mobility and self-care.

outcome: Association of study-level and country-level covariates with mean observed TTO utilities
statement: In meta-regressions of 17 commonly valued health states across 10 countries, mild states were unaffected by any covariate, while a higher percentage of male respondents and higher educational attainment were associated with higher utilities for some moderate and severe states, a higher urban population share with lower utilities for some moderate states, and higher health expenditure as a share of GDP with higher utilities for the most severe states.

outcome: Association of study-level and country-level covariates with mean observed TTO utilities
statement: Response rate, percentage of respondents excluded, GDP per capita, inflation and unemployment rate were not significantly associated with observed utilities for any health state, and higher CREATE scores showed only a non-significant tendency toward lower observed utilities.

outcome: Reporting completeness of valuation studies measured by CREATE score
statement: The authors developed CREATE, a 35-item reporting checklist scored 0 to 35 covering health state selection, sampling and target population, recruitment and survey administration, elicitation technique and transformation, respondent flow and data quality definitions, modelling and goodness-of-fit, and presentation of the final algorithm and value set; CREATE scores of reviewed studies ranged from 20 to 34.

outcome: Reporting completeness of valuation studies measured by CREATE score
statement: Reporting gaps were common: sample size calculations were described in only three valuation studies, recruitment strategies were rarely reported, and there was no consensus on defining or handling inconsistent or incomplete valuation data, with inconsistent respondents included in some countries and excluded in others.

outcome: Caregiver perceived burden of caring measured by the Zarit Burden Interview and its claudication categories
statement: Caregiver HRQOL was inversely and statistically significantly correlated with perceived burden of caring, although the effect size was small.

outcome: Caregiver EQ-5D-5L dimension response levels and EQ VAS score
statement: In the anxiety/depression dimension model, absence of claudication and higher satisfaction with the National Health System were protective, and female caregivers were more likely than male caregivers to report slight problems.

outcome: Caregiver EQ-5D-5L dimension response levels and EQ VAS score
statement: Care hours per week of the main caregiver and the family relationship with the patient did not significantly influence any EQ-5D dimension.

outcome: Caregiver EQ-5D index derived by crosswalk from EQ-5D-5L responses (UK, Spanish and French value sets)
statement: Truncated multiple regression models of caregiver EQ-5D scores fitted poorly and were not presented.

outcome: Ability of EQ-5D to discriminate HRQOL between caregiver burden groups (known-groups validity)
statement: Mean caregiver EQ-5D index differed between Zarit burden groups: the absence-of-claudication group differed significantly from both the mild and the high claudication groups, while mild and high claudication did not differ from each other.

outcome: Caregiver EQ-5D index derived by crosswalk from EQ-5D-5L responses (UK, Spanish and French value sets)
statement: Caregiver EQ-5D index and EQ VAS were markedly higher than those of the patients they cared for.

outcome: Caregiver EQ-5D-5L dimension response levels and EQ VAS score
statement: More than 20% of caregivers reported moderate, severe or extreme problems in pain/discomfort or anxiety/depression, whereas over 80% reported no or only slight problems in mobility and self-care.

outcome: Caregiver perceived burden of caring measured by the Zarit Burden Interview and its claudication categories
statement: Most caregivers were women, parents of the patient and employed, and 84% reported absence of claudication on the Zarit Burden Interview.

outcome: Caregiver EQ-5D-5L dimension response levels and EQ VAS score
statement: In the mobility dimension model, patient age, care hours per week of a secondary caregiver, patient sex and patient utility index were significantly associated with reported problems.

outcome: Caregiver EQ-5D-5L dimension response levels and EQ VAS score
