statement: In the self-care dimension model, shorter duration of caring, caregiver sex, patient sex and patient utility index were significantly associated with reported problems.

outcome: Caregiver EQ-5D-5L dimension response levels and EQ VAS score
statement: In the usual activities dimension model, patient age, Zarit burden category and patient utility index significantly predicted the level of problems.

outcome: Caregiver EQ-5D-5L dimension response levels and EQ VAS score
statement: In the pain/discomfort dimension model, employed caregivers were significantly less likely than unemployed caregivers to report slight problems, and older patient age and lower patient utility index were associated with more problems.

outcome: Classification of valuation exercises by health state, reference person, time frame, rater group and type of experience
statement: Forty-nine valuation exercises from 22 papers were classified in the framework; the role of experience is usually disregarded or reduced to personal experience in the present, linked to self-reported health.

outcome: Classification of valuation exercises by health state, reference person, time frame, rater group and type of experience
statement: Only two papers analysed the impact of experience on reported values while controlling for the other elements of the valuation exercise; no reviewed study eliciting public preferences used a past time frame, and no study of vested interest groups specified vicarious experience.

outcome: Reported effect of experience with a health state on elicited health state values
statement: In the reviewed evidence, people currently experiencing mild EQ-5D-3L states gave higher VAS values than those not experiencing them, while for a more severe state the reverse held; differences were small and only significant for one profile.

outcome: Reported effect of experience with a health state on elicited health state values
statement: Providing disease adaptation information (treated here as non-affective vicarious experience) systematically increased values, and the increase was largest among respondents with no experience of the condition.

outcome: Reported effect of experience with a health state on elicited health state values
statement: In one reviewed TTO study, respondents reporting full health (11111) were more likely to trade time and gave lower values than respondents self-reporting any impaired profile, for all three states valued.

outcome: Test-retest reliability of EQ-5D-5L dimensions, utility index and EQ VAS over 10 days (absolute ICC)
statement: Test-retest agreement over 10 days was above the 0.7 acceptability threshold for every EQ-5D-5L dimension, for the utility index and for EQ VAS, with the lowest value on pain/discomfort.

outcome: Feasibility of self-completion, judged by the proportion of missing or inappropriate responses
statement: Only four of 501 completed questionnaires had missing EQ-5D-5L or EQ VAS responses, which the authors read as evidence that self-completion of the Amharic EQ-5D-5L is feasible in adolescents.

outcome: Floor and ceiling effects on EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: Floor effects were uncommon and ceiling effects were high on all dimensions except anxiety/depression and pain/discomfort; 94.5% of school-sample adolescents reported no mobility problems.

outcome: EQ VAS scores and EQ-5D-5L utility index scores by disease group
statement: Mean EQ VAS and mean EQ-5D-5L utility index were highest in the school sample and lower in each mental health disorder group.

outcome: Known-group (discriminant) validity of EQ-5D-5L dimensions, utility index and EQ VAS across disease group, chronic illness experience, sex and education
statement: The EQ-5D-5L utility index and EQ VAS discriminated significantly between the school sample and adolescents with major mental health disorders, and between levels of chronic illness experience.

outcome: Known-group (discriminant) validity of EQ-5D-5L dimensions, utility index and EQ VAS across disease group, chronic illness experience, sex and education
statement: Group differences were significant on self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression, but not on mobility.

outcome: Known-group (discriminant) validity of EQ-5D-5L dimensions, utility index and EQ VAS across disease group, chronic illness experience, sex and education
statement: Pairwise comparisons showed significant differences in EQ VAS and utility index between the school sample and each disorder group, and a significant utility difference between depression and bipolar disorder.

outcome: Known-group (discriminant) validity of EQ-5D-5L dimensions, utility index and EQ VAS across disease group, chronic illness experience, sex and education
statement: Known-group differences by educational status were significant for the utility index, EQ VAS and four dimensions, whereas differences by sex were significant only for mobility, pain/discomfort and the utility index.
Postoperative haematuria and pain were the most frequent outcomes across procedures, and side effects were common but generally mild.
TURBT produced a greater early symptom and care burden than TULA or cystoscopy, including more haematuria, pain, acute urinary retention, catheter use, analgesic use, and healthcare contacts.

Health-related quality of life was worse after TURBT than after TULA on postoperative day 1, but the difference was absent by day 14; TULA and cystoscopy did not differ significantly at either time point.

Male TURBT patients generally reported worse lower urinary tract symptom scores than male TULA or cystoscopy patients, with voiding and nocturia having the greatest impact; overall LUTS scores changed little over time.
TULA outcomes were more similar to cystoscopy-only outcomes than to TURBT outcomes during early recovery.

Only the EQ-5D-Y-3L had a ceiling effect in the total sample of children with special healthcare needs; the EQ-5D-Y-5L was below the prespecified threshold in the total sample, and no instrument had a floor effect.

In the total sample, EQ-5D-Y-5L and CHU9D met the prespecified criteria across all evaluated psychometric attributes. PedsQL and EQ-5D-Y-3L performed well on most attributes, while AQoL-6D and HUI3 could not be assessed conclusively for reliability or responsiveness.
PedsQL, EQ-5D-Y-3L, and EQ-5D-Y-5L had good test-retest agreement in the total sample, while CHU9D had moderate agreement. AQoL-6D and HUI3 results were inconclusive because the samples were small.

EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, and CHU9D were responsive to improvements in general health and main health condition. PedsQL, EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, and CHU9D were responsive to worsening health. The response effect sizes were small in the main analysis.

Ceiling effects, test-retest reliability, and responsiveness varied by age and report type. EQ-5D-Y-5L did not show acceptable test-retest reliability in proxy reports, and CHU9D did not show acceptable test-retest reliability among children aged 13–18 years.

All six instruments demonstrated known-group validity with statistically significant, large differences across the tested known groups, and instrument items generally supported the prespecified convergent and divergent validity hypotheses against PedsQL items.
The likelihood of choosing death increased with longer health-state duration and greater EQ-5D-Y-3L severity across perspectives.

Worse-than-dead responses were substantially more common in binary better-than-dead choices with explicit duration than in ranking tasks without duration; even state 23333 for one year had a worse-than-dead proportion above 40%, compared with about 25% in the ranking data.

Maximal endurable time patterns increased with health-state severity, but their distributions differed little across perspectives or religious-affiliation groups. Irregular response patterns were more common than maximal endurable time patterns for every state and perspective.

With duration included, respondents reported more worse-than-dead preferences under the self-perspective than under either proxy perspective. Self and proxy responses remained strongly aligned, and proxy1 and proxy2 did not differ significantly from each other.

When duration was omitted, the rank of death and the full ranking distributions did not differ systematically between self and proxy perspectives or between religious and nonreligious groups; death had a median rank of 6 in all groups.

Religious affiliation was negatively associated with worse-than-dead preferences. Nonreligious respondents were more likely to choose death across all perspectives, and the association remained in the stricter analysis of respondents for whom religion was important.

Stronger support for euthanasia, female gender, and not having children were associated with a higher likelihood of a worse-than-dead preference, while higher expected age at death for oneself was associated with a lower likelihood. Belief in life after death was not significant in the fully adjusted model.
The arthritis literature used many inconsistent or inaccurate names for EQ-5D and its versions and sometimes described the instrument as a weighted index, index score, or index scale.
Of the first 20 publications reviewed, half did not mention EQ-5D in the abstract; the 10 that did used several different names, including expansions that treated EQ-5D as an abbreviation.
The 62-publication PubMed sample included spacing and capitalization errors and inaccurate expansions of EQ-5D in abbreviation lists.
Across the limited samples, published reports applied the established nomenclature for EQ-5D and its components inconsistently.

outcome: Time to first unplanned readmission, defined as an emergency department visit or acute care hospital readmission for a nonelective medical condition
statement: In the 11,177-person analysis cohort, observed unplanned readmission increased from 5.6% within 30 days to 18.4% within 180 days and 25.0% within 360 days of discharge.

outcome: Prediction-model discrimination measured with C-index and time-dependent AUC
statement: For the 180-day prediction window in the full sample, the administrative-data Base model had a C-index of 0.762; adding EQ-5D-5L increased it to 0.774, and adding VR-12 increased it to 0.782.

outcome: Prediction-model discrimination measured with C-index and time-dependent AUC
statement: Across 30-, 180-, and 360-day windows in the full sample, EQ-5D-5L increased C-index by 0.011 to 0.014, while VR-12 increased it by 0.020 to 0.021.

outcome: Prediction-model discrimination measured with C-index and time-dependent AUC
statement: In the ACSC subgroup, VR-12 improved discrimination by 2.2 to 3.4 percentage points across prediction windows; EQ-5D-5L gains were smaller and did not significantly improve discrimination.

outcome: Prediction-model calibration and predictive accuracy measured with calibration slope and Brier score
statement: All full-sample and ACSC models showed adequate calibration, with calibration slopes close to 1.0.

Age, comorbidity count, length of stay, admission acuity, and prior hospital or emergency department use were leading Base-model predictors; VR-12 current health and physical limitations and EQ-5D-5L mobility and EQ VAS were leading PROM predictors.

outcome: Prediction-model calibration and predictive accuracy measured with calibration slope and Brier score
statement: Brier scores were about 0.03 to 0.04 for 30-day predictions and 0.12 to 0.13 for 180-day predictions, which showed lower absolute accuracy for the longer horizon.
Time-varying Cox, complete-case, and logistic-regression sensitivity analyses gave results consistent with the primary landmark analyses.

Anxiety/depression severity correlated with every physical EQ-5D-5L dimension; the association was strongest for pain/discomfort, moderate for usual activities and mobility, and smaller for self-care.
Survey-mode stratified generalized ordered logistic and linear regression analyses gave results that were largely consistent with the combined analysis.

After adjustment for age, sex, education, caregiving status, and health condition, higher anxiety/depression severity had a graded association with greater odds of reporting problems in mobility, self-care, usual activities, and pain/discomfort.
Higher anxiety/depression severity had a graded association with lower Chinese EQ-5D-5L utility values and lower EQ VAS scores in crude and adjusted models.

outcome: Internal consistency
statement: All three Basque questionnaires exceeded the prespecified Cronbach alpha threshold of 0.70.

outcome: Convergent validity against SF-36
statement: The Barthel Index, EQ-5D-5L utility index, EQ VAS, and PHQ-9 correlated with the SF-36 physical component as hypothesized; PHQ-9 also correlated with the SF-36 mental component, while Barthel Index did not and the EQ-5D measures had low mental-component correlations.

outcome: Score distributions and floor and ceiling effects
statement: The Barthel Index and EQ-5D-5L utility index had ceiling effects, the PHQ-9 had a floor effect, and the EQ VAS had neither a floor nor a ceiling effect under the prespecified 15% criterion.
Responsiveness was not assessed, and some PHQ-9 known-groups comparisons were not statistically significant in small subgroups.

outcome: Known-groups validity by comorbidity burden
statement: Barthel Index, EQ-5D-5L utility, and EQ VAS distinguished comorbidity groups; PHQ-9 differed by number of comorbidities but not by Charlson Comorbidity Index group.

outcome: Comprehensibility and feasibility during cognitive debriefing
statement: Cognitive debriefing led the team to replace some Standard Basque terms with informal terms for better comprehension and to correct syntactic and grammatical problems in the EQ-5D-5L; EuroQol Research Foundation accepted the revised version.

outcome: Functional independence, utility, perceived health, and depression symptom scores
statement: The cohort had high functional independence and health status and low depression symptom scores.

outcome: Unidimensional structure validity
statement: Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a single dimension for each questionnaire, with acceptable confirmatory model fit.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index scored with the United States value set
statement: Mean HRQoL of the New York sample during the first COVID-19 wave was 0.82 for the EQ-5D-5L index, 7.5 for the level sum score, and 79.3 for the EQ VAS.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index scored with the United States value set
statement: HRQoL improved with increasing age, with the youngest group (18–24 years) reporting the lowest EQ-5D-5L index and most problems across all five dimensions, while gender had no noticeable effect.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index scored with the United States value set
statement: EQ outcome scores declined with each additional chronic condition and with worse recalled access to health care.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index scored with the United States value set
statement: Respondents reporting COVID-19 infection without recovery had by far the lowest EQ-5D-5L index and highest level sum score.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index scored with the United States value set
statement: Loss of health insurance due to COVID-19, being unable to work, and low disaster preparedness were each associated with markedly lower EQ-5D-5L index scores in the univariable analysis.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index scored with the United States value set
statement: In multivariable analysis restricted to healthy respondents only a few factors remained significant (race/ethnicity, education, living situation, disaster preparedness, smoking, and experienced access to health care), whereas in diseased respondents most factors were significant, with number of chronic conditions, inability to work, and bad access to care showing the largest negative coefficients.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L index scored with the United States value set
statement: Deprivation factors such as race/ethnicity and household income showed moderate univariable effects that largely disappeared in the stratified multivariable analyses.

outcome: EQ VAS self-rated health (0–100)
statement: Modifying effects of the determinants were generally larger for the EQ-5D-5L index and level sum score than for the EQ VAS.
An administration error produced multiple assessments for some residents: seven self-reports and seven staff proxy reports were repeated at different time points, and all were included in analysis.

EQ-5D-5L had moderate to strong positive correlations with QoL-ACC across respondent types. Correlations with EQ-HWB-S were weaker than hypothesized for residents and family proxies and strong only for staff proxies. Correlations with ASCOT were generally absent or weak.
No instrument met the prespecified threshold for a floor or ceiling effect. The largest near-ceiling proportion was for ASCOT staff proxy-person responses, at 14%, below the 15% threshold.

EQ-5D-5L index scores had excellent resident-staff reliability and good resident-family and staff-family reliability. Resident-staff reliability was also good for QoL-ACC, EQ-HWB, EQ-HWB-S, and EQ VAS, but only moderate for ASCOT; ASCOT and EQ VAS performed poorly for some family comparisons.
Item-level agreement was better for observable domains such as mobility, personal care, and activities than for emotional well-being, feelings, or cognition.
Only staff-reported EQ-5D-5L scores significantly distinguished residents with no or mild cognitive impairment from residents with moderate or severe impairment.

EQ-5D-5L scores from residents, staff proxies, and family proxies all significantly distinguished higher from lower dependency. Other measures generally showed poorer quality of life with greater dependency, but several comparisons did not reach significance in the small subsamples.
The EQ-5D-5L had the fewest missing values among the four measures. Missingness differed by respondent, with little missing staff data and more missing family and resident data.

EQ-HWB(-S), QoL-ACC, and ASCOT showed minimal missing data overall, no floor or ceiling effects, and generally moderate to good interrater reliability, but their small assigned subsamples made the validity results exploratory.

Across measures, resident self-reported preference-weighted scores were higher than proxy scores, and family proxy scores were lower than staff proxy scores. For EQ-5D-5L, mean scores were 0.57 for residents, 0.50 for staff proxies, and 0.37 for family proxies.
Caregivers accepted the EQ-5D-Y layout, wording, and recall period and generally understood the EQ VAS; eating, communication, and movement were the most frequent additional suggestions.
The final bank contained behaviour, communication, eating, independence, play, mood, movement, pain, relationships, sickness or general health, and sleep.

The final items represented physical, emotional, social, and functional HRQoL and mapped to ICF-CY body structure and function, activities, and participation, but not environmental or personal-factor categories.
The candidate pool grew from 36 literature-derived items to 53 after caregiver interviews, then fell to 28 after Delphi round 1, 15 for second-round consideration, and 11 final items.
The review found no generic child HRQoL measure based solely on observable behaviour; the greatest unmet need was for children younger than three years.
PROMIS-16 items generally had lower ceiling percentages and higher informativity than matched EQ-5D-5L items.
Conceptually matched items showed good cross-instrument convergence for physical functioning and anxiety or depression.
The PROMIS-16 cognitive-function items showed high floor percentages, weak alignment with other constructs, and anomalous positive EQ VAS transitions at the worst response level.
Most severity increments in both instruments were associated with lower EQ VAS scores, but EQ-5D-5L retained stronger independent associations with EQ VAS in instrument-level models.
Exploratory factor analysis identified six factors: physical function, social roles and activities, anxiety or depression, pain interference, cognitive function, and sleep or fatigue.
Compared with prior item-testing evidence, stand-alone PROMIS-16 administration produced higher ceilings for social-role items and higher floors for cognitive-function items.

All participants traded some length of life for better health in at least one task, but willingness to trade varied and reflected time with loved ones, hope for medical advances, the inherent value of life, quality of life, burden on others, and judgments that some states were worse than death.

Almost half of participants showed maximum endurable time preferences: they preferred a poor health state to immediate death but preferred a shorter rather than a longer period in that state. Reported tipping points ranged from 3 months to 2 years.

Most participants gave special value to one or three final weeks of life because this time allowed preparation for death, farewells, practical arrangements, and closure; some participants did not consider the short extension important.

The interviews did not give clear additional evidence of discounting future time. Some participants gave little weight to duration differences in the far future, some treated equal absolute differences alike, and two described judgments consistent with constant proportional trade-off.

Participants used both multiplicative and additive decision strategies. Some considered duration conditional on the health state, while others separated health and duration and ignored health attributes that were constant across profiles even when duration differed.

Colour shading and bold text often helped participants identify severity and matching attributes, but heavy reliance on colour sometimes caused colour-counting heuristics or the omission of constant attributes when duration varied.

Death-related wording changed interpretation and emotional response. Views on pass away versus dying were mixed, immediate death was emotive for some, and participants recommended consistent wording across alternatives.

Participants sometimes struggled with hypothetical or unfamiliar health attributes, inferred treatments or causes of death, overlooked duration, selected profiles close to their own health, tried to select a greyed-out option, or misunderstood the dead state.
Participants generally engaged carefully and had few overt difficulties, but some fully engaged participants still gave inconsistent choices as their considerations changed during the interview.

outcome: Bolt-on development methods and wording characteristics
statement: The review found substantially more differentiated five-level than three-level vision and hearing bolt-on wordings.

outcome: Test-retest reliability and patient-proxy agreement
statement: No included publication assessed test-retest reliability or patient-proxy agreement, and evidence on responsiveness and content validity was limited.

outcome: Patterns of bolt-on use, valuation, and evidence coverage
statement: Five vision publications and two hearing publications valued EQ-5D plus bolt-on health states using diverse methods; one publication developed a full EQ-5D-5L plus vision value set that five later publications applied.
The evidence base was larger for vision than hearing and was more developed for five-level than three-level bolt-ons.

outcome: Bolt-on development methods and wording characteristics
statement: Six vision publications and six hearing publications proposed new wordings; only three publications in each stream used qualitative techniques during item development.
Most included source studies were cross-sectional, and most assessed self-reported health; face-to-face and online administration were the most common channels.

outcome: Ceiling and floor effects
statement: Adding vision or hearing bolt-ons reduced EQ-5D ceiling effects across adult general-population and patient samples.

outcome: Absolute and relative informativity
statement: Where assessed, adding a bolt-on increased both absolute and relative informativity compared with EQ-5D alone.

outcome: Divergent, convergent, known-group, and structural validity
statement: Vision and hearing bolt-ons generally had weak correlations with the five core EQ-5D dimensions, which supported divergent validity; convergence was stronger with relevant patient-reported sensory measures than with some clinical measures.

outcome: Divergent, convergent, known-group, and structural validity
statement: Known-group validity was shown for several relevant characteristics, including visual acuity, severity of visual impairment, visual functioning problems, presence of hearing problems, bilateral disability classification, and better-ear performance, although some comparisons were not significant.

outcome: Responsiveness of vision bolt-ons
statement: The two publications that assessed responsiveness found that vision bolt-ons improved detection of change relative to standard EQ-5D; no hearing publication assessed responsiveness.

outcome: Divergent, convergent, known-group, and structural validity
statement: One structural-validity study placed vision and hearing bolt-ons on an other-physical-symptoms factor that did not contain core EQ-5D dimensions; adding vision improved explained variance in EQ VAS only slightly.
The review included 53 articles; data from 42 articles were extracted for construct validity, test-retest reliability, and responsiveness.

Seven articles were related to content validity. All content-validity articles reported comprehensibility, but only three reported comprehensiveness and three reported relevance; the evidence was too limited for population-specific synthesis.
For self-reported AQoL-6D, low-quality evidence indicated sufficient construct validity; no evidence was available for responsiveness or test-retest reliability.

For self-reported CHU9D, high-quality evidence supported sufficient construct validity and high-quality evidence indicated inconsistent test-retest reliability; no responsiveness data were available. For proxy-reported CHU9D, high-quality evidence supported sufficient construct validity and responsiveness.

For self-reported EQ-5D-Y, high-quality evidence supported sufficient construct validity, while low-quality evidence supported sufficient responsiveness and test-retest reliability. For the proxy version, high-quality evidence supported sufficient construct validity and moderate-quality evidence indicated inconsistent test-retest reliability. Most EQ-5D-Y results used unweighted summative scores because value sets were unavailable before 2019.

For self-reported HUI2, high-quality evidence supported sufficient construct validity and responsiveness, while low-quality evidence indicated insufficient test-retest reliability. For proxy-reported HUI2, high-quality evidence indicated inconsistent construct validity and insufficient responsiveness.

For self-reported HUI3, high-quality evidence supported sufficient construct validity and responsiveness. For proxy-reported HUI3, high-quality evidence supported sufficient construct validity but indicated insufficient responsiveness.

Population-specific synthesis found high-quality evidence of sufficient construct validity for CHU9D in general-population children in Australia, China, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom; for EQ-5D-Y in general-population children, children with musculoskeletal or connective-tissue diseases, and South Africa; and for HUI2 and HUI3 in children with neoplasm and in Canada.

Evidence was concentrated unevenly: CHU9D evidence was mainly from general-population samples, while HUI evidence was concentrated in pediatric neoplasm and North American samples. Evidence for test-retest reliability and responsiveness was scarce and often methodologically weak.

The final confirmatory factor analysis measurement model comprised seven factors: physical functioning, psychological symptoms, energy/sleep, physical pain, social functioning, needs and satisfaction, and showed good fit.
The ONS-4 happiness item loaded on the satisfaction factor rather than psychological symptoms, and all WEMWBS items loaded on the psychological symptoms factor despite content differences.
Psychological symptoms was the factor with the most items (23) and satisfaction the fewest (4); standardised factor loadings were generally large.
Tests of unidimensionality supported single factors for psychological symptoms and for energy/sleep, because the global factor explained most of the common variance.

Health measures covered five of the seven factors (physical functioning, psychological symptoms, social functioning, energy/sleep and pain), wellbeing measures covered three (psychological symptoms, needs and satisfaction), and the social care measure covered one (needs).
The EQ-5D-5L items loaded on three constructs only: physical functioning (mobility, self-care, usual activities), pain and psychological symptoms.

Candidate bolt-ons were identified for constructs missing from the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system (energy/sleep, social functioning, needs and satisfaction) and for the partially covered mental health area (items loading on psychological symptoms), for example cognition, energy and dignity items.

The ASCOT dignity item was poorly associated with all identified factors, showing large local dependencies and residual correlations, and was removed from the factor analysis; the ASCOT social participation item loaded on the needs factor rather than social functioning.

Five of the seven factors, and identical factor structures for the EQ-5D-5L and ONS-4, reproduced the measurement model previously identified in the Multi-Instrument Comparison (MIC) dataset; ICECAP items were better represented (by the needs factor) than in the MIC.
Exploratory factor analyses gave a variable number of factors, between six (parallel analysis) and eleven (eigenvalues greater than one).

outcome: Test-retest reliability of EQ-5D-Y dimensions and VAS
statement: Test-retest agreement over 24 to 48 hours was moderate to good for Mobility, Looking After Myself and Worried/Sad/Unhappy, fair for Pain or Discomfort, and poor for Usual Activities; the VAS showed strong agreement.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y dimension profiles and VAS scores by health group
statement: EQ-5D-Y dimensions discriminated between the acutely ill children and the other three groups, and the special school group reported more mobility problems than mainstream children; the acutely ill group had the worst Composite Score and the lowest VAS.

outcome: Discriminant, concurrent and convergent validity of the EQ-5D-Y
statement: The Composite Score correlated with the VAS only in the acutely ill children; there was no significant correlation in the healthy, chronically disabled or chronically ill groups.

outcome: Discriminant, concurrent and convergent validity of the EQ-5D-Y
statement: Convergent validity between all matching EQ-5D-Y and PedsQL dimensions, and between Pain or Discomfort and the Faces Pain Scale, was seen only in the acutely ill children, while EQ-5D-Y Mobility and Looking After Myself correlated with the matching WeeFIM dimensions in all three groups with health conditions.

outcome: Responsiveness of EQ-5D-Y Composite Score and VAS between baseline and three months
statement: The EQ-5D-Y Composite Score and VAS showed a medium effect size between baseline and three months in the two groups expected to improve (chronically ill and acutely ill), and only a small effect in the mainstream and special school groups.

outcome: Feasibility and clinical usefulness of routine EQ-5D-Y administration
statement: The EQ-5D-Y was feasible in routine use: all children completed it within the recommended five minutes, six of nine therapists found it very easy to use and would continue using it, and all found it useful for planning management, especially the Pain or Discomfort and Worried/Sad/Unhappy information.

outcome: EQ-5D-Y dimension profiles and VAS scores by health group
statement: Unexpected responses appeared in healthy children: 14% reported Mobility problems that the WeeFIM did not confirm and 21% reported Pain or Discomfort problems not reflected in the Faces Pain Scale, while children with chronic conditions reported dimension problems but a median VAS of 100.

outcome: Internal consistency
statement: PedsQL scores generally had acceptable internal consistency, but school functioning in the Generic Core Scales and treatment adherence in the Cardiac Module were below the prespecified alpha threshold of 0.70.

outcome: Convergent validity
statement: Convergent validity was supported for all three preference-based instruments against the PedsQL Generic Core Scales, although selected self-care, worried, tired, and daily-routine correlations were weaker than expected.

outcome: Score distributions, ceiling effects, and floor effects
statement: At baseline, both EQ-5D-Y versions had substantial ceiling effects, while CHU9D had a much lower ceiling effect; no instrument showed a floor effect.

outcome: Known-group validity and discriminative ability
statement: The PedsQL Generic Core Scales showed the strongest known-group discrimination. EQ-5D-Y instruments discriminated functional status and general health better than clinical severity, and CHU9D showed significant differences only for general health.

outcome: Responsiveness to change
statement: Among participants reporting improved general health at 12 months, EQ-5D-Y-5L was the most responsive instrument. EQ-5D-Y-3L and CHU9D had small responsiveness, and PedsQL instruments were minimally responsive.

outcome: Responsiveness to change
statement: Among participants reporting worsened general health at 12 months, none of the overall instruments showed meaningful responsiveness. The PedsQL Cardiac Module treatment-anxiety domain was the exception.

outcome: Test-retest reliability
statement: Test-retest reliability in the stable subgroup was satisfactory for most scores. CHU9D had the highest reliability among preference-based instruments, and EQ-5D-Y-3L was just below the prespecified threshold.
In the total sample, tiredness and sleep produced the largest reductions in the EQ-5D-5L ceiling and were the only individual bolt-ons to improve relative informativity.

Most bolt-ons loaded on factors distinct from the core EQ-5D-5L dimensions; tiredness and sleep represented vitality, cognition represented cognitive functioning, and social participation and social relationships represented social functioning.

Condition-relevant bolt-ons improved known-groups validity. Breathing performed best for respiratory conditions, cognition for memory problems, dizziness for stroke consequences, and muscle weakness or swollen ankles/feet for relevant musculoskeletal groups.

Tiredness had the strongest and most consistent added explanatory power for EQ VAS and WHO-5, while condition-specific symptom bolt-ons sometimes added explanatory value in relevant chronic conditions.
All tested bolt-ons had excellent item-level and instrument-level test-retest reliability; social participation had the lowest reliability among them.

Most bolt-ons improved instrument responsiveness in respondents who reported worse health, but only tiredness, sleep, cognition, and smell/taste improved responsiveness in those who reported health improvement.
Cognition and breathing added little in the full general-population sample but performed better in relevant chronic-condition subgroups.
Social participation improved known-groups validity in the depression/anxiety subgroup and added explanatory power for mental well-being rather than health in the general population.

Participants had mixed preferences, but they allocated the highest equal vote shares to 1-week and 4-week recall periods; ease of recall favored 1 week, while familiarity and representativeness favored 4 weeks.
The variants were more responsive than standard EQ-5D-5L for distinguishing patients who improved from those who were stable or worsened, whether change was defined by SGRQ or clinical assessment.
Among 120 follow-up participants, SGRQ change classified 35.8% as better, 36.7% as stable, and 27.5% as worse; clinical assessment classified 43.3%, 33.3%, and 23.3%, respectively.

All interview participants considered the proposed variants relevant, acceptable, easy to understand, and easy to answer; votes were equally divided between intensity-based and frequency-based response options.

The review assessed documentation from 46 countries, excluded 12 countries, and included 34 official national pharmacoeconomic guidelines.
Among the 34 included guidelines, EQ-5D was named in 29, SF-6D in 11, Health Utilities Index in 10, Quality of Well-Being in 3, Assessment of Quality of Life in 2, and CHU9D in 1.

Fifteen guidelines preferred or encouraged a specified multi-attribute utility instrument. All 15 included EQ-5D: 13 preferred only EQ-5D and 2 preferred EQ-5D with another measure. No guideline preferred another MAUI without also recommending EQ-5D.

Nineteen guidelines recommended cost-utility analysis but did not prefer a specific MAUI. Fourteen gave MAUI examples, all of which included EQ-5D; 12 preferred domestic population preference weights. Five gave no MAUI examples.
Most guidelines referred to EQ-5D in general or to EQ-5D-3L. Six recommended EQ-5D-3L; EQ-5D-5L was an alternative in four guidelines and the preferred version in the Netherlands and Portugal.
Guidelines commonly justified EQ-5D preference by its widespread use, comparability and consistency across analyses, and the availability of national value sets.

The review included 187 studies with 116,525 participants; cohort studies were most common and Europe contributed most studies.
Included-study quality varied: most studies were moderate quality, followed by high quality; few were low quality.

EQ-5D-5L was used in most included studies. Face-to-face and digital administration were the most frequently reported modes. Reporting of index scores, EQ VAS, profiles, and value sets was inconsistent.
The pooled mean EQ-5D utility score among patients with COVID-19 was 0.76, with extreme between-study heterogeneity.
The pooled mean EQ VAS score among patients with COVID-19 was 70.76, with extreme between-study heterogeneity.
Pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression were the most affected EQ-5D dimensions; self-care was least affected.

Utility scores differed significantly by geographic region and national income category. Asia had the highest regional pooled utility and Europe had the lowest; low- and middle-income settings had higher pooled utility than high-income settings.
Pooled utility did not differ significantly by EQ-5D version, study design, measurement before versus after 12 weeks, or age below versus at least 60 years.

Across 42 studies, common predictors of lower HRQoL included older age, female sex, greater acute disease severity, comorbidities, hospitalization or intensive treatment, and persistent post-COVID-19 symptoms. Socioeconomic disadvantage and weaker psychosocial resources were also reported.
Leave-one-out and study-exclusion sensitivity analyses did not materially change the pooled utility estimate, and Egger's test did not show significant publication bias.
