statement: Among the five mapping algorithms, response mapping from SF-12 summary scores to EQ-5D item responses came closest to the observed EQ-5D results, while response-mapping functions gave wider error margins around utility estimates than direct-mapping functions.
The initial access site was changed most often in procedures initiated through radial access.
Any puncture-site complication and local hematoma were most common with brachial access, least common with radial access, and intermediate with femoral access.
Follow-up groups did not differ significantly in reported myocardial infarction, stroke or transient ischemic attack, repeated coronarography, PCI, or coronary artery bypass grafting.

Patients most often preferred radial access for a hypothetical future procedure. Among patients who had experienced more than one access, 70.4% selected radial access as most convenient and none selected brachial access.
Access groups did not differ significantly in vascular complications during PCI; radial-access PCI used the lowest median contrast volume.
Overall EQ-5D-3L results and adapted EQ VAS ratings did not differ significantly by access site, but brachial access was associated with more frequent self-care problems and slower improvement.

Both bolt-ons reduced the full-sample ceiling effect only slightly; R2 produced the larger reduction. In the respiratory-condition group, R1 did not reduce the ceiling and R2 produced only a small reduction.
All 10,033 respondents had complete EQ-5D-5L index, EQ VAS, respiratory bolt-on, WHODAS, and mMRC data and were included in analysis.

R1 had strong correlations with EQ-5D-5L usual activities and WHODAS long-distance walking. R2 had moderate correlations with almost all EQ-5D-5L and WHODAS dimensions, while the two bolt-ons were strongly correlated with each other.

All measures discriminated between respiratory-condition groups, but the R2 utility score had the largest standardized effect size. Smoking-history groups showed only small and similar differences across measures.
The bolt-on descriptive systems represented more observed health profiles than the core EQ-5D-5L: 843 core profiles, 1,511 EQ-5D-5L plus R1 profiles, and 1,492 EQ-5D-5L plus R2 profiles.

Utility scores decreased with greater mMRC breathlessness severity. In respondents with a respiratory condition, bolt-on utilities were lower than the core EQ-5D-5L utility, with the lowest mean for R2; correlations with mMRC were also strongest for R2.

Fifty studies using eight different preference-based quality of life instruments met the inclusion criteria; the QOL-AD was the most used instrument (32 studies, 64%) and the EQ-5D was second (13 studies, 26%), with ICECAP-O (2), DEMQOL (2), SF-36, SF-12, DQOL and DQI also used.

outcome: QualSyst methodological quality scores of the included studies
statement: Methodological quality of the included studies was generally high on the QualSyst tool, with scores ranging from 0.77 to 1.00 and duplicate-assessed agreement of 87% on a 10% sample.

outcome: Inter-rater agreement between self-report and proxy-report of quality of life, measured by intraclass correlation coefficients for overall or index scores
statement: Agreement between self-report and proxy-report was generally poor irrespective of the instrument applied, the proxy type or the perspective adopted: of the 19 papers reporting ICC for overall or index scores, 12 reported poor agreement and 7 moderate agreement, and no paper reported good or excellent agreement.

outcome: Mean self-reported and proxy-reported quality of life scores (raw scores or utility scores) and the direction of their difference
statement: Proxies generally rated the older person's quality of life lower than the older person did: of the 40 papers reporting mean self and proxy scores, 38 reported lower proxy ratings; exceptions were higher proxy ratings on the ICECAP-O in one study and on the QOL-AD in another.

outcome: Dimension-level inter-rater agreement measured by kappa statistics
statement: Agreement tended to be higher on more observable domains such as physical health and mobility than on less observable domains such as emotional well-being and mental health, although one study reported the reverse pattern with only slight agreement for physical health.

The two studies that asked paid-carer proxies to adopt both perspectives found higher agreement when the proxy adopted the older person perspective; in one, EQ-5D agreement was moderate under the older person perspective and poor under the proxy's own perspective, while EQ VAS agreement was low under either perspective.

outcome: Reporting of cognitive assessments, thresholds, proxy perspective and scoring algorithms across the included studies
statement: A wide and inconsistent range of cognitive assessments and thresholds was applied; the MMSE was used in 36 studies (72%) and the CDR in 16 (32%), with eight different MMSE thresholds used to describe participants with probable or possible Alzheimer's disease and seven different criteria for established dementia.

Most included studies were cross-sectional (36 studies, 72%) so few tracked quality of life over time; the studies that followed dyads for at least a year found self-reported quality of life stayed broadly steady while proxy ratings declined, widening the self-proxy gap in line with rising disease severity markers.

Family members, mostly spouses and adult offspring, were the most common proxies (33 studies, 66%); 8 studies (16%) used professional carers, 7 studies (14%) used both groups, and the remainder used a mix or did not specify proxy type.
Only 12 of the 50 studies reported the scoring algorithm applied to generate utility scores, which the authors attribute to none of the included studies being economic evaluations.
Negative values made up 44.3% of analyzed cTTO responses; observed mean state values decreased with severity and ranged from -0.844 for 55555 to 0.960 for 11112.
In the analytic sample, 36.4% reported state 11111; pain/discomfort was the most frequently reported problem dimension, and the mean EQ VAS score was 75.9.
The study completed a cTTO-only valuation design with 20 tasks per participant and approximately half the standard recommended sample size, without a discrete-choice experiment.

All candidate models had logically ordered coefficients and similar cross-validation accuracy; the constrained-intercept Tobit model corrected for heteroskedasticity was preferred because it predicted mild states best while retaining comparable cross-validation performance.
Of 545 participants with complete data, 53 with severe response inconsistency were excluded, which left 492 participants and 9840 cTTO responses in the primary analysis.
Reinclusion of inconsistent responses and sequential exclusion of each interviewer produced almost identical or only marginally different preferred-model estimates.
The Uganda EQ-5D-5L value set ranged from -1.116 for 55555 to 1 for 11111; pain/discomfort had the largest effect and anxiety/depression had the smallest effect.
A representative sample of 1,079 adults completed 10 cTTO and 12 DCE tasks each, and the response rate was 34%.

The hybrid heteroskedastic Tobit model produced internally consistent and statistically significant coefficients and was selected because it performed best for out-of-sample prediction when single health states were omitted.
Pain/discomfort had the largest utility weight, followed by mobility, anxiety/depression, self-care, and usual activities; the final value for state 55555 was -0.563.
The new directly elicited EQ-VT value set gave lower values, more negative health states, and a wider range than the existing crosswalk value set.
The new EQ-VT and crosswalk value sets differed substantially but remained positively correlated.
The cTTO data showed heteroskedasticity and censoring-relevant response patterns, which supported the use of a heteroskedastic Tobit specification.
The expanded DCE design permitted mixed logit estimation, and the rescaled mixed logit results were similar to the cTTO-only and hybrid results.
Quality control flagged 164 interviews, minor interviewer effects remained, and only two respondents were non-traders.

Across the 11 health states, mean utilities ranged from 0.78 for non-transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia with low anemia burden and oral ICT to 0.37 for high transfusion burden with subcutaneous ICT; high burden with oral-or-subcutaneous ICT also had a mean of 0.37.
Within non-transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia, greater anemia burden was associated with lower utility.

Within transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia, utility decreased consistently as transfusion burden increased; every pairwise comparison between burden levels within an ICT strategy was significant at p<0.00001.

Iron chelation modality had a smaller and less consistent effect than transfusion burden. Oral ICT was preferred to subcutaneous ICT at high and medium burden, while differences within the low-burden group were small and not uniformly ordered.

No significant utility differences by gender were found. Participants older than 55 years gave significantly lower utilities than younger groups for LOSC, MSC, and HO, but the other eight health states did not differ significantly by age.

The interview data showed acceptable protocol performance and face validity. Forty-one analyzed participants gave at least one worse-than-dead value, and the distributions showed more disagreement for severe states but no substantial interviewer effect.
Scenario analyses that included the 12 excluded non-traders or removed respondent-flagged observations produced little change in utilities and largely preserved the health-state ranking.
All five pilot participants reported that the health-state language and content were clear and coherent; only minor formatting changes were needed.

outcome: VAS values assigned to EQ-5D-Y health states under each perspective
statement: Mean values for EQ-5D-Y health states were lower in all three countries when the states were ascribed to a 10-year-old child than when ascribed to the respondent or to another adult, while the rank order of states stayed largely consistent across perspectives.

outcome: Within-respondent differences in value between perspectives (SELF-ADULT, SELF-CHILD)
statement: Paired comparisons of within-respondent differences showed that SELF versus CHILD values differed significantly for 16 of 24 state comparisons, whereas SELF versus ADULT values differed significantly for only 4 of 24.

outcome: Within-respondent differences in value between perspectives (SELF-ADULT, SELF-CHILD)
statement: The largest perspective differences (absolute mean difference above 5.0 VAS points, the upper 20% of differences) were almost all SELF-CHILD differences, concentrated in the German and English data, with none in the Spanish SELF-CHILD data exceeding that cut point.

outcome: Within-respondent differences in value between perspectives (SELF-ADULT, SELF-CHILD)
statement: The pattern of SELF versus ADULT values differed by country: German and Spanish respondents generally gave higher values when states applied to another adult, but English respondents gave higher values for another adult in only 2 of 8 states, and no recorded respondent characteristic accounted for this difference.

outcome: Within-respondent differences in value between perspectives (SELF-ADULT, SELF-CHILD)
statement: Parenting experience showed no systematic association with the SELF-CHILD value difference in analysis of variance or in regression with respondent characteristics as dummy variables, although the direction and size of differences varied by country.

outcome: Self-reported health of respondents (EQ-5D-3L profile and EQ VAS)
statement: Achieved samples differed markedly between countries in age, sex, marital status, education, parenting experience and self-reported health, with Spanish respondents youngest and healthiest.

outcome: Completeness and discrimination of VAS valuation responses
statement: Quality screening of valuation responses (no more than four missing values and at least four distinct values assigned) removed about a fifth of respondents from the aggregated analysis.

outcome: Patient-caregiver agreement on EQ-5D-Y descriptive-system dimensions
statement: Patient-caregiver agreement on the descriptive-system dimensions was moderate to good for both Y-3L and Y-5L at baseline and follow-up.

outcome: Patient-caregiver agreement on EQ VAS
statement: Patient-caregiver agreement on EQ VAS was poor at baseline and improved at follow-up, but remained below the prespecified ICC threshold of 0.7 for good reliability.

outcome: Ceiling effects of Y-3L and Y-5L descriptive systems
statement: Y-5L identified slightly more problems and had only slightly lower ceiling effects than Y-3L; its test-retest reliability was slightly poorer.

outcome: Missing responses
statement: There were no missing descriptive-system or EQ VAS responses for any of the four tested EQ-5D-Y variants at baseline or follow-up.

outcome: Test-retest reliability of EQ-5D-Y descriptive-system dimensions
statement: Among respondents with unchanged self-rated health, descriptive-system test-retest reliability was good to very good for patient Y-3L, moderate to good for patient Y-5L, and fair to good overall for both proxy versions; the proxy pain/discomfort and Y-5L mobility results were weaker.

outcome: Test-retest reliability of EQ VAS
statement: EQ VAS showed good test-retest reliability in both patient self-report and caregiver proxy report.
Of 115 invited patient-caregiver dyads, 96 completed baseline and 84 completed follow-up; the mean retest interval was 2.8 days.
At baseline, patients rated their health higher on EQ VAS than caregivers rated the patients.
Results for patients aged 8-10 years were similar to the full sample, with moderate to very good agreement and test-retest reliability.

outcome: Difference between self- and proxy-rated EQ-5D-5L index scores
statement: People living with dementia rated their HRQoL higher than their proxies did, based on mean EQ-5D-5L index scores.

outcome: Agreement and individual-response discrepancies between self- and proxy-rated EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: Only 5% of dyads gave identical five-dimension ratings; 95% differed on at least one EQ-5D-5L dimension.

outcome: Agreement and individual-response discrepancies between self- and proxy-rated EQ-5D-5L dimensions
statement: Dimension-level agreement was lowest for usual activities and highest for pain/discomfort.

outcome: Proxy overestimation, underestimation, and central-tendency response behavior
statement: Proxies rated health worse when the person with dementia reported no problems, but rated health better when the person reported problems; caregivers selected middle response options twice as often, especially for mobility, usual activities, and self-care.
The crosswalk produced values for all 3,125 EQ-5D-5L health states and retained the Slovenian EQ-5D-3L value-set range from perfect health to the worst state.
The interim EQ-5D-5L values were narrower and more densely distributed around the median than the EQ-5D-3L values.
The EQ-5D-5L crosswalk values had a higher mean and median, lower dispersion, and negative rather than near-zero skewness compared with the EQ-5D-3L values.
The added slight level separated nearby health states only a little, whereas the severe level covered a larger share of the utility scale.
The EQ-5D-5L crosswalk had proportionally fewer health states valued below zero and fewer valued above 0.8 than the EQ-5D-3L value set.
Blepharospasm severity and frequency improved markedly after botulinum toxin A treatment, with the largest effect at 1 month and partial recurrence by 3 months.
EQ-5D-5L utility scores improved after treatment and remained above baseline at 3 months.
EQ VAS scores improved after treatment and remained above baseline at 3 months.
NEI-VFQ-25 vision-related quality of life improved at 1 month and remained above baseline at 3 months.
Most generic and vision-specific HRQoL dimensions improved after treatment; EQ-5D-5L self-care and NEI-VFQ-25 ocular pain did not show significant improvement.

The median perceived duration of botulinum toxin A action was about 10 weeks, with almost all participants reporting recurrent symptoms by 12 weeks; duration did not differ between the two formulations.
Minor treatment complications were reported by about one fifth of participants and resolved within 4 weeks.

Higher baseline blepharospasm severity was associated with greater improvement in utility and NEI-VFQ-25 composite scores; sex, age, underlying disease, and employment also affected quality-of-life improvement.

outcome: Pool of candidate severity labels generated per country and per dimension
statement: The review of HRQoL instruments and the focus groups produced 233 candidate severity labels in total, with the largest pool in Germany and the smallest in the UK, where the team applied strict grammatical and child-friendliness criteria.
The resulting EQ-5D-Y-5L defines 3125 possible health states, compared with 243 for the EQ-5D-Y-3L.

Between 7 and 16 labels per dimension per language were carried forward to the sorting and response scaling interviews, with the same label set used for mobility, looking after myself and usual activities, and a different set for pain or discomfort and for feeling worried, sad or unhappy.

outcome: Rated severity position of each candidate label on the health continuum (median, mode, standard deviation)
statement: A total of 255 sorting and response scaling interviews was completed across the four countries, and the rated labels covered an appropriate range of severity on the health continuum in all countries, with ratings from participants aged 8-10 comparable to those from older participants.

Qualitative comments overrode the quantitative ratings for some labels: the Swedish labels pyttelite and nagot were interpreted differently by the two age groups and were dropped, and the German level-2 label for feeling worried, sad or unhappy became ein bisschen because participants said they would not use leicht or ein wenig in that context.

outcome: Feasibility of completing the draft 4L and 5L versions, including missing data
statement: Participants in all countries found both draft versions feasible and easily understood, no questions about labels arose in Germany or Sweden, and the UK 5L test produced no questions and no missing data.

outcome: Preference for the 5L over the 4L version
statement: The majority of participants, irrespective of health status, preferred the 5L version over the 4L version, saying it allowed a more precise rating and had a middle answer category; two participants criticised the central option as a possible non-decision choice.

outcome: Comprehensibility of the severity labels and of the draft 4L and 5L versions
statement: Cognitive interviews led to Spanish label changes: un poco de problema became algun pequeno problema, moderados/moderadamente was replaced by bastante, muchisimos became muchos/mucho, and algo became un poco.

outcome: Comprehensibility of the severity labels and of the draft 4L and 5L versions
statement: In the UK, the level-5 labels terrible/terribly for pain or discomfort and for feeling worried, sad or unhappy were problematic for primary school children and were replaced by extreme/extremely, confirmed in four further interviews.

outcome: Final set of severity level labels forming the EQ-5D-Y-5L descriptive system in four languages
statement: Back-translation and comparison of the German, Spanish, Swedish and UK English 5L versions showed only slight wording discrepancies, for example the German level-4 label grosse against a lot of in English and Swedish, and all labels remained as developed by the national teams.

Utility agreement was excellent between EQ-HWB-9 and HUI3 and lower with SWEMWBS and ICECAP-A. Bland-Altman plots showed convergence toward full health or well-being, slight positive bias versus ICECAP-A, and slightly lower EQ-HWB-9 scores than SWEMWBS.
Differences by carer status and adjacent age categories were small; mean EQ-HWB-9 utilities were lower for carers and generally increased with age.
Potential item-level ceiling effects occurred for mobility and activities in the full sample, but the EQ-HWB-9 had no instrument-level ceiling or floor effect under the prespecified thresholds.

Exhaustion was the most frequently reported EQ-HWB-9 problem and was often reported even when comparator well-being measures indicated no problems, which suggests that EQ-HWB-9 captures an aspect not fully represented by those measures.

EQ-HWB-9 items had strong correlations with conceptually overlapping comparator items, except that trouble concentrating or thinking clearly had only a moderate correlation with HUI3 cognition. Pain and mobility had the strongest physical-domain correlations.

EQ-HWB-9 distinguished healthy from unhealthy respondents and groups with different mental well-being, disability, and life satisfaction. Effects were largest for groups with poorer mental well-being, lower life satisfaction, or more severe disability.
EQ-HWB-9 utility scores correlated strongly with SWEMWBS, ICECAP-A, and HUI3 utilities, with the strongest correlation for HUI3.

WOMAC scores generally increased as problems increased across adjacent EQ-5D-5L response levels. Total WOMAC scores correlated negatively with both EQ-5D-5L utility and EQ VAS scores, which supported construct validity.

All 151 participants completed the baseline electronic EQ-5D-5L without missing data. Completion took a mean of about 130 seconds. Education level was not significantly associated with EQ-5D-5L dimension, utility, or EQ VAS results.
Two-week test-retest reliability was good for utility and EQ VAS scores. Agreement for the five dimension responses was moderate to good.
Participants who reported better global health at three months had statistically significant improvements in utility and EQ VAS scores and fewer reported problems across all five dimensions.
Participants who reported worse global health had decreases in utility and EQ VAS scores and more reported problems, but the score changes were not statistically significant in this small subgroup.
Participants reporting unchanged global health had a statistically significant increase in utility score, although their EQ VAS increase was not significant.

The electronic EQ-5D-5L distinguished the prespecified known groups. Participants with mild pain, general outpatient clinic patients, and patients with knee rather than back problems generally had better utility and EQ VAS results than their comparison groups. Utility and EQ VAS group-difference effect sizes were moderate to large.

Three-class censored normal mixture models best fit both the utility and EQ VAS longitudinal data. Most participants remained in the high utility class, whereas most remained in the middle EQ VAS class.
Across respondents, 13% always prioritized the worse-off group and 34% always prioritized the group with the greatest health improvement.
Of 625 recruited individuals, 606 completed the interview.
In the adjusted model, female and religious respondents were more likely to prioritize the worse-off group, whereas the oldest age group was less likely to do so.
When the two alternatives had equal health improvement, respondents prioritized the worse-off group in 45% of tasks.
The main DCE analysis included 468 respondents; the software excluded 133 based on achieved health-state values and 5 more were excluded because of an application coding error.
The two-stage design using individual-level TTO values to construct later priority-setting tasks was feasible, with important trade-offs and scope for development.
A larger difference in health improvement reduced the odds of prioritizing the worse-off group.
The difference in pretreatment health-state value was not significantly associated with prioritizing the worse-off group.
Sensitivity analyses did not show an overall preference for prioritizing the worse-off group; the ratio specification indicated less priority as inequality increased.
Respondents usually supplied a varied individual value set, but logical-dominance violations occurred in many sets.
Of 1378 conducted interviews, the final analysis used 974 main-study interviews after removal of pilot, incomplete, and protocol-noncompliant interviews.

outcome: Protocol compliance, response consistency, model fit, and prediction accuracy
statement: The final sample supplied 9740 cTTO and 6818 DCE responses; the feedback module reduced cTTO inconsistencies and the main analysis excluded flagged valuations.

The authors selected model 4, a heteroskedastic model based on cTTO data, because it was logically consistent, had significant dimension decrements, handled increasing error variance, and had strong prediction accuracy.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state values and national tariff
statement: The preferred tariff assigned negative values to more than one third of the 3125 EQ-5D-5L states, with the worst state 55555 valued at -0.933.

outcome: EQ-5D-5L health-state values and national tariff
statement: Mobility had the largest effect on health-state values in all tested models; in the preferred model it was followed by pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression, self-care, and usual activities.

outcome: Feasibility and cultural appropriateness of the EQ-VT protocol
statement: Pilot testing found the standard wheelchair practice example culturally unsuitable for many participants, so the team replaced it with a migraine example and added tested pictorial and colour-card aids for participants with low literacy.

outcome: Participants' self-reported EQ-5D-5L health and EQ VAS scores
statement: In the analyzed sample, anxiety/depression was the most common self-reported EQ-5D-5L problem, self-care was the least common, and the mean EQ VAS score was 76.9.

outcome: Protocol compliance, response consistency, model fit, and prediction accuracy
statement: Sensitivity analysis that restored health states flagged in the feedback module worsened model performance, which supported their exclusion from the main analysis.

outcome: Protocol compliance, response consistency, model fit, and prediction accuracy
statement: All cTTO candidate models were logically consistent, while the DCE conditional-logit model had minor ordering inconsistencies for self-care level 3 and usual-activities level 3.
In adjusted country-specific and pooled models, chronic disease and unemployment were the strongest and most consistent correlates of poorer LSS and EQ VAS outcomes.

Adjusted education and income associations were heterogeneous across countries. Unemployment remained associated with poorer HRQoL in every country, while gender was generally not associated with the outcomes and age associations varied by outcome and country.

HRQoL differed across countries. China had the lowest median LSS and the highest median EQ VAS; Italy, Sweden, and the United States had the highest median LSS values. Rank-sum differences across countries were significant for both outcomes.

Unadjusted LSS results showed poorer HRQoL for the low-education group than for the high-education group in the pooled sample. Significant rank differences appeared in every country except Italy, and the largest median education gap was in the United Kingdom. EQ VAS education gradients were smaller and less consistent.

Low-income respondents had poorer unadjusted LSS and EQ VAS outcomes than high-income respondents in the pooled sample. Income gradients appeared in the Netherlands, Sweden, the United Kingdom, and the United States, but not in China or Italy.
The LSS and EQ VAS models identified chronic disease and unemployment as the same main determinants, but EQ VAS appeared more responsive to education and income differences than LSS.
In the full analytic sample, the median EQ-5D-5L LSS was 6.00 and the median EQ VAS was 80.0.

Unemployed respondents had poorer LSS and EQ VAS outcomes than employed respondents in the pooled sample and in every country. Work status produced larger and more consistent HRQoL disparities than education or income.
Bland-Altman plots suggested no significant systematic differences between T1 and T2 for EQ-5D-5L summary index, EQ VAS, or reworded QOLIBRI-OS level sum score.

EQ-5D-5L index and reworded QOLIBRI-OS sum scores were strongly correlated at both time points, as were Anxiety/Depression and Emotion, but Usual Activities and Function in Daily Life did not reach the prespecified strong-correlation threshold.
Most EQ-5D-5L and reworded QOLIBRI-OS reliability results differed significantly between countries.
Across the three countries, EQ-5D-5L dimension agreement was substantial to almost perfect, summary-index reliability was good, and EQ VAS reliability was moderate.
The reworded QOLIBRI-OS had lower test-retest reliability than EQ-5D-5L, with item agreement ranging from fair to substantial and sum-score reliability ranging from moderate to good.

outcome: Anchored EQ-5D-5L health state utility values from the DCE with duration
statement: The DCE with duration produced generally logically ordered coefficients for the EQ-5D-5L; only mobility level 2 interacted with duration was disordered and it was not statistically significant.

outcome: Anchored EQ-5D-5L health state utility values from the DCE with duration
statement: The distribution of predicted values for all 3125 EQ-5D-5L states was unimodal with no gap between the best and next best state, and a substantial share of states were worse than dead.

outcome: Anchored EQ-5D-5L health state utility values from the DCE with duration
statement: Five-level coefficients were broadly comparable with the earlier three-level EQ-5D study, the main difference being the worst mobility level, whose wording changed from 'confined to bed' to 'unable to walk about'.

outcome: Time trading behaviour and learning or fatigue effects across the choice sequence
statement: Most respondents traded duration: among the 1597 respondents facing at least one task where duration differed, most showed mixed trading, while a minority never or always chose the shorter duration.

outcome: Logical consistency and stability of choice model coefficients across sample sizes and numbers of tasks
statement: Individual ordinal preferences generally agreed with aggregate cardinal QALY values; disagreement occurred only where the QALY difference between scenarios was very small.

outcome: Time trading behaviour and learning or fatigue effects across the choice sequence
statement: Predicted values from the three single-module batches were very highly correlated, but scale parameters fell across modules, indicating a fatigue effect, and preference homogeneity across batches was narrowly rejected.

outcome: Logical consistency and stability of choice model coefficients across sample sizes and numbers of tasks
statement: Holding the design and total number of observations constant, batches of 10 tasks with an intermediate sample and 15 tasks with a smaller sample gave results closer to the whole-sample model than 5 tasks with a large sample.
The achieved sample was broadly representative of the UK population on observable characteristics.
Self-reported or interviewer-reported understanding was high across all three studies.
The qualitative findings showed misunderstanding of some OPUF steps, including anchoring on dead.
The EQ-VT and OPUF studies had limited inconsistent or illogical responses, while the PAPRIKA study excluded a large share of responses under its prespecified criteria.
Pain, activity, mobility, and sadness or depression were the most important EQ-HWB-S dimensions in all three studies.
The three approaches produced different negative values for the worst EQ-HWB-S state.
Dimension weights differed by approach; PAPRIKA gave less weight to mobility and more weight to cognition than the other approaches.

outcome: Chinese laypeople quality-of-life framework
statement: The analysis generated 221 QoL-related codes. After application of five predefined exclusion criteria, 187 codes remained, of which 97 were inductively developed.

outcome: Chinese laypeople quality-of-life framework
statement: The 187 retained codes formed 57 sub-themes in eight themes: feeling and emotion, cognition, self-identity, coping, physical sensation, relationship, activity, and mindset.

outcome: Comprehensiveness of the EQ-HWB conceptual framework in the Chinese context
statement: The Chinese QoL framework and EQ-HWB framework aligned for 18 of 57 sub-themes and seven of eight themes.
Mindset was a new theme not present in the EQ-HWB framework. It included life attitude, adjustment of mindset, and positive or negative energy.

outcome: Comprehensiveness of the EQ-HWB conceptual framework in the Chinese context
statement: The EQ-HWB conceptual framework was almost entirely represented in the Chinese QoL framework; hearing was the only EQ-HWB sub-theme not reported by respondents.

New or differently represented content included regret, boredom, stress, emotional abilities, cognitive impairment, self-assessment, adaptation, weakness, appetite, appearance, relationship formation, judgment, betrayal, physical function, sleep, and diet.

outcome: Comprehensiveness of the EQ-HWB conceptual framework in the Chinese context
statement: Boredom and sleep were assigned to different themes across the two frameworks, and the Chinese autonomy concept included dependence as a negative aspect.

outcome: Qualitative data saturation
statement: The researchers judged that saturation was reached: the last three interviews added no new themes, and similar QoL views recurred among the last ten participants.

outcome: Ceiling effect (proportion reporting no problems and state 11111)
statement: The 5L version showed a considerably reduced ceiling effect: 47.6 % of 5L respondents reported state 11111 compared with 56.2 % of 3L respondents, and level 1 reporting was lower on the 5L in every dimension.

outcome: Ceiling effect (proportion reporting no problems and state 11111)
statement: The 5L identified more respondents with severe health problems than the 3L; for example 6.1 % reported level 4 or 5 problems in usual activities on the 5L versus 1.5 % reporting level 3 on the 3L.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D profile, EQ-5D index and EQ VAS scores in the English general population
statement: Respondents used a wider spread of health states on the 5L: three 3L states accounted for almost 75 % of respondents whereas 12 states were needed on the 5L; the worst state 55555 was never reported while 33333 was reported by 4 respondents (0.1 %).

outcome: Discriminatory power across age, sex and education groups
statement: Both versions showed poorer health in older respondents, females, and respondents without a degree; the 5L descriptive system discriminated better between age groups, for example a 35.6 percentage point gap between the oldest and youngest groups in reporting no usual activity problems on the 5L versus 20.6 points on the 3L.

outcome: Discriminatory power across age, sex and education groups
statement: EQ-5D index and EQ VAS scores fell with age on both versions; 3L index scores were higher than crosswalk-derived 5L index scores in all age groups, significantly so only in the oldest group, and the age-group differences seen in the descriptive system largely disappeared in the index.

outcome: Self-reported EQ-5D profile, EQ-5D index and EQ VAS scores in the English general population
statement: EQ VAS results were similar across versions, with digit preference around multiples of ten in both, the two most frequent scores being 90 and 80, and 8 of the 10 most frequent 3L scores also among the most frequent 5L scores.
HRQoL evidence was geographically concentrated: 698 studies were conducted in 31 countries, and Nigeria, Ethiopia, and South Africa together contributed more than half of all included studies.
Most included studies were descriptive, used patient populations, and were conducted in hospitals; interventional and mixed-methods research was uncommon.
Interviewer administration was the dominant collection mode, and convenience and consecutive sampling were the most common sampling methods; 15.6% of studies did not report a sampling method.
HIV/AIDS, cancer, and diabetes were the most frequently studied health conditions.
WHOQOL-BREF, SF-36, and EQ-5D were the three most frequently used generic HRQoL measures.
Among 96 EQ-5D studies, EQ-5D-3L was used more often than EQ-5D-5L; some studies used EQ VAS alone or did not identify the EQ-5D version.
EQ-5D reporting was inconsistent. Complete reporting of descriptive profile, index score, and EQ VAS was much more frequent for EQ-5D-5L studies than for EQ-5D-3L studies.
Study sample sizes varied widely, with a median of 210 participants and an interquartile range of 101 to 394.
The mixed-logit model fitted the DCE data better than the conditional logit model by BIC; all level coefficients in both models were statistically significant and severity-monotonic.

Of 2790 people who accepted the DCE survey, 1152 were analyzed; 1365 did not complete all tasks and 273 were too fast or failed a dominant pair. All 211 cTTO attendees were analyzed, although two interviews were flagged as potentially poor quality.
The linear mapping without an intercept was selected because it had lower RMSE and MAE than the other tested mappings and predicted moderate states relatively well.
The final value set ranged from 1 for full health (11111) to -0.0059 for the worst health state (33333); 33333 was the only profile with a negative modeled utility.
In the preferred mixed-logit model, pain or discomfort had the largest weight, followed by mobility, self-care, usual activities, and anxiety/depression.
The mean observed cTTO value for profile 33333 was substantially lower than its final modeled value, showing poor prediction of the most severe state.

Item non-response on the EQ-5D-3L was low in the elderly European SHARE sample: only 3% of respondents had at least one missing EQ-5D value, the whole descriptive system was missing for 1.32%, the whole instrument for 0.4% and the EQ VAS for 2.8%.

In this sample the proportion reporting no problems and the mean EQ VAS decreased monotonically with age, with the largest drop in the 80+ group, and women, less educated persons and persons without a partner reported worse health.

Missing values stayed below about 3% across all dimensions and gender strata, were highest for self-care and anxiety/depression, were similar for men and women, and increased with age, with the steepest increase for the EQ VAS in the oldest panellists.

Item non-response varied markedly between countries; the Czech Republic had the most missing dimension responses while Denmark, Germany and Sweden had many more missing EQ VAS than dimension responses, and Spain, Italy, Slovenia and Sweden had consistently few missing dimension responses.

All EQ-5D-3L dimensions except anxiety/depression correlated moderately to strongly with physical measures, while anxiety/depression correlated strongly with the EURO-D scale, supporting convergent and divergent construct validity.

EQ-5D-3L dimensions and the EQ VAS correlated at least moderately with generic self-perceived health measures (CASP, self-perceived health, number of symptoms), with the strongest correlations for usual activities with ADL limitations and for EQ VAS with self-perceived health.
Correlations with divergent measures (BMI, maximum grip strength and all cognitive measures) were small, ranging from 0 to 0.308.

Correlations of the EQ VAS with physical and cognitive measures increased with age, roughly doubling between the youngest and oldest age groups for ADL and IADL, whereas the correlation with self-perceived health was stable across age groups.

The EQ VAS discriminated best between groups defined by general health measures, followed by activity limitations and depression case status, while associations with sociodemographic variables were small and those with cognitive measures, age and job situation were moderate.

Each EQ-5D-3L dimension discriminated best in its corresponding domain, for example anxiety/depression between depressed and non-depressed persons, self-care between persons with and without ADL limitations, and pain/discomfort between persons with and without IADL limitations.
